The edges are directed; electrical signals propagate in just one direction along the wires in the brain. Outgoing edges are called axons and incoming edges are called dendrites. A neuron fires, sending a pulse down its axon, when the incoming pulses, from the dendrites, exceed a threshold.
concepts.motivation_md: The biological brain provides a proof-of-concept for a complex system capable of learning and pattern recognition, serving as the original inspiration for artificial neural network architectures.
concepts.recap_md:
- Neurons act as nodes in a graph with directed edges representing connections.
- Signals travel from dendrites (inputs) to axons (outputs).
- A neuron "fires" or activates only when incoming signals exceed a specific threshold.

concepts.title: Linear Layer

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A linear layer computes an affine function of its inputs by calculating a weighted sum plus a bias.
concepts.content:
$$z = f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b = \mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x} + b$$

Mathematically, $f$ is an affine function, but by convention we call it a "linear layer." One way to think of it is $f$ is a linear function of $\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}\\ 1\end{bmatrix}$. It computes a linear function of the inputs; if the result exceeds a threshold (here 0), the neuron fires.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear layers serve as the fundamental building block of neural networks, aggregating multiple input signals into a single scalar value through weighted summation.
concepts.recap_md:
- A linear layer calculates $z = \mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x} + b$.
- Although technically an affine function, it is conventionally referred to as a linear layer.
- It can be viewed as a linear function of the augmented input vector including a constant 1.

concepts.title: Activation Function

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: An activation function decides whether a neuron fires based on the weighted sum of its inputs.
concepts.content:
The function $g$ is called the activation function because it decides whether the neuron activates (fires). A common example is the step function:

$$g(z) = \begin{cases} 1, &\text{if} \quad z > 0\\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

It operates on the value $z = \mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x} + b$, which consists of the weighted inputs plus a bias, $b$.
concepts.motivation_md: Activation functions introduce non-linearity into neural networks, allowing them to model complex relationships beyond simple linear transformations.
concepts.recap_md:
- The activation function determines the output (firing) of a neuron.
- It typically takes the result of a linear layer as its input.
- A simple version is a threshold function that outputs 1 if the input is positive and 0 otherwise.

concepts.title: Bias Parameter

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: The bias is an additive constant in a linear layer that shifts the activation threshold.
concepts.content: The bias, $b$, is an additive term added to the weighted sum of inputs $\mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Without a bias, a linear layer would always produce zero when the input is zero. The bias allows the decision boundary to be shifted away from the origin.
concepts.recap_md:
- The bias $b$ is added to the dot product of weights and inputs.
- It allows the model to represent offsets in the data.

concepts.title: Perceptron as a Classifier

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A perceptron can learn to classify data by assigning labels based on which side of a decision boundary the input falls.
concepts.content: Perceptrons can learn to classify data. Consider a perceptron with two inputs, $x_1$ and $x_2$, and one output, $y$. Let the incoming connection weights be $w_1 = 2$, $w_2 = 1$, and $b=0$. The values of $z$ and $y$, as a function of $x_1$ and $x_2$, are shown in (see figure: Value of hidden unit ($z$) and output unit ($y$) in a perceptron, as a function of the input data.). Notice that $y$ takes on values 0 or 1, so you can think of this as a classifier that assigns a class label of 1 to the upper-right half of the plotted region.
concepts.motivation_md: The perceptron was one of the first models to demonstrate that simple artificial neurons could perform binary classification tasks, sparking early interest in artificial intelligence.
concepts.recap_md:
- A perceptron maps inputs to a binary output (0 or 1).
- It acts as a linear classifier, dividing the input space into two regions.
- The classification is determined by the sign of the weighted sum of inputs plus bias.

concepts.title: Perceptron Learning Problem

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: Learning in a perceptron involves adjusting weights and bias to minimize the number of misclassifications in a dataset.
concepts.content:
To use a perceptron for learning, given data $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, we adjust the weights $\mathbf{w}$ and the bias $b$ in order to minimize a classification loss, $\mathcal{L}$, that scores the number of misclassifications:

$$\mathbf{w}^*, b^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\mathbf{w}, b} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b, y^{(i)})$$
concepts.motivation_md: To make a perceptron useful, we need a systematic way to find the parameters that best fit the observed data, which is framed as an optimization problem.
concepts.recap_md:
- Learning is framed as an optimization problem to find optimal weights $\mathbf{w}^*$ and bias $b^*$.
- The objective is to minimize the average classification loss across the training set.
- The loss function $\mathcal{L}$ typically penalizes the model for incorrect predictions.

concepts.title: Image Classification
concepts.one_liner: The decade of 2000–2010 in computer vision was characterized by a significant focus on image classification and object recognition.
concepts.content: The decade of 2000–2010 focused on image classification and object recognition, utilizing various methodologies to categorize visual data.
concepts.motivation_md: Image classification is a fundamental task in computer vision that allows systems to automatically categorize images into predefined classes, enabling automated organization and search of visual data.
concepts.recap_md: - Focuses on assigning a categorical label to an entire image.

concepts.title: Object Recognition
concepts.one_liner: Object recognition was a primary research focus in the field of computer vision between 2000 and 2010.
concepts.content: The decade of 2000–2010 focused on image classification and object recognition, driving the development of algorithms capable of identifying specific entities within images.
concepts.motivation_md: Object recognition allows computers to identify and locate specific objects within a scene, which is essential for tasks like autonomous driving, robotics, and image-based search.
concepts.recap_md: - Involves identifying and locating specific objects within digital images.

concepts.title: Computer Vision Benchmarks
concepts.one_liner: Medium-sized benchmarks with tens of thousands of images drive progress by popularizing new metrics and guidelines for reproducible research.
concepts.content: The creation of medium size benchmarks, with tens of thousands of images, started driving progress in the field. Examples include Caltech 101, PASCAL, LabelMe, and CIFAR. The introduction of benchmarks popularized new metrics and guidelines for reproducible research in the field.
concepts.motivation_md: Benchmarks provide standardized datasets and evaluation metrics, allowing researchers to compare different algorithms fairly and ensure that progress is measurable and reproducible.
concepts.recap_md: - Consist of datasets with tens of thousands of images for training and testing.

concepts.title: GIST Descriptor
concepts.one_liner: GIST is an image descriptor that is often combined with machine learning techniques like decision trees.
concepts.content: GIST is an image descriptor that, when combined with machine learning techniques such as decision trees, is used for processing and analyzing visual information.
concepts.motivation_md: GIST descriptors are designed to represent the global spatial structure of a scene, making them useful for rapid scene recognition and categorization.
concepts.recap_md: - A global image descriptor used to represent scene structure.

concepts.title: Bag of Words (BoW)
concepts.one_liner: Bag of Words (BoW) is a type of image descriptor used in computer vision.
concepts.content: Bag of Words (BoW) is an image descriptor used to represent visual data by treating image features as a collection of unordered visual "words."
concepts.motivation_md: BoW simplifies complex image data into a histogram of visual features, making it easier for standard machine learning algorithms to classify images.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents images as a frequency distribution of visual features.

concepts.title: Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT)
concepts.one_liner: Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) is a descriptor used to identify local features in images.
concepts.content: Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) is an image descriptor used to detect and describe local features in images that are invariant to changes in scale or rotation.
concepts.motivation_md: SIFT allows for robust matching of objects across different images even when they are viewed from different angles, distances, or under different lighting conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - A local feature descriptor invariant to scale and rotation.

concepts.title: Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG)
concepts.one_liner: Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) is an image descriptor used for object detection.
concepts.content: Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) is an image descriptor that captures the distribution of intensity gradients or edge directions to represent object appearance.
concepts.motivation_md: HOG is particularly effective for detecting objects with distinct shapes, such as humans, because it focuses on the orientation of edges within local image regions.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses gradient orientations to describe the shape and appearance of objects.

concepts.title: Decision Trees
concepts.one_liner: Decision trees are a machine learning technique often combined with image descriptors for visual tasks.
concepts.content: Decision trees are a machine learning technique that, when combined with image descriptors, are used for computer vision tasks. They are often used alongside other methods like boosting and support vector machines.
concepts.motivation_md: Decision trees provide a clear, hierarchical structure for making classification decisions based on specific features, offering both efficiency and interpretability.
concepts.recap_md: - A machine learning model that classifies data through a series of binary decisions.

concepts.title: Fovea
concepts.one_liner: The fovea is a region of the eye where there are no rods and the cones are close-packed.
concepts.content: The fovea is a region of the eye characterized by a specific sampling pattern where there are no rods and the cones are close-packed.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the fovea is essential for modeling how the eye samples light at its highest resolution, as the absence of rods and dense packing of cones define our central vision.
concepts.recap_md: The fovea contains no rods.

concepts.title: Cone Response Matrix Equation
concepts.one_liner: Photoreceptor responses can be described using matrix algebra as the product of a spectral sensitivity matrix and an incident light vector.
concepts.content: We can describe the photoreceptor responses using matrix algebra. If the matrix $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$ consists of the spectral sensitivities of the L, M, and S cones in three rows, and the vector $\mathbf{t}$ is a column vector of the spectrum of light incident on the eye, then the L, M, and S cone responses will be the product: $$\begin{bmatrix} L \\ M \\ S \\ \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}} \, \mathbf{t}$$
concepts.motivation_md: This matrix representation allows for a computationally efficient way to predict how the human eye will respond to any given light spectrum.
concepts.recap_md: - The matrix $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$ contains spectral sensitivities for L, M, and S cones.

concepts.title: Color Matching Principles
concepts.one_liner: Color matching is the process of adjusting primary colors to reproduce a target color, based on the principle that any color appearance can be matched by a linear combination of three primaries.
concepts.content: Color science provides methods to analyze and reproduce color, allowing image displays to match target colors and ensuring consistency in manufactured items and food standards. (see figure: The USDA color standards for French fried potatoes, one of many color standards @Munsell2020) A key task is predicting when two colors will be perceived as a match, such as adjusting a display to match a reflecting surface. Despite different spectra, colors can almost always be made to match. This performance is inferred from the spectral sensitivity curves of receptors. Experimentation shows that any color appearance can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors, due to the three classes of photoreceptors in the eye. These matches are transitive: if color A and color B both match the same combination of primaries, they match each other. The amounts of each primary required serve as coordinates for the color.
concepts.motivation_md: Color matching is the foundation of the color industry, enabling the consistent reproduction of colors across different media, from digital displays to physical products like food and branded materials.
concepts.recap_md: - Any color can be matched by a linear combination of three primary colors.

concepts.title: Primary Colors
concepts.one_liner: Primary colors are reference colors whose linear combination can match the appearance of any other color.
concepts.content: Primary colors are reference colors used to match a target color. Through experimentation, it has been discovered that the appearance of any color can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors. This phenomenon is a direct result of the presence of three classes of photoreceptors in human eyes. These color matches are transitive; if color A matches a specific combination of primaries and color B matches that same combination, then color A will match color B. Consequently, the amount of each primary required to match a color can serve as a set of coordinates indicating that color.
concepts.motivation_md: Primary colors exist because humans have three types of cone cells; they provide a basis for representing the entire gamut of human color perception using only three variables.
concepts.recap_md: - Any color appearance can be matched by a linear combination of three primary colors.

concepts.title: Color Metamerism
concepts.one_liner: Color metamerism occurs when two different light spectra appear to be the same color because they produce the same response in the eye's photoreceptors.
concepts.content: Two different spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes. There is a large space of metamers: any two vectors describing light power spectra that give the same projection onto a set of color matching functions will look the same. While light spectra exist in a high-dimensional space, human vision only perceives projections onto a 3D subspace.
concepts.motivation_md: Metamerism is what makes color reproduction possible; we don't need to replicate the exact physical spectrum of an object to make it look the same to a human observer.
concepts.recap_md: - Metamers are different light spectra that are perceived as the same color.

concepts.title: Color Reproduction System
concepts.one_liner: A color reproduction system is defined by three spectral sensitivity curves that are linear combinations of the eye's spectral sensitivities.
concepts.content: A color reproduction system is defined by first specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves. These are organized into a $3 \times N$ matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, where $N$ is the number of spectral samples over the visible range. The three curves should be a linear combination of the eye's spectral sensitivity curves, or $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \, \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$, where $\mathbf{R}$ is any full-rank $3 \times 3$ matrix. This allows translation between different color spaces by applying a $3 \times 3$ matrix transformation to change basis vectors, which do not need to be orthogonal. (see figure: A color reproduction system. Light sensors a, b, and c respond to the input light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$, giving sensor activations $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. Combinations of those activations drive the...)
concepts.motivation_md: This framework allows engineers to design cameras and displays that accurately capture and recreate colors by ensuring the system's sensors relate mathematically to human visual sensitivities.
concepts.recap_md: - A color reproduction system is characterized by a $3 \times N$ matrix of spectral sensitivity curves.

concepts.title: Derivation of Color Matching Conditions
concepts.one_liner: The derivation of color matching conditions identifies the relationship between primary lights, sensor sensitivities, and mixing matrices required for perfect color reproduction.
concepts.content: (see figure: A color reproduction system. Light sensors a, b, and c respond to the input light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$, giving sensor activations $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. Combinations of those activations drive the...) For a given set of primary lights $\mathbf{P}$, we seek a matrix of color sensitivity curves $\mathbf{C}$ and a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{M}$ to allow perfect color reproduction. The eye's response to a light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$ is $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}} \mathbf{t}$. In a reproduction system, sensors produce $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$, which are mixed by $\mathbf{M}$ to control primaries $\mathbf{P}$, resulting in an output spectrum $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. For perfect reproduction, the eye's response to this output must match its response to the original: $\mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{t}$. Since this must hold for any $\mathbf{t}$, the condition is $\mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}_{eye}$. By requiring the sensor subspace $\mathbf{C}$ to be a linear combination of the eye's subspace ($\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{C}_{eye}$), we derive the condition $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I}_3$, where $\mathbf{I}_3$ is the identity matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: This derivation provides the mathematical constraints necessary to ensure that a camera-display system produces colors that are perceptually identical to the original scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Perfect reproduction requires the eye's response to the output spectrum to match its response to the input.

concepts.title: Primary Lights
concepts.one_liner: Primary lights are a set of three lights whose combination can be controlled to match the eye's response to a given light spectrum.
concepts.content: A color reproduction system measures an input light and produces an output light that matches the color appearance of the input. A camera with a screen display is an example, where colors in the world are measured and then reproduced. We can match the eye's response to a given light spectrum through the appropriate control of a sum of three lights, called the primary lights. In a display screen, the three color elements of each pixel serve as the primary lights.
concepts.motivation_md: Primary lights are the physical components (like LED subpixels) that allow electronic devices to generate a wide range of perceived colors by stimulating the eye's three cone types in specific proportions.
concepts.recap_md: - Primary lights are the physical light sources used to reproduce colors in a system.

concepts.title: Fast Activations and Slow Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Activations are fast functions of individual datapoints, while parameters are slow functions of entire datasets learned via optimization.
concepts.content: Activations and parameters differ in how they relate to data. Activations are fast functions of a datapoint, resulting from a few layers of processing that specific input. Parameters are also functions of the data, but they are slow functions of datasets, arrived at via an optimization procedure over a whole dataset. Both are statistics of the data that organize or summarize it. Parameters act as a kind of metasummary because they specify the functional transformation that produces activations, while activations themselves are a summary of the data.
concepts.motivation_md: This distinction helps clarify the different roles of data-dependent values in a neural network: activations represent the immediate response to an input, while parameters represent the long-term knowledge extracted from the training set.
concepts.recap_md: - Activations are fast functions of individual datapoints generated by layer processing.

concepts.title: Deep Neural Networks
concepts.one_liner: Deep nets are neural networks that stack linear-nonlinear motifs many times to perform powerful nonlinear mappings.
concepts.content:
Deep nets are neural nets that stack the linear-nonlinear motif many times:

(see figure: Deep nets consist of linear layers interleaved with nonlinearities.)

Each layer is a function. Therefore, a deep net is a composition of many functions:
$$\begin{aligned}
    f(\mathbf{x}) = f_{L}(f_{L-1}(\ldots f_2(f_1(\mathbf{x}))))
\end{aligned}$$
The $L$ is the number of layers in the net. These functions are parameterized by weights $[\mathbf{W}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{W}_L]$ and biases $[\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_L]$. Collectively, the concatenation of all parameters in a deep net is referred to as $\theta$. Deep nets are powerful because they can perform nonlinear mappings; a deep net with sufficiently many neurons can fit almost any desired function arbitrarily closely.
concepts.motivation_md: Deep neural networks allow for the learning of complex, nonlinear relationships that simple linear models cannot capture, enabling the approximation of nearly any continuous function.
concepts.recap_md: - A deep net is a composition of $L$ functions, each representing a layer.

concepts.title: Nonlinear Classification with Deep Nets
concepts.one_liner: Deep networks can solve nonlinear classification problems by stacking multiple layers to separate data that is not linearly separable.
concepts.content:
Deep networks can solve binary classification problems where classes are not linearly separable. In such cases, no single line can separate the data points. However, a multilayer network, such as a two-layer MLP, can solve this problem by adding more layers.

(see figure: Dataset that is not linearly separable.)

(see figure: A simple MLP network.)

By using specific settings for weights $\mathbf{W}_1$ and $\mathbf{W}_2$, the network performs a sequence of operations: linear transformations, followed by a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) nonlinearity, another linear transformation, and finally a threshold indicator function to produce the output $y$. 

(see figure: Values of hidden units and output unit for the MLP shown in \fig{\ref{fig-neural_nets-simple_MLP_network}}.)

As shown in the output visualization, the neural net successfully assigns values to regions of the dataspace corresponding to the labels. While parameters can be found through enumeration, they are typically learned using gradient descent.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple linear classifiers fail on complex datasets where classes are intermingled or non-linearly arranged; deep nets provide the necessary flexibility to create complex decision boundaries.
concepts.recap_md: - Multilayer networks can separate data that is not linearly separable by composing linear and nonlinear operations.

concepts.title: Indicator Function
concepts.one_liner: The indicator function $\mathbb{1}(x)$ returns 1 if the condition $x$ is true and 0 otherwise.
concepts.motivation_md: The indicator function is a fundamental mathematical tool used to convert logical conditions into numerical values, which is essential for defining classification outputs and loss functions.
concepts.recap_md: - The indicator function maps true conditions to 1 and false conditions to 0.

concepts.title: Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
concepts.one_liner: The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is a pointwise nonlinearity that yields non-zero gradients over half its domain, making it suitable for gradient-based learning.
concepts.content: The Rectified linear unit (relu) is a pointwise nonlinearity. It is described as a graded version of a threshold function. It has the advantage of yielding non-zero gradients over half its domain, which makes it amenable to gradient-based learning.
concepts.motivation_md: ReLU solves the vanishing gradient problem found in other activation functions like sigmoid, allowing for more efficient training of deep neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - ReLU is a pointwise nonlinearity used in neural networks to enable gradient-based learning.

concepts.title: Universal Approximation Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The universal approximation theorem states that deep nets can, in principle, perform any continuous input-output mapping.
concepts.content:
The universal approximation theorem states that deep nets can perform any continuous input-output mapping, even with just a single hidden layer. However, the number of neurons in the hidden layer may need to be very large to fit complicated functions. Technically, this theorem holds for continuous functions on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^N$.

To understand this intuitively, consider approximating a function from $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with a relu-MLP. Any function can be approximated by a sum of indicator functions (bumps):
$$\begin{aligned}
    f(x) \approx \sum_i w_i \mathbb{1}(\alpha_i < x < \beta_i)
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Any function from $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ can be approximated arbitrarily well by a sum of elementary bumps.)

A relu-MLP can represent these bumps because a single bump $\mathbb{1}(\alpha < x < \beta)$ can be approximated by a combination of four ReLU functions:
$$\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{1}(\alpha < x < \beta)\\
&\approx \\
&\texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-(\alpha-\gamma)}{\gamma}\bigg) - \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-\alpha}{\gamma}\bigg) - \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-(\beta-\gamma)}{\gamma}\bigg) + \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-\beta}{\gamma}\bigg)
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: A bump can be represented as a weighted sum of shifted and scaled relu functions.)

As $\gamma \rightarrow 0$, the approximation becomes exact. This construction can be implemented as a `linear`-`relu`-`linear` network. By summing many such bumps, a network can approximate any curve to arbitrary precision, though it may require an unbounded number of neurons.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the theoretical foundation for neural networks, proving that they are expressive enough to represent any complex continuous relationship given enough capacity.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural networks with at least one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set.

concepts.title: Network Width
concepts.one_liner: Network width refers to the number of neurons in a single hidden layer of a neural network.
concepts.content: The number of neurons on a single hidden layer is called its width. If different layers have different numbers of neurons, the width may be specified per layer. Often, it is assumed all layers have the same width when speaking generally of the width of the network. A hidden layer with $N$ neurons can fit a scalar function with $\mathcal{O}(N)$ bumps.
concepts.motivation_md: Width is a primary hyperparameter that determines the parallel processing capacity of a layer and its ability to represent multiple features simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md: - Width is defined as the number of neurons in a hidden layer.

concepts.title: Network Depth
concepts.one_liner: Network depth refers to the number of layers in a neural network, which can increase capacity more efficiently than width.
concepts.content: Depth refers to the number of layers in a network. Increasing depth is an effective way to increase the capacity of the net, and its effect differs from increasing width. Empirically, deeper nets often work better in practice and may require far fewer parameters to fit data than wide nets. Mathematical theory suggests that certain classes of functions can be represented with a polynomial number of neurons in a deep network but would require an exponential number of neurons in a shallower network. These theoretical arguments are known as depth separations.
concepts.motivation_md: Increasing depth allows a network to learn hierarchical representations of data, where later layers compose features from earlier layers, often leading to better generalization and efficiency.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth is the total number of layers in a neural network.

concepts.title: Linear Layers
concepts.one_liner: Linear layers are the workhorses of deep nets, containing almost all parameters in the form of weights and biases.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear layers provide the fundamental learnable transformations in a neural network, allowing the model to scale and shift input data through weights and biases.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear layers contain the majority of a network's learnable parameters.

concepts.title: Activation Layers
concepts.one_liner: Activation layers add nonlinearity to neural networks, typically through pointwise functions applied to each dimension of the input vector.
concepts.motivation_md: Without activation layers, a multi-layer neural network would collapse into a single linear transformation, making it unable to model complex, non-linear relationships in data.
concepts.recap_md: - Activation layers introduce nonlinearity to prevent the network from being a simple linear function.

concepts.title: Sigmoid Activation
concepts.one_liner: The sigmoid activation function maps input values to a range between 0 and 1.
concepts.content:
The sigmoid activation function is defined as:

$$\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{out}}}[i] = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{in}}}[i]}} \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{sigmoid}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Sigmoid functions are used to squash input values into a probability-like range between 0 and 1.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps inputs to the $(0, 1)$ range.

concepts.title: Tanh Activation
concepts.one_liner: The tanh activation function is a scaled and shifted sigmoid that maps inputs to a range between -1 and 1.
concepts.content:
The hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation function is defined in terms of the sigmoid function:

$$\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{out}}}[i] = 2*\texttt{sigmoid}(2*\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{in}}}[i])-1 \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{tanh}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Tanh is often preferred over sigmoid because it is zero-centered, mapping inputs to a range between -1 and 1.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps inputs to the $(-1, 1)$ range.

concepts.title: Leaky ReLU Activation
concepts.one_liner: Leaky ReLU is an activation function that allows a small, non-zero gradient when the input is negative.
concepts.motivation_md: Leaky ReLU addresses the 'dying ReLU' problem by ensuring that neurons still have a small gradient when their input is negative.
concepts.recap_md: - Provides a small slope $\alpha$ for negative inputs instead of zeroing them out.

concepts.title: Normalization Layers
concepts.one_liner: Normalization layers are nonlinearities that perturb neurons based on the collective behavior of a set of neurons.
concepts.content: Normalization layers add another kind of nonlinearity. Instead of being a pointwise nonlinearity, like in activation layers, they are nonlinearities that perturb each neuron based on the collective behavior of a set of neurons.
concepts.motivation_md: Normalization layers help stabilize and speed up training by ensuring that the distribution of activations remains consistent across layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Perturbs neurons based on collective behavior rather than pointwise mapping.

concepts.title: Batch Normalization (Batchnorm)
concepts.one_liner: Batchnorm standardizes neural activations with respect to their mean and variance over a batch of datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Batchnorm is used to stabilize training and allow for higher learning rates by reducing internal covariate shift through standardization.
concepts.recap_md: - Standardizes activations using batch mean and variance.

concepts.title: Standard Score
concepts.one_liner: The standard score represents how many standard deviations a random variable draw differs from the mean.
concepts.content: The standard score of a draw of a random variable is how many standard deviations it differs from the mean: $z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard scores allow for the comparison of data points from different distributions by placing them on a common scale.
concepts.recap_md: - Calculated as $z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

concepts.title: Checkpoint
concepts.one_liner: A checkpoint is a record of the parameter vector at a specific iteration of training.
concepts.content: A checkpoint is a record of the parameters at some iteration of training. Specifically, if the iterates of the parameter vector are $\theta^0, \theta^1, \ldots, \theta^T$, then any $\theta^k$ can be recorded as a checkpoint. These records allow for the visualization of how a network transforms a training dataset, layer by layer, at different stages over the course of training.
concepts.motivation_md: Checkpoints allow researchers to save and analyze the state of a model at various points during the optimization process, enabling progress tracking and the visualization of how representations evolve over time.
concepts.recap_md: - A checkpoint captures the parameter vector $\theta^k$ at a specific training iteration $k$.

concepts.title: Dimensionality reduction

position.section_title: How High-Dimensional Datapoints Get Remapped by Deep Net

concepts.one_liner: Dimensionality reduction tools project high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional spaces, such as 2D, to enable visualization.
concepts.content:
Deep representations are typically high-dimensional, making them difficult to visualize directly. Dimensionality reduction tools project high-dimensional data to a lower dimensionality, for example 2D, which can be visualized. A common objective is to perform the projection such that the distance between two datapoints in the 2D projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space. While these techniques provide a rough view of the network's internal state, they are essential for understanding how modern deep nets (like transformers with tens of thousands of dimensions) represent datasets.

(see figure: How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer...)
concepts.motivation_md: Because humans cannot visualize data beyond three dimensions, dimensionality reduction is necessary to inspect the high-dimensional feature spaces and internal representations learned by deep neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - Projects high-dimensional data into lower dimensions (usually 2D or 3D).

concepts.title: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE)

position.section_title: How High-Dimensional Datapoints Get Remapped by Deep Net

concepts.one_liner: t-SNE is a dimensionality reduction technique used to visualize high-dimensional deep net embeddings in a 2D space.
concepts.content:
t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a specific dimensionality reduction technique used to visualize how different layers of a modern deep net represent a dataset. It projects high-dimensional embeddings (which can be tens of thousands of dimensions) down to 2D. The projection aims to keep the distance between two datapoints in the 2D view roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space. This allows for the visualization of how semantic classes are separated or disentangled within the network's representation.

(see figure: How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer...)
concepts.motivation_md: t-SNE is particularly effective at preserving local structure, making it a popular choice for visualizing the clusters and semantic separations that emerge in deep learning feature spaces.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps high-dimensional embeddings down to a 2D plane.

concepts.title: Computation Graph
concepts.one_liner: A computation graph represents a neural network as a series of modular blocks or layers chained together.
concepts.content:
A key idea of neural nets is to decompose computation into a series of layers. Layers are treated as modular blocks that can be chained together into a computation graph. For example, a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) can be visualized as a sequence of these modular layers.

(see figure: In this chapter we will visualize neural nets as a sequence of layers, which we call a computation graph.)
concepts.motivation_md: Decomposing complex functions into a graph of simpler operations makes it easier to implement automatic differentiation and organize the architecture of deep learning models.
concepts.recap_md: - Decomposes complex computations into modular, chained blocks.

concepts.title: Forward Pass for a Layer
concepts.one_liner: The forward pass is the operation where a layer transforms inputs into outputs.
concepts.content:
Each layer takes in some inputs and transforms them into some outputs; this is called the $\texttt{forward}$ pass through the layer. If the layer has parameters $\theta$, they are considered an input to a parameter-free transformation:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}},\theta) \end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Forward operation of a neural net layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: The forward pass is the fundamental mechanism by which a neural network processes input data to generate a prediction or representation.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps input $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and parameters $\theta$ to an output $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$.

concepts.title: Backward Operation
concepts.one_liner: The backward operation is a layer-specific function used in computation graphs to calculate gradients.
concepts.content: The backward operation is a special operation defined for each layer in a computation graph. Just like the forward pass, it is modular and relies on the structure of the graph to propagate information.
concepts.motivation_md: To train a network, we need to know how the loss changes with respect to every parameter; the backward operation provides a modular way to compute these gradients using the chain rule.
concepts.recap_md: - A modular operation defined for each layer to facilitate gradient calculation.

concepts.title: Backpropagation: Reuse of Computation

position.section_title: The Trick of Backpropagation: Reuse of Computation

concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation efficiently computes gradients by reusing shared terms from the chain rule across different layers.
concepts.content:
Consider a computation graph that is a chain of functions $f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots f_2 \circ f_1$, where each function $f_l$ is parameterized by $\theta_l$. To optimize these parameters with respect to a scalar loss $J$, we compute gradients like $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_2}$ using the chain rule. 

(see figure: Basic sequential computation graph.)

(see figure: Computation graph as a tree.)

When writing out these gradients, many terms are shared:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_1} &= \left( \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_3}{\partial \mathbf{x}_2} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_2}{\partial \mathbf{x}_1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_1}{\partial \theta_1} \\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_2} &= \left( \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_3}{\partial \mathbf{x}_2} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_2}{\partial \theta_2} \end{aligned}$$

The trick of backpropagation is to evaluate the shared product (highlighted in parentheses) only once and reuse it for all subsequent gradient calculations, rather than computing each layer's gradients independently.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculating gradients independently for every parameter in a deep network would be computationally prohibitive. Reusing intermediate results reduces the complexity from exponential to linear with respect to the number of layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies shared terms in the chain rule expansion of gradients.

concepts.title: Backpropagation as Dynamic Programming
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation is an application of dynamic programming, as it stores and reuses intermediate results to solve a complex problem.
concepts.content: The strategy of calculating shared terms once and reusing them in subsequent calculations is known as dynamic programming. Backpropagation applies this general algorithmic strategy to the computation of gradients in a neural network.
concepts.motivation_md: By framing backpropagation as dynamic programming, we can understand it as an efficient way to solve the sub-problems of gradient calculation by caching intermediate results.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses dynamic programming to avoid redundant calculations.

concepts.title: System
concepts.one_liner: A system is a process or function that transforms a signal into another.
concepts.content: A system is a process or function that transforms a signal into another signal, typically across domains such as time, space, or wavelength.
concepts.motivation_md: In signal processing, we need a way to describe the mechanisms that modify or react to signals. Defining a 'system' provides a mathematical framework for these transformations.
concepts.recap_md: - A system acts as a function mapping an input signal to an output signal.

concepts.title: Continuous and Discrete Signals Comparison
concepts.one_liner: Continuous signals in nature are sampled and transformed into finite sequences of numbers called discrete signals for computer processing.
concepts.content:
Although most signals that exist in nature are infinite continuous signals, when we introduce them into a computer they are sampled and transformed into a finite sequence of numbers, also called a discrete signal. As is common in signal processing, we use parentheses to indicate continuous variables and brackets to denote discrete variables. For instance, if we sample the signal shown in @fig-contdiscsignal (a) once every second ($\Delta T = 1$ s) we get the discrete signal shown in @fig-contdiscsignal (b).

(see figure: Fig (a) A continuous signal, and (b) a discrete signal obtained by sampling the continuous signal at the times $t=n$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Computers cannot process infinite, continuous data directly. Sampling allows us to represent real-world phenomena as finite sequences that digital hardware can manipulate.
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous signals use parentheses $(t)$ while discrete signals use brackets $[n]$.

concepts.title: Continuous Signal
concepts.one_liner: Continuous signals are infinite signals that typically exist in nature.
concepts.content: Most of the signals that exist in nature are infinite continuous signals.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous signals represent physical quantities as they exist in the real world, varying smoothly over an uncountable set of time or space points.
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous signals are the standard form of signals found in nature.

concepts.title: Discrete Signal
concepts.one_liner: A discrete signal is a finite sequence of numbers obtained by sampling a continuous signal.
concepts.content: A discrete signal is a finite sequence of numbers created when a continuous signal is sampled and transformed for use in a computer.
concepts.motivation_md: Discrete signals are the fundamental data format for digital signal processing, allowing mathematical operations to be performed by computers.
concepts.recap_md: - Discrete signals consist of a finite sequence of numerical values.

concepts.title: Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Sampling is the process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one.
concepts.content: Sampling is the process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one.
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling bridges the gap between the continuous physical world and the discrete digital world of computers.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling converts continuous-time data into discrete-time sequences.

concepts.title: Signal Sampling Process
concepts.one_liner: Signal sampling captures values at discrete time instants, such as a camera recording video at 30 frames per second.
concepts.content: If we consider the light that reaches one camera photo sensor, we could write it as a one dimensional function of time, $\ell(t)$, where $\ell(t)$ denotes the incident light at time $t$, and $t$ is a continuous variable that can take on any real value. The signal $\ell(t)$ is then sampled in time by the camera where the values are only captured at discrete times (e.g., 30 times per second). In that case, the signal $\ell$ will be defined only on discrete time instants and we will write the sequence of measured values as: $\ell\left[ n \right]$, where $n$ can only take on integer values.
concepts.motivation_md: Using a camera as an example helps visualize how continuous physical phenomena (light) are captured at specific intervals to create digital data (video frames).
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous signals $\ell(t)$ use real-valued time $t$.

concepts.title: Sampling Equation
concepts.one_liner: The sampling equation $\ell[n] = \ell(n \Delta T)$ relates discrete and continuous signals via the sampling period $\Delta T$.
concepts.content: The relationship between discrete and continuous signals is given by the sampling equation: $$\ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left(n~\Delta T \right)$$ where $\Delta T$ is the sampling period. For instance, $\Delta T = 1/30$ s in the case of sampling a signal 30 times per second.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation provides the mathematical link between a continuous function and its discrete representation, defining exactly which points in time are preserved.
concepts.recap_md: - The sampling equation is $\ell[n] = \ell(n \Delta T)$.

concepts.title: Discrete Signal Vector Notation
concepts.one_liner: Discrete signals can be conveniently represented as column vectors.
concepts.content: In many cases it is convenient to write discrete signals as vectors. Using vector notation, we can write a signal in the interval $n \in \left[0,6 \right]$ as a column vector $\boldsymbol\ell= \left[3, 2, 1, 4, 0, 0, 0\right]^T$, where $T$ denotes transpose. In this example, several values are zero, $\ell\left[n\right] = 0$.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing signals as vectors allows us to use the powerful tools of linear algebra to process and analyze digital signals.
concepts.recap_md: - Discrete signals can be expressed as column vectors $\boldsymbol\ell$.

concepts.title: Local Gradient Arrays (g and L)
concepts.one_liner: The local gradient arrays $\mathbf{g}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ represent partial derivatives of the cost and the layer output, respectively, at a single operating point.
concepts.content:
(see figure: A generic layer in the computation graph. The braces represent the part of the computation graph we need to consider in order to evaluate $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$, $\mathbf{L}$, and $\mathbf{g}in$.)

Two key shorthand arrays are used to track partial derivatives for backpropagation:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_l&\triangleq \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_l} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{grad of cost with respect to } \mathbf{x}_l \quad [1 \times |\mathbf{x}_l|]\\
    \mathbf{L}&\triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta]} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{grad of layer}\\
    &\quad\quad \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} \triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{\quad with respect to layer input data} \quad [|\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}| \times |\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}|]\\
    &\quad\quad \mathbf{L}^{\theta} \triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \theta} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{\quad with respect to layer params} \quad [|\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}| \times |\theta|]
\end{aligned}$$

All these arrays represent the gradient at a single operating point, defined by the current values of the data and parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: To perform backpropagation efficiently, we need a standardized way to represent the sensitivity of the cost function and the layer outputs to their inputs and parameters. These arrays provide the necessary building blocks for applying the chain rule across layers.
concepts.recap_md: - $\mathbf{g}_l$ is the gradient of the cost $J$ with respect to the layer activations $\mathbf{x}_l$.

concepts.title: Parameter Update Rule
concepts.one_liner: The parameter update rule uses the product of the output gradient and the layer's parameter gradient to adjust weights and minimize cost.
concepts.motivation_md: The ultimate goal of training a neural network is to find parameters that minimize the cost function. This rule provides the specific mechanism for adjusting those parameters based on the calculated gradients.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient with respect to parameters is the product of the output gradient $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ and the local parameter gradient $\mathbf{L}^{\theta}$.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Recurrence Relation
concepts.one_liner: The backpropagation recurrence relation allows for the iterative computation of error signals by sending gradients backward through the network.
concepts.content:
Computing the gradient of the cost with respect to inputs, $\mathbf{g}$, requires evaluating the chain rule across all layers between $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ and $J$. This can be computed iteratively: once $\mathbf{g}_l$ is known, $\mathbf{g}_{l-1}$ is found via a single matrix multiplication. This is summarized by the recurrence relation:

$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{backpropagation of errors}
\end{aligned}$$

This recurrence is the essence of backpropagation: it sends error signals (gradients) backward through the network, starting at the last layer and iteratively applying the relation to compute $\mathbf{g}$ for each previous layer. In deep learning libraries like PyTorch, this value is typically stored in a `.grad` field associated with each variable.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculating gradients for deep networks would be computationally prohibitive without an efficient method. This recurrence relation breaks the complex global gradient calculation into simple local matrix multiplications.
concepts.recap_md: - Error signals $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ are computed by multiplying the subsequent gradient $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ by the local Jacobian $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}$.

concepts.title: Backward Function for a Generic Layer
concepts.one_liner: The backward function for a generic layer takes the input data, parameters, and output gradient to produce the input gradient and parameter gradient.
concepts.content: The `backward` function for a generic layer consists of an operation that takes three inputs ($\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$) and produces two outputs ($\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}$). ![`backward` for a generic layer. We use the color to indicate parameter gradients.](figures/backpropagation/mod_block_backward.png) In this process, the color red is used for data/activation gradients being passed backward through the network, while yellow indicates parameter gradients.
concepts.motivation_md: Modularizing the backward pass into a standard function for every layer allows complex neural architectures to be automatically differentiated by simply chaining these local operations.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward function maps $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ to $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}$.

concepts.title: Forward Pass through the Network

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

concepts.one_liner: The forward pass evaluates the network layer by layer, starting from the input data to produce a sequence of activations.
concepts.content:
To prepare for gradient updates, we first compute a forward pass through the entire network. This involves starting with input data $\mathbf{x}_0$ and evaluating each layer sequentially to produce the sequence $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.

(see figure: Forward pass.)

During this pass, data and activations are passed forward through the network, often represented visually with green indicators.
concepts.motivation_md: Gradients depend on the specific values of activations at each layer. The forward pass is necessary to establish these "operating points" before the backward pass can calculate derivatives.
concepts.recap_md: - The forward pass computes activations $\mathbf{x}_l$ sequentially from $l=0$ to $L$.

concepts.title: Backward Pass through the Network

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

concepts.one_liner: The backward pass iteratively evaluates gradients from the last layer to the first to obtain parameter gradients for the entire network.
concepts.content:
Following the forward pass, we compute a backward pass by iteratively evaluating the gradients $\mathbf{g}$ and obtaining the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer.

(see figure: A schematic diagram of the backpropagation process in a neural network. Red arrows flow from right to left, starting with a value of 1 entering a loss derivative block $\mathcal{L}'$, then passing...)
concepts.motivation_md: The backward pass is the core algorithm for training; it efficiently propagates the error from the output back to every weight in the network, allowing for simultaneous optimization of all parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass computes the sequence of gradients $\mathbf{g}_l$ in reverse order.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Over Data Batches
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation in batch mode computes the average gradient over a set of datapoints to update parameters for the entire batch.
concepts.motivation_md: Training on single examples can be noisy and inefficient. Batch mode allows for more stable gradient estimates and takes advantage of parallel computing hardware like GPUs.
concepts.recap_md: - The batch gradient is the average of the gradients calculated for each individual datapoint.

concepts.title: Linearity of Gradients
concepts.one_liner: The gradient of a sum of terms is equal to the sum of the gradients of each individual term.
concepts.motivation_md: This property is fundamental to machine learning because it justifies why we can compute gradients on individual examples or small batches and combine them to optimize a global objective function.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient of a sum is the sum of the gradients.

concepts.title: Operating Point
concepts.one_liner: The operating point refers to a particular setting of parameters where the loss function is currently being evaluated.
concepts.content: The term operating point refers to a particular point, or setting of the parameters, where we are currently evaluating the loss.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a specific reference point in the parameter space to evaluate the current state of a model's performance during optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - An operating point is a specific setting of parameters $\theta$.

concepts.title: Zeroth-Order Optimization
concepts.one_liner: Zeroth-order optimization minimizes loss by sampling different parameter values and moving toward those with lower costs, observing only the loss value itself.
concepts.content: In the simplest setting, called zeroth-order optimization, the update function only gets to observe the value $J(\theta)$. The only way, then, to find $\theta$'s that minimize the loss is to sample different values for $\theta$ and move toward the values that are lower.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach is used when gradient information is unavailable or too difficult to compute, relying solely on function evaluations to explore the parameter space.
concepts.recap_md: - Only the loss value $J(\theta)$ is observed during optimization.

concepts.title: First-Order Optimization
concepts.one_liner: First-order optimization uses the gradient of the cost function to determine the direction of steepest descent for minimizing the loss.
concepts.content: For gradient-based optimization, also called first-order optimization, the update function takes as input the gradient of the cost with respect to the parameters at the current operating point, $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$. This reveals hugely useful information about the loss that directly tells us how to minimize it: just move in the direction of steepest descent, that is, the gradient direction.
concepts.motivation_md: By using the gradient, the optimizer knows exactly which direction reduces the loss most efficiently, making it much more powerful than random sampling.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses the gradient $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$ at the current operating point.

concepts.title: Higher-Order Optimization
concepts.one_liner: Higher-order optimization methods utilize higher-order derivatives, such as the Hessian, to account for the local curvature of the loss landscape.
concepts.content: Higher-order optimization methods observe higher-order derivatives of the loss, such as the Hessian $H$, which tells you how the landscape is locally curving. The Hessian is costly to compute, but many methods use approximations to the Hessian, or other properties related to loss curvature, and these are growing in popularity.
concepts.motivation_md: While gradients show the direction of descent, higher-order derivatives provide information about the curvature, allowing for more precise steps and potentially faster convergence.
concepts.recap_md: - Utilizes higher-order derivatives like the Hessian $H$.

concepts.title: Basic Gradient Descent
concepts.one_liner: Basic gradient descent updates parameters by taking steps in the gradient direction with a length proportional to the gradient magnitude.
concepts.content:
The simplest version of gradient descent just takes a step in the gradient direction of length proportional to the gradient magnitude. This algorithm is described in @alg-gradient_descent_basic_gradient_descent.

(see figure: Gradient descent `GD`. Optimizing a cost function $J: \theta \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by descending the gradient $\nabla_{\theta} J$.)

This algorithm has two hyperparameters, the learning rate $\eta$, which controls the step size (learning rate times gradient magnitude), and the number of steps $K$. If the learning rate is sufficiently small and the initial parameter vector $\theta^0$ is random, then this algorithm will almost surely converge to a local minimum of $J$ as $K \rightarrow \infty$. However, to descend more quickly, it can be useful to set the learning rate to a higher value.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a fundamental iterative method for finding local minima of a function by following the steepest downward path.
concepts.recap_md: - Steps are taken in the direction of the gradient $\nabla_{\theta} J$.

concepts.title: Learning Rate
concepts.one_liner: The learning rate is a hyperparameter that controls the step size in gradient descent by scaling the gradient magnitude.
concepts.content: The learning rate $\eta$ is a hyperparameter that controls the step size in gradient descent, calculated as the learning rate times the gradient magnitude. If the learning rate is sufficiently small and the initial parameter vector $\theta^0$ is random, then this algorithm will almost surely converge to a local minimum of $J$ as $K \rightarrow \infty$. However, to descend more quickly, it can be useful to set the learning rate to a higher value.
concepts.motivation_md: It is a critical tuning parameter that balances the speed of learning against the risk of overshooting the minimum or failing to converge.
concepts.recap_md: - Represented by $\eta$, it scales the gradient to determine step size.

concepts.title: Learning Rate Schedules
concepts.one_liner: A learning rate schedule is a strategy that adjusts the learning rate over time, typically decaying it to take smaller steps as optimization approaches a minimizer.
concepts.content:
A generally useful strategy is to start with a high value for $\eta$ and then decay it until convergence according to a learning rate schedule. Schedules generally work by calling some function $\texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k)$ to get the learning rate on each iteration of descent:
$$
\eta^{k} = \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k)
$$
Generally, we want an update rule where $\eta^{k+1} < \eta^k$, so that we take smaller steps as we approach the minimizer. A few simple and popular approaches include exponential decay, stepwise exponential decay, and linear decay:
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \beta^{-k} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{exponential decay}\\
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \beta^{-\lfloor k/M \rfloor} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{stepwise exponential decay}\\
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \frac{(K - k)}{K} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{linear decay}
\end{aligned}
$$
One downside of linear decay is that it depends on the total number of steps $K$. Variations on this algorithm include only decaying the learning rate when a plateau is reached or using more complex nonlinear schedules, such as cosine decay.

(see figure: Gradient descent with learning rate decay algorithm.)
concepts.motivation_md: Schedules allow for fast initial progress with large steps while ensuring fine-grained convergence by reducing step sizes as the optimizer nears the solution.
concepts.recap_md: - Adjusts the learning rate $\eta$ dynamically during training.

concepts.title: Momentum
concepts.one_liner: Momentum is an optimization technique that incorporates previous update directions into the current step to smooth the trajectory and accelerate descent.
concepts.content:
Momentum makes the analogy to skiing: it is like the inertia of the skier, carrying them over little bumps and increasing their speed as they descend along a straight path. In math, momentum means that we set the parameter update to be a direction $\mathbf{v}^{k+1}$, given by a weighted combination of the previous update direction, $\mathbf{v}^{k}$, plus the current negative gradient:
$$
\mathbf{v}^{k+1} = \mu \mathbf{v}^{k} - \eta\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta^k)
$$
The weight $\mu$ is a hyperparameter sometimes simply called the momentum. 

(see figure: Gradient descent with momentum algorithm.)

Some momentum can help the convergence rate, but too much momentum will cause the trajectory to overshoot the optimum and might prevent the trajectory from stopping even when the optimum loss is achieved.

(see figure: (left) A simple loss function $J = \texttt{abs}(\theta)$. (right) Optimization trajectory for three different settings of momentum $\mu$. White line indicates value of the parameter at each iteration...)
concepts.motivation_md: It helps the optimizer navigate noisy gradients or flat regions by maintaining a "velocity" from previous steps, leading to faster and smoother convergence.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines the current gradient with a fraction $\mu$ of the previous update.

concepts.title: Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient
concepts.one_liner: A type of momentum that biases the update direction based on accumulated information from previous updates.
concepts.content: Nesterov's accelerated gradient is a kind of momentum that biases the update direction based on accumulated information from previous updates.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard gradient descent can oscillate or converge slowly; Nesterov's method uses historical update trends to refine the search direction and accelerate convergence.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a momentum-based optimization technique.

concepts.title: Adam Optimizer
concepts.one_liner: A popular optimization method that biases the update direction based on accumulated information from previous updates.
concepts.content: Adam is a popular alternative for optimization that incorporates momentum, biasing the update direction based on accumulated information from previous updates.
concepts.motivation_md: Adam is designed to improve optimization efficiency by using adaptive estimates of lower-order moments to handle sparse gradients and noisy objectives.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a popular alternative to standard gradient descent.

concepts.title: One-Sided Derivative

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

concepts.one_liner: A derivative calculated at a discontinuity by taking the gradient value an infinitesimal step away in a fixed arbitrary direction.
concepts.content:
In cases where a function is discontinuous and the analytical derivative is undefined, gradient descent can still function by using a one-sided derivative. This involves setting the gradient at the discontinuity to be equal to the gradient value an infinitesimal step away from the discontinuity in a fixed arbitrary direction. For each atomic discontinuous operation, frameworks like Pytorch require defining gradients at discontinuities, where the one-sided gradient is a standard choice. This allows the use of functions with discontinuous gradients, such as rectified nonlinear units (ReLU), in deep learning.

(see figure: How gradient descent behaves on various functions.** In each subplot, the left shows the function $J$, with the red point representing the solution found by gradient descent (GD) with $\eta=0.01$ and...)
concepts.motivation_md: Many common deep learning functions, like ReLU, are non-differentiable at specific points; one-sided derivatives allow optimization algorithms to handle these discontinuities gracefully.
concepts.recap_md: - It defines the gradient at a discontinuity as the value an infinitesimal step away.

concepts.title: Vanishing Gradient

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

concepts.one_liner: A condition where the gradient is near zero everywhere, causing gradient descent with a fixed learning rate to be extremely slow.
concepts.content:
A vanishing gradient occurs when a function's gradient is near zero everywhere. In such cases, gradient descent with a fixed learning rate will be slow because the updates to the parameters are minimal.

(see figure: How gradient descent behaves on various functions.** In each subplot, the left shows the function $J$, with the red point representing the solution found by gradient descent (GD) with $\eta=0.01$ and...)
concepts.motivation_md: When gradients become too small, learning effectively stops; identifying this phenomenon is crucial for diagnosing training failures in deep networks.
concepts.recap_md: - It refers to gradients that are near zero across the function's domain.

concepts.title: Exploding Gradient

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

concepts.one_liner: A condition where the gradient goes to infinity at the minimizer, leading to failures in convergence during gradient descent.
concepts.content:
An exploding gradient is a scenario where the gradient at the minimizer goes to infinity. This behavior leads to failures of convergence in gradient descent.

(see figure: How gradient descent behaves on various functions.** In each subplot, the left shows the function $J$, with the red point representing the solution found by gradient descent (GD) with $\eta=0.01$ and...)
concepts.motivation_md: Extremely large gradients can cause weight updates to overshoot the minimum, leading to unstable training and divergence.
concepts.recap_md: - It occurs when the gradient magnitude approaches infinity near the optimum.

concepts.title: Evolution Strategies

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

concepts.one_liner: An optimization approach that estimates update directions by sampling perturbations of parameters and moving toward those that decrease the loss.
concepts.content:
Evolution strategies are approaches to finding an update direction $\mathbf{v}$ by sampling perturbations of $\theta$ and observing which perturbations lead to a lower loss. In this strategy, $J(\theta+\epsilon)$ is evaluated for a set of perturbations $\epsilon$, and the parameters are moved toward the $\epsilon$'s that decreased the loss. A basic version of this algorithm is given in (see figure: Evolution strategy algorithm.). This algorithm can successfully minimize functions where the true gradient might be zero or otherwise unhelpful.

(see figure: Using @alg-gradient_descent_ES) to minimize a nondifferentiable (zero-gradient) loss, using $\sigma=1$, $M=10$, and $\eta=0.02$.)
concepts.motivation_md: When true gradients are unavailable, zero, or unreliable, evolution strategies provide a way to optimize functions using only point evaluations.
concepts.recap_md: - They compute update directions by sampling random perturbations of the parameters.

concepts.title: Surrogate Loss

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

concepts.one_liner: A function $J_{\texttt{surr}}$ with meaningful gradients that approximates the original loss function $J$ to facilitate optimization.
concepts.content: A surrogate loss function, $J_{\texttt{surr}}$, is a function with meaningful (non-zero) gradients that approximates the original loss function $J$. It is used as a choice for the update direction $\mathbf{v}$ when the true gradient is not ideal. An example of a surrogate loss might be a smoothed version of $J$.
concepts.motivation_md: If a loss function is non-differentiable or has zero gradients in many places, a surrogate loss provides a differentiable approximation that guides the optimizer.
concepts.recap_md: - It is an approximation of the target loss function designed to have useful gradients.

concepts.title: Gradient Clipping

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

concepts.one_liner: A technique to combat exploding gradients by clamping the magnitude of the gradient to a specified maximum value.
concepts.content:
Gradient clipping is a technique used to combat exploding gradients by clamping the magnitude of the gradient to some maximum value. The approach is described in (see figure: Gradient clipping algorithm.). The clipping function is defined as $\texttt{clip}(v, -m, m) = \max(\min(v,m),-m)$. This algorithm can successfully minimize functions with exploding gradients, preventing the optimization from failing.

(see figure: Using `GD` with clipping to minimize a loss with exploding gradients, using $m=0.1$.)
concepts.motivation_md: To prevent large gradient values from causing numerical instability or divergence, clipping ensures updates remain within a manageable range.
concepts.recap_md: - It clamps the gradient magnitude to a predefined maximum value $m$.

concepts.title: Systems Overview
concepts.one_liner: A system takes an input signal, performs a computation, and produces an output signal.
concepts.content:
The kind of systems that we will study here take a signal, $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, as input, perform some computation, $f$, and output another signal, $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}= f(\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}})$.

(see figure: System processing one signal.)

This transformation is very general and it can do all sorts of complex things: it could detect edges in images, recognize objects, detect motion in sequences, or apply aesthetic transformations to a picture. The function $f$ could be specified as a mathematical operation or as an algorithm. As a consequence, it is very difficult to find a simple way of characterizing what the function $f$ does. In the next section we will study a simple class of functions $f$ that allow for a simple analytical characterization: linear systems.
concepts.motivation_md: Systems provide a mathematical framework for processing signals, such as images. While general systems can be arbitrarily complex, defining them as functions allows us to categorize and analyze specific transformations like edge detection or object recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - A system is a function $f$ that transforms an input signal $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ into an output signal $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}$.

concepts.title: Linear System
concepts.one_liner: A system is linear if it satisfies the properties of additivity and homogeneity.
concepts.content:
Linear systems represent a very small portion of all the possible systems one could implement, but they are capable of creating very interesting image transformations. A function $f$ is linear if it satisfies the following two properties:

$$\begin{aligned}
f\left( \boldsymbol\ell_1+\boldsymbol\ell_2 \right) &=& f(\boldsymbol\ell_1)+ f(\boldsymbol\ell_2) \\ \nonumber
f(a\boldsymbol\ell) &=& af(\boldsymbol\ell) ~~\text{~for any scalar~} a
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Linearity simplifies the analysis of complex systems by allowing us to decompose inputs and study their effects independently. This property is foundational for many image processing techniques.
concepts.recap_md: - Linearity requires additivity: $f(\ell_1 + \ell_2) = f(\ell_1) + f(\ell_2)$.

concepts.title: Linear System Matrix Formulation
concepts.one_liner: A linear system can be expressed as a matrix-vector multiplication where the output is a linear combination of input values.
concepts.content:
To make things more concrete, assume the input is a 1D signal with length $N$ written as $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$, and the output is another 1D signal with length $M$ written as $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right]$. Most of the times we will work with input and output pairs with the same length $M=N$. A linear system, in its most general form, can be written as follows:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[n,k\right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right] ~~~ for ~~~ n \in \left[0, M-1 \right]
$$ where each output value $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right]$ is a linear combination of values of the input signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n \right]$ with weights $h \left[n,k\right]$. The value $h \left[n,k\right]$ is the weight applied to the input sample $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$ to compute the output sample $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right]$. To help visualizing the operation performed by the linear filter it is useful to write it in matrix form:
$$\begin{bmatrix}\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 0 \right] \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ 1 \right] \\
\vdots \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ n \right] \\
\vdots \\
\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ M-1 \right]
\end{bmatrix}
 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  h\left[0,0\right] ~&~ h\left[0,1\right] ~&~ ... ~&~ h\left[0,N-1\right] \\
  h\left[1,0\right] ~&~ h\left[1,1\right] ~&~ ... ~&~ h\left[1,N-1\right] \\
  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots \\
  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  h \left[n,k\right] ~&~  \vdots \\
\vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots ~&~  \vdots \\
  h\left[M-1,0\right] ~&~ h\left[M-1,1\right] ~&~ ... ~&~ h\left[M-1,N-1\right] 
 \end{bmatrix}
~
 \begin{bmatrix}
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[0\right] \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[1\right] \\
  \vdots \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k\right] \\
  \vdots \\
  \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[N-1\right]
 \end{bmatrix}$$
which we will write in short form as $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$. The matrix $\mathbf{H}$ has size $M \times N$.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing linear systems as matrices allows us to use the powerful tools of linear algebra to analyze and implement signal transformations efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear systems can be written as $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}} = \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$.

concepts.title: Linear System as Fully Connected Layer
concepts.one_liner: A linear function can be represented as a fully connected layer in a neural network.
concepts.content:
A linear function can also be drawn as a **fully connected layer** in a neural network, with weights $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{H}$, where the output unit $i$, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[i \right]$, is a linear combination of the input signal $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ with weights given by the row vectors of $\mathbf{H}$. Graphically it looks like this:

(see figure: A linear function drawn as a **fully connected layer** in a neural network.)
concepts.motivation_md: Connecting linear systems to neural network architectures helps bridge the gap between classical signal processing and modern deep learning models.
concepts.recap_md: - A fully connected layer is a graphical representation of a linear system.

concepts.title: 2D Linear Systems
concepts.one_liner: In 2D, linear systems compute output pixels as a linear combination of input pixels, often represented by flattening images into vectors.
concepts.content:
In two dimensions the equations are analogous. Each pixel of the output image, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right]$, is computed as a linear combination of pixels of the input image, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n, m\right]$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1} \sum_{l=0}^{N-1} h \left[n,m,k,l \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k,l \right]
$$ By writing the images as column vectors, concatenating all the image columns into a long vector, we can also write the previous equation using matrices and vectors: $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Extending linear systems to 2D is essential for image processing, where data is naturally organized in grids rather than 1D sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - 2D linear systems use double summations to process pixel grids.

concepts.title: Linear Translation Invariant (LTI) System
concepts.one_liner: Linear translation invariant (LTI) systems apply the same processing algorithm at every spatial position.
concepts.content:
