Linear systems are still too general for us. So let's consider an even smaller family of systems: **linear translation invariant** (LTI) **systems**.

[FIGURE:b7749e9467b10dd1 | A Venn diagram showing nested subsets of mathematical functions. The largest set is 'All functions' (red), which contains 'Differentiable' functions (yellow), which in turn contains 'Linear'...]

Translation invariant systems are motivated by the following observation: typically, we don't know where within the image we expect to find any given item, so we often want to process the image in a spatially invariant manner, the same processing algorithm at every pixel.
concepts.motivation_md: Since objects can appear anywhere in an image, it is efficient and logical to use systems that treat all spatial locations identically.
concepts.recap_md: - LTI systems are a subset of linear systems that are spatially invariant.

concepts.title: Translation Equivariance
concepts.one_liner: A system is translation equivariant if translating the input results in a corresponding translation of the output.
concepts.content:
A system is an LTI system if it is linear and when we translate the input signal by $n_0, m_0$, then output is also translated by $n_0, m_0$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[ n - n_0, m-m_0 \right] = f \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[ n-n_0, m-m_0 \right] \right)$$
for any $n_0,m_0$. This property is called **equivariant** with respect to translation. Translation invariance and linearity impose a strong constraint on the form of the general linear filter equation.
concepts.motivation_md: Equivariance ensures that the system's response is consistent regardless of where the input signal is located in the domain.
concepts.recap_md: - Translation equivariance means $f(\text{shifted input}) = \text{shifted output}$.

concepts.title: Convolution and Convolution Kernel
concepts.one_liner: An LTI system can be expressed as a convolution of the input data with a convolution kernel.
concepts.content: In the case of a linear translation invariant system, the linear system becomes a **convolution** of the image data with some **convolution kernel**. This operation is very important and we devote the rest of this chapter to study its properties.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution provides a computationally efficient and mathematically elegant way to implement LTI systems.
concepts.recap_md: - LTI systems are mathematically equivalent to convolution operations.

concepts.title: Associative Property of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolutions can be applied in any order, allowing the grouping of multiple kernels or signals without changing the result.
concepts.content:
Convolutions are associative, meaning they can be applied in any order:
$$\ell_1 [n] \circ \ell_2 [n] \circ \ell_3 [n] = \ell_1[n] \circ (\ell_2[n] \circ \ell_3[n]) = (\ell_1[n] \circ \ell_2[n]) \circ \ell_3[n]$$
In practice, for finite length signals, the associative property might be affected by how boundary conditions are implemented.
concepts.motivation_md: Associativity allows for the pre-computation of multiple filters into a single equivalent kernel, which can significantly improve computational efficiency in signal processing and neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution is associative, meaning $(\ell_1 \circ \ell_2) \circ \ell_3 = \ell_1 \circ (\ell_2 \circ \ell_3)$.

concepts.title: Distributive Property of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolution is distributive with respect to addition, allowing a kernel to be applied to a sum of signals individually.
concepts.content:
Convolution is distributive with respect to the sum:
$$\ell_1[n] \circ (\ell_2[n] + \ell_3[n] ) = \ell_1[n] \circ \ell_2[n] +  \ell_1 [n] \circ \ell_3 [n]$$
concepts.motivation_md: This property ensures that filtering a combined signal is the same as filtering each component separately and then adding them, which is fundamental to linear system theory.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution distributes over addition: $f \circ (g + h) = f \circ g + f \circ h$.

concepts.title: Shift Property of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Translating either the input signal or the kernel by a constant results in an output translated by that same constant.
concepts.content:
Another interesting property involves shifting the two convolved functions. Consider the convolution $\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n] = h[n] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$. If the input signal, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$, is translated by a constant $n_0$, i.e. $\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n - n_0]$, the result of the convolution with the same kernel, $h[n]$, is the same output as before but translated by the same constant $n_0$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n-n_0] =  h[n] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n-n_0]$$
Translating the kernel is equivalent:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}[n-n_0] =  h[n] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n-n_0]  = h[n-n_0] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n]$$
concepts.motivation_md: This property, also known as shift-invariance, ensures that a feature detected by a kernel will be recognized regardless of its position in the input signal.
concepts.recap_md: - Shifting the input signal by $n_0$ shifts the convolution output by $n_0$.

concepts.title: Support of Convolution
concepts.one_liner: The convolution of signals with lengths $N$ and $M$ results in a signal with length at most $M+N-1$.
concepts.content: The convolution of a discrete signal of length $N$ with another discrete signal of length $M$ results in a discrete signal with length $L \leq M+N-1$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the support (length) of the output is critical for memory allocation and for deciding how to handle boundaries when processing finite signals.
concepts.recap_md: - The output length $L$ of convolving signals of length $N$ and $M$ is $L \leq M+N-1$.

concepts.title: Convolution Identity (Impulse)
concepts.one_liner: The impulse function $\delta[n]$ acts as the identity for convolution, returning the original signal unchanged.
concepts.content:
The convolution has an identity function, the impulse $\delta [n]$, which takes the value 1 for $n=0$ and is zero everywhere else:
$$\delta [n] = \begin{cases} 1 & \quad \text{if } n=0\\ 0 & \quad \text{if } n \neq 0 \end{cases}$$
The convolution of the impulse with any other signal, $\ell[n]$, returns the same signal:
$$\delta [n] \circ \ell[n] = \ell[n]$$
The impulse function is
[FIGURE:c145f3f27c246168 | A discrete-time graph of the unit impulse function $\delta[n)$. A vertical blue line with a blue dot at the top is located at $n=0$ with a height of $1$. For all other integer values of $n$ from $-4$...]
concepts.motivation_md: The impulse function is the mathematical 'unit' of convolution, allowing us to represent any signal as a sum of shifted and scaled impulses.
concepts.recap_md: - The impulse $\delta[n]$ is 1 at $n=0$ and 0 otherwise.

concepts.title: Handling Convolution Boundaries
concepts.one_liner: Boundary handling addresses the ambiguity of computing convolution values where the kernel overlaps the edge of the input signal.
concepts.content:
When implementing a convolution, one is confronted with the question of what to do at the image boundaries. There's really no satisfactory answer for how to handle the boundaries that works well for all applications. One solution consists in omitting from the output any pixels that are affected by the input boundary. The issue with this is that the output will have a different size than the input and, for large convolutional kernels, there might be a large portion of the output image missing.

Only the green region contains values that can be computed, the rest will be affected by how we decide to handle the boundaries:

[FIGURE:6b79adcf26f0dfd2 | A diagram showing three nested rectangles representing different convolution output sizes. The largest, outer yellow rectangle with a dashed border is labeled 'Full convolution'. Inside it, a...]
concepts.motivation_md: Since real-world signals are finite, kernels eventually 'fall off' the edge during sliding. We need strategies to define these missing values or manage the resulting reduction in output size.
concepts.recap_md: - Boundary handling is necessary because kernels overlap the edges of finite signals.

concepts.title: Zero Padding
concepts.one_liner: Zero padding sets pixels outside the signal boundary to zero or another constant to maintain output size.
concepts.content: Zero padding involves setting the pixels outside the boundary to zero (or to some other constant such as the mean image value). This is the default option in most neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: Zero padding is a simple and computationally efficient way to ensure the output of a convolution has the same spatial dimensions as the input.
concepts.recap_md: - Values outside the boundary are treated as zero or a constant.

concepts.title: Circular Padding
concepts.one_liner: Circular padding extends a signal by replicating pixels from the opposite side, treating the signal as periodic.
concepts.content:
Circular padding extends the image by replicating the pixels from the other side. If the image has size $P \times Q$, circular padding consists of the following:
$$\ell_{\texttt{in}}[n,m] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}[(n)_P,(m)_Q]$$
where $(n)_P$ denotes the modulo operation and $(n)_P$ is the reminder of $n/P$.

This padding transforms the finite length signal into a periodic infinite length signal. Although this will introduce many artifacts, it is a convenient extension for analytical derivations.
concepts.motivation_md: Circular padding is mathematically useful because it aligns with the properties of the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), where signals are inherently treated as periodic.
concepts.recap_md: - Circular padding uses modulo arithmetic to wrap the signal around its boundaries.

concepts.title: Depth Separations
concepts.one_liner: Depth separations are arguments comparing networks of different depths to demonstrate the benefits of deeper architectures.
concepts.content: Arguments comparing networks where $d^\prime < d$ are called depth separations. This line of research explores the theoretical benefits and representational advantages of deeper neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: Depth separations exist to provide a theoretical framework for understanding why deeper networks can be more efficient or powerful than shallower ones.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth separations compare the capabilities of networks with different depths $d$ and $d^\prime$.

concepts.title: Hebbian Learning

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Hebbian learning is a bottom-up approach where neurons strengthen connections based on simultaneous activity, summarized as "fire together, wire together."
concepts.content: Hebbian learning is a bottom-up alternative to backpropagation where neurons wire up based on the feedforward pattern of activity in the net. Unlike backpropagation, which is a top-down feedback-based algorithm that minimizes a loss function, Hebbian methods use Hebb's rule: "fire together, wire together." This means the weight of the connection between two neurons increases whenever they are active at the same time. Although this rule does not explicitly minimize a loss function, it can learn effective representations like infomax representations or act as memory banks. Hebbian learning is considered more biologically plausible than backpropagation because it is computed locally at each neuron rather than requiring global coordination.
concepts.motivation_md: Hebbian learning provides a biologically plausible model for how learning might occur in the brain through local interactions without global error signals.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a bottom-up learning approach based on local feedforward activity.

concepts.title: Hebb's Rule

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Hebb's rule is the principle that the connection weight between two neurons increases whenever they are active at the same time.
concepts.content: The canonical learning rule in Hebbian methods is Hebb's rule: "fire together, wire together." This rule states that we increase the weight of the connection between two neurons whenever the two neurons are active at the same time.
concepts.motivation_md: Hebb's rule provides the fundamental mechanism for local learning, explaining how neural connections strengthen through shared activity.
concepts.recap_md: - It is summarized by the phrase "fire together, wire together."

concepts.title: Infomax Representations

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Infomax representations are neural activations that capture as much information as possible about the input signal.
concepts.content: Hebb-like rules can learn infomax representations, which capture, in the neural activations, as much information as possible about the input signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Infomax representations aim to maximize the efficiency of information encoding within a neural network's activations.
concepts.recap_md: - These representations maximize the information captured from an input signal.

concepts.title: Tensors in Deep Learning

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: A tensor is a multidimensional array that serves as the primary data structure for representing all components of a deep learning model.
concepts.content: The main data structure in deep learning is the tensor, which is a multidimensional array. Everything in deep learning is represented as tensors, including inputs, activations, weights, and outputs. If data is not natively in this format, it must be converted into a tensor before being fed to a deep net. Most often, these tensors consist of real numbers in $\mathbb{R}$. For example, a dataset of images and labels can be viewed as two tensors: $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C_0 \times H \times W }$ (representing $N$ images with $C_0$ channels, height $H$, and width $W$) and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}$ (representing $K$-way classification labels).
concepts.motivation_md: Tensors provide a unified and efficient way to handle the high-dimensional data required for modern neural network computations.
concepts.recap_md: - Tensors are multidimensional arrays used for all data in deep learning.

concepts.title: Channels

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Channels refer to the number of neurons in a layer, analogous to the color channels of an input image.
concepts.content: The activations in a network are tensors. For MLP networks, activation tensors have shape $N \times C_{\ell}$, where $C_{\ell}$ is the number of neurons on layer $\ell$. These are sometimes called channels in analogy to the color channels of the input image. In other architectures like convolutional networks, activation layers have additional dimensions, such as shape $N \times C_{\ell} \times H_{\ell} \times W_{\ell}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of channels allows for a consistent description of feature dimensions across different types of neural network layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Channels represent the number of neurons or feature maps in a specific layer.

concepts.title: Batch Processing

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Batch processing is the technique of running multiple data points through a neural network simultaneously in parallel.
concepts.content: Normally, we don't process one image at a time through a neural net. Instead, we run a batch of images all at once, and they are processed in parallel. A batch sampled from the training data can be denoted as $\{\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{batch}}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}_{\texttt{batch}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\texttt{batch}}}$. When represented as a tensor, the batch has shape $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times C_0 \times H \times W}$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times K}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Batch processing is used to leverage the parallel computing power of modern hardware, significantly speeding up training and inference.
concepts.recap_md: - Batches allow for parallel processing of multiple data points.

concepts.title: Visualizing Tensors and Batches

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Visualizing tensors in 3D or higher dimensions helps conceptualize how batches of data are processed through neural network layers.
concepts.content: Visualizing the tensors associated with a batch of datapoints helps illustrate how they are processed by a network. For an MLP, the input is a set of vectors $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times C_0}$ and the output is $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times 1}$. (see figure: The tensors that represent one pass through the MLP in @fig-neural_nets-simple_MLP_network) While simple for 1D data, vision systems typically work with higher-dimensional tensors. Image data often uses four-dimensional tensors (batch $\times$ channels $\times$ height $\times$ width), while videos may use five or six dimensions. Visualizing these as 3D tensors can be a useful step toward imagining data processing as operating on $N$-dimensional tensors. (see figure: A 3D tensor that could represent an $C \times H \times W$ color image.)
concepts.motivation_md: Visualization aids in understanding the complex, multi-dimensional transformations that occur as data passes through a deep learning model.
concepts.recap_md: - Tensors for images are typically 4D, while videos can be 5D or 6D.

concepts.title: Image
concepts.one_liner: An image is a two-dimensional array of values $\boldsymbol\ell\in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$ representing intensity levels.
concepts.motivation_md: To process images computationally, we must represent visual information as a structured mathematical object. Treating an image as a matrix of intensity values allows us to apply linear algebra and signal processing techniques to visual data.
concepts.recap_md: - An image is mathematically defined as a 2D array $\boldsymbol\ell\in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$.

concepts.title: Pixel Indexing
concepts.one_liner: Pixel location is denoted by $\ell[n, m]$, where $n$ and $m$ are horizontal and vertical indices representing intensity at that location.
concepts.content: When we want to make explicit the location of a pixel we will write $\ell\left[n, m \right]$, where $n \in \left[0,N-1 \right]$ and $m \in \left[0,M-1 \right]$ are the indices for the horizontal and vertical dimensions, respectively. Each value in the array indicates the intensity of the image in that location. For color images we will have three channels, one for each color.
concepts.motivation_md: Indexing provides a standardized way to reference specific locations within an image, which is essential for operations like filtering, edge detection, or pixel-wise transformations.
concepts.recap_md: - Pixels are indexed as $\ell[n, m]$ for horizontal index $n$ and vertical index $m$.

concepts.title: Continuous Image Representation
concepts.one_liner: Working in the continuous domain as $\ell(x,y)$ simplifies the derivation of analytical solutions for discrete signals.
concepts.content: Although images are discrete signals, in some cases it is useful to work on the continuous domain as it simplifies the derivation of analytical solutions. This is useful for tasks such as using the image gradient in the continuous domain and then approximating it in the discrete space domain. In those cases we will write images as $\ell(x,y)$ and video sequences as $\ell(x,y,t)$.
concepts.motivation_md: While digital images are discrete, calculus is often easier to perform on continuous functions. Representing images continuously allows for the use of derivatives and integrals to derive theoretical models before discretizing them for implementation.
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous images are represented as $\ell(x,y)$ and video as $\ell(x,y,t)$.

concepts.title: Signal Length Classification
concepts.one_liner: Signals are classified as infinite length if they extend over the entire support or finite length if they are zero outside a compact interval.
concepts.content: Both continuous and discrete signals can be classified according to their extent. **Infinite length** signals are signals that extend over the entire support $\ell\left[n \right]$ for $n \in (-\infty, \infty)$. **Finite length** signals have non-zero values on a compact time interval and they are zero outside, i.e. $\ell\left[n \right] = 0$ for $n \notin S$ where $S$ is a finite length interval.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between finite and infinite signals is crucial for determining which mathematical tools (like specific transforms or summation methods) are applicable and for understanding the memory requirements of a signal.
concepts.recap_md: - Infinite length signals extend for $n \in (-\infty, \infty)$.

concepts.title: Periodic Signal
concepts.one_liner: A signal $\ell[n]$ is periodic if there exists a value $N$ such that $\ell[n] = \ell[n + kN]$ for all $n$ and $k$.
concepts.content: A signal $\ell\left[n \right]$ is **periodic** if there is a value $N$ such that $\ell\left[n \right] = \ell\left[n + k N\right]$ for all $n$ and $k$. A periodic signal is an infinite length signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Periodicity is a fundamental property in signal processing that allows us to represent complex signals as sums of simpler oscillating components, such as in Fourier analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - A signal is periodic if $\ell[n] = \ell[n + kN]$ for some period $N$.

concepts.title: DC Value
concepts.one_liner: The DC value is the mean value of a signal, representing the average intensity in the case of an image.
concepts.content: The mean value of a signal is often called the **DC value**. DC means **direct current** and it comes from electrical engineering. Although most signals have nothing to do with currents, the term DC is still commonly used. In the case of an image, the DC component is the average intensity of the image. For a finite signal of length $N$ (or a periodic signal), the **DC value** is $$\mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \ell\left[n\right]$$ If the signal is infinite, the average value is $$\mu = \lim_{N \xrightarrow{} \infty} \frac{1}{2N+1} \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \ell\left[n\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: The DC value represents the baseline or 'offset' of a signal. In image processing, it corresponds to the overall brightness, and separating it from the 'AC' (varying) components is a key step in many compression and enhancement algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - The DC value $\mu$ is the average intensity or mean value of a signal.

concepts.title: Energy of a Signal
concepts.one_liner: The energy of a signal is defined as the sum of its squared magnitude values.
concepts.content: The **energy of a signal** is defined as the sum of squared magnitude values: $$E = \sum_{n = -\infty}^{\infty} \left| \ell\left[n\right] \right| ^2$$ Signal energy and general energy are equivalent up to a normalization constant. For instance, the energy dissipated by a resistance $R$ with voltage $v(t)$ is \begin{equation} E = \frac{1}{R} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} v(t) ^2 dt \end{equation} Signals are further classified as **finite energy** and **infinite energy** signals. Finite length signals are finite energy and periodic signals are infinite energy signals when measuring the energy in the whole time axis.
concepts.motivation_md: Energy provides a measure of the 'strength' or 'size' of a signal. It is a critical concept for understanding signal stability, noise levels, and the physical constraints of transmitting or storing data.
concepts.recap_md: - Signal energy $E$ is the sum of squared magnitudes $\sum |\ell[n]|^2$.

concepts.title: Squared Euclidean Distance for Signals
concepts.one_liner: The squared Euclidean distance (L2 norm) is used to compare two signals by summing the squared differences of their values.
concepts.content: If we want to compare two signals, we can use the squared Euclidean distance (squared L2 norm) between them: $$D^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \left| \ell_1 \left[n\right] - \ell_2 \left[n\right] \right| ^2$$ However, the euclidean distance (L2) is a poor metric when we are interested in comparing the content of the two images and building better metrics is an important area of research. Sometimes, the metric is L2 but in a different representation space than pixel values.
concepts.motivation_md: Quantifying the difference between two signals is necessary for tasks like image compression, pattern recognition, and quality assessment. While L2 is mathematically simple, it doesn't always align with human perception of similarity.
concepts.recap_md: - Squared Euclidean distance $D^2$ measures the average squared difference between two signals.

concepts.title: Decision Boundary

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A decision boundary is a line or surface that separates data labeled with different classes in a classification problem.
concepts.content:
In the optimization process of a perceptron, the decision boundary is shifted and rotated until a line is found that separates data labeled as $y = 0$ from data labeled as $y = 1$.

(see figure: Different possible decision surfaces of a perceptron.)
concepts.motivation_md: To solve classification problems, we need a geometric way to partition the input space so that different regions correspond to different predicted labels.
concepts.recap_md: - The decision boundary is the line or surface that separates different classes in the data.

concepts.title: Perceptron Learning Algorithm

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: The perceptron learning algorithm is a specific optimizer tailored to the structure of the original perceptron to find a separating line between classes.
concepts.content: The original perceptron paper proposed the "perceptron learning algorithm," an optimizer tailored to the specific structure of the perceptron. Older papers on neural nets are full of specific learning rules for specific architectures, such as the delta rule or the Rescorla-Wagner model. Nowadays, these special-purpose algorithms are rarely used. Instead, general-purpose optimizers like gradient descent (for differentiable objectives) or zeroth-order methods (for nondifferentiable objectives) are preferred. For the perceptron objective, because it has a nondifferentiable threshold function, a zeroth order optimizer would be used instead of backpropagation.
concepts.motivation_md: Early neural networks required specialized rules to adjust weights; understanding these helps contextualize the shift toward modern general-purpose optimization like backpropagation.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a specialized optimization rule designed for the original perceptron architecture.

concepts.title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
concepts.one_liner: A multilayer perceptron (MLP) is a network of stacked layers consisting of linear transformations followed by pointwise nonlinear activation functions.
concepts.content:
Perceptrons can solve linearly separable binary classification problems, but they are otherwise limited, such as only producing a single output. Multiple outputs can be achieved by adding edges that fan out after the perceptron.

(see figure: Multiple outputs fan out from a neuron.)

This network maps an input layer of data $\mathbf{x}$ to a layer of outputs $\mathbf{y}$. The neurons in between inputs and outputs are called hidden units. A stack of many hidden units is called a multilayer perceptron (MLP).

(see figure: Mutilayer perceptron.)

Because this network has multiple layers of neurons, and because each neuron in this net acts as a perceptron, we call it a multilayer perceptron (MLP). The equation for this MLP is:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{z} &= \mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1 &\triangleleft \quad \text{linear layer}\\
    \mathbf{h} &= g(\mathbf{z}) &\triangleleft \quad \text{activation function}\\
    \mathbf{y} &= \mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{b}_2 &\triangleleft \quad \text{linear layer}
\end{aligned}$$

In general, MLPs can be constructed with any number of layers following this pattern: linear layer, activation function, linear layer, activation function, and so on. The activation function $g$ can be any pointwise nonlinearity, mapping $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. This sequence is the prototypical motif in almost all neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: Single perceptrons are limited to linearly separable problems; MLPs overcome this by stacking layers, allowing the network to learn complex, non-linear mappings and multiple outputs.
concepts.recap_md: - MLPs consist of alternating linear layers and pointwise nonlinear activation functions.

concepts.title: Hidden Units
concepts.one_liner: Hidden units are the neurons located between the input and output layers of a neural network.
concepts.content: The neurons in between inputs and outputs are called hidden units. For example, $z$ is a hidden unit and $h$ is a hidden unit, where $h = g(z)$ and $g(\cdot)$ is an activation function.
concepts.motivation_md: Hidden units allow a network to create intermediate representations of data, which is essential for learning complex patterns that aren't visible in the raw input.
concepts.recap_md: - Hidden units are internal neurons that are neither raw inputs nor final outputs.

concepts.title: Pointwise Nonlinearity
concepts.one_liner: A pointwise nonlinearity is an activation function applied independently to each element of a vector.
concepts.content: The activation function $g$ can be any pointwise nonlinearity, that is, $g(\mathbf{h}) = [\tilde{g}(h_1), \ldots, \tilde{g}(h_N)]$ where $\tilde{g}$ is any nonlinear function that maps $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Without nonlinearity, a stack of linear layers would just be another linear layer; pointwise nonlinearities allow neural networks to approximate complex, non-linear functions.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a function applied to each component of a vector individually.

concepts.title: Neural Activations
concepts.one_liner: Neural activations are the values that neurons take on as representations of the data being processed through the network.
concepts.content:
Activations are the values that the neurons take on, denoted as $[\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{h}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{z}_{L-1}, \mathbf{h}_{L-1}, \mathbf{y}]$. This term is used for both preactivation function neurons and postactivation function neurons. The activations are the neural representations of the data being processed. Often, we refer to all data and neural activations in a network, layer by layer, as a sequence $[\mathbf{x}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L]$, in which case $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the raw input data.

[FIGURE:e4b298598d24ed71 | A multilayer network is a sequence of transformations $f_1, \ldots, f_L$ that produce a series of activations $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.]
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between the data flowing through the net (activations) and the learned weights (parameters) is fundamental for understanding how information is represented and transformed.
concepts.recap_md: - Activations are the internal values or representations produced by neurons during processing.

concepts.title: Network Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Network parameters are the learnable weights and biases that define the transformations within a neural network.
concepts.content: Parameters are the weights and biases of the network. These are the variables being learned. Both activations and parameters are tensors of variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Parameters are the "memory" of the network; by adjusting them, the model learns to map specific inputs to desired outputs.
concepts.recap_md: - Parameters consist of the weights and biases that the optimization algorithm modifies.

concepts.title: Interchangeability of Activations and Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Activations and parameters are interchangeable in the sense that both act as inputs to a layer's function and can be varied to achieve an objective.
concepts.content: Each layer can be viewed as a function $\mathbf{x}_{l+1} = f_{l+1}(\mathbf{x}_{l}, \theta_{l+1})$ that takes the activations from the previous layer and the parameters of the current layer as input to produce the next layer's activations. Varying either the input activations or the input parameters will affect the output of the layer. From this perspective, anything we can do with parameters, we can do with activations instead, and vice versa. For example, while normally we learn the values of the parameters, we could instead hold the parameters fixed and learn the values of the activations that achieve some objective, which is the basis for methods like network prompting, adversarial attacks, and network visualization.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing that activations and parameters are both just inputs to a function allows for advanced techniques like "learning" the input (visualization) or "learning" prompts rather than weights.
concepts.recap_md: - Both activations and parameters serve as inputs to the function defining a network layer.

concepts.title: Mirror Padding
concepts.one_liner: Mirror padding reflects the valid image pixels over the boundary of valid output pixels.
concepts.content: Mirror padding is a technique where valid image pixels are reflected over the boundary of valid output pixels. This is the most common approach for extending signal boundaries and typically yields the best results.
concepts.motivation_md: When performing convolutions, boundary artifacts occur because the kernel extends beyond the image edges. Mirror padding solves this by creating a natural-looking extension based on the image's own content.
concepts.recap_md:
- Reflects existing pixels across the image boundary.
- Generally considered the most effective padding method for reducing artifacts.

concepts.title: Repeat Padding
concepts.one_liner: Repeat padding sets boundary values to that of the nearest output image pixel with valid mask inputs.
concepts.content: Repeat padding is a boundary extension method where the value of a pixel outside the valid range is set to the value of the nearest output image pixel that has valid mask inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: This method provides a simple way to handle boundaries in convolution by assuming the signal remains constant beyond its edges.
concepts.recap_md:
- Extends the image by duplicating the edge pixel values.
- Useful for simple boundary handling where complex reflection is not required.

concepts.title: Circular Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Circular convolution uses circular padding to convolve a finite length signal by treating it as an infinite periodic extension.
concepts.content: [FIGURE:adb812066d7186ad | A square diagram representing a circulant matrix structure. A thick black main diagonal is flanked by two red diagonals and two green diagonals. Small segments of the red and green diagonals wrap...] When convolving a finite length signal with a kernel, it can be convenient to extend the signal beyond its boundary to reduce boundary artifacts. This trick is also very useful analytically and leads to a special case: the circular convolution, which uses circular padding. The circular convolution of two signals, $h$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$, of length $N$ is defined as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n\right] = h \left[n\right] \circ_N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[(n-k)_N \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$$ In this formulation, the signal $h \left[ (n)_N \right]$ is the infinite periodic extension, with period $N$, of the finite length signal $h \left[n \right]$. The output of the circular convolution is a periodic signal with period $N$, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n \right] = \ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[(n)_N \right]$. The circular convolution has the same properties as standard convolution, such as being commutative.
concepts.motivation_md: Circular convolution is used to simplify mathematical analysis of discrete signals and to eliminate boundary artifacts by treating the signal as if it wraps around in a circle.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses circular padding to treat finite signals as periodic.
- Defined by the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h \left[(n-k)_N \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k \right]$.
- Results in a periodic output signal with the same period $N$.

concepts.title: Continuous Domain Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Continuous domain convolution replaces the discrete sum with an integral to combine two continuous signals.
concepts.content: The convolution in the continuous domain is defined in the same way as with discrete signals but replacing the sums by integrals. Given two continuous signals $h(t)$ and $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(t)$, the convolution operator is defined as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = h(t) \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$$ The properties of the continuous domain convolution are analogous to the properties of the discrete convolution, with the commutative, associative, and distributive relationships still holding.
concepts.motivation_md: To apply the concept of linear translation-invariant filtering to continuous-time signals, we must transition from discrete summations to continuous integrations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Defined by the integral $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau) \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\tau) d\tau$.
- Maintains standard algebraic properties like commutativity and associativity.
- Acts as the continuous-domain counterpart to discrete convolution.

concepts.title: Continuous Impulse (Dirac Delta Function)
concepts.one_liner: The Dirac delta function is a continuous impulse that is zero everywhere except at the origin, with an integral equal to one.
concepts.content: The impulse, $\delta (t)$, in the continuous domain is defined such that $\ell(t) \circ \delta(t) = \ell(t)$. The impulse is defined as being zero everywhere but at the origin, where it takes an infinitely high value so that its integral is equal to 1: $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t) dt = 1$$ The impulse function is also called the impulse distribution (as it is not a function in the strict sense) or the Dirac delta function. [FIGURE:3bb6012ff85cabfe | A graph of the Dirac delta function $\delta(t-a)$ on a coordinate system with horizontal axis $t$ and vertical axis $\delta(t-a)$. A single blue vertical arrow is positioned at $t=a$ on the...]
concepts.motivation_md: The Dirac delta function serves as the identity element for convolution in the continuous domain, allowing us to model instantaneous events or point sources.
concepts.recap_md:
- Defined by $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t) dt = 1$ and $\delta(t)=0$ for $t \neq 0$.
- Acts as the identity for continuous convolution: $\ell(t) \circ \delta(t) = \ell(t)$.
- Technically a distribution rather than a standard function.

concepts.title: Properties of the Dirac Delta Distribution
concepts.one_liner: The Dirac delta distribution possesses unique scaling, symmetry, and sampling properties that facilitate signal analysis.
concepts.content:
The impulse has several important properties:

- Scaling property: $\delta (at) = \delta (t) / |a|$
- Symmetry: $\delta (-t) = \delta (t)$
- Sampling property: $\ell(t) \delta (t-a) = \ell(a) \delta (t-a)$ where $a$ is a constant. From this, we have the following: $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell(t) \delta (t-a) dt = \ell(a)$$
- As in the discrete case, the continuous impulse is also the identity for the convolution: $\ell(t) \circ \delta (t) = \ell(t)$.
concepts.motivation_md: These properties allow mathematicians and engineers to extract specific values from signals (sampling) and simplify complex integrals involving impulses.
concepts.recap_md:
- The sampling property extracts the value of a function at a specific point: $\int \ell(t) \delta (t-a) dt = \ell(a)$.
- It is symmetric ($\delta(-t) = \delta(t)$) and scales inversely with the absolute value of $a$.
- It serves as the identity element for continuous convolution.

concepts.title: Cross-Correlation
concepts.one_liner: Cross-correlation is a translation-invariant operator used to locate templates in an image without inverting the kernel.
concepts.content: The cross-correlation operator provides a simple technique to locate a template in an image and is closely related to convolution. The cross-correlation operator (denoted by $\star$) between the image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and the kernel $h$ is written as follows: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\star h = \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n+k,m+l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$ where the sum is performed over the support of the filter $h$, assumed to be a square $(-N,N)\times(-N,N)$. In the convolution, the kernel is inverted left-right and up-down, while in the cross-correlation it is not. For comparison, the convolution between image $\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ and kernel $h$ is: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = \ell_{\texttt{in}}\circ h = \sum_{k,l=-N}^N \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-k,m-l \right] h \left[k,l \right]$$.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-correlation is primarily used for template matching, as it measures the similarity between a kernel and different parts of an image without the need for the kernel flipping required by convolution.
concepts.recap_md:
- Used to locate templates within a larger image.
- Unlike convolution, the kernel $h$ is not inverted (flipped) during the operation.
- Mathematically defined as $\sum \ell_{\texttt{in}}[n+k, m+l] h[k, l]$.

concepts.title: Template Matching
concepts.one_liner: Template matching is a technique used to find a small image patch within a larger image.
concepts.content: The goal of template matching is to find a small image patch within a larger image. (see figure: Fig (a) Template. (b) Input image. (c) Correlation between input (b) and template (a). (d) Normalized correlation. e) Locations with cross-correlation above 75 percent of its maximum value.) For example, template matching can be used to detect all occurrences of a specific letter within an image of text by calculating the correlation between the input and the template.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique is essential for object detection and pattern recognition, allowing a system to identify specific known shapes or characters within a complex scene.
concepts.recap_md:
- Identifies the location of a small template patch in a larger image.
- Often utilizes cross-correlation or normalized correlation to find matches.
- Can be used for tasks like character recognition in text images.

concepts.title: Cosine Series
concepts.one_liner: Fourier series can be expressed as sums of cosine functions, representing a function through its harmonic components.
concepts.content:
Fourier series can be written as sums of different sets of harmonic functions. For instance, using cosine functions we can describe the ramp function as:
$$\frac{1}{2} t =  \frac{\pi}{4}  - \frac{2}{\pi} \cos (t) - \frac{2}{3^2 \pi}  \cos (3t) - \frac{2}{5^2 \pi}  \cos (5t) - ...$$
The cosine and sine series of the same function are only equal in the interval $t \in (0, \pi)$, and result in different periodic extensions outside that interval.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing functions using only cosine terms is useful for analyzing signals with even symmetry or for creating specific periodic extensions of a function defined on a finite interval.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fourier series can be constructed using a set of harmonic cosine functions.
- The cosine series and sine series of a function generally differ outside the interval $(0, \pi)$.

concepts.title: Continuous Time Sine Wave
concepts.one_liner: The continuous time sine wave is defined by its amplitude, frequency, and phase.
concepts.content:
The **continuous time sine wave** is
$$s\left(t\right) = A \sin\left(w ~t - \theta \right)$$
where $A$ is the **amplitude**, $w$ is the **frequency**, and $\theta$ is the **phase**. The wave signal is periodic with a period $T=2 \pi / w$.

[FIGURE:61cdacec6e8491fb | A graph of a continuous sine wave $s(t)$ plotted against time $t$. A horizontal double-headed arrow between two consecutive peaks is labeled 'Period', and a vertical double-headed arrow from the...]
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous sine waves are the fundamental building blocks of signal processing and harmonic analysis, representing pure oscillations in physical systems.
concepts.recap_md:
- The standard form is $s(t) = A \sin(wt - \theta)$.
- The period $T$ is determined by the frequency $w$ as $T = 2\pi/w$.

concepts.title: Discrete Time Sine Wave
concepts.one_liner: A discrete time sine wave is a sampled version of a sinusoid that is periodic only for specific rational frequencies.
concepts.content:
In discrete time, the **discrete time sine wave** is defined as:
$$s\left[n\right] = A \sin\left(w ~n  - \theta \right)$$
Note that the discrete sine wave will not be periodic for any arbitrary value of $w$. A discrete signal $\ell\left[n\right]$ is periodic if there exists $T \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n+mT\right]$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$. For the discrete sine (and cosine) wave to be periodic, the frequency must be $w = 2 \pi K / N$ for $K,N \in \mathbb{N}$. If $K/N$ is an irreducible fraction, then the period of the wave will be $T = N$ samples.

Although $\theta$ can have any value, we often consider $\theta=0$ and $\theta = \pi/2$, which correspond to the sine and cosine waves, respectively. To make the periodicity explicit, we use the form:
$$s_k\left[n\right] = \sin\left( \frac{2 \pi}{N} \, k \, n \right)$$
$$c_k\left[n\right] = \cos\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N} \,k\,n \right)$$
This notation is useful for signals with period $N$ or finite support of length $N$ where $n \in [0, N-1]$. Here, $k \in [1, N/2]$ denotes the frequency. Note that if $k=0$, then $s[n] = 0$ and $c[n]=1$. Also, $c_{N-k} = c_k$ and $s_{N-k} = -s_k$, meaning frequencies $k > N/2$ mirror those in the interval $[1, N/2]$.

(see figure: Sine and cosine waves with $A=1$ and $N=20$. Each row corresponds to $k=1$, $k=2$ and $k=3$. Note that for $k=3$ the waves oscillates three times in the interval $\left[0,N-1\right)$, but the samples in each oscillation are not identical, and it is only truly periodic once every $N$ samples. This is because $3/20$ is an irreducible fraction.]
concepts.motivation_md: Discrete sine waves are essential for digital signal processing, but unlike continuous waves, they require specific frequency conditions to remain periodic.
concepts.recap_md:
- Periodicity requires the frequency $w$ to be a rational multiple of $2\pi$.
- The frequency $k$ represents the number of cycles within a support region of length $N$.

concepts.title: Sines and Cosines in 2D
concepts.one_liner: Two-dimensional discrete sine and cosine waves are defined by spatial frequencies that determine the rate of change along two dimensions.
concepts.content:
The analysis of discrete waves can be extended to two dimensions (2D). In 2D, the discrete sine and cosine waves are defined as:
$$s_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = A \sin \left(2 \pi \left( \frac{u\,n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
$$c_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = A \cos \left(2 \pi \left( \frac{u\,n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
where $A$ is the amplitude and $u$ and $v$ are the two spatial frequencies. These frequencies define how fast or slow the waves change along the spatial dimensions $n$ and $m$.

(see figure: 2D sine waves with $N=M=20$. The frequency values are (a) $u=2, v=0$; (b) $u=3, v=1$; (c) $u=7,v=-5$.)
concepts.motivation_md: 2D sinusoids are the basis for image processing and spatial frequency analysis, allowing images to be decomposed into directional patterns.
concepts.recap_md:
- 2D waves use two spatial frequencies, $u$ and $v$, to define oscillations across a grid.
- The indices $n$ and $m$ represent spatial coordinates in the discrete 2D plane.

concepts.title: Complex Exponential Wave
concepts.one_liner: The complex exponential wave is a fundamental signal relating real and imaginary components through Euler's formula.
concepts.content:
The complex exponential wave is defined as:
$$e_{u}\left[n\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j   \frac{u\, n}{N}   \right)$$
Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula: $\exp(ja) = \cos(a) + j\sin(a)$. As $n$ goes from 0 to $N-1$, the function rotates along the complex circle of unit magnitude. In a plot of the real component ($x$-axis) versus the imaginary component ($y$-axis), this rotation becomes visible.

(see figure: Complex exponential wave with (a) $N=40$, $k=1$, $A=1$; and (b) $N=40$, $k=3$, $A=1$. The red and green curves show the real and imaginary waves. The black line is the complex exponential. The dots...)
concepts.motivation_md: Complex exponentials simplify the mathematics of waves and oscillations, turning trigonometric identities into algebraic operations with exponents.
concepts.recap_md:
- Defined as $e_u[n] = \exp(2\pi j u n / N)$.
- Represents a rotation around the unit circle in the complex plane as $n$ increases.

concepts.title: Euler's Formula
concepts.one_liner: Euler's formula relates complex exponentials to trigonometric functions: $\exp(ja) = \cos(a) + j\sin(a)$.
concepts.content:
Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula:
$$\exp \left(j a\right) = \cos (a) + j \sin (a)$$ 
This formula provides the link between circular motion in the complex plane and oscillatory trigonometric functions.
concepts.motivation_md: Euler's formula is the bridge between trigonometry and complex analysis, allowing for much easier manipulation of periodic signals.
concepts.recap_md:
- Connects complex exponentials to sine and cosine functions.
- Fundamental for representing signals in the frequency domain.

concepts.title: Separability of Complex Exponentials
concepts.one_liner: Two-dimensional complex exponentials are separable, meaning they can be expressed as the product of two one-dimensional signals.
concepts.content:
In 2D, the complex exponential wave is defined as:
$$e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j \left(  \frac{u\, n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
where $u$ and $v$ are the two spatial frequencies. A key property is that complex exponentials in 2D are separable. This means they can be written as the product of two 1D signals:
$$e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right]   = e_{u}\left[n\right] e_{v}\left[m\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Separability allows complex 2D operations, like the Fourier Transform, to be computed as a series of simpler 1D operations, greatly improving computational efficiency.
concepts.recap_md:
- A 2D complex exponential is the product of a horizontal and a vertical 1D complex exponential.
- This property simplifies the analysis and processing of 2D signals like images.

concepts.title: Orthogonality of Complex Exponentials
concepts.one_liner: Complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis, allowing any finite discrete signal to be decomposed into a linear combination of them.
concepts.content:
A remarkable property is that the complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length. For images of size $N \times M$, the inner product is given by:
$$\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] e^*_{u',v'}\left[n,m\right] = MN \delta \left[u-u'\right]\delta \left[v-v'\right]$$
Therefore, any finite length discrete image can be decomposed as a linear combination of complex exponentials.
concepts.motivation_md: Orthogonality ensures that each frequency component in a signal can be analyzed independently, which is the theoretical foundation of the Fourier Transform.
concepts.recap_md:
- Complex exponentials serve as an orthogonal basis for finite discrete signals.
- Any discrete image can be represented as a sum of these basis functions.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of the Delta Distribution
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of the delta function $\delta \left[n,m \right]$ is equal to 1.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform of the delta function $\delta \left[n,m \right]$ is $$\mathcal{F} \left\{ \delta \left[n,m \right] \right\} = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \delta \left[n,m \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} = 1$$ where the Fourier transform of the delta signal is 1: $$\delta \left[n,m \right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 1$$ If we think in terms of the inverse Fourier transform, this means that if we sum all the complex exponentials with a coefficient of 1, then all the values will cancel but the one at the origin, which results in a delta function: $$\delta \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=-N/2}^{N/2} \sum_{v=-M/2}^{M/2} \exp{ \left(2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }$$
concepts.motivation_md: The delta function is the simplest possible signal in the spatial domain, representing a single point. Understanding its Fourier transform—which is a constant—establishes the fundamental relationship between localization in space and spread in frequency.
concepts.recap_md: - The Fourier transform of a discrete delta function $\delta[n,m]$ is a constant value of 1.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of Cosine and Sine Waves
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transforms of cosine and sine waves result in pairs of shifted delta functions in the frequency domain.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform of the cosine wave, $\cos{ \left( 2\pi \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right) }$, is: $$\begin{aligned} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \cos{ \left( 2\pi \left( \frac{u_0 \, n}{N} + \frac{v_0 \, m}{M} \right) \right) } \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} = \\ =\frac{1}{2} \left( \delta \left[u-u_0, v-v_0 \right] +  \delta \left[u+u_0, v+v_0 \right] \right) \end{aligned}$$ This can be proven using Euler's equation and the orthogonality between complex exponentials. This results in the Fourier transform relationship: $$\cos{ \left( 2\pi \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right) } \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \frac{1}{2} \left( \delta \left[u-u_0, v-v_0 \right] +  \delta \left[u+u_0, v+v_0 \right] \right)$$ And for the sine wave, $\sin{ \left( 2\pi \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0 m}{M} \right) \right) }$, we have a similar relationship: $$\sin{ \left( 2\pi \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0 m}{M} \right) \right) } \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \frac{1}{2j} \left( \delta \left[u-u_0, v-v_0 \right] - \delta \left[u+u_0, v+v_0 \right]\right)$$ (see figure: Some 2D Fourier transform pairs. Images are $64 \times 64$ pixels. The waves are cosine with frequencies $(1,2)$, $(5,0)$, $(10,7)$, $(11,-15)$. The last two examples show the sum of two waves and...)
concepts.motivation_md: Cosine and sine waves are the building blocks of the Fourier transform. Knowing their transforms allows us to identify specific frequency components and orientations in 2D signals like images.
concepts.recap_md: - A cosine wave transforms into two real delta functions at $\pm(u_0, v_0)$.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of Real and Even Signals
concepts.one_liner: Real and even input signals result in Fourier transforms that are also real and even.
concepts.content: From the Fourier transform equation, one can show that real and even input signals transform to real and even outputs. For signals symmetric about the spatial origin, the imaginary component of the Fourier transform happens to be zero. In such cases, the magnitude of the Fourier transform is simply the absolute value of the real component. Additionally, if an image is separable (it can be written as the product of two 1D signals), its DFT is also the product of 1D DFTs.
concepts.motivation_md: Symmetry in the spatial domain simplifies calculations in the frequency domain. Recognizing real and even signals allows us to ignore the imaginary part of the transform, making analysis more efficient.
concepts.recap_md: - Real and even signals produce real and even Fourier transforms.

concepts.title: 2D Box Function and its DFT
concepts.one_liner: The 2D DFT of a box function is the product of two 1D DFTs due to its separability.
concepts.content: A 2D box is a separable function and can be written as the product of two box functions: $\text{box}_{L_n, L_m} \left[n,m\right] = \text{box}_{L_n} \left[n\right] \text{box}_{L_m}\left[m\right]$. Because of this property, the DFT is also the product of the two 1D DFTs: $$\text{Box}_{L_n, L_m} \left[ u,v \right] = \text{Box}_{L_n} \left[ u\right] \text{Box}_{L_m} \left[ v\right].$$ As the support of the image in one domain gets larger, the magnitude in the other domain becomes more localized.
concepts.motivation_md: The 2D box function is a standard model for rectangular apertures or simple filters. Leveraging its separability simplifies the computation of its 2D Fourier transform into two 1D problems.
concepts.recap_md: - A 2D box function is separable into the product of two 1D box functions.

concepts.title: Box Function Definition
concepts.one_liner: The box function is defined as 1 inside a specific interval $[-L, L]$ and 0 elsewhere.
concepts.content: The box function is defined as follows: $$\text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] = \begin{cases} 1 & \quad \text{if } -L \leq n \leq L \\ 0 & \quad \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$ The box function takes values of 1 inside the interval $\left[ -L,L \right]$ and it is 0 outside. The duration of the box is $2L+1$. It is useful to think of the box function as a finite length signal of length $N$ and to visualize its periodic extension outside of that interval. [FIGURE:e9ca46281c35c8d1 | Box function for $L=5$ and $N=32$.]
concepts.motivation_md: The box function (or rectangular pulse) is the simplest windowing function. It is used to model finite-duration signals and serves as a fundamental building block for more complex signal processing operations.
concepts.recap_md: - The box function has a value of 1 for $n \in [-L, L]$ and 0 otherwise.

concepts.title: Derivation of the DFT of the Box Function
concepts.one_liner: The DFT of a box function is derived using the geometric series formula to arrive at a ratio of sine functions.
concepts.content: To compute the DFT of the finite length box function with length $N$, we use the DFT definition and the periodic nature of the terms: $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F} \left\{ \text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] \right\} &= \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \, \text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)} \\ &= \sum_{n=-L}^{L} \, \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)} \end{aligned}$$ Using the equation for the sum of a geometric series $\sum_{n=-L}^{L} a^n = \frac{a^{-(2L+1)/2}-a^{(2L+1)/2}}{a^{-1/2}-a^{1/2}}$ with $a = \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u}{N} \right)}$, we can write the sum as: $$\begin{aligned} \sum_{n=-L}^{L} \, \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)} &= \frac{\exp{ \left( \pi j \frac{u(2L+1)}{N} \right)} - \exp{ \left( -\pi j \frac{u(2L+1)}{N} \right)}} {\exp{ \left( \pi j \frac{u}{N} \right)} - \exp{ \left( - \pi j \frac{u}{N} \right)} } \\ &= \frac{\sin \left( \pi u(2L+1)/N \right)}{\sin \left( \pi u/N \right)} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Deriving the DFT of the box function provides a concrete example of how to apply the geometric series formula and Euler's identities to solve discrete transforms.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivation relies on the geometric series sum formula.

concepts.title: Discrete Sinc Function
concepts.one_liner: The discrete sinc function is a symmetrical periodic function defined as a ratio of sines.
concepts.content: The discrete sinc function **sincd** is defined as follows: $$ \text{sincd}(x;a) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{a \sin (\pi x/a)} $$ where $a$ is a constant. This is a symmetrical periodic function with a maximum value of 1.
concepts.motivation_md: The discrete sinc function is the natural counterpart to the continuous sinc function in discrete-time signal processing, appearing whenever a signal is truncated or windowed by a box function.
concepts.recap_md: - The discrete sinc is defined as $\text{sincd}(x;a) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{a \sin (\pi x/a)}$.

concepts.title: DFT of the Box Function
concepts.one_liner: The DFT of the box function is the discrete sinc function.
concepts.content: The DFT of the box function is the discrete sinc function: $$\text{box}_{L} \left[n \right]\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \frac{\sin \pi u (2L+1)/N}{\sin \pi u/N} $$ We denote the DFT of the box function, $\text{box}_{L} \left[n \right]$, by capitalizing the first letter: $\text{Box}_{L} \left[u \right]$. This function has its maximum value at $u=0$ and is a symmetric real function. (see figure: DFT of the box filter with $L=5$, and $N=32$.) One period of the DFT is contained in the interval $\left[ -16, 15 \right]$ and the rest is a periodic extension.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the result of the box function's DFT is essential for understanding spectral leakage and the frequency response of simple moving average filters.
concepts.recap_md: - The DFT of a box function is a real, symmetric discrete sinc function.

concepts.title: Shift Property (Translation in Space)
concepts.one_liner: Translating a signal in the spatial domain results in multiplying its Fourier transform by a complex exponential.
concepts.content:
A shift corresponds to a translation in space. Translating a signal $\ell[n,m]$ in the spatial domain by $(n_0, m_0)$ pixels results in multiplying its Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$ by a complex exponential. Specifically, for an image with period $N,M$, the Fourier transform of the displaced image $\ell[n-n_0,m-m_0]$ is given by:

$$\begin{split} \mathcal{F} \{ \ell[n-n_0,m-m_0] \} &= \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell[n-n_0,m-m_0] \exp{ \left( -2
\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} \\ &= \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell[n,m] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, (n+n_0)}{N} + \frac{v\, (m+m_0)}{M} \right) \right)} \\ &= \mathscr{L}[u,v] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)} \end{split}$$

Because the signal $\ell$ and the complex exponentials have period $N,M$, the sum indices can be changed over any range of size $N \times M$ samples. In practice, this property is strictly true only for a circular shift, where pixels disappearing on one boundary reappear on the opposite side. For standard translations, such as those caused by camera motion, boundary artifacts and new pixels appearing mean the shift property is only an approximation.
concepts.motivation_md: The shift property allows us to understand how spatial movement affects the frequency domain. It is fundamental for tasks like motion estimation, image registration, and understanding the phase information of the Fourier transform.
concepts.recap_md:
- A spatial translation by $(n_0, m_0)$ results in a phase shift in the frequency domain.
- The Fourier transform is multiplied by $\exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)}$.

concepts.title: Circular Shift and Boundary Artifacts
concepts.one_liner: The DFT shift property is strictly true only for circular shifts, otherwise boundary artifacts make it an approximation.
concepts.content: In practice, applying a translation to an image results in boundary artifacts. The DFT shift property is generally only true if a circular shift is applied, meaning pixels that disappear on one boundary due to translation reappear on the opposite side. This requirement is a consequence of the periodic structure of the signal $\ell$ assumed by the DFT. In real-world scenarios, such as camera motion, translations are not circular and new pixels appear at the boundaries; therefore, the shift property serves only as an approximation.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the difference between theoretical circular shifts and real-world translations is crucial for correctly applying Fourier methods to finite digital images.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DFT assumes a periodic signal structure, necessitating circular shifts for exact property adherence.
- Real-world translations introduce boundary artifacts that make the shift property an approximation.

concepts.title: Global Displacement Estimation using DFT
concepts.one_liner: Global displacement between two images can be estimated by locating the maximum in the Fourier domain, though it lacks robustness.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Translation in space. Image (c) corresponds to image (a) after a translation of 16 pixels to the right and four pixels down. Images (b) and (d) show the real parts of their corresponding DFTs (with...)

Locating the maximum on (see figure: Translation in space. Image (c) corresponds to image (a) after a translation of 16 pixels to the right and four pixels down. Images (b) and (d) show the real parts of their corresponding DFTs (with...) (f) can be used to estimate the displacement between two images when the translation corresponds to a global translation. However, this method is not very robust and it is rarely used in practice.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explores how the shift property can theoretically be used to detect motion or alignment between two frames.
concepts.recap_md:
- Global translation can be estimated by finding the maximum in a specific Fourier-based representation.
- The method is generally considered non-robust for practical applications.

concepts.title: Modulation Property (Translation in Frequency)
concepts.one_liner: Multiplying an image by a complex exponential translates its Fourier transform, a process known as modulation.
concepts.content:
If an image is multiplied by a complex exponential, its Fourier transform is translated. This is known as the modulation property:

$$\ell[n,m] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)} \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}[u-u_0,v-v_0]$$

This relationship can be proven using the dual convolution property. Because the resulting signal is not real, its Fourier Transform does not exhibit symmetries around $u,v=0$. A related relationship involving a cosine wave is:

$$\ell[n,m] \cos{ \left( 2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)} \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}[u-u_0,v-v_0] + \mathscr{L}[u+u_0,v+v_0]$$

Multiplying a signal by a wave is called signal modulation, a fundamental operation in communications and image analysis. (see figure: Modulation in space. Multiplying an image by a cosine wave results in a new image with a Fourier transform with two copies of the Fourier transform of the original image. Only the magnitude of the...) shows an example of modulating an image by a diagonal wave, resulting in two copies of the original Fourier transform.
concepts.motivation_md: Modulation is essential for shifting signal information to different frequency bands, which is a cornerstone of communication systems and certain image processing filters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multiplying by a complex exponential results in a single translation in the frequency domain.
- Multiplying by a cosine wave creates two shifted copies of the Fourier transform.
- Modulation is a dual to the spatial shift property.

concepts.title: Duality of Shift and Modulation
concepts.one_liner: A shift in one domain is equivalent to modulation in the other domain.
concepts.content: A shift and a modulation are equivalent operations in different domains. Specifically, a shift in the spatial domain corresponds to a modulation in the frequency domain, while a shift in the frequency domain corresponds to a modulation in the spatial domain.
concepts.motivation_md: This duality simplifies the analysis of signals by allowing us to choose the domain where an operation is easiest to compute or visualize.
concepts.recap_md:
- Spatial shift equals frequency modulation.
- Frequency shift equals spatial modulation.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform for Continuous Signals
concepts.one_liner: The continuous Fourier transform is used for infinite length signals and operations like derivatives that are best defined in the continuous domain.
concepts.content:
The continuous domain is convenient for functions and operations not defined in the discrete domain, such as the derivative operator or the Gaussian distribution. For infinite length signals in the continuous domain, the Fourier transform is defined as:

$$\mathscr{L}(w) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell(t) \exp{ \left( - j w t \right)} \, dt$$

where $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a continuous function of frequency $w$ (in radians). The inverse Fourier transform is given by:

$$\ell(t) = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L}(w) \exp{ \left( j w t \right) } \, dw$$

Most properties of the DFT apply to the continuous domain by replacing sums with integrals.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous formulations are often mathematically more elegant and allow for the use of calculus tools like derivatives that are only approximated in discrete space.
concepts.recap_md:
- The continuous Fourier transform uses integrals over an infinite domain.
- It is particularly useful for operations like differentiation and continuous distributions like the Gaussian.
- Frequency $w$ is a continuous variable in radians.

concepts.title: Continuous Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Convolution between two continuous signals is defined by an integral across the spatial variables.
concepts.content:
The convolution between two continuous signals is defined as:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}(t) = \ell_1 \circ \ell_2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell_1 (t-t') \ell_2(t') \, d t'$$
This definition can be extended to 2D by using double integrals across spatial variables $x$ and $y$. While images and filters are typically discrete in practice, it is often convenient to treat them as continuous signals for theoretical formulation.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous convolution provides the mathematical foundation for filtering and system analysis before discretization occurs.
concepts.recap_md:
- Continuous convolution is defined by an integral of the product of two functions, one of which is shifted.
- The concept extends to 2D for image processing using double integrals.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform for Infinite Length Discrete Signals
aliases: Fourier Transform for Infinite Length Discrete Signals
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform for infinite length discrete signals results in a continuous, periodic frequency representation.
concepts.content:
For discrete signals with infinite length, the Fourier transform sum becomes infinite. By replacing $w = 2 \pi u / N$, the transform is written as:
$$\mathscr{L}(w) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell[n] \exp{(- j w n)}$$
In this case, the frequency $w$ is a continuous variable, and the Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a periodic function with period $2 \pi$. The inverse Fourier transform is:
$$\ell[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{2 \pi} \mathscr{L}(w) \exp{(j w n)} d w$$
where the integration is performed over a single period.
concepts.motivation_md: This tool bridges the gap between discrete sequences and continuous frequency analysis, useful for analyzing systems with infinite impulse responses.
concepts.recap_md:
- The transform for infinite discrete signals results in a continuous and $2\pi$-periodic frequency domain.
- The inverse transform requires integration over only one period of the frequency spectrum.

concepts.title: Polar Form of the Fourier Transform

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of an image can be expressed in polar form as the product of an amplitude component and an exponential phase component.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform of an image can be written in polar form:
$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  = A \left[u,v \right] \, \exp{\left( j\, \theta\left[u,v \right]  \right)}$$
where $A \left[u,v \right] = \left| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  \right|$ and $\theta \left[u,v \right] = \angle  \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Decomposing the Fourier transform into polar form allows for the separate analysis of magnitude (intensity/strength) and phase (spatial location), which is essential for understanding image structure and processing.
concepts.recap_md: - The polar form is given by $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = A \left[u,v \right] e^{j\theta[u,v]}$.

concepts.title: Fourier Amplitude

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier amplitude is the magnitude of the Fourier transform at each frequency coordinate.
concepts.content: $A \left[u,v \right] = \left| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  \right|$
concepts.motivation_md: The amplitude represents the strength or weight of each complex exponential (sinusoid) present in the signal.
concepts.recap_md: - $A[u,v]$ is defined as the absolute value of the Fourier transform.

concepts.title: Fourier Phase

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier phase represents the angular component of the Fourier transform, determining the alignment of sinusoids.
concepts.content: $\theta \left[u,v \right] = \angle  \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: The phase determines the spatial location of features; it specifies how sinusoids must line up to create observed contours and edges.
concepts.recap_md: - $\theta[u,v]$ is the angle or argument of the complex Fourier transform.

concepts.title: Interpretation of Fourier Amplitude and Phase

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: Location information typically resides in the phase, while intensity scaling and signal strength reside in the magnitude.
concepts.content:
Decomposing the Fourier transform of a signal into its amplitude and phase is a useful image representation. In terms of the inverse Fourier transform, $A \left[u,v \right]$ gives the strength of the weight for each complex exponential, while the phase $\theta \left[u,v \right]$ translates the complex exponential. 

The phase carries information about where image contours are by specifying how the phases of the sinusoids must line up to create observed edges. Translating an image in space only modifies the phase of its Fourier transform. In short, location information goes into the phase while intensity scaling goes into the magnitude.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the distinct roles of amplitude and phase helps in tasks like image registration, edge detection, and understanding how spatial shifts affect frequency data.
concepts.recap_md: - Amplitude $A[u,v]$ represents the strength of frequency components.

concepts.title: Phase Dominance in Natural Images

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: In many natural images, the phase component dominates the visual appearance and determines the location of edges and colors.
concepts.content:
The appearance of natural images is often dominated by the phase of their Fourier transform. This is demonstrated by experiments swapping the phases and amplitudes of two different images.

(see figure: Swapping the amplitude and the phase of the Fourier Transform of two images. Each color channel is processed in the same way.)

When an image is reconstructed using the amplitude of one image and the phase of another, the resulting image's appearance mostly resembles the source of the phase. For example, an image built with the phase of a stop sign will look like a stop sign even if the amplitude comes from a different image. The phase signal determines where the edges and colors are located, though final colors may be altered if amplitudes change.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights that spatial structure is primarily encoded in the phase, explaining why phase preservation is critical in image processing.
concepts.recap_md: - Phase determines the location of edges and structural features.

concepts.title: DFT Magnitude Decay in Natural Images

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The magnitude of the DFT for natural images typically peaks at the origin and decays inversely proportional to radial frequency.
concepts.content: A remarkable property of natural images is that the magnitude of their DFT generally has its maximum at the origin and decays inversely proportional to the radial frequency. The magnitude of the DFT of natural images is quite similar across different scenes and can be approximated by $A \left[u,v \right] = a/ (u^2+v^2)^b$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. This typical structure has been used as a prior for many tasks such as image denoising.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing that natural images share a common power spectrum shape allows researchers to develop effective priors for image restoration and denoising.
concepts.recap_md: - DFT magnitude of natural images peaks at the origin (DC component).

concepts.title: Relative Importance of Phase and Amplitude

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The relative importance of phase and amplitude in defining image content varies depending on the specific characteristics of the image.
concepts.content:
While phase is often dominant, the amplitude also contains very useful information. The relative importance of these components depends on the image type. 

In experiments where one component is kept and the other is replaced with noninformative data (randomized phase or a generic $1/f$ amplitude), different patterns emerge. For some images, the phase carries most of the information. However, as shown in (Figure 1.1.6), for other images—such as those showing pseudo-periodic textures—the amplitude becomes the most important component in defining the image content.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept corrects the misconception that phase is always the only important factor, showing that amplitude is crucial for textures and periodic structures.
concepts.recap_md: - Phase dominance is not universal across all image types.

concepts.title: Amplitude and Periodic Patterns

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier amplitude is particularly effective at capturing and representing images that contain strong periodic patterns.
concepts.content: The amplitude is great for capturing images that contain strong periodic patterns. In such cases, the amplitude can be more informative than the phase. This observation has served as the basis for many image descriptors. While the amplitude is somewhat invariant to location, the phase is a complex signal that does not always make image information explicit in the same way.
concepts.motivation_md: Amplitude's relative invariance to translation and its sensitivity to periodicity make it an ideal feature for texture analysis and pattern recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Amplitude excels at representing periodic textures.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Linear Layer
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for a linear layer involves computing gradients with respect to inputs, weights, and biases using matrix multiplications and outer products.
concepts.content:
