A linear layer is defined in the forward direction as $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$, where $\mathbf{W}$ is an $[M \times N]$ matrix and $\mathbf{b}$ is an $M$-dimensional vector. To perform backpropagation, we require the gradients of this function with respect to its inputs and parameters. The individual scalar gradients are:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}[i,j] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial x_{\texttt{in}}[j]} = \mathbf{W}[i,j] \\ \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{W}}[i,jk] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial \mathbf{W}[j,k]} = \begin{cases} x_{\texttt{in}}[k], &\text{if} \quad i == j\\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\ \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}}[i,j] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial \mathbf{b}[j]} = \begin{cases} 1, &\text{if} \quad i == j\\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

These imply that $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{I}$. The `backward` implementation for a linear layer uses these to compute:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}\\ \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{b}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \end{aligned}$$

(see figure: The forward and backward matrix multiples for a linear layer.)

The gradient with respect to the weights, $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}}$, simplifies to an outer product between the input vector and the output gradient:

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$$

(see figure: Matrix multiply for parameter gradient of a linear layer.)

(see figure: Linear layer forward and backward.)

These operations are easily implemented using matrix multiplication primitives as shown in the following pseudocode:

```python
class linear():
    def __init__(self, W, b, lr):
        self.W = W
        self.b = b
        self.lr = lr
        
    def forward(self, x_in):
        self.x_in = x_in
        return matmul(W,x)+b
    
    def backward(self,J_out):
        J_in = matmul(J_out,W)
        dJdW = matmul(self.x_in,J_out)
        dJdb = J_out
        return J_in, dJdW, dJdb
    
    def update(self, dJdW, dJdb):
        self.W -= self.lr*dJdW.transpose()
        self.b -= self.lr*dJdb
```
concepts.motivation_md: To train a neural network, we must calculate how changes in weights and biases affect the loss. For linear layers, these gradients allow us to update parameters and propagate error signals back to previous layers efficiently using standard matrix algebra.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient with respect to the input is the product of the output gradient and the weight matrix.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Pointwise Nonlinearity
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for pointwise nonlinearities involves an element-wise multiplication of the incoming gradient by the derivative of the activation function.
concepts.content:
Pointwise nonlinearities have very simple `backward` functions. For a parameterless scalar nonlinearity $h: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with derivative $h^{\prime}$, a pointwise layer is defined as $f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = [h(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}$. The Jacobian is a diagonal matrix of the derivatives: $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \texttt{diag}([h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}) \triangleq \mathbf{H}^\prime$. Since there are no parameters, the backward operation only calculates $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{H}^\prime$.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)

This simplifies to an element-wise product:
$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}[i] = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[i]h^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[i]) \quad \forall i$$

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: Nonlinearities are essential for neural networks to learn complex patterns. We need a way to pass gradients through these functions so that layers earlier in the network can be updated based on the final loss.
concepts.recap_md: - The Jacobian of a pointwise nonlinearity is a diagonal matrix of its derivatives.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a ReLU Layer
concepts.one_liner: The backward pass for a ReLU layer acts as a mask, passing gradients only where the input was non-negative.
concepts.content:
For a `relu` layer, the derivative function is:
$$\begin{aligned} h^\prime(x) = \begin{cases} 1 &\text{if} \quad x \geq 0\\ 0 &\text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$
As a matrix multiply, the `backward` operation uses this derivative to gate the incoming gradients.
concepts.motivation_md: ReLU is a standard activation function. Its gradient is computationally efficient (either 0 or 1), allowing for fast backpropagation while avoiding vanishing gradients for positive inputs.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of ReLU is 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative inputs.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for an L2 Loss Layer
concepts.one_liner: The backward signal from an $L_2$ loss layer is a row vector representing the per-dimension errors between the prediction and the target.
concepts.content:
For an $L_2$ loss function $\left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2$, where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the prediction and $\mathbf{y}$ is the ground truth, the layer has no parameters. We only derive the gradient with respect to the input:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &= \frac{\partial \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{y}}} = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) \\ \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}*2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) \end{aligned}$$
Because the output of the loss layer is the cost $J$, $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1$. The backward signal is a row vector of per-dimension errors.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of an $L_2$ loss layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: The loss layer is the starting point of backpropagation. We need to calculate the initial gradient of the loss with respect to the network's final output to begin the chain rule process.
concepts.recap_md: - The gradient of the $L_2$ loss with respect to the network output is twice the difference between the prediction and the ground truth.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through an MLP
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through an MLP involves sequential matrix multiplications where the backward pass for linear layers uses transposed weight matrices.
concepts.content:
In an MLP, the forward pass involves sequential transformations through linear and nonlinear layers.

(see figure: Forward pass through an MLP.)

For the backward pass, if we treat gradients $\mathbf{g}$ as column vectors, the operation for a linear layer becomes $\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{W}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. This reveals that the backward pass for a linear layer is the same operation as the forward pass, just with the weights transposed. 

(see figure: Backward pass through an MLP.)

In contrast, the `relu` layer acts as a gating matrix parameterized by the forward pass activations, masking out gradients where the activation was negative. Parameter gradients at each step are computed as an outer product between the layer's input activations $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and the gradients $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: To train multi-layer networks, we need a systematic way to apply the chain rule across many layers. Understanding the MLP backward pass as a sequence of matrix operations allows for efficient implementation in modern hardware.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass through linear layers uses the transpose of the forward weight matrices.

concepts.title: Backpropagation as a Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: The entire backpropagation process can be viewed as a single large neural network where the backward pass is a linear network parameterized by the forward pass.
concepts.content:
The backward pass through a neural network can be implemented as another neural network, specifically a linear network with parameters determined by the weight matrices and activations of the original network. Consequently, the full backpropagation algorithm—comprising both the forward and backward passes—can be viewed as one large neural network. Parameter gradients are computed from this network via one additional matrix multiply for each layer of the backward network.

(see figure: The computation graph for backpropagation through a three-layer MLP. It's just another neural net! Solid lines are involved in computing data/activation gradients and dotted lines are involved in...)
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing backpropagation as a neural network itself helps in understanding the symmetry between forward and backward passes and facilitates the design of automated differentiation systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation is a composite computation graph consisting of both forward and backward passes.

concepts.title: Hypernetwork
concepts.one_liner: A hypernetwork is a neural network setup where one network outputs the values that parameterize another neural network.
concepts.content: A hypernetwork is a general setup where one neural network outputs values that parameterize another neural network. In the context of backpropagation, the forward network acts as a hypernetwork that parameterizes the backward network, such as when activations from `relu` layers are transformed to become parameters (gating masks) for the linear layers of the backward pass.
concepts.motivation_md: Hypernetworks provide a flexible framework for dynamic parameter generation, allowing a model to adapt its behavior based on the specific input it receives.
concepts.recap_md: - Hypernetworks are networks that generate parameters for other networks.

concepts.title: Linearity of the Backward Pass
concepts.one_liner: The backward pass of any computation graph consists exclusively of linear layers because the chain rule is a product of Jacobian matrices.
concepts.content: The backward network consists only of linear layers, regardless of the forward network's composition. This occurs because backpropagation implements the chain rule, which is always a product of Jacobian matrices. Since a Jacobian is a matrix, it represents a linear function. Intuitively, each Jacobian can be viewed as a locally linear approximation to the loss surface, which is represented by a linear layer in the backward pass.
concepts.motivation_md: This property explains why backpropagation is computationally predictable and why it can be implemented efficiently using standard linear algebra libraries.
concepts.recap_md: - The backward pass is always linear because it is composed of Jacobian matrix multiplications.

concepts.title: Linearity of the Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform and its inverse are linear transformations.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform and its inverse are linear transformations:
$$\alpha \ell_1 \left[n,m \right] + \beta \ell_2 \left[ n,m \right]  
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
\alpha \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v \right] + \beta \mathscr{L}_2 \left[ u,v \right]$$
where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are complex numbers. This property can be easily proven from the definition of the DFT.
concepts.motivation_md: Linearity allows us to compute the Fourier transform of a complex signal by breaking it down into a weighted sum of simpler components, facilitating easier analysis and processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DFT of a linear combination of signals is the same linear combination of their individual DFTs.
- This property applies to both the forward and inverse Fourier transforms.

concepts.title: Separability of the Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: If an image is separable, then its Fourier transform is also separable.
concepts.content: An image is separable if it can be written as the product of two 1D signals, $\ell\left[n,m \right] = \ell_1\left[n \right] \ell_2\left[m \right]$. If an image is separable, then its Fourier transform is separable: $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] = \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u \right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[v \right]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Separability simplifies the computation of a 2D DFT by allowing it to be calculated as a sequence of 1D DFTs, significantly reducing computational complexity.
concepts.recap_md:
- A 2D signal is separable if it is the product of two 1D signals.
- The 2D DFT of a separable signal is the product of the 1D DFTs of its components.

concepts.title: Separable Approximation using SVD
concepts.one_liner: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) can be used to find a separable approximation of a non-separable image.
concepts.content:
Although almost all images are not separable, some can be approximated by a separable image. 

[FIGURE:4c9735cdf9d9b2ef | A photograph of a building facade featuring a $3 \times 3$ grid of windows with green shutters. The repetitive horizontal and vertical structure of the windows serves as a real-world example of a...]

We can use the SVD decomposition to find a separable approximation to this image. The result is:

[FIGURE:544fb3db7ed43ca4 | A color visualization of a complex-valued matrix representing a 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). It features a grid-like pattern of intersecting horizontal and vertical bands in shades of muted...]

This last image can be written as the product of two 1D signals.
concepts.motivation_md: Most real-world images are not perfectly separable, but finding a separable approximation allows for more efficient processing and storage using 1D techniques.
concepts.recap_md:
- Most images are not naturally separable but can be approximated as such.
- SVD decomposition is a mathematical tool used to find the best separable approximation of an image.

concepts.title: Parseval's Theorem
concepts.one_liner: Parseval's theorem states that the dot product and norm of signals are preserved after a Fourier basis change.
concepts.content:
### Parseval's Theorem

As the DFT is a change of basis, the dot product between two signals and the norm of a vector is preserved (up to a constant factor) after the basis change. This is stated by Parseval's theorem:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \ell_1 \left[n,m \right] \ell_2^* \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v \right] \mathscr{L}_2^* \left[u,v \right]$$
In particular, if $\ell_1=\ell_2$ this reduces to the **Plancherel theorem**:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \ell\left[n,m \right] \|^2 = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \|^2$$
This relationship is important because it tells us that the energy of a signal can be computed as the sum of the squared magnitude of the values of its Fourier transform.
concepts.motivation_md: Parseval's theorem ensures that the total energy of a signal remains consistent whether it is measured in the spatial domain or the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DFT preserves the dot product and norm of signals up to a constant factor $1/NM$.
- The energy of a signal can be computed by summing the squared magnitudes in either the spatial or frequency domain.

concepts.title: Plancherel Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Plancherel theorem relates the sum of squared magnitudes of a signal to those of its Fourier transform.
concepts.content:
If $\ell_1=\ell_2$, Parseval's theorem reduces to the **Plancherel theorem**:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \ell\left[n,m \right] \|^2 = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \|^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a direct way to calculate signal energy in the frequency domain, which is often more convenient for filtering and analysis tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Plancherel's theorem is a specific case of Parseval's theorem where a signal is compared to itself.
- It equates the spatial energy sum to the frequency energy sum scaled by $1/NM$.

concepts.title: Convolution Property of the DFT
concepts.one_liner: The operation of a convolution in the spatial domain corresponds to multiplication in the Fourier domain.
concepts.content:
### Convolution

Consider a signal $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$ that is the result of applying (circular) convolution of two signals, $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$, both of size $N \times M$: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \ell_1 \circ \ell_2$$

If we take the Fourier transform of both sides and use the definition of the Fourier transform, we obtain:
$$\begin{split}
\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] & =  \mathcal{F}  \left\{ \ell_1 \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 \right\} \\
& =  
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}  \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} 
\left\{
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1} 
\ell_1 \left[n-k, m-l \right] \ell_2 \left[k,l \right]
\right\}
\exp \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{nu}{N} + \frac{mv}{M} \right) \right)
\end{split}$$
In these sums, the finite signal $\ell_1 \left[n, m \right]$ is extended periodically. Changing the dummy variables ($n' = n - k$ and $m' = m - l$) and recognizing the DFT of $x[n,m]$ using circular boundary conditions, we find:
$$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1}  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \exp{ \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{ku}{N}+\frac{lv}{M} \right ) \right)} \ell_2 \left[k,l\right]$$
Performing the final DFT gives the desired result:
$$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v\right] = \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$

Thus, the operation of a convolution, in the Fourier domain, is just a multiplication of the Fourier transform of each term:
$$\ell_1 \left[n,m\right] \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 \left[n,m\right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution is computationally expensive in the spatial domain. This property allows us to perform convolution much faster by multiplying in the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md:
- Spatial circular convolution corresponds to point-wise multiplication in the frequency domain.
- This relationship is fundamental for efficient linear filtering of images.

concepts.title: Fourier Bases as Eigenfunctions of LSI Systems
concepts.one_liner: Fourier bases are the eigenfunctions of all space-invariant linear operators.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform lets us characterize images by their spatial frequency content. It's also the natural domain in which to analyze space-invariant linear processes, because the Fourier bases are the eigenfunctions of all space-invariant linear operators. In other words, if you apply any linear, space-invariant operator to a complex exponential, the result is always a complex exponential of that same frequency, though generally with a different amplitude and phase.
concepts.motivation_md: This property explains why the Fourier transform is so powerful for LSI systems: it diagonalizes the operator, turning complex convolutions into simple scalar multiplications.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fourier bases are eigenfunctions of linear space-invariant (LSI) systems.
- Applying an LSI operator to a complex exponential preserves its frequency, only altering amplitude and phase.

concepts.title: Dual Convolution Property (Product in Space)
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of the product of two images is the circular convolution of their individual DFTs.
concepts.content:
### Dual Convolution

Another common operation when working with images is to compute products between images. For instance, this occurs when applying a mask to an image, which corresponds to multiplying the image by a mask that has zeros in the pixels to be excluded.

It turns out that the Fourier transform of the product of two images is the (circular) convolution of their DFTs:

$$\ell_1 \left[n,m\right] \ell_2 \left[n,m\right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \frac{1}{NM} \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \circ \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: This property is the dual of the convolution theorem; it explains how point-wise operations like masking or windowing affect the frequency spectrum of a signal.
concepts.recap_md:
- Point-wise multiplication in the spatial domain corresponds to circular convolution in the frequency domain.
- The resulting frequency convolution is scaled by a factor of $1/NM$.

concepts.title: Receptive Field
concepts.one_liner: The receptive field of a neuron corresponds to the region of the input stimulus space that has to be stimulated in order to produce a response in the neuron.
concepts.content: The receptive field of a neuron corresponds to the region of the input stimulus space (the retina in the case of a visual neuron) that has to be stimulated in order to produce a response in the neuron. Most neurons in the visual processing stream are activated only when light shines on a precise portion of the retina. Only stimulation within the receptive field (RF) of a neuron produces a response. [FIGURE:542154188035b8df | A schematic diagram of a large rectangular area labeled 'Image/visual field'. Inside this field, a smaller circular region with a dashed border and light gray fill is labeled 'RF', representing the...]
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding receptive fields is fundamental to mapping how sensory information is spatially organized and processed by individual neurons in the visual system.
concepts.recap_md: - The receptive field is the specific area in the visual field where a stimulus triggers a neuronal response.

concepts.title: Center-Surround Receptive Field Organization
concepts.one_liner: Ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization that enables contrast enhancement.
concepts.content: Ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization. There are two primary types: on-center cells, which activate when light hits the middle of the receptive field and deactivate when light hits the surrounding ring, and off-center cells, which exhibit the opposite behavior. This organization reveals that the retina performs contrast enhancing operations. In an ON-center receptive field, illumination of the inner part increases the firing rate, while stimulation of the outer part inhibits the response.
concepts.motivation_md: This organization allows the retina to perform contrast enhancement and edge detection before signals reach the brain, serving as an efficient way to process visual information.
concepts.recap_md: - Receptive fields are organized into a central disk and a surrounding ring with antagonistic responses.

concepts.title: On-center and Off-center Ganglion Cells
concepts.one_liner: On-center and off-center cells are ganglion cells that respond antagonistically to light in the center versus the surround of their receptive fields.
concepts.content: There are two types of ganglion cells: on-center and off-center. On-center cells are activated when a spot of light is inside a small region in the middle of the receptive field and are deactivated (firing below their average rate) when the light is projected inside a ring around the center. Off-center cells exhibit the opposite behavior, being inhibited by light in the center and excited by light in the surround.
concepts.motivation_md: These two cell types provide a dual representation of the visual scene, allowing the brain to detect both increases and decreases in local illumination efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - On-center cells fire more rapidly when light hits the center of their receptive field.

concepts.title: Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN)
concepts.one_liner: The lateral geniculate nucleus is a six-layered relay structure that transmits monocular visual information from the retina to the cortex.
concepts.content: The axons of ganglion cells from both eyes project to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a structure composed of six layers of neurons that outputs to the visual cortex. The LGN receives inputs from both eyes, but the signals are not mixed and the neurons remain monocular. LGN neurons have concentric center-surround receptive fields. While its role is not completely understood, it may be involved in temporal decorrelation, attention modulation, and saccadic suppression. Interestingly, only 5 percent of the input connections come from the retina, while 95 percent are feedback connections from the primary visual cortex and other areas.
concepts.motivation_md: The LGN acts as a sophisticated relay station that filters and modulates visual information from the retina before it reaches the cortex, influenced heavily by top-down feedback.
concepts.recap_md: - The LGN is a six-layered relay center in the thalamus for the visual pathway.

concepts.title: Simple, Complex, and Hypercomplex Cells
concepts.one_liner: Visual cortex neurons are classified as simple, complex, or hypercomplex based on their selectivity for orientation and spatial position.
concepts.content: Neurons in the visual cortex are classified according to attributes such as spatial selectivity, orientation preference, eye preference, and type, which includes simple, complex, or hypercomplex cells. Some neurons are best stimulated by an oriented bar at a specific orientation when it appears at the center of the receptive field. An oriented simple cell shows an increased firing rate when stimulated with an oriented bar in the positive region of the receptive field with the preferred orientation.
concepts.motivation_md: This classification describes how the visual system builds complex representations of shapes and edges from basic light-dark patterns.
concepts.recap_md: - Simple cells respond to oriented bars at specific locations in the receptive field.

concepts.title: Functional Organization of V1: Columns and Hypercolumns
concepts.one_liner: A section of around 1 $\times$ 3 mm (called a hypercolumn) covers all orientations and both eyes for a small portion of the visual field.
concepts.content: The first visual area in the visual cortex, called V1, is a sheet of neurons arranged along several layers. Neurons in V1 are organized along columns; cells within a vertical column are selective to the same orientation. When moving an electrode horizontally, the preferred orientation changes smoothly (orientation columns), while moving in the perpendicular horizontal direction changes eye preference (ocular dominance columns). A section of around 1 $\times$ 3 mm, called a hypercolumn, covers all orientations and both eyes for a small portion of the visual field. Color-sensitive neurons are also organized in blobs surrounded by orientation-sensitive neurons.
concepts.motivation_md: This modular organization ensures that every point in the visual field is systematically processed for all possible orientations and inputs from both eyes.
concepts.recap_md: - V1 is organized into vertical columns where neurons share specific stimulus preferences.

concepts.title: Ventral and Dorsal Visual Streams
concepts.one_liner: Visual information is processed through ventral and dorsal streams specialized for object recognition and motion processing, respectively.
concepts.content: Cells in the visual cortex project their outputs to other visual areas following two main streams: the ventral stream and the dorsal stream. These project into specialized areas performing motion processing (area MT), face processing (fusiform face area [FFA]), and object recognition (IT).
concepts.motivation_md: Dividing visual processing into two streams allows the brain to simultaneously solve the "what" (object identity) and "where/how" (spatial location and motion) problems.
concepts.recap_md: - The ventral stream is primarily involved in identifying objects and faces.

concepts.title: Linear Filter Approximation of Visual Neurons
concepts.one_liner: Many of the neurons in the early layer of visual processing can be approximated by linear filters with rectifying nonlinearities and contrast control mechanisms.
concepts.content: Many of the neurons in the early layer of visual processing (retina, LGN, and visual cortex) can be approximated by linear filters with rectifying nonlinearities and contrast control mechanisms. These models form the basis of many computer vision algorithms.
concepts.motivation_md: Approximating biological neurons as linear filters provides a mathematical framework that bridges neuroscience and computer vision, enabling the development of biologically inspired algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - Early visual neurons are often modeled as linear filters with non-linear components.

concepts.title: Central Difference Operator (d1)
concepts.one_liner: The central difference operator $d_1 = [1, 0, -1]/2$ approximates spatial derivatives by calculating the difference between neighboring samples divided by two.
concepts.content:
The spatial derivative can be approximated using the central difference operator $d_1 = [1, 0, -1]/2$. In one dimension, convolving a signal $\ell [n]$ with $d_1 [n]$ results in:
$$
\ell \circ d_1 = \frac{\ell [n+1] - \ell [n-1]}{2}
$$
The output of this filter shows the highest magnitude at the midpoint where there is variation in the input signal, effectively centering the derivative estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: This operator addresses the spatial misalignment issues found in simpler forward or backward difference approximations by centering the derivative calculation on the current sample.
concepts.recap_md: - The operator is defined by the kernel $d_1 = [1, 0, -1]/2$.

concepts.title: Derivative in the Fourier Domain
concepts.one_liner: In the continuous domain, differentiation is equivalent to multiplying the Fourier transform of a function by $jw$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding derivatives in the Fourier domain allows for the analysis of how different discrete derivative approximations behave across various frequencies.
concepts.recap_md: - Differentiation in the spatial domain corresponds to multiplication by $jw$ in the frequency domain.

concepts.title: DFT of Discrete Derivative Approximations
concepts.one_liner: The DFT of discrete derivative approximations reveals their frequency response and phase shifts compared to the ideal continuous derivative.
concepts.content:
In the discrete domain, the DFT of a signal derivative depends on the approximation used. For the operator $d_0 [n]$, the DFT is:
$$
\begin{split}
D_0 [u] & = 1 - \exp \left( -2 \pi j \frac{u}{N} \right)  \\
& = \exp \left( - \pi j \frac{u}{N} \right) 2 j \sin (\pi u /N)
\end{split}
$$
The first term represents a pure phase shift causing a half-sample delay, while the second term is the amplitude gain. For the central difference operator $d_1 [n]$, the DFT is:
$$
\begin{split}
D_1 [u] & =  1/2\exp \left( 2 \pi j \frac{u}{N} \right) - 1/2 \exp \left( -2 \pi j \frac{u}{N} \right)  \\
& =  j \sin (2 \pi u /N)
\end{split}
$$
While $D_0[u]$ provides a better amplitude approximation to the ideal derivative $|2 \pi u/N|$, it introduces a phase shift. Conversely, $D_1[u]$ has no shift but approximates the derivative over a smaller frequency range and produces smoother outputs. Note that $D_1[u] = D_0[u] B_1[u]$, where $B_1[u]$ is the DFT of a binomial filter.
concepts.motivation_md: Analyzing the DFT helps engineers choose between derivative approximations based on the trade-off between phase accuracy (alignment) and frequency range.
concepts.recap_md: - $D_0$ provides better amplitude approximation but introduces a half-sample phase shift.

concepts.title: 2D Image Derivative Discretization
concepts.one_liner: Two-dimensional image derivatives can be approximated along vertical and horizontal components using discrete kernels.
concepts.motivation_md: Approximating derivatives in 2D is essential for detecting edges and features that occur in different directions within an image.
concepts.recap_md: - 2D derivatives are computed using kernels for horizontal and vertical changes.

concepts.title: Roberts Cross Operator
concepts.one_liner: The Roberts cross operator uses a rotated reference frame to compute image derivatives while avoiding spatial misalignment.
concepts.motivation_md: It was designed to provide spatially aligned derivative outputs, which is critical for accurate edge localization in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses diagonal kernels to calculate differences in a rotated frame.

concepts.title: Sobel Operator
concepts.one_liner: The Sobel operator is a spatially aligned derivative discretization based on the $[-1, 0, 1]$ kernel.
concepts.content: The Sobel operator is a discretization of the image derivative that ensures both outputs are spatially aligned because they are shifted in the same way. It is based on the $[-1, 0, 1]$ kernel.
concepts.motivation_md: The Sobel operator provides a more robust and aligned estimate of the image gradient compared to simpler 2x2 operators.
concepts.recap_md: - Utilizes a 3-element kernel to maintain spatial alignment.

concepts.title: Utility of Simple Derivative Operators
concepts.one_liner: Simple derivative operators remain essential in modern computer vision for their efficiency and foundational role in feature descriptors.
concepts.content: While newer algorithms for edge extraction have been developed, simple derivative operators still hold value where efficiency is important. These operators continue to be used as fundamental components in modern computer vision descriptors, including the Scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) and the histogram of oriented gradients (HOG).
concepts.motivation_md: Despite their simplicity, these operators provide the computational efficiency required for real-time applications and large-scale feature extraction.
concepts.recap_md: - Valued for computational efficiency in real-time systems.

concepts.title: Image Reconstruction from Derivatives
concepts.one_liner: Original signals and images can be recovered from their derivatives through the process of integration.
concepts.content: Derivatives are powerful tools for representing images and extracting information. Although it may seem that information is lost during differentiation, the original signal can be recovered by integrating its derivative. This process involves examining what specific information (such as the constant of integration) is lost and how the integration can be performed in both 1D and 2D cases.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding reconstruction proves that the derivative representation is a complete (or near-complete) description of the original signal's structure.
concepts.recap_md: - Integration allows for the recovery of the original signal from its derivative.

concepts.title: Perceptron Learning Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt published the perceptron learning algorithm, a model of biological brains that could learn to recognize simple visual patterns.
concepts.content: In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt published one of the first formal learning algorithms, called the perceptron learning algorithm, and showed that it can, in principle, learn to recognize certain simple visual patterns. The perceptron was also one of the first artificial neural nets, a computational model of biological brains. The ability of perceptrons to learn to solve recognition problems created an explosion of interest in neural nets.
concepts.motivation_md: The perceptron was developed to show that a formal learning algorithm could, in principle, learn to recognize simple visual patterns, serving as a computational model of biological brains.
concepts.recap_md: - Introduced by Frank Rosenblatt in 1958 as one of the first formal learning algorithms. - Designed as a computational model of biological brains to solve recognition problems.

concepts.title: Artificial Neural Networks
concepts.one_liner: Artificial neural nets are computational models of biological brains designed to solve recognition problems through learning.
concepts.content: Artificial neural nets are computational models of biological brains. The ability of early models like perceptrons to learn to solve recognition problems created an explosion of interest in neural nets.
concepts.motivation_md: Artificial neural nets exist as computational models of biological brains, designed to solve recognition problems through learning.
concepts.recap_md: - Computational models inspired by the structure and function of biological brains. - Capable of learning to solve complex recognition problems.

concepts.title: Cycles of Interest in Neural Networks
concepts.one_liner: Interest in neural networks has historically fluctuated in cycles, sometimes independent of the broader field of learning algorithms.
concepts.content: Interest in neural nets has since gone through a series of ebbs and flows. These cycles have partially lined up with interest in learning algorithms more generally, but there have also been phases where interest in neural nets was low but interest in other learning algorithms was high.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these cycles helps explain why interest in neural networks has fluctuated over time, even when interest in other learning algorithms remained high.
concepts.recap_md: - Interest in neural networks has historically fluctuated in cycles of ebbs and flows. - These cycles do not always coincide with general interest in other learning algorithms.

concepts.title: Deep Learning
concepts.one_liner: Deep learning systems are multi-layered networks of perceptrons capable of complex operations and logic that dominate modern AI.
concepts.content: In the 1980s, interest in learning algorithms and neural nets began to surge again because researchers showed that perceptrons could be stacked to create systems capable of complex operations, including logic. These systems were the precursors to the deep learning systems that dominate today.
concepts.motivation_md: Deep learning systems were developed because researchers showed that stacking perceptrons allowed for complex operations and logic that single-layer systems could not achieve.
concepts.recap_md: - Formed by stacking perceptrons to perform complex logical and computational operations. - Emerged as a dominant approach in modern artificial intelligence.

concepts.title: Neocognitron
concepts.one_liner: The neocognitron is a vision-specific architecture introduced by Kunihiko Fukushima in the 1980s as a precursor to modern convolutional neural networks.
concepts.content: In the 1980s, several architectures specific to vision were introduced, including Kunihiko Fukushima's neocognitron, which was a precursor to modern convolutional neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: The neocognitron was introduced as a specialized architecture for vision, providing a foundation for modern systems that process visual information.
concepts.recap_md: - A vision-specific architecture introduced by Kunihiko Fukushima in the 1980s. - Served as a critical precursor to modern convolutional neural networks.

concepts.title: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
concepts.one_liner: Convolutional neural networks are specialized architectures for vision that evolved from earlier models like the neocognitron.
concepts.content: In the 1980s, several architectures specific to vision were introduced, including Kunihiko Fukushima's neocognitron, which was a precursor to modern convolutional neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: CNNs solve the problem of efficiently recognizing visual patterns by using architectures specifically designed for vision tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Specialized architectures designed for processing and recognizing visual information. - Evolved from earlier 1980s models like the neocognitron.

concepts.title: Backpropagation
concepts.one_liner: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. showed how neural networks can be efficiently trained, leading to practical applications like digit recognition.
concepts.content: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. showed how these kinds of networks can be efficiently trained, and their system was put into use for recognizing handwritten digits by the US Postal Service.
concepts.motivation_md: Backpropagation was introduced to provide an efficient way to train neural networks, enabling them to be used for practical tasks like digit recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - An efficient training method for neural networks demonstrated by Yann LeCun et al. in 1989. - Successfully used for practical tasks like handwritten digit recognition.

concepts.title: AI Winter
concepts.one_liner: The AI winter was a period around 2000 when interest in learning algorithms declined after the promises of the 1980s failed to materialize.
concepts.content: By the year 2000, the field of AI as a whole was firmly in a "winter"; the promises of the 1980s had failed to materialize and the study of learning algorithms continued on without much fanfare in just a few corners of academia.
concepts.motivation_md: The "winter" describes a period where the field had to continue in academia without much fanfare after failing to meet the high expectations of the previous decade.
concepts.recap_md: - A period of low interest and funding in AI around the year 2000. - Resulted from the failure of 1980s promises to materialize.

concepts.title: Separability of the Box Filter
concepts.one_liner: The two-dimensional box filter is separable because it can be expressed as the convolution of two one-dimensional kernels.
concepts.content: The two-dimensional (2D) box filter is separable as it can be written as the convolution of two 1D kernels: $\text{box}_{N,M} \left[n,m \right] = \text{box}_{N,0} \circ \text{box}_{0,M}$. When the box is large, it can be implemented efficiently using the integral image.
concepts.motivation_md: Separability allows a 2D convolution to be computed as two 1D convolutions, significantly reducing the computational cost from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$ per pixel.
concepts.recap_md: - A 2D box filter is the convolution of a horizontal 1D box and a vertical 1D box.

concepts.title: DC Gain of the Box Filter
concepts.one_liner: The DC gain of a box filter is the gain it applies to a constant input signal, equal to the sum of its kernel values.
concepts.content:
One important property of a low-pass filter is the DC gain, which is the gain it has for a constant value input (the lowest possible input frequency). If the input signal is a constant $\ell[n,m] = a$, the result of convolving the image with the box filter $h_{N,M}$ is also a constant:

$$\ell_{\text{out}} \left[n,m\right] = \sum_{k,l} a \text{box}_{N,M} \left[k,l \right] = a \sum_{k,l} \text{box}_{N,M} \left[k,l \right] = a (2N+1)(2M+1)$$

The DC value of a signal is its mean value. In the frequency domain, the DC gain refers to the filter's gain at a frequency of 0, represented by $H[0,0]$ where $H$ is the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the filter's kernel. One can verify in (see figure: 1D Box Filter.) and (see figure: Fourier transform of Box Filter.) that the value of $| \text{Box}_1[0] |$ is 3. The DC gain of a filter will change the mean value of the input signal.

Fig (a) A one-dimensional (1D) box filter ($[1,1,1]$), and (b) its Fourier transform over 20 samples. Note that the frequency gain is not monotonically decreasing with spatial frequency.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding DC gain is essential for predicting how a filter affects the overall brightness or average intensity of an image.
concepts.recap_md: - DC gain is the filter's response to a constant input signal or zero frequency.

concepts.title: General DC Gain of a Filter
concepts.one_liner: The DC gain of an arbitrary filter is calculated as the sum of all its kernel values.
concepts.content:
In general, the DC gain of an arbitrary filter $h [n,m]$ is the sum of its kernel values:

$$\text{DC~gain} = \sum_{n,m} h [n,m]$$
concepts.motivation_md: This general definition allows for the calculation of the scaling effect of any linear filter on the average intensity of a signal.
concepts.recap_md: - The DC gain of any filter $h[n,m]$ is simply $\sum_{n,m} h[n,m]$.

concepts.title: Blur Filter Normalization
concepts.one_liner: Blur kernels are typically normalized so their values sum to 1, ensuring the output image maintains the same mean intensity as the input.
concepts.content: When designing blur kernels (low-pass filters), we generally want to have a DC gain of 1. The reason is that if we have an image with grayscale levels in the range of 0 to 256 and with an average around 128, we will want to preserve the same mean value in the output. For this reason, in most applications, we will normalize the kernel values so that they sum to 1. In the case of the box filter, this means dividing the kernel values by $(2N+1)(2M+1)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Normalization prevents the filtered image from becoming significantly brighter or darker than the original image.
concepts.recap_md: - A DC gain of 1 preserves the mean grayscale value of the input image.

concepts.title: Limitations of the Box Filter
concepts.one_liner: The box filter is simple but suffers from non-monotonic frequency attenuation and potential artifacts.
concepts.content:
The box filter is simple to implement and to understand, but it has a number of limitations:

- **The box filter is not a perfect blurring filter.** A blur filter should attenuate high spatial frequencies with stronger attenuation for higher spatial frequencies. However, the attenuation of a box filter is not monotonic with spatial frequency. For example, a high-frequency oscillating signal $[..., 1, -1, 1, -1, ...]$ filtered with $\text{box}_{1}$ results in the same oscillating signal, while a lower frequency wave might be completely zeroed out. This can cause artifacts to appear. 

While this could be addressed using an even size box filter $[1,1]$, even filters are not centered around the origin and cause a half-pixel translation in the output. Therefore, odd filter sizes are preferred.

The oscillating signal:

[FIGURE:b08aebefbd75544f | A discrete 1D signal plot representing a box filter. It shows blue stems with circular heads at integer positions along the horizontal $n$-axis. Stems at $n = -1, 0, 1$ have a height of 1, while all...]

convolved with the kernel $[1,1,1]$ results in:

[FIGURE:87007ce110b1a43f | A discrete stem plot representing a 1D signal on a horizontal axis labeled $n$. The signal alternates between positive and negative values at integer intervals, with blue dots at the end of each...]
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying these limitations explains why more sophisticated filters, like the Gaussian filter, are often preferred for high-quality image blurring.
concepts.recap_md: - Box filters do not attenuate frequencies monotonically, which can lead to artifacts.

concepts.title: Triangular Filter
concepts.one_liner: A triangular filter is the result of convolving two box filters, meaning repeated box blurring is not equivalent to a single larger box blur.
concepts.content:
If you convolve two boxes, you do not get another box; instead, you get a triangle. For instance, in the simple case where $N=1, M=0$:

$$\text{box}_{1,0} \circ \text{box}_{1,0} = \left[1, 1, 1\right] \circ \left[1, 1, 1\right] = \left[1,2,3,2,1\right]$$

The output is a triangular filter with length $2 \times (L-1)$, where $L$ is the length of the box filter. When convolving two box filters of different lengths, the result will be a truncated triangle. This means that if you blur an image twice with box filters, the result is not equivalent to blurring only once with a larger box filter.
concepts.motivation_md: This property highlights that the box filter family is not closed under convolution, unlike the Gaussian filter family.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolving two box filters produces a triangular filter.

concepts.title: Gaussian Filter
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian filter is a symmetric low-pass filter that models many natural processes and allows for adjustable levels of image detail.
concepts.content:
The Gaussian filter is one of the most important blurring (low-pass) filters in computer vision because it is a good model for many naturally occurring filters and possesses unique properties. 

The Gaussian distribution is defined in continuous variables. In one dimension:

$$g(x; \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp{ \left( -\frac{x^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$

And in two dimensions:

$$g(x,y; \sigma) = \frac{1}{2 \pi \sigma^2} \exp{ \left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$

The parameter $\sigma$ adjusts the spatial extent of the Gaussian. The normalization constant ensures the function integrates to 1. The Gaussian kernel is positive and symmetric (a zero-phase filter). By adjusting the standard deviation $\sigma$, it is possible to adjust the level of image detail in the blurred image, as seen in (see figure: Gaussian filter with $\sigma=2$.), (see figure: Gaussian filter with $\sigma=4$.), and (see figure: Gaussian filter with $\sigma=8$.).
concepts.motivation_md: The Gaussian filter is preferred because it provides smooth blurring without the artifacts associated with box filters and mimics natural optical blur.
concepts.recap_md: - The Gaussian filter is a symmetric, positive, zero-phase low-pass filter.

concepts.title: Discretization of the Gaussian Filter
concepts.one_liner: To use a Gaussian filter in practice, it must be sampled at discrete locations and truncated to a finite support, typically within three standard deviations.
concepts.content:
To use the Gaussian filter in practice, we must consider discrete locations and approximate the function with a finite support. In practice, we only need to consider samples within three standard deviations $x \in (-3\sigma, 3\sigma)$, where the amplitude is around 1% of its central value. 

For a given standard deviation $\sigma$, the discretized Gaussian kernel $g[n, m; \sigma]$ is:

$$g \left[ n,m; σ \right] = \exp{ \left( -\frac{n^2 + m^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$

[FIGURE:750fb1caf06dd3e4 | A discrete stem plot of a 1D Gaussian function $g[n)$ centered at $n=0$. The plot shows blue dots at integer values from $n=-4$ to $n=4$, with a peak value of 1 at $n=0$ and values decreasing...]

In this discrete form, the normalization constant is often removed so that the value at the origin is 1. However, in practice, the discrete kernel should be normalized by the sum of its values to ensure the DC gain is 1, as the sum of the discrete samples differs from the continuous integral.
concepts.motivation_md: Discretization is necessary for implementing Gaussian blurs in digital image processing software and hardware.
concepts.recap_md: - Discrete Gaussian kernels are typically truncated at $3\sigma$.

concepts.title: sequence representation
concepts.one_liner: Sequences are represented as functions $\ell (x,y,t)$ of spatial coordinates and time, typically discretized as $\ell [n,m,t]$ for processing.
concepts.content: Sequences are represented as functions $\ell (x,y,t)$, where $x,y$ are the spatial coordinates and $t$ is time. When processing sequences, we work with the discretized version represented as $\ell [n,m,t]$, where $n,m$ are the pixel indices and $t$ is the frame number. Discrete sequences are bounded in space and time and can be stored as arrays of size $N \times M \times P$.
concepts.motivation_md: To process video or time-varying visual data, we need a mathematical framework that extends 2D image representations into a third dimension representing time.
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous sequences are functions of space $(x,y)$ and time $t$.

concepts.title: globally moving image model
concepts.one_liner: A globally moving image model describes a sequence where an initial image translates with a constant velocity $(v_x, v_y)$ over time.
concepts.content:
A special sequence occurs when the image has a global motion with constant velocity $(v_x,v_y)$. In such a case, we can write:
$$
\ell (x,y,t) = \ell _0 (x-v_xt,y-v_yt)
$$
where $\ell _0(x,y)= \ell (x,y,0)$ is the image being translated, and $v_x$ and $v_y$ are constants. At time $t$, the image $\ell _0(x,y)$ is translated by the vector $(v_x t, v_y t)$. Consequently, the pixel value at location $(x=0, y=0)$ at time $t=0$ will appear at time $T$ in location $(x=v_x T, y=v_y T)$.
concepts.motivation_md: This model provides a simple mathematical way to describe uniform motion across an entire frame, serving as a building block for more complex motion estimation.
concepts.recap_md: - Global motion is modeled by translating the initial image $\ell_0$ by $(v_x t, v_y t)$.

concepts.title: constant brightness assumption
concepts.one_liner: The constant brightness assumption hypothesizes that the brightness of pixels remains unchanged as they move through a scene.
concepts.content: The constant brightness assumption assumes that the brightness of the pixels does not change while the scene is moving. Using continuous values for $x$, $y$, and $t$, along with continuous images $\ell _0(x,y)$, allows for the handling of any velocity values under this assumption. This hypothesis serves as the initial basis for most motion estimation algorithms.
concepts.motivation_md: Without assuming that an object's appearance stays relatively constant as it moves, it would be mathematically difficult to track pixels from one frame to the next.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes pixel intensity is invariant to motion.

concepts.title: moving object over static background model
concepts.one_liner: This model represents a sequence as a moving object with a binary mask occluding a static background.
concepts.content:
A sequence containing a moving object over a static background can be modeled as:
$$
\ell (x,y,t) = b(x,y) (1-m(x-v_xt,y-v_yt)) + o(x-v_xt,y-v_yt) m(x-v_x t,y-v_y t)
$$
where $b(x,y)$ is the static background image, $o(x,y)$ is the object image moving with speed $(v_x,v_y)$, and $m(x,y)$ is a binary mask that moves with the object. This mask models the fact that the object occludes the background as it moves.
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world video often involves specific objects moving independently of their surroundings; this model mathematically separates the foreground motion from the static environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines a static background $b(x,y)$ and a moving object $o(x,y)$.

concepts.title: Fourier transform of a globally moving image

position.section_title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of a globally moving image relates spatial frequencies to temporal frequency via a Dirac delta function.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform (FT) of a globally moving image is derived using the shift property:
$$
\mathscr{L} (w_x,w_y,w_t) = \mathscr{L}_0 (w_x, w_y) \delta (w_t + v_x w_x + v_y w_y)
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Analyzing motion in the frequency domain reveals that the energy of a moving image lies on a specific plane, which is useful for velocity estimation and filter design.
concepts.recap_md: - The FT of a moving image is constrained by a delta function $\delta (w_t + v_x w_x + v_y w_y)$.

concepts.title: sinc function

position.section_title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

concepts.one_liner: The sinc function is the Fourier transform of a box kernel, characterized by a central maximum and decreasing oscillations.
concepts.content:
The sinc function is the Fourier transform of a box kernel. In the continuous domain, the sinc function has the form:
$$
\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin (\pi x)}{\pi x}
$$
This function has its maximum at $x=0$ and then has decreasing oscillations.

[FIGURE:cddd5de71ef162b7 | A graph of the normalized sinc function, $\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x}$. The curve has a global maximum of 1 at $x=0$ and crosses the x-axis at integer values including $x = -1, 1, 2...]
concepts.motivation_md: The sinc function is fundamental in signal processing for understanding ideal low-pass filtering and the effects of rectangular windowing.
concepts.recap_md: - Defined as $\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin (\pi x)}{\pi x}$.

concepts.title: causal filters
concepts.one_liner: Causal filters are systems where the output at any time depends only on current and past values of the input.
concepts.content: Causal filters are filters with output variations that only depend on the past values of the input. This requirement imposes the constraint that $h [n,m,t]=0$ for all $t<0$. This means that if the input is an impulse at $t=0$, the output will only have non-zero values for $t>0$. If this condition is satisfied, the filter output will only depend on the input's past for all possible inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: In real-time systems, we cannot use information from the future; causality ensures a filter can be implemented in a physical, time-forward system.
concepts.recap_md: - Output depends only on past and present inputs.

concepts.title: non-causal filters
concepts.one_liner: Non-causal filters are systems where the output depends on future values of the input.
concepts.content: Non-causal filters are filters where the output has a dependency on future inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: While not implementable in real-time, non-causal filters are useful in post-processing applications where the entire signal or video sequence is already recorded.
concepts.recap_md: - Output depends on future input values.

concepts.title: Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: Graphical models, along with belief propagation, provided the basis to address many computer vision tasks.
concepts.content: Graphical models, along with techniques like belief propagation, provided the basis to address many computer vision tasks in the early 2000s.
concepts.motivation_md: Graphical models allow for the representation of complex dependencies between variables, providing a structured way to handle uncertainty in vision problems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Graphical models provide a basis for addressing complex vision tasks.
- They are often used in conjunction with belief propagation.

concepts.title: Boosting
concepts.one_liner: Boosting is a learning algorithm used to detect objects, such as faces in photos, by combining simple learners.
concepts.content: Boosting is a learning algorithm that gained prominence in the early 2000s. For example, in 2001, Paul Viola and Michael Jones published a method that used a simple learning algorithm called boosting to detect faces in photos.
concepts.motivation_md: Boosting solves the problem of creating a strong classifier by combining many simple, "weak" learners, making it efficient for real-time tasks like face detection.
concepts.recap_md:
- Boosting is a learning algorithm used for object detection.
- It was famously applied by Viola and Jones for face detection in 2001.

concepts.title: Support Vector Machines (SVM)
concepts.one_liner: Support vector machines are shallow learning machines used to process input data for vision tasks.
concepts.content: Support vector machines (SVM) are a type of shallow learning machine. In early vision research, features were often extracted and then provided as input to an SVM to perform classification or regression tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: SVMs provide a robust way to find the optimal hyperplane that separates data classes, which was a standard approach for classification before the rise of deep learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- SVMs are categorized as shallow learning machines.
- They were widely used for vision tasks following feature extraction.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Belief propagation, along with graphical models, provided the basis to address many computer vision tasks.
concepts.content: Belief propagation is an inference algorithm that, along with graphical models, provided the basis to address many computer vision tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Belief propagation allows for efficient inference in graphical models, helping to calculate marginal distributions in complex networks of variables.
concepts.recap_md:
- Belief propagation is an inference technique for graphical models.
- It was a foundational method for addressing various vision tasks.

concepts.title: Large Image Databases
concepts.one_liner: Large image databases containing millions of images provide the data necessary for modern vision tasks.
concepts.content: The first very large image databases, containing millions of images such as Tiny Images, ImageNet, and COCO, appeared with the hypothesis that most vision tasks could be solved with sufficient data.
concepts.motivation_md: Large databases solve the problem of data scarcity, allowing learning-based models to generalize better by training on millions of diverse examples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Databases like ImageNet and COCO contain millions of images.
- They support the hypothesis that large amounts of data are key to vision.

concepts.title: Learning-Based vs. Model-Based Perception
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision focuses on data and flexible architectures rather than predefined models of how perception works.
concepts.content: While many previous perspectives on perception began with models about how perception might work, learning-based approaches take a different path. They rely on flexible architectures that incorporate as few hypotheses about perception as possible, and instead focus on data to learn to build the right model for perception.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional model-based approaches often rely on rigid assumptions that may not capture the complexity of the real world; learning-based methods allow the data to define the model.
concepts.recap_md:
- Learning-based approaches minimize initial hypotheses about perception.
- They prioritize data-driven model building over predefined theoretical models.

concepts.title: Empiricism vs. Rationalism in Vision
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision is rooted in empiricism, the philosophy that knowledge is acquired through experience and data rather than pure reason.
concepts.content: Learning-based vision has its roots in the philosophical tradition of empiricism, which holds that knowledge about the world should be acquired by experience, rather than solely through reason (an approach known as rationalism). The modern day term for experience is "data," and learning is really all about data.
concepts.motivation_md: This distinction helps explain the shift from hand-coded rules (rationalism) to data-driven algorithms (empiricism) in artificial intelligence.
concepts.recap_md:
- Empiricism emphasizes knowledge through experience and data.
- Rationalism emphasizes knowledge through reason and predefined models.

concepts.title: Three Approaches to Programming Vision Algorithms
concepts.one_liner: Vision algorithms can be programmed directly, derived from world models, or learned from data by fitting functions to examples.
concepts.content: Learning derives vision algorithms by fitting functions to data. One way to think about it is that our goal is to "program" a vision algorithm and there are a few ways to do so (@fig-taxonomy-programming_vs_learning). One way is to write the algorithm directly in Python code: first we will compare the intensity of this pixel and that pixel, then we will threshold about some such value, and so on. Another approach is to derive the algorithm as the rational thing to do given some underlying model of the world; for example, because overlapping objects generically produce contrast edges in the image, the optimal way to detect boundaries between objects is to look for a particular kind of contrast. The third approach—the learning approach—is to program algorithms via data: first collect a bunch of examples of inputs and the correct output, then fit a function that replicates these exemplar mappings from input to output. ![Two ways of programming an algorithm. Left: traditional way, Right: the machine learning way. You will learn about the machine learning "compiler", called Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), in .](figures/taxonomy/programming_vs_learning.png){#fig-taxonomy-programming_vs_learning width="100%"}
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these three approaches helps clarify the evolution from manual feature engineering and physical modeling to modern data-driven machine learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Direct programming involves manual coding of pixel-level logic.
- Model-based derivation uses rational principles of the physical world.
- The learning approach fits functions to input-output data pairs.

concepts.title: Limitations of Discrete Gaussian Approximations
concepts.one_liner: Directly sampling a continuous Gaussian at discrete locations results in an approximation that fails to preserve the Gaussian's fundamental convolution properties.
concepts.content: Many properties of the Gaussian are only true for the continuous version and do not work for its discrete approximation $g[n,m;\sigma]$ obtained by directly sampling values at discrete locations. For example, consider a 1D Gaussian with variance $\sigma^2=1/2$ approximated by five samples: $$g_5[n] = [0.0183, 0.3679, 1.0000, 0.3679, 0.0183]$$ If you compute the approximation for $\sigma^2=1$ by discretizing the Gaussian, the result is not equal to $g_5 \circ g_5$. Therefore, as you apply successive convolutions of discretized Gaussians, the errors accumulate and the result is no longer a Gaussian. Additionally, the convolution of $g_5[n]$ with the wave $[1,-1,1,-1,...]$ is not zero, which is expected from the form of the Fourier Transform of the Gaussian. While this is not always a strong limitation, it is important in cases like antialiasing filters where highest frequencies must be completely canceled.
concepts.motivation_md: While continuous Gaussians have elegant mathematical properties, simply sampling them to create discrete filters breaks the property that the convolution of two Gaussians is another Gaussian. This concept explains why naive discretization leads to accumulating errors in image processing pipelines.
concepts.recap_md:
- Discrete approximations of Gaussians obtained by direct sampling do not preserve the convolution property $g_{\sigma_1} \circ g_{\sigma_2} = g_{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}}$.
 - Successive convolutions of discretized Gaussians lead to accumulating errors and a non-Gaussian result.
 - Discretized Gaussians may fail to completely cancel highest frequencies, which is problematic for specific tasks like antialiasing.

concepts.title: Binomial Filters
concepts.one_liner: Binomial filters are efficient discrete approximations to the Gaussian filter obtained by successive convolutions of the box filter $[1,1]$.
concepts.content: Binomial filters are very efficient discrete approximations to the Gaussian filter that, for certain $\sigma$ values, have nicer properties than discretized Gaussians. These filters are obtained by successive convolutions of the box filter $[1,1]$. They utilize the central limit theorem to approximate a Gaussian as successive convolutions of a very simple function.
concepts.motivation_md: Binomial filters were developed to overcome the mathematical inconsistencies of naive discrete Gaussians while providing a computationally efficient way to perform low-pass filtering using simple integer arithmetic.
concepts.recap_md:
- Binomial filters are discrete approximations of the Gaussian filter.
 - They are constructed through successive convolutions of the simple box filter $[1,1]$.
 - Their design is motivated by the central limit theorem.

concepts.title: Binomial Coefficients and Pascal's Triangle
concepts.one_liner: The coefficients of binomial filters are organized into Pascal's triangle, where each row represents a 1D binomial kernel.
concepts.motivation_md: Pascal's triangle provides a simple, recursive method to generate the coefficients for binomial filters of any order, mapping specific rows to specific spatial variances.
concepts.recap_md:
- Each row in Pascal's triangle corresponds to a 1D binomial kernel $b_n$.
 - The coefficients are generated by summing the two adjacent numbers in the row above.
 - The variance $\sigma^2$ increases by $1/4$ with each subsequent row.

concepts.title: Compact Integer Approximation of Gaussian Coefficients
concepts.one_liner: Binomial coefficients provide a compact approximation of Gaussian coefficients using only integers.
concepts.content: Binomial coefficients provide a compact approximation of the Gaussian coefficients using only integers. Note that the values of $b_2$ are different from $g_5$ despite that both will be used as approximations to a Gaussian with the same variance $\sigma^2 = 1/2$. The thing to note is that the variance of $g_5$ is not really $\sigma^2 = 1/2$ despite being obtained by discretizing a Gaussian with that variance.
concepts.motivation_md: Using integer coefficients instead of floating-point values makes filtering operations significantly faster and more hardware-friendly while maintaining a more accurate variance than naive discretization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Binomial filters use integer coefficients for efficient computation.
 - They provide a more reliable variance approximation than direct discretization of a Gaussian.
 - $b_2$ and $g_5$ both approximate $\sigma^2=1/2$ but use different values and have different actual variances.

concepts.title: DC Gain and Spatial Variance of Binomial Filters
concepts.one_liner: The DC gain of a binomial filter $b_n$ is $2^n$ and its spatial variance is $\sigma^2 = n/4$.
concepts.content: The sum of all the coefficients (DC gain) for each binomial filter $b_n$ is $2^n$, and their spatial variance is $\sigma^2 = n/4$.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the DC gain and variance allows for proper normalization of the filter and predictable control over the amount of blurring applied to an image.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DC gain (sum of coefficients) for $b_n$ is $2^n$.
 - The spatial variance of $b_n$ is defined as $\sigma^2 = n/4$.

concepts.title: Convolution Property of Binomial Filters
concepts.one_liner: The convolution of two binomial filters results in another binomial filter, mirroring the continuous Gaussian property.
concepts.content: One remarkable property of the binomial filters is that $b_n \circ b_m = b_{n+m}$, and, therefore, $\sigma_n^2 + \sigma_m^2 = \sigma_{n+m}^2$, which is analogous to the Gaussian property in the continuous domain. That is, the convolution of two binomial filters is another binomial filter.
concepts.motivation_md: This property ensures that applying multiple binomial filters in sequence is mathematically consistent and predictable, unlike naive discrete Gaussian approximations.
concepts.recap_md:
- $b_n \circ b_m = b_{n+m}$.
 - The variances add linearly: $\sigma_n^2 + \sigma_m^2 = \sigma_{n+m}^2$.
 - This property makes binomial filters a mathematically sound discrete alternative to Gaussians.

concepts.title: Three-tap Binomial Kernel
concepts.one_liner: The 3-tap binomial kernel $b_2 = [1, 2, 1]$ is the simplest even approximation to a Gaussian filter.
concepts.content: The simplest approximation to the Gaussian filter is the 3-tap binomial kernel: $$b_2 = [1, 2, 1]$$ This filter is interesting because it is even (so it can be applied to an image without producing any translation) and its discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is: $$B_2 [u] = 2+2 \cos (2 \pi u/N)$$ The frequency gain decreases monotonically with spatial frequency $u$ and becomes zero at the highest frequency. (see figure: 1D Binomial Filter.) (see figure: Fourier Transform of Binomial Filter.) Fig (a) A one-dimensional three-tap approximation to the Gaussian filter ($[1,2,1]$) and, (b) its Fourier transform for $N=20$ samples.
concepts.motivation_md: The $[1, 2, 1]$ kernel is a fundamental building block in image processing, offering a zero-phase (no shift) low-pass filter that is extremely fast to compute.
concepts.recap_md:
- The kernel $b_2 = [1, 2, 1]$ is the simplest even binomial filter.
 - It has a monotonic frequency response with no ripples.
 - It completely eliminates the highest spatial frequencies.

concepts.title: Monotonicity and Fourier Transform of Even Binomial Filters
concepts.one_liner: Even binomial filters are successive convolutions of the $[1,2,1]$ kernel and possess monotonic Fourier transforms.
concepts.content: All the even binomial filters can be written as successive convolutions with the kernel $[1,2,1]$. Therefore, their Fourier transform is a power of the Fourier transform of the filter $[1,2,1]$ and therefore they are also monotonic: $$B_{2n} [u] = (2+2 \cos (2 \pi u/N))^n$$
concepts.motivation_md: Monotonicity in the frequency domain is desirable because it ensures that the filter smoothly attenuates high frequencies without introducing artificial 'ripples' or artifacts in the image.
concepts.recap_md:
- Even binomial filters $b_{2n}$ are formed by convolving $b_2$ with itself $n$ times.
 - Their Fourier transforms are powers of the $b_2$ transform.
 - They maintain a monotonic decrease in gain across spatial frequencies.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through DAGs

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation can be extended to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) by introducing special merge and branch modules to handle nodes with multiple inputs and outputs.
concepts.content:
Backpropagation is not limited to chain-like graphs; it can also handle Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). In a DAG, nodes can have multiple inputs and multiple outputs. To work with general DAGs, it helps to introduce two special modules that construct the topology of the graph: `merge` and `branch` (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.).

Mathematically, these are defined as variable concatenation and copying:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{merge}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b) &\triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b] \triangleq \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}\\
    \texttt{branch}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) &\triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}] \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]
\end{aligned}$$

The shape of the data tensors (e.g., images as two-dimensional arrays) does not impact the underlying math. The `merge` operator concatenates inputs, and its backward pass simply picks out the corresponding parts of the gradient vector. The `branch` operator sends copies of the same output to multiple downstream nodes; its backward pass sums the gradients coming back from those different paths. Both modules have no parameters, so no parameter gradients are needed. These layers allow for the construction of any DAG computation graph (see figure: Merge and branch layers `forward` and `backward`.).
concepts.motivation_md: Standard backpropagation is often introduced for simple sequential chains. However, modern neural architectures like ResNets or Inception modules involve complex branching and merging. Extending backprop to DAGs allows for the training of these more sophisticated and non-linear topologies.
concepts.recap_md: - Backpropagation handles DAGs by using `merge` (concatenation) and `branch` (copying) operations.

concepts.title: Merge Operator

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: The merge operator constructs graph topology by concatenating multiple input variables into a single multidimensional output.
concepts.content:
The `merge` operator is a special module used to construct the topology of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.). It takes two inputs and concatenates them to result in a new multidimensional variable:
$$\texttt{merge}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b) \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b] \triangleq \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$$

While binary merging is standard, $N$-way merging can be done analogously or by repeating the operator. The backward pass equation is straightforward: to compute the gradient of the cost with respect to an input $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}$, we have:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^{a} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}^a} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\Big[\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}, \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{b}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\Big]^\mathsf{T}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[1, 0]^\mathsf{T}
\end{aligned}$$
This means the backward pass simply picks out the first half of the $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ gradient vector for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^a$ and the second half for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^b$.
concepts.motivation_md: The merge operator is necessary for layers that require multiple distinct inputs, such as combining features from different branches of a neural network into a single vector for further processing.
concepts.recap_md: - The merge operator concatenates multiple inputs into a single multidimensional variable.

concepts.title: Branch Operator

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: The branch operator sends copies of a single input to multiple downstream nodes, resulting in the summation of gradients during the backward pass.
concepts.content:
The `branch` operator is a module used to construct Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) by sending copies of the same output to multiple downstream nodes (see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.). Mathematically, it is defined as:
$$\texttt{branch}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}] \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]$$

In the backward pass, the module receives multiple gradients from different downstream paths, represented as the gradient vector $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b]$. The backward pass output is computed as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}&= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}\\
    &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] \frac{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}}\\
    &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] [1, 1]^\mathsf{T}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a + \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b
\end{aligned}$$
Thus, branching simply sums all the gradients passed backward to it. While binary branching is shown, $N$-way branching follows the same logic.
concepts.motivation_md: Branching allows a single piece of data or a parameter to influence multiple parts of a model. Summing the gradients during backpropagation ensures that the total influence of that variable on the final loss is correctly accounted for.
concepts.recap_md: - The branch operator copies a single input to multiple outputs.

concepts.title: Parameter Sharing
concepts.one_liner: Parameter sharing occurs when a single parameter is sent as input to multiple layers, causing their gradients to sum during backpropagation.
concepts.content:
Parameter sharing consists of a single parameter being sent as input to multiple different layers. This can be viewed as a branching operation in the computation graph (see figure: Parameter sharing is equivalent to branching a parameter in the computation graph.).
