concepts.motivation_md: Standard neural network weights are fixed after training, but different inputs often require focusing on different parts of the data. The attention matrix allows the network to dynamically adjust its focus based on the specific input it is currently processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- The attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is data-dependent rather than fixed.
 - It typically consists of non-negative values.
 - It functions by allocating attention weights across the input data.

concepts.title: Dynamic Pooling

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Dynamic pooling is a form of mean pooling where weights are dynamically decided based on the input data.
concepts.content: Attention can be described as fully connected layers with data-dependent weights. Alternatively, attention can be viewed as a kind of dynamic pooling. This is similar to mean pooling but uses a weighted average where the weights are dynamically decided based on the input data.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard pooling operations like mean or max pooling treat all elements in a window the same way regardless of their content. Dynamic pooling allows the network to prioritize more relevant information within the pooling operation based on the input itself.
concepts.recap_md:
- Dynamic pooling is a weighted average pooling operation.
 - Weights are determined dynamically based on the input data.
 - It provides a different perspective on the attention mechanism.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Query-key-value attention is the specific attention allocation function used in transformer architectures.
concepts.content: Query-key-value attention is the particular version of the attention allocation function $f$ that appears in transformers. It defines how attention is distributed across inputs by associating tokens with specific roles defined by queries, keys, and values.
concepts.motivation_md: To effectively retrieve information from a set of inputs, a system needs a way to specify what it is looking for (query), what each input contains (key), and what information should actually be extracted (value).
concepts.recap_md:
- It is the standard attention mechanism used in transformers.
 - It uses a specific allocation function $f$ to determine weights.
 - It relies on the interaction between queries, keys, and values.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Transformers use query-key-value attention, where each token is associated with a query, a key, and a value vector.
concepts.content: Transformers use a particular kind of attention based on the idea of queries, keys, and values. In query-key-value attention, each token is associated with a query vector, a key vector, and a value vector. The idea of queries, keys, and values comes from databases, where a database cell holds a value, which is retrieved when a query matches the cell's key. Tokens are like database cells and attention is like retrieving information from the database of tokens. These vectors are defined as linear transformations of the token's code vector, projecting to query/key/value vectors of length $m$. For a token $\mathbf{t}$, we have: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ query}\\ \mathbf{k} &= \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ key}\\ \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{W}_v \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ value} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: This mechanism allows a model to selectively attend to relevant information by comparing a search criteria (query) against labels (keys) to extract content (values).
concepts.recap_md:
- Each token is transformed into query (q), key (k), and value (v) vectors.
 - Transformations are performed via learned weight matrices $\mathbf{W}_q, \mathbf{W}_k, \mathbf{W}_v$.
 - It mimics database retrieval where a query matches a key to return a value.

concepts.title: Query, Key, and Value Vectors

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Query, key, and value vectors are linear transformations of a token's code vector used to facilitate information retrieval.
concepts.content: In query-key-value attention, each token is associated with a query vector, a key vector, and a value vector. This concept is inspired by databases, where a cell holds a value that is retrieved when a query matches the cell's key. In this context, tokens act like database cells. We define these vectors as linear transformations of the token's code vector $\mathbf{t}$, projecting them to a length $m$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ query}\\ \mathbf{k} &= \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ key}\\ \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{W}_v \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ value} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: By projecting a single token into three distinct vectors, the model can separately represent what the token is looking for, what it contains for others to find, and the actual content it contributes.
concepts.recap_md:
- $\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}, \mathbf{v}$ are generated by multiplying the token vector by learned matrices.
 - The query represents the search, the key represents the label, and the value represents the content.
 - All three vectors typically have the same length $m$.

concepts.title: Database Analogy for Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: The database analogy describes attention as a process where a query matches a key to retrieve a value.
concepts.content: The idea of queries, keys, and values comes from databases, where a database cell holds a value, which is retrieved when a query matches the cell's key. In the context of neural networks, tokens are like database cells and attention is like retrieving information from the database of tokens.
concepts.motivation_md: This analogy helps humans understand the abstract mathematical operations of attention by comparing them to the familiar process of looking up information in a structured database.
concepts.recap_md:
- Tokens function as database cells.
 - Queries are matched against keys to determine relevance.
 - Values represent the information being retrieved.

concepts.title: Attention Layer Mechanics

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Attention mechanics involve matching query vectors against keys to compute weights for a weighted sum of value vectors.
concepts.content: In transformers, inputs are tokenized. For example, a textual question is represented as a token which submits its query vector, $\mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}$, to be matched against the keys of other tokens (such as patches in an image). The similarity between the query and the key, most commonly measured by the dot product $\mathbf{q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}$, determines the attention weight. Querying each token in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ results in a vector of similarities: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{s} = [s_1, \ldots, s_N]^\mathsf{T}&= [\mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_N]^\mathsf{T} \end{aligned}$$ We then normalize $\mathbf{s}$ using the softmax function to produce attention weights $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$. Finally, we take a weighted sum over token value vectors to obtain the output $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= \texttt{softmax}(\mathbf{s})\\ \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \begin{bmatrix} a_1\mathbf{v}_1^\mathsf{T}\\ \vdots \\ a_N\mathbf{v}_N^\mathsf{T}\\ \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ [FIGURE:afb7764c48883324 | A legend showing the color coding for attention components: 'query' is represented by a yellow vertical rectangle, 'key' by a magenta vertical rectangle, and 'value' by a teal vertical rectangle.] (see figure: Mechanics of an attention layer. Queries from the question match keys from the tokens representing the impala; value vectors of the impala tokens then contribute the most to the sum that yields...)
concepts.motivation_md: This process allows the model to compute a context-aware representation of an input by aggregating information from all other inputs based on their relevance to the current task.
concepts.recap_md:
- Similarity is calculated using the dot product of queries and keys.
 - Similarities are normalized via softmax to create a probability distribution of weights.
 - The final output is a weighted sum of value vectors.

concepts.title: Dot Product Similarity for Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: The dot product $\mathbf{q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}$ is the most common measure of similarity between a query and a key in attention mechanisms.
concepts.content: The most common measure of similarity between a query $\mathbf{q}$ and a key $\mathbf{k}$ is the dot product $\mathbf{q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}$. Querying each token in the input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ using this method produces a vector of similarities $\mathbf{s}$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{s} = [s_1, \ldots, s_N]^\mathsf{T}&= [\mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_N]^\mathsf{T} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The dot product provides a computationally efficient way to determine how much two vectors align, which serves as a proxy for how relevant a specific key is to a given query.
concepts.recap_md:
- Similarity is defined as $s = \mathbf{q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}$.
 - It results in a scalar value for each query-key pair.
 - These scalars are collected into a similarity vector $\mathbf{s}$.

concepts.title: Tokens as a Data Type

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A token is an encapsulated group of neurons, often represented as a vector, that serves as a fundamental data structure in deep learning.
concepts.content: A token is a fundamental data structure and group of neurons that can be viewed as a new data type. Unlike channels or batches, tokens are encapsulated groups of information where operators defined over them serve as the primary interface for accessing and modifying their internal contents. In this context, a token's internal content is a vector of neurons, represented by a column vector $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 1}$, which is also referred to as the token's code vector.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard neural networks operate on individual scalar neurons, many data types (like text or image patches) are naturally grouped. Treating these groups as "tokens"—encapsulated data types with their own defined operators—allows for more structured and expressive processing than treating every neuron independently.
concepts.recap_md: - A token is an encapsulated group of neurons, typically represented as a vector $\mathbf{t}$.

concepts.title: Tokenizing Data

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Tokenization is the process of converting raw input data, such as image patches, into a set of vectors for processing by subsequent layers.
concepts.content:
The first step to working with tokens is to tokenize the raw input data. Once tokenized, all subsequent layers operate over tokens until the output layer makes a prediction. To tokenize an image, each patch of pixels is represented by a token. The token vector is either the vectorized patch (stacking color channels) or a lower-dimensional projection of that vectorized patch. Consequently, a full image corresponds to an array of tokens.

(see figure: Tokenization: converting an image to a set of vectors. $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{tokenize}}$ is a learnable linear projection from the dimensionality of the vectorized crops to $d$ dimensions. This is...)
concepts.motivation_md: Before a transformer or token-based network can process raw data like an image, the data must be converted into a discrete set of vector embeddings. Tokenization provides this bridge, turning continuous or high-dimensional raw inputs into a structured format the model can manipulate.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokenization converts raw data into a set of vectors (tokens) for model processing.

concepts.title: Matrix Representation of Tokens

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A sequence or set of tokens is represented by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$, where each row is a transposed token vector.
concepts.content:
A sequence of tokens is denoted by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$, where each token $\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N$ is transposed to become a row of the matrix:

$$\mathbf{T} = 
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\
    \vdots \\
    \mathbf{t}_N^\mathsf{T}\\
\end{bmatrix}$$

Graphically, $\mathbf{T}$ is constructed from the tokens as shown in Figure 1.1.6:

(see figure: In this chapter, we will represent a set of tokens as a matrix whose rows are the token vectors.)

Transformers are invariant to permutations of the input sequence, so groups of tokens are effectively treated as sets rather than ordered sequences. This notation emphasizes that tokens are to transformers as neurons are to neural nets; while an MLP takes a column vector of scalar neurons, a transformer operates over a matrix $\mathbf{T}$ representing an array of vector-valued tokens.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing tokens as rows in a matrix allows us to use efficient linear algebra operations to process entire sets of data simultaneously. It also highlights the structural shift from scalar-based processing (MLPs) to vector-based processing (Transformers).
concepts.recap_md: - A set of $N$ tokens of dimension $d$ is represented as an $N \times d$ matrix.

concepts.title: Mixing Tokens

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Mixing tokens involves taking a weighted sum of vector-valued tokens to produce new token representations.
concepts.content:
Mixing tokens is the operation of taking a linear combination of tokens. Unlike a fully connected layer in a standard neural net which takes a weighted sum of scalar neurons, this operation takes a weighted sum of vector-valued tokens.

(see figure: Linear combination of neurons versus tokens.)

The general equations for linear combinations of neurons versus tokens are:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{linear combination of neurons}\\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{linear combination of tokens}
\end{aligned}$$

Operations over tokens are defined analogously to operations over neurons, with the primary difference being that tokens are vector-valued rather than scalar-valued.
concepts.motivation_md: To process information across different parts of an input (like different patches of an image), the model needs a way to combine information from multiple tokens. Linear mixing provides a fundamental mechanism for tokens to interact and share information.
concepts.recap_md: - Token mixing is a linear combination of vector-valued tokens, analogous to weighted sums of neurons.

concepts.title: Fully Connected Layer over Tokens

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A fully connected layer over tokens maps input tokens to output tokens using a weight matrix and optional token biases.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard fully connected layers operate on individual features. By defining them over tokens, we can transform the entire set of tokens simultaneously, allowing the network to learn relationships between different token positions in a sequence.
concepts.recap_md: - An FC layer over tokens uses the formula $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}} + \mathbf{b}$.

concepts.title: Modifying Tokens (Tokenwise Operators)

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Tokenwise operators apply nonlinear transformations to each token individually and independently to enable the modeling of nonlinear functions.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear operations alone cannot model complex, non-linear relationships. Tokenwise operators allow the model to transform the internal representation of each token independently, increasing the network's expressive power without prematurely mixing information between tokens.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokenwise operators apply a function $F_{\theta}$ to each token independently.

concepts.title: Token Nets

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Token nets are computation graphs that use tokens as primary nodes, alternating between linear mixing layers and tokenwise nonlinearities.
concepts.content:
Token nets are computation graphs that use tokens as the primary nodes rather than individual neurons. They function similarly to neural nets by alternating between layers that mix nodes in linear combinations (such as fully connected or convolutional layers) and layers that apply pointwise nonlinearities (such as per-token MLPs). Because tokens are groups of neurons, a token net is essentially a neural net viewed as a "net of subnets."

(see figure: Neural nets versus token nets. The arrows here represent any functional dependency between the nodes (note that different arrows represent different types of functions).)
concepts.motivation_md: By organizing neurons into tokens, we can design architectures that are more intuitive for structured data. Token nets provide a framework for understanding how modern architectures like Transformers operate on higher-level primitives than simple scalar values.
concepts.recap_md: - Token nets use tokens as primary nodes instead of individual neurons.

concepts.title: The Attention Layer

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: An attention layer is a linear combination of tokens where the weights are dynamically determined by the input data rather than being fixed parameters.
concepts.content:
Attention layers define a special kind of linear combination of tokens using an attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$ instead of a fixed weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$. The key distinction is that $\mathbf{A}$ is data-dependent; its values are a function $f$ of the input data. $\mathbf{A}$ typically contains non-negative values, representing the amount of "attention" paid to each input token.

(see figure: Fully-connected layers versus attention layers.)

The equation for an attention layer is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{A} &= f(\ldots) \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ attention}\\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}
\end{aligned}$$

Attention can be viewed as a form of dynamic pooling or a weighted average where weights are decided based on the input. For example, in an image query task, $f$ might assign high weights to tokens matching a specific text query (like "animal heads") and low weights to others. This allows the layer to dynamically change its behavior in response to different inputs.

(see figure: How attention can be allocated across different regions (tokens) in an image. The token code vectors consist of multiple dimensions and each can encode a different attribute of the token. To the left...)
concepts.motivation_md: Fixed weights in standard layers mean the model always looks at the same locations for information. Attention allows the model to focus on different parts of the input depending on the context, enabling it to answer specific queries or handle variable-length data more effectively.
concepts.recap_md: - Attention layers use data-dependent weights $\mathbf{A} = f(\text{data})$ to combine tokens.

concepts.title: Filter Decomposition via SVD
concepts.one_liner: Any $M \times N$ filter can be decomposed as a linear sum of separable filters by applying the singular value decomposition (SVD) to the kernel array.
concepts.content: Any $M \times N$ filter can be decomposed as a linear sum of $\min(N,M)$ separable filters. These separable filters are obtained by applying the singular value decomposition (SVD) to the kernel array $\mathbf{w}$. The SVD results in three matrices, $\mathbf{U}$, $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{V}$, such that $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T}$, where the columns of $\mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ are the separable 1D filters and the diagonal values of the diagonal matrix $\mathbf{S}$ are the linear weights. Computational benefits are only obtained when using small linear combinations for large kernels. In a neural network, one could use only separable filters for all the units, allowing the learning process to discover ways of combining them to build more complex, nonseparable kernels.
concepts.motivation_md: Decomposing large filters into separable 1D components significantly reduces the number of multiplications required for convolution, improving computational efficiency while allowing networks to learn complex spatial patterns from simpler building blocks.
concepts.recap_md: - SVD decomposes an $M \times N$ kernel into a weighted sum of separable 1D filters.

concepts.title: Downsampling and Upsampling Pyramids in CNNs
concepts.one_liner: CNNs can be structured as analysis and synthesis pyramids by using downsampling and upsampling layers to process signals at multiple scales.
concepts.content: CNNs can be structured as analysis and synthesis pyramids, which serve as a powerful tool for image processing. To create a pyramid, a method of downsampling the signal during analysis and upsampling during synthesis must be introduced. In CNNs, these operations are performed using specialized downsampling and upsampling layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Image pyramids allow neural networks to process information at multiple resolutions, enabling the model to capture both fine-grained local details and broad global context within a single architecture.
concepts.recap_md: - Analysis pyramids use downsampling to reduce signal resolution for feature extraction.

concepts.title: Downsampling Layer
concepts.one_liner: Downsampling layers transform input tensors into smaller spatial dimensions, typically through strided convolution or pooling.
concepts.content: Downsampling layers transform the input tensor to an output tensor that is smaller in the spatial dimensions: $\mathbb{R}^{N \times M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N/s_n \times M/s_m}$. One common kind of downsampling layer is strided convolution, which is equivalent to convolution followed by subsampling. Another frequent implementation is the pooling layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Downsampling reduces the spatial resolution of feature maps, which decreases the computational cost of subsequent layers and increases the effective receptive field of the filters.
concepts.recap_md: - These layers reduce the spatial dimensions of a tensor from $(N, M)$ to $(N/s_n, M/s_m)$.

concepts.title: Upsampling Layer
concepts.one_liner: Upsampling layers increase the spatial dimensions of a tensor, often by dilating the signal with zeros before applying a convolution.
concepts.content: Upsampling layers perform the opposite transformation of downsampling, outputting a tensor that is larger in the spatial dimensions than the input: $\mathbb{R}^{N \times M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{Ns_n \times Ms_m}$. One kind of upsampling layer is the analogue of strided convolution; instead of subsampling, it dilates the signal then convolves. Starting with a blank image of zeros, $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$, the operation is defined as: $$\begin{aligned} h[ns_n, ms_m] &= x_{\texttt{in}}[n, m] & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{dilation}\\ \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{w} \star \mathbf{h} + b & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv} \end{aligned}$$ This equation applies for all integer values of $n \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ and $m \in \{1,\ldots,M\}$. These layers are sometimes called UpConv or deconvolution layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Upsampling is necessary for tasks that require high-resolution output from low-resolution feature maps, such as image segmentation, super-resolution, and generative modeling.
concepts.recap_md: - Upsampling layers increase spatial dimensions from $(N, M)$ to $(Ns_n, Ms_m)$.

concepts.title: UpConv Layer (Deconvolution Layer)
concepts.one_liner: An UpConv layer is a combination of dilation and convolution used to increase the spatial resolution of a tensor.
concepts.content: Sometimes the combination of dilation and convolution layers is called an UpConv layer or a deconvolution layer. It is important to note that in this context, the term deconvolution has a different meaning than its standard definition in signal processing.
concepts.motivation_md: The UpConv layer provides a learnable way to increase spatial resolution, allowing the network to reconstruct spatial details from compressed feature representations.
concepts.recap_md: - UpConv layers combine signal dilation with convolution for upsampling.

concepts.title: Nonlinear Filtering Layer
concepts.one_liner: Nonlinear filtering layers process local windows of an input tensor using a nonlinear function instead of a standard linear convolution.
concepts.content: Nonlinear filtering layers define filters that are nonlinear rather than linear or affine. Like convolutional filters, these filters slide across the input tensor and process each window identically and independently, but the operation they perform is a nonlinear function of the local window.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard convolutions are linear; nonlinear filtering layers allow the network to capture complex, non-additive local relationships that linear filters cannot represent.
concepts.recap_md: - These filters slide across the input and process each window independently.

concepts.title: Pooling Layer
concepts.one_liner: Pooling layers are downsampling layers that summarize local patches using aggregate statistics like the mean or maximum value.
concepts.content: Pooling layers are downsampling layers that summarize the information in a patch using some aggregate statistic, such as the patch's mean value (mean pooling) or its max value (max pooling), defined as follows: $$\begin{aligned} x_{\texttt{out}}[i]= \max_{i \in \mathcal{N}(i)} x_{\texttt{in}}[i]& \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{max pooling}\\ x_{\texttt{out}}[i]= \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}(i)} x_{\texttt{in}}[i]& \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{mean pooling} \end{aligned}$$ The term $\mathcal{N}(i)$ indicates the set of indices in the same patch as index $i$.
concepts.motivation_md: Pooling reduces the spatial size of representation to reduce the amount of parameters and computation in the network, and also to control overfitting by providing a form of translation invariance.
concepts.recap_md: - Pooling summarizes a local patch into a single representative statistic.

concepts.title: Mean Pooling
concepts.one_liner: Mean pooling is a downsampling operation that summarizes a patch by calculating the average value of its elements.
concepts.content: Mean pooling is a downsampling technique that summarizes a patch's information by calculating its mean value. It is defined as: $$x_{\texttt{out}}[i]= \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}(i)} x_{\texttt{in}}[i]$$ The $\mathcal{N}(i)$ indicates the set of indices in the same patch as index $i$.
concepts.motivation_md: Mean pooling is used to reduce spatial resolution while preserving the average signal intensity of a region, often resulting in a smoother downsampled feature map compared to max pooling.
concepts.recap_md: - Mean pooling calculates the average of all values within a local patch.

concepts.title: Locality in Vision

position.section_title: Why Process Images Patch by Patch?

concepts.one_liner: The world exhibits locality where related things clump together in small patches, while distant things are often independent.
concepts.content: The world exhibits locality, meaning that related things tend to clump together within a single small patch, while things that are far apart can often be safely assumed to be independent. Because of this property, chopping an image into small patches is sufficient for solving many vision problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Locality allows computer vision systems to focus on local regions rather than processing every pixel's relationship to every other pixel, significantly reducing complexity.
concepts.recap_md: - Related visual elements tend to be located near each other in small patches.

concepts.title: Property #2: Processing Each Patch Identically (Translation Invariance)

position.section_title: Why Process Images Patch by Patch?

concepts.one_liner: Convolution is suitable for images because visual content is translation invariant, meaning objects retain their identity regardless of their position.
concepts.content: For images, convolution is an especially suitable strategy because visual content tends to be translation invariant. Typically, objects can appear anywhere in an image and look the same; as objects move across the frame, their position changes but their identity and appearance do not. Similarly, as a camera pans across a scene, the content shifts in position but is otherwise unchanged. Because the visual world is roughly translation invariant, it is justified to process each patch identically using the same function $f$, regardless of its position. In the context of convolutions, this means that if the input signal is shifted by some translation, the output signal will be shifted by the same amount.
concepts.motivation_md: Since objects maintain their identity regardless of where they appear in a frame, neural networks should use a mathematical operation like convolution that treats every location the same way.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual objects generally look the same regardless of their specific coordinates in an image.

concepts.title: Encoder
concepts.one_liner: An encoder is an analysis network that maps data to a representation, usually of lower dimensionality.
concepts.content: In the context of deep networks, an analysis network is called an encoder. An encoder maps from data to a representation of that data, which is usually lower dimensional. In convolutional neural networks (CNNs), encoders are typically nets that take an image as input and then downsample it, layer by layer, until producing a much lower-dimensional feature map as output. An example of an encoder is an image classifier. These networks can be made from many different architectures, including those that are not neural nets. (see figure: A convolutional encoder (top) and a convolutional decoder (bottom). The exact ordering of the operations (e.g., downsample before or after the non-linearity) is just an example and may vary in...)
concepts.motivation_md: Encoders are used to compress high-dimensional raw data into a compact, meaningful representation that captures essential features while discarding noise.
concepts.recap_md: - An encoder transforms input data into a lower-dimensional representation.

concepts.title: Decoder
concepts.one_liner: A decoder is a synthesis network that maps from a representation back to the original data format, such as an image.
concepts.content: In the context of deep networks, a synthesis network is called a decoder. A decoder performs the inverse operation of an encoder, mapping from a representation back to the data. In convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a decoder takes a set of low-dimensional features as input and then upsampling them, layer by layer, until producing an image as the final output. An example of a decoder is an image generator. These networks can be made from many different architectures, including those that are not neural nets. (see figure: A convolutional encoder (top) and a convolutional decoder (bottom). The exact ordering of the operations (e.g., downsample before or after the non-linearity) is just an example and may vary in...)
concepts.motivation_md: Decoders allow a system to reconstruct or generate complex data (like images) from a compressed or abstract set of features.
concepts.recap_md: - A decoder maps a low-dimensional representation back to the original data space.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder Architecture
concepts.one_liner: An encoder-decoder architecture combines an analysis network and a synthesis network to process images through a low-dimensional bottleneck.
concepts.content: An encoder-decoder architecture is formed by putting an encoder and a decoder together. This architecture first encodes the input image into a low-dimensional representation, then decodes the representation back into an image output. This is a suitable architecture for image-to-image problems and offers several advantages: 1) by downsampling, the internal feature maps are smaller, which uses less memory and computation; 2) it introduces an information bottleneck—a low-dimensional representation that can only transmit limited information—which forces the network to learn abstractions. (see figure: Encoder-decoder architecture. In this example, the input is an image and the output is a segmentation map.)
concepts.motivation_md: This architecture is essential for image-to-image tasks like segmentation or translation, where the model must understand the scene globally before reconstructing it.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines an encoder for feature extraction and a decoder for image reconstruction.

concepts.title: Information Bottleneck
concepts.one_liner: An information bottleneck is a low-dimensional representation between an encoder and decoder that forces the network to abstract and compress data.
concepts.content: An information bottleneck is a low-dimensional representation situated between an encoder and a decoder. Because it is low-dimensional, it can only transmit a limited amount of information, which forces the network to perform abstraction and compress the signal.
concepts.motivation_md: By restricting the flow of information, the network is forced to prioritize the most important features of the data, leading to better generalization and abstraction.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a low-dimensional layer that restricts the amount of data passed through the network.

concepts.title: Skip Connection
concepts.one_liner: A skip connection is an identity pathway that connects two disparate layers of a network to shuttle information directly across blocks.
concepts.content: A skip connection is an identity pathway that connects two disparate layers of a network, defined by the function $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$. These connections are used to shuttle information directly across blocks of layers in the net, helping to circumvent problems that arise when information must pass through many sequential layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Skip connections help solve the vanishing gradient problem and prevent the loss of fine-grained spatial information as data passes through deep or downsampling layers.
concepts.recap_md: - It provides an identity path $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$ between non-adjacent layers.

concepts.title: U-Net
concepts.one_liner: A U-Net is an encoder-decoder architecture with mirrored skip connections that concatenate activations to preserve high-frequency spatial details.
concepts.content: A U-Net is an architecture formed by adding skip connections to an encoder-decoder. In this architecture, skip connections are arranged in a mirror pattern, where layer $l$ is connected directly to layer $(L-l)$. The output of a skip connection is reintegrated into the network by concatenating the activations from the prior layer to the activations on the later layer along the channel dimension. This architecture maintains the information-bottleneck benefits of an encoder-decoder, such as memory efficiency and forced abstraction, while allowing residual information to flow through skip connections. This ensures the network does not sacrifice the ability to output high-frequency spatial predictions. U-Nets are similar to steerable pyramids, consisting of a downsampling analysis path and an upsampling synthesis path, but they utilize learned filters and nonlinearities. (see figure: U-net architecture. Each block contains a series of layers. The skip connections concatenate activations.)
concepts.motivation_md: U-Nets solve the problem of losing fine spatial detail in encoder-decoders by providing a direct path for high-resolution features to reach the output layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Arranges skip connections in a mirror pattern between encoder and decoder stages.

concepts.title: Coring Function
concepts.one_liner: A coring function modifies noisy observations by setting coefficient values near zero to zero, based on the high prior probability of zero values.
concepts.content:
A coring function is used to modify a noisy observation to reach the MAP estimate for a denoised coefficient value. If a coefficient value is observed near zero, it is set to zero, based on the very high prior probability of zero coefficient values.

(see figure: Input/output coring curve for maximum posterior denoising for the example of @fig-waveletBayes)
concepts.motivation_md: In denoising, small coefficient values are often more likely to be noise than signal. Coring leverages the statistical prior that many natural image coefficients are zero to suppress this noise.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sets coefficient values near zero to exactly zero.
 - Implements a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate for denoising.

concepts.title: Markov Random Field (MRF) Models

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: Markov random field (MRF) models assume a pixel's probability distribution is independent of the rest of the image if enough surrounding pixels are specified.
concepts.content: Markov random field (MRF) models are a powerful class of image models. The core intuition for these models is that if the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image. To fit and sample from the MRF structure requires the mathematical tools of graphical models. This Markov structure can be exploited to synthesize textures that are visually compelling.
concepts.motivation_md: MRFs provide a mathematically precise way to model local dependencies in images, allowing for complex global structures to emerge from simple local rules.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes local pixel neighborhoods determine a pixel's probability distribution.
 - Requires graphical model tools for fitting and sampling.

concepts.title: Efros and Leung Texture Synthesis

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: The Efros and Leung algorithm synthesizes textures by conditioning the value of a central pixel on a large enough region of nearby pixels.
concepts.content: Efros and Leung introduced an algorithm for texture synthesis that exploits intuitions about the Markov structure of images to synthesize textures that are visually compelling. The intuition of the Efros and Leung texture generation model is that if you condition on a large enough region of nearby pixels around a center pixel, that effectively determines the value of the central pixel.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique solves the problem of generating new texture samples that look like a given example by assuming that local neighborhoods contain enough information to predict missing pixels.
concepts.recap_md:
- Exploits Markov structure for texture generation.
 - Determines central pixel values based on surrounding local regions.

concepts.title: Nonlocal Means Denoising

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: Nonlocal means denoising computes a pixel's value as a weighted sum of all other pixels, weighted by the similarity of their local neighborhoods.
concepts.content:
The nonlocal means denoising algorithm defines the denoised image as a weighted sum of all other pixels in the image, weighted by the similarity of the local neighborhoods of each pair of pixels. More formally,
$$\ell_{\mbox{NLM}}[n,m] = \sum_{k,l} w_{n,m}[k,l] \ell[k,l]$$ where
$$w_{n,m}[k,l] = \frac{1}{Z_{n,m}} \exp{\frac{- \left| \ell[N_{k,l}] - ℓ[N_{n,m}] \right| ^2}{h^2}},$$
where $N_{i, j}$ denotes an $h \times h$ region of pixels centered at $i, j$, and $Z_{n,m}$ is set so that the weights over the image sum to one, that is $\sum_{kl} w_{n,m}[k,l] = 1$.

(see figure: Nonlocal means denoising algorithm results. (left) Original image without noise. (middle) Noisy image. (right) Denoised image.*Source*:Figure from @Baudes2011)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard filters only look at nearby pixels; nonlocal means recognizes that similar patterns (like a texture or edge) may recur far away in the image and uses them to improve the denoising estimate.
concepts.recap_md:
- Denoises by averaging pixels with similar local neighborhoods.
 - Uses a global weighted sum where weights depend on patch similarity.

concepts.title: Nonlocal Means Weighting Functions

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: The weighting function in nonlocal means determines which pixels are averaged together based on the similarity of their local structures to the target pixel.
concepts.content:
The weighting function $w_{n,m}[k,l]$ indicates which pixels are averaged together to yield the nonlocal mean value placed at a specific location in the denoised image. The parameter $h$ is typically set to $10 \sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the estimated image noise standard deviation. Sampling occurs at image regions with similar local structure as the image position to be denoised.

[FIGURE:c5b8102b308188df | Four square panels demonstrating the Non-Local Means weighting function. The first pair shows a brick wall texture with a white dot at the center; its corresponding weight map shows a grid of white...]
concepts.motivation_md: Defining weights based on neighborhood similarity allows the algorithm to preserve sharp edges and repetitive textures that simple spatial blurring would destroy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Weights are determined by the similarity of $h \times h$ pixel regions.
 - The parameter $h$ is usually scaled relative to the noise standard deviation $\sigma$.

concepts.title: Statistical Image Regularities
concepts.one_liner: Statistical image models utilize low-level regularities to constrain the space of natural images for tasks like synthesis and denoising.
concepts.content:
Statistical image models utilize low-level regularities of images in order to build a statistical model without trying to understand the content of the pictures. Modeling these statistical regularities enables many tasks, including both image synthesis and image denoising. While these models help constrain the space of natural images, simple models often fail to provide a strong enough model to sample entirely new, realistic images, as the space of natural images is a very small part of the space of all possible images.

(see figure: The space of natural images is just very small part of the space of all possible images. In the case of color images with $32 \times 32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like...)
concepts.motivation_md: By identifying patterns common to almost all natural images (like smoothness or edge statistics), we can distinguish signal from noise and generate realistic textures.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses low-level patterns rather than high-level semantic understanding.
 - Helps reduce the search space from all possible images to 'natural' images.

concepts.title: Definition of Texture
concepts.one_liner: A texture is an image composed of similar-looking elements where the representation focuses on the statistics of the constituents rather than individual elements.
concepts.content: A texture is a type of image that is composed by a set of similar looking elements. A texture representation contains information about the statistics of its constituent elements, but not about the elements individually. This concept is intimately related to human perception.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining texture statistically allows us to describe complex surfaces (like grass or sand) without needing to model every individual blade or grain.
concepts.recap_md:
- Composed of a set of similar-looking constituent elements.
 - Defined by the statistics of elements rather than their individual identities.

concepts.title: Texture Analysis and Synthesis Overview
concepts.one_liner: Texture analysis and synthesis serve as foundational problems for exploring image representations and precursors to modern deep learning approaches.
concepts.content: Texture analysis and synthesis are problems used to explore texture representations. These models are precursors of more modern approaches using deep learning. Many of the concepts and intuitions regarding why these models are successful are best understood by first exploring simple yet powerful statistical models.
concepts.motivation_md: Studying classical texture models provides the necessary intuition for how local patterns combine to form global structures, which is fundamental to understanding modern neural networks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Serves as a gateway to understanding complex image representations.
 - Provides foundational intuitions for modern deep learning methods.

concepts.title: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a general class of architecture for processing sets by forming a graph of operations over the set.
concepts.content: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a very general class of architecture for processing sets by forming a graph of operations over the set. Transformers can be considered a special case of GNNs, as they perform exactly this type of operation. While GNNs are highly versatile, they are not yet as popular in computer vision as other architectures, with the notable exception of transformers.
concepts.motivation_md: GNNs provide a flexible framework for processing data that doesn't fit into standard grids, treating elements as nodes in a graph to capture complex relationships.
concepts.recap_md: - GNNs process sets by forming a graph of operations over the set elements.

concepts.title: Definition of Natural Image
concepts.one_liner: A natural image is a sample from the relatively small subset of all possible pixel arrays that represent real-world visual scenes.
concepts.content: An image is a very high dimensional array of pixels $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. The space of all possible images is extremely large; for example, even $32\times32$ pixel thumbnails with three color channels and 8 bits per channel result in more than $10^{7,398}$ possible images. Most of these possible images consist of random noise. Natural images occupy only a very small part of this total space. (see figure: The space of natural images is just very small part of the space of all possible images. In the case of color images with $32\times32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like...) A typical sample from the set of all images consists of pixels independently sampled from a uniform distribution, whereas natural images possess specific structures and properties.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that natural images occupy a tiny manifold within the space of all possible pixel combinations is fundamental for developing effective compression, denoising, and generative models.
concepts.recap_md: - Natural images are a tiny subset of the high-dimensional space of all possible pixel arrays.

concepts.title: Visual Worlds
concepts.one_liner: Visual worlds are simplified image sets used to characterize specific properties of natural images through analytic tools and generative models.
concepts.content: As natural images are complex, researchers use simple visual worlds that retain important properties of natural images while allowing for analytic characterization. These worlds range from white noise and Gabor patches to CGI and real street scenes. (see figure: Different visual worlds, some real, some synthetic. (a) White noise. (b) Gabor patches. (c) Mondrian. (d) Stars. (e) Clouds. (f) Line drawing. (g) Computer graphic imagery (CGI). (h) A real street...) Each world has unique visual characteristics that can be captured by specific models. These models help in understanding what makes the set of real images unique and can be applied to tasks like noise removal, predicting missing high-frequencies, and filling in occluded regions.
concepts.motivation_md: By studying simplified synthetic environments, researchers can isolate and model specific visual phenomena before tackling the full complexity of the natural world.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual worlds are simplified sets of images used to study specific visual characteristics.

concepts.title: Differentiating Noise from Texture

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Differentiating noise from texture involves determining if a pattern is an independent corruption of the image or an intrinsic property of a 3D surface.
concepts.content: (see figure: Telling noise from surface texture. Which one is which?) Stationary image noise is an independent process from the image content. It is not affected by object boundaries, does not deform according to the 3D orientation of surfaces, and does not change frequency with distance from the camera. In contrast, a surface texture is part of the world; if noise were truly in the world, it would have to conspire with the observer's viewpoint to appear stationary. [FIGURE:680c813998d8644a | @fig-noiseInTheWorld (b) has noise added] Image denoising relies on this distinction, aiming to separate an image into a clean component and a noise component based on statistical models.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between sensor noise and physical surface patterns is crucial for image restoration and for understanding how the human visual system interprets scene content.
concepts.recap_md: - Stationary noise is independent of scene content and geometry, unlike surface textures.

concepts.title: Additive Stationary Noise

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Additive stationary noise is noise with statistical properties independent of location that is added to an observation.
concepts.content: Additive stationary noise is defined as noise whose statistical properties are independent of its spatial location within an image. This noise is added to the underlying clean observation. A more precise mathematical treatment of this concept can be found in the context of Gaussian image denoising models.
concepts.motivation_md: This model provides a mathematically tractable way to represent common types of electronic or sensor interference in image acquisition.
concepts.recap_md: - Stationary noise has statistical properties that do not change across different image locations.

concepts.title: Procedural vs. Statistical Image Models

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Image models can be built either through procedural descriptions like rendering engines or through statistical models that capture local neighborhood properties.
concepts.content: There are two primary ways to build image models that represent the uniqueness of real photographs. The first is a procedural description, which uses a list of objects, poses, and styles combined with a rendering engine (similar to CGI). However, this requires an exhaustive list of everything in the world. The second approach is building statistical models of images. These models attempt to capture the properties of small image neighborhoods, starting from the simplest case of a single pixel. Statistical models are foundational in fields like natural language modeling and offer a way to handle the complexity of the visual world without explicit procedural lists.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing between procedural and statistical modeling allows researchers to balance explicit scene knowledge against the ability to learn patterns directly from data.
concepts.recap_md: - Procedural models use rendering rules, while statistical models use probability distributions of pixels.

concepts.title: Independent Pixel Model
concepts.one_liner: The independent pixel model assumes all pixels are independent and their intensities are drawn from a stationary distribution.
concepts.content: The simplest image model assumes that all pixels are independent and their intensity values are drawn from a stationary distribution, meaning the distribution is independent of the pixel's location. The probability $p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell)$ of an image $\ell[n,m]$ of size $N \times M$ is given by: $$p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{m=1}^{M} p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$$ Here, $p_{\theta}$ denotes a parameterized probability model where the vector $\theta$ contains parameters that can be fitted to data using maximum likelihood or other loss functions.
concepts.motivation_md: This model serves as a baseline for image analysis, demonstrating the limitations of ignoring spatial correlations between neighboring pixels.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes every pixel's value is independent of its neighbors.

concepts.title: Sampling from a Statistical Image Model
concepts.one_liner: Sampling from a statistical image model involves generating new images based on a learned probability distribution to assess the model's accuracy.
concepts.content: One way to assess a statistical image model is to sample from it and view the resulting images. This requires knowing the distribution $p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$. For a discrete gray-scale image with 256 levels, $p_{\theta}$ is a vector of 256 values; for color images, it involves $256^3$ bins. (see figure: Fitting a statistical image model to a set of training images. Once the model is learned we can use the model to sample new images.) The parameters $\theta$ can be estimated as the average histogram of a training set or a single image. To sample a new image, each pixel is sampled independently using the intensity distribution. (see figure: Estimation of the image model parameters using one image, and then sampling a new image by sampling pixels independently using the histogram of the training image.) In the multinomial model, the probability of a pixel at $(n,m)$ having value $k$ is $p_{\theta}(\ell [n,m] = k) = \theta_k$. (see figure: Examples of images and corresponding random samples with the same distribution of pixel intensities. Only the image with stars (a) has some visual similarity with the randomly sampled image.) While this works for simple cases like star fields, it fails for complex images because treating pixels as independent observations ignores the inherent structure of images.
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling allows for a qualitative visual inspection of what a statistical model has actually learned, revealing whether it captures the essential structures of the target data.
concepts.recap_md: - New images are generated by sampling each pixel independently from a learned histogram.

concepts.title: Maximal Clique
concepts.one_liner: A maximal clique is a clique that cannot include more nodes of the graph without losing the clique property.
concepts.content:
A **maximal clique** is a clique that can't include more nodes of the graph without losing the clique property. The sets of nodes below form maximal cliques (left), or do not (right):

[FIGURE:a834d415de54d03b | A maximal clique is the largest possible clique.]
concepts.motivation_md: In graph theory and graphical models, identifying maximal cliques is essential for understanding the largest possible sets of fully interconnected variables, which often define the factors in a probability distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - A maximal clique is a clique that cannot be extended by adding another adjacent vertex.

concepts.title: Markov Chain
concepts.one_liner: A Markov chain is a graphical model structure where variables form a linear sequence and satisfy the Markov property.
concepts.content:
In perception problems, we typically have both observed and unobserved variables. A simple **Markov chain** structure consists of observed variables $y_i$ and unobserved variables $x_i$:

(see figure: Same three-node Markov chain of @fig-chain.)

This is a chain because the variables form a linear sequence. It's a Markov chain structure because the hidden variables have the Markov property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all the variables shown here is $p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) = \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$. Using $p(a,b) = p(a \bigm | b) p(b)$, we can also write the probability of the $x$ variables conditioned on the observations $y$,

$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3 \bigm | y_1, y_2, y_3) = \frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3).$$

For brevity, we write $p(\mathbf{y})$ for $p(y_1, y_2, y_3)$. Thus, to form the conditional distribution, within a normalization factor, we simply include the observed variable values into the joint probability. For vision applications, we often use such Markov chain structures to describe events over time.
concepts.motivation_md: Markov chains are used to model sequences where the future state depends only on the current state, making them ideal for describing temporal events or linear dependencies in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Variables in a Markov chain form a linear sequence where hidden variables satisfy the Markov property.

concepts.title: Markov Random Field (MRF)
concepts.one_liner: A Markov random field (MRF) is a two-dimensional graphical structure used to capture spatial relationships between variables.
concepts.content:
To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is useful, called a **Markov random field** (MRF):

(see figure: Two-dimensional Markov random field.)

Then the joint probability over all the variables factorizes into this product:

$$p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \prod_{(i,j)} \phi_{ij}(x_i, x_j) \prod_i \psi_i(x_i, y_i),$$

where the first product is over all spatial neighbors $i$ and $j$, and the second product is over all nodes $i$. An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is depicted in (see figure: A low-resolution photograph of a tree branch with green leaves against a gray background. A small rectangular red box highlights a specific region of the image, likely to illustrate a local...), which shows a small image region and its context. (see figure: A grid of nodes representing pixels in an image, connected in a Markov Random Field (MRF) structure. Each node is colored either blue or red, representing a binary segmentation of the image into two...) shows an MRF with each node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel. The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are shown as the color of each node in this illustration.
concepts.motivation_md: While Markov chains handle linear sequences, MRFs are designed to model spatial dependencies in 2D data, such as pixel relationships in image segmentation.
concepts.recap_md: - MRFs use a 2D grid structure to model spatial dependencies between neighboring nodes.

concepts.title: Directed Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: Directed graphical models describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of conditional probability distributions.
concepts.content:
In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical model is commonly used. **Directed graphical models** describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating arrows pointing into it. So this graph

(see figure: A directed graphical model with three variables.)

denotes the joint probability,

$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3) = p(x_2) p(x_1 \bigm | x_2) p(x_3 \bigm | x_2)$$

The general rule for writing the joint probability described by a directed graph is this: Each node, $x_n$, contributes the factor $p(x_n \bigm | x_{\Xi})$, where $\Xi$ is the set of nodes with arrows pointing in to node $x_n$. Directed graphical models are often used to describe causal processes.
concepts.motivation_md: Directed graphical models are particularly useful for representing causal relationships and hierarchical dependencies where the direction of influence is known.
concepts.recap_md: - Each node contributes a conditional probability factor based on its parent nodes.

concepts.title: Likelihood Term
concepts.one_liner: The likelihood term $p(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.content: The **likelihood term** $p(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The likelihood term is a fundamental component of Bayesian inference, quantifying how well a specific model or scene explains the observed data.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the probability of observations given a specific state or scene.

concepts.title: Prior Probability
concepts.one_liner: The prior probability $p(\mathbf{x})$ tells the probability of any given scene $\mathbf{x}$ occurring.
concepts.content: The **prior probability**, $p(\mathbf{x})$, tells the probability of any given scene $\mathbf{x}$ occurring.
concepts.motivation_md: Priors allow us to incorporate existing knowledge or assumptions about the world into our probabilistic models before any data is observed.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the probability of a state occurring independently of any observations.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.one_liner: The evidence is the denominator $P(\mathbf{y})$ in Bayes' rule, which is constant with respect to the variables being estimated.
concepts.content: The denominator, $P(\mathbf{y})$, is called the **evidence**. In inference, it is often ignored as it is constant with respect to the variables we seek to estimate, $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The evidence acts as a normalization constant in Bayes' rule, ensuring that the posterior distribution sums to one.
concepts.recap_md: - The evidence $P(\mathbf{y})$ is the total probability of the observed data.

concepts.title: Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) Estimate
concepts.one_liner: The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability $p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y})$.
concepts.content: Selecting the best estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ requires specifying a penalty for making a wrong guess. If we penalize all wrong answers equally, the best strategy is to guess the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability, $p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y})$. This is because any other explanation $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ for the observations $\mathbf{y}$ would be less probable. This approach is called the **maximum a posteriori** (MAP) estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: MAP estimation provides a single 'best' guess for an unknown variable by combining observed data with prior knowledge.
concepts.recap_md: - The MAP estimate is the mode of the posterior distribution.

concepts.title: Histogram Matching
concepts.one_liner: Histogram matching is a pixelwise transformation that modifies an image so its intensity distribution matches the histogram of another image.
concepts.content: Manipulating image histograms is a very useful operation. Given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ with histograms $\mathbf{h}_1$ and $\mathbf{h}_2$, we look for a pixelwise transformation $f\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$ so that the histogram of the transformed image, $f\left(\ell_1 [n,m] \right)$, matches the histogram of $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. There are many ways in which histograms can be transformed. One natural choice is a transformation that preserves the ordering of pixels intensities.
concepts.motivation_md: While simple histogram models are poor generative models for creating realistic images, histogram manipulation is a powerful tool for image processing and adjusting visual characteristics.
concepts.recap_md:
- It seeks a pixelwise function $f$ to align the intensity distribution of one image with another.
- A common approach is to use transformations that preserve the original ordering of pixel intensities.

concepts.title: Perceptual Importance of Histogram Manipulations
concepts.one_liner: Simple histogram manipulations can significantly alter the perceived material properties of objects, such as changing a surface from shiny to matte.
concepts.content:
The perceptual importance of simple histogram manipulations can be illustrated by spheres reflecting complex ambient illumination. By simply changing the image histogram, we can transform how we perceive the material of each sphere: from shiny to matte. For example, a sphere rendered with illumination from a campus photograph or from pink noise (random noise with a $\frac{1}{|w_x^2+w_y^2|}$ power spectrum) can have its histogram swapped with another. Modifying the image histograms within the pixels of the sphere creates a different sense of gloss, making the sphere appear to be made of a different type of material.

(see figure: Perceptual importance of simple histogram manipulations. Figure from @Fleming2001)
concepts.motivation_md: This concept demonstrates that low-level statistical properties like histograms are crucial for high-level visual tasks like material perception.
concepts.recap_md:
- Histogram swapping can change the perceived gloss or material of a rendered object.
- These manipulations show that material perception is tied to the distribution of pixel intensities.

concepts.title: Pixel Correlation Function
concepts.one_liner: The pixel correlation function measures the statistical relationship between the intensities of two pixels as a function of their spatial separation.
concepts.content:
In the quest to find what makes photographs of everyday scenes special, the next simplest image structure is a set of two pixels. If one plots the value of the intensity of one pixel as a function of the intensity value of a nearby pixel, the scatterplot is concentrated on the identity line. As we look at the correlation between pixels that are farther away, the correlation value slowly decays. The correlation, $C$, between two pixels separated by offsets of $\Delta n$ and $\Delta m$, is:
$$C(\Delta n, \Delta m) = \rho \left( \ell[n+\Delta n,m+ \Delta m], \ell[n,m] \right)$$
where
$$\rho \left( a, b \right) = \frac{E \left( (a-\bar{a})( b- \bar{b}) \right)}{\sigma_a \sigma_b},$$
and $\sigma_a$ is the standard deviation of the variable $a$, and $\bar{a}$ is the mean of $a$.

(see figure: (center) Scatter plots of pairs of pixels intensities as a function of distance and (right) cross-correlation as a function for vertical (green) and horizontal (red) displacements for the street...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the statistical dependencies between neighboring pixels is a fundamental step in modeling the structure of natural images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pixel intensities in natural images are highly correlated with their neighbors.
- This correlation typically decays as the spatial distance between pixels increases.

concepts.title: Gaussian Image Model
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian image model is a maximum entropy statistical model that accounts for the correlation and power spectrum of natural images.
concepts.content:
(see figure: (center) Scatter plots of pairs of pixels intensities as a function of distance and (right) cross-correlation as a function for vertical (green) and horizontal (red) displacements for the street...)

A statistical image model can be constructed to account for the correlation statistics and the power spectrum of natural images. If the only constraint is the correlation function among pixels, the maximum entropy distribution is the Gaussian distribution:
$$p(\boldsymbol\ell) \propto \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol\ell^\mathsf{T}{\bf C}^{-1} \boldsymbol\ell\right)$$
where ${\bf C}$ is the covariance matrix of all image pixels. This model accounts for the correlation of intensity values between different pixels rather than assuming independence.

For stationary signals, the covariance matrix ${\bf C}$ has a circulant structure and can be diagonalized using the Fourier transform: ${\bf C} = {\bf F}{\bf D}{\bf F}^\mathsf{T}$. Here, ${\bf F}$ contains the Fourier basis and the diagonal matrix ${\bf D}$ contains values $1/ w ^\alpha$ for all radial frequencies $w$, where $\alpha$ is typically set to 1.5.
concepts.motivation_md: The Gaussian model provides a mathematically tractable way to capture the primary spatial correlations found in natural scenes using the principle of maximum entropy.
concepts.recap_md:
- It models image probability using a Gaussian distribution based on a pixel covariance matrix.
- The covariance matrix is often diagonalized in the Fourier domain using a power-law decay.

concepts.title: Dead Leaves Model
concepts.one_liner: The dead leaves model is a simplified image formation model that represents an image as a random superposition of overlapping shapes.
concepts.content:
The dead leaves model is a simplified image formation model that tries to approximate some of the properties observed for natural images. Introduced by Matheron in the 1960s and popularized by Ruderman in the 1990s, the model is best described by a procedure: an image is modeled as a set of shapes (dead leaves) that fall on a flat surface, generating a random superposition.

![Images sampled from the dead leaves model, for different shapes of dead leaves. (a) Circles, and (b) Squares. ](figures/statistical_image_models/dead_leaves_squares_and_circles.png){width="100%" #fig-deadleaves}
concepts.motivation_md: This model provides a more realistic approximation of natural image properties, such as occlusion and edges, compared to simpler noise models.
concepts.recap_md:
- It simulates image creation by randomly dropping and overlapping geometric shapes.
- It captures key structural properties of natural images like occlusion.

concepts.title: Power Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The power spectrum of a signal is defined as the square of the magnitude of its Fourier transform.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform of the autocorrelation of a signal is the square of the magnitude of its Fourier Transform. The square of the magnitude of the FT, $\lVert \mathscr{L}(u,v) \rVert ^2$, is the power spectrum of a signal.
concepts.motivation_md: The power spectrum is a fundamental tool for analyzing the frequency content and energy distribution of signals and images.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is the squared magnitude of the Fourier transform: $\lVert \mathscr{L}(u,v) \rVert ^2$.
- It is mathematically equivalent to the Fourier transform of the signal's autocorrelation.

concepts.title: Power Law of Natural Images
concepts.one_liner: The magnitude of the Fourier transform of most natural images follows a power law, falling off as $1/w^\alpha$ with frequency.
concepts.content:
One remarkable property of most natural images is that if you take the 2D Fourier transform of an image, its magnitude falls off as a power law in frequency:
$$\lVert \mathscr{L}(u,v) \rVert \simeq \frac{1}{ w ^ \alpha}$$
where $w$ denotes the radial spatial frequency ($w = \sqrt{u + v}$), $\mathscr{L}(u,v)$ is the Fourier transform of the image $\ell[n,m]$, and $\alpha \simeq 1$. This property holds across all orientations.

In natural images, the largest amplitudes concentrate in the low spatial frequencies, whereas random images have similar spectral content at all frequencies. By calculating the average magnitude of the FT over all angular directions, it can be seen that the decay along the radial frequency roughly follows a $1/w^{1.5}$ decay in many examples. This property is shared across images despite very distinct appearances.

(see figure: (top) Three natural images with size 512 $\times$ 512 pixels, and one random image. (middle) The magnitude of their Fourier transforms (FT), images are transformed to grayscale by averaging the three...)
concepts.motivation_md: This power-law decay is a universal statistical signature of natural scenes, distinguishing them from random noise and providing a basis for image compression and modeling.
concepts.recap_md:
- Natural images exhibit a characteristic $1/w^\alpha$ decay in their Fourier magnitude.
- This indicates that low-frequency components (coarse structures) dominate over high-frequency components.

concepts.title: Sampling from the Gaussian Model
concepts.one_liner: Images can be sampled from a Gaussian model by specifying a covariance matrix with a power-law power spectrum.
concepts.content:
Once a distribution is defined, it can be used to sample new images. This requires specifying the parameters of the distribution, specifically the covariance matrix ${\bf C}$. Images can be generated using the $1/ w^\alpha$ model to fill the diagonal values of the matrix ${\bf D}$. These images are created by combining a random phase with a power spectrum magnitude following $1/(1+w ^\alpha)$, typically with $\alpha=1.5$. The addition of 1 to the denominator avoids division by zero. This generative process can also be applied to color images by sampling each color channel independently.

(see figure: (top) Images are generated by making an image with a random phase and with a magnitude of the power spectrum following $1/ (1+w ^\alpha)$ with $\alpha=1.5$. (bottom) Same generative process applied...)
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling allows researchers to visualize what features are captured by a statistical model and to verify if the model produces images that look 'natural'.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sampling involves using a random phase and a power-law magnitude in the Fourier domain.
- The parameter $\alpha$ (often 1.5) controls the 'roughness' or frequency decay of the sampled image.

concepts.title: Softmax Normalization of Attention Weights

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Attention weights are computed by applying the softmax function to similarity scores, which are then used to take a weighted sum over token value vectors.
concepts.motivation_md: Softmax normalization ensures that attention weights are non-negative and sum to one, allowing the model to interpret them as a probability distribution over the input tokens when aggregating information.
concepts.recap_md: - Normalize similarity scores into weights using the softmax function.

concepts.title: Self-Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Self-attention is an architecture where every token in a layer submits a query and computes a weighted sum over all other tokens in that same layer.
concepts.content:
Self-attention is a generic architecture where we don't have to hand-design which tokens interact in which ways. The idea is that on a self-attention layer, *all* tokens submit queries, and for each of these queries, we take a weighted sum over *all* tokens in that layer. If $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ is a set of $N$ input tokens, then we have $N$ queries, $N$ weighted sums, and $N$ output tokens to form $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. This is visualized below in @fig-transformers-self_attn_layer.

(see figure: A self-attention layer.)
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a general-purpose way to dynamically pool information within a single set of tokens without requiring manual specification of which tokens should interact.
concepts.recap_md: - Every token acts as both a query and a source of information.

concepts.title: Self-Attention Matrix Computation

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Self-attention transforms input tokens into query, key, and value matrices to compute an attention matrix and a weighted output representation.
concepts.motivation_md: This matrix-based approach allows for efficient, parallelized computation of all token interactions simultaneously using standard linear algebra operations.
concepts.recap_md: - Project inputs into Q, K, and V matrices using learnable weights.

concepts.title: Intuition of Self-Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Self-attention allows tokens to refine their representations by aggregating context from other relevant tokens, such as grouping patches of the same object in an image.
concepts.content:
The intuition of self-attention is that it's easier to recognize a patch given the context of other relevant patches around it. For example, in semantic segmentation, a token $\mathbf{t}_2$ representing an impala torso can be updated by attending to other impala patches to refine its representation into a more abstracted vector capturing the label *impala*. This refinement sums over token code vectors, reducing noise and amplifying commonalities. Further, a query could retrieve information from related context, such as giraffe or zebra patches, which provide informative biome context.

(see figure: One way self-attention could be used to aggregate information across all patches containing the same object, and thereby arrive at a better representation of the object in $\mathbf{t}_2$, the query...)

Actual usage is determined by training data. Tokens on hidden layers do not necessarily represent spatially localized patches; attention layers can mix information across spatially distant tokens, meaning $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}[0,:]$ may not represent the same spatial region as $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[0,:]$.

(see figure: Example of self-attention maps where each token is an image patch and the query and key vectors are both set to the mean color of the patch, normalized to be a unit vector.)
