concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the 'why' behind self-attention helps explain how transformers capture global context and relationships that local operations like standard convolutions might miss.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokens refine their meaning by attending to other relevant tokens in the sequence.

concepts.title: Multihead Self-Attention (MSA)

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Multihead self-attention runs multiple attention layers in parallel to capture different types of token similarities simultaneously.
concepts.content:
A single self-attention layer measures similarity in just one way, defined by the matrix $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}_k$. To measure similarity in multiple ways (e.g., color, texture, and shape), transformers use **multihead self-attention** (**MSA**), which runs $k$ attention layers in parallel on the same input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$. The $k$ outputs are concatenated and projected back to the original dimensionality:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^i &= \texttt{attn}^i(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}) \quad \text{for } i \in \{1,\ldots,k\}\\
    \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}} &= \begin{bmatrix}
        \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1[0,:] & \ldots & \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k[0,:]\\
        \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
        \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1[N-1,:] & \ldots & \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k[N-1,:]\\
    \end{bmatrix}\\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}
\end{aligned}$$

where $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$ is a learnable matrix that merges the heads. Unlike single-headed attention, the value vectors in MSA do not need to match the token code dimensionality because of this final projection. MSA allows for adding parallel complexity, complementary to adding sequential depth.
concepts.motivation_md: Single-head attention is limited to one 'view' of the data; multihead attention allows the model to attend to different aspects of the input (like color vs. shape) at the same time.
concepts.recap_md: - Parallel attention heads allow the model to learn different similarity metrics.

concepts.title: Token Normalization

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Token normalization standardizes the dimensions of each individual token code vector using its own mean and variance.
concepts.content: This architecture uses layer normalization before each attention layer and before each token-wise MLP layer. The normalization is performed *within* each token: the token code vector is treated akin to a layer, and each dimension of this vector is standardized by the mean and variance over all its dimensions. This `token norm` is a tokenwise operation without learnable parameters. Residual connections are typically added around these layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Normalizing within each token helps stabilize training and ensures that the scale of features remains consistent across the network's layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Standardizes each token vector independently based on its own internal statistics.

concepts.title: Permutation Equivariance of Transformers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Transformers are permutation equivariant, meaning scrambling the input token order results in an identically scrambled output order.
concepts.content:
An important property of transformers is that they are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence. This follows from the fact that both tokenwise layers, $F_{\theta}$, and attention layers, $\texttt{attn}$, are **permutation equivariant**:

$$\begin{aligned}
    F_{\theta}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))\\
    \texttt{attn}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{attn}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

where $\texttt{permute}$ reorders the rows of the matrix. Since the full transformer is a composition of these layers (along with residual connections and token normalization, which are also equivariant), the entire architecture is permutation equivariant:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{transformer}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{transformer}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Transformers are permutation equivariant. For notational simplicity, we omit layer indices on the token variables here.)
concepts.motivation_md: This property reflects that the basic attention mechanism treats the input as a set rather than a sequence, making it naturally flexible for data where order might be arbitrary or should be handled explicitly.
concepts.recap_md: - Scrambling input tokens results in an identically scrambled output.

concepts.title: Layer Selection Based on Symmetries

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Selecting neural network layers that reflect the symmetries of the data, such as translation or permutation equivariance, is a key architectural strategy.
concepts.content: A generally good strategy is to select layers that reflect the symmetries in your data or task. For example, in object detection, translation equivariance is useful because an object's identity remains the same regardless of its location. Permutation equivariance is also relevant, though scrambling image patches can disrupt spatial layout important for recognition. Transformers address this by using positional codes to reinsert spatial information into the permutation-equivariant architecture.
concepts.motivation_md: Inductive biases, like equivariance, help models generalize better by baking known properties of the problem domain into the network structure.
concepts.recap_md: - Match layer properties (like equivariance) to the natural symmetries of the task.

concepts.title: Residual Network (ResNet)
concepts.one_liner: A popular neural network architecture that uses skip connections, known as residual connections, to additively perturb inputs through blocks of layers.
concepts.content: Residual Networks, or ResNets, are a popular architecture that uses skip connections called residual connections. In a ResNet, this connection is added to the output of a block of layers $F$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{residual block} \end{aligned}$$ In a residual block, $F$ acts as a residual that additively perturbs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ to transform it into an improved $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$. If the dimensionality of $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ differs from $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$, a linear mapping can be added to convert the dimensions: $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$. Residual blocks can easily perform identity mappings by learning to set $F$ to zero. Consequently, if many residual blocks are stacked in a row, the network can learn to use only a subset of them. By setting the number of blocks to be very large, the net can essentially learn how deep to make itself to solve the task. ResNets often exploit this by being hundreds of blocks deep. (see figure: ResNet architecture. Each block contains a series of layers. The skip connections add activations from one block to the next.)
concepts.motivation_md: Deep networks often suffer from optimization difficulties; ResNets solve this by using residual connections that allow the network to learn identity mappings easily, enabling the training of much deeper architectures.
concepts.recap_md: - Residual connections add the input of a block directly to its output.

concepts.title: Residual Connection
concepts.one_liner: A type of skip connection in ResNets where the input is added to the output of a block of layers.
concepts.content: In the context of ResNets, skip connections are called residual connections. This kind of skip connection is added to the output of a block of layers $F$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{residual block} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Residual connections facilitate the training of very deep networks by providing a direct path for gradients and allowing layers to learn incremental changes to the input.
concepts.recap_md: - Residual connections are skip connections that use addition to combine inputs and outputs.

concepts.title: Residual Block
concepts.one_liner: A fundamental unit in ResNets where a block of layers learns a residual mapping that is added back to the original input.
concepts.content: A residual block is a structure where a skip connection, known as a residual connection, is added to the output of a block of layers $F$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{residual block} \end{aligned}$$ In this setup, $F$ is viewed as a residual that additively perturbs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ to produce an improved $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$. If $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ have different dimensions, a linear mapping $\mathbf{W}$ can be used: $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$. Because a block can learn an identity mapping by setting $F$ to zero, stacking many blocks allows the network to adaptively determine its depth. (see figure: ResNet architecture. Each block contains a series of layers. The skip connections add activations from one block to the next.)
concepts.motivation_md: Residual blocks allow for the construction of extremely deep networks by making it easy for layers to represent identity functions, preventing performance degradation as depth increases.
concepts.recap_md: - The block learns a residual function $F$ that perturbs the input.

concepts.title: Transformer Architecture
concepts.one_liner: A neural network architecture that processes data patches independently and then interleaves stages to globalize information across those patches.
concepts.content: The transformer is an architecture that has recently begun to supplant CNNs as a successful model for vision problems. While different from CNNs, transformers embody similar underlying principles of sensory processing. Specifically, they include stages that process each patch identically and independently, but they interleave these stages with other stages that globalize information across patches. This combination of local processing and global information exchange is a key property shared with many modern architectures beyond CNNs.
concepts.motivation_md: Transformers provide an alternative to CNNs that can capture global dependencies more effectively while still utilizing the principles of local processing and shared weights.
concepts.recap_md: - Transformers process patches independently before globalizing information across them.

concepts.title: Recurrent Neural Nets (RNNs)
concepts.one_liner: A neural network architecture with feedback connections designed for sequential computation and modeling sequences.
concepts.content: Recurrent Neural Nets (RNNs) are a neural net architecture for modeling sequences through sequential computation rather than parallel computation. Unlike feedforward neural net architectures, which are represented by directed acyclical computation graphs, RNNs are neural nets with feedback connections. A feedback connection defines a recurrence in the computational graph, meaning their computation graphs have cycles. This allows the outputs of one layer to send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline. To make this well-defined, RNNs introduce the notion of a timestep, where one timestep corresponds to one functional call to each layer (or computation node) in the RNN, mapping that layer's inputs to its outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: RNNs are designed to handle sequential data where the order of inputs matters, allowing the network to maintain a state and process information over time.
concepts.recap_md: - RNNs use feedback connections to create cycles in their computation graphs.

concepts.title: Feedforward Neural Net
concepts.one_liner: A neural network architecture represented by a directed acyclical computation graph without feedback connections.
concepts.content: Feedforward neural net architectures are models that can be represented by directed acyclical computation graphs. In these architectures, information flows in a single direction from input to output without any feedback loops or cycles.
concepts.motivation_md: Feedforward networks provide a straightforward way to map inputs to outputs for tasks where sequential dependency or memory of previous states is not required.
concepts.recap_md: - Information flows in a single direction without cycles.

concepts.title: RNN Timestep
concepts.one_liner: A single functional call to each layer in an RNN that maps inputs to outputs and defines the progression of sequential computation.
concepts.content: In Recurrent Neural Nets (RNNs), the computation graph contains cycles where outputs can send messages back to earlier stages. To make this well-defined, RNNs introduce the notion of a timestep. One timestep of running an RNN corresponds to one functional call to each layer (or computation node) in the RNN, mapping that layer's inputs to its outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Timesteps provide a discrete structure for recurrent computations, allowing the network to update its state and process sequences of data one element at a time.
concepts.recap_md: - A timestep represents one full pass through the RNN's layers.

concepts.title: Memory Propagation in RNNs
concepts.one_liner: The process by which recurrent feedback loops in an RNN propagate information across timesteps, acting as a form of memory.
concepts.content: The recurrent feedback loops in an RNN function as a kind of memory by propagating information from timestep $t$ to timestep $t+1$. This allows the network to remember information about timestep $t$ when processing new information at timestep $t+1$. By induction, an RNN can potentially remember information over arbitrarily long time intervals. Consequently, RNNs are Turing complete, meaning they can perform any computation a computer can.
concepts.motivation_md: Memory propagation allows RNNs to solve tasks that require context from previous inputs, such as language modeling or time-series prediction.
concepts.recap_md: - Feedback loops allow information to persist from one timestep to the next.

concepts.title: Separability of the Gaussian Filter
concepts.one_liner: The $n$-dimensional Gaussian filter has the computational advantage that it can be applied as a concatenation of $n$ 1D Gaussian filters.
concepts.content: The $n$-dimensional Gaussian filter has the computational advantage that it can be applied as a concatenation of $n$ 1D Gaussian filters. This is seen by writing the 2D Gaussian in the convolution equation. Letting $g^x$ and $g^y$ be the 1D Gaussian convolution kernels in the horizontal and vertical directions (where $g^x [n]=g[n,0]$ and $g^y[m]=g[0,m]$), we have: $$g \left[n,m \right] \circ \ell \left[n,m\right] = \sum_{k,l} g \left[n-k,m-l \right] \ell \left[k,l \right] = \sum_{k,l} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(n-k)^2 + (m-l)^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) } \circ \ell \left[n,m \right]$$ $$= \sum_{k} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(n-k)^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) } \left( \sum_{l} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(m-l)^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) } \ell \left[k,l \right] \right) = g^x \circ (g^y \circ \ell \left[n,m \right])$$ This saves significant computation time. If the 2D convolution kernel is $N \times N$ samples, a direct convolution scales in proportion to $N^2$. Using a cascade of two 1D kernels scales in proportion to $2N$.
concepts.motivation_md: Direct 2D convolution is computationally expensive, scaling quadratically with the kernel size. Separability allows the same operation to be performed using 1D convolutions, reducing the complexity to linear scaling.
concepts.recap_md: - An $n$-dimensional Gaussian can be decomposed into a sequence of $n$ 1D Gaussian convolutions.\n- This decomposition reduces computational complexity from $O(N^2)$ to $O(2N)$ for a 2D kernel of size $N \times N$.

concepts.title: Circular Symmetry and Separability of the Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: The $n$-dimensional Gaussian is the only completely circularly symmetric operator that is separable.
concepts.content: The $n$-dimensional Gaussian is the only completely circularly symmetric operator that is separable.
concepts.motivation_md: In image processing, it is often desirable to have a filter that treats all directions equally while remaining computationally efficient. The Gaussian is unique in satisfying both.
concepts.recap_md: - The Gaussian is the only operator that possesses both circular symmetry and separability.\n- This makes it ideal for isotropic filtering without the high cost of non-separable 2D kernels.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of the Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: The continuous Fourier transform of a Gaussian is also a Gaussian.
concepts.content: The continuous Fourier transform (FT) of a Gaussian is also a Gaussian. For a 1D Gaussian, its Fourier transform is: $$G (w; \sigma) = \exp{ \left( -\frac{w^2 \sigma^2} {2} \right) }$$ and in 2D the Fourier transform is: $$G (w_x, w_y; \sigma) = \exp{ \left(- \frac{(w_x^2+w_y^2) \sigma^2} {2} \right) }$$ Note that this function is monotonically decreasing in magnitude for increasing frequencies, and it is also radially symmetric.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing that the Fourier transform of a Gaussian is another Gaussian simplifies frequency domain analysis and explains why Gaussian filters act as low-pass filters without ringing.
concepts.recap_md: - The Fourier transform of a Gaussian is another Gaussian in the frequency domain.\n- The resulting frequency response is monotonically decreasing and radially symmetric.

concepts.title: Gaussian Fourier Transform Width Property
concepts.one_liner: The width of the Gaussian Fourier transform decreases with $\sigma$.
concepts.content: The width of the Gaussian Fourier transform decreases with $\sigma$. This is the opposite behavior to the Gaussian in the spatial domain.
concepts.motivation_md: This property illustrates the uncertainty principle in signal processing, showing that a function cannot be simultaneously narrow in both the spatial and frequency domains.
concepts.recap_md: - Increasing the spatial width $\sigma$ of a Gaussian results in a narrower Fourier transform.\n- This inverse relationship defines the trade-off between spatial localization and frequency localization.

concepts.title: Convolution of Two Gaussians
concepts.one_liner: The convolution of two $n$-dimensional Gaussians is an $n$-dimensional Gaussian.
concepts.content: The convolution of two $n$-dimensional Gaussians is an $n$-dimensional Gaussian: $$g (x,y; \sigma_1 ) \circ g (x,y; \sigma_2) = g (x,y; \sigma_3)$$ where the variance of the result is the sum $\sigma_3^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2$. This property of Gaussian filters is the basis of the Gaussian pyramid. To prove this, one can use the Fourier transform of the Gaussian and the fact that convolution is the product of Fourier transforms.
concepts.motivation_md: This property allows for the efficient computation of multi-scale representations, as seen in Gaussian pyramids, by iteratively applying smaller Gaussian filters.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolving two Gaussians yields a new Gaussian.\n- The variance of the resulting Gaussian is the sum of the variances of the input Gaussians: $\sigma_3^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2$.

concepts.title: Gaussian as Solution to the Heat Equation
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian is the solution to the heat equation.
concepts.content: The Gaussian is the solution to the heat equation.
concepts.motivation_md: The heat equation describes how physical quantities diffuse over time. In image processing, Gaussian blurring is mathematically equivalent to the diffusion of pixel intensities.
concepts.recap_md: - The Gaussian function is the fundamental solution to the heat (or diffusion) equation.\n- This links image blurring to physical diffusion processes.

concepts.title: Central Limit Theorem and the Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: Repeated convolutions of any function concentrated in the origin result in a Gaussian.
concepts.content: Repeated convolutions of any function concentrated in the origin result in a Gaussian (central limit theorem).
concepts.motivation_md: This explains why the Gaussian distribution appears so frequently in nature and signal processing as the limiting shape for repeated filtering operations.
concepts.recap_md: - Repeatedly convolving a function with itself or others leads to a Gaussian shape.\n- This property is a direct consequence of the central limit theorem.

concepts.title: Gaussian Impulse Limit
concepts.one_liner: In the limit $\sigma \rightarrow 0$ the Gaussian becomes an impulse.
concepts.content: In the limit $\sigma \rightarrow 0$ the Gaussian becomes an impulse. This property is shared by many other functions, but it is a useful thing to know.
concepts.motivation_md: This limit represents the identity operation in convolution; as the filter width vanishes, the output becomes identical to the input signal.
concepts.recap_md: - A Gaussian with $\sigma \rightarrow 0$ acts as a Dirac delta function.\n- In this limit, the convolution of a signal with the Gaussian returns the signal itself.

concepts.title: Matching Natural Image Parameters
concepts.one_liner: New images can be sampled by matching the Fourier Transform magnitude of individual natural images while replacing the phase with random noise.
concepts.content:
We can sample new images by matching the parameters of individual natural images. To process color images, we first look for a color space that decorrelates color information for each image. This is achieved by applying principal component analysis (PCA) to the three color channels, resulting in a $3 \times 3$ matrix that produces three decorrelated channels. For each channel, we compute the Fourier Transform (FT), keep the magnitude, and replace the phase with random noise. Finally, we compute the new generated image by performing the inverse FT and applying the inverse of the PCA matrix to return to the original color space. This process results in images that maintain a similar color distribution to the inputs.

(see figure: Examples of images and random samples with the same magnitude of the FT of the corresponding image. We use PCA in color space to find decorrelated color components. Then, each decorrelated color...)
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for the generation of synthetic textures or images that share the statistical properties (specifically the power spectrum and color distribution) of a specific reference image, which is useful for studying visual perception and image statistics.
concepts.recap_md:
- Use PCA to decorrelate color channels into a $3 \times 3$ matrix.
 - Keep the FT magnitude of the original image but randomize the phase.
 - Apply the inverse FT and inverse PCA to reconstruct the image in the original color space.

concepts.title: Image Denoising: Wiener Filter
concepts.one_liner: Image denoising under a Gaussian model can be solved using a Wiener filter, which provides a closed-form MAP estimate in both spatial and Fourier domains.
concepts.content:
Image denoising can be formulated using a prior on the correlation structure of natural images. In this problem, we observe a noisy image $\boldsymbol\ell_g$ corrupted with white Gaussian noise: $$\ell_g[n, m] = \ell[n, m] + g[n, m]$$ The goal is to recover the uncorrupted image $\ell[n,m]$, where the noise $g[m, n]$ has variance $\sigma_g^2$. This is formulated as finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate: $$\max_{\boldsymbol\ell} p(\boldsymbol\ell\bigm | \boldsymbol\ell_g) = \max_{\boldsymbol\ell} p({\boldsymbol\ell}_g \bigm | {\boldsymbol\ell}) p({\boldsymbol\ell})$$ The likelihood and prior functions are defined as: $$\begin{aligned} p({\boldsymbol\ell}_g \bigm | {\boldsymbol\ell}) & \propto \exp( - \left| {\boldsymbol\ell}_g - {\boldsymbol\ell} ight| ^2 / \sigma_g^2) \\ p({\boldsymbol\ell}) & \propto \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} {\boldsymbol\ell}^T {\bf C}^{-1} {\boldsymbol\ell} \right) \end{aligned}$$ The closed-form solution is a linear operation: $${\boldsymbol\ell} = {\bf C} \left( {\bf C} + \sigma_g^2 \mathbf{I} \right)^{-1} {\boldsymbol\ell}_g$$ In the Fourier domain, this is expressed as: $$\mathscr{L}(v) = \frac{A/|v|^{2\alpha}}{A/|v|^{2\alpha} + \sigma_g^2} \mathscr{L}_g(v)$$

(see figure: (Top row) Ground truth decomposition of image into Gaussian white noise and the image, uncorrupted by noise. (bottom row) Gaussian image model denoising results. Note that the estimated noise image...)
concepts.motivation_md: The Wiener filter provides an optimal way to recover an image from Gaussian noise by leveraging the known power-law correlation structure of natural images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Formulates denoising as a MAP estimation problem using a Gaussian prior.
 - The solution is a linear operation involving the image covariance matrix.
 - In the Fourier domain, the filter attenuates frequencies based on the signal-to-noise ratio.

concepts.title: Wavelet Marginal Model
concepts.one_liner: The Wavelet Marginal Model extends Gaussian models by using localized filter banks and measuring the histogram shape of filter responses to capture edges and lines.
concepts.content: The Wavelet Marginal Model extends the Gaussian prior to better capture image properties like flat regions, edges, and lines. It does this in two ways: (1) using localized filters (such as Gaussian derivatives, Gabor filters, or steerable pyramids) instead of global sinusoids, and (2) measuring the histogram shape of all filter responses rather than just mean power. For a filter bank of $K$ filters with kernels $h_k [n,m]$, and assuming filter outputs are independent, the prior model for natural images is: $$p(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{k=0}^{K-1} \prod_{n,m} p_k(\ell_k [n,m])$$ This distribution is the product over all filters and locations of the likelihood of each filtered value, where $p_k$ typically follows a generalized Laplacian distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard Gaussian models generate cloud-like images because they only capture correlation; the Wavelet Marginal Model is needed to represent the sparse, localized structures like edges found in real-world scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a bank of localized band-pass filters to capture local image structure.
 - Assumes independence between filter outputs to simplify the joint probability.
 - Models the distribution of filter responses using non-Gaussian histograms.

concepts.title: Non-Gaussian Distribution of Filter Responses
concepts.one_liner: Band-pass filtered natural images exhibit a characteristic non-Gaussian distribution with a sharp peak at zero and heavy tails.
concepts.content:
When natural images are processed with band-pass filters, such as image derivatives or Gabor filters, the resulting output follows a non-Gaussian distribution. While the histogram of an unfiltered image lacks a consistent structure across different images, the histograms of filter outputs (like horizontal or vertical derivatives) are remarkably clean, symmetric, and have a unique maximum around zero. This observation contradicts the Gaussian image model; if the Gaussian model were correct, any linear operation like filtering would result in a Gaussian output. Instead, natural images produce highly kurtotic distributions when filtered.

(see figure: (a) Input image. (b) Horizontal and (c) vertical derivatives of the input image. (d) Histogram of pixel intensities of the input image. (e and f) Histograms of the two derivatives of the original...)

(see figure: Comparison of histograms of images from different visual worlds, and band-pass filtered versions of those images. (top row) Gaussian noise. Band-pass filtered Gaussian noise is still Gaussian...)
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing that filter responses are non-Gaussian is crucial for building more accurate statistical models of images, as it reveals the sparse nature of edges and details in natural scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Band-pass filter outputs of natural images are non-Gaussian and symmetric.
 - These distributions typically feature a sharp peak at zero, representing sparse features.
 - This property distinguishes natural images from pure Gaussian noise models.

concepts.title: Generalized Laplacian Distribution
concepts.one_liner: The generalized Laplacian distribution parameterizes the non-Gaussian outputs of band-pass filters using shape and scale parameters.
concepts.content:
The distribution of intensity values in an image filtered by a band-pass filter $h$ can be parameterized by the generalized Laplacian distribution: $$p(\ell_h[n,m] = x) = \frac{\exp \left(- \left| x/s \right|^r \right)}{2 (s/r) \Gamma(1/r)}$$ This distribution has two parameters: the exponent $r$, which determines the shape, and the scale parameter $s$, which influences variance. In natural images, $r$ typically lies between $0.4$ and $0.8$. Special cases include $r=2$ (Gaussian), $r=1$ (standard Laplacian), $r \to \infty$ (uniform distribution), and $r \to 0$ (delta function).

(see figure: Generalized Laplacian distribution with $s=1$ and (a) $r=0.1$, (b) $r=1$, (c) $r=2$, and (d) $r=10$. %Changing the exponent $r$ changes the shape of the distribution, generating some special case...)
concepts.motivation_md: This distribution provides a flexible mathematical framework to model the heavy-tailed, sparse nature of image derivatives, which is essential for tasks like denoising and inpainting.
concepts.recap_md:
- Parameterizes filter responses using shape $r$ and scale $s$.
 - Natural images typically exhibit $r < 1$, indicating a highly kurtotic (sparse) distribution.
 - It generalizes the Gaussian ($r=2$) and Laplacian ($r=1$) distributions.

concepts.title: Toy Model of Image Inpainting Derivation
concepts.one_liner: The optimal value for a missing pixel depends on the shape parameter $r$ of the image prior, with $r < 1$ favoring sharp edges.
concepts.motivation_md: This derivation demonstrates why non-Gaussian priors ($r < 1$) are superior for image restoration tasks like inpainting, as they correctly preserve sharp boundaries instead of blurring them.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaussian priors ($r=2$) result in smooth, averaged interpolations.
 - Sparse priors ($r < 1$) favor sharp edges by choosing values that minimize the number of non-zero derivatives.
 - The transition in behavior occurs at $r=1$.

concepts.title: Bayesian Image Denoising
concepts.one_liner: Bayesian image denoising uses the heavy-tailed distribution of filter responses as a prior to estimate true coefficients from noisy observations.
concepts.content:
The highly kurtotic distribution of band-pass filter responses provides a regularity useful for image denoising. Assuming additive Gaussian noise with variance $\sigma^2$, the likelihood of a true coefficient $x$ given an observed noisy coefficient $\hat{x}$ is: $$p(\hat{x} \bigm | x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - �\hat{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$ Using a Laplacian prior ($r=1$) for the subbands, $p(x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right) }$, the posterior probability is: $$P(x \bigm | \hat{x}) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right)} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - \hat{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$ This Bayesian approach allows for estimating the true coefficient value. For small observed values, the posterior peak remains at zero, effectively shrinking noise toward zero, while larger observations yield estimates closer to the observed value.

(see figure: Showing the likelihood, prior, and posterior terms for the estimation of a subband coefficient from several noisy observations. (a) A zero subband coefficient is observed. (b) An observation of 0.26...)
concepts.motivation_md: By combining a Gaussian noise model with a sparse Laplacian prior, we can more effectively distinguish between actual image features (which are sparse) and noise (which is pervasive).
concepts.recap_md:
- Combines a Gaussian likelihood (noise) with a Laplacian prior (image structure).
 - The posterior distribution determines the most likely original coefficient.
 - This method naturally performs 'shrinkage,' where small noisy coefficients are suppressed toward zero.

concepts.title: Laplacian Image Prior
concepts.one_liner: The Laplacian image prior models the probability of subband coefficients using an exponential function of their absolute values.
concepts.content: The prior probability of any subband coefficient value $x$ in a natural image can be modeled using the Laplacian distribution (the generalized Laplacian with $r=1$): $$p(x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right) }$$ This prior reflects the observation that most filter responses in natural images are near zero, with occasional large values corresponding to edges.
concepts.motivation_md: The Laplacian prior is a mathematically convenient way to enforce sparsity in image representations, which is a fundamental property of natural scenes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes a shape parameter of $r=1$ in the generalized Laplacian model.
 - Represents the sparse distribution of edges and features in images.
 - Used as a prior in Bayesian estimation and denoising.

concepts.title: Minimum Mean Squared Error (MMSE) Estimate
concepts.one_liner: The minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimate is the point estimate that minimizes the average squared distance from the correct answer, resulting in the mean of the posterior distribution.
concepts.content:
If the penalty function for an estimate is the squared distance in $\mathbf{x}$, then the point estimate that minimizes the average value of that error is called the **minimum mean squared error** estimate (MMSE). To find this estimate, we seek the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that minimizes the squared error, weighted by the probability of each outcome:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \mbox{argmin}_{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} \int_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}})' (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}}) d\mathbf{x}$$

Differentiating with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ to solve for the stationary point, which is the global minimum for this convex function, we find:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \int_{\mathbf{x}} \mathbf{x} p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y})  d\mathbf{x}.$$

Thus, the minimum mean squared error estimate, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE}$, is the mean of the posterior distribution. If $\mathbf{x}$ represents a discretized space, then the marginalization integrals over $d\mathbf{x}$ become sums over the corresponding discrete states of $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In estimation, we often want to penalize errors based on how far they are from the truth. The MMSE estimate specifically minimizes the expected squared error, providing a mathematically convenient and intuitive estimate that corresponds to the center of mass (mean) of the posterior probability distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - The MMSE estimate minimizes the expected value of the squared distance between the estimate and the true value.

concepts.title: Marginalization in Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: For discrete variables, the marginal probability at a node is computed by summing the joint probability over the states of all other nodes.
concepts.content:
For the case of discrete variables, we compute the marginal probability at a node by summing over the states at all the other nodes:

$$p\left(x_i \mid \mathbf{y}\right)=\sum_{\lambda_i} \sum_{x_j} p\left(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_i, \ldots, x_N \mid \mathbf{y}\right),$$

where the notation $j \backslash i$ means "all possible values of $j$ except for $j = i$."
concepts.motivation_md: Marginalization allows us to focus on the probability distribution of a specific variable of interest by removing the influence of all other nuisance variables in a complex system.
concepts.recap_md: - Marginalization involves summing (discrete) or integrating (continuous) the joint distribution over all variables except the one of interest.

concepts.title: Messages in Belief Propagation

position.section_title: Simple Example of Inference in a Graphical Model

concepts.one_liner: Messages in belief propagation are partial sums that pass information about node states from one node to another.
concepts.content: The partial sums used in marginalization calculations are named **messages** because they pass information from one node to another. For example, a message from node 3 to node 2 is denoted $m_{32}(x_2) = \sum_{x_3} \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) m_{63}(x_3)$. Similarly, the message from node 2 to node 1 is $m_{21}(x_1) = \sum_{x_2} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) m_{52}(x_2) m_{32}(x_2)$. Note that the messages are always about the states of the node that the message is being sent to; that is, the arguments of the message $m_{ij}$ are the states $x_j$ of node $j$. The algorithm corresponding to these calculations is called **belief propagation**.
concepts.motivation_md: Direct marginalization is computationally expensive. By treating partial sums as 'messages' passed between nodes, we can efficiently compute marginals using local computations.
concepts.recap_md: - Messages represent the summarized influence of a subtree on a specific node.

concepts.title: Derivation of Message-Passing Rule
concepts.one_liner: The belief propagation message-passing rule is derived by distributing marginalization sums over a tree-structured network of pairwise potentials.
concepts.content:
This derivation describes belief propagation for graphical models with pairwise potentials $\psi_{ij}(x_j, x_i)$. Extensions to higher-order potentials can be achieved by augmenting node states until only pairwise potentials are required. 

Consider a section of a general network with pairwise potentials as shown in (see figure: Example motivating belief propagation update rule. (a) Marginalization of a graph with no loops. (b) Shows how the partial sums at $x_j$ distribute over nodes.). In a network of $N+1$ nodes, we marginalize over nodes $x_1 \ldots x_N$. If we assume the nodes form a tree, we can distribute the marginalization sum past nodes for which the sum is a constant value. 

A **belief propagation message** $m_{ij}$, from node $i$ to node $j$, is defined as the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$. By passing the summations over node states through nodes that are constant over those summations, we arrive at a factorization where we can read off the recursive message update rule. As illustrated in (see figure: Example motivating belief propagation update rule. (a) Marginalization of a graph with no loops. (b) Shows how the partial sums at $x_j$ distribute over nodes.), marginalization over the states of all nodes leaving node $j$ (not including node $i$) leads to the belief propagation message passing rule.
concepts.motivation_md: To justify the local update rules of Belief Propagation, we must show they are mathematically equivalent to the global marginalization of the joint probability distribution on a tree.
concepts.recap_md: - The rule is derived by exploiting the distributive law to push summations inside products.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation Message
concepts.one_liner: A belief propagation message $m_{ij}$ is the sum of probabilities over all states of all nodes in the subtree leaving node $i$ excluding node $j$.
concepts.content: We define a **belief propagation message**: A message $m_{ij}$, from node $i$ to node $j$, is the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining a message as a sum over a subtree allows the algorithm to recursively aggregate information from distant parts of a graph into local computations.
concepts.recap_md: - A message $m_{ij}$ summarizes all information from the subtree 'behind' node $i$ relative to node $j$.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation Message Passing Rule
concepts.one_liner: The message from node $j$ to $i$ is computed by multiplying incoming messages (excluding $i$'s) with the pairwise potential and marginalizing over $x_j$.
concepts.content:
To compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:

1. Multiply together all messages (independent probabilities) coming in to node $j$, except for the message from node $i$ back to node $j$.
2. Multiply by the pairwise compatibility function $\psi_{ij}(x_i, x_j)$.
3. Marginalize over the variable $x_j$.

These steps are summarized in this equation to compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:

$$m_{j i}\left(x_i\right)=\sum_{x_j} \psi_{i j}\left(x_i, x_j\right) \prod_{k \in \eta(j) \backslash i} m_{k j}\left(x_j\right)$$

where $\eta(j) \backslash i$ means "the neighbors of node $j$ except for node $i$." (see figure: Pictorial depiction of belief propagation message passing rules of equation (@eq-bpupdate), where $\odot$ indicates elementwise multiplication (i.e., the Hadamard product).) shows this equation in a graphical form. Any local potential functions $\phi_{j}(x_j)$ are treated as an additional message into node $j$, such that $m_{0j}(x_j) = \phi_{j}(x_j)$. For continuous variables, the sum over the states of $x_j$ is replaced by an integral over the domain of $x_j$.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule provides a local, recursive way to compute global marginals. It ensures that information is propagated through the network without redundant 'echoes' from the receiving node.
concepts.recap_md: - To send a message to node $i$, node $j$ aggregates all incoming information except what came from $i$.

concepts.title: Nosey Neighbor Rule
concepts.one_liner: The 'nosey neighbor rule' describes how BP messages convey a neighbor's belief about a node's internal state based on all other available information.
concepts.content: Belief Propagation (BP) messages are partial sums in the marginalization calculation. The arguments of messages are always the state of the node that the message is going to. BP follows the "nosey neighbor rule" (attributed to Brendan Frey): Every node is a house in some neighborhood. Your nosey neighbor says to you, "Given what I've seen myself and everything I've heard from my neighbors, here's what I think is going on inside your house."
concepts.motivation_md: This metaphor provides an intuitive way to remember that messages are directed and represent a summary of 'external' evidence regarding a specific node's state.
concepts.recap_md: - A message $m_{ij}(x_j)$ is node $i$ telling node $j$ what it believes $j$'s state should be.

concepts.title: Marginal Probability in Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: In a loop-free network, the marginal probability at a node is the product of all incoming messages and its local potential.
concepts.content:
The marginal probability at a node $i$ is the sum over the joint probabilities of all states except those of $x_i$. In a network with no loops, the conditional independence structure ensures that the marginal probability at node $i$ is the product of the sum of all states of all nodes in each subtree connected to node $i$. Because probabilities within each subtree are independent when conditioned on node $i$, the marginal probability at node $i$ is the product of all incoming messages:

$$p_{i}(x_i) = \prod_{j\in \eta(i)}  m_{ji}(x_i)$$

(see figure: To compute the marginal probability at node $i$, we multiply together all the incoming messages at that node: $p_{i}$ as another message.)

Note that the local clique potential at node $i$, $\psi_i(x_i)$, is included as one of the messages in the product of all messages into node $i$.
concepts.motivation_md: Once messages have been propagated through a tree, this rule allows for the immediate calculation of the exact marginal distribution for any node using only local information.
concepts.recap_md: - The marginal at a node is found by multiplying all messages arriving at that node.

concepts.title: Message Update Sequence
concepts.one_liner: The belief propagation update rule can be applied whenever all the incoming messages required for an outgoing message are defined.
concepts.content: To find all the messages in a graphical model, we invoke the recursive BP update rule. We can apply the update whenever all the incoming messages in the rule are defined. If there are no incoming messages to a node, such as at the leaf nodes of a tree, then its outgoing message is well-defined. This allows us to start the recursive algorithm. A node can send a message whenever all the incoming messages it needs have been computed. In a graphical model tree, we can compute the outgoing messages from leaf nodes because they have no incoming messages other than from the node to which they are sending a message, which does not enter into that specific outgoing message computation.
concepts.motivation_md: This sequence provides a systematic way to compute marginals in tree-structured graphs by identifying a starting point (the leaves) and a recursive order that ensures all necessary information is available for each computation.
concepts.recap_md: [object Object]

concepts.title: Depth-First Update Schedule
concepts.one_liner: In a depth-first update, messages are passed from the leaves up to an arbitrary root and then back down to the leaves.
concepts.content:
In depth-first update, one node is arbitrarily picked as the root. Messages are then passed from the leaves of the tree (relative to that root node) up to the root, then back down to the leaves. When computing marginals at many nodes, we reuse messages with the BP algorithm. A single message-passing sweep through all the nodes lets us calculate the marginal at any node (using the depth-first update rules to calculate the marginal at the root node). A second sweep from the root node back to all the leaf nodes calculates all the messages needed to find the marginal probability at every node. It takes only twice the number of computations to calculate the incoming messages to every node, and thus the marginal probabilities everywhere, as it does to calculate the incoming messages for the marginal probability at a single node.

[FIGURE:9560b6515cfb38e6 | A tree-structured graph with five nodes. A central vertical edge connects a top-center node to a bottom-center node. The top node is connected horizontally to two leaf nodes, and the bottom node is...]

[FIGURE:455ef9a295437c12 | A diagram of a tree-structured graph with six circular nodes. Three blue arrows originate from the top-center node, pointing towards its three neighbors: the top-left node, the top-right node, and...]

[FIGURE:a33008ecd7f522ba | A tree graph with six nodes. A central vertical edge connects a top-center node to a bottom-center node. The top node is connected horizontally to two leaf nodes. The bottom node is connected...]

**Depth-first BP message passing schedule**. Select a root node. (a) Start at leaves; (b) proceed to root; (c), perform an outgoing sweep; and (d) compute remaining messages, ending at leaf nodes.
concepts.motivation_md: This schedule is highly efficient for computing marginals at every node in a tree, requiring only two passes (inward and outward) to provide all necessary messages.

concepts.title: Synchronous Parallel Update Schedule
concepts.one_liner: In a parallel update, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has received the necessary incoming messages at each turn.
concepts.content:
In parallel update, at each turn, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has received all the necessary incoming messages. Each node sends an outgoing message as soon as it receives the necessary incoming messages.

[FIGURE:05fcd402b5e6435d | A diagram of a tree-structured graph with five nodes. Blue arrows indicate message passing from the four leaf nodes toward the two central internal nodes, representing the first step of a...]

[FIGURE:642603864966b118 | A tree graph with two internal nodes and four leaf nodes. Two blue arrows indicate bidirectional message passing along the central vertical edge connecting the two internal nodes.]

[FIGURE:8a28a6db9b463c3e | A tree-structured graph with five nodes. A central vertical edge connects a top-center node to a bottom-center node. The top node is connected horizontally to two leaf nodes, and the bottom node is...]

**Synchronous parallel update schedule** for BP message passing: Each node sends an outgoing message as soon as it receives the necessary incoming messages. Iterations: (a) one, (b) two, and (c) three.
concepts.motivation_md: Parallel updates allow for a synchronous, decentralized approach to message passing where nodes act as soon as local data is available, which is often easier to implement in distributed systems.

concepts.title: Disparity
concepts.one_liner: Disparity represents the depth of pixels as the difference in position between left and right camera images.
concepts.content: In graphical models for stereo vision, each unobserved variable represents the unknown depth of a pixel in a scan line. Often, we represent this depth as the **disparity** between the left and right camera images.
concepts.motivation_md: Disparity is a computationally convenient way to represent depth in stereo vision, as it relates directly to the observable shift of objects between two different camera perspectives.

concepts.title: Potts Model
concepts.one_liner: The Potts Model is a compatibility matrix where identical neighboring states have a weight of 1 and different states have a weight of $\delta$.
concepts.content:
The prior probability of any configuration of pixel disparity states is described by setting the compatibility matrices, $\mathbf{\phi}[s_i, s_{i+1}]$, of a Markov chain. The Potts Model defines this compatibility matrix as:

$$\mathbf{\phi}[s_i, s_{i+1}] = 
    \begin{cases}
      1, & \text{if}\ s_i = s_{i+1} \\
      \delta, & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}$$

In typical stereo vision examples, a value such as $\delta = 0.001$ is used.
concepts.motivation_md: The Potts Model is used to encourage piecewise constant solutions in image processing, penalizing differences between neighboring pixels to promote smoothness while allowing for occasional sharp transitions.
concepts.recap_md: [object Object]

concepts.title: Loopy Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Loopy belief propagation applies standard BP update rules to graphs with cycles to find approximate marginal probabilities.
concepts.content:
The BP message update rules only provide exact marginals when the network topology is a tree or a chain. For graphs with loops, exact computation depends on the treewidth, which can be intractably large for models like 2D Markov random fields. However, applying message update rules locally remains a useful operation even without global guarantees. This is the **loopy belief propagation algorithm**:

1. Convert the graph to pairwise potentials.
2. Initialize all messages to all ones, or to random values between 0 and 1.
3. Run the belief propagation update rules until convergence.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard BP is only exact on trees, many real-world problems (like image processing) involve loops. Loopy BP provides a practical, though approximate, way to perform inference in these complex graphs.
concepts.recap_md: [object Object]

concepts.title: Treewidth
concepts.one_liner: Treewidth is a graph-theoretic quantity that determines the complexity of exact marginal probability computation in graphs with loops.
concepts.content: The BP message update rules only work to give the exact marginals when the topology of the network is that of a tree or a chain. In general, exact computation of marginal probabilities for graphs with loops depends on a graph-theoretic quantity known as the **treewidth** of the graph.
concepts.motivation_md: Treewidth measures how 'tree-like' a graph is. It is a critical concept because the computational cost of exact inference algorithms grows exponentially with the treewidth of the underlying graphical model.
concepts.recap_md: [object Object]

concepts.title: Bethe Free Energy
concepts.one_liner: Fixed points of the belief propagation algorithm in loopy networks correspond to minima of the Bethe free energy approximation.
concepts.content: In networks with loops, fixed points of the belief propagation algorithm—defined as message configurations where messages do not change with an update—correspond to minima of a well-known approximation from statistical physics known as the Bethe free energy. In practice, the solutions found by the loopy belief propagation algorithm can be quite good.
concepts.motivation_md: Connecting BP to Bethe free energy provides a theoretical foundation for why loopy BP works, framing the algorithm as an optimization process that minimizes an approximation of the true energy of the system.
concepts.recap_md: [object Object]

concepts.title: Steering Equation for First-order Gaussian Derivatives
concepts.one_liner: The steering equation for the first derivative of a Gaussian filter allows synthesizing a directional derivative in any direction as a linear combination of horizontal and vertical derivatives.
concepts.content: A directional derivative in any direction can be synthesized as a linear combination of derivatives in the horizontal and vertical directions. By the linearity of convolution, this applies to the derivative applied to any filter or image. The steering equation for the first derivative of a Gaussian filter is $$g_{x}(x,y,	heta) = \cos(\theta) g_x(x,y) + \sin(\theta) g_y(x,y)$$ where $g_x$ and $g_y$ are the Gaussian derivatives along $x$ and $y$, and $g_{x}(x,y,\theta)$ is the derivative along the direction defined by the angle $\theta$. The interpolation functions are $k_1(\theta) = \cos(\theta)$ and $k_2(\theta) = \sin(\theta)$. A first-order derivative filter of any orientation can be synthesized from a linear combination of two basis filter derivatives.
concepts.motivation_md: It allows for the computation of image derivatives at any arbitrary orientation without having to re-convolve the image with a new filter for every angle, saving significant computation time.
concepts.recap_md: - A first-order Gaussian derivative at any angle $\theta$ is a linear combination of $x$ and $y$ derivatives. - The interpolation functions are $k_1(\theta) = \cos(\theta)$ and $k_2(\theta) = \sin(\theta)$.

concepts.title: Steering Equation for Second-order Gaussian Derivatives
concepts.one_liner: The steering equation for second-order Gaussian derivatives synthesizes a derivative at any orientation using a linear combination of three basis filters.
concepts.content: All higher order Gaussian derivatives have the property of being steerable, but the number of basis filters changes with the order. For second-order Gaussian derivatives, the steering equation is: $$\begin{split} g_{x,x}(x,y,\theta) & = g_{xx}(\cos(\theta) x - \sin (\theta) y, \sin(\theta) x + \cos (\theta)y) = \\ &= \cos^2(\theta) g_{xx}(x,y) + \sin^2(\theta) g_{yy}(x,y) - 2 \cos(\theta) \sin(\theta) g_{xy}(x,y) \end{split}$$ To interpolate the derivative along any orientation requires three basis filters and the interpolation functions are $k_1(\theta) = \cos^2(\theta)$, $k_2(\theta) = \sin^2(\theta)$, and $k_3(\theta) = -2\cos(\theta)\sin(\theta)$. The minus sign in $k_3$ is due to the positive direction of $\theta$ being counter-clockwise. A second-order derivative needs three basis filters.
concepts.motivation_md: Higher-order derivatives are needed for detecting features like ridges or blobs. Steering allows these features to be analyzed at any orientation using a fixed set of basis filters.
concepts.recap_md: - Second-order steering requires three basis filters: $g_{xx}$, $g_{yy}$, and $g_{xy}$. - The interpolation functions involve $\cos^2(\theta)$, $\sin^2(\theta)$, and $-2\cos(\theta)\sin(\theta)$.

concepts.title: Steerable Filter Architecture
concepts.one_liner: Steerable filter architecture uses a set of basis filters and gain maps to synthesize oriented filters at any position in an image.
concepts.content: This architecture for processing images with oriented steerable filters involves passing input images through a set of basis filters. The outputs of those filters are then modulated with a set of gain maps, which can be different at each pixel. These gain maps adjust the linear combinations of the basis filters, allowing the input filter to be steered to the desired orientations at each position. (see figure: Architecture for steerable filters. This architecture computes the second-order image derivative along orientation $\theta$.)
concepts.motivation_md: This architecture provides a computationally efficient way to apply filters at different orientations across an image, which is essential for tasks like edge detection and texture analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - Input images are processed by a fixed set of basis filters. - Gain maps modulate the basis filter outputs to achieve the desired orientation at each pixel.

concepts.title: Basis Filters
concepts.one_liner: Basis filters are a fixed set of filters whose linear combination can synthesize a rotated version of the same filter.
concepts.content: In an architecture for processing images with oriented steerable filters, input images pass through a set of basis filters. The outputs of those filters are modulated with a set of gain maps to adjust the linear combinations, allowing the filter to be steered to desired orientations at each position. (see figure: Architecture for steerable filters. This architecture computes the second-order image derivative along orientation $\theta$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Basis filters serve as the fundamental building blocks for steerable filters, allowing a continuous range of orientations to be represented by a small, discrete set of pre-computed filter responses.
concepts.recap_md: - Basis filters are the primary filters through which an input image passes. - Their outputs are combined using gain maps to synthesize filters at arbitrary orientations.

concepts.title: Gain Maps
concepts.one_liner: Gain maps are pixel-specific weights used to linearly combine basis filter outputs to achieve a desired filter orientation.
concepts.content: In the architecture for steerable filters, the outputs of basis filters are modulated with a set of gain maps. These gain maps can be different at each pixel and adjust the linear combinations of the basis filters. This allows the input filter to be steered to the desired orientations at each position in the image. (see figure: Architecture for steerable filters. This architecture computes the second-order image derivative along orientation $\theta$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Gain maps provide the mechanism for spatially varying the orientation of a filter, enabling the detection of features that change direction across an image.
concepts.recap_md: - Gain maps modulate the outputs of basis filters. - They allow for pixel-by-pixel control over the steering orientation.

concepts.title: Steering Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Steering Theorem defines the conditions and number of basis filters required to synthesize a rotated version of a filter as a linear combination of its basis.
concepts.content: The Steering Theorem quantifies how many basis filters are required to steer a given filter, which depends on how sharply oriented the filter is. For a filter with impulse response $h(x,y)$, or $h(r,\phi)$ in polar coordinates, the steering condition is the requirement that the rotated filter, $h(r,\phi - \theta)$, be a linear combination of a set of basis filters that are rotated versions of itself, $h(r,\phi - \theta_m)$ with $m \in (1,M)$: $$h(r,\phi - \theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} k_{m}(\theta) h(r,\phi - \theta_m) .$$ If the filter is expressed as a Fourier series in angle, $h(r,\phi) = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} a_n(r) \exp \left( j n \phi \right)$, the steering condition holds if and only if the interpolation functions $k_{j}(\theta)$ are solutions of: $$\left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ \exp (j \theta) \\ \ldots \\ \exp (j N \theta) \\ \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\ \exp (j \theta_{1}) & \exp (j \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j \theta_{M}) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \exp (j N \theta_{1}) & \exp (j N \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j N \theta_{M}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} k_{1}(\theta) \\ k_{2}(\theta) \\ \vdots \\ k_{M}(\theta) \end{array} \right].$$
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the mathematical foundation for steerable filters, determining the minimum number of basis filters needed to perfectly reconstruct a filter at any orientation.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates the number of basis filters to the angular frequency content of the filter. - Provides a matrix equation to solve for the interpolation functions $k_m(\theta)$.

concepts.title: Steering Condition
concepts.one_liner: The steering condition is the requirement that a rotated filter can be expressed as a linear combination of a fixed set of basis filters.
concepts.content: For a filter with impulse response $h(x,y)$, or $h(r,\phi)$ in polar coordinates, the steering condition is the requirement that the rotated filter, $h(r,\phi - \theta)$, be a linear combination of a set of basis filters that are rotated versions of itself, $h(r,\phi - \theta_m)$ with $m \in (1,M)$. The steering condition is: $$h(r,\phi - \theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} k_{m}(\theta) h(r,\phi - \theta_m) .$$
concepts.motivation_md: Defining this condition is the first step in determining if a filter is "steerable" and how to implement it efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - Requires a rotated filter to be a linear combination of basis filters. - Basis filters are typically rotated versions of the original filter.

concepts.title: Steering Theorem Derivation via Fourier Series
concepts.one_liner: The steering theorem can be derived by expressing a filter as a Fourier series in angle and solving for the interpolation functions.
concepts.content: If a filter to be steered is expressed as a Fourier series in angle, $h(r,\phi) = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} a_n(r) \exp \left( j n \phi \right)$, we can substitute this into the steering condition to find the interpolation functions $k_{j}(\theta)$. The steering condition holds for functions expandable in this form if and only if the interpolation functions $k_{j}(\theta)$ are solutions of: $$\left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ \exp (j \theta) \\ \ldots \\ \exp (j N \theta) \\ \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\ \exp (j \theta_{1}) & \exp (j \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j \theta_{M}) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \exp (j N \theta_{1}) & \exp (j N \theta_{2}) & \ldots & \exp (j N \theta_{M}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} k_{1}(\theta) \\ k_{2}(\theta) \\ \vdots \\ k_{M}(\theta) \end{array} \right].$$
concepts.motivation_md: Using Fourier series allows for a general derivation that applies to any filter, linking its angular complexity to the number of basis filters required for steering.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses complex exponentials to represent the filter's angular dependence. - Results in a system of linear equations for the interpolation functions.

concepts.title: Bottleneck
concepts.one_liner: A bottleneck is a low-dimensional representational constraint in an autoencoder.
concepts.content: A low-dimensional representational **bottleneck** is used to constrain the latent space of an autoencoder.
concepts.motivation_md: Bottlenecks force a neural network to compress data into its most essential features, preventing the model from simply learning an identity mapping and instead discovering meaningful structure.
concepts.recap_md: - A bottleneck is a low-dimensional representation space.

concepts.title: Dimensionality Reduction
concepts.one_liner: Dimensionality reduction occurs when the latent representation $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^M$ has fewer dimensions than the input $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$.
concepts.content: Typically, the key property of an autoencoder is that $M < N$, where $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^M$ is the representation. In this case, we have performed **dimensionality reduction**. While autoencoders can be constructed without this property, those versions do not perform dimensionality reduction and instead may place other explicit or implicit constraints on $\mathbf{z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Dimensionality reduction is used to find a compact representation of data, removing noise and redundant information while retaining the core features necessary for reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Occurs when the latent space dimension $M$ is less than the input dimension $N$.

concepts.title: Reconstruction Loss
concepts.one_liner: Reconstruction loss measures the difference between the original input and its reconstructed version.
concepts.content: A typical choice for measuring the quality of an autoencoder's output is the squared error **reconstruction loss**, defined as $\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{recon}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{x}) = \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2$.
concepts.motivation_md: To train an autoencoder, we need a quantitative measure of how well the decoder can recreate the original input from the compressed representation.
concepts.recap_md: - Quantifies the error between input $\mathbf{x}$ and reconstruction $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

concepts.title: Autoencoder Learning Problem
concepts.one_liner: The autoencoder learning problem seeks to minimize the expected squared reconstruction error over the data distribution.
concepts.content:
The learning problem for an autoencoder is defined as finding the optimal encoder $f^*$ and decoder $g^*$ such that:
$$f^*,g^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{f,g} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}} \left\lVert g(f(\mathbf{x})) - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2 $$
concepts.motivation_md: This optimization problem formalizes the goal of learning a representation that preserves as much information as possible under the constraints of the bottleneck.
concepts.recap_md: - Minimizes the expected $L_2$ distance between input and reconstruction.

concepts.title: L2 Reconstruction Loss Properties
concepts.one_liner: The $L_2$ loss decomposes into a sum of per-pixel errors, prioritizing individual pixel intensities over patch-level statistics.
concepts.content: The particular loss function determines what kind of information is preferred when the bottleneck cannot support preserving all the information. The $L_2$ loss decomposes as $\left\lVert g(f(\mathbf{x})) - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2 = \sqrt{\sum_i (g(f(\mathbf{x}))_i - x_i)^2}$, which is a sum over individual pixel errors. This means it only cares about matching each individual pixel intensity $g(f(\mathbf{x}))_i$ to the ground truth $x_i$ and does not directly penalize patch-level statistics of $\mathbf{x}$ (i.e., statistics $\phi(\mathbf{x})$ that do not factorize as a sum $\sum_i \psi_i(x_i)$ over per-pixel functions). Alternatively, autoencoders can use loss functions that penalize higher-order statistics, allowing for the reconstruction of edges, textures, and other perceptual structures.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the $L_2$ loss decomposition helps explain why standard autoencoders might produce blurry results; they optimize for pixel-wise accuracy rather than structural or perceptual coherence.
concepts.recap_md: - $L_2$ loss focuses on individual pixel intensities.

concepts.title: Examples of Autoencoders
concepts.one_liner: Many diverse methods, such as steerable pyramids and CycleGAN, can be viewed as specialized autoencoders.
concepts.content: Autoencoders appear in many forms throughout machine learning. For instance, the steerable pyramid and the CycleGAN algorithm can both be considered special kinds of autoencoders. Many methods in representation learning can be interpreted through the lens of autoencoding if viewed broadly.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing the autoencoder structure in complex algorithms helps unify different concepts in computer vision and generative modeling under a single framework of compression and reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Steerable pyramids are a form of autoencoder.

concepts.title: Relationship of Autoencoders to PCA
concepts.one_liner: A linear autoencoder with $L_2$ loss learns the same subspace as Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
concepts.content: Closely related to autoencoders are other dimensionality reduction algorithms like **principle components analysis** (**PCA**). In fact, an $L_2$ autoencoder, for which both $f$ and $g$ are linear functions, learns an $M$-dimensional embedding that spans the same subspace as a PCA projection to $M$-dimensions.
concepts.motivation_md: This relationship provides a theoretical bridge between classical statistical methods like PCA and modern neural network-based representation learning.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear autoencoders with $L_2$ loss are equivalent to PCA in terms of the subspace they span.

concepts.title: Evaluating Representation Quality via Nearest Neighbors
concepts.one_liner: Representation quality can be evaluated by checking if nearest neighbors in the embedding space are semantically meaningful.
concepts.content:
To evaluate if an autoencoder obtains a good representation, we can use a simple approach: see if the nearest neighbors in representational space are meaningful. This can be tested in two ways: (1) for a given query, visualize the images in the dataset whose embeddings are nearest neighbors to the query's embedding, and (2) measure the accuracy of a one-nearest-neighbor classifier in embedding space.

(see figure: A grid of images showing five query shapes on the left and their five nearest neighbors in the representation space of layer 6 on the right. Each row represents a query: a pink triangle, an orange...)

(see figure: A line graph showing classification accuracy (%) versus layer (0 to 6) for two properties: shape and color. The 'shape' curve (dashed line) starts at approximately 75% at layer 0 and increases...)

Every layer of a neural net can be considered as an embedding of the data. Using the layer 6 embeddings (the bottleneck layer) as the feature space, we can measure distance. If the neighbors are similar to the queries in terms of colors, shapes, positions, and rotations, the autoencoder has produced a meaningful representation of the data.
concepts.motivation_md: Since "representation quality" is abstract, nearest-neighbor analysis provides a concrete, visual, and measurable way to verify that the network has captured relevant semantic features.
concepts.recap_md: - Visualizing nearest neighbors helps verify semantic similarity in latent space.

concepts.title: Predictive Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Predictive encoding uses a prediction task as a pretext to train a useful data representation by mapping data through an embedding to a target prediction.
concepts.content:
In predictive representation learning, the goal is to use prediction as a way to train a useful representation rather than to make predictions per se. The method involves first encoding the data into an embedding $\mathbf{z}$, then mapping from that embedding to a target prediction. This creates a composition of functions, similar to an autoencoder, that can be trained with a prediction task to yield a high-quality data encoder. The prediction task serves as a **pretext task** for learning good representations.

Different types of prediction tasks are proposed depending on the desired properties of the representation. Examples include predicting future frames in a video, predicting the next pixel in an image sequence, or using an image's semantic class as the target. In the latter case, while the problem is identical to training an image classifier, the goal is to obtain a good image encoding predictive of semantics rather than the classifier itself. These examples are visualized below (@fig-representation_learning-predictive_learning_examples).

(see figure: Examples of different pretext tasks.)
concepts.motivation_md: Predictive encoding exists because many useful features of data are implicitly learned when trying to solve a prediction problem. By framing learning as a prediction task, we can force a model to extract meaningful structures into an embedding space, which can then be used for other downstream applications.
concepts.recap_md: - Predictive encoding trains an encoder by mapping data to an embedding $\mathbf{z}$ that must be sufficient to predict a target.

concepts.title: Pretext Task
concepts.one_liner: A pretext task is a prediction problem used as a means to train a useful data representation rather than for the sake of the prediction itself.
concepts.content: In predictive representation learning, the goal is not to make predictions per se, but to use prediction as a way to train a useful representation. The way to do this is first encode the data into an embedding $\mathbf{z}$, then map from the embedding to your target prediction. This gives a composition of functions, just like with the autoencoder, that can be trained with a prediction task and yield a good data encoder. The prediction task is a **pretext task** for learning good representations.
concepts.motivation_md: Pretext tasks provide a supervised signal to guide the learning of internal representations when the primary goal is feature extraction rather than the specific output of the task.
concepts.recap_md: - A pretext task is a proxy problem used to learn embeddings.

concepts.title: Predictive Coding
concepts.one_liner: Predictive coding is the theory that the sensory cortex only transmits the difference between its predictions and actual observed signals.
concepts.content: Neuroscientists suggest the brain uses prediction to better encode sensory signals. The idea of **predictive coding** states that the sensory cortex only transmits the difference between its predictions and the actual observed signal. While representation learning focuses on learning to make good predictions initially, predictive coding focuses on using such representations to compress future signals by transmitting only the "surprises" or prediction errors.
concepts.motivation_md: Predictive coding explains how biological systems can efficiently process vast amounts of sensory data by focusing resources on unexpected information rather than redundant, predictable signals.
concepts.recap_md: - The brain may transmit only the difference between predictions and observations.

concepts.title: Predictive Representation Learning Problem
concepts.one_liner: Predictive representation learning formally maps input data through an encoder and a predictor to minimize the distance between the prediction and a target.
concepts.content:
Formally, let $\mathbf{y}$ be the prediction target. Predictive representation learning is illustrated as follows:

[FIGURE:4b90715c8d8cd84b | A flow diagram illustrating predictive representation learning. On the left, input data is represented as a set {x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}}_{i=1}^n. An arrow points into a central box labeled 'Predictive...]

In this framework, $D$ is a distance function, such as $L_2$. The functions $f$ (the encoder) and $g$ (the predictor) are typically neural networks, though $g$ is often just a single linear layer. Unlike autoencoders, there is no standard setting for the relative dimensionalities of the input $N$, embedding $M$, and target $K$; these depend on the specific task. For example, in image classification, $N$ is the high dimensionality of pixels, $M$ is usually lower, and $K$ is the number of classes.
concepts.motivation_md: This formalization provides a mathematical structure to optimize feature extractors using standard loss functions and backpropagation.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses an encoder $f$ and a predictor $g$ to map inputs to targets.

concepts.title: Emergent structure in z-space
concepts.one_liner: Solving pretext tasks can lead to the emergence of structured representations in the embedding space that were not explicitly part of the training data.
concepts.content:
The power of pretext tasks lies in acquiring useful image embeddings $\mathbf{z}$ as a byproduct. Often, the $z$-space develops *emergent structure* not explicit in the raw data or the task itself. For example, researchers found that a CNN trained for scene classification (e.g., identifying a kitchen or bedroom) developed internal neurons that selectively fired for specific objects like staircases or rafts, even though it was never explicitly trained to detect objects. 

(see figure: Visualizing two neural receptive fields in a scene classifier neural net. Images taken from @zhou2014object)

This shows that object detectors emerge in the hidden layers of a CNN as a necessary step for recognizing scenes. This suggests that the internal parsing of scenes in CNNs may match how humans recognize and parse visual information.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding emergent structure helps explain why deep learning models generalize well and reveals how complex high-level concepts can be learned from simpler supervision.
concepts.recap_md: - Hidden layers may develop specific detectors for concepts not explicitly labeled.

concepts.title: Self-supervision
concepts.one_liner: Self-supervision is a form of predictive learning where the training targets are automatically generated from the raw data itself.
concepts.content:
Self-supervision is used when labeled targets are not provided. Instead, targets are "cooked up" from the raw data. For example, one might use the color of a specific pixel as a label for the rest of the image. Formally, it looks like this:

[FIGURE:62baf82aec2fdf08 | A flowchart illustrating self-supervised representation learning. It shows input data {X^{(i)}}_{i=1}^n entering a box labeled 'Self-supervised representation learning'. Inside the box, the...]

Here, $V_1$ and $V_2$ are functions of the full data tensor $\mathbf{X}$. A common pretext task is to predict one part of the data from another, such as predicting the right side of an image from the left, or predicting future video frames from past ones. This allows for predictive learning without manual labeling.
concepts.motivation_md: Self-supervision solves the problem of data scarcity by allowing models to learn from vast amounts of unlabeled data by creating their own supervision signals.
concepts.recap_md: - Targets are derived directly from the input data without manual labels.

concepts.title: Perceptual groups
concepts.one_liner: Perceptual groups are fundamental structures, such as objects, that visual systems naturally arrive at when tasked with understanding the world.
concepts.content:
Object detectors emerge as a byproduct of various pretext tasks, including scene classification, colorization, and inpainting. 

(see figure: Visualizing two neural receptive fields in the colorization model from @zhang2016colorful. Images generated by Andrew Owens and Richard Zhang.)
