This consistency across different tasks suggests that "objects" are not just a human quirk but represent fundamentally useful structures in the world. Any visual system attempting to understand the environment likely arrives at a similar representation, carving the sensory array into objects and other **perceptual groups**.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of perceptual groups explains why different learning tasks often converge on similar internal representations of the physical world.
concepts.recap_md: - Diverse pretext tasks often lead to the emergence of similar object detectors.

concepts.title: Abstract pretext tasks
concepts.one_liner: Abstract pretext tasks involve predicting properties like image rotation or relative patch positions to induce semantic and geometric understanding.
concepts.content: Some varieties of self-supervised learning use abstract prediction problems rather than predicting missing data. Examples include predicting if an image has been rotated 90 degrees or determining the relative position of two image patches. These tasks induce effective visual representations because solving them requires the model to learn semantic and geometric regularities, such as the fact that clouds appear at the top of images or tree trunks appear below branches.
concepts.motivation_md: Abstract tasks force the model to learn high-level global context and spatial relationships that simple pixel-level prediction might ignore.
concepts.recap_md: - Tasks like rotation prediction force models to learn geometric and semantic regularities.

concepts.title: K-means update rules
concepts.one_liner: The k-means algorithm iteratively assigns datapoints to the nearest cluster center and then updates each center to be the mean of its assigned points.
concepts.content:
The $k$-means algorithm relies on two primary update rules. First, each datapoint is assigned to the nearest cluster by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance to the current code vectors:

$$\begin{aligned} a_i &\leftarrow \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,k\}} \left\lVert\mathbf{z}_j - \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2 \end{aligned}$$

This step is a brute force enumeration of all $k$ possible assignments to select the one that minimizes the objective for that datapoint. Second, the code vectors (cluster centers) are updated given the current assignments:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{z}_j &\leftarrow \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}(a_i = j)\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \end{aligned}$$

This update is optimal because the point that minimizes the sum of squared distances from a dataset is the mean of that dataset. Thus, each code vector is set to the mean of all datapoints currently assigned to its cluster.
concepts.motivation_md: These rules provide a computationally efficient way to minimize the k-means objective function. By alternating between optimal assignments and optimal means, the algorithm iteratively improves the representation of the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Assign each point $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ to the cluster $j$ with the closest mean $\mathbf{z}_j$.

concepts.title: K-means from multiple perspectives
concepts.one_liner: K-means can be viewed as a representation learning algorithm, a simple generative model, or a discrete version of a Gaussian mixture model.
concepts.content: K-means can be understood from multiple complementary perspectives. While often presented as a representation learning algorithm, it is also a way of interpreting data or a simple generative model. Specifically, $k$-means acts like an autoencoder with a discrete bottleneck. It can also be viewed as a vanilla form of a Gaussian mixture model (GMM). These relationships form a rich tapestry: autoencoders and variational autoencoders (VAEs) are continuous versions of $k$-means and GMMs, respectively. Identifying the "delta" or difference between these models helps in understanding how new methods relate to established ones.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding k-means from multiple perspectives allows researchers to see connections between seemingly different fields like clustering, probabilistic modeling, and neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - K-means is an autoencoder with a discrete bottleneck.

concepts.title: Perceptual grouping in vision
concepts.one_liner: Perceptual grouping is the process by which humans organize visual elements into higher-level structures like contours, surfaces, and objects.
concepts.content: In vision, the problem of clustering is related to the idea of perceptual grouping. Humans see the world as organized into different levels of perceptual structure, such as contours, surfaces, objects, and events. These structures are groupings, or clusters, of related visual elements. For example, a contour is a group of points forming a line, and an object is a group of parts forming a cohesive whole. Algorithms like $k$-means, when applied in a suitable feature space, can discover these natural groupings.
concepts.motivation_md: Perceptual grouping explains how the brain simplifies complex visual input into meaningful entities, a process that clustering algorithms attempt to emulate.
concepts.recap_md: - Humans organize visual elements into clusters like contours and objects.

concepts.title: Contrastive learning
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive learning learns compressed representations by supervising the model to be invariant to different viewing transformations of the same data.
concepts.content: Contrastive learning is an approach to representation learning where a model is supervised to be invariant to certain viewing transformations. This results in a compressed representation that captures only the properties common between different data views, such as two different cameras or different modalities like color and depth. It is closely related to clustering; while clustering maps similar points to exactly $k$ distinct embeddings, contrastive learning maps similar points to similar embeddings in a continuous space. Unlike CNNs that bake invariance into the architecture, contrastive learning incentivizes invariance through the objective function.
concepts.motivation_md: Contrastive learning allows models to learn useful features without manual labels by identifying which information is essential across different versions of the same data.
concepts.recap_md: - Learns representations invariant to transformations by pulling similar views together.

concepts.title: Data views
concepts.one_liner: Data views are different versions or co-occurring signals of the same underlying data, such as different sensor modalities or transformations.
concepts.content: Data views refer to different signals or transformations derived from a total data tensor $\mathbf{X}$. For example, color and grayscale versions of an image can be considered two different views, denoted as $\mathbf{x} = V_1(\mathbf{X})$ and $\mathbf{y} = V_2(\mathbf{X})$. These views can result from sensory co-occurrences (like different cameras) or from specific transformations (like channel dropping). Ultimately, any two signals can be considered transformations of a combined signal, and any signal and its transformation can be viewed as two ways of measuring the same underlying world.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining data views allows contrastive learning algorithms to identify which features are consistent across different observations of the same object.
concepts.recap_md: - Views can be different sensory modalities or mathematical transformations of data.

concepts.title: Alignment loss
concepts.one_liner: Alignment loss penalizes the difference between representations of a datapoint and its transformed version to encourage invariance.
concepts.content: Alignment loss is a technique used to learn an encoder $f$ that is invariant to a specific transformation $T$. The idea is to penalize deviations from the desired invariance using a loss of the form $\left\lVert f(T(\mathbf{x}))-f(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert_2^2$. By minimizing this loss, the model learns to map both the original and the transformed data to the same region in the representation space.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a direct mathematical way to enforce that a model's output does not change when the input undergoes certain irrelevant transformations.
concepts.recap_md: - Penalizes the squared distance between embeddings of a point and its transformation.

concepts.title: Representational collapse
concepts.one_liner: Representational collapse occurs when a model achieves trivial invariance by mapping all different datapoints to the same constant vector.
concepts.content: Representational collapse is a failure mode in representation learning where the encoder $f$ learns a trivial solution. For example, if the goal is to minimize alignment loss, the model might learn to output the zero vector for every input. In this state, all datapoints are mapped to the same arbitrary vector, achieving perfect but useless invariance because the representation no longer carries any information about the input.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying representational collapse is crucial for designing contrastive objectives that force the model to learn meaningful, discriminative features.
concepts.recap_md: - A failure where the model maps all inputs to a single constant output.

concepts.title: Positive and negative pairs
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive learning uses positive pairs to encourage similarity and negative pairs to prevent representational collapse by pushing embeddings apart.
concepts.content:
Contrastive learning prevents representational collapse by using two types of data pairings. Positive pairs, denoted as $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{+}\}$, consist of two datapoints we wish to align (e.g., $\mathbf{x}^{+} = T(\mathbf{x})$). Negative pairs, $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{-}\}$, are datapoints that should be represented differently. Negative pairs are commonly constructed by sampling two datapoints independently from the data distribution. The objective is to pull together the positive pairs and push apart the negative pairs.

(see figure: Contrastive learning.)

This approach can be extended to achieve invariance to a set of transformations $\{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$ by applying the loss for each transformation.
concepts.motivation_md: By explicitly pushing unrelated points apart, negative pairs ensure the model doesn't find the trivial solution of mapping everything to the same point.
concepts.recap_md: - Positive pairs are versions of the same data that should have similar embeddings.

concepts.title: Attention Layers vs. Convolutional Layers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Attention layers perform global operations where all input tokens can interact, unlike convolutional layers which are restricted to local receptive fields.
concepts.content: Attention layers are not convolutional. They do not factor the processing into independent chunks but instead perform a global operation, in which all input tokens can interact. The linear combination of tokens that results is not a mixing operation found in CNNs and addresses the limitation of CNNs being myopic, with each filter only seeing information in its receptive field.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolutional layers are limited by their local receptive fields, making them "myopic." Attention layers solve this by allowing global interactions between all tokens in a sequence or image.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Attention layers perform global operations rather than local ones.", "- Unlike CNNs, attention allows every input token to interact with every other token.", "- This global interaction overcomes the 'myopic' limitation of fixed convolutional receptive fields." ]

concepts.title: Masked Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Masked attention restricts which tokens can attend to others by fixing specific weights in the attention matrix to zero.
concepts.content:
Sometimes we want to restrict which tokens can attend to which. This can be done by masking the attention matrix, which just means fixing some of the weights to be zero. This can be useful for many settings, including learning features via masked autoencoding, cross-attention between different data modalities, and for sequential prediction. 

To illustrate, we will describe the sequential prediction use case. For simplicity, in this section we depict tokens with one-dimensional code vectors, but remember $\mathbf{T}$ would have $d$ columns for $d$-dimensional code vectors. A common problem is to predict the $(n+1)$-th token in a sequence given the previous $n$ tokens. For example, we may be trying to predict tokens that represent the next frame in a video, the next word in a sentence, or the weather on the next day. The $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$ is shorthand for the sequence of tokens $\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf{t}_{n}^\mathsf{T} \end{bmatrix}$.

A simple way to model this prediction problem is with a linear layer: $\mathbf{y}_{n+1} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$. Here is what this looks like diagrammatically, and on the right is the layer shown as matrix multiplication:

(see figure: Masked prediction of time index 4 from time indices 1-3.)

During training, we will give examples like this: $$\begin{aligned} \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_n\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n+1}\\ \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-1}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_n\\ \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-2}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n-1} \end{aligned}$$ and so on. We can make all these predictions at once with a single matrix multiply:

(see figure: Masked attention to make multiple causal predictions at once. Black cells are masked; they are filled with zeros.)

This way, one forward pass makes $N$ predictions rather than one prediction. This is equivalent to doing a single next token prediction $N$ times, but it all happens in a single matrix multiply, using the matrix shown on the right.
concepts.motivation_md: Masking is used to control information flow, such as preventing a model from 'cheating' by looking at future tokens during sequential prediction or for specific tasks like masked autoencoding.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Masking involves setting specific attention weights to zero to restrict token interaction.", "- It enables efficient training for sequential prediction by processing multiple sub-sequences in one pass.", "- Common applications include causal prediction, cross-attention, and masked autoencoding." ]

concepts.title: Causal Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Causal attention is a masking strategy where each token can only attend to previous tokens in a sequence.
concepts.content: This kind of matrix is called causal because each output index $i$ only depends on input indices $j$ such that $j < i$. If $\mathbf{A}$ is an attention matrix, then this strategy is called causal attention. This is a masking strategy where each token can only attend to previous tokens in the sequence. This approach can dramatically speed up training because all the sub-sequence prediction problems (predict $\mathbf{t}_{n-1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-2}$, predict $\mathbf{t}_{n}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-1}$, predict $\mathbf{t}_{n+1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$) are supervised at the same time.
concepts.motivation_md: In sequential tasks, we must ensure the model does not use information from the future to predict the present. Causal attention enforces this constraint while allowing parallel training on all prefixes of a sequence.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Causal attention ensures output at index $i$ only depends on inputs at indices $j < i$.", "- It prevents the model from looking at 'future' tokens during training.", "- This strategy allows for simultaneous supervision of multiple sub-sequence predictions, speeding up training." ]

concepts.title: Multilayer Masked Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Multilayer masked attention maintains causal dependencies across deep networks by sharing computation between overlapping prediction sub-networks.
concepts.content: This also works for transformers with more than one layer, where the masking strategy looks like shown in (see figure: Multilayer masked attention achieves causal prediction with a deep net.). Notice that the output tokens on every layer $l$ have the property that $\mathbf{t}^l_n$ only depends on $\mathbf{T}^0_{1:n-1}$, where $\mathbf{T}^0$ are the initial set of tokens input into the transformer. Also notice that, after the first layer, all subsequent layers can use causal attention that is not shifted in time, and the previous property is still maintained. Finally, notice that the subnetwork that predicts each subsequent output token overlaps substantially with the subnetworks that predict each previous token. That is, there is sharing of computation between all the prediction problems. We will see a more concrete application of this strategy when we get to autoregressive models.
concepts.motivation_md: To build deep autoregressive models, causality must be preserved through every layer. Multilayer masked attention ensures that information from future tokens never leaks into earlier positions, even through intermediate representations.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Ensures output token $\mathbf{t}^l_n$ only depends on initial tokens $\mathbf{T}^0_{1:n-1}$ across all layers.", "- Subsequent layers use causal attention without needing additional time shifts.", "- Computation is shared between overlapping subnetworks that predict different sequence positions." ]

concepts.title: Positional Encodings

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Positional encodings concatenate a code representing a token's position within a signal to retain spatial or sequential knowledge.
concepts.content:
Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, which means that we can shuffle the positions of the tokens and nothing substantial changes. A consequence is that tokens do not encode their position within the representation of the signal. Sometimes, however, we may wish to retain positional knowledge. For example, knowing that a token is a representation of the top region of an image can help us identify that the token is likely to represent sky. 

Positional encoding concatenates a code representing position within the signal onto each token. If the signal is an image, then the positional code should represent the x- and y-coordinates. However, it need not represent these coordinates as scalars; more commonly we use a periodic representation of position, where the coordinates are encoded as the vector of values a set of sinusoidal waves take on at each position: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{p}_x &= [\sin(x), \sin(x/B), \sin(x/B^2), \ldots, \sin(x/B^P)]^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{p}_y &= [\sin(y), \sin(y/B), \sin(y/B^2), \ldots, \sin(y/B^P)]^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{p} &= \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}_x\\ \mathbf{p}_y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ where $x$ and $y$ are the coordinates of the token. This representation is visualized in (see figure: Positional codes.). 

Another strategy is to simply let the positional codes be learned by the model, which could potentially result in a better representation of space than sinusoidal codes. While positional encoding is useful and common in transformers, it is not specific to this architecture. The same kind of encodings can be useful for CNNs as well, as a way to make convolutional filters that are conditioned on position. Positional encodings also appear in radiance fields.
concepts.motivation_md: Because transformer operations are permutation equivariant, they are 'position-blind.' Positional encodings are necessary to give the model information about where tokens are located in a sequence or image.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Transformers are naturally permutation equivariant and do not inherently know token positions.", "- Positional encodings add spatial or sequential information by concatenating codes to tokens.", "- Codes can be fixed sinusoidal functions or learned parameters." ]

concepts.title: Permutation Equivariance in Transformers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, meaning shuffling input positions only permutes the outputs without changing the underlying computation.
concepts.content: Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, which means that we can shuffle the positions of the tokens and nothing substantial changes (the only change is that the outputs get permuted). A consequence is that tokens do not encode their position within the representation of the signal. This property explains why transformers require additional mechanisms, like positional encodings, if the order or location of data points is important for the task.
concepts.motivation_md: Permutation equivariance allows transformers to process sets of data where order doesn't matter, but it creates a challenge for tasks like language or image processing where position is critical.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Shuffling input tokens results in a corresponding shuffling of output tokens.", "- The core computation is independent of the absolute or relative positions of tokens.", "- This property necessitates positional encodings to handle ordered data like text or images." ]

concepts.title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer
position.section_title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

concepts.one_liner: Fully connected, convolutional, and self-attention layers are all affine transformations that differ in how their weight matrices are structured and determined.
concepts.content:
Many layers in deep nets are special kinds of affine transformations. Three common types are fully-connected layers (`fc`), convolutional layers (`conv`), and self-attention layers (`attn`). All these layers are alike in that their forward pass can be written as $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$ for some matrix $\mathbf{W}$ and some vector $\mathbf{b}$. 

In `conv` and `attn` layers, $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are determined as some function of the input $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. In `conv` layers this function is very simple: just make a Toeplitz matrix that repeats the convolutional kernel(s) to match the dimensionality of $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. In `attn` layers the function that determines $\mathbf{W}$ is more involved, and typically biases $\mathbf{b}$ are not used. 

Each of these layers can be represented as a matrix. The matrix for an `fc` layer is full rank, whereas the matrices for `conv` and `attn` layers have low-rank structure, but different kinds of low-rank structure. (see figure: A comparison of three neural network layer types: fully connected (fc), convolutional (conv), and self-attention (attn). For each, it shows a wiring graph of connections between input and output...) catalog some of the other important properties of each of these layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding different layer types as variations of affine transformations helps unify deep learning theory and highlights how architectural constraints (like weight sharing in CNNs or input-dependency in Attention) affect the model's capacity.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- All three layer types can be expressed as $\mathbf{X}_{\text{out}} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\text{in}} + \mathbf{b}$.", "- Convolutional and attention layers use input-dependent weight matrices with low-rank structures.", "- Fully connected layers typically use full-rank matrices that are independent of the specific input values." ]

concepts.title: Transformers as Graph Neural Networks

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Transformers can be viewed as a special case of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that process sets of tokens by forming a graph of operations.
concepts.content:
Transformers are the dominant architecture in computer vision and most fields of artificial intelligence. They combine ideas from earlier architectures—convolutional patchwise processing, residual connections, ReLU nonlinearities, and normalization layers—with newer innovations like vector-valued tokens, attention layers, and positional codes. 

Transformers can also be considered as a special case of graph neural networks (GNNs). GNNs are a very general class of architecture for processing sets by forming a graph of operations over the set. A transformer does exactly that: it takes an input set of tokens and, layer by layer, applies a network of transformations over that set until a final representation or prediction is read out.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing transformers as GNNs provides a theoretical framework for understanding how they process unstructured sets of data through relational operations rather than just fixed grids or sequences.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Transformers process sets of tokens using a graph of operations, similar to GNNs.", "- They integrate classical deep learning components with modern attention-based mechanisms.", "- The architecture applies successive transformations to a set of tokens to produce a final representation." ]

concepts.title: CNNs in Disguise

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Most of the transformer architecture can be viewed as a convolutional neural network in disguise.
concepts.content: Transformers provide a new way of thinking about data processing, and it may seem like they are very different from past architectures. However, they actually have many commonalities with CNNs. In fact, most (but not all) of the transformer architecture can be viewed as a CNN in disguise. Several of the layers in a transformer are in fact performing convolutions.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept bridges the gap between traditional convolutional architectures and modern transformers, helping learners understand that transformers are not a complete departure from established signal processing principles but rather a specific evolution of them.
concepts.recap_md: - Transformers share significant architectural commonalities with CNNs.

concepts.title: Tokenization as Convolution

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Tokenization can be written as a convolutional layer with kernel size and stride both equal to the patch size $K$.
concepts.content:
The first step in working with transformers is to tokenize the input. The most basic way to do this is to chop up the input image into non-overlapping patches of size $K \times K$, then convert these patches to vectors via a linear projection. This operation can be written as convolution; the whole idea of CNNs is to chop the signal into patches. In particular, this form of tokenization can be written as a convolutional layer with kernel size and stride both equal to $K$:
$$\begin{aligned}
&\mathbf{T}[n(N/K)+m,c_{\texttt{2}}] = \nonumber\\
&b[c_{\texttt{2}}] +  \sum_{c_{\texttt{1}}=1}^{C_{\texttt{in}}} \sum_{k_1,k_2=-K}^K w[c_{\texttt{1}},c_{\texttt{2}},k_1,k_2] x_{\texttt{in}}[c_{\texttt{1}},K n-k_1,K m-k_2] \quad \triangleleft \quad \text{(tokenization)}
\end{aligned}$$
where, for RGB images, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N \times M}$, $C_{\texttt{in}}=3$, and $C_{\texttt{out}}=d$ (the token dimensionality). This math assumes $N$ and $M$ are evenly divisible by $K$; if they aren't then the input can be resized or padded until they are. This is just a $\texttt{conv}$ operator with the following parameters:

```python
T = conv(x_in, channels_in=3, channels_out=d, kernel=K, stride=K) # tokenize
```
concepts.motivation_md: By framing tokenization as a convolution, we can implement the initial patch-embedding step of a transformer using highly optimized standard convolutional layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Image tokenization is equivalent to a convolution with kernel size and stride equal to the patch size.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Projections as Convolutions

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: The query, key, and value projections in transformers are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.
concepts.content:
The query, key, and value projections that are part of the attention layers can be viewed as convolutions. For simplicity, consider the query projection, since key and value follow the same pattern. This operation is typically written as a matrix multiply $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}$, which applies the same linear transformation ($\mathbf{W}_q$) to each token vector. Applying the same linear operation to each element in a sequence is exactly what convolution does. Specifically, the query operation can be written as convolving the set of $N$ $d$-channel tokens with a filter bank of $m$ filters, with kernel size 1, producing a new set of $N$ $m$-channel tokens. This equivalence is visualized below:

(see figure: The query, key, and value projections in transformers can be written either as a convolution or a matrix multiply.)

Therefore, the query, key, and value projections are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding QKV projections as $1 \times 1$ convolutions highlights that these layers process each token independently, emphasizing the local nature of the linear transformation before the global attention mechanism takes over.
concepts.recap_md: - QKV projections apply the same linear transformation to every token in a sequence.

concepts.title: Matrix Product as Convolution

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Every matrix product can be written as a convolution of a multichannel filter bank with a signal.
concepts.content: Convolution actually appears all over in linear algebra, and in fact every matrix product can be written as a convolution! Whenever you see a product $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$, you can think of it as the convolution of a multichannel filter bank $\mathbf{B}$ (one filter in each row; kernel size 1) with the signal $\mathbf{A}$ (time indexes rows, channels in the columns).
concepts.motivation_md: This mathematical identity provides a unified view of linear algebra and signal processing, showing that matrix multiplications—the backbone of deep learning—are fundamentally a form of convolution.
concepts.recap_md: - Any matrix product $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$ is equivalent to a convolution with a $1 \times 1$ kernel.

concepts.title: Tokenwise MLP

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A token-wise MLP can be written as a series of convolutions interleaved with neuronwise-nonlinearities, effectively acting as a CNN.
concepts.motivation_md: The MLP block in a transformer is responsible for processing the information within each token. Recognizing it as a $1 \times 1$ CNN helps explain why transformers are so effective at feature transformation.
concepts.recap_md: - Token-wise MLPs apply the same transformation to every token independently.

concepts.title: Similarities between CNNs and Transformers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Most layers in transformers are convolutional, breaking the signal into chunks and processing them independently and identically.
concepts.content: Most layers in transformers are convolutional. These layers break up the signal processing problem into chunks, then process each chunk independently and identically. Other operations in transformers—such as normalization layers and residual connections—are also common in CNNs. Breaking up a problem into chunks is a fundamentally useful idea often called factorizing a problem into smaller pieces.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying similarities between these two dominant architectures helps students transfer their knowledge of CNNs (like normalization and residuals) to the study of transformers.
concepts.recap_md: - Both CNNs and transformers factorize problems by processing signal chunks independently.

concepts.title: Permutation Invariance and 1x1 Filters in Transformers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Transformers use $1 \times 1$ filters to maintain permutation invariance, unlike CNNs which use larger kernels to process adjacent regions together.
concepts.content: When written as convolutions, the query-key-value projections and token-wise MLPs in transformers only use $1 \times 1$ filters. This is necessary because using a larger kernel would break the permutation invariance property of transformers; the output of the filters would depend on which token is next to which. This is a key difference between CNNs and transformers: CNNs use $K \times K$ filters to process adjacent image regions together, while transformers use $1 \times 1$ filters and have no architectural way of knowing about spatial structure. For vision problems where spatial structure is important, transformers are instead given knowledge of position through the inputs (positional encodings) rather than through the architectural structure.
concepts.motivation_md: This explains why transformers require positional encodings: their core linear layers are spatially 'blind' due to the use of $1 \times 1$ kernels, a design choice that preserves permutation invariance.
concepts.recap_md: - Transformers use $1 \times 1$ filters to ensure the network is permutation invariant.

concepts.title: 1x1 Filter

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A $1 \times 1$ filter refers to any filter whose kernel size is 1 in all its dimensions.
concepts.content: The term "1x1 filter" refers to any filter whose kernel size is 1 in all its dimensions, regardless of whether the signal is one-dimensional, two-dimensional, three-dimensional, etc.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition clarifies a common piece of deep learning jargon, ensuring that the '1x1' label is understood as a constraint on spatial extent across any number of dimensions.
concepts.recap_md: - A $1 \times 1$ filter has a kernel size of 1 across all spatial dimensions.

concepts.title: Infinite Texture Generation Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm that crops pieces from a very large reference image to create new images.
concepts.content: Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm as shown in (see figure: The infinite texture generation algorithm. If we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images.). However, such an algorithm, although successful in practice, provides little understanding of how human perception works or how to modify textures to create new ones. Additionally, it does not help in identifying what representations can be useful to measure similarity between textures.
concepts.motivation_md: This trivial approach serves as a baseline for texture synthesis, highlighting the need for more sophisticated models that explain human perception and allow for texture manipulation.
concepts.recap_md: - Texture synthesis can be achieved by simply cropping pieces from a large reference image.

concepts.title: Intuition for Texture Perception

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Most observers perceive images with many similar elements as a single texture rather than a composition of individual, countable objects.
concepts.content: Most observers perceive an image of a stone wall, such as the one in [FIGURE:ecffb3dd8eb68d4d | A close-up photograph of a rustic stone wall composed of irregularly shaped, flat, and rounded stones of various sizes and earthy tones like grey, tan, and reddish-brown. The stones are tightly...], as a rock texture rather than a composition of countable rocks. While the rocks are indeed countable, doing so requires a significant effort, and most people do not care about the specific number of elements unless they are in the business of selling them.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why we treat complex visual scenes as textures, simplifying our visual processing by focusing on global patterns rather than individual components.
concepts.recap_md: - Observers naturally group numerous similar objects into a single texture representation.

concepts.title: Perception of Sets

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Human vision processes small groups of objects instantly but relies on linear counting or statistical set representation for larger groups.
concepts.content: When an image is composed of one or a few distinct objects, we can easily pay attention to each of them individually and count them in parallel. For displays with fewer than five elements, the time required to report the number does not depend on the count, as shown in (see figure: When looking at these images, we can count the number of circles at a glance if there are less than five circles. When an image has more than five items, we have to count them one by one.). However, when images are composed of more than five similarly looking elements, counting them requires looking at each one by one, and the time to count them grows linearly. In these cases, we seem to pay attention only to a few of them and represent the rest as a set.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how the brain transitions from individual object recognition to set-based perception is crucial for modeling how humans handle complex visual environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Humans can count up to four or five objects instantly through a process called subitizing.

concepts.title: Subitizing

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Subitizing is the ability to instantly determine the number of objects in a display without counting them, typically limited to fewer than five items.
concepts.content: The ability to know how many objects are in a display without counting them is called subitizing. This phenomenon only works when there are fewer than five elements in a display.
concepts.motivation_md: Subitizing represents a specialized, high-speed visual process for small quantities, distinct from the serial counting used for larger sets.
concepts.recap_md: - Subitizing allows for the near-instantaneous recognition of small quantities.

concepts.title: Visual Crowding

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Visual crowding is a phenomenon where objects in peripheral vision become difficult to recognize when surrounded by other similar features.
concepts.content: Crowding is a visual phenomenon where objects in the periphery become hard to identify when surrounded by other elements, as illustrated in (see figure: Crowding. If you look at the central cross, the letter R on the right can be recognized, however the letter B on the left is hard to read.). This occurs because the features of the target and its neighbors get entangled as if the pooling window for image features was larger than the items together. While fixating on a central point, it is easy to see that a peripheral region contains text, but it is hard to bind the features together to perceive individual letters. The circles in (see figure: Crowding. If you look at the central cross, the letter R on the right can be recognized, however the letter B on the left is hard to read.) represent an approximation of the size of the visual regions over which visual features are pooled.
concepts.motivation_md: Crowding demonstrates that peripheral vision relies on statistical representations of image features rather than high-resolution individual object recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Crowding makes it difficult to distinguish individual objects in the periphery when they are closely spaced.

concepts.title: Textons

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Textons are fundamental texture elements, such as junctions and corners, whose statistical relationships define a texture's appearance.
concepts.content: Bela Julesz proposed that textures are analyzed in terms of statistical relationships between fundamental texture elements called textons. According to this model, textons might be represented by features such as the number of junctions, terminators, corners, and intersections within patterns. These models were often restricted to binary images formed by simple elements as shown in (see figure: Texture discrimination using textons.). While it is often easy to see the boundary between textures pre-attentively, the challenge is that detecting specific texton elements can be unreliable, making the representation non-robust.
concepts.motivation_md: Textons were an early attempt to define the "atoms" of texture, helping researchers understand how the human visual system discriminates between different patterns.
concepts.recap_md: - Textons are basic units like corners or terminators used to model texture perception.

concepts.title: Pre-Attentive Texture Discrimination

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Pre-attentive texture discrimination is the ability to distinguish between different textures instantly and without conscious effort.
concepts.content: Pre-attentive texture discrimination refers to the ability to see boundaries between textures without making a conscious effort. Models based on filter banks, introduced by Bergen, Adelson, Malik, and Perona, demonstrated that filter outputs could explain several discrimination results. These features based on filter outputs can also be used for texture-based image segmentation.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept identifies the low-level visual processes that allow us to segment scenes into different regions based on texture automatically.
concepts.recap_md: - Pre-attentive discrimination occurs instantly without requiring focused attention.

concepts.title: The Problem of Texture Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: The problem of texture synthesis involves creating new random samples of a texture that match the statistical characteristics of a reference image.
concepts.content: The problem of texture synthesis involves building a process that, given a reference texture, outputs images with new random samples of the same texture. This is often achieved by transforming a reference texture into a representation using texture analysis (an encoder) to find parameters $\theta$. The synthesis procedure then takes a random noise image and these parameters to generate the desired output. Texture synthesis is important for computer graphics applications and for studying what representations of a texture are useful for visual recognition.
concepts.motivation_md: Texture synthesis allows for the generation of infinite variations of a pattern, which is useful for realistic rendering and testing theories of texture perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Texture synthesis aims to generate new images that are perceived as the same texture as a reference.

concepts.title: Vector Embedding
concepts.one_liner: A vector embedding is a high-dimensional vector representation $\mathbf{z}$ produced by an encoding function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$.
concepts.content: An encoding is a mapping defined by a function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$. Typically both the input $\mathbf{x}$ and the output $\mathbf{z}$ are high-dimensional vectors, where $\mathbf{z}$ is called a vector embedding of $\mathbf{x}$. The mapping $f$ is trained to produce these representations for further use.
concepts.motivation_md: Vector embeddings allow raw data to be transformed into a structured numerical format that can be processed by machine learning models while preserving relevant information.
concepts.recap_md: - A vector embedding $\mathbf{z}$ is the output of an encoding function $f(\mathbf{x})$.

concepts.title: Disentangled Representation
concepts.one_liner: A disentangled representation is one where the dimensions of the embedding $\mathbf{z}$ correspond to independent factors of variation.
concepts.content: A representation is considered disentangled when the dimensions of the vector $\mathbf{z}$ are independent factors of variation in the data. In this way, the representation space $\mathcal{Z}$ captures distinct, non-overlapping characteristics of the input.
concepts.motivation_md: Disentangling factors of variation makes representations more interpretable and useful for downstream tasks by separating independent features like shape, color, or lighting.
concepts.recap_md: - Dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ should represent independent factors of variation.

concepts.title: Compression as a Desideratum for Representation

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

concepts.one_liner: A good representation is parsimonious, capturing only the essential characteristics of data necessary for human-interest tasks.
concepts.content:
A good representation is one that is parsimonious and captures just the essential characteristics of the data necessary for tasks of human interest. There are at least three senses in which compressed representations are desirable:

1. Compressed representations require less memory to store.
2. Compression is a way to achieve invariance to nuisance factors, such as camera noise, lighting conditions, and viewing angle. By factoring out and discarding these nuisances, the representation becomes more useful for tasks like object recognition.
3. Compression embodies Occam's razor: among competing hypotheses that explain the data equally well, the simplest is most likely to be true. Many algorithms, such as autoencoders, seek simple representations from which raw data can be regenerated, assigning high likelihood to the data.

Many representation learning algorithms capture these goals by penalizing or constraining the complexity of the learned representation. This penalty is usually paired with an objective to preserve specific information while compressing the signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Compression reduces storage costs, improves robustness by removing irrelevant 'nuisance' noise, and follows the principle of simplicity to improve generalization.
concepts.recap_md: - Compression reduces memory usage and storage requirements.

concepts.title: Occam's Razor in Representation Learning

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

concepts.one_liner: Among two representations that fit the data equally well, preference should be given to the more compressed one.
concepts.content: Compression is an embodiment of Occam's razor: among competing hypotheses that all explain the data equally well, the simplest is most likely to be true. Many representation learning algorithms seek simple representations from which you can regenerate the raw data (e.g., autoencoders). Such representations explain the data in the formal sense that they assign high likelihood to the data. This aligns with the idea of Bayesian Occam's razor. Therefore, for representation learning, the principle states that among two representations that fit the data equally well, the more compressed one is preferred.
concepts.motivation_md: Applying Occam's razor helps prevent overfitting by favoring simpler, more compressed models that are more likely to capture true underlying patterns rather than noise.
concepts.recap_md: - Simpler hypotheses that explain data well are more likely to be true.

concepts.title: Minimum Description Length Principle

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

concepts.one_liner: The minimum description length principle is a version of Occam's razor applied to data representation.
concepts.content: The minimum description length (MDL) principle is a version of Occam's razor used in representation learning. It suggests that the best representation is the one that leads to the greatest compression of the data.
concepts.motivation_md: MDL provides a formal framework for balancing model complexity and data fit, ensuring that representations remain efficient and generalizable.
concepts.recap_md: - MDL is a formalization of Occam's razor for data compression.

concepts.title: Prediction as a Desideratum for Representation

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

concepts.one_liner: A defining property of a good representation is its ability to facilitate the prediction of important world properties.
concepts.content:
The purpose of a visual system is to take actions that achieve desirable future outcomes, making prediction a critical goal for representations. Prediction can be generalized beyond the future to include the past, gaps in measurements (imputation), or abstract properties like the mental states of others (theory of mind). In general, prediction refers to the inference of any arbitrary property of the world given observed data.

Most representation learning algorithms in vision aim to learn compressed encodings that are also predictive of the future to support decision-making. Other goals include making representations disentangled, interpretable, and actionable. These goals often overlap; for instance, more compressed representations may be simpler and easier for a human to interpret.
concepts.motivation_md: Representations exist to support action; being able to predict future states or hidden properties is essential for effective decision-making and interaction with the world.
concepts.recap_md: - Prediction involves inferring arbitrary world properties from observed data.

concepts.title: Imputation

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

concepts.one_liner: Imputation is the problem of predicting gaps or missing values in measurements.
concepts.content: Imputation is the problem of predicting gaps in measurements. Examples include filling in missing pixels in a corrupted image or superresolving a movie to play at a higher framerate.
concepts.motivation_md: Imputation allows systems to recover information from incomplete or noisy datasets, which is common in real-world sensor data.
concepts.recap_md: - Imputation involves filling in missing data points or pixels.

concepts.title: Autoencoder
concepts.one_liner: An autoencoder is a function that maps data back to itself via a low-dimensional representational bottleneck.
concepts.content:
Autoencoders are common representation learners consisting of a function that maps data back to itself via a low-dimensional representational bottleneck.

(see figure: {\small (left) An autoencoder maps from points in data space, to points in representation space, and back. (right) An example of running an autoencoder on an input image of a bird.)

While the output is intended to be the same as the input, the key trick is to impose constraints on the intermediate representation $\mathbf{z}$ so that it becomes useful. The most common constraint is compression, where $\mathbf{z}$ is a low-dimensional, compressed representation of the input $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: By forcing data through a narrow 'bottleneck,' autoencoders are compelled to learn the most essential features of the data to successfully reconstruct the input.
concepts.recap_md: - Autoencoders map data to a representation space and back to the original space.

concepts.title: Affinity-Based Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Affinity-based segmentation groups items by modeling a distance metric that measures the similarity between patterns or the likelihood they belong to the same object.
concepts.content:
Affinity-based segmentation is based on the idea of affinity, where a distance metric is modeled to determine whether two items should be grouped. This metric usually measures how similar two patterns are or how likely they are to be part of the same object. For example, a simple affinity function over pixel pairs could be the Euclidean distance between their color values. Pixels with high affinity should belong to the same group, while pixels with low affinity should belong to different groups.

Methods using this principle include graph cuts, spectral clustering, and Markov random field (MRF)-based clustering. A modern approach involves contrastive learning, which is a natural fit because it learns from similarities (positive pairs) and differences (negative pairs). Contrastive methods learn an embedding where datapoints with high affinity are nearby and those with low affinity are far apart. Once this embedding is established, clustering can be performed using an algorithm like $k$-means.

While color distance can serve as an affinity, the method becomes more interesting with nontrivial affinities, such as those derived from human judgments or self-supervised measures. Self-supervised contrastive learning methods like SimCLR, MoCo, and DINO train mappings from image patches to embedding vectors. By running these methods densely across an image, a feature map is created where each pixel's value is an embedding vector similar to other pixels likely to appear in the same scene. Applying $k$-means to this feature map results in effective segmentation.

(see figure: Image segmentation using $k$-means over DINO @caron2021emerging features)
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional clustering often struggles with complex visual structures. Affinity-based segmentation solves this by defining a similarity metric (affinity) between elements. This allows the system to group pixels or regions based on learned relationships rather than just raw pixel values, making it possible to capture semantic or perceptual coherence in an image.
concepts.recap_md: - Affinity measures the similarity or likelihood that two items belong to the same group.

concepts.title: Edge Detection
concepts.one_liner: Edge detection aims to represent image content through sparse, stable boundaries that often correspond to scene geometry like depth discontinuities.
concepts.content: Edge detection is a complementary problem to segmentation, as an image partition can be represented either by segment assignments or by the boundaries between them. Early vision algorithms focused on edge detection under the premise that edges form a compact representation of image content. Edges are relatively sparse and remain stable despite nuisances like noise and lighting. Furthermore, specific edge structures relate to scene geometry; for instance, an edge representing an occluding contour indicates a depth discontinuity at that location in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Edges provide a sparse and robust representation of an image, filtering out noise and lighting variations while preserving essential structural information like object boundaries and depth changes.
concepts.recap_md: - Edges provide a compact, sparse representation of an image that is stable against noise.

concepts.title: Line Drawings
concepts.one_liner: Line drawings represent the edge structure of an image in a way that is highly intuitive to humans, though their utility for machine vision remains an active area of research.
concepts.content: Line drawings are a method of representing the edge structure in an image. Their high interest to humans suggests that representing images via edge structure may be fundamentally useful. While there is active research in computer graphics regarding the modeling of line drawings, it remains unclear if this representation will eventually prove as compelling for visually intelligent machines as it is for humans.
concepts.motivation_md: Humans can easily recognize objects from simple lines, suggesting that edge-based representations contain the most critical information for visual understanding.
concepts.recap_md: - Line drawings represent images through their essential edge structures.

concepts.title: Layer-Based Representations
concepts.one_liner: Layer-based representations capture depth by modeling a scene as a stack of planes, approximating 3D structure through parallax.
concepts.content:
Layer-based representations capture aspects of depth by modeling a scene as a stack of planes, similar to the multiplane camera used in early animation. In this approach, different elements of a scene—such as the sky, mountains, and foreground characters—are drawn on separate glass planes. Shifting these planes creates parallax, where foreground layers move faster than background layers. This serves as a rough approximation of the 3D world and is often referred to as a 2.5D representation, providing a way to handle depth without the computational expense of full 3D modeling.

[FIGURE:2af0dbf22adfc9da | A technical patent drawing of a multiplane camera system labeled 'FIG. 1'. It shows a tall vertical frame with multiple horizontal layers (labeled A through E) stacked vertically, which are used to...]
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling the full 3D geometry of a scene is computationally expensive. Layer-based representations provide a simpler alternative that still captures essential depth cues like occlusion and parallax.
concepts.recap_md: - Scenes are modeled as a stack of planes to approximate 3D depth.

concepts.title: 2.5D Representations
concepts.one_liner: 2.5D representations are pseudo-3D models, such as layers, that capture depth aspects without the full expense of 3D modeling.
concepts.content: In computer vision, layer-based representations are popular for capturing aspects of depth without the expense of modeling a fully 3D world. These layers and other related pseudo-3D representations are sometimes called 2.5D representations.
concepts.motivation_md: 2.5D representations bridge the gap between flat 2D images and complex 3D models, allowing systems to reason about depth and layering efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - 2.5D representations are pseudo-3D models that capture depth via layers.

concepts.title: Ordinal Structure
concepts.one_liner: Ordinal structure refers to the relative depth ordering of objects, such as which item is on top of another.
concepts.content: Layers in a representation capture ordinal structure, which describes the relative ordering of objects rather than their exact position in metric space. This is often the primary structure of interest in tasks where relative depth is key; for example, determining which piece of paper is on top of a pile.
concepts.motivation_md: In many practical tasks, knowing the exact distance to an object is less important than knowing its relative order (e.g., what is in front of what).
concepts.recap_md: - Ordinal structure captures the relative depth ordering of objects.

concepts.title: Emergent Groups
concepts.one_liner: In modern neural networks, structures like objects and contours are emergent properties of hidden layers rather than explicit human-designed components.
concepts.content: While traditional methods like edge detection and bottom-up segmentation are less common in modern vision systems, perceptual organization remains present. In these systems, structures such as objects, contours, and layers are emergent in the hidden layers of neural networks rather than being explicitly designed by humans. For instance, object detectors have been observed to emerge within neural networks trained for tasks like colorization.
concepts.motivation_md: Modern deep learning suggests that explicit manual definitions of visual parts are not always necessary, as networks naturally learn to organize visual information to solve complex tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Perceptual structures like objects and contours emerge naturally in the hidden layers of deep networks.

concepts.title: Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: Generative models are stochastic functions that map labels or descriptions to data, performing the synthesis of data in a one-to-many fashion.
concepts.content:
Generative models perform or describe the synthesis of data. While an image classifier is a many-to-one function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ mapping images to labels, a generative model is a function in the opposite direction $g: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Because there are many possible outputs for any given input (one-to-many), generative models handle this ambiguity by treating $g$ as a stochastic function.

(see figure: A classifier maps images to labels.)

(see figure: A generator maps labels (or other descriptions) to images.)
concepts.motivation_md: Generative models allow us to create new data samples and understand the underlying distribution of a dataset, which is useful for tasks like image synthesis and data augmentation.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models map labels or descriptions to data (synthesis).

concepts.title: Max-Product Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: The max-product version of belief propagation replaces the summation in the update rule with an argmax operator to compute a MAP estimate of hidden states.
concepts.content: Instead of summing over the states of other nodes, we are sometimes interested in finding the $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the joint probability. The argmax operator passes through constant variables just as the summation sign did. This leads to an alternate version of the BP algorithm where the summation (of multiplying the vector message products by the node compatibility matrix) is replaced with argmax. This is called the max-product version of belief propagation, and it computes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate of the hidden states.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard belief propagation computes marginal probabilities, we often need to find the single most likely configuration of all hidden states (the MAP estimate).
concepts.recap_md: - The max-product algorithm replaces the summation in the belief propagation update rule with an argmax operator. - This variant is used to compute the MAP estimate of hidden states rather than marginal probabilities.

concepts.title: Computational Complexity of Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Belief propagation enables efficient inference by reducing marginalization cost from exponential to linear in the number of nodes for tree-structured graphs.
concepts.content: Running belief propagation within a tree computes exact marginal probabilities at each node by reusing intermediate sums across different marginalizations and exploiting the structure of the joint probability to perform the computation efficiently. If nothing were known about the joint probability structure, the marginalization cost would grow exponentially with the number of nodes in the network. However, if the graph structure corresponding to the joint probability is known to be a chain or a tree, then the marginalization cost only grows linearly with the number of nodes and is quadratic in the node state dimensions. The belief propagation algorithm enables inference in many large-scale problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Direct marginalization of joint distributions is computationally intractable for large networks because the cost grows exponentially with the number of variables.
concepts.recap_md: - In tree or chain structures, belief propagation reduces the computational cost of marginalization from exponential to linear. - The algorithm achieves efficiency by reusing intermediate sums and exploiting the factorization of the joint probability.

concepts.title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

position.section_title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

concepts.one_liner: Probabilistic graphical models and neural networks both use graph structures but differ significantly in the meaning of nodes, edges, and their underlying computational goals.
concepts.content: Probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) and neural networks (NNs) share a graph structure with nodes and edges, but these components represent different concepts. In NNs, nodes typically represent real-valued scalar activations, while in PGMs, they represent random variables (scalar or vector, discrete or continuous). Edges in PGMs determine statistical dependencies, whereas in NNs, they define the linear summations passed to the next layer. The primary difference lies in computation: PGMs represent factorized probability distributions to compute probabilities like marginals, while NNs compute results that minimize an expected loss or an energy function. This goal of minimizing loss rather than calculating probabilities allows NNs more general computations at the cost of less interpretable, non-probabilistic outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the distinction between PGMs and NNs helps clarify when to use probabilistic inference versus optimization-based learning for a given problem.
concepts.recap_md: - PGMs represent random variables and statistical dependencies to compute probabilities through message passing. - Neural networks use nodes for activations and edges for weights to minimize a loss function rather than calculating probabilities.

concepts.title: Nodes in Neural Networks vs. PGMs

position.section_title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

concepts.one_liner: Nodes in neural networks represent scalar activations, whereas nodes in probabilistic graphical models represent random variables.
concepts.content: The nodes of a neural network diagram typically represent real-valued scalar activations. The nodes of a probabilistic graphical model represent a random variable, which can be real or discrete-valued, and either a scalar or a vector.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing what a node represents is fundamental to understanding whether a graph describes a computational flow or a statistical dependency structure.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural network nodes represent scalar activations. - PGM nodes represent random variables, which can be discrete or continuous and scalar or vector.

concepts.title: Edges in Neural Networks vs. PGMs

position.section_title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

concepts.one_liner: Edges in PGMs represent statistical dependencies, while edges in neural networks represent participation in linear summations for subsequent layers.
concepts.content: Edges in probabilistic graphical models determine statistical dependencies. Edges in neural networks determine which nodes are involved in a linear summation to the next layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining the role of edges clarifies how information or influence propagates through the different types of graphical structures.
concepts.recap_md: - PGM edges signify statistical dependencies between variables. - Neural network edges define the connectivity for linear summations between layers.

concepts.title: Computation in Neural Networks vs. PGMs

position.section_title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

concepts.one_liner: PGMs compute probabilities through factorized distributions, while neural networks focus on minimizing expected loss or energy functions.
concepts.content: The fundamental difference between PGMs and NNs lies in what they calculate. PGMs represent factorized probability distributions and pass messages that allow for the computation of probabilities, such as the marginal probability at a node. In contrast, NNs compute results that minimize some expected loss or an energy function. This different goal of minimizing an expected loss rather than calculating a probability allows for more general computations by a neural network at the cost of output that may be less modular or less interpretable because they are not probabilities.
concepts.motivation_md: The choice between calculating exact probabilities and optimizing a loss function determines the interpretability and flexibility of the model.
concepts.recap_md: - PGMs focus on calculating probabilities like marginals using factorized distributions. - Neural networks optimize for loss minimization, allowing for more general but less interpretable computations.

concepts.title: Representation Learning
concepts.one_liner: Representation learning is the process of identifying objective functions that allow deep networks to transform data into the most effective representational space.
concepts.content: The choice of representation is critical because each type of representation makes some operations easy and others hard. Deep neural networks can be thought of as transforming the data, layer by layer, from one representation into another. Representation learning is primarily an investigation of objectives; it identifies different objective functions that capture properties of what it means to be a good representation. By training deep nets to optimize these objectives, we can investigate and develop the best possible representations for data.
concepts.motivation_md: Since the effectiveness of an algorithm often depends on how data is represented, we want to automate the discovery of representations that make tasks easier.
concepts.recap_md: - Representation learning aims to find the best possible way to represent data for specific tasks. - It involves optimizing objective functions that define what makes a representation "good."

concepts.title: Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Encoding is a mapping function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ that transforms raw datapoints into simpler, more useful abstract representations or vector embeddings.
concepts.content:
The goal of representation learning is to learn to map from datapoints, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$, to abstract representations, $\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}$, as schematized in @fig-representation_learning-rep_learning_schematic:

(see figure: The goal in this chapter is to learn to map from datapoints to abstract representations, which are typically simpler and more useful than the raw data.)

We call this mapping an encoding and learn a function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$. Typically both $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ are high-dimensional vectors, and $\mathbf{z}$ is called a vector embedding of $\mathbf{x}$. The mapping $f$ is trained so that $\mathbf{z}$ has certain desirable properties: common desiderata include that $\mathbf{z}$ be lower dimensional than $\mathbf{x}$; that the distribution of $\mathbf{z}$ values, $p(\mathbf{z})$, has a simple structure (such as being the unit normal distribution); and that the dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ be independent factors of variation, meaning the representation should be disentangled. In this way $\mathcal{Z}$ is a simpler, more abstracted, or better organized representational space than $\mathcal{X}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw data is often high-dimensional and noisy; encoding transforms it into a more structured space that is easier for models to process.
concepts.recap_md: - An encoding is a function $f$ that maps raw data $\mathbf{x}$ to an abstract representation $\mathbf{z}$. - Desirable properties for the embedding $\mathbf{z}$ include lower dimensionality, simple distributions, and disentangled factors of variation.

concepts.title: Generator Stochastic Function
concepts.one_liner: A generator is a function that produces stochastic outputs by mapping a randomized input vector and an optional label to a deterministic output.
concepts.content:
One way to make a function stochastic is to make it a deterministic function of a stochastic input. We define $g$ as a function, called a **generator**, that takes a randomized vector $\mathbf{z}$ as input along with the label/description $\mathbf{y}$, and produces an image $\mathbf{x}$ as output, that is, $g: \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Then this function can output a different image $\mathbf{x}$ for each different setting of $\mathbf{z}$. The generative process is as follows: first sample $\mathbf{z}$ from a prior $p(Z)$, then deterministically generate an image based on $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{y}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{z} \sim p(Z)\\
    \mathbf{x} = g(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}
$$

Graphical model for generating $X \| Y, Z$.

[FIGURE:b59cceb106ac5b5a | A directed acyclic graph (DAG) representing a generative process. Two source nodes, $Y$ and $Z$, have directed arrows pointing towards a single target node $X$. Nodes $X$ and $Y$ are shaded light...]

This procedure is shown in @fig-generative_models-image_generation_with_z:

(see figure: Making a generator stochastic by conditioning on a random variable.)
concepts.motivation_md: To create models that can synthesize varied and realistic data, we need a way to introduce randomness into a function's output. By treating the generator as a deterministic function of a random 'noise' vector, we can produce a diverse set of outputs from a single learned mapping.
concepts.recap_md: - A generator $g$ maps a random vector $\mathbf{z}$ and a label $\mathbf{y}$ to an output $\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Latent Variables
concepts.one_liner: Latent variables are unobserved inputs that specify attributes of the generated data not determined by the label.
concepts.content: Usually we draw $\mathbf{z}$ from a simple distribution such as Gaussian noise, that is, $p(Z) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1})$. The way to think of $\mathbf{z}$ is that it is a vector of **latent variables**, which specify all the attributes of the images other than those determined by the label. These variables are called latent because they are not directly observed in the training data (it just consists of images $\mathbf{x}$ and their labels $\mathbf{y}$). In our example, $\mathbf{y}$ tells $g$ to make a bird but the $\mathbf{z}$-vector is what specifies exactly which bird. Different dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ specify different attributes, such as the size, color, pose, background, and so on; everything necessary to fully determine the output image.
concepts.motivation_md: Training data often lacks explicit labels for every possible visual detail (like lighting or pose). Latent variables provide a mathematical way to represent these hidden factors, allowing the model to account for all the variation present in the real data.
concepts.recap_md: - Latent variables are not directly observed in the training data.

concepts.title: Unconditional Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: An unconditional generative model produces data from scratch by modeling the distribution $p(X)$ without dependency on an input label.
concepts.content:
Sometimes we wish to simply make up data from scratch; in fact, this is the canonical setting in which generative models are often studied. To do so, we can simply drop the dependency on the input $\mathbf{y}$. This yields a procedure for making data from scratch:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{z} \sim p(Z)\\
    \mathbf{x} = g(\mathbf{z})
\end{aligned}$$

Graphical model for an unconditional generative model.
[FIGURE:1d3827bf44b3fbcc | A simple directed graphical model with two nodes. An unshaded circle labeled $Z$ at the top has a downward-pointing arrow directed toward a shaded circle labeled $X$ at the bottom, representing a...]

We call this an **unconditional generative model** because it is a model of the unconditional distribution $p(X)$. Generally we will refer to unconditional generative models simply as generative models.
concepts.motivation_md: Unconditional models are useful when we want to learn the general structure of a dataset without needing specific labels, or when the goal is to synthesize entirely new examples that belong to a general category.
concepts.recap_md: - Models the unconditional distribution $p(X)$ by dropping the dependency on label $\mathbf{y}$.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: A conditional generative model is a model of a conditional distribution $p(X | Y)$.
concepts.content: A **conditional generative model** is a model of any conditional distribution $p(X \bigm | Y)$. These models focus on generating data $\mathbf{x}$ given a specific input or label $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In many applications, we don't just want a random image; we want an image of a specific thing (like a 'cat' or a 'dog'). Conditional models allow us to control the output of the generation process using external information.
concepts.recap_md: - Models the conditional distribution $p(X | Y)$.

concepts.title: Content Creation: Procedural Rivers
concepts.one_liner: Generative models can be used for content creation, such as procedurally generating landscapes or river paths in video games.
concepts.content:
One reason to use unconditional generative models is content creation. Suppose we are making a video game and we want to automatically generate a bunch of exciting levels for the player to explore. We would like a procedure for making up new levels from scratch. Such procedures have been successfully used to generate random landscapes and cities for virtual realities. Suppose we want to add a river to a landscape. We need to decide what path the river should take. A simple program for generating the path could be "walk an increment forward, flip a coin to decide whether to turn left or right, repeat."

Here is that program in pseudocode:

(see figure: A simple generative model that draws images of rivers.)

Here are a few rivers this program draws (@fig-generative_models-rivers1):

(see figure: Procedurally generated rivers.)

This program relies on a sequence of coin flips to generate the path of the river. In other words, the program took a randomized vector (noise) as input, and converted this vector into an image of the path of the river. It's exactly the same idea as generating images of birds, just this time the generator is a program that makes rivers (@fig-generative_models-gen_model_of_rivers_diagram):
concepts.motivation_md: Manually designing every asset in a large-scale virtual world is time-consuming and expensive. Procedural generation using stochastic models allows for the creation of infinite, varied content with minimal manual effort.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models enable automatic content creation for virtual environments.

concepts.title: Sampling from a Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: Sampling is the process of querying a learned generator with new, randomized vectors to produce novel outputs.
concepts.content:
To learn to synthesize realistic images, we start with a training set of examples of real images, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. In this context, an example is an {`input`, `output`} pair where the `input` is the null set. We feed these examples to a learner, which produces a generator function. Later, we may query the generator with new, randomized $\mathbf{z}$-vectors to produce novel outputs, a process called **sampling** from the model. This two-stage procedure is shown in @fig-generative_models-gen_model_training_vs_sampling:
