(see figure: Learning and using a generator.)
concepts.motivation_md: Once a model has learned the underlying distribution of a dataset, we need a way to use that knowledge. Sampling allows us to 'draw' from that distribution to create new, never-before-seen examples.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling involves inputting random noise into a trained generator to create new data.

concepts.title: Objective of Generative Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The objective of generative modeling is to create a generator that produces synthetic data identically distributed to the real training data.
concepts.content:
The objective of the learner is to create a generator that produces *synthetic* data, $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, that looks like the *real* data, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. There are different ways to define "looks like":

1. Synthetic data matches the real data in terms of certain marginal statistics (e.g., mean color, variance, or edge statistics).
2. Synthetic data has high probability under a density model fit to the real data.

The first approach works well when we only want to match certain properties. The second approach is better when we want to produce synthetic data that matches *all* statistics of the training examples. In practice, we may not be able to match all statistics due to limits of the model's capacity. To be precise, the goal of deep generative models is to produce synthetic data that is *identically distributed* as the training data, that is, we want $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ where $p_{\texttt{data}}$ is the true process that produced the training data.
concepts.motivation_md: The goal is to capture the 'essence' of a dataset so perfectly that the model's creations are indistinguishable from real-world observations, effectively learning the underlying probability distribution of the data.
concepts.recap_md: - The goal is to produce synthetic data that is identically distributed as the training data.

concepts.title: Generalization in Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: A good generative model must generalize by producing synthetic samples that look like the training data without simply memorizing and regurgitating them.
concepts.content: A property of a good generative model is that it be a simple, or smooth, function, so that it generalizes to producing synthetic samples that look like the training data but are not identical to it. A generator that only regurgitates the training data is overfit in the same way a classifier that memorizes the training data is overfit. In both cases, the true goal is to fit the training data and to do so with a function that generalizes. While memorized training samples satisfy the goal of making synthetic data look real, they fail the requirement of generalization.
concepts.motivation_md: If a model only repeats what it has seen, it hasn't truly learned the 'rules' of the data. Generalization ensures the model can create novel content that follows the same patterns as the original data.
concepts.recap_md: - Generalization prevents the model from simply memorizing and regurgitating training examples.

concepts.title: Contrastive learning from co-occurrence
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive learning from co-occurrence aims to learn a common representation of all signals that occur together, such as audiovisual pairs or different color channels of the same image.
concepts.content:
Contrastive learning can be based on co-occurrence, where the goal is to learn a common representation of all co-occurring signals. This form of contrastive learning is useful for learning, for example, an audiovisual representation where the embedding of an image matches the embedding of the sound for that same scene. Similarly, we can learn an image representation where the embedding of the grayscale channels matches the embedding of the color channels. In both cases, the objective is to align co-occurring sensory signals.

(see figure: Contrastive learning from multiple views of the data. Figure inspired by \cite{tian2020contrastive)

In this framework, co-occurring signals—such as color and grayscale—are referred to as two different **views** of the total data tensor $\mathbf{X}$, denoted as $\mathbf{x} = V_1(\mathbf{X})$ and $\mathbf{y} = V_2(\mathbf{X})$. These views can result from sensory co-occurrences or transformations of $\mathbf{X}$, such as channel dropping. Ultimately, the two kinds of contrastive learning (transformations and co-occurrences) are fundamentally the same: any two signals can be considered transformations of a combined total signal, and any signal and its transformation can be considered two co-occurring ways of measuring the underlying world.

[FIGURE:699660d27bc5fbbc | A block diagram illustrating contrastive learning with transformations. It shows input data {x^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N, T entering a box labeled 'Contrastive learning (transformations)'. Inside the box...]

[FIGURE:8ce923f69bb6f5a1 | A flowchart for contrastive learning showing data input, a processing box, and output functions. The input is data pairs {x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N. The central box defines the objective as a sum...]
concepts.motivation_md: This approach allows models to learn meaningful representations by exploiting the natural relationships between different modalities or parts of the data. By aligning signals that naturally occur together, the model captures the underlying structure of the world without requiring explicit human labels.
concepts.recap_md: - It learns a shared embedding space for signals that appear together, like audio and video.

concepts.title: Hadsell et al. contrastive loss
concepts.one_liner: The Hadsell et al. contrastive loss pulls positive samples together and pushes negative samples apart, using a margin to define when points are sufficiently separated.
concepts.content:
Hadsell et al. proposed a "contrastive loss" that pulls together positive samples and pushes apart negative samples. This definition is now part of a broader family of contrastive losses. This specific loss adds the concept of a **margin** to the vanilla formulation: it only pushes or pulls when the distance is less than a specified amount $m$ (the margin); otherwise, points are considered far enough apart or close enough together. The general formulation takes as input an anchor $\mathbf{x}$, a positive example $\mathbf{x}^+$, and one or more negative examples $\mathbf{x}^-$. The full learning objective sums over many samples:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}^-) &= \max(D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^+)-m_{\texttt{pos}},0) - \\ &\quad \max(m_{\texttt{neg}} - D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^-),0) \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Standard distance metrics might try to push negative samples infinitely far apart. The margin ensures the model only focuses on correcting pairs that are incorrectly close, preventing the loss from being dominated by already well-separated examples.
concepts.recap_md: - Pulls positive pairs together and pushes negative pairs apart.

concepts.title: Triplet loss
concepts.one_liner: The triplet loss optimizes representations by ensuring the distance between an anchor and a positive sample is smaller than the distance between the anchor and a negative sample by at least a margin.
concepts.content:
The **triplet loss** is a popular contrastive loss that incorporates a **margin** $m$ into its formulation. It ensures that the distance between an anchor and a positive sample is smaller than the distance between the anchor and a negative sample. The loss only applies when the relative distances do not satisfy the margin requirement; otherwise, the points are considered sufficiently separated. The loss function is defined as:
$$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}^-) = \max(D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^+)) - D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^-)) + m, 0)$$ 
This objective takes as input an anchor $\mathbf{x}$, a positive example $\mathbf{x}^+$, and a negative example $\mathbf{x}^-$.
concepts.motivation_md: Unlike simple pairwise losses, triplet loss focuses on the relative distance between positive and negative pairs, which is often more important for tasks like retrieval or face recognition than absolute distances.
concepts.recap_md: - Compares an anchor to both a positive and a negative sample simultaneously.

concepts.title: InfoNCE loss
concepts.one_liner: The InfoNCE loss treats contrastive learning as a classification problem, using a log softmax to distinguish a positive sample from multiple negative samples.
concepts.content:
The **InfoNCE loss** is a variation of contrastive loss that treats establishing a contrast as a classification problem. It attempts to move points apart until the positive sample for a given anchor can be classified separately from all negatives. The loss is defined as a log softmax over a vector of scores $f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(c)/\tau$ where $c$ is either the positive sample $\mathbf{x}^+$ or one of the negative samples $\{\mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N$:
$$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \{\mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N) = -\log \frac{e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}^+)/\tau}}{e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}^+)/\tau} + \sum_i e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)/\tau}}$$
You can think of this loss as a classification problem where the ground truth class is $\mathbf{x}^+$ and the other possible classes are the negative samples.
concepts.motivation_md: By using multiple negative samples and a softmax-based objective, InfoNCE provides a stronger training signal than single-pair losses, effectively maximizing the mutual information between the anchor and the positive sample.
concepts.recap_md: - Formulates contrastive learning as a multi-class classification task.

concepts.title: Margin in contrastive loss
concepts.one_liner: A margin in contrastive loss defines a distance threshold beyond which the model stops pushing or pulling points.
concepts.content: Hadsell et al.'s contrastive loss and the triplet loss add the concept of a **margin** to the vanilla formulation. They only push or pull when the distance is less than a specified amount $m$ (called the margin); otherwise, points are considered far enough apart or close enough together.
concepts.motivation_md: Without a margin, a model might waste capacity trying to push already-distinct samples even further apart, which can lead to unstable training or poor generalization.
concepts.recap_md: - Acts as a threshold for the loss function to ignore well-separated samples.

concepts.title: Why Group?
concepts.one_liner: Grouping is a form of representation learning that discovers language-like structures, such as objects and relationships, from unsupervised principles.
concepts.content:
Grouping is a special case of representation learning, serving as a substrate for downstream analysis and processing. Perceptual organization involves structures like objects, spatial relationships, shapes, and events. While current trends in computer vision map images to text to use natural language processing tools, perceptual organization aims to achieve similarly powerful representations through bottom-up grouping rules rather than human-language supervision. It is about discovering language-like structures from unsupervised principles to understand what constitutes an "object." Perceptual groups can also extend beyond the limits of language, representing coherent structures in our minds that may not have specific names.

(see figure: How many objects do you see?)
concepts.motivation_md: To interact with the world, we need to move beyond raw pixels to meaningful entities. Grouping provides the necessary structure for reasoning, planning, and high-level understanding.
concepts.recap_md: - Grouping provides a foundation for downstream tasks like object recognition.

concepts.title: Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities.
concepts.content:
**Segmentation** is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities. There is no single definition of what constitutes a coherent entity, as it varies by task; a segment might be a nameable object, a region of a single material, or a physically distinct piece of geometry.

(see figure: There are multiple ways you might segment any given image, and each way will highlight different world properties. This cactus branch could be viewed as (a) a single segment (the "branch"), (b) two...)

Segmentation can be framed as a clustering problem where each pixel is assigned to one of $k$ clusters. Two common approaches to this problem include assigning similar pixels to the same cluster or assigning pixels to the same cluster if there is no boundary between them.
concepts.motivation_md: Segmentation is a fundamental step in computer vision that allows machines to isolate individual objects or regions from a complex scene for further analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - Partitions an image into coherent, task-dependent regions.

concepts.title: K-Means Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: K-means segmentation clusters pixels based on feature similarity, such as color, to partition an image into regions of constant appearance.
concepts.content:
$K$-means is a simple clustering algorithm that can be applied to segmentation by treating each pixel as a datapoint. The simplest approach uses the pixel's color as its feature vector. For example, using $ab$ color values allows an image to be visualized as a scatter plot of color distributions.

(see figure: Different regions of coherent color in the image correspond to clusters in the scatter plot of all the $ab$-values of the image's pixels. In general, segmentation can be reduced to the problem of...)

$K$-means finds clusters in this color space and segments the image by assigning each pixel to the cluster of its color value. Each pixel in a cluster can then be colored by the mean color of that cluster.

(see figure: $K$-means segmentation on the fruits example.)

This method effectively finds segments with roughly constant color. While it can succeed on images where objects are defined by color similarity (like a zebra against a background), it fails on complex patterns not defined by color similarity.

(see figure: (top row): $k$-means segmentation succeeds on a seemingly hard image. *Photo source*: Fredo Durand. (bottom row): $k$-means fails on an image that, to our eye, looks no more complex.)
concepts.motivation_md: K-means provides a computationally efficient way to perform basic segmentation by assuming that objects are composed of pixels with similar visual features like color.
concepts.recap_md: - Clusters pixels based on color features (e.g., $ab$ values).

concepts.title: Diffusion Model
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models are a class of generative models that break the hard problem of image generation into many simple corruption and restoration steps.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models use a strategy similar to autoregressive models by breaking a hard problem into many simple pieces. They can be understood by looking at what autoregressive models do in the reverse direction: starting with a complete image, they remove one pixel, then the next, and the next.

(see figure: An autoregressive sequence in reverse is a corruption process that removes one pixel at a time.)
concepts.motivation_md: Generating complex data like high-resolution images in a single step is computationally difficult. Diffusion models solve this by decomposing the generation process into a sequence of small, manageable denoising steps, making the learning process more stable and effective.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffusion models break complex generation tasks into a series of simple steps. - They are conceptually related to autoregressive models viewed in a reverse corruption direction.

concepts.title: Reverse Diffusion Process
concepts.one_liner: The reverse diffusion process uses a neural network to learn the mapping from a noisier image back to a less noisy version.
concepts.content:
Just like autoregressive models, diffusion models train a neural net, $f_{\theta}$, to reverse the corruption process. It can be trained via supervised learning on example sequences of different images getting noisier and noisier. For example, as shown in the figure below, the sequence of images of a bird getting noisier can be flipped in time to provide a sequence of training examples of the mapping $\mathbf{x}_t \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$. These examples are then fit by a predictor $f_{\theta}$.

(see figure: Reverse diffusion process. The forward process creates supervision to train the reverse process.)
concepts.motivation_md: To generate data from noise, a model must learn how to undo the effects of corruption. By training on a reversed sequence of noise addition, the model learns to incrementally recover structure from chaos.
concepts.recap_md: - A neural network $f_{\theta}$ is trained to reverse the image corruption process. - Training data is created by flipping a sequence of increasingly noisy images in time. - The model learns the specific mapping $\mathbf{x}_t \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$ using supervised learning.

concepts.title: Denoiser
concepts.one_liner: A denoiser is a neural network that learns to remove small amounts of noise from an image to eventually recover a noise-less version.
concepts.content: We call $f_{\theta}$ a denoiser; it learns to remove a little bit of noise from an image. If we apply this denoiser over and over, starting with pure noise, the process should coalesce on a noise-less image that looks like one of our training examples.
concepts.motivation_md: The denoiser is the core functional unit of a diffusion model, responsible for the iterative refinement of data from a high-entropy state (noise) to a low-entropy state (a clean image).
concepts.recap_md: - The denoiser $f_{\theta}$ is trained to remove small increments of noise. - Repeated application of the denoiser transforms pure noise into a structured image.

concepts.title: Training Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Training a diffusion model involves generating noisy data through a forward process and training a neural network to invert those steps.
concepts.content:
The steps to train a diffusion model are as follows:

1. Generate training data by corrupting a bunch of images (forward process; noising).
2. Train a neural net to invert each step of corruption (reverse process; denoising).

As an additional trick, it can help to let the denoising function observe time step $t$ as input, so that we have:
$$\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t) \end{aligned}$$
This can help the denoiser to make better predictions, because knowing $t$ helps us know if we are looking at a normal scene that has been corrupted by noise (likely if $t$ is large) or a scene where the actual physical structure is full of chaotic, rough textures that happen to look like noise (likely if $t$ is small, because for small $t$ we haven't added much noise yet).

(see figure: Training a diffusion model consists of first producing training pairs of the form {noisy image, less noisy image}. Then do supervised learning on these pairs.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard supervised learning requires input-output pairs. By intentionally noising images, we create a synthetic dataset where the 'ground truth' is the less-noisy version, allowing us to train models to reverse the entropy increase.
concepts.recap_md: - Training involves a forward noising process and a reverse denoising process. - Including the time step $t$ as an input helps the model distinguish between added noise and natural image texture.

concepts.title: Probabilistic Interpretation of Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models can be interpreted probabilistically as Gaussian density models or variational autoencoders.
concepts.content: Diffusion models are trained using a loss $\mathcal{L}$, which could be the $L_2$ distance. In many diffusion models, $f_{\theta}$ is instead trained to output the parameters (mean and variance) as a Gaussian density model fit to the data. This formulation yields useful probabilistic interpretations; in fact, such a diffusion model can be framed as a variational autoencoder. However, diffusion models can still work well without these interpretations, instead using a wide variety of prediction models for $f_{\theta}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Framing diffusion models probabilistically allows researchers to use established tools from information theory and Bayesian inference, such as variational bounds, to improve and analyze model performance.
concepts.recap_md: - Models can be trained to output Gaussian parameters (mean and variance) rather than just a point estimate. - This approach allows diffusion models to be framed as variational autoencoders.

concepts.title: Noise Prediction Reparameterization
concepts.one_liner: A common training trick is to reparameterize the model to predict the noise added to an image rather than the clean signal itself.
concepts.content:
One useful trick for training diffusion models is to reparameterize the learning problem as predicting the noise rather than the signal:
$$\begin{aligned} f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t) &= \epsilon_t &\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{first predict noise}\\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} &= \mathbf{x}_t + \epsilon_t &\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{then remove this noise} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Predicting the noise component is often numerically more stable and easier for the neural network to learn than directly reconstructing the original image signal from a highly corrupted state.
concepts.recap_md: - The model is reparameterized to predict the noise $\epsilon_t$ instead of the signal $\mathbf{x}_{t-1}$. - The final prediction is reached by subtracting the predicted noise from the current noisy state.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) directly sample complex distributions in a single step by using a classifier to distinguish between real and synthetic data.
concepts.content: While autoregressive and diffusion models build up complex distributions step by step, the generative adversarial network (GAN) creates a system that directly outputs samples from the complex distribution in one step. The goal of generative modeling is to make synthetic data that looks like real data. GANs take a direct and intuitive approach: synthetic data looks like real data if a classifier cannot distinguish between synthetic images and real images.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs were developed to avoid the iterative sampling required by other models, aiming for a more direct 'one-shot' generation process driven by a competitive learning framework.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs generate samples from complex distributions in a single step. - They rely on a classifier's inability to distinguish between real and synthetic data as a measure of quality.

concepts.title: GAN Generator
concepts.one_liner: The generator in a GAN is a neural network that maps latent variables to synthetic data samples.
concepts.content: GANs consist of two neural networks, the generator, $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, which synthesizes data.
concepts.motivation_md: The generator's role is to learn a mapping from a simple, known distribution (like Gaussian noise) to the complex distribution of the target data, effectively 'creating' new samples.
concepts.recap_md: - The generator $g_{\theta}$ is one of the two primary components of a GAN. - It maps a latent space $\mathcal{Z}$ to the data space $\mathcal{X}$.

concepts.title: Reverse KL Divergence
concepts.one_liner: The reverse KL divergence, $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \| p_{\text {data }})$, measures the probability of the model's samples under the true data distribution.
concepts.content: $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta)$ is sometimes called the forward KL divergence, and it measures the probability of the data under the model distribution. The reverse KL divergence, $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \| p_{\text {data }})$, does the converse, measuring the probability of the model's samples under the data distribution. Because we do not have access to the true data distribution, the reverse KL divergence usually cannot be computed.
concepts.motivation_md: While forward KL divergence is standard for maximum likelihood, reverse KL divergence provides an alternative perspective by evaluating how likely model-generated samples are to have come from the real data distribution. It is a fundamental concept in variational inference and generative modeling, even if it is often intractable to compute directly.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the probability of model samples $p_\theta$ under the true data distribution $p_{\text{data}}$.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood Learning for Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Maximum likelihood learning for density models attempts to increase the probability density at observed datapoints while implicitly decreasing it elsewhere.
concepts.content:
Maximizing the likelihood objective is a form of maximum likelihood learning. Pictorially, we can visualize this objective as trying to push up the density over each observed datapoint:

(see figure: Fitting a max likelihood density model to data. The gray region holds a constant amount of mass; think of it as piles of dirt. To increase the amount of dirt at the locations of the green arrows you...)

Remember that a probability density function (pdf) is a function $p_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow [0,\infty)$ with $\int_{\mathbf{x}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = 1$. To learn a pdf, we typically learn the parameters of a family of pdfs, such as the Gaussian family. All members of such a family are normalized nonnegative functions; because they are normalized, whenever we push up density over datapoints, we are forced to sacrifice density over other regions. This implicitly removes density from places where there is no data.
concepts.motivation_md: Maximum likelihood provides a principled way to fit statistical models to data by ensuring the model assigns the highest possible probability to the observed samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Aims to maximize the probability density $p_\theta(\mathbf{x})$ for all observed data points.

concepts.title: Energy-Based Models (EBMs)
concepts.one_liner: Energy-based models (EBMs) learn an unnormalized function $E_\theta$ to represent data, avoiding the difficult constraint of ensuring the total probability integrates to one.
concepts.content:
Density models constrain the learned function to be normalized, such that $\int_{\mathbf{x}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = 1$. This constraint is often hard to realize. One approach is to learn an unnormalized function $E_{\theta}$, then convert it to a normalized density. Note that low energy implies high probability; thus, we minimize energy to maximize probability.

Energy-based models (EBMs) address the normalization challenge by skipping the normalization step and letting the output of the learner just be $E_\theta$. Even though it is not a true probability density, $E_{\theta}$ can still be used for many applications because we can compare relative probabilities. In sum, energy functions can do most of what probability densities can do, except they do not give normalized probabilities. Therefore, they are insufficient for applications where communicating true probabilities is important for interpretability or interfacing with downstream systems, such as a medical imaging system communicating the likelihood of cancer.
concepts.motivation_md: Normalizing a complex probability distribution is often computationally intractable. EBMs allow us to model the structure of data without the overhead of calculating a partition function.
concepts.recap_md: - Learns an unnormalized energy function $E_\theta$ where lower energy corresponds to higher probability.

concepts.title: Normalizing Constant (Partition Function)
concepts.one_liner: The normalizing constant $Z(\theta)$, or partition function, is the integral of the unnormalized density over all possible data values.
concepts.content: A density can be defined as $p_{\theta} = \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$, where $Z(\theta) = \int_{\mathbf{x}} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x}$ is the normalizing constant. The $Z(\theta)$ can be very expensive to compute and often can only be approximated. Notice that $Z$ is a function of model parameters $\theta$ but not of the datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, since we integrate over all possible data values.
concepts.motivation_md: To turn an arbitrary non-negative function into a valid probability distribution, we must divide by the sum (or integral) of all its possible values so that the total probability equals one.
concepts.recap_md: - Defined as $Z(\theta) = \int_{\mathbf{x}} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Boltzmann or Gibbs Distribution
concepts.one_liner: The parametric form $\frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$ is referred to as a Boltzmann or Gibbs distribution.
concepts.content: The parametric form $\frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$ is sometimes referred to as a Boltzmann or Gibbs distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: This functional form originates in statistical mechanics to describe the probability of a system being in a certain state as a function of that state's energy and the temperature.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents a probability distribution defined by an energy function $E_\theta$.

concepts.title: Relative Probabilities in Energy-Based Models
concepts.one_liner: Energy-based models allow for the comparison of relative probabilities because the normalizing constant $Z(\theta)$ cancels out.
concepts.content: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)} = \frac{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}/Z(\theta)}{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)}/Z(\theta)} = \frac{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}}{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)}} \end{aligned}$$ Knowing relative probabilities is all that is required for sampling (via MCMC), for outlier detection (where the relatively lowest probability datapoint is the outlier), and even for optimizing over a space of data to find the datapoint with maximum probability, because $\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}} -E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculating the absolute probability in an EBM is hard due to the partition function, but many tasks only require knowing if one point is more likely than another.
concepts.recap_md: - Relative probabilities are calculated as the ratio of unnormalized exponentials, bypassing $Z(\theta)$.

concepts.title: Gradient of Log Density in EBMs
concepts.one_liner: The gradient of the log probability density with respect to the input $\mathbf{x}$ is identical to the negative gradient of the energy function.
concepts.content:
To solve a maximization problem over $\mathbf{x}$, we might want to find the gradient of the log probability density with respect to $\mathbf{x}$. It turns out this gradient is identical to the gradient of $-E_{	heta}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$:

$$ egin{aligned} 
abla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p_{	heta}(\mathbf{x}) &= 
abla_{\mathbf{x}} \log  rac{e^{-E_{	heta}(\mathbf{x})}}{Z(	heta)}\ &= -
abla_{\mathbf{x}} E_{	heta}(\mathbf{x}) - 
abla_{\mathbf{x}} \log Z(	heta)\ &= -
abla_{\mathbf{x}} E_{	heta}(\mathbf{x}) \end{aligned}$$

In sum, energy functions can do most of what probability densities can do, except that they do not give normalized probabilities.
concepts.motivation_md: This identity allows us to perform gradient-based optimization or Langevin dynamics sampling on the data space without ever needing to compute the normalizing constant $Z(\theta)$.
concepts.recap_md: - $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = -\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$.

concepts.title: Contrastive Divergence
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive divergence is an optimization method for energy-based models that modifies the energy function to decrease energy for data samples and increase it for model samples.
concepts.content:
Contrastive divergence is a method that modifies the energy function on each iteration of optimization to decrease the energy assigned to samples from the data (positive term) and to increase the energy assigned to samples from the model (negative term):

(see figure: Fitting a max likelihood energy function to data, using contrastive divergence. @hinton2002training)

Once the energy function perfectly adheres to the data, samples from the model are identical to samples from the data and the positive and negative terms cancel out. Mathematically, this procedure approximates the gradient of the log likelihood function. Defining $p_{\theta} = \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$, we decompose the gradient of the log likelihood:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] - \nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) \end{aligned}$$

The first term is the positive term gradient. The second term, the negative term gradient, is an intractable integral that we rewrite as an expectation to be approximated via sampling:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] \end{aligned}$$

Plugging this back in, we arrive at:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] \end{aligned}$$

By taking $N$ samples $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \sim p_{\theta}$, we approximate the gradient as $\frac{1}{N} \nabla_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N (-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + E_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}))$. This establishes a contrast between data and model samples, bringing the model closer to the data. Contrastive divergence is an optimizer specifically built for max likelihood objectives over energy functions.
concepts.motivation_md: Directly maximizing the likelihood of an EBM is difficult because the gradient of the log partition function is intractable. Contrastive divergence provides a practical way to approximate this gradient using samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Approximates the log-likelihood gradient by contrasting real data samples with samples generated by the model.

concepts.title: Closed-form KL divergence for Gaussians
concepts.one_liner: The KL divergence between an encoder's Gaussian distribution and a unit Gaussian prior can be computed in closed form.
concepts.content:
For each datapoint $x$, the KL term can be computed in closed form since it is between two normal distributions:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid x) \| p_z\right)&=\operatorname{KL}\left(\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_z, \sigma_z^2\right) \| \mathcal{N}(0,1)\right)\\
    &= \frac{1}{2}(\mu_z^2 + \sigma_z^2 - \log(\sigma_z^2) - 1)
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Computing KL divergence generally requires integration, which is computationally expensive. For the specific case of two Gaussians, a closed-form solution exists, allowing for efficient and exact gradient-based optimization of the VAE objective.
concepts.recap_md:
- The KL divergence between $\mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma_z^2)$ and $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ has a simple algebraic form.
- This closed-form expression eliminates the need for sampling when calculating the KL term of the ELBO.

concepts.title: Approximating the VAE likelihood term via sampling
concepts.one_liner: The likelihood term in a VAE is approximated by sampling a latent variable $z$ from the encoder and measuring the probability of the input $x$ under the decoder's distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: The expected log-likelihood in the VAE objective is often intractable to compute analytically. Approximating it with a single sample provides an unbiased estimate that is computationally efficient for stochastic gradient descent.
concepts.recap_md:
- The process involves encoding an input, sampling from the resulting latent distribution, and decoding the sample.
- Likelihood is measured as the log-probability of the original input under the decoder's output distribution.

concepts.title: Reconstruction error
concepts.one_liner: Reconstruction error measures the difference between the original input and the output of the decoder after encoding and decoding.
concepts.motivation_md: Reconstruction error provides a training signal that forces the latent representation to preserve enough information to accurately recreate the original input.
concepts.recap_md:
- It represents the $(x - \mu_x)^2$ term in the Gaussian log-likelihood.
- Minimizing this error ensures the VAE functions as an effective autoencoder.

concepts.title: Reparameterization trick
concepts.one_liner: The reparameterization trick allows backpropagation through a sampling step by expressing the stochastic variable as a deterministic function of a fixed noise source.
concepts.content:
To train a VAE, we must backpropagate through the sampling step. We do this by reparameterizing the sampling from $\mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2_z)$ as a deterministic transformation of a fixed noise source:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\\
    z = \mu_z + \epsilon \sigma_z
\end{aligned}$$

This step is known as the reparameterization trick. It reparameterizes a stochastic function to be a deterministic transformation of a unit Gaussian. To optimize the encoder parameters, we only need to backpropagate through $\mu_z$ and $\sigma_z$, which are deterministic functions of $x$, sidestepping the need to handle backpropagation through a stochastic function.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard backpropagation cannot pass through random sampling. By separating the randomness into an external variable $\epsilon$, the gradients can flow through the parameters of the distribution ($\mu$ and $\sigma$).
concepts.recap_md:
- It transforms a stochastic sampling process into a differentiable deterministic function.
- It enables the use of standard gradient descent to optimize encoder parameters.

concepts.title: Tension between KL term and reconstruction error
concepts.one_liner: A VAE works through the tension between the KL term, which squashes latents toward the origin, and reconstruction error, which spreads them out to preserve information.
concepts.content:
The KL term encourages the encodings $z^{(i)}$ to be near a unit Gaussian distribution. If we fix $\sigma_{z^{(i)}}$ to 1, the KL term reduces to $\frac{1}{2}(\mu_{z^{(i)}}^2 - 1) \propto \mu_{z^{(i)}}^2$, which encourages the encodings $\mu_{z^{(i)}}$ to be as close to zero as possible. In other words, the KL term squashes the distribution of latents ($q_{\psi}(Z)$) toward the origin. Minimizing the reconstruction error, conversely, requires that the latents do not collapse; it wants them to be as spread out as possible to preserve information about the inputs $x^{(i)}$. The tension between these two terms causes the VAE to produce a tightly packed latent space that can be densely sampled, unlike standard autoencoders which may have gaps.

(see figure: Training a VAE to model the blue distribution. The Gaussian components spread out to tile both the embedding space and the data space.)
concepts.motivation_md: Without this tension, the model would either collapse all inputs to a single point (minimizing KL) or create a disorganized, sparse latent space (minimizing reconstruction error) that is useless for generation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The KL term acts as a regularizer that squashes latent codes toward the origin.
- Reconstruction error forces latent codes to spread out to maintain input information.
- This balance results in a continuous, densely packed latent space suitable for sampling.

concepts.title: VAEs as representation learning
concepts.one_liner: VAEs serve as representation learning tools by mapping data to low-dimensional latent codes that preserve input information and can exhibit properties like disentanglement.
concepts.content: One perspective on VAEs is that they are generative models where the encoder is scaffolding for the decoder. However, the encoder is also useful as an end in itself for representation learning. Like autoencoders, the VAE encoder maps data to a low-dimensional latent code that preserves information about the input. VAEs can even go beyond autoencoders: if the prior is $p_{\mathbf{z}} = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, the loss encourages the dimensions of the embedding to be independent, a property called disentanglement.
concepts.motivation_md: Beyond just generating new data, we often want to find meaningful, compressed ways to represent complex data for downstream tasks or to understand the underlying factors of variation.
concepts.recap_md:
- VAE encoders provide compressed embeddings similar to standard autoencoders.
- The choice of prior can encourage specific desirable properties in the learned representation.
- VAEs often learn independent dimensions of variation through the KL divergence constraint.

concepts.title: Disentanglement
concepts.one_liner: Disentanglement is a property where individual dimensions of a latent embedding correspond to independent factors of variation in the data.
concepts.content: Disentanglement means that we can vary one dimension of the embedding at a time, and just one independent factor of variation in the generated images will change. For example, one dimension might control the direction of light in a scene while another dimension controls the intensity of light. In VAEs, using a prior like $p_{\mathbf{z}} = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ encourages the loss to make the dimensions of the embedding independent.
concepts.motivation_md: Disentangled representations are highly desirable because they are more interpretable and allow for precise control over specific features when generating or manipulating data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Each latent dimension ideally controls exactly one independent feature of the data.
- It allows for "walking" along a single axis to change one specific attribute (e.g., lighting or rotation).

concepts.title: Nonidentifiability of true parameters
concepts.one_liner: Nonidentifiability refers to the issue where a model may find mechanisms that explain the data without necessarily recovering the true causal parameters that generated it.
concepts.content:
VAEs and most representation learning methods do not necessarily recover the true causal mechanisms that generated the data; instead, they might find other mechanisms that can equivalently explain the data. For example, a VAE might discover a latent dimension that summarizes a global mode of behavior (like river curvature) even if that behavior was generated by a different process in the original data source. A formal name for this issue is the nonidentifiability of the true parameters that generated a dataset.

(see figure: Walking along two axes of latent space generates images that show variation in two distinct attributes, demonstrating that this model is, to a degree, disentangled.)
concepts.motivation_md: It is important to understand that while a model's latent space might be useful and disentangled, it does not guarantee that the model has discovered the 'real' underlying physics or logic of the data source.
concepts.recap_md:
- Models can explain data using parameters that differ from the true generating process.
- Disentangled dimensions may represent summaries of behavior rather than the original causal factors.
- Nonidentifiability is a fundamental challenge in recovering true parameters from observed data.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Networks as Representation Learners

position.section_title: Generative Adversarial Networks Are Representation Learners Too

concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can discover disentangled latent variables that control specific data attributes, similar to Variational Autoencoders.
concepts.content:
Generative adversarial networks (GANs), like VAEs, train a mapping from latent variables to synthesized data, $g: \mathbf{z} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$. Experiments with powerful models like BigGAN, trained on ImageNet, demonstrate that GANs also learn meaningful and disentangled latents. For example, walking along specific latent dimensions can reveal variables that control distinct features such as background color or an object's orientation.

(see figure: Walking in in two orthogonal directions in BigGAN @brock2018large)

This behavior is expected because the GAN generator is structurally similar to the VAE decoder. Both map a low-dimensional random variable $\mathbf{z}$ (typically $p_{\mathbf{z}} = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$) to high-dimensional data. Since the dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ are independent a priori, and the goal is to create synthetic data with the properties of real data, both models tend to learn latent representations with similar disentangled properties. These models belong to a large class that maps simple, high-entropy distributions to structured, low-entropy data.
concepts.motivation_md: While GANs are primarily known for high-quality data synthesis, understanding them as representation learners reveals that their latent space is not just random noise. It provides a structured way to manipulate and understand the underlying features of the data manifold.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs map low-dimensional latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ to high-dimensional data $\mathbf{y}$.

concepts.title: Connection Between Representation Learning and Generative Modeling
concepts.one_liner: Representation learning and generative modeling are intimately connected and can be viewed as inverses of each other.
concepts.content: Representation learning and generative modeling are intimately connected; they can be viewed as inverses of each other. This view reveals an important property of the latent variables in generative models. While these variables have simple prior distributions like noise, they are not unimportant nuisances. Instead, latent variables act as a powerful representation of the data. They can be thought of as underlying control knobs that generate the data. A user can spin these knobs randomly to produce a random image, or tune them to navigate the natural image manifold in a systematic way to arrive at a specific desired image.
concepts.motivation_md: This connection explains why generative models are useful beyond just making pretty pictures; they provide a structured 'control panel' for complex data by learning its underlying factors.
concepts.recap_md: - Representation learning and generative modeling act as inverse processes.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Models for Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Generative models can be used to solve prediction problems by modeling the relationship between inputs and outputs.
concepts.content: Generative models have three primary uses: synthesizing realistic but novel data, learning representations of data, and solving prediction problems. This third use is arguably the most widespread application of generative models in practice.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard regression often fails when there are multiple valid answers for a single input; conditional generative models provide a framework to handle this ambiguity by modeling the full output distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models can synthesize data, learn representations, or solve prediction problems.

concepts.title: Point Prediction
concepts.one_liner: A point prediction is a single output value for a given input, often formulated via least-squares regression.
concepts.content:
Point prediction occurs when a model outputs just a single prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y}$ for every input $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$. This is often formulated as least-squares regression, where a function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ is trained to output a vector of real-valued numbers (such as RGB pixel values) by penalizing the squared distance between the output and the ground truth.

(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

Point prediction fails when there are multiple equally valid answers. For example, colorizing a grayscale image is a many-to-one mapping; a single grayscale value could correspond to many different color values. Because a point estimate can only predict one of these multiple possible solutions, it is a poor inference method for fundamentally ambiguous problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Point prediction is the simplest form of regression, but it is insufficient for complex, real-world tasks where data is ambiguous or multimodal.
concepts.recap_md: - Point prediction outputs a single value $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ for a given input $\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Multimodal Distributions in Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Point predictions fail in multimodal distributions by 'splitting the difference' between valid modes, often resulting in impossible outputs.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

In ambiguous problems like colorization, the true data distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}$ may be multimodal. For instance, a shirt might be either teal or pink with equal probability. Least-squares regression results in a model that predicts the mean of the data distribution. In this case, the point prediction would be gray—a color that has zero probability under the true data distribution. 

While a point prediction $\hat{a} = f_{\theta}(l)$ can be interpreted as a predictive distribution $p_{\theta}(A = a | l) = \delta(a - \hat{a})$ using the Dirac delta function, it remains fundamentally limited. Even using different loss functions like $L_1$ will not solve the problem, because a single point prediction can only ever represent one mode, whereas the true distribution may have multiple equally probable modes.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the failure of point predictions on multimodal data motivates the need for models that can represent multiple possible outcomes simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md: - Least-squares regression predicts the mean, which may have zero probability in multimodal data.

concepts.title: Predictive Distribution Modeling
concepts.one_liner: Predictive distribution modeling improves on point estimates by predicting the parameters of a probability distribution rather than a single value.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

Instead of a point estimate, we can predict a distribution. For example, a least-squares regression model can be viewed as outputting the mean of a Gaussian fit to $p_{\theta}(A | l)$. By also predicting the variance, we obtain a better sense of possible outcomes, though a single Gaussian remains unimodal. 

To capture bimodal or complex data, we can predict the parameters of a more expressive parametric family, such as a mixture of Gaussians. For a mixture of $N$ Gaussians, the model outputs $3N$ numbers: the mean, variance, and weight for each component. The loss function is then the data likelihood under the mixture parameterized by these outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Predicting a distribution allows a model to express uncertainty and handle multiple possible outcomes that a single point prediction cannot capture.
concepts.recap_md: - Models can output parameters (like mean and variance) of a distribution instead of a single point.

concepts.title: Categorical Distribution for Expressive Predictions
concepts.one_liner: The categorical distribution provides a highly expressive way to model multimodal predictions by quantizing the output space.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

The categorical distribution, $\texttt{Cat}$, is a common choice for modeling expressive, multimodal distributions. Because it applies to discrete variables, the output values must first be quantized into bins. For example, an $a$-value in color space can be quantized into ten bins, making the categorical distribution a ten-dimensional vector of non-negative numbers that sum to 1. This parameterization is powerful because all probability mass functions over $k$ classes are members of the family $\texttt{Cat}(k)$, allowing the model to represent any number of modes up to the resolution of the quantization.
concepts.motivation_md: Quantizing continuous outputs into categories allows us to use standard classification tools to model complex, multi-peaked probability distributions without assuming a specific functional form like a Gaussian.
concepts.recap_md: - Categorical distributions require quantizing continuous output values into discrete bins.

concepts.title: Softmax Regression and Expressive Distributions
concepts.one_liner: Softmax regression is a ubiquitous tool because it models a maximally expressive predictive distribution over a quantized space.
concepts.content: Softmax regression is a critical application of the categorical distribution. It is a ubiquitous modeling tool because it models a maximally expressive predictive distribution over a quantized decision space, which explains its effectiveness in classification tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing classification through the lens of generative modeling explains why softmax is so effective: it doesn't just pick a label, it models the most flexible possible distribution over the available choices.
concepts.recap_md: - Softmax regression utilizes the categorical distribution for maximum expressivity in discrete spaces.

concepts.title: Data Log Likelihood Function
concepts.one_liner: The data log likelihood function $L(\{\mathbf{x}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta)$ measures the log likelihood of the observed data under a model $p_{\theta}$.
concepts.content:
One of the most important quantities we will measure is the data log likelihood function $L(\{\mathbf{x}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta)$, which measures the log likelihood of the data under the model $p_{\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned}
    L(\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$
Many methods use a max likelihood objective, optimizing $L$ with respect to $\theta$. To compute the likelihood function, we need to compute $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Maximum likelihood estimation is a fundamental principle in statistics and machine learning for finding the model parameters that best explain the observed data.
concepts.recap_md: - The log likelihood is the sum of the log probabilities of each individual data point under the model.

concepts.title: Marginal Likelihood
concepts.one_liner: The marginal likelihood expresses the probability of observed data by marginalizing over all unobserved latent variables.
concepts.motivation_md: When a model depends on hidden or latent factors that aren't directly observed, we must integrate them out to find the total probability of the data we actually see.
concepts.recap_md: - Marginal likelihood is calculated by integrating the joint distribution of data and latent variables over the latent space.

concepts.title: Infinite Mixture of Gaussians
concepts.one_liner: Variational Autoencoders model an infinite mixture of Gaussians by making the mean and variance functions of a continuous latent variable.
concepts.motivation_md: Finite mixture models are limited in their representational power; using an infinite mixture allows for a much more flexible distribution that can capture complex data structures.
concepts.recap_md: - VAEs represent an infinite mixture by treating Gaussian parameters as neural network outputs of a latent variable.

concepts.title: VAE Learning Problem
concepts.one_liner: The VAE learning problem involves maximizing the data log likelihood, which requires approximating an intractable integral over latent variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard maximum likelihood is impossible to compute directly for VAEs because the integral over the latent space cannot be solved analytically for deep neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - The VAE objective is to maximize the log of the marginal likelihood.

concepts.title: Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)
concepts.one_liner: The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood that provides a differentiable objective for training VAEs.
concepts.content:
The VAE objective $J$, often called the Evidence Lower Bound or ELBO, is a lower-bound on the data log-likelihood $\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$. It is used because the exact log-likelihood is intractable and its Monte Carlo estimate is biased. By applying Jensen's inequality, we derive $J$ as:
$$\begin{aligned}    J_p &= \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\\
    &= \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big]\\
    &\geq \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log \big(\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\big)\Big] \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{Jensen's inequality}\\
    &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[-\log q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) + \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) + \log p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z}) \Big] = J
\end{aligned}$$
Using the definition of KL-divergence, $J$ can be rewritten as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    J &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) \Big] - \mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi(Z \mid \mathbf{x}) \| p_{\mathbf{z}}\right)
\end{aligned}$$
In this form, the objective is the sum of a term measuring data log likelihood under samples from $q_{\psi}$ and a term measuring the gap between $q_{\psi}$ and the prior $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. The learning problem for both $\theta$ and $\psi$ is to maximize this shared objective over the dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: Directly maximizing the log-likelihood is difficult due to bias in Monte Carlo estimates of the log-expectation. The ELBO provides a surrogate objective that is easy to estimate and optimize.
concepts.recap_md: - The ELBO is a lower bound on the log-likelihood derived via Jensen's inequality.

concepts.title: Jensen's Inequality in VAE Derivation
concepts.one_liner: Jensen's inequality is used in VAEs to show that the expectation of the log is a lower bound of the log of the expectation.
concepts.content:
The fact that the VAE objective $J$ is a lower-bound on the log-likelihood $J_p$ follows from Jensen's inequality:
$$\begin{aligned}    J_p &= \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\\
    &= \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\Big]\\
    &\geq \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[\log \big(\frac{p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})}{q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})\big)\Big] \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{Jensen's inequality}\\
    &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})}\Big[-\log q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) + \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z}) + \log p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z}) \Big]\\
    &= J \quad\quad\triangleleft\quad\text{VAE objective}\\
    &\Rightarrow \quad J \leq J_p
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Jensen's inequality allows us to move the logarithm inside the expectation, transforming an intractable log-integral into a tractable expectation of logs.
concepts.recap_md: - Jensen's inequality proves that $J \leq \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$.

concepts.title: Connection between VAEs and Autoencoders
concepts.one_liner: VAEs can be viewed as autoencoders where the reconstruction error is measured as the likelihood of the input given a sampled latent code.
concepts.content:
VAEs use an encoder $f_{\psi}$ (parameterizing $q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x})$) and a decoder $g_{\theta}$ (parameterizing $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z})$), mirroring the structure of an autoencoder. For 1D data and latent space, we define means and variances:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mu_z &= f^{\mu}_{\psi}(x), & \sigma^2_z &= f^{\Sigma}_{\psi}(x)\\
    \mu_x &= g^{\mu}_{\theta}(z), & \sigma^2_x &= g^{\Sigma}_{\theta}(z)
\end{aligned}$$
The VAE objective maximizes the sum of a likelihood term and a KL term. The likelihood term is approximated by sampling: we encode $x$ to get $\mu_z, \sigma^2_z$, sample $z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2_z)$, and then decode $z$ to get $\mu_x, \sigma^2_x$. The log-likelihood $\log p_{\theta}(x | z)$ is:
$$\begin{aligned}  
    \log p_{\theta}(x | z) &= \log\frac{1}{\sigma_x\sqrt{2\pi}} - \frac{\overbrace{(x - \mu_x)^2}^{\text{reconstruction error}}}{2\sigma_x^2}
\end{aligned}$$
Measuring the probability the decoder places on the original input $x$ corresponds to measuring the reconstruction error, just like an autoencoder.

(see figure: To evaluate the likelihood a VAE places on a datapoint $x$, we encode $x$ into $z$-space and then decode back and compute the reconstruction error. This corresponds to one importance sample for...)
concepts.motivation_md: Connecting VAEs to autoencoders provides an intuitive framework for understanding how generative models can learn compressed representations of data.
concepts.recap_md: - VAEs encode inputs into a distribution in latent space and decode samples to reconstruct the input.

concepts.title: Maximizing the VAE objective
concepts.one_liner: The VAE learning problem seeks to maximize an objective consisting of a likelihood term and a KL-divergence term.
concepts.content:
The VAE learning problem seeks to maximize the following objective:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Big( \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{z\sim q_{\psi}(Z \bigm | x^{(i)})}\Big[ \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)} \bigm | z) \Big]}_{\text{likelihood term}} - \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\left(q_\psi\left(Z \mid x^{(i)}\right) \| p_z\right)}_{\text{KL term}} \Big)
\end{aligned}$$
On each step of optimization, we compute this objective over a batch of datapoints, and then apply backpropagation to update the parameters to increase the objective.
concepts.motivation_md: This specific decomposition allows the model to balance accurate reconstruction of the data with a well-behaved, regularized latent space.
concepts.recap_md: - The objective is maximized using backpropagation over batches of data.

concepts.title: Heeger-Bergen Texture Synthesis Method
concepts.one_liner: A wavelet-based texture synthesis method that matches histograms of filter responses across multiple orientations and scales to generate new images from noise.
concepts.content: The Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis method, published in 1995, is an influential wavelet-based algorithm for image synthesis. It is based on the conjecture that two textures appear identical to a human observer if they produce the same distribution of filter responses for all filters. The algorithm consists of two stages: texture analysis and texture synthesis. In the analysis stage, a reference texture is decomposed into multiple orientations and scales using a steerable pyramid, typically with six orientations and three scales. The final texture representation, $\theta$, is the concatenation of the 18 subband histograms, the low-pass residual histogram, and the input image histogram. (see figure: (a) Texture analysis (encoder) using a steerable pyramid with six orientations and three scales. The output representation is the concatenation of the 18 subband histograms, the low-pass residual...) The synthesis stage is an iterative procedure that begins with a random noise image and uses the parameters $\theta$ to produce a new improved image. (see figure: The steps of the Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis algorithm. The process starts with white noise input image. Each step takes as input the previous output, and it is modified by a function...) The crux of the algorithm is to alternate matching the intensity domain pixel histogram of the image and then matching the histograms of each subband in the transform domain. Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity. (see figure: Histogram matching for one of the subbands. The same operation is done for all the subbands independently.) After several iterations, the algorithm converges to a synthesized texture. While effective for many textures, it may poorly depict large-scale structures as it does not capture correlations across scales. (see figure: Two examples of synthesized textures. Inputs have a size of 256 $\times$ 256 pixels, outputs are 512 $\times$ 512. In these examples, the algorithm runs for 15 iterations, using a pyramid of six...)
concepts.motivation_md: The method was developed to test the hypothesis that textures are perceptually identical if they share the same distribution of filter responses, providing a way to synthesize textures using multi-scale statistical matching.
concepts.recap_md: - Decomposes a reference texture into subbands using a steerable pyramid. - Iteratively matches histograms of the image and its filter subbands. - Represents texture as a concatenation of subband, low-pass residual, and image histograms.

concepts.title: Texture Analysis
concepts.one_liner: The process of extracting a texture representation, $\theta$, from a reference texture image.
concepts.content: Texture analysis of a reference texture extracts a texture representation, $\theta$. This representation captures the essential parameters or statistical properties of the reference image required to characterize its texture.
concepts.motivation_md: To create a compact mathematical or statistical description of a visual texture that can be used to generate new, similar samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Extracts a representation $\theta$ from a reference image. - Serves as the encoder stage in texture synthesis workflows.

concepts.title: Texture Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: The procedure of using a texture representation, $\theta$, to generate new random samples that appear visually similar to the original texture.
concepts.content: Texture synthesis uses a representation, $\theta$, to generate new random samples of the same texture. In general, two textures are perceived as similar when they seem to be generated by the same physical process.
concepts.motivation_md: To generate large or infinite amounts of a specific texture from a small sample, which is useful in computer graphics and image editing.
concepts.recap_md: - Generates new samples based on a representation $\theta$. - Aims to produce images perceived as originating from the same process as the reference.

concepts.title: Histogram Matching for Texture Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: A technique that uses a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity to modify image or subband values so their distribution matches a target histogram.
concepts.content: Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity. In texture synthesis, it is used to transform the subbands of a noise image to match the Laplacian-shaped histograms typical of natural textures. For example, the subband of input white noise has a Gaussian distribution; histogram matching modifies each subband pixel so the resulting subband looks sparser, with many values set to zero, matching the target reference. (see figure: Histogram matching for one of the subbands. The same operation is done for all the subbands independently.)
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a way to force the statistical distribution of a generated image to match the known statistics of a reference texture across different scales and orientations.
concepts.recap_md: - Employs a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity to adjust pixel value distributions. - Transforms Gaussian noise subbands to match the sparse distributions of natural textures.

concepts.title: Parametric Texture Models

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: Texture models that represent a texture using a fixed, low-dimensional set of statistical parameters.
concepts.content: Parametric texture models represent textures using a specific set of parameters, $\theta$, extracted during analysis. These models were the primary approach to texture synthesis until the emergence of nonparametric methods around the year 2000.
concepts.motivation_md: To provide a compact, efficient representation of texture that captures essential statistical properties without needing to store the entire original image.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a low-dimensional representation $\theta$ to characterize textures. - Predominant in the field until the rise of nonparametric models.

concepts.title: Nonparametric Texture Models

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: Texture models that use the reference image itself as the representation, rather than a fixed set of parameters.
concepts.content: Nonparametric texture models became dominant after 2000, succeeding parametric models until the rise of neural generative models in 2014. In these models, the representation of a texture is typically the reference image itself. The advantage of this approach is that no information is lost in the representation.
concepts.motivation_md: To avoid the information loss inherent in low-dimensional parametric models and better capture complex, high-order spatial structures.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses the reference image itself as the texture representation. - Dominant between 2000 and the advent of deep learning generative models.

concepts.title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: A nonparametric texture synthesis model based on Markov random fields that generates pixels by sampling from similar neighborhoods in a reference image.
concepts.content: The Efros-Leung model is a nonparametric Markov random field image model where the probability distribution of a pixel is dependent on the neighborhood around it. In this model, the representation of a texture is the reference image itself, ensuring no information is lost. The synthesized texture changes as a function of the context region size: small regions may fail to capture complete structures, while larger regions enforce spatial regularities. (see figure: In the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99) (see figure: A source texture image consisting of five white rings arranged in a quincunx pattern (four in the corners and one in the center) against a solid black background.) (see figure: A black and white image showing a source texture of thin, white, squiggly lines and small loops scattered across a black background. The lines are irregular and vary in length and curvature...) (see figure: A black and white texture image showing many small, white, ring-shaped circles scattered across a solid black background. The circles are roughly uniform in size but are distributed with some...) (see figure: A source texture image consisting of a regular grid of white rings on a black background. The rings are arranged in a staggered, hexagonal-like pattern across the entire frame.) (see figure: Image synthesis results from the Efros-Leung algorithm. The small crops are used to synthesize the larger texture regions. Input images are 128 $\times$ 128 pixels, and the outputs are 256 $\times$...)
concepts.motivation_md: It solves the problem of synthesizing textures with complex spatial structures that parametric models fail to capture by directly leveraging the local statistics of the source image.
concepts.recap_md: - Models texture as a Markov random field where pixels depend on their neighborhood. - Synthesizes images by finding and copying matching patches from a reference sample. - Neighborhood size controls the balance between local variety and global structure.

concepts.title: Efros-Leung Algorithm

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: An iterative process that synthesizes texture by matching local neighborhoods in a reference image and copying corresponding pixel values.
concepts.content: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an iterative procedure for texture synthesis. At each iteration, the algorithm identifies the synthesized pixels in the neighborhood of the target pixel. It searches the input reference image for examples of similar pixel configurations, defined by a sum of squared intensity differences lower than a specific threshold. One of these matching instances is randomly selected, and its pixel value is copied to the synthesized image. This process is typically performed in a raster-scan ordering. Pixels without sufficient neighboring context can be randomly sampled from the input texture. (see figure: In the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99)
concepts.motivation_md: To provide a simple yet effective way to grow textures by mimicking the local conditional probability distributions found in a sample image.
concepts.recap_md: - Iteratively fills pixels based on local neighborhood similarity to the source. - Uses sum of squared differences (SSD) to find matching patches. - Can be implemented using a raster-scan ordering for synthesis.

concepts.title: Representation Learning as Pretraining
concepts.one_liner: Representation learning algorithms are specifically designed pretraining phases meant to serve as a warm-up for a subsequent real-world task.
concepts.content: The pretraining phase can be regular training that is only labeled as "pretraining" in retrospect once adaptation to a new problem begins. Alternatively, pretraining algorithms can be specifically designed to serve only as a warm-up for the real event. Representation learning algorithms are of this latter variety, intended to provide a foundation for future tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Pretraining allows a model to learn useful features or representations from a large dataset before being adapted to a specific target task, which can improve performance and efficiency.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pretraining can be standard training repurposed for a new task.
 - Representation learning algorithms are specifically designed as a warm-up phase.
 - The goal is to prepare the model for the 'real event' of solving a specific problem.

concepts.title: Finetuning
concepts.one_liner: Finetuning consists of initializing a new classifier with the parameter vector from a pretrained model and then training it as usual.
concepts.content: Finetuning consists of initializing a new classifier with the parameter vector from the pretrained model, and then training it as usual. In other words, finetuning is making small (fine) adjustments (tuning) to the parameters of your model to adapt it to do something slightly different than what it did before, or even something a lot different.
concepts.motivation_md: Finetuning allows a model to leverage knowledge from a previous task to solve a new task, often requiring less data and time than training from scratch.
concepts.recap_md:
- Initialize a new model using parameters from a pretrained model.
 - Perform 'fine' adjustments to adapt the model to a new task.
 - Can be used for tasks that are slightly or significantly different from the original.

concepts.title: Finetuning Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: The finetuning algorithm involves pretraining a model, initializing a new model with those parameters, and then training it on a new task.
concepts.content:
There are three stages to the finetuning process: (1) pretrain $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, (2) initialize $f^{\prime} = f$, and (3) finetune $f^{\prime}: \mathcal{X}^{\prime} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}^{\prime}$. The full algorithm is represented as a continually learning $f_{\theta}$ with different iterates of $\theta$ as learning progresses.

(see figure: Finetuning. Using gradient descent to train one model and then finetuning to produce a second model.)
concepts.motivation_md: This structured approach provides a formal method for transferring knowledge from a source domain to a target domain using gradient-based optimization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Stage 1: Pretrain the initial model $f$.
 - Stage 2: Initialize the new model $f^{\prime}$ with the pretrained parameters.
 - Stage 3: Finetune the new model on the target domain.

concepts.title: Network Surgery for Finetuning
concepts.one_liner: Network surgery involves replacing the first or last layers of a pretrained network to accommodate changes in input or output dimensionality.
concepts.content:
To handle changes in dimensionality during transfer learning, it is common to cut off the last layer of the network and replace it with a new final layer that outputs the correct dimensionality. If the input dimensionality changes, you can do the same with the first layer of the network. Both these changes are shown in the process of adapting a model.

(see figure: A diagram illustrating the process of pretraining and finetuning a neural network with changing input/output dimensions. In the 'Pretraining' stage, a model $f = f_3 \circ f_2 \circ f_1$ is trained...)
concepts.motivation_md: Pretrained models often have fixed input and output sizes; network surgery allows these models to be adapted to tasks with different data formats or class counts.
concepts.recap_md:
- Replace the final layer to match the target output dimensionality.
 - Replace the first layer if the input dimensionality changes.
 - This allows the reuse of internal layers that have learned general features.

concepts.title: Finetuning Subparts of a Network
concepts.one_liner: Finetuning can be applied selectively to specific layers or subparts of a computation graph while others remain frozen or are initialized from scratch.
concepts.content:
(see figure: A diagram illustrating the process of pretraining and finetuning a neural network with changing input/output dimensions. In the 'Pretraining' stage, a model $f = f_3 \circ f_2 \circ f_1$ is trained...)

### Finetuning Subparts of a Network

You do not have to finetune all layers in your network; you can selectively finetune some and initialize others from scratch. This strategy can be applied generally, where some parts of a computation graph are initialized from pretrained models and others from scratch. There are many reasons for this: you might have pretrained models that perform only specific parts of a full system's requirements, allowing you to compose them with new layers. Alternatively, you may want to freeze certain layers to prevent them from forgetting their prior knowledge.
concepts.motivation_md: Selective finetuning saves computational resources and prevents 'catastrophic forgetting' by preserving specialized knowledge in certain parts of the network.
concepts.recap_md:
- Selectively finetune specific layers while keeping others fixed.
 - Compose pretrained modules with layers initialized from scratch.
 - Freeze layers to preserve prior knowledge during the adaptation process.

concepts.title: Freezing Layers
concepts.one_liner: Freezing layers involves preventing specific modules or parameters from being updated during training to preserve their prior knowledge.
