concepts.content:
Freezing certain layers is a technique used to prevent them from forgetting their prior knowledge during the training process. This is often indicated in diagrams using a specific symbol.

We will use the symbol [FIGURE:29db42ece472b20d | A black silhouette icon of a padlock with a circular dial in the center, used as a symbol to indicate that a module or parameter is frozen and not updated during training.]
concepts.motivation_md: Freezing layers is essential when you want to maintain the feature extraction capabilities of a pretrained model while only training the task-specific parts.
concepts.recap_md:
- Prevents parameters from being updated during backpropagation.
 - Used to preserve knowledge and reduce the number of trainable parameters.
 - Often represented by a padlock icon in architectural diagrams.

concepts.title: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
concepts.one_liner: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates only a subspace of the full weight matrix to save memory and regularize adaptation.
concepts.content: Within a single layer, it is possible to update just a subspace of the full weight matrix. This can be an effective way to save memory, as there are fewer weight gradients to track during backpropagation, or to regularize the amount of adaptation being performed. One popular way to do so is to apply a low-rank update to the weight matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: Updating massive weight matrices is computationally expensive; LoRA provides a way to adapt large models by only training a small number of additional parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Updates a subspace of the weight matrix rather than the whole matrix.
 - Reduces memory usage by tracking fewer gradients.
 - Acts as a form of regularization for model adaptation.

concepts.title: Read Out Module
concepts.one_liner: A read out module takes features from a computation graph as input and produces a new prediction as output.
concepts.content: A read out module is a specific kind of module that takes features from the computation graph as input and produces a new prediction as output. When these modules are linear, they are referred to as linear read outs.
concepts.motivation_md: Read out modules are necessary to translate the internal representations (features) learned by a network into a format suitable for a specific task's predictions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Takes features from the computation graph as input.
 - Produces the final prediction as output.
 - Often implemented as a linear layer.

concepts.title: Data Bias and Shift
concepts.one_liner: Machine learning theory often assumes future data is identically distributed as past data, but in reality, discrepancies between training and deployment distributions frequently lead to system failures.
concepts.content: The goal of learning is to acquire rules from past data that work well on future data. In the theory of machine learning, it is almost always assumed that the future is identically distributed as the past. In reality, it is almost always the case that this is not true. Many of the failures of machine learning in industry and in society are due to this discrepancy between theory and practice. When a learned system is deployed on data that is unlike what it was trained on, various issues can arise regarding the reliability and accuracy of the model.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard machine learning theory relies on the assumption that training and test data come from the same distribution. However, real-world applications often break this assumption. Understanding data bias and shift is critical for diagnosing why models that perform perfectly in the lab fail when deployed in the real world.
concepts.recap_md: - Machine learning typically assumes training and test data are identically distributed.

concepts.title: Distribution Shift
concepts.one_liner: Distribution shift occurs when training data and test data are sampled from different parts of the total data space.
concepts.content:
Distribution shift occurs when the training data is sampled from one part of the total data space and the test data is sampled from another part. There is a gap between the training distribution and test distribution, which can be visualized as a domain gap.

(see figure: Domain gap between training data and test data in the ColorizeBot example.)

In these cases, we are confounded by a shifting data distribution. Shifting data is the rule, not the exception, and it challenges the probabilistic guarantees we expect over future results.
concepts.motivation_md: In practice, the environment in which a model operates changes over time or differs from the controlled environment where data was collected. Recognizing distribution shift is the first step in building robust systems that can generalize beyond their specific training sets.
concepts.recap_md: - Distribution shift is the discrepancy between training and test data distributions.

concepts.title: Name That Dataset! Game
concepts.one_liner: The 'Name That Dataset!' game demonstrates that computer vision datasets have distinct styles, making them biased samples of the visual world.
concepts.content:
In the paper by Torralba et al. (2011), the authors propose a game called *Name That Dataset!*. The game consists of matching random images from famous computer vision datasets with their corresponding dataset names. The point of the game is to show that it is easy to recognize the *style* of images and to identify the dataset they belong to. If the datasets were unbiased samples of the same visual world, it would be impossible to win the game; however, researchers can correctly match them about 75 percent of the time.

(see figure: Let's play the *Name That Dataset!* game. Modified from @Torralba2011. The game consists in associating each set of three images with the name of the dataset, from the list on the right, they belong...)
concepts.motivation_md: This game serves as a pedagogical tool to prove that datasets are not neutral representations of reality. By showing that humans can identify a dataset just by looking at a few images, it highlights the inherent 'signature' or bias present in data collection processes.
concepts.recap_md: - Researchers can identify specific datasets with high accuracy based on image style.

concepts.title: The Value of Training Examples
concepts.one_liner: The market value of a training example varies across datasets, often requiring more data to achieve the same performance when testing on a different distribution.
concepts.content:
The value of a training example from one dataset can be measured by its effectiveness when used to test on another. A value of 0.25, for instance, means that you need 4 times more training examples than when using a sample derived from the same testing distribution. This 'Market Value' for specific categories, such as a 'car' sample, shows how datasets like LabelMe, PASCAL, ImageNet, and Caltech101 relate to one another in terms of cross-dataset generalization.

|                     | LabelMe market | PASCAL mkt. | ImageNet mkt. | Caltech101 mkt. |
|---------------------|----------------|-------------|---------------|-----------------|
| 1 LabelMe is worth  | 1 LabelMe      | 0.26 Pascal | 0.31 ImageNet | 0 Caltech       |
| 1 Pascal is worth   | 0.50 LabelMe   | 1 Pascal    | 0.88 ImageNet | 0 Caltech       |
| 1 ImageNet is worth | 0.24 LabelMe   | 0.40 Pascal | 1 ImageNet    | 0 Caltech       |
| 1 Caltech101 is worth | 0.23 LabelMe | 0 Pascal    | 0.28 ImageNet | 1 Caltech       |
: "Market Value" for a "car" sample across datasets. Modified from @Torralba2011. {#tbl-market_bias}
concepts.motivation_md: Quantifying the 'value' of data helps researchers understand how much 'transferable' information exists between datasets. It illustrates that not all data is created equal; data from a different distribution is often significantly less efficient for training than data from the target distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Market value measures how many examples from one dataset equal one example from the target distribution.

concepts.title: Photographer Bias
concepts.one_liner: Photographer bias refers to the tendency of humans to capture objects and scenes from preferred, canonical viewpoints rather than random ones.
concepts.content:
Photographer bias is one of the most common biases in image databases and is difficult to eliminate. Studies show that participants have consistent preferences for particular viewpoints of objects, which often correlate with how easy the object is to recognize. People recognize objects better when presented in a canonical orientation.

(see figure: Cannonical viewpoints for 12 objects. Figure from @Palmer1981)

The views recognized faster match the viewpoints preferred when taking a picture. This preference introduces biases in object pose statistics in photographs compared to how objects are actually seen in the world. This bias extends to scenes, involving camera orientation (e.g., the horizon's position), object locations (like the rule of thirds), arrangements, shadows, occlusions, and lighting conditions. Photographers consciously or unconsciously consider these factors when deciding which pictures to take.
concepts.motivation_md: Because humans take the photos used in datasets, those datasets reflect human psychology and aesthetic preferences rather than a raw, objective view of the world. This can lead to models that fail when they encounter objects from 'unnatural' or non-canonical angles.
concepts.recap_md: - Humans prefer 'canonical' viewpoints that make objects easier to recognize.

concepts.title: Canonical Orientation
concepts.one_liner: A canonical orientation is a preferred viewpoint from which an object is most easily recognized by humans.
concepts.content:
A canonical orientation refers to the viewpoint from which people recognize objects most effectively. Studies have shown that speed and accuracy in object classification are higher when objects are presented in these preferred orientations.

(see figure: Cannonical viewpoints for 12 objects. Figure from @Palmer1981)
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of canonical orientation explains why certain viewpoints dominate image datasets. Understanding this helps identify why a model might be 'brittle' when seeing an object from an unusual angle that was never captured by a human photographer.
concepts.recap_md: - Canonical orientations are viewpoints that maximize recognition speed and accuracy.

concepts.title: Collection Bias
concepts.one_liner: Collection bias arises from the specific protocols or sources used to gather data, such as internet searches or specific capture techniques.
concepts.content:
Collection bias stems from the fact that different data sources—such as egocentric videos, internet images, or vacation photographs—carry significant and identifiable biases. For example, a Google image search for "mug" typically returns images against flat, white backgrounds from canonical viewpoints, rather than the diverse settings where mugs are actually found (like inside a dishwasher or a sink).

(see figure: Pictures of mugs returned by a Google image search. There are many types of biases present in this small image collection.)

Such collections often lack diversity, featuring specific traits like handles appearing on the right side or a lack of occlusions. These biases are a direct result of the collection protocol used, such as the ranking algorithms of search engines or the types of images people choose to upload to the internet.
concepts.motivation_md: Models are only as good as the data they see. If the collection process (like web scraping) only captures 'clean' or 'ideal' versions of an object, the resulting AI will likely fail in messy, real-world environments where those objects are occluded or poorly lit.
concepts.recap_md: - Collection bias is the result of the specific protocol or source used to gather images.

concepts.title: Annotation Bias
concepts.one_liner: Annotation bias occurs when the choices made by human annotators regarding which images to label and what terms to use introduce systematic errors.
concepts.content: Annotation bias occurs when image annotators choose which images to annotate and which labels to apply. This often correlates with viewpoint preferences and photographer biases, as easier-to-recognize images are more likely to be segmented and labeled, potentially compounding existing biases. Furthermore, the language choices made during annotation are a significant source of bias, particularly social bias.
concepts.motivation_md: Even if the images themselves were perfect, the human act of labeling them introduces subjectivity. Annotators might ignore difficult cases or use inconsistent terminology, which teaches the model to replicate those same human shortcuts and prejudices.
concepts.recap_md: - Annotators tend to label images that are easier to recognize, reinforcing photographer bias.

concepts.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
concepts.one_liner: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a variant of gradient descent that uses a randomly sampled batch of training data to estimate the gradient at each iteration.
concepts.content:
One problem with gradient-based methods is that the gradient may be very expensive to compute, especially for learning problems where the objective $J$ is the average of losses incurred on each training datapoint. Computing $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$ requires computing the gradient for each element in the average. For a training set of size $N$, $\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta, \{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)})$. For large $N$, computing this sum is very expensive. 

Instead, we can randomly subsample (without replacement) a batch of terms from this sum, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(b)}, \mathbf{y}^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^B$, where $B$ is the batch size. We then compute an estimate of the total gradient as the average gradient over this batch: $$\tilde{\mathbf{g}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{b=1}^B \nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(b)}), \mathbf{y}^{(b)})$$. This variant is called stochastic gradient descent (SGD) because each iteration uses a different randomly (stochastically) sampled batch. 

(see figure: Stochastic gradient descent algorithm. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a stochastic subset (batch) of the full training data, and makes an update on that basis.)

Beyond speed, SGD has useful properties: it can jump over small bumps in the loss landscape that disappear for some batches, and it can implicitly regularize the learning problem. For linear problems with multiple parameter settings that minimize loss, SGD often converges to the solution with the minimum parameter norm.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard gradient descent is computationally prohibitive on large datasets because it requires calculating the gradient for every single training point before making a single update. SGD solves this by using small random subsets of data to estimate the gradient, enabling much faster iterations.
concepts.recap_md: - SGD estimates the true gradient using a randomly sampled subset (batch) of the training data.

concepts.title: Batch Size
concepts.one_liner: The batch size $B$ is the number of randomly subsampled training points used to compute an estimate of the total gradient.
concepts.content: For large datasets of size $N$, computing the full gradient sum is very expensive. Suppose instead we randomly subsample (without replacement) a batch of terms from this sum, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(b)}, \mathbf{y}^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^B$, where $B$ is the batch size. We then compute an estimate of the total gradient as the average gradient over this batch as follows: $$\tilde{\mathbf{g}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{b=1}^B \nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(b)}), \mathbf{y}^{(b)})$$.
concepts.motivation_md: Batch size acts as a hyperparameter to navigate the tradeoff between gradient accuracy and computational speed. Larger batches provide more accurate estimates but require more computation per step.
concepts.recap_md: - The batch size $B$ determines how many samples are used to estimate the gradient in each iteration.

concepts.title: Overfitting
concepts.one_liner: Overfitting occurs when a model fits properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, leading to high training performance but low test performance.
concepts.content: Learning theory studies the settings under which optimization on the training set yields good results on the test set. In general it may not, since the test set may have different properties from the training set. When we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, we call this overfitting. When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not generalize to the test data.
concepts.motivation_md: Overfitting is a central challenge in machine learning where a model becomes too specialized to its training examples, losing its ability to make accurate predictions on new, unseen data.
concepts.recap_md: - Overfitting happens when a model captures noise or specific training set quirks instead of the underlying relationship.

concepts.title: Generalization
concepts.one_liner: Generalization is the ability of a model to apply what it learned from training data to perform well on unseen test data.
concepts.content: Learning theory studies the settings under which optimization on the training set yields good results on the test set. In general it may not, since the test set may have different properties from the training set. When we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, we call this overfitting. When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not generalize to the test data.
concepts.motivation_md: The ultimate goal of machine learning is not just to memorize training data, but to generalize—to perform accurately on new data the model has never encountered before.
concepts.recap_md: - Generalization refers to how well a model's learned patterns apply to a separate test set.

concepts.title: Underfitting
concepts.one_liner: Underfitting occurs when a learner fails to optimize the objective on the training data.
concepts.content: A learner may perform poorly for one of two reasons: either it failed to optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting. The former is called underfitting and the latter is called overfitting.
concepts.motivation_md: Underfitting identifies when a model is too simple or training has not progressed enough to capture the basic patterns in the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Underfitting is characterized by poor performance even on the training data itself.

concepts.title: Polynomial Regression
concepts.one_liner: Polynomial regression is a learning problem where the hypothesis space consists of polynomial functions of a specified degree $K$.
concepts.content: Polynomial regression is just like linear regression except that the hypothesis space is polynomial functions rather than linear functions, that is, $$y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$$ where $K$, the degree of the polynomial, is a hyperparameter of the hypothesis space. In the setting where we use the least-squares ($L_2$) loss function, polynomial regression is highly related to linear regression; in fact, we can transform a polynomial regression problem into a linear regression problem.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear models are often too simple to capture curved relationships in data. Polynomial regression allows for more flexible curves while still benefiting from the well-understood optimization techniques of linear regression.
concepts.recap_md: - Polynomial regression uses a hypothesis space of the form $f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$.

concepts.title: Polynomial Regression as Linear Regression
concepts.one_liner: Polynomial regression can be treated as a linear regression problem by featurizing the input $x$ into a vector of its powers.
concepts.content: We can rewrite a polynomial as a linear function in the parameters $\theta$: $$\sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)$$ where $$\phi(x) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x \\ x^2 \\ \vdots \\ x^K \end{bmatrix}$$. By featurizing $x$ and representing each datapoint with the feature vector $\phi(x)$, we arrive at a linear regression problem in this feature space. The learning problem and closed-form optimizer for $L_2$ polynomial regression are almost identical to $L_2$ linear regression, using a data matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$: $$\mathbf{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x^{(1)} & x^{(1)^2} & ... & x^{(1)^K} \\ 1 & x^{(2)} & x^{(2)^2} & ... & x^{(2)^K} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x^{(N)} & x^{(N)^2} & ... & x^{(N)^K} \end{bmatrix}$$. The matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$ is an array of the features (columns) for each datapoint (rows).
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows us to solve non-linear problems using the powerful and efficient tools developed for linear regression, simply by changing how we represent the input data.
concepts.recap_md: - Featurizing $x$ into $\phi(x)$ makes the polynomial function linear with respect to the parameters $\theta$.

concepts.title: Data Generating Process
concepts.one_liner: The data generating process is the full process, including the true underlying relationship and observation noise, that produces observed data.
concepts.content: The observed data $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ is sampled from a ground truth relationship plus observation noise. We refer to the full process that generates the data as the data generating process. For example, if the true relationship is $Y = X^2 + 1$ and the observation noise is $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, then the noisy observations $Y^\prime = Y + \epsilon$ and the resulting samples $x,y \sim p(X,Y^{\prime})$ constitute the data-generating process.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the data generating process helps distinguish between the actual signal we want to learn and the random noise that we should ignore.
concepts.recap_md: - The data generating process combines a true underlying relationship with random observation noise.

concepts.title: Gradient of Log Identity
concepts.one_liner: The gradient of the log of a function is equal to the gradient of the function divided by the function itself.
concepts.content: A very useful identity from the chain rule of calculus, which appears often in machine learning, is: $$\nabla_{x} \log f(x) = \frac{1}{f(x)} \nabla_{x} f(x)$$ This identity allows for the simplification of gradients involving log-likelihoods.
concepts.motivation_md: This identity is a fundamental tool in machine learning for optimizing objectives involving probability densities, as it converts the gradient of a log-function into a more manageable form involving the function's own gradient.
concepts.recap_md: - The identity is defined as $\nabla_{x} \log f(x) = \frac{1}{f(x)} \nabla_{x} f(x)$.

concepts.title: Comparing Different Kinds of Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: Generative models can be categorized by whether they provide density functions, energy functions, or generator functions.
concepts.content:
Generative models can be summarized by whether they produce density functions $p_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow [0,\infty)$, energy functions $E_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, or generators $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Each family has distinct trade-offs. Generators utilize latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ to control properties of the generated output, allowing meaningful changes by varying these inputs. In contrast, density and energy models lack direct latent control but provide scores related to data likelihood, which are useful for anomaly detection or synthesizing high-quality data through optimization.

Models are roughly categorized by their straightforward usage, though some properties can be added with extra effort (e.g., sampling from a density model or estimating density from a VAE). 

| Method | Latents? | Density/Energy? | Generator? |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Energy-based models | ❌ | ✅ (energy only) | ❌|
| Gaussian | ❌ | ✅ | ❌|
| Autoregressive models | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (slow) |
| Diffusion models | ✅ (high-dimensional) | ❌ | ✅ (slow) |
| GANs | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| VAEs | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |

Generative models also differ in their objectives, hypothesis spaces, and optimization algorithms. Some, like autoregressive models, refer to a hypothesis space, while others, like VAEs, refer to a specific conjunction of objective, hypothesis space, and optimization algorithm.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the trade-offs between different generative architectures helps in selecting the right model for a specific task, such as representation learning, likelihood estimation, or efficient sampling.
concepts.recap_md: - Generators use latent variables for controllable synthesis, while density/energy models provide likelihood scores.

concepts.title: Gaussian Density Model
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian distribution is a simple density model defined by its mean and variance parameters.
concepts.content: One of the simplest and most useful density models is the Gaussian distribution, which in one dimension (1D) is: $$p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)}$$ This density has two parameters, $\theta_1$ (mean) and $\theta_2$ (variance). The normalization constant $Z$ ensures the function is normalized. The typical strategy in defining density models is to create a parameterized family of functions where every member is normalized, then search over the parameters to optimize a generative modeling objective.
concepts.motivation_md: The Gaussian model serves as a foundational building block for density estimation, providing a mathematically tractable way to represent data distributions using only two parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - The 1D Gaussian density is $p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)}$.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood Objective for Density Models
concepts.one_liner: The maximum likelihood objective for density models seeks to maximize the expected log-probability of the data.
concepts.content: For density models, the most common objective is maximum likelihood: $$\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(x)] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)})$$ This objective measures how well the model's probability distribution aligns with the observed data samples.
concepts.motivation_md: Maximum likelihood estimation provides a principled statistical framework for fitting model parameters to observed data by maximizing the probability that the model generated that data.
concepts.recap_md: - The objective is to maximize the average log-likelihood $\frac{1}{N} \sum \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)})$.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation for 1D Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: Maximum likelihood estimation for a 1D Gaussian results in setting the parameters to the empirical mean and variance of the data.
concepts.content:
For a 1D Gaussian, the log-likelihood objective takes the form: $$\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)} = -\log(Z) + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)$$ While optimization can be done via gradient descent, an analytical solution exists by setting the gradient to zero. For the mean $\theta_1^*$, the solution is the empirical mean: $$\theta_1^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x^{(i)}$$ For the variance $\theta_2^*$, noting that $\frac{\partial (-\log Z)}{\partial \theta_2^*} = \frac{1}{2\theta_2^*}$, the solution is the empirical variance: $$\theta_2^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2$$ This shows that to maximize the probability of the data under a Gaussian, one should set the model parameters to the data's empirical mean and variance.

[FIGURE:36e43cf75cec6f8d | A block diagram representing a 1D Gaussian density model. On the left, input data {x^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N enters a central box labeled '1D Gaussian density model'. Inside the box, three components are...]
concepts.motivation_md: Deriving the MLE for a Gaussian demonstrates why empirical statistics are the optimal parameters for this specific distribution, providing a clear example of an analytical solution to a learning problem.
concepts.recap_md: - The optimal mean $\theta_1^*$ is the empirical average of the data points.

concepts.title: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)
concepts.one_liner: A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) represents complex densities by combining multiple Gaussian distributions.
concepts.content: To model a more complicated density, we may use a mixture of multiple Gaussian distributions, called a Gaussian mixture model (GMM).
concepts.motivation_md: Single Gaussians are limited to unimodal distributions; GMMs allow for modeling more complex, multimodal data by combining several simple distributions.
concepts.recap_md: - A GMM is a weighted sum of multiple Gaussian distributions.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Model
concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive models synthesize data sequentially, predicting each new element based on the previously generated sequence.
concepts.content:
An autoregressive model synthesizes an image pixel by pixel, where each new pixel is decided based on the sequence already generated. This is treated as a sequence prediction problem: given a sequence of observed pixels, a learned function $f_{\theta}$ predicts the color of the next one. 

As shown in (see figure: An autoregressive model, f_{\theta}, that generates an image pixel by pixel. The black pixels are the remaining pixels to synthesize. Compare with the Efros-Leung model in @fig-sampling_efros_leung.), the model predicts each next pixel from a partial image. The context is the region the prediction is based on, which could be the entire synthesized image or a smaller window. After predicting the distribution for the next pixel, a color is chosen—either the most likely or by sampling to introduce randomness—and the context window slides forward to repeat the process.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models simplify the complex task of high-dimensional data generation by breaking it down into a series of simpler conditional 1D prediction steps.
concepts.recap_md: - Data is generated sequentially, with each step conditioned on a 'context' of previous outputs.

concepts.title: Categorical Distribution for Pixel Modeling
concepts.one_liner: A categorical distribution can fully represent the probability mass function of a single grayscale pixel's 256 possible values.
concepts.content: Synthesizing a single grayscale pixel is straightforward because it can take on one of 256 possible values (for standard 8-bit images). A categorical distribution is used to represent the probability of each value. This distribution is fully expressive, meaning it can represent any possible probability mass function (pmf) over those 256 values. Fitting the distribution to training data involves counting the frequency of each value in the training set and normalizing by the total count. Once fit, we can sample from this distribution to synthesize a random one-pixel image.
concepts.motivation_md: Using a categorical distribution for pixels avoids making assumptions about the shape of the color distribution, allowing the model to learn any arbitrary frequency of pixel intensities from the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Grayscale pixels are modeled as categorical variables with 256 possible outcomes.

concepts.title: Conditional Variational Autoencoders (cVAEs)

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: A conditional VAE (cVAE) defines a conditional distribution as a marginal over latent variables that are independent of the conditioning inputs.
concepts.content:
A variational autoencoder (VAE) is an infinite mixture model based on the identity $p_{	heta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{	heta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z}$. Analogously, any conditional distribution can be defined as the marginal over some latent variable: $p_{	heta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{	heta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})d\mathbf{z}$. In conditional VAEs (cVAEs), we restrict our attention to latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ that are independent of the inputs we are conditioning on, resulting in the cVAE likelihood model: $$p_{	heta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{	heta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z}$$

This corresponds to the following graphical model:
[FIGURE:184e45370a8359cb | A directed acyclic graph (DAG) representing a conditional generative model. It consists of three circular nodes: $X$ and $Z$ at the top, and $Y$ at the bottom. Directed arrows point from $X$ to $Y$...]

The idea is that $\mathbf{z}$ should only encode information about $\mathbf{y}$ that is independent from what $\mathbf{x}$ already provides. For example, in predicting the next frame of a bouncing billiard ball from a single frame $\mathbf{x}$, the color and rough position are known from $\mathbf{x}$, but the velocity is missing. If the model learns to interpret $\mathbf{z}$ as velocity, it achieves a high-likelihood prediction. Just like regular VAEs, cVAEs use an encoder to predict the optimal importance sampling distribution $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$. In practice, the encoder takes both $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ as input, and the decoder takes both $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$.

(see figure: A scenario where a yellow ball is moving across a plane. The observation, $\mathbf{x}$, is a static frame. From that observation, we know what will be the color and rough position of the ball in the...)

(see figure: cVAE architecture. The dotted lines indicate that the *target encoder* is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path.)
concepts.motivation_md: cVAEs allow for generative modeling when we have specific conditioning information (like a class label or a previous video frame). They solve the problem of modeling the remaining uncertainty in a prediction by using latent variables to capture only the information not already provided by the conditioning input.
concepts.recap_md: - cVAEs model $p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})$ by marginalizing over a latent variable $\mathbf{z}$ that is independent of the input $\mathbf{x}$.

concepts.title: Conditional Autoregressive Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional autoregressive models treat conditioning inputs as a prefix to the sequence of values being modeled.
concepts.content: Autoregressive models already model a sequence of conditional distributions. To condition them on some inputs $\mathbf{x}$, we can simply concatenate $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the sequence of $y$ values we are modeling, yielding the new sequence: $[x_1, \ldots, x_m, y_1, \ldots, y_n]$. The probability model factorizes as: $$p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^n p_{\theta}(y_i \bigm | y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, x_1, \ldots, x_m)$$ Each distribution in this product is a prediction of the next item in a sequence given the previous items, which is no different than what we had for unconditional autoregressive models. Therefore, the tools for modeling unconditional autoregressive distributions are also appropriate for modeling conditional autoregressive distributions. From an implementation perspective, the same exact code will handle both cases, just depending on whether you prefix the sequence or not.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach allows standard sequence-to-sequence modeling (like translation or text-to-speech) to use the same architectural foundations as unconditional language models by simply prepending the context.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditioning is achieved by concatenating the input $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the target sequence $\mathbf{y}$.

concepts.title: Conditional Diffusion Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models incorporate conditioning variables by concatenating them into the input of the denoising function.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models can be made conditional by concatenating the conditioning variables, $\mathbf{x}$, into the input to the denoising function: $$\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_t, t, \mathbf{x})$$ Both diffusion models and autoregressive models convert generative modeling into a sequence of supervised prediction problems. To make them conditional is therefore just as easy as conditioning a supervised learner on more observations. If the original training pairs are $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, we can condition on additional paired observations $\mathbf{c}$ by augmenting the pairs to become $\{[\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{c}^{(i)}], \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. 

An example where we condition on text is shown in (see figure: Text-conditional diffusion model.). The intuition is that if we give $f_{\theta}$ a description of the image as an additional input, then it can do a better job at solving its prediction task. Because of this, $f_{\theta}$ will become sensitive to the text command, and if you give different text it will denoise toward a different image that matches that text.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional diffusion models enable tasks like text-to-image synthesis by allowing the denoising process to be guided by external information, ensuring the generated output aligns with specific user requirements.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditioning is implemented by adding the context $\mathbf{x}$ as an input to the denoising function $f_{\theta}$.

concepts.title: Structured Prediction in Vision
concepts.one_liner: Structured prediction in vision involves predicting high-dimensional, structured objects like label maps, depth maps, or meshes from an input image.
concepts.content: Whenever you want to make a prediction of an image, conditional generative models are a suitable modeling choice. While image colorization is a classic example, most problems in vision involve predicting labels or geometry. In image classification, the output might be a single class, but in object detection and semantic segmentation, we want a label for each part of the image. The target output in these problems is high-dimensional and structured. Similarly, in geometry estimation, the output is a depth map, a voxel grid, or a mesh. All these are high-dimensional structured objects. The tool needed for solving these problems is structured prediction, and conditional generative models are therefore a good choice for these tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard classification or regression is insufficient for tasks where the output has internal spatial or structural dependencies, such as segmentation or 3D reconstruction. Structured prediction frameworks handle these complex outputs.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision tasks like segmentation and depth estimation require predicting high-dimensional, structured outputs.

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation is the problem of mapping an input image to an output image, effectively translating between different views of data.
concepts.content: Image-to-image problems are mapping problems where the input is an image and the output is also an image, defined here as any array of size $N \times M \times C$ (height by width by number of channels). These problems are very common in computer vision and include examples such as colorization, next frame prediction, depth map estimation, and semantic segmentation. One way to think about all these problems is as translating from one view of the data to another. For example, semantic segmentation is a translation from viewing the world in terms of its colors to viewing the world in terms of its semantics. This perspective defines the problem of image-to-image translation, analogous to translating between languages like English and French.
concepts.motivation_md: Many vision tasks can be unified under a single framework where the goal is to transform one representation of a scene (like a sketch or a label map) into another (like a photo).
concepts.recap_md: - Defines vision tasks as a mapping from an input image array to an output image array.

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation with a Conditional GAN
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation can be performed using a conditional GAN where a generator maps an input image to an output image and a discriminator evaluates the result.
concepts.content:
One approach to image-to-image translation is to use a conditional GAN, as popularized by the "pix2pix" method. For example, in translating a facade layout map into a photo, the conditioning information (input) is a semantic segmentation image, and the output is a matching photo. The generator maps an image to an image using an architecture like a U-Net (a CNN with skip connections). The discriminator maps the output image to a real-versus-synthetic scalar score using a regular CNN. 

(see figure: The pix2pix @pix2pix2017 model applied to translating a facade layout map into a photo of the facade. The model was trained on the CMP Facades Database @Tylecek13 and the input and ground truth...)

In this setting, noise inputs are often omitted because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ has enough entropy to create variety, though this means the model typically produces only one prediction $\mathbf{y}$ for each input $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional GANs provide a powerful framework for generating realistic, high-resolution images that are strictly constrained by an input structure, such as a map or a sketch.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a U-Net generator to map input images to output images and a CNN discriminator for scoring.

concepts.title: GAN Discriminator as a Learned Loss Function
concepts.one_liner: The discriminator of a conditional GAN can be viewed as a learned loss function that adapts to penalize relevant errors made by the generator.
concepts.content:
The setup of a conditional GAN can be viewed as a regression problem with a learned loss function $d_{\phi}$. This loss function adapts to the structure of the data and the behavior of the generator to penalize just the relevant errors the generator is currently making. To stabilize the optimization process, it can be helpful to add a conventional regression loss, such as the $L_1$ loss, to the objective: $$\arg\min_G\max_D \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert_1 \big]$$

(see figure: The discriminator of a GAN as a learned loss function.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard losses like Mean Squared Error often produce blurry results in image generation; a learned discriminator loss can capture complex, high-level features of 'realness' that are hard to define mathematically.
concepts.recap_md: - The discriminator acts as a dynamic loss function that penalizes specific generator errors.

concepts.title: PatchGAN Discriminator
concepts.one_liner: A PatchGAN discriminator scores individual image patches as real or fake and averages these scores to determine the total loss.
concepts.content: The architecture of the learned loss function $d_{\phi}$ determines what kinds of errors it penalizes. A popular architecture for image-to-image tasks is the PatchGAN discriminator, which scores each patch in the output image as real or fake and takes the average over patch scores as the total loss: $$d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i=0}^N \sum_{j=0}^M d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}(\mathbf{x}[i:i+k,j:j+k], \mathbf{y}[i:i+k,j:j+k])$$ where $k \times k$ is the patch size. This operation is equivalent to the sliding window action of a CNN, so $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ can be implemented as a CNN that outputs a $2 \times N \times M$ feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores. Patches can be sampled at different strides and resolutions depending on the CNN architecture.
concepts.motivation_md: By focusing on local patches rather than the whole image, PatchGAN encourages high-frequency detail and texture realism while reducing the number of parameters in the discriminator.
concepts.recap_md: - Scores local $k \times k$ patches to enforce local consistency and high-frequency detail.

concepts.title: PatchGAN Properties
concepts.one_liner: PatchGAN discriminators offer statistical advantages by modeling local patches rather than entire images, requiring fewer parameters while training on more data samples.
concepts.content:
The PatchGAN strategy has two advantages over just scoring the whole image as real or synthetic with a classifier architecture: (1) it can be easier to model if a patch is real or synthetic than to model if an entire image is real or synthetic ($d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ needs fewer parameters), (2) there are more patches in the training data than there are images. These two properties give PatchGAN discriminators a statistical advantage over whole image discriminators (fewer parameters fit to more data). 

The disadvantage is that the PatchGAN only has the architectural capacity to penalize errors that are observable within a single patch. This can be seen by training models with different discriminator patch sizes and observing the results. 

(see figure: Varying the receptive field (patch size) of the convolutional discriminator affects what kinds of structure the discriminator enforces. These results are from @pix2pix2017)

A $1\times1$ discriminator can only observe a single pixel at a time and cannot penalize errors in joint pixel statistics such as edge structure, hence the blurry results. Larger receptive fields can enforce higher order patch realism, but cannot model structure larger than the patch size (hence the tiling artifacts that occur with a period roughly equal to the patch size). Quality degrades with the $286\times286$ discriminator possibly because this discriminator has too hard a task given the limited training data (in any given training set, there are fewer examples of $286\times286$ regions than there are of, say, $70\times70$ regions).
concepts.motivation_md: Whole-image discriminators often require massive parameter counts and struggle with limited data. PatchGAN solves this by focusing on local patches, which increases the effective number of training examples and simplifies the modeling task, allowing the network to focus on high-frequency details like texture and local structure.
concepts.recap_md: - PatchGANs use fewer parameters and more training samples by treating each image patch as a separate data point.

concepts.title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired image-to-image translation maps images between domains without requiring direct training pairs of corresponding images.
concepts.content:
In image-to-image translation, we can treat the task like a supervised regression problem using a learned loss function given by a GAN discriminator. This approach works well when we have lots of training data pairs $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$ to learn from. Unfortunately, very often, paired training data is hard to obtain. For example, consider the task of translating a photo into a Cezanne painting:

(see figure: A style transfer example from the CycleGAN paper @CycleGAN2017 *Input photo source*: Alexei A. Efros.)

This task requires predicting what a scene would look like if a specific artist had painted it. We cannot solve this with paired training data because such data is extremely hard to come by; we would need the artist to paint new scenes for every photo in our training set. However, humans can imagine the answer because we know the artist's style and can reason about the changes needed to make a photo match that style, even without seeing them paired with the exact same scenes. This setting is called the unpaired translation setting, distinguished from paired translation as indicated in the figure below.

(see figure: (left) An example of paired image-to-image translation (colorization) versus (right) unpaired translation (photo to Cezanne). Figure adapted from @CycleGAN2017)
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world scenarios, such as style transfer or domain adaptation, it is impossible or prohibitively expensive to collect exact pairs of corresponding images (e.g., a photo and its exact oil painting equivalent). Unpaired translation allows models to learn these mappings using independent sets of images from each domain.
concepts.recap_md: - Unpaired translation eliminates the need for one-to-one training pairs $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$.

concepts.title: Emergent Pairing in GANs
concepts.one_liner: In GANs, the specific mapping between input vectors and output data is not predetermined but emerges during training to satisfy the objective.
concepts.content: GANs have a very useful property well-suited to unpaired translation. They train a mapping from a noise distribution to a data distribution $p(Z) \rightarrow p(X)$. They do this without knowing the pairing between $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ values in the training data. Instead, this pairing is emergent. Which $\mathbf{z}$-vector corresponds to which $\mathbf{x}$ is not predetermined but self-organizes to satisfy the GAN objective: all $\mathbf{z}$-vectors should map to realistic images, and collectively they should map to the data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Because GANs naturally learn to map one distribution to another without explicit supervision of which input maps to which output, they are inherently capable of discovering structure in data where explicit labels or pairs are missing.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs learn a mapping $p(Z) \rightarrow p(X)$ without explicit pairing between individual samples.

concepts.title: Unpaired Learning with GANs
concepts.one_liner: GANs can learn to map between two image domains without paired supervision by matching the output distribution to the target domain.
concepts.content:
Consider training a GAN to map from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{y}$ values:

$$\begin{aligned}    \arg\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{y})) \big]
\end{aligned}$$

This is a regular GAN objective where $\mathbf{y}$ plays the role of the target data and $\mathbf{x}$ plays the role of the noise input. Such a GAN self-organizes so that outputs are realistic $\mathbf{y}$ values and different inputs map to different outputs to collectively match the data distribution over $\mathbf{y}$. No paired supervision is required.

While such a GAN may learn the correct mapping, there are many symmetries in this learning problem. Many different mappings achieve equivalent loss; for example, a permutation of the mapping (shifting which $\mathbf{x}$ maps to which $\mathbf{y}$) achieves the same loss because the GAN objective only cares about the output distribution, not the specific instance-level mapping.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard GAN objectives focus on distribution matching. This allows for learning transformations between domains without pairs, but it introduces the problem of 'identifiability'—the model might learn a valid-looking mapping that is semantically incorrect because many different mappings can produce the same output distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Unpaired GANs match the distribution of outputs to the target domain without needing specific $\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{y}$ pairs.

concepts.title: Set-level vs Instance-level Supervision
concepts.one_liner: GANs utilize set-level supervision by checking if an output belongs to an admissible set rather than matching a specific target instance.
concepts.content:
The GAN discriminator differs from a normal loss function. Rather than checking if the output matches a target instance (that $g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$ matches $\mathbf{y}^{(i)}$), it checks if the output is part of an admissible set—the set of things that look like realistic $\mathbf{y}$ values. This property makes GANs perfect for working with unpaired data, where we don't have instance-level supervision but only have set-level supervision.

We call this unpaired learning rather than unsupervised because we still have supervision in the form of labels indicating which set each datapoint belongs to (i.e., we know whether each image is an $\mathbf{x}$ or a $\mathbf{y}$).
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional supervised learning requires knowing exactly what the output should be for every input. Set-level supervision relaxes this, allowing models to learn from collections of data (like 'photos' and 'paintings') where we know the category but not the specific correspondences.
concepts.recap_md: - Instance-level supervision requires specific target pairs, while set-level supervision only requires knowing which domain a sample belongs to.

concepts.title: Cycle-consistency
concepts.one_liner: Cycle-consistency is the principle that translating an image to a new domain and back should return it to its original state.
concepts.content:
A regular GAN objective applied to mapping from $X$ to $Y$ solves the unpaired translation problem but does not distinguish between the correct mapping and many other mappings that achieve the same output distribution. To break this symmetry, we add constraints like cycle-consistency. The idea is that if we translate from $X$ to $Y$ and then translate back (from $Y$ to $X$), we should arrive where we started. 

In natural language processing, this is known as backtranslation. For example, translating "apple" to French ("pomme") and then back to English should return "apple." Cycle-consistency losses are regularizers that encourage a learned mapping to be roughly one-to-one. The cycle-consistency losses are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{x};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1\\
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{y};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1
\end{aligned}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Without cycle-consistency, an unpaired GAN might map an image of a cat to a random image of a dog. Cycle-consistency forces the model to preserve the structural information of the original image so that the transformation can be reversed, effectively narrowing the space of possible mappings to those that are semantically meaningful.
concepts.recap_md: - Cycle-consistency requires that $f(g(x)) \approx x$ and $g(f(y)) \approx y$.

concepts.title: CycleGAN
concepts.one_liner: CycleGAN is a framework for unpaired image-to-image translation that combines adversarial losses with cycle-consistency constraints to learn one-to-one mappings.
concepts.content:
The complete CycleGAN objective combines adversarial losses with cycle-consistency losses:
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \arg\min_{\theta,\psi}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}^{Y}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{Y}(\mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1 + \\
    \log d_{\phi}^{X}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{X}(\mathbf{x})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \big]
\end{aligned}
$$
This model translates from domain $X$ to domain $Y$ and back, ensuring outputs in each domain look realistic according to their respective discriminators and that the mappings are cycle-consistent. 

(see figure: CycleGAN schematic. Figure derived from @CycleGAN2017)

The cycle-consistency losses encourage the translation to be a one-to-one function, reducing the number of valid solutions. This is effective when the true solution is indeed one-to-one. However, symmetries may still exist: if the $X$-to-$Y$ mapping and its inverse are both permuted incorrectly, CycleGAN may still be satisfied despite the mapping being incorrect.
concepts.motivation_md: CycleGAN was developed to enable high-quality image-to-image translation in the absence of paired data. By training two generators and two discriminators simultaneously with a consistency constraint, it successfully captures the style of a target domain while preserving the content of the source domain.
concepts.recap_md: - CycleGAN uses two sets of GAN losses and two cycle-consistency losses to learn bidirectional mappings.

concepts.title: Trend toward General-Purpose Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The current trend in AI is to replace specialized, task-specific systems with general-purpose conditional generative models.
concepts.content: Many problems in vision can be phrased as structured prediction, and conditional generative models provide a unified and simple solution to a diverse array of these problems. A current trend in computer vision and artificial intelligence is to replace bespoke systems for specific kinds of structured prediction—such as object detectors or image captioning systems—with general-purpose conditional generative models. This shift toward general-purpose modeling tools reduces the need for special-purpose systems designed for specific vision tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Historically, computer vision relied on hand-engineered pipelines for every unique task. Moving toward general-purpose generative models allows for a more unified architecture that can solve many different problems (translation, detection, synthesis) using the same underlying principles and training objectives.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditional generative models are increasingly used as general-purpose tools for various structured prediction tasks.

concepts.title: Target Invariance in Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Target invariance assumes that the target outputs $y$ remain unchanged when the input $x$ undergoes specific transformations.
concepts.content: When applying data augmentation, we often assume that the target outputs $\mathbf{y}$ are invariant to the augmentations of the inputs $\mathbf{x}$. Let $y(\mathbf{x})$ be the true $\mathbf{y}$ for an input $\mathbf{x}$; then we assume that $y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$ for all $\theta$, meaning $y$ is invariant to the transformation $T$. For example, in scene classification, mirror augmentation is appropriate because mirroring a scene does not change its class label. However, in optical character recognition, mirror augmentation is unsuitable because the mirror image of a character like 'b' looks like 'd', meaning $y(\texttt{mirror}(\mathbf{x})) \neq y(\mathbf{x})$. Similarly, molecular data with chiral structures may behave differently from their mirror images, violating the invariance assumption.
concepts.motivation_md: Data augmentation relies on the assumption that certain transformations of the input data do not change the underlying label. Understanding target invariance helps practitioners choose augmentations that preserve the semantic meaning of the data, ensuring the model learns the correct relationships rather than being confused by transformations that alter the ground truth.
concepts.recap_md: - Target invariance occurs when $y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$, meaning the label is unaffected by the transformation.

concepts.title: Target Equivariance in Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Target equivariance involves transforming both inputs and targets simultaneously so that the relationship between them is preserved.
concepts.content: To handle cases where $y(\mathbf{x}) \neq y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$, we use a more advanced kind of data augmentation where we transform the $\mathbf{y}$ values at the same time as the $\mathbf{x}$ values using transforms $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$. This results in an augmented dataset of the form $\{T_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), T_{\mathcal{Y}}(\mathbf{y}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)})\}_{j=1}^M$. This requires that $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$ express an equivariance between the two domains, defined as $T_{\mathcal{Y}}(y(x),\theta_{\mathcal{Y}}) = y(T_{\mathcal{X}}(x,\theta_{\mathcal{X}}))$ for all $\theta$. This is standard when $\mathbf{y}$ has spatial or temporal structure aligned with $\mathbf{x}$, such as semantic segmentation. In such cases, if we perform a random crop on the image $\mathbf{x}$, we must apply the same crop to the label map $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In many tasks, such as object detection or segmentation, the target label is spatially dependent on the input. If the input is cropped or rotated, the label must be updated accordingly. Equivariance ensures that the model learns the correct spatial mapping even when the input data is transformed.
concepts.recap_md: - Equivariance requires transforming the target $y$ in tandem with the input $x$ to maintain their relationship.

concepts.title: Domain Randomization
concepts.one_liner: Domain randomization broadens a model's experience by randomizing the parameters of a simulator rather than transforming a static dataset.
concepts.content: When data is generated by a simulator rather than sampled from a static dataset, we can apply domain randomization. Instead of adding random transformations to existing data points, we randomize the parameters of the simulator itself. For example, lighting conditions may be randomized so that each interaction with the simulation looks slightly different. The effect is analogous to data augmentation: it converts a narrow set of experiences (simulation with one lighting condition) into a much broader set of experiences (simulation with many different lighting conditions) for the model to learn from.
concepts.motivation_md: Simulators often fail to capture the full complexity of the real world, leading to a 'reality gap.' Domain randomization helps bridge this gap by exposing the model to a wide variety of simulated environments, making the resulting model more robust to variations it will encounter in real-world data.
concepts.recap_md: - Domain randomization involves varying simulator parameters like lighting or physics to create diverse training data.

concepts.title: Out-of-Distribution Data
concepts.one_liner: Out-of-distribution data refers to test cases that differ significantly in characteristics or distribution from the training data.
concepts.content:
Data augmentation works by broadening the distribution of training data to reduce the gap between training and test data. When test images look quite different from training data—for instance, having lower resolution or different object categories—we say the test data are out-of-distribution relative to the training data. Data augmentation adds variation to the training data, broadening its distribution so that the test data become more in-distribution. With sufficient augmentation, test data may eventually look like random samples from the training distribution.

![Data augmentation broadens the training distribution so that it might better cover the test cases. (a) Training data are from Caltech256 @griffin2007caltech and test data are from CIFAR100 @cifar100. The scatter plots show these data in a 2D feature space [the first two principle components (pcs) of CLIP @radford2021learning]. (b) Training data after `mirror` augmentations (random horizontal flips). (c) The same plus `crops` (crop then rescale to the original size). (d) The same plus `color jitter` (random shifts in color and contrast).](./figures/data_augmentation/data_aug_real_example.png){width="100%" #fig-data_augmentation-data_aug_real_example}
concepts.motivation_md: Models often fail when deployed because real-world data (test data) differs from the curated training set. Identifying and addressing out-of-distribution gaps through techniques like data augmentation is critical for building models that generalize to new environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Out-of-distribution (OOD) data is test data that does not match the statistical distribution of the training set.

concepts.title: Learned Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Learned data augmentation uses algorithms to discover complex transformations that a model should be invariant to, rather than coding them by hand.
concepts.content: While simple transformations like flipping or cropping are effective and easy to implement, they represent only a small fraction of possible transformations. For complex tasks like pedestrian detection, we might want a model to be invariant to variations in a pedestrian's pose. Because such variations are difficult to code by hand, we can use learning algorithms to learn how to augment our data and achieve the desired invariances. After learning, the model will be invariant (or equivariant) with respect to these discovered transformations.
concepts.motivation_md: Manual augmentation is limited by human intuition and coding effort. Learned augmentation allows the system to automatically find the most useful variations for a specific task, which is especially valuable for complex, high-dimensional transformations like human pose or lighting changes.
concepts.recap_md: - Learned data augmentation automates the discovery of transformations that improve model invariance.

concepts.title: Generative Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Generative data augmentation uses models like GANs or VAEs to create new training samples by perturbing latent variables.
concepts.content:
One way to perform learned data augmentation is to use generative models such as GANs or VAEs. These models are suitable because latent variables can control factors of variation. Given a datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, an encoder $f_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, and a generator $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, we can create an augmented copy as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x} = g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{w}) \end{aligned}$$ where $\mathbf{w}$ is a small perturbation to the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$. If the generative model lacks an encoder, one can be trained via supervised learning on pairs $\{g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}), \mathbf{z}\}$. By using various settings of $\mathbf{w}$, such as Gaussian perturbations $\mathbf{w} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, we produce a set of output images that are slight variations of one another.

(see figure: Generative data augmentation `genaug`)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard augmentations are often restricted to simple geometric or color changes. Generative models can produce highly realistic and diverse variations of data that capture complex semantic changes, potentially providing a richer training signal than manual heuristics.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative data augmentation creates new samples by adding noise to the latent representation of existing data.

concepts.title: Circularity in Learned Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Circularity in learned augmentation occurs when the augmentation model is trained on the same data it is intended to augment.
concepts.content: Training a generative model $g_{\theta}$ on a dataset $X$ and then using $g_{\theta}$ to augment $X$ for training a function $f$ introduces a circularity. If we denote the learner as a function $L$ that maps data to a learned function $f$, then without augmentation $f = L(X)$. With augmentation, $f = L(\tilde{X})$. If $\tilde{X}$ is generated by an algorithm like $\texttt{genaug}(X)$, then $\tilde{X}$ is simply a function of $X$. This implies the existence of a new learner $\tilde{L} = L \circ \texttt{genaug}$ such that $f = \tilde{L}(X)$. Thus, a learning algorithm using unaugmented data can be functionally equivalent to one using augmented data when the augmentation itself is derived from that same data.
concepts.motivation_md: It is important to recognize that learned augmentation doesn't 'create' new information out of thin air if it's trained on the same set. Understanding this circularity helps researchers distinguish between true information gain and complex forms of regularization.
concepts.recap_md: - Circularity occurs when augmented data $\tilde{X}$ is a deterministic function of the original data $X$.

concepts.title: Robust Optimization
concepts.one_liner: Robust optimization is a general approach in optimization where models are trained to perform well under adversarial or worst-case conditions.
concepts.content: Robust optimization is a general approach in the optimization literature that encompasses techniques like adversarial training. It is used for various purposes, including training generative adversarial networks, encouraging exploration in reinforcement learning, and training agents to compete against others. The core idea is to optimize for performance that is resilient to variations or adversarial perturbations in the input or environment.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard optimization might produce models that are fragile to small changes. Robust optimization seeks to ensure that a model's performance remains stable even when faced with the worst-case scenarios or noisy environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Robust optimization focuses on maintaining performance under perturbations or adversarial conditions.

concepts.title: Quantization Error in Classification
concepts.one_liner: Quantization error occurs when continuous values are mapped to a discrete set of bins, potentially lowering resolution and causing ambiguity between similar values.
concepts.content: Quantization error is a consequence of treating continuous values as discrete classes. For example, in color prediction, true colors like teal and bright pink may be mapped to discrete bins; if the quantization resolution is low, it becomes impossible to distinguish between similar shades that fall into the same bin. This can result in predictions appearing slightly duller than the true data distribution, such as when a bin is colored with the floor of its range. Generally, this error can be mitigated by increasing the number of classes $k$. In image formats with 256 possible values, setting $k=256$ eliminates quantization error entirely.
concepts.motivation_md: Quantization allows us to apply classification techniques to continuous regression problems, but it introduces a trade-off between the number of classes and the precision of the representation.
concepts.recap_md: - Quantization error arises when continuous data is discretized into a finite number of bins.

concepts.title: Curse of Dimensionality in Quantization
concepts.one_liner: The number of classes required for quantization grows exponentially with the number of dimensions, making joint pixel prediction computationally astronomical.
concepts.content: While quantizing a single value into $k$ classes is manageable, the approach suffers from the curse of dimensionality when extended to multiple dimensions. To tile a two-dimensional space (like $ab$ color values) while retaining a resolution of $k$ for both dimensions requires $k^2$ classes. (see figure: The funny shape of the $lab$ color gamut is because not every $ab$ value maps to a valid pixel color. When working with predictions over $lab$ color space, we may map $ab$ values that fall outside...) The problem becomes severe when predicting multiple pixels: quantizing the $ab$-values of $N$ pixels requires $k^{2N}$ classes. For a standard $256 \times 256$ resolution image, the number of classes required becomes astronomical.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why simple classification cannot be directly scaled to high-dimensional outputs like full images without more sophisticated modeling strategies.
concepts.recap_md: - Quantizing $N$ pixels with $k$ resolution levels per dimension requires $k^{2N}$ discrete classes.

concepts.title: Conditional Independence Assumption in Prediction
concepts.one_liner: The conditional independence assumption treats each output dimension as independent of others given the input, a common but often inaccurate simplification in image modeling.
concepts.content: To circumvent the curse of dimensionality, models often factorize the joint distribution by making independent predictions for each pixel. This corresponds to the factorization: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{ab} \bigm | \mathbf{l}) = \prod_{n=1}^N\prod_{m=1}^M p_{\theta}(ab[n,m,:] \bigm | \mathbf{l}) \end{aligned}$$ This model assumes pixel colors are conditionally independent given the luminance image. This same assumption is implicit in least-squares regression ($L_2$ loss) for multidimensional prediction. Because the $L_2$ loss factorizes as a product over pairwise potentials, the Hammersley-Clifford theorem implies a probability distribution where all true values $y_i$ are independent given the predictions $\hat{y}_i$ (and thus given the input $\mathbf{x}$). While computationally efficient, this assumption is rarely true in computer vision problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Factorizing the joint distribution into independent conditional probabilities makes high-dimensional prediction computationally feasible, though it ignores the structural relationships between output dimensions.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditional independence assumes $p(y_1, y_2 | x) = p(y_1 | x)p(y_2 | x)$. - Least-squares regression ($L_2$ loss) implicitly assumes conditional independence between output dimensions.

concepts.title: Unstructured Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Unstructured prediction refers to fitting models that assume independence between output dimensions, such as pixels, conditioned on the input.
concepts.content: Unstructured prediction occurs when using methods like per-pixel classification or least-squares regression that implicitly assume independence between all output pixels, conditioned on the input.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying unstructured prediction helps researchers understand why certain models fail to capture global coherence or spatial relationships in complex outputs.
concepts.recap_md: - Unstructured prediction assumes independence between output components given the input.

concepts.title: Color Flipping in Unstructured Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Color flipping is a failure in unstructured prediction where independent pixel choices cause chaotic transitions between colors in regions of uncertainty.
concepts.content: Color flipping occurs when an unstructured classifier makes independent hard decisions for each pixel in a multi-modal distribution. If a model learns roughly equal probabilities for two modes (e.g., teal and pink), slight changes in input luminance can cause the prediction to wiggle between these modes. Because choices are made independently per pixel, the output may chaotically alternate between colors. (see figure: Color flipping can arise from a smooth underlying predictive distribution, on top of which independent choices are made.) A real example from @zhang2016colorful shows a model alternating between blue and red for a shirt and background because it is unsure of the correct color. [FIGURE:b268dfef8da91f88 | A photograph of a male tennis player on a court, used to illustrate the challenges of colorization. His shirt exhibits a mix of pink and teal hues, demonstrating how a classifier might struggle to...]
concepts.motivation_md: Color flipping illustrates the visual artifacts that arise when a model fails to account for the joint structure and spatial consistency of an image.
concepts.recap_md: - Color flipping results from independent pixel-wise decisions in the presence of multi-modal uncertainty.

concepts.title: Structured Prediction

position.section_title: Conditional Generative Models Solve Multimodal Structured Prediction

concepts.one_liner: Structured prediction methods model the joint structure of the output space rather than factorizing it into independent potentials.
concepts.content: Structured prediction methods model joint structure in the output space and do not factorize the output into independent potentials conditioned on the input. Conditional generative modeling is a structured prediction approach that models a full distribution of possibilities over the joint configuration of outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Structured prediction is necessary for tasks where the output components (like pixels in an image) are highly correlated and must be consistent with one another.
concepts.recap_md: - Structured prediction models the joint distribution of outputs rather than independent components.

concepts.title: Amortized Inference

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Amortized inference uses a neural network to learn a direct mapping from inputs to outputs, distributing the cost of inference over the training phase.
concepts.content: Amortized inference refers to an approach where the cost of inference is amortized over a training phase. A neural network learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs, approximating the solution that would have been obtained through exact inference on a given input.
concepts.motivation_md: Amortized inference allows for extremely fast predictions at test time by shifting the heavy computational burden to the offline training stage.
concepts.recap_md: - Amortized inference replaces expensive per-instance optimization with a learned mapping function.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs)

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional GANs extend the GAN framework by providing an input to both the generator and discriminator, enabling the modeling of conditional distributions.
concepts.content: A conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) is created by adding an input $\mathbf{x}$ to both the generator and the discriminator: $$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) \big] \end{aligned}$$ This changes the discriminator's task to determining if the input-output pair $(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$ is real or synthetic. A pair may be flagged as synthetic if the output itself looks fake or if the output does not match the input. If both conditions are satisfied, the samples produced are $iid$ with respect to the true conditional distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}(Y \bigm | \mathbf{x})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional GANs allow for targeted generation, such as generating an image based on a specific label or a source image, rather than just generating random samples from a dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - cGANs add an auxiliary input $\mathbf{x}$ to the generator and discriminator. - The discriminator evaluates the consistency of the input-output pair.

concepts.title: Reprojection Error
concepts.one_liner: The reprojection error is the difference between the estimated image coordinates of a 3D point and its ground-truth image coordinates.
concepts.content: The reprojection error is the difference between the estimated image coordinates of a 3D point and its ground-truth image coordinates.
