Given 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and their corresponding 2D projections $\mathbf{p}_i$, we can use estimated camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{R}$, and $\mathbf{T}$ to project the 3D points and obtain estimated 2D locations $\mathbf{p}'_i$ of their projections. The reprojection error is the distance between these points, as shown in (see figure: Reprojection error indicated by the red lines on the image plane.).
concepts.motivation_md: Reprojection error provides a geometric measure of how well a camera model and its estimated parameters (intrinsic and extrinsic) explain the observed 2D image data. It is the standard metric used to refine camera calibration through optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - It measures the distance between a point's observed 2D location and its projected 2D location based on a camera model.

concepts.title: Reprojection Loss Function
concepts.one_liner: The reprojection loss is the sum of squared distances between observed 2D points and their estimated projections based on camera parameters.
concepts.content: The reprojection error can be evaluated with the loss: $$\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}'_i \|^2=\sum_{i=1}^N \| \mathbf{p}_i - \pi \left( \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} ~ \mid ~ -\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}_i \right) \| ^2 $$ where $\pi()$ is the function that transforms homogeneous coordinates to heterogeneous coordinates. This function can also incorporate other camera parameters to account for geometric distortion introduced by the camera optics.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining a formal loss function allows for the use of numerical optimization techniques to find the most accurate camera parameters by minimizing the total error across all observed points.
concepts.recap_md: - The loss is calculated as the sum of squared Euclidean distances between observed and projected points.

concepts.title: Minimizing Reprojection Loss via Gradient Descent
concepts.one_liner: Reprojection loss can be minimized by gradient descent to optimize the camera's intrinsic and extrinsic parameter matrices.
concepts.content: The reprojection loss can be minimized by gradient descent, optimizing the three matrices $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{R}$, and $\mathbf{T}$ directly. For the minimization to converge, it is usually initialized with the solution obtained using the Direct Linear Transform (DLT).
concepts.motivation_md: While linear methods like DLT provide a good initial estimate, they do not directly minimize geometric error. Nonlinear optimization via gradient descent refines these parameters to achieve the highest possible accuracy.
concepts.recap_md: - Optimization is performed directly on the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and extrinsic matrices $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$.

concepts.title: Toy Example: Office Camera Calibration
concepts.one_liner: A practical test using office measurements demonstrates how camera parameters can be recovered from real-world 3D-to-2D correspondences.
concepts.content: To test if the theory meets practice, a simple calibration was performed using an office picture and measured distances (see figure: Office picture and real distances between a sparse set of points measured in centimeters.). By placing the origin on the ground floor and collecting 12 manually identified 3D-to-2D correspondences (see figure: Office picture and a table with the 3D world coordinates of 12 points, extracted using the measurements from @fig-office_measurements), the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ was estimated using the DLT algorithm. The resulting mean reprojection error was 12.3 pixels, less than 0.5 percent of the image height. From $\mathbf{M}$, the translation vector $\mathbf{T}$ was recovered, yielding a camera height of 171.8 cm, very close to the initial guess. Further decomposition using QR decomposition yielded the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$. The recovered $\mathbf{K}$ suggested square pixels and an optical center near the image center, while $\mathbf{R}$ allowed for the calculation of the camera's viewing angle (20.5 degrees), consistent with the physical setup.
concepts.motivation_md: This example serves to validate the mathematical models of camera calibration using real-world, noisy data, proving that the theory is robust enough for practical applications.
concepts.recap_md: - Real-world calibration can be achieved with as few as 8-12 point correspondences.

concepts.title: Privacy and Camera Calibration
concepts.one_liner: A picture reveals information about the camera and the photographer, even when there is no one in the picture.
concepts.content: A picture reveals information about the camera and the photographer, even when there is no one in the picture. It is important to keep this in mind when thinking about privacy.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that metadata and geometric information can be extracted from images is crucial for recognizing the privacy implications of sharing photos.
concepts.recap_md: - Camera calibration techniques can uncover the location and orientation of the photographer.

concepts.title: Camera Orientation Extraction Tip
concepts.one_liner: When extracting camera orientation, ensure you use the correct rotation matrix convention to avoid errors.
concepts.content: A potential bug when extracting the camera orientation is to use the rotation matrix instead of its inverse. In this context, $\mathbf{R}^\mathsf{T}$ is defined as the rotation needed to move the world coordinate axes to be aligned with the camera-coordinate axes.
concepts.motivation_md: Coordinate system conventions in computer vision can be confusing; explicitly defining the role of the rotation matrix prevents common implementation errors.
concepts.recap_md: - Be careful to distinguish between the rotation of the world to the camera versus camera to the world.

concepts.title: Visualizing camera orientation
concepts.one_liner: Visualizing annotated 3D points alongside inferred camera locations helps verify the accuracy of the calibration.
concepts.content: It is always important to visualize everything to make sure that all is correct. (see figure: Inferred camera location for the office picture. The figure shows three different viewpoints.) shows a visualization of the annotated 3D points and the inferred camera location and orientation from three different viewpoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Visualization acts as a sanity check to ensure that the mathematical results of calibration correspond to a physically plausible scene.
concepts.recap_md: - 3D visualization of camera poses helps identify errors in orientation or translation.

concepts.title: Stereo anaglyph
concepts.one_liner: A stereo anaglyph uses color filtering to deliver separate images to each eye, creating a 3D effect.
concepts.content: (see figure: (a) Stereo anaglyph of the Titanic @McManus2022. The red image shows the right eye's view, and cyan the left eye's view. (b) When viewed through red/cyan stereo glasses the cyan variations appear in...) shows a stereo anaglyph of the Titanic. This was taken with two cameras, one displaced laterally from the other. The right camera's image appears in red, and the left camera image is in cyan. If viewed with a red filter covering the left eye and a cyan filter covering the right, the right eye sees only the right camera's image (and vice versa), allowing the ship to appear as a 3D stereo image. The relative displacement between each camera's image of objects changes as a function of their depth, enabling a 3D interpretation.
concepts.motivation_md: Stereo anaglyphs provide a simple way to represent 3D depth information on a 2D surface using inexpensive color-coded glasses.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses red and cyan color channels to encode left and right eye views.

concepts.title: Linear Probes
concepts.one_liner: Linear probes are lightweight linear modules added to a neural network's feature maps to perform new tasks or assess the knowledge represented in specific layers.
concepts.content: Linear probes are linear modules used as a way of repurposing a neural net to perform a new task. These modules are relatively lightweight, having few parameters, and can be optimized with tools from linear optimization where there are often closed form solutions. Because of this, linear probes are very popular for adapting models. These modules are also useful as a way of assessing what kind of knowledge each feature map in the original network represents; if a feature map can linearly classify some attribute of the data, then that feature map knows something about that attribute. In this usage, linear probes are probing the knowledge represented in some layer of a neural net.
concepts.motivation_md: They provide a computationally efficient way to repurpose existing models for new tasks and offer a diagnostic tool to interpret what specific layers of a neural network have learned.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear probes are lightweight modules optimized with linear optimization tools to repurpose networks.

concepts.title: Learning from a Teacher
concepts.one_liner: Learning from a teacher involves a student model observing a well-trained teacher model's outputs or intermediate activations to improve its own performance.
concepts.content:
One way of formalizing this setting is to consider the teacher as a well-trained model $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ that maps input queries to output answers. The student (the learner) observes both data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ and has access to the teacher model $t$. The student can learn to imitate the teacher's outputs or can learn to match how the teacher processes the queries by matching intermediate activations of the teacher model.

[FIGURE:872a10889f557ebb | A block diagram representing the process of learning from a teacher. On the left, the inputs are a dataset $\{x^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and a teacher model $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$. An arrow...]
concepts.motivation_md: This framework allows a smaller or newer model to benefit from the expertise of a pre-trained high-performance model, potentially speeding up training or improving accuracy.
concepts.recap_md: - The student model observes both raw data and the outputs or internal states of a teacher model.

concepts.title: Knowledge Distillation
concepts.one_liner: Knowledge distillation is an algorithm where a student model learns to imitate the probability mass function outputs of a well-trained teacher classifier.
concepts.content:
Knowledge distillation is a simple and popular algorithm for learning a classifier from a teacher. We assume that the teacher is a well-trained classifier that outputs a $K-1$-dimensional probability mass function (pmf), $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$. The student, a model $f_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$, simply tries to imitate the teacher's output pmf: for each input $x$ that the student sees, its goal is to output the same pmf vector as the teacher outputs for $x$.

[FIGURE:d0121ab0dd8a499c | A block diagram illustrating the knowledge distillation process. On the left, input data $\{x^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and a teacher model $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \Delta^{K-1}$ are fed into a central box...]

In knowledge distillation, the targets are not one-hot but rather are more graded. The teacher outputs a probability vector that reflects the teacher's belief as to the class of the input, rather than the ground truth class. These beliefs may assign partial credit to classes that are similar to the ground truth, which can make the teacher more informative than learning from ground truth labels.

(see figure: Comparing knowledge distillation to supervised learning from labels.)

For example, the pmf vector for a domestic cat might be "90 percent domestic cat, but also 10 percent tiger." This tells the student something about both classes, providing more information than a one-hot label and potentially accelerating learning.
concepts.motivation_md: It allows a student model to capture the nuanced "dark knowledge" of a teacher, such as inter-class similarities, which is more informative than simple hard labels.
concepts.recap_md: - The student model minimizes the difference between its output probability distribution and the teacher's distribution.

concepts.title: Prompting
concepts.one_liner: Prompting edits the input data, such as prepending natural language instructions, to solve new problems without changing the model's parameters.
concepts.content: Prompting edits the input data to solve a new problem. Prompting is very popular in natural language processing (NLP), where text-to-text systems can have natural language prompts prepended to the string that is input to the model. For example, a general-purpose language model can be prompted with [`Make sure to answer in French`, `X`], for some arbitrary input `X`. Then the output will be a French translation of whatever the model would have responded to when queried with `X`.
concepts.motivation_md: It enables a single pre-trained model to perform a wide variety of tasks simply by changing the input context, avoiding the need for task-specific fine-tuning.
concepts.recap_md: - Prompting involves modifying the input data rather than the model parameters to achieve a new task.

concepts.title: Visual Prompting
concepts.one_liner: Visual prompting applies the concept of prompting to vision systems by prepending or adding visual data, such as pixels or tokens, to the model's input.
concepts.content:
The same can be done for vision systems. First, prompting methods from NLP can be directly used for prompting the text inputs to vision-language models. Second, prompting can also be applied to visual inputs. Just like we can prepend a textual input with text, we can prepend a visual input with visual data, yielding a method called visual prompting. This can be done by concatenating pixels, tokens, or other visual formats to a vision model's inputs. This requires a model that takes variable-sized inputs, such as CNNs, RNNs, and transformers. Alternatively, we can combine the visual prompt with the input query in other ways, such as by addition.

(see figure: Prompting: a prompt $\mathbf{p}$ is combined with the input $x$ to change the output $y$.)
concepts.motivation_md: It allows vision models to be repurposed for new tasks using only input modifications, similar to how text prompts guide language models.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual prompts can be implemented by concatenating pixels or tokens to the input of a vision model.

concepts.title: Adversarial Reprogramming
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial reprogramming is an early term for prompting, highlighting its similarity to the way adversarial examples manipulate model behavior.
concepts.content: Because of its similarity to adversarial examples, early papers on prompting sometimes referred to it as adversarial reprogramming.
concepts.motivation_md: The term emphasizes that modifying inputs to change a model's task is conceptually similar to how adversarial perturbations "reprogram" a model's output.
concepts.recap_md: - This is an alternative name for prompting used in early research literature.

concepts.title: Token Prompting
concepts.one_liner: Token prompting is a technique where a learnable code vector is concatenated to the input tokens of a vision transformer to modulate its behavior.
concepts.content:
Rather than adding a prompt in pixel space, it is also possible to add a prompt to an intermediate feature space. One way to do this is to use a token as the prompt for a vision transformer architecture. This new token is a $d$-dimensional code vector concatenated to the input of the transformer, which is a set of tokens representing image patches.

(see figure: Prompting a transformer with a learnable input token. The prompt token is mixed into the network via attention; therefore \textit{no} parameters of the original network have to be updated (see...)

This vector is optimized to change the behavior of the transformer to achieve a desired result. The attention mechanism works as usual except now all the input tokens also attend to the prompt. The prompt thereby modulates the transformation applied to the input tokens on the first layer, affecting the transformer's behavior without updating original network parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a way to adapt transformers to new tasks by optimizing only a small set of prompt parameters while keeping the large pre-trained model frozen.
concepts.recap_md: - A learnable code vector is concatenated to the transformer's input tokens.

concepts.title: Promptable Systems
concepts.one_liner: Promptable systems are models trained to adapt their behavior at test time based on human-interpretable inputs like text instructions or user-drawn strokes.
concepts.content: It is also possible to train a model to be promptable, so that at test time it adapts better to user prompts. An advantage of this approach is that we can train a model to understand human-interpretable prompts, such as text instructions or user-drawn strokes. In fact, any system that interactively adapts to user inputs can be considered a promptable system. Many such systems use the tools of conditional generative modeling to train systems that are conditioned on user text instructions, such as DALL-E.
concepts.motivation_md: Training models to be promptable ensures they can be intuitively controlled by users in real-time without needing further training or technical adjustments.
concepts.recap_md: - These systems are designed to adapt to human-interpretable prompts like text or sketches.

concepts.title: Estimating boat distance using the horizon
concepts.one_liner: Estimate the distance of a boat from a single elevated observation point by measuring the angle between the horizon and the boat's position.
concepts.content:
The first method measures the location of the boat relative to the horizon line. An observer is standing on top of an elevated point (a mountain, tower, or building) at a known height, $h$. The observer measures the angle $\alpha$ between the horizontal (obtained by pointing toward the horizon) and the position of the boat. We can then derive the boat distance to the base of the point of observation, $d$, by the simple trigonometric relation: $$d = \frac{h}{\tan (\alpha)}$$ (see figure: Two methods to estimate the distance of a boat from the coast. (left) The first method uses a single observation point, with knowledge of the observer's height above the water. (right) The second...)

This method allows us to estimate the boat position with a single observation point if the observer's height above the water is known. However, it is not very accurate and might require high observation points which might not be available. It also requires incorporating the earth curvature when the boat is far away.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique provides a way to estimate distance when only one observation point is available, provided the observer's height is known.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a single observation point at a known height $h$.
 - Measures the angle $\alpha$ between the horizon and the target.
 - Calculates distance using the formula $d = h / \tan(\alpha)$.

concepts.title: Estimating boat distance using triangulation
concepts.one_liner: Triangulation estimates the distance to a boat by measuring angles from two separate observation points along a coast.
concepts.content:
The second method requires two different observation points along the coast separated by a distance $t$. At each point, we measure the angles, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, between the direction of the boat and the line connecting the two observation points. Then we can apply the following relation: $$d = t \frac{\sin (\alpha) \sin (\beta)}{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}$$ (see figure: Two methods to estimate the distance of a boat from the coast. (left) The first method uses a single observation point, with knowledge of the observer's height above the water. (right) The second...)

This method is called triangulation. For it to work, we need a large distance $t$ so that the angles are significantly different from $90$ degrees.
concepts.motivation_md: Triangulation allows for distance estimation without needing to know the observer's height, relying instead on a known baseline distance between two points.
concepts.recap_md:
- Requires two observation points separated by a known distance $t$.
 - Measures angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from each point to the target.
 - Uses the sine rule relationship $d = t \frac{\sin (\alpha) \sin (\beta)}{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}$.

concepts.title: Parallax effect
concepts.one_liner: The parallax effect is the relative displacement of features across two images related to the distance between the observer and the scene.
concepts.content: The relative displacement of features across two images is known as the parallax effect. This displacement is related to the distance between the observer and the observed scene. Just as in the example of estimating the distance to boats in the sea, our brain uses disparities across the two eye views to measure distances to objects.
concepts.motivation_md: The parallax effect is the fundamental geometric principle that allows biological and artificial systems to perceive depth from two different viewpoints.
concepts.recap_md:
- Refers to the relative displacement of features between two viewpoints.
 - The magnitude of displacement is directly related to the distance of the object.
 - Serves as a primary depth cue for human vision.

concepts.title: Free fusion
concepts.one_liner: Free fusion consists in making the eyes converge or diverge in order to fuse a stereogram without needing a stereoscope.
concepts.content: Free fusion consists in making the eyes converge or diverge in order to fuse a stereogram without needing a stereoscope. Making it work requires practice.
concepts.motivation_md: Free fusion allows a person to perceive 3D depth from 2D stereograms using only their eyes, bypassing the need for specialized viewing hardware.
concepts.recap_md:
- Involves manual control of eye convergence or divergence.
 - Allows viewing stereograms in 3D without a stereoscope.
 - Requires practice to master the technique.

concepts.title: Random dot stereograms
concepts.one_liner: Random dot stereograms demonstrate that humans can perceive depth using only relative displacement, even without recognizable features or other depth cues.
concepts.content:
Random dot stereograms, introduced by Bela Julesz, are a beautiful demonstration that humans can perceive depth using the relative displacement of features across two views even in the absence of any other depth cues. The random images contain no recognizable features and are quite different from the statistics of the natural world. But this seems not to affect our ability to compute the displacements between the two images and perceive 3D structure.

(see figure: Random dot stereogram. Both images are almost identical. The difference is that there is a square in the middle that is displaced by a few pixels left-right between the two images. When each image it...)
concepts.motivation_md: These stereograms prove that the brain can process depth information solely from binocular disparity, independent of object recognition or perspective cues.
concepts.recap_md:
- Created by Bela Julesz to study depth perception.
 - Contain no recognizable features, only random noise.
 - Depth is perceived solely through the relative displacement of pixels between two views.

concepts.title: Anaglyph pinhole camera
concepts.one_liner: An anaglyph pinhole camera uses two pinholes with different color filters to capture a 3D image in a single shot.
concepts.content:
We can build a stereo pinhole camera that produces anaglyph images in a single shot by making two pinholes instead of just one. We transform the pinhole camera into an anaglyph pinhole camera by making two holes and placing different color filters on each hole. This produces an image that is the superposition of two images taken from slightly different viewpoints, each with a different color. To see the 3D image, we look at the picture by placing the same color filters in front of our eyes, such as color glasses with blue and red filters.

(see figure: One way of playing with pinhole cameras is to build an anaglyph pinhole camera. The anaglyph pinhole camera captures stereo images by projecting an anaglyph image on the projection plane.)

Experimental details involve adjusting the distance between the two pinholes (e.g., 1.5 in to 3 in). Once color filters are placed on each pinhole, longer exposure times are required because less light enters the camera. Increasing the distance between pinholes increases the parallax effect and the range of 3D information, but if the images are too far apart, the visual system will be unable to fuse them into a 3D image.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for the creation of 3D stereo images using a simple, low-cost device without needing complex electronic sensors or synchronized shutters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses two pinholes with distinct color filters (e.g., red and blue).
 - Captures two viewpoints simultaneously as a single superimposed image.
 - Requires longer exposure times and specific pinhole spacing for optimal 3D fusion.

concepts.title: Stereo triangulation
concepts.one_liner: Stereo triangulation is the task of determining the depth of points in the world by comparing images from two spatially offset cameras.
concepts.content: The task of stereo is to triangulate the depth of points in the world by comparing the images from two spatially offset cameras. To triangulate depth, we need to describe how image positions in the stereo pair relate to depth in the 3D world.
concepts.motivation_md: Triangulation is the mathematical foundation for computer vision systems to reconstruct 3D environments from 2D image pairs.
concepts.recap_md:
- Compares images from two spatially offset cameras.
 - Relates 2D image positions to 3D world depth.
 - Forms the basis of stereo vision systems.

concepts.title: Multiview stereo
concepts.one_liner: Multiview stereo is the task of triangulating depth using more than two cameras.
concepts.content: If more than two cameras are used, the task is referred to as multiview stereo.
concepts.motivation_md: Using multiple cameras improves the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstructions compared to simple two-camera stereo systems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Extends stereo triangulation to three or more cameras.
 - Used for complex 3D scene reconstruction.

concepts.title: Definition of Camera Calibration
concepts.one_liner: A camera is calibrated if the transformations relating 3D world coordinates to pixel coordinates within the camera are known.
concepts.content: A camera is said to be **calibrated** if we know the transformations relating 3D world coordinates to pixel coordinates within the camera. Those transformations involve two types of parameters: (1) parameters that depend on where the camera is physically located in the world, and (2) parameters that are a function of the camera itself. These two types of parameters are called extrinsic and intrinsic parameters, respectively.
concepts.motivation_md: To interpret images or reconstruct 3D scenes, we must understand the mathematical relationship between the physical world and the digital pixels. Calibration provides the necessary parameters to map these two spaces.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Calibration involves determining the mapping between 3D world coordinates and 2D pixel coordinates.",
  "- It requires identifying both extrinsic parameters (location/orientation) and intrinsic parameters (camera properties)."
]

concepts.title: Extrinsic Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Extrinsic parameters are the set of camera parameters that depend on where the camera is physically located in the world.
concepts.content: In the context of camera calibration, transformations involve parameters that depend on where the camera is physically located in the world. These are called extrinsic parameters. They describe the camera's position and orientation relative to a global coordinate system.
concepts.motivation_md: Extrinsic parameters are necessary to understand the camera's pose in the world, allowing us to relate observations from different viewpoints or to a fixed world map.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Extrinsic parameters define the physical location and orientation of the camera in the 3D world.",
  "- They are one of two primary components required for full camera calibration."
]

concepts.title: Intrinsic Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Intrinsic parameters are the set of parameters that are a function of the camera itself.
concepts.content: In the context of camera calibration, transformations involve parameters that are a function of the camera itself. These are called intrinsic parameters. They describe internal characteristics such as focal length and the optical center.
concepts.motivation_md: Intrinsic parameters allow us to model how the camera's internal geometry projects light onto the sensor, independent of where the camera is placed.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Intrinsic parameters are internal to the camera hardware and do not change with camera movement.",
  "- They are essential for mapping the 3D rays entering the lens to 2D pixel locations."
]

concepts.title: Direct Linear Transform (DLT) Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: The Direct Linear Transform (DLT) recovers the camera projection matrix by solving a linear system derived from 3D-to-2D point correspondences.
concepts.content:
If we have at least six correspondences between 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and their image projections $\mathbf{p}_i$, we can recover the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ by solving a linear system of equations. For each pair, we have the relationship:

$$\mathbf{p}_i = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{P}_i = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{m}_0^\mathsf{T} \\ \mathbf{m}_1^\mathsf{T} \\ \mathbf{m}_2^\mathsf{T} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}_i$$

Writing the heterogeneous coordinates of $\mathbf{p}$ as $x_i = \frac{\mathbf{m}_0^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P}_i}{\mathbf{m}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P}_i}$ and $y_i = \frac{\mathbf{m}_1^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P}_i}{\mathbf{m}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P}_i}$, we can rearrange terms to get two linear equations per correspondence:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{m}_0 - x_i \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{m}_2 &= 0 \\ \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{m}_1 - y_i \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{m}_2 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Stacking these for $N$ correspondences yields a system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{0}$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is a $2N \times 12$ matrix and $\mathbf{m}$ is the vectorized projection matrix. Since measurements are often noisy, we typically use more than six correspondences and find the solution that minimizes the residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{m} \|^2$, which is the smallest eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$. This method requires that the $N$ points do not all lie in a single plane.
concepts.motivation_md: DLT provides a straightforward algebraic way to estimate a camera's projection matrix from known 3D points and their 2D images, serving as a fundamental tool for camera calibration.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- DLT estimates the $3 \times 4$ projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ using 3D-to-2D point correspondences.",
  "- It requires at least six points and solves a homogeneous linear system $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{m}=0$.",
  "- The optimal solution under noise is the smallest eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$."
]

concepts.title: DLT Implementation Tip
concepts.one_liner: Verify DLT implementations by simulating 3D points and projecting them with a known matrix to ensure the recovered values match up to a scale factor.
concepts.content: Rearranging the vector $\mathbf{m}$ into the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is a potential source of bugs. Try first simulating some 3D points and project them with a known $\mathbf{M}$ matrix, and check that you recover the same values (up to a scale factor).
concepts.motivation_md: Vector-to-matrix indexing is error-prone; simulation provides a ground-truth test to ensure the algorithm is implemented correctly before using real, noisy data.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Use simulated data with a known projection matrix to validate the DLT implementation.",
  "- Ensure the recovered matrix matches the original up to a global scale factor."
]

concepts.title: Recovering Intrinsic and Extrinsic Parameters from Projection Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The intrinsic and extrinsic parameters can be recovered from the projection matrix by decomposing it into its constituent components.
concepts.content:
Once $\mathbf{M}$ is estimated, it is possible to decompose it to recover the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$, rotation $\mathbf{R}$, and translation $\mathbf{T}$. The matrix is written as:

$$\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{K}\mathbf{R} ~ \mid ~ -\mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T} \end{bmatrix}$$

By splitting $\mathbf{M}$ into a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}$ and a $3 \times 1$ vector $\mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T}$, we can estimate the camera translation as $\mathbf{T} = - \mathbf{B}^{-1} \mathbf{b}$. To find $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{R}$, we use the QR decomposition of $\mathbf{B}^{-1}$. Since $\mathbf{K}$ is upper triangular and $\mathbf{R}$ is orthonormal, this decomposition (with appropriate sign adjustments to ensure $\mathbf{K}$'s diagonal is positive) uniquely identifies the parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: The projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is a 'black box' that maps 3D to 2D; decomposing it allows us to understand the physical pose and internal settings of the camera separately.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- The projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is decomposed into $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T}$.",
  "- Translation $\mathbf{T}$ is recovered via $\mathbf{T} = -\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$.",
  "- Intrinsic $\mathbf{K}$ and rotation $\mathbf{R}$ are found using QR decomposition on $\mathbf{B}^{-1}$."
]

concepts.title: QR Decomposition for Parameter Recovery
concepts.one_liner: QR decomposition of the inverse of the projection submatrix allows for the recovery of the upper-triangular intrinsic matrix and the orthonormal rotation matrix.
concepts.content: To estimate the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$, we can use the QR decomposition of the matrix $\mathbf{B}^{-1}$. The QR decomposition decomposes a matrix into the product of a unitary matrix and an upper triangular one. Because we want the product in the order $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}$ (upper triangular times orthonormal), we apply the decomposition to the inverse of $\mathbf{B}$. The resulting decomposition is not unique; however, since the diagonal elements of $\mathbf{K}$ must be positive, we can resolve ambiguity by changing the signs of columns in $\mathbf{K}$ and the corresponding rows in $\mathbf{R}$.
concepts.motivation_md: QR decomposition is a standard linear algebra tool that perfectly matches the physical constraints of camera parameters: an upper-triangular matrix for internal geometry and an orthonormal matrix for rotation.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- QR decomposition on $\mathbf{B}^{-1}$ yields the rotation and intrinsic matrices.",
  "- Ambiguity in the decomposition is resolved by enforcing positive diagonal elements in the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$."
]

concepts.title: Multiplane Calibration Method (Zhang's Method)
concepts.one_liner: Zhang's method is a popular calibration technique that uses multiple images of a planar chart in different orientations.
concepts.content: A popular method for camera calibration is to use a planar calibration chart and to take multiple pictures of it by placing the chart in different locations and orientations relative to a fixed camera. This method was introduced by Zhang in 1999 and it remains commonly used today.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional calibration often required complex 3D targets; Zhang's method simplified the process by allowing users to use a simple flat pattern (like a chessboard) moved in front of the camera.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Zhang's method uses a 2D planar chart rather than a 3D calibration object.",
  "- It requires multiple images of the chart at different orientations to solve for camera parameters."
]

concepts.title: Finding the Epipoles
concepts.one_liner: The epipoles can be computed as the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues of the essential matrix and its transpose.
concepts.content: As the epipoles, $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$, belong to the epipolar lines, they satisfy $\mathbf{p}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} \mathbf{p}_1 = 0$. Since the epipoles are the intersection of all the epipolar lines, both relationships must be true for any points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$. Therefore, $\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} = 0$. As the matrix $\mathbf{E}$ is likely to be noisy, we can compute the epipoles as the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{E}^\mathsf{T}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In stereo vision, finding the epipoles is necessary to define the geometry of the camera system. Because real-world data is noisy, a robust numerical method like eigenvalue decomposition is needed to find these points accurately.
concepts.recap_md: - Epipoles satisfy the null-space conditions $\mathbf{E} \mathbf{e}_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{e}_2^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{E} = 0$.

concepts.title: Image Rectification
concepts.one_liner: Image rectification warps stereo images so that epipolar lines align with image scanlines, simplifying the search for matching points.
concepts.content: One only needs to search along epipolar lines to find matching points in the second image. If the sensor planes of each camera are coplanar, and if the pixel rows are colinear across the two cameras, then the epipolar lines will be along image scanlines, simplifying the stereo search. Using homography transformations, we can warp observed stereo camera images taken under general conditions to synthesize the images that would have been recorded had the cameras been aligned to yield epipolar lines along scan rows.
concepts.motivation_md: Searching for matching points across two images is computationally expensive. Rectification reduces this 2D search problem into a 1D search along horizontal scanlines, significantly increasing efficiency.
concepts.recap_md: - Rectification aligns camera sensor planes to be coplanar and pixel rows to be colinear.

concepts.title: Image Rectification Procedure
concepts.one_liner: A standard rectification procedure involves rotating cameras to be parallel and scaling images to match size.
concepts.content: Many configurations of the two cameras satisfy the desired image rectification constraints: (1) that epipolar lines are along image scanlines, and (2) that matching points are within the same rows in each camera image. One procedure that will satisfy those constraints is as follows. First, rotate each camera to be parallel with each other and with optical axes perpendicular to the line joining the two camera centers. Second, rotate each of the cameras about its optical axis to align the rows of each camera with those of the other. Third, uniformly scale one camera's image to be the same size as the other, if necessary. The resulting image pair will thus satisfy the two requirements above for image rectification. Image rectification uses image warping with bilinear (or other) interpolation.
concepts.motivation_md: To achieve the computational benefits of rectified images, a systematic geometric transformation (rotation and scaling) must be applied to the raw camera inputs to satisfy specific alignment constraints.
concepts.recap_md: - Rotate cameras to be parallel with optical axes perpendicular to the baseline.

concepts.title: Stereo Rectification Algorithms
concepts.one_liner: Various rectification algorithms exist to minimize distortions or work with weaker conditions like the fundamental matrix.
concepts.content: Other algorithms are optimized to minimize image distortions and may give better performance for stereo algorithms. We assume camera calibrations are known, but other rectification algorithms can use weaker conditions, such as knowing the fundamental matrix. Many software packages provide image rectification code.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard rectification can introduce significant image distortion. Specialized algorithms aim to preserve image quality or function when full camera calibration parameters are unavailable.
concepts.recap_md: - Some algorithms minimize image distortion for better stereo matching performance.

concepts.title: Introduction to Learning-Based Stereo Methods
concepts.one_liner: Neural network approaches now dominate stereo methods, implementing matching and filtering either separately or in end-to-end architectures.
concepts.content: As is the case for most other vision tasks, neural network approaches now dominate stereo methods. The two stages of a stereo algorithm, matching and filtering, can be implemented separately by neural networks, or together in a single, end-to-end optimization.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional hand-crafted stereo algorithms often struggle with complex textures or lighting. Learning-based methods can learn more robust features and filtering strategies directly from data.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural networks can handle stereo matching and filtering as separate stages or a single end-to-end task.

concepts.title: Output Representation: Disparity vs Depth
concepts.one_liner: Stereo systems can represent output as disparity or depth, each offering different advantages for noise modeling and estimation.
concepts.content: One important question is how we want to represent the output. We are ultimately interested in estimating the 3D structure of the scene. We can estimate the disparity or the depth. Disparity might be easier to estimate as it is independent of the camera parameters. It is also easier to model noise, as we can assume that noise is independent of disparity. However, when using depth, estimation error will be larger for distant points.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing between disparity and depth affects how errors are distributed and how easily the system can be calibrated. Disparity is often preferred for initial estimation due to its simpler noise characteristics.
concepts.recap_md: - Disparity is independent of camera parameters and allows for simpler noise modeling.

concepts.title: Planarity Property of Disparity
concepts.one_liner: For flat surfaces, the second-order derivative of disparity along any spatial direction is zero.
concepts.content: Another interesting property of disparity is that for flat surfaces, the second-order derivative along any spatial direction, $\mathbf{x}$, is zero: $$\frac{\partial^2 d}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2}  = 0.$$ This equality does not hold for depth. This property allows introducing a simple regularization term that favors planarity.
concepts.motivation_md: Many real-world scenes contain flat surfaces. This mathematical property of disparity allows researchers to build "planarity priors" into their algorithms to improve reconstruction of walls, floors, and tables.
concepts.recap_md: - The second-order derivative of disparity is zero for flat surfaces, unlike depth.

concepts.title: Converting Disparity to Depth
concepts.one_liner: To convert disparity into depth values, one must calculate the inverse of the disparity.
concepts.content: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d\left[n,m \right]$ into depth values $z\left[n,m \right]$, we need to invert the disparity, that is $$\begin{aligned} z \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{ d \left[n,m \right] }$$
concepts.motivation_md: While disparity is useful for matching, most robotics and 3D applications require actual distance (depth) to objects in the scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth is the reciprocal of disparity: $z = 1/d$.

concepts.title: Shearing Transformation
concepts.one_liner: Shearing involves scale factors in the off-diagonal matrix locations, displacing points along lines by a distance proportional to their coordinate.
concepts.content:
Shearing involves scale factors in the off-diagonal matrix locations, as shown in the matrix $\mathbf{Q}$:

$$\mathbf{Q} =             
    \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & q_x & 0 \\
    q_y & 1 & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 1
    \end{bmatrix}$$

(see figure: Three examples of shear transformation.)

In the example of a horizontal shear ($q_x=1, q_y=0$), points are displaced along horizontal lines by a displacement proportional to the $y$ coordinate, $x'=x+q_y y$. In a shear, lines are mapped to lines and parallel lines remain parallel, but (non-zero) angles between lines change.
concepts.motivation_md: Shearing is used to skew or tilt an image or object. It allows for transformations where parallel lines are preserved but the relative angles between axes change, which is useful for simulating perspective or creating italicized effects.
concepts.recap_md: [FIGURE:fig-shear | Three examples of shear transformation.]

concepts.title: Chaining Transformations
concepts.one_liner: Complex geometric operations can be built by multiplying the matrices of individual transformations in a specific order.
concepts.motivation_md: Chaining allows for the creation of complex movements and orientations by breaking them down into simple, fundamental operations like translation, rotation, and scaling.
concepts.recap_md:
- Complex transformations are achieved through matrix multiplication.
- The order of operations matters because matrix multiplication is noncommutative.
- To transform around a specific point, translate that point to the origin first.

concepts.title: Euclidean Transformation
concepts.one_liner: A Euclidean transformation is the result of chaining rotations and translations, preserving both lengths and angles.
concepts.content: When chaining rotations and translations only, we will have a euclidean transformation. In this type of transformation, lengths and angles between lines are preserved.
concepts.motivation_md: Euclidean transformations represent rigid body motions where the shape and size of an object do not change, only its position and orientation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Formed by chaining only rotations and translations.
- Preserves both lengths and angles between lines.

concepts.title: Similarity Transform
concepts.one_liner: A similarity transform chains rotation, translation, and uniform scaling, preserving angles but not lengths.
concepts.content: A similarity transform is the result of chaining a rotation, translation, and scaling (specifically with uniform scaling, where $s_x=s_y$). In this case, angles are preserved but lengths are not.
concepts.motivation_md: Similarity transforms are used when an object's shape must be maintained while its size and position change, such as zooming in on a map.
concepts.recap_md:
- Combines rotation, translation, and uniform scaling.
- Preserves angles but changes lengths.

concepts.title: Affine Transformation
concepts.one_liner: An affine transformation chains translations, scalings, rotations, and shears, preserving parallel lines but not necessarily lengths or angles.
concepts.content:
Chaining translations, scalings, rotations, and shears results in an affine transformation. In general, this results in a generic matrix with the form:

$$\mathbf{p}' = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a & b & c \\
    d & e & f \\
    0 & 0 & 1
    \end{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{p}$$

Any transformation with this form (6 degrees of freedom) is an affine transformation. An affine transformation has the property that parallel lines will remain parallel after the transformation; however, lengths and non-zero angles might change.
concepts.motivation_md: Affine transformations provide a flexible way to map coordinates while maintaining linear structures, which is essential for image registration and computer graphics.
concepts.recap_md:
- Includes translations, scalings, rotations, and shears.
- Parallel lines remain parallel after transformation.
- Represented by a matrix with 6 degrees of freedom.

concepts.title: Projective Transformation
concepts.one_liner: Projective transformations use a full 3x3 matrix with 8 degrees of freedom to represent more general geometric mappings.
concepts.content:
A projective transformation occurs when we use a full $3 \times 3$ matrix with 9 parameters:

$$\mathbf{p}' = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a & b & c \\
    d & e & f \\
    g & h & i
    \end{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{p}$$

In fact, we only have 8 degrees of freedom because a global scaling of the matrix does not change the homogeneous coordinates. This set of transformations is more general than affine transformations and includes elations.
concepts.motivation_md: Projective transformations are necessary to model how 3D scenes are projected onto 2D surfaces, accounting for perspective effects where parallel lines appear to converge.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a full matrix with 8 degrees of freedom.
- More general than affine transformations.
- Global scaling of the matrix does not affect the result in homogeneous coordinates.

concepts.title: Elation
concepts.one_liner: An elation is a specific type of projective transformation arising from the additional degrees of freedom in a full transformation matrix.
concepts.content: Elations are a subset of transformations described by the full $3 \times 3$ projective matrix. They represent additional degrees of freedom beyond those found in affine transformations.
concepts.motivation_md: Elations are specific projective transformations used in geometry to describe mappings that fix all points on a line and all lines through a point on that line.
concepts.recap_md:
- A type of projective transformation.
- Enabled by the 8 degrees of freedom in a general homogeneous matrix.

concepts.title: Geometric Transformations as Convolutions
concepts.one_liner: When geometry is explicitly added to image representation, transformations like rotations and shears can be implemented as 1D convolutions over locations.
concepts.content:
Once geometry is added to the image representation, transformations such as rotations, scalings, and shears can be implemented as one-dimensional (1D) convolutions over the locations.

(see figure: Geometric transformation as a convolution. The input and output signals are represented as pixel sets with explicit geometry. The convolution kernels are $w_x$ and $w_y$, corresponding to one...)

In this representation, each input element is a vector $(x_i, y_i, \ell_i)$ where $x_i, y_i$ are the pixel location and $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity. The convolution kernels are $w_x = [\cos(\theta), \sin(\theta)]$ and $w_y = [-\sin(\theta), \cos(\theta)]$. The weights are the same for all inputs, and the output is also represented using explicit positions $(x'_i, y'_i, \ell'_i)$. Note that performing a convolution on the output intensity requires translating the position encoding back into a rectangular grid, as transformations like rotation move pixels off the original grid.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach unifies geometric transformations and signal processing, allowing complex spatial changes to be treated with the same mathematical framework as linear filtering.
concepts.recap_md:
- Transformations are modeled as 1D convolutions over coordinate vectors $(x, y, \ell)$.
- Convolution kernels like $w_x$ and $w_y$ apply the transformation weights to all inputs.
- Output positions must be re-mapped to a rectangular grid for standard image processing.

concepts.title: Social Bias
concepts.one_liner: Social bias refers to biases associated with how groups of people might be reflected differently in data due to collection protocols or existing societal stereotypes.
concepts.content: Social bias can affect both images and their associated labels. It refers to biases associated with how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data. These biases can originate from the data collection protocol or from existing social biases. For instance, images can be captured in certain world regions or contain stereotypes, while labels can reflect social assumptions. An example of social bias is a dataset of images and labels that associates doctors with males and nurses with females. Besides impacting overall model performance, these types of biases can have a negative social impact once deployed. It is important to be aware of these biases and incorporate techniques to mitigate their effects.
concepts.motivation_md: Social bias exists because datasets often mirror the prejudices and structural inequalities of the real world. If left unaddressed, models trained on this data will perpetuate harmful stereotypes and perform poorly for marginalized groups.
concepts.recap_md:
- Social bias stems from data collection protocols or existing societal stereotypes.
 - It manifests in both image content (e.g., regional representation) and label associations.
 - Mitigation is necessary to prevent negative social impacts and performance disparities upon deployment.

concepts.title: Testing and Benchmark Bias
concepts.one_liner: Biases in the test set can lead to misleading conclusions about model performance and the effectiveness of training data.
concepts.content: While bias is often associated with training sets, biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on final system behavior. The test set is the primary tool researchers and engineers use to decide which algorithm is best or which data collection is more effective. However, there might be little correlation between performance measured on a biased test set and the final performance of the system during deployment. In particular, if we compare two training datasets—one biased and another less biased—by evaluating them on a biased test dataset, we could incorrectly conclude that the biased training dataset is superior.
concepts.motivation_md: Testing and benchmark bias occurs because our evaluation metrics are only as good as the data we use to measure them. If the 'ruler' (the test set) is skewed, we cannot accurately judge which models are truly robust or fair.
concepts.recap_md:
- Test set bias can be more damaging than training bias because it misguides model selection.
 - High performance on a biased test set does not guarantee good performance in real-world deployment.
 - Biased benchmarks can erroneously favor biased training data over more representative datasets.

concepts.title: Bias as a Relative Term
concepts.one_liner: Bias is a relative term comparing two datasets, or a dataset against the real world or a desired distribution.
concepts.content: Bias is a relative term between two datasets, or between a dataset and the real world, or a desired distribution. We only have access to the real world via datasets, which are inevitably biased.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept clarifies that 'bias' isn't an absolute property of a single dataset in isolation, but a measure of divergence from a reference point, acknowledging that no dataset perfectly captures reality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Bias describes the relationship between a dataset and a reference distribution.
 - All datasets are inevitably biased representations of the real world.

concepts.title: Adversarial Shifts
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial shifts occur when data changes are malicious and controlled by a competing agent trying to fool a system.
concepts.content: Data shifts can be random, but they can also be adversarial. This occurs whenever the test setting is under the control of a competing agent, such as someone trying to hack a system (computer security), another animal trying to eat us (evolution), or a trader trying to outperform us on the stock market (finance). Neural networks are notably easy for an adversary to fool.
concepts.motivation_md: Unlike random noise, adversarial shifts are specifically designed to exploit a model's weaknesses, making them a critical security concern for deployed AI systems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Adversarial shifts are malicious rather than random.
 - They occur in competitive environments like security, finance, or biology.
 - Standard neural networks are highly vulnerable to these targeted manipulations.

concepts.title: Adversarial Attacks
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks involve adding imperceptible noise to inputs to force a neural network into making specific, incorrect predictions.
concepts.content:
Adversarial attacks involve adding imperceptible noise to an image that fools neural net classifiers despite looking innocuous to a human. The noise pattern can be selected to force the network to produce any output the attacker desires. The adversary optimizes the noise pattern $\mathbf{\epsilon}$ to cause a particular output while restricting the noise to a small $r$-radius ball around the original image. For example, to cause a classifier $f$ to misclassify a cat as an ostrich, an attacker finds the noise via:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{\epsilon}} H(\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{ostrich}}, f(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{\epsilon})), \quad\quad \text{subject to} \quad\quad \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r
\end{aligned}$$
where $H$ is the cross-entropy loss.

(see figure: An adversarial attack that adds subtle changes to the cat photo to make a neural net classify it instead as an ostrich. The noise image color values are scaled 20x for visualization.)

This type of attack requires the attacker to have access to the system to optimize $\mathbf{\epsilon}$. Deploying a system to the public provides this access, making it vulnerable. While simple vulnerabilities can be found manually through architecture analysis or aliasing, large-scale adversarial attacks are generated via optimization procedures to ensure the noise has small amplitude and high confidence in causing failure.
concepts.motivation_md: Adversarial attacks demonstrate that neural networks do not 'see' the world like humans do; they rely on features that can be manipulated by tiny, calculated perturbations to cause catastrophic failures.
concepts.recap_md:
- Attacks use optimized, imperceptible noise to force specific incorrect outputs.
 - The noise is typically constrained within a small $r$-radius ball around the original input.
 - Publicly accessible models are vulnerable because attackers can use them to optimize their perturbations.

concepts.title: Adversarial Robustness
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial robustness is the goal of minimizing a system's worst-case error rather than just its mean error.
concepts.content: Adversarial analysis is worst-case analysis. Typically, systems are trained to minimize empirical risk, defined as the mean error over the training data. Because the focus is only on the mean, the worst case might be arbitrarily bad. Alternative approaches try to minimize worst-case error, resulting in systems that are more adversarially robust.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard training only ensures a model works well on average. Adversarial robustness is necessary for safety-critical applications where a single failure caused by a worst-case input could be unacceptable.
concepts.recap_md:
- Standard training minimizes mean error (empirical risk), ignoring worst-case scenarios.
 - Adversarial robustness focuses on minimizing the maximum possible error.
 - It provides a safeguard against inputs specifically designed to exploit model weaknesses.

concepts.title: Adversarial Training
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial training increases model robustness by augmenting the training process with worst-case transformations or perturbations.
concepts.content:
Adversarial training is a technique used to increase the robustness of models to adversarial attacks. While standard data augmentation applies random transformations to data to minimize expected loss:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim p_{\theta}}[\mathcal{L}(f(T(\mathbf{x};\theta)),\mathbf{y})]]
\end{aligned}$$
adversarial training instead considers augmenting with worst-case transformations that incur the highest possible loss:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\theta \in \Theta}[\mathcal{L}(f(T(\mathbf{x};\theta)),\mathbf{y})]] 
\end{aligned}$$
In the context of adversarial robustness, one form of this is to set $T$ to be an epsilon-ball attack, $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}$:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_f \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} [\max_{\mathbf{\epsilon} \, s.t. \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r}[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{\epsilon}),\mathbf{y})]]
\end{aligned}$$
This increases robustness against perturbations at test time. Beyond robustness, adversarial training is used for generative adversarial networks, reinforcement learning exploration, and competitive agents. It is also known as robust optimization.
concepts.motivation_md: By training on the very examples that would normally fool it, a model learns to ignore malicious noise and focus on more stable, meaningful features.
concepts.recap_md:
- It replaces random data augmentation with worst-case perturbations during training.
 - The objective is to minimize the maximum loss within a defined transformation space (e.g., an epsilon-ball).
 - It is a specific application of the broader field of robust optimization.

concepts.title: Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Data augmentation expands a dataset by adding synthetic versions of data points created through random transformations.
concepts.content:
Data augmentation expands a dataset by adding random transformations of each datapoint. For each $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}$ pair in the original dataset, you add $M$ new synthetic pairs $\{T(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^M$, where $T$ is a transformation function with stochastic parameters $\theta$. For example, $T$ might be a `crop` function with $\theta$ representing coordinates.

(see figure: A few common types of data augmentation.)

By mapping a smaller dataset to a larger one, data augmentation simulates the effect of adding more real data. It is a critical tool in machine learning because larger datasets generally lead to better performance.

[FIGURE:d88031ceb8315562 | A flowchart showing the process of data augmentation. It starts with a 'Small dataset' represented by the set {x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N, which passes through a 'Data augmentation' block...]
concepts.motivation_md: Data is the fuel for machine learning, but collecting real-world data is expensive. Data augmentation allows us to bake domain knowledge (like 'a cat is still a cat if cropped') into the model while artificially increasing the dataset size.
concepts.recap_md:
- It creates synthetic training examples using stochastic transformations like cropping or rotating.
 - It effectively increases dataset size, which typically improves model performance.
 - The labels remain the same for the transformed versions of the original data points.

concepts.title: Image Representation: Set of Pixels
concepts.one_liner: An image can be represented as a collection of points, indicating its color and location explicitly as a set of pixels.
concepts.content: An image can be represented as a collection of points, indicating its color and location explicitly. In this case, an image is represented as a **set of pixels**: $$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}$$ where $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity (or color) recorded at location $(x_i,y_i)$. This representation makes the geometry explicit. While it might seem like a trivial representation, it makes some operations easy. For instance, we can apply geometric transformations easily by directly working with the spatial coordinates. If you want to translate an image to the right by one pixel, you can do that easily by simply creating the new image defined by the set of translated pixels: $\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i+1,y_i] : i \right\}$. Representing images as sets of points is very common in geometry-based computer vision.
concepts.motivation_md: This representation makes the geometric properties of an image explicit, facilitating operations like spatial transformations (translation, rotation) that are more complex in standard grid-based formats.
concepts.recap_md: - An image is defined as a set of tuples containing intensity and spatial coordinates.

concepts.title: Image Representation: Continuous Function
concepts.one_liner: An image can be represented as a continuous function whose input is a location and whose output is an intensity or color.
concepts.content: Another option is to represent an image as a continuous function whose input is a location $(x, y)$ and whose output is an intensity, or a color, $\ell$: $$\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$$ This image representation is commonly used when we want to make image priors more explicit. The function $f_{\theta}$ is parameterized by the coefficients $\theta$. This function becomes especially interesting when the parameters $\theta$ are different than the original pixel values, requiring them to be estimated from the original image. Once learned, the function $f$ should be able to take as input continuous spatial variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing images as continuous functions allows for the use of continuous spatial variables and makes image priors explicit, which is useful for tasks like super-resolution or image modeling.
concepts.recap_md: - Images are modeled as functions $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ mapping coordinates to intensities.

concepts.title: Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$, where all non-zero scalings are equivalent.
concepts.content: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$. The transformation rule from heterogeneous to homogeneous coordinates is simply to add an additional coordinate, 1, to the heterogeneous coordinates: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ It is the same if the vector has three dimensions: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Homogeneous coordinates have the additional rule that all (non-zero) scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix}$$ for any non-zero scalar, $\lambda$. To go from homogeneous coordinates back to the heterogeneous representation, we divide all the entries of the homogeneous coordinate vector by their last dimension: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ w \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} x/w \\ y/w \end{pmatrix}$$ A point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant, which is closely related to perspective projection. (see figure: Transformation rule between heterogeneous and homogeneous coordinates in 2D. All the points along the dotted line correspond to the same point in heterogeneous coordinates. Note that the points...) While you can add two points in heterogeneous coordinates, you cannot do the same in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates simplify geometric transformations like translation and perspective projection by allowing them to be expressed as linear matrix multiplications.
concepts.recap_md: - Convert to homogeneous by appending a 1; convert back by dividing by the last coordinate.

concepts.title: Heterogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Heterogeneous coordinates are conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of points in 2D or 3D space.
concepts.content: Heterogeneous coordinates refer to conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of a point in 2D, such as $(x,y)$, or 3D, such as $(x,y,z)$. In mathematical notation, these are typically written with rounded brackets, whereas their corresponding homogeneous coordinate representations are denoted by square bracketed vectors.
concepts.motivation_md: These are the standard coordinates used in Euclidean geometry to represent positions in space relative to an origin.
concepts.recap_md: - Standard Cartesian coordinates like $(x, y)$ or $(x, y, z)$. - Typically denoted with rounded brackets to distinguish them from homogeneous vectors.

concepts.title: Scaling Invariance of Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: In homogeneous coordinates, all non-zero scalings of a coordinate vector are equivalent and represent the same point.
concepts.content: The homogeneous coordinates have the rule that all (non-zero) scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent. For example, to represent a 2D point, we have: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix}$$ for any non-zero scalar, $\lambda$. This property implies that a point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant, meaning any point within the line that passes through the origin translates into the same point in heterogeneous coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Scaling invariance allows the representation of points at infinity and simplifies the math of perspective projection, where distance from the camera scales the observed coordinates.
concepts.recap_md: - Multiplying a homogeneous vector by a non-zero scalar does not change the point it represents.

concepts.title: Conversion from Homogeneous to Heterogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: To convert from homogeneous to heterogeneous coordinates, divide all entries of the vector by its last dimension.
concepts.content: To go from homogeneous coordinates back to the heterogeneous representation of a point, we divide all the entries of the homogeneous coordinate vector by their last dimension: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ w \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} x/w \\ y/w \end{pmatrix}$$ This normalization step recovers the standard Cartesian coordinates from the projective representation.
concepts.motivation_md: This conversion is necessary to extract physical spatial coordinates from the projective space used during matrix transformations.
concepts.recap_md: - Divide every component of the vector by the final coordinate $w$.

concepts.title: 2D Translation in Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Translation in homogeneous coordinates is represented as a matrix-vector product rather than vector addition.
concepts.content: Consider a translation by a 2D vector $(t_x, t_y)$. In heterogeneous coordinates, we have $$\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} t_x \\ t_y \end{pmatrix}$$ We can write this translation in homogeneous coordinates by the product: $$ \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ This transforms an addition into a product by a matrix, $\mathbf{T}$, and a vector, $\mathbf{p}$, in homogeneous coordinates: $$ \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{T} \mathbf{p}, $$ with the homogeneous matrix, $\mathbf{T}$, defined as $$ \mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ For calculations in homogeneous coordinates, both matrices and vectors are only defined up to an arbitrary (non-zero) multiplicative scaling factor. (see figure: (left) Translation. (right) Composition of two consecutive translations.)
concepts.motivation_md: Using homogeneous coordinates allows translations to be treated as linear transformations, enabling the composition of multiple transformations into a single matrix.
concepts.recap_md: - Translation is represented by a matrix with the translation vector in the last column. - This converts the operation from vector addition to matrix multiplication.

concepts.title: Small Angle Rotation Approximation
concepts.one_liner: For very small angles, the rotation matrix can be approximated using a Taylor development where $\sin(x) \approx x$ and $\cos(x) \approx 1$.
concepts.content: If the angle of rotation is very small, then we can approximate the rotation matrix by its Taylor development: $$\mathbf{R} \simeq \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta & 0 \\ -\theta & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ This approximation is valid because for small $x$, $\sin(x) \approx x$ and $\cos(x) \approx 1$. For small angles, a rotation becomes a shear. In general, for all angles, a rotation can be written as two shears and a scaling.
concepts.motivation_md: Small angle approximations simplify the math in iterative algorithms, tracking, or when dealing with incremental changes in orientation.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses the approximations $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$ and $\cos(\theta) \approx 1$. - The resulting matrix represents a shear operation.

concepts.title: Simple stereo geometry
concepts.one_liner: Simple stereo geometry assumes two identical, horizontally translated cameras with parallel optical axes to estimate depth from point projections.
concepts.content: In a simple stereo setting, two identical cameras with the same intrinsic parameters are aligned so that one is translated horizontally with respect to the other, ensuring their optical axes are parallel. Assuming calibrated cameras, this geometry reveals the essence of depth estimation. Consider a point $\mathbf{P}$ in 3D space that projects onto the left camera at $[x_L,y_L]^\mathsf{T}$ and the right camera at $[x_R,y_R]^\mathsf{T}$. Because the cameras are aligned horizontally, the $y$-coordinates for the projection in both cameras are equal ($y_L=y_R$). This allows for depth estimation to be analyzed within a single image row by looking at a top-down view of the setting.
concepts.motivation_md: This simplified configuration reduces the complex 3D reconstruction problem to a 1D search along horizontal lines, making it easier to derive the fundamental relationship between image displacement and physical depth.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes identical cameras with parallel optical axes and horizontal translation.

concepts.title: Depth derivation from similar triangles
concepts.one_liner: Depth can be triangulated by relating the ratio of camera baseline and focal length to the horizontal disparity of a point in two images.
concepts.content: A simple way to triangulate the depth, $Z$, of a point visible in both images is through similar triangles. By comparing a triangle formed by the cameras and the 3D point to a smaller triangle involving the focal length and image coordinates, the ratios of their height to base must be the same. This leads to the relationship: $$\frac{T+x_R-x_L}{Z-f} = \frac{T}{Z}$$ Solving for $Z$ gives the depth equation: $$Z =  \frac{fT}{x_L-x_R}$$ where $f$ is the focal length, $T$ is the offset (baseline) between cameras, and $x_L-x_R$ is the horizontal disparity.
concepts.motivation_md: This derivation provides a direct mathematical formula to calculate the distance of an object from the camera based on how much its position shifts between two viewpoints.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses similar triangles to relate camera baseline $T$ and focal length $f$ to depth $Z$.

concepts.title: Stereo matching problem
concepts.one_liner: The stereo matching problem involves automatically identifying which points in two different camera views correspond to the same 3D point.
concepts.content:
In reality, stereo images are complex, and it is not immediately known which points in one camera correspond to the same 3D point in the other. This requires solving the stereo matching problem. Visually, this involves localizing a feature point in one image and finding the corresponding point in the other image based on the visual similarity of the local image region. The displacements between these corresponding points, or disparities, are what reveal depth.

[FIGURE:5b3ceb105441e961 | A photograph of an office interior with several objects highlighted by colored bounding boxes to demonstrate stereo matching and disparity. A potted plant is in white, a framed picture in purple, a...]

[FIGURE:8bc44da026c71495 | A photograph of an office space with several colored bounding boxes and yellow arrows indicating horizontal displacement (disparity) between two stereo views. A purple box on a wall picture, a white...]
concepts.motivation_md: To calculate depth using triangulation, we must first know which pixels represent the same physical object; stereo matching automates this correspondence search.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies corresponding points between two images to measure disparity.

concepts.title: Intensity-based stereo matching
concepts.one_liner: Intensity-based matching attempts to find disparities by comparing pixel values, but it is often unreliable due to noise, lack of texture, and occlusions.
concepts.content: A naive algorithm for finding the disparity of any pixel in the left image is to search for a pixel of the same intensity in the corresponding row of the right image. However, local intensity matches often don't reliably indicate disparity. This unreliability stems from several factors: lack of texture leading to noisy matches among identical pixels, image intensity noise, specularities that change location between views, and occlusions where scene points appear in only one image. An effective approach to mitigate this noise is to use a disparity space image, where matching errors are plotted for various offsets, and then apply an edge-preserving filter to smooth the results and find the best-matched disparities.
concepts.motivation_md: While simple to implement, direct pixel-to-pixel intensity matching fails in real-world scenes, necessitating more robust filtering and feature-based techniques.
concepts.recap_md: - Searches for pixels with similar intensities along the same image row.

concepts.title: Disparity space image
concepts.one_liner: A disparity space image is a configuration where matching errors for a range of disparity offsets are plotted, typically vertically, against horizontal position.
concepts.content: A disparity space image is a configuration where the matching error (such as squared difference of intensities) for a range of disparity offsets is plotted vertically as a function of horizontal position. In this representation, the disparity corresponding to the minimum error matches can be identified, often visualized as a path or set of points (sometimes plotted in red) representing the best estimates for depth across the image row.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a structured way to visualize and analyze all possible matches for a row of pixels, allowing for global optimization or filtering to find the most likely depth profile.
concepts.recap_md: - Plots matching errors for various disparity offsets against horizontal image position.

concepts.title: Matching and filtering steps in stereo
concepts.one_liner: The process of finding disparity is often divided into matching features across images and then filtering to interpolate a complete disparity map.
concepts.content: The task of finding disparity at each point is often broken into two parts: (1) finding features and matching them across images, and (2) interpolating between, or adjusting, the feature matches to obtain a reliable disparity estimate everywhere.
