position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud requires mapping each pixel to a 3D point using intrinsic camera parameters.
concepts.content:
Translating a depth map into a point cloud requires a calibrated camera with known intrinsic parameters. Each pixel $(n,m)$ is mapped into a 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, by using the depth, $z[n,m]$, at that location.

Using homogeneous coordinates, the equation translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud for each pixel is:
$$\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$$
where $\mathbf{p}$ are the pixel coordinates, $z(\mathbf{p})$ is the depth measured at that location, and $\mathbf{P}$ are the final 3D point coordinates. In heterogeneous coordinates, making the pixel locations explicit, the equation can be rewritten as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    X[n,m] &= \left( n-c_x \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \\
    Y[n,m] &= \left( m-c_y \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \\
    Z[n,m] &= z[n,m] 
\end{aligned}$$
where $a$, $c_x$ and $c_y$ are the intrinsic camera parameters in pixel units. This shows that the 3D point coordinates are represented by three images $X[n,m]$, $Y[n,m]$, and $Z[n,m]$ of the same size as the input image.
concepts.motivation_md: To perform 3D reasoning or navigation, we must convert 2D image-plane depth measurements into a standard 3D coordinate system (X, Y, Z).
concepts.recap_md: [ - The transformation uses the inverse of the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and the depth value $z$. ]

concepts.title: Turbo and Jet Colormaps for Depth Visualization

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The turbo colormap is a modified version of the jet colormap used to visualize depth maps and distinguish them from grayscale images.
concepts.content:
Depth maps are usually visualized using the **turbo colormap**, which is a modification of the **jet colormap** from Matlab. We use this convention to differentiate a depth map from a natural gray-scale image.

[FIGURE:5e64d445bf392d94 | Two vertical color bars labeled 'Jet' and 'Turbo' showing rainbow color maps used for depth visualization. Both bars transition from dark blue at the bottom, labeled 'Near', through cyan, green...]

The jet colormap can be problematic as it has a nonmonotonic intensity profile.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard grayscale images represent intensity, while depth maps represent distance; using a specific colormap like Turbo helps humans visually interpret depth gradients more clearly.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Turbo and Jet colormaps use color to represent depth values. ]

concepts.title: Point Clouds vs. Meshes

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Point clouds consist of isolated 3D points, while meshes connect points into surfaces using triangles.
concepts.content: In a point cloud, there is no notion of grouping of 3D points; points are isolated and not connected to each other. Translating a depth map or a point cloud into a mesh requires solving the perceptual organization problem first. A mesh connects points with triangles, but it only makes sense to connect points that belong to the same surface or that are in contact.
concepts.motivation_md: Point clouds are the direct output of many sensors, but meshes are necessary for defining continuous surfaces and volumes in graphics and simulation.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Point clouds contain isolated points with no connectivity information. ]

concepts.title: Supervised Depth Estimation Formulation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Supervised depth estimation is formulated as a pixelwise regression problem where a model learns to predict depth maps from images.
concepts.content:
In the supervised setting, we assume a training set containing $N$ images, $\ell^{(i)} [n,m]$, and their associated depth maps, $z^{(i)} [n,m]$. Depth estimation is formulated as a pixelwise regression problem. Typically, $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}$ and $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$ are images of the same size. The goal is to estimate depth at each pixel, $\hat{z}^{(i)}[n,m]$, from a single image using a learnable function $h_\theta$:
$$\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)} = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)} \right)$$
The parameters $\theta$ are learned by minimizing the loss over the training set:
$$\theta^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}, \mathbf{z}^{(i)} \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: By treating depth estimation as a supervised regression task, we can leverage deep learning to predict 3D structure from 2D images using ground-truth data.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Supervised depth estimation uses a learnable function to map images to depth maps. ]

concepts.title: Recovering World Coordinates from Depth
concepts.one_liner: World coordinates for every pixel can be recovered using depth information and the intrinsic camera parameters matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: In computer vision, simply knowing the 2D pixel location and depth is often insufficient; we need to map these back to 3D space to reconstruct the physical scene. This technique provides the mathematical bridge to transform image-space data into a metric 3D camera reference frame.
concepts.recap_md: - World coordinates are recovered by multiplying the inverse of the intrinsic matrix by the homogeneous pixel coordinates and scaling by depth.

concepts.title: Two-Stage Neural Networks for Stereo
concepts.one_liner: Two-stage networks compute disparity by extracting features with shared weights and then processing a 3D cost volume with a convolutional neural network.
concepts.content:
Given two images, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$, the disparity at each location can be computed by a function $\hat{\mathbf{d}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$. The objective is that the estimated disparities $\hat{\mathbf{d}}$ should be close to ground truth disparities $\mathbf{d}$, often optimized using a squared loss $J(\theta) = \sum_t | \mathbf{d} - f_{\theta} (\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) |^2$.

When matching and filtering are implemented separately, one common formulation uses one neural network to extract features from both images, $g(\mathbf{i}_1)$ and $g(\mathbf{i}_2)$, and another to compute the matching cost and estimate disparities:
$$f(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) = c ( g(\mathbf{v}_1), g(\mathbf{v}_2) )$$

A common approach, depicted in (see figure: Block diagram of CNN stereo processing, abstracted from the block diagrams of @Chang2018, @Zhang2019GANet, @Kendall2017), involves:
- Rectifying the stereo pair so scanlines depict the same world points.
- Extracting features using a pair of networks with shared weights.
- Forming a 3D cost volume indicating local visual evidence of a match for each pixel and disparity.
- Training and applying a 3D convolutional neural net (CNN) to aggregate costs over the volume to estimate the best disparity for each pixel.

This 3D CNN performs the regularization step found in non-neural approaches like SGM, but with better performance. While effective, 3D cost volume processing can be expensive; recent work has explored iterative algorithms to avoid 3D filtering for improved speed.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional stereo matching relies on handcrafted features and rigid regularization. Two-stage neural networks replace these with learned feature extractors and cost-aggregation layers, significantly improving accuracy and robustness in complex scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Disparity is estimated by processing a 3D cost volume formed from shared-weight feature maps.

concepts.title: Stereo Algorithm Evaluation and Middlebury Dataset
concepts.one_liner: The Middlebury stereo web page provides a comprehensive comparison of stereo algorithms on a common dataset.
concepts.content: The Middlebury stereo web page provides a comprehensive comparison of many stereo algorithms, compared on a common dataset, with pointers to algorithm descriptions and code. One can use the web page to evaluate the improvement of stereo reconstruction algorithms over time. The advancement of the field over time is very impressive.
concepts.motivation_md: Standardized benchmarks are essential for tracking progress in computer vision. The Middlebury dataset allows researchers to compare different stereo matching techniques under identical conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - Middlebury serves as a central benchmark for evaluating stereo reconstruction algorithm performance.

concepts.title: Introduction to Homographies
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a general geometric image transformation that maps pixels between views when the scene is planar or the camera only rotates.
concepts.content:
A homography is a general geometric image transformation that relates corresponding points across two images. While general viewpoints require 3D scene structure and relative camera motion to find a mapping, a simple transformation exists in specific scenarios: when the scene is planar or when two cameras are related only by a rotation. In these cases, the coordinates of corresponding points are related by a homography.

[FIGURE:d89ebe83f072de38 | A photograph of a row of academic books on a shelf, focusing on titles related to computer vision and perception. The books are arranged vertically, showing their spines with titles such as 'The...]

[FIGURE:4c2d17b07db71aed | A photograph of a bookshelf containing several academic books related to computer vision and perception. Visible titles include 'Perception as Bayesian Inference', 'The Retina', 'Foundations of...]

These two images are (approximately) related by a homography. Homographies are used in applications such as perspective correction, augmented reality, image stitching, creating bird's-eye views, and correcting keystone distortions.
concepts.motivation_md: Mapping one image to another usually requires complex 3D information. Homographies provide a powerful shortcut for common tasks like panoramic stitching or document scanning where the geometry is constrained.
concepts.recap_md: - Homographies relate views when the scene is flat or the camera rotation is the only change.

concepts.title: Definition of Homography
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines and can be represented by a 3x3 matrix in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content:
A homography (or projective transformation) is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines. It is a function $h$ that maps points such that if $\mathbf{p}_1$, $\mathbf{p}_2$, and $\mathbf{p}_3$ are colinear, their transformed points are also colinear. In homogeneous coordinates, this mapping $\mathbf{p}' = h(\mathbf{p})$ is written as a product with a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{H}$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This is expressed in short form as $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$. In a general homography, angles and lengths are not preserved; parallel lines might not remain parallel, and lines of identical length might change. (see figure: Homography. Colinear points remain colinear after transformation. Angles between lines are not preserved.)
concepts.motivation_md: To mathematically manipulate images for tasks like perspective correction, we need a formal definition of how points move. The homography provides a linear representation (in homogeneous space) for these non-linear 2D projections.
concepts.recap_md: - A homography maps points to points while maintaining collinearity.

concepts.title: Collinearity Preservation of Homographies
concepts.one_liner: Colinear points remain colinear after a homography transformation, as shown by the transformation of the line equation in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content: To prove that colinear points remain colinear after the homography, we use the equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates, $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$. Given the homography relationship $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$, we have $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{p}'$. Substituting this into the line equation yields $(\mathbf{H}^{-\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{l})^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p'}=0$, which is the equation of a line for the projected points $\mathbf{p}'$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem confirms the fundamental property of homographies: they are projective transformations that preserve the 'straightness' of lines, which is critical for maintaining the structure of objects in warped images.
concepts.recap_md: - The transformation of a line equation under a homography results in a new line equation.

concepts.title: Homography from Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: When a camera rotates around its center without translation, the mapping between corresponding points in different views is a homography.
concepts.content:
When images are taken from the same point by rotating the camera with no translation, the coordinates of corresponding points across pairs of images are related by a homography, regardless of their distance from the camera.

[FIGURE:1db46673e5bbe185 | A photograph of the Stata Center at MIT, taken at a tilted angle...]
[FIGURE:8267e250a2c64ddf | A photograph of the Stata Center at MIT, featuring complex, non-rectilinear architecture...]
[FIGURE:83ad2f9f3b5c333e | A photograph of a modern brick and metal building with complex, non-orthogonal geometry...]

As shown in (see figure: Camera rotation generates two images related by a homography.), we align the world coordinate system with camera 1. The projection of a 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ into camera 1 (with zero translation) is $\lambda_1 [x, y, 1]^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{K} [X, Y, Z]^\mathsf{T}$. For camera 2, with rotation $\mathbf{R}$, the projection is $\lambda_2 [x', y', 1]^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} [X, Y, Z]^\mathsf{T}$.

Inverting these equations to relate the common 3D point yields:
$$\begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = \lambda_1 \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \lambda_2 \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This establishes the relationship:
$$\lambda_2 / \lambda_1 \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Thus, $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$ is the $3\times3$ homography matrix relating the views. This holds even if the cameras have different intrinsic parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle is the foundation of panoramic image stitching. Because the transformation depends only on camera rotation and not on the depth of objects, we can perfectly align images taken from a tripod even if the scene has complex 3D structure.
concepts.recap_md: - Pure camera rotation creates a homography $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{K}_2 \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}_1^{-1}$.

concepts.title: Homography from Planar Surfaces
concepts.one_liner: When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points on that plane are related by a homography.
concepts.content:
When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points inside that plane are related by a homography. This is illustrated in [FIGURE:8d12e88a6496cd81 | A photograph of a stone building facade...] and [FIGURE:d33152acf9add1c2 | A photograph of a stone building facade...], where points on a building facade are related across views.

To prove this, we place the world-coordinate system on the plane such that $Z=0$, as shown in (see figure: Geometry of a the projection of a planar scene.). The projection equation is:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Setting $Z=0$ and letting $\mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2$ be the first two columns of the rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$, we get:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This shows that points on the plane are related to image points by a homography. Since this holds for any camera, the relationship between corresponding points across two cameras for a planar scene is also a homography. While the epipolar constraint always holds, the homography is a stronger constraint that applies specifically to these planar conditions.
concepts.motivation_md: Many man-made environments consist of flat surfaces like walls or floors. Recognizing that these surfaces follow a homography allows for specialized processing, such as rectifying a perspective view of a document into a flat, top-down image.
concepts.recap_md: - Points on a 3D plane map to 2D image points via a homography matrix.

concepts.title: Multitask Training
concepts.one_liner: Multitask training defines a new task for which multiple specific tasks are special cases, allowing the model to be trained on data from all tasks.
concepts.content: Because we have finite data for any given task, it can help to share data between tasks. One approach is to not just broaden the data but to also broaden the task by defining a new task, $AB$, for which tasks $A$ and $B$ are special cases. Then we can train $AB$ on both the data for task $A$ and for task $B$. An example of a metatask like $AB$ is data imputation. For instance, predicting missing color channels is the colorization problem (task $A$), while predicting a chunk of pixels masked out of an image is the inpainting problem (task $B$). We can train a joint colorization–inpainting model by setting up both as data imputation and training a general data imputation model on both sets of training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Data scarcity is a common bottleneck in deep learning. Multitask training solves this by allowing a model to borrow data from related tasks, improving generalization and efficiency.
concepts.recap_md:
- Define a broad metatask that encompasses multiple specific sub-tasks. 
- Train a single model on the combined datasets of all included tasks. 
- Use shared representations to improve performance on tasks with limited data.

concepts.title: Data Imputation Framework
concepts.one_liner: Data imputation is an incredibly general framework where models learn to predict missing data, such as color channels or masked pixels.
concepts.content: Data imputation is an incredibly general framework. For example, predicting missing color channels is the colorization problem, and predicting a chunk of pixels masked out of an image is the inpainting problem. We can train a joint colorization–inpainting model if we simply set up both as data imputation and train a general data imputation model. This model can be trained on both colorization training data and inpainting training data. This raises the question of which vision problems can be formulated as data imputation, and which ones cannot.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a unified way to frame diverse self-supervised tasks, allowing models to learn from the structure of the data itself without explicit labels for every sub-task.
concepts.recap_md:
- Formulates learning as predicting missing or corrupted parts of the input data. 
- Acts as a metatask for specific problems like colorization and inpainting. 
- Enables joint training across different types of data missingness.

concepts.title: One-Shot Learning
concepts.one_liner: Humans can learn to recognize a new kind of animal after seeing it just once, an ability known as one-shot learning.
concepts.content: A common criticism of deep learning systems is that they are data hungry. To learn a new concept (e.g., "is this a dog?") may require showing a deep net thousands of labeled examples of that concept. Conversely, humans can learn to recognize a new kind of animal after seeing it just once, an ability known as one-shot learning.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard deep learning requires massive datasets, which are often unavailable. One-shot learning aims to mimic human-like efficiency in learning from minimal information.
concepts.recap_md:
- Refers to learning a new category or concept from a single example. 
- Contrasts with traditional data-intensive deep learning approaches. 
- Aims to improve the data efficiency of artificial intelligence models.

concepts.title: Few-Shot Learning
concepts.one_liner: Few-shot learning refers to learning from just a few examples.
concepts.content: Few-shot learning refers to learning from just a few examples. It is part of a spectrum of data efficiency that also includes the zero-shot setting, where a model works out of the box on a new problem without any adaptation.
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world applications, collecting thousands of labels is impossible. Few-shot learning allows models to adapt to new tasks with very limited supervision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Involves adapting a model to a new task using a very small support set. 
- Sits between one-shot learning and standard supervised learning in terms of data requirements.

concepts.title: Zero-Shot Learning
concepts.one_liner: The zero-shot setting refers to when a model works out of the box on a new problem, with zero adaptation whatsoever.
concepts.content: The zero-shot setting refers to when a model works out of the box on a new problem, with zero adaptation whatsoever. This is related to few-shot learning, which refers to learning from just a few examples.
concepts.motivation_md: Zero-shot learning is the ultimate goal for generalizable AI, where a model can handle tasks it has never explicitly seen during training by leveraging broad prior knowledge.
concepts.recap_md:
- Requires a model to perform a task without any task-specific training data. 
- Relies on the model's ability to generalize from its pre-existing knowledge.

concepts.title: Transfer Learning
concepts.one_liner: Transfer learning deals with how to use prior knowledge to solve new learning problems quickly.
concepts.content: Deep nets are data hungry when they are trained from scratch, but they can be data efficient if we give them appropriate prior knowledge and the means to use their priors to accelerate learning. Transfer learning deals with how to use prior knowledge to solve new learning problems quickly. Humans do this by bringing extensive prior knowledge to bear when learning new concepts.
concepts.motivation_md: Training models from scratch for every new task is computationally expensive and data-intensive. Transfer learning leverages existing knowledge to make learning new tasks faster and easier.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses knowledge gained from one task to improve learning in a related task. 
- Reduces the amount of data and time required to train models for new problems. 
- Mimics the human ability to apply prior experience to new situations.

concepts.title: Pretraining
concepts.one_liner: Pretraining is the phase of transfer learning focused on how to acquire prior knowledge in the first place.
concepts.content: Pretraining is the process of acquiring prior knowledge in the first place. (see figure: Transfer learning consists of two phases: first we pretrain a model on one task and then we adapt that model to perform a new task.)
concepts.motivation_md: To transfer knowledge, a model must first possess it. Pretraining provides a foundation of features or patterns that can be reused later.
concepts.recap_md:
- The first stage of the transfer learning process. 
- Involves training a model on a large, general dataset to learn useful features.

concepts.title: Adaptation
concepts.one_liner: Adaptation is the phase of transfer learning focused on how to use prior knowledge to solve a new task.
concepts.content: Adaptation is the process of using prior knowledge to solve a new task. (see figure: Transfer learning consists of two phases: first we pretrain a model on one task and then we adapt that model to perform a new task.)
concepts.motivation_md: Once a model has general knowledge, it must be specialized to be useful for a specific target problem. Adaptation bridges the gap between general pretraining and specific application.
concepts.recap_md:
- The second stage of the transfer learning process. 
- Involves fine-tuning or modifying a pretrained model for a specific target task.

concepts.title: LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging)

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: LiDAR is a device that calculates distances by measuring the time taken for emitted light to return after reflecting off a surface.
concepts.content: LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) is a device that calculates distances by measuring the time taken for emitted light to return after reflecting off a surface (time of flight). A LiDAR produces a range image by scanning multiple directions. The output of this process is a point cloud. It is a common data capture method for depth sensing, alongside other sensors such as RGB-D cameras.
concepts.motivation_md: LiDAR provides a direct way to measure 3D geometry by using light pulses, solving the problem of estimating distance from 2D images alone.
concepts.recap_md:
- Measures distance using the time of flight of emitted light.
 - Scans multiple directions to produce a range image.
 - Generates a point cloud as its primary output.

concepts.title: Data Collection for Supervised Depth Estimation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Supervised depth estimation relies on datasets captured via sensors like Kinect and LiDAR, or reconstructed through multiview geometry and stereo pairs.
concepts.content: Datasets for supervised depth estimation are collected using various methods. Examples include the NYUv2 dataset, captured using a handheld Microsoft Kinect sensor in indoor environments, and the KITTI dataset, collected from a moving vehicle equipped with a LiDAR scan. Other methods utilize stereo pairs for training or multiview geometry techniques to provide accurate 3D estimates. For instance, MegaDepth uses scenes captured with multiple cameras to generate 3D reconstructions via structure from motion, creating datasets of images and associated depth maps for training single-image depth estimation models.
concepts.motivation_md: To train neural networks for depth estimation, large-scale ground truth data is required to teach the model the relationship between 2D pixels and 3D distance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Sensors like Kinect (RGB-D) and LiDAR provide direct ground truth depth maps.
 - Structure from motion and multiview geometry can generate depth data from multiple images.
 - Stereo pairs are also used as a source of training data for depth estimation.

concepts.title: L2 Loss for Depth Estimation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The L2 loss for depth estimation calculates the sum of squared differences between estimated and ground truth depth values.
concepts.content:
One simple loss used to optimize the parameters of a depth estimator is the L2 loss. This loss measures the difference between the estimated depth, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$, and the ground truth depth, $\mathbf{z}$:

$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{z} \right) =  \sum_{n,m} \left( \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m] \right) ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: The L2 loss provides a straightforward mathematical objective to minimize the distance between predicted and actual depth values during training.
concepts.recap_md:
- Computes the squared difference between predicted and actual depth at each pixel.
 - Sums these differences across all pixels $(n, m)$ in the image.
 - Serves as a basic optimization target for depth estimation parameters.

concepts.title: Scale-Invariant Loss

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The scale-invariant loss addresses global scale factors by eliminating the average difference between estimated and ground truth depth.
concepts.content:
The scale-invariant loss addresses the issue of global scale factors by eliminating the global scale factor from the calculation:
$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{z} \right) =  \sum_{n,m} \left( \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m] - \alpha\right) ^2$$
where $\alpha = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{n,m} \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m]$. This loss compares the estimated and ground truth depth at each pixel while accounting for a constant offset.
concepts.motivation_md: In many depth estimation tasks, the relative depth is more important than the absolute scale, which might be unknown or inconsistent across datasets.
concepts.recap_md:
- Eliminates global scale factors using a calculated offset $\alpha$.
 - $\alpha$ represents the mean difference between estimated and ground truth depth.
 - Focuses on the relative depth structure rather than absolute distance values.

concepts.title: Log-Depth and Disparity Optimization

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Optimizing for log-depth or disparity helps mitigate large errors associated with distant points in depth estimation.
concepts.content: Standard depth estimation can result in large errors for points with large depth values. One way to mitigate this is to optimize the reconstruction of the log of the depth, $\log \left( z[n,m] \right)$, or the disparity, which corresponds to the inverse of the depth, $1/z[n,m]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear depth scales penalize errors at long distances too heavily; log-depth and disparity provide a more balanced error distribution.
concepts.recap_md:
- Log-depth optimization uses $\log(z)$ to handle large depth ranges.
 - Disparity optimization uses $1/z$, the inverse of depth.
 - These methods reduce the impact of high-magnitude errors at large distances.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Depth Estimation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Depth estimation is typically implemented using an encoder-decoder neural network with skip connections to map RGB images to depth maps.
concepts.content:
The depth estimation function is usually implemented with a neural network using an encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections. The input is a red-green-blue (RGB) image and the output is a depth map. While this architecture is generic and not specific to depth estimation, one could add constraints such as a preference for planar shapes or other structural priors. However, most current approaches use a fairly generic architecture and let the data and the loss function determine the best mapping.

(see figure: Typical architecture for depth estimation from a single image @Xian2018)
concepts.motivation_md: Encoder-decoder structures are effective at capturing global context while preserving local spatial details necessary for accurate per-pixel depth prediction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses an encoder-decoder structure to transform RGB inputs into depth maps.
 - Skip connections help preserve spatial detail from the input image.
 - Often relies on data-driven learning rather than hard-coded structural priors.

concepts.title: Generalization in Learning-Based Depth Estimation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Existing depth estimation methods rely on massive datasets to achieve generalization across diverse visual scenes.
concepts.content: Existing methods rely on training on massive amounts of data to achieve good generalization across a wide set of images. [FIGURE:ff0296d2898fb6f0 | A photograph of an office interior used as a sample input for depth estimation. The scene includes a wooden bookshelf filled with books, a round wooden table with a white chair, a concrete pillar...] [FIGURE:3125eeb80587cef3 | A depth map of an office scene using a jet color scheme. Closer objects like a round table in the foreground are shown in cool blue and cyan, while more distant areas like a doorway in the background...] (a) Office scene. (b) Estimated $Z$ component by the approach from @Ranftl2021, @Ranftl2022.
concepts.motivation_md: Generalization is critical because depth estimation models must work on real-world scenes that differ significantly from their training data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Generalization is achieved by training on very large, diverse datasets.
 - Models can estimate depth for complex indoor scenes like offices.
 - Visualizations often use color schemes (like jet) to represent depth levels.

concepts.title: Visualizing 3D Reconstruction Quality

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The best way to evaluate a 3D reconstruction is to translate the depth map into a point cloud and view it from different perspectives.
concepts.content:
Just looking at a 2D depth map might make estimates appear good, but it is hard to tell the true quality of the estimation with that visualization. The best way of appreciating the quality of a 3D reconstruction is by translating the depth map into a point cloud and then reconstructing the scene under different view points. Points near regions of depth discontinuities are often removed to improve the clarity of the visualization, as these points are frequently incorrect and tend to have depth values that are the average of the values on each side of the discontinuity.

[FIGURE:349fd762fb7f8019 | A 3D point cloud reconstruction of an office scene viewed from a perspective angle. The image shows a bookshelf filled with books on the left, a small round wooden table in the foreground, and a desk...]

[FIGURE:ab4a3ae0938f2ef6 | A 3D point cloud reconstruction of an office scene, viewed from a high-angle perspective. The reconstruction shows a blue carpeted floor, some furniture elements like a wooden table or desk, and wall...]

Reconstructed point cloud of the office scene with two different view points. Results are good, but not great.
concepts.motivation_md: 2D depth maps can hide errors in geometry; 3D point cloud visualization reveals artifacts and inaccuracies in the reconstructed spatial structure.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth maps are converted to point clouds for better quality assessment.
 - Viewing the reconstruction from multiple angles reveals geometric errors.
 - Depth discontinuities are often filtered out because they contain averaged, inaccurate values.

concepts.title: SFM Degrees of Freedom Analysis

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Degrees of freedom analysis determines the minimal number of observations required to solve the Structure from Motion problem by comparing the number of unknowns to the number of image coordinates.
concepts.content: To determine the minimal number of observations needed to solve the Structure from Motion (SFM) problem, we analyze the degrees of freedom. Assuming calibrated cameras with known intrinsic parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, we count the unknowns: the 3D coordinates of $N$ points and the extrinsic camera parameters for $M$ images. This results in $3N$ unknowns for the 3D points. For the camera parameters, assuming the first camera is at the origin, we solve for $M-1$ cameras. Rotations contribute $3(M-1)$ unknowns, and translations (up to a scale factor) contribute $3(M-1)-1$ unknowns, totaling $3N + 6(M-1)-1$ unknowns. Given image coordinates of $N$ points across $M$ images, we have $2NM$ observations. A solution is possible when $$2NM \geq 3N + 6(M-1)-1$$ Note that if $M=1$, the problem cannot be solved. If cameras are uncalibrated, an additional $3M$ unknowns are typically added, depending on the camera type.
concepts.motivation_md: This analysis identifies the theoretical limits of reconstruction. It helps researchers understand the minimum number of points and camera views necessary before an optimization or algebraic solution can even be attempted.
concepts.recap_md:
- The total unknowns for $N$ points and $M$ calibrated cameras is $3N + 6(M-1)-1$.
 - A solution requires the number of observations ($2NM$) to be greater than or equal to the number of unknowns.
 - Uncalibrated cameras increase the complexity by adding approximately $3M$ additional unknowns.

concepts.title: Scale Drift

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Scale drift is the accumulation of slight numerical errors in scale factors when sequentially triangulating new camera frames in a reconstruction.
concepts.content: In Structure from Motion, we often assume every point is visible in every view to perform tasks like fundamental matrix estimation and triangulation relative to a reference view. However, if this visibility criterion is not met, each new image added to the reconstruction must be triangulated with respect to its closest image. During this process, slight numerical errors can occur, causing the new frame to have a slightly different scale factor relative to the existing reconstruction. This error accumulates over time, a phenomenon known as scale drift.
concepts.motivation_md: In long-range camera trajectories or video sequences, points disappear and reappear. Understanding scale drift is crucial for developing loop closure and global optimization techniques that prevent the reconstructed map from warping over time.
concepts.recap_md:
- Scale drift occurs when new images are triangulated sequentially rather than against a single global reference.
 - Small numerical errors in scale factor for each new frame accumulate over the course of the reconstruction.
 - It is primarily caused by limited visibility where points do not persist across all views.

concepts.title: Visibility Term in Reprojection Error

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The visibility term $v_i^{(j)}$ is a binary variable used in the reprojection error equation to account for 3D points that are only visible in a subset of camera views.
concepts.content: To calculate the final reprojection error, a visibility term $v_i^{(j)}$ is added to account for 3D points that are only visible in a subset of the views. The binary variable $v_i^{(j)}$ indicates if point $i$ is seen from camera $j$. For all points not visible in a specific view, $v_i^{(j)}$ is set to 0, meaning their reprojection error is ignored. This is expressed as: $$\sum_{j=1}^M \sum_{i=1}^N v_i^{(j)} \left\lVert \mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i - \pi \left( \mathbf{K}^{(j)} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}^{(j)} ~ \mid ~ -\mathbf{R}^{(j)}\mathbf{T}^{(j)} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}^{(j)}_i \right) \right\rVert ^2 $$
concepts.motivation_md: In real-world scenarios, points are frequently occluded or move out of the camera's field of view. This term allows the optimization algorithm to handle incomplete data without penalizing the model for missing observations.
concepts.recap_md:
- $v_i^{(j)}$ is a binary indicator: 1 if point $i$ is visible in camera $j$, and 0 otherwise.
 - Setting $v_i^{(j)}=0$ effectively removes that point-camera pair from the total error summation.
 - This term is essential for defining a valid reprojection error across multiple views with partial visibility.

concepts.title: Bundle Adjustment

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Bundle adjustment is the process of optimizing the 'bundle of rays' connecting camera centers and 3D point coordinates to minimize reprojection error.
concepts.content: The optimization of the reprojection error is called bundle adjustment. The term refers to the process of optimizing the "bundle of rays" connecting the camera centers and the coordinates of the 3D points. A common simplification in this process is to assume that all cameras share the same intrinsic parameters ($\mathbf{K}^{(j)}=\mathbf{K}$), which typically occurs when views are captured by a single moving camera with a fixed focal length.
concepts.motivation_md: Initial estimates of camera positions and 3D points are often noisy. Bundle adjustment provides a globally optimal refinement, ensuring that the reconstructed geometry is as consistent as possible with the observed image data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Bundle adjustment minimizes the total reprojection error across all points and all camera views.
 - It simultaneously refines both 3D point positions and camera extrinsic (and sometimes intrinsic) parameters.
 - The name comes from the adjustment of the "bundle" of light rays passing from points to camera centers.

concepts.title: Challenges and Ambiguities in Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Structure from Motion faces challenges such as local minima and noisy matches, alongside inherent ambiguities like global scale and coordinate system orientation.
concepts.content: When optimizing the reprojection error, several ambiguities exist that cannot be recovered: a global translation and rotation of the world-coordinate system, the global scale, and a projective ambiguity when the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ is unknown. Additionally, SFM faces two main challenges: the requirement for reliable matching points and the difficulty of optimizing the error equation, which is prone to local minima and sensitive to noisy matches.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing these limitations is vital for interpreting SFM results; for instance, knowing that the absolute size of an object cannot be determined without a known reference object (due to scale ambiguity).
concepts.recap_md:
- Ambiguities include global rotation, translation, scale, and potential projective distortion.
 - Reliable feature matching is a prerequisite for successful reconstruction.
 - Optimization is difficult because the error surface contains many local minima and is sensitive to noise.

concepts.title: Interest Points

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Interest points are image locations that remain stable under various geometric transformations and illumination changes.
concepts.content: The goal of finding image features is to locate image locations that are likely to be stable under different sets of geometric transformations (translation, scaling, rotation, skew, and projective) and illumination changes. These stable regions are called interest points.
concepts.motivation_md: To track objects or reconstruct scenes, we need landmarks that look the same even if the camera moves or the lighting changes. Interest points provide these reliable anchors.
concepts.recap_md:
- Interest points must be stable across geometric changes like rotation and scaling.
 - They should be robust to changes in scene illumination.
 - They serve as the foundational features for matching across different images.

concepts.title: Moving Element

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Initially, interest points were called moving elements, referring to identifiable image points like corners or texture elements that could be followed over time.
concepts.content: Initially, interest points were called moving elements. A moving element was defined as any image point that could be identified and followed over time, such as a corner, a line termination point, or a texture element.
concepts.motivation_md: This historical term reflects the early focus of computer vision on motion analysis and tracking specific points through a temporal sequence of frames.
concepts.recap_md:
- "Moving element" is an early term for what are now called interest points.
 - Examples include corners, line endings, and specific texture elements.
 - The concept emphasizes the ability to track a point across a time sequence.

concepts.title: Hand-engineered Interest Point Detectors

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Hand-engineered detectors, such as the Harris corner detector and SIFT, use mathematical heuristics to identify distinct and stable image regions.
concepts.content: Hand-engineered procedures to detect interest points include the Harris corner detector, which identifies corners as regions likely to be distinct and stable under geometric transformations. Other important detectors include local extrema of the Laplacian pyramid across space and scale (as seen in SIFT), Harris-Laplace, and maximally stable regions (MSER). These detectors aim to find regions that remain identifiable despite various image transformations.
concepts.motivation_md: Before deep learning, these mathematical operators were the primary way to extract repeatable features from images, providing a robust way to perform matching without needing to learn from data.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Harris corner detector is a fundamental tool for finding distinct, stable points.
 - Laplacian pyramid extrema allow for scale-invariant interest point detection.
 - These detectors are designed to ensure that features like corners remain detectable after rotation or scaling.

concepts.title: Representing Scenes with Fields
concepts.one_liner: Fields are general-purpose functions that vary over space, mapping coordinates to values to represent scenes.
concepts.content: Fields are a way to represent functions that vary over space and are used as a scene representation in many contexts. For example, every image is a field: it is a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values. While images in computer vision are often discrete fields where input coordinates are discrete-valued, fields can also be continuous. Furthermore, fields can be more than two-dimensional and can even be defined over non-Euclidean geometries like the surface of a sphere. Radiance fields are a specific example of vector fields, which assign a vector to each position in space, such as a mapping $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$ where $X, Y, Z$ are coordinates and $v_1, v_2$ are values.
concepts.motivation_md: Fields provide a unified mathematical framework for representing diverse spatial data, from 2D images to 3D volumes and complex physical properties like light radiance.
concepts.recap_md: - Fields map spatial coordinates to specific values or vectors.

concepts.title: Vector Fields
concepts.one_liner: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector to each position in space.
concepts.content: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector to each position in space. For example, we might have a vector field $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$, where $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are coordinates and $v_1$ and $v_2$ are some values. Radiance fields are a specific example of this type of function.
concepts.motivation_md: Vector fields allow us to describe properties that have both magnitude and direction (or multiple components) at every point in a spatial domain.
concepts.recap_md: - A vector field maps spatial coordinates to a vector of values.

concepts.title: Pixel Images as Fields
concepts.one_liner: Pixel images are discrete fields mapping 2D coordinates to color values.
concepts.content: Pixel images, $f: x, y \rightarrow r, g, b$, are fields with the property that the input domain is discrete, or, equivalently, the field is piecewise constant over little squares that tile the space.
concepts.motivation_md: Treating an image as a field allows us to apply signal processing and functional analysis tools to digital pictures.
concepts.recap_md: - Pixel images are discrete fields mapping $(x, y)$ to $(r, g, b)$ values.

concepts.title: Voxel Fields
concepts.one_liner: Voxel fields are discrete 3D fields representing values like occupancy or color in a volume.
concepts.content: Voxel fields, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow \mathbf{v}$ are discrete fields that can represent values $\mathbf{v}$ like spatial occupancy, flux, or color in a volume. They are like 3D pixels. Like pixels, they have the special property that they are piecewise constant over cubes the size of their resolution.
concepts.motivation_md: Voxels extend the concept of 2D pixels into 3D space to represent volumetric data.
concepts.recap_md: - Voxel fields are the 3D equivalent of pixel images.

concepts.title: Optical Flow Fields
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow fields measure motion by mapping image coordinates and time to velocity vectors.
concepts.content: Optical flow fields, $f: x, y, t \rightarrow u, v$, measure motion in a video in terms of how scene content flows across the image plane.
concepts.motivation_md: Optical flow is essential for tracking objects and understanding temporal dynamics in video sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Optical flow maps $(x, y, t)$ to motion vectors $(u, v)$.

concepts.title: Signed Distance Functions (SDFs)
concepts.one_liner: Signed distance functions represent geometry by mapping points to their distance from the closest surface.
concepts.content: Signed distance functions (SDFs), $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow d$, represent the distance to the closest surface to point $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$. This is a useful representation of geometry.
concepts.motivation_md: SDFs provide a mathematically clean way to define surfaces and perform geometric operations like boolean unions or intersections.
concepts.recap_md: - SDFs map 3D coordinates to the distance to the nearest surface.

concepts.title: Implicit vs. Explicit Representations

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Implicit representations use parameterized functions to represent continuous fields with infinite resolution.
concepts.content: Continuous fields are powerful because they have infinite resolution. However, we cannot represent a continuous field explicitly by recording the value at all infinite possible positions. Instead, we use an implicit representation: we record a finite set of parameters for a function that can tell us the value of the field at any coordinate. These parameterized functions take as input any continuous position and return the field value at that location.
concepts.motivation_md: Implicit representations allow us to store and manipulate continuous, high-resolution data using a manageable, finite number of parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - Implicit representations store function parameters rather than raw values.

concepts.title: Differentiable Radiance Fields

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Differentiable radiance fields use gradient-based optimization to fit parameterized functions to scene images.
concepts.content: There are many different parameterized functions $L_{\theta}$ that could represent a target radiance field $L$, such as neural networks or mixtures of Gaussians. The important property is that the field $L_{\theta}$ is a differentiable function of the parameters $\theta$. This allows the use of gradient-based optimization to find parameter settings that yield a desirable field. Whatever function family is used, it takes coordinates as input and produces colors and densities as output (see figure: Module for a parameterized radiance field. We use $\mathbf{R}$ to denote the vector of coordinates $L_\theta$ takes as input.). Because these functions are differentiable, they can be treated as modules in a computation graph, allowing for the use of backpropagation to fit the field to a set of images.
concepts.motivation_md: By making the radiance field differentiable, we can use standard machine learning optimization techniques to reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md: - Radiance fields are represented by differentiable functions $L_{\theta}$.

concepts.title: Learning-based Interest Point Detection

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Interest point detection can be formulated as a learning problem where a classifier is trained to automatically label image patches as being centered on a keypoint or not.
concepts.content:
The problem of detecting points of interest has been formulated as a learning problem. Given a set of examples of points of interest manually annotated on images, we can train a classifier to automatically label image patches as being centered on a keypoint or not. Some examples of learning-based approaches are Quad-Networks and SuperPoint.

(see figure: Keypoint detector formulated as a patch classification problem. The classifier labels the patch as containing a keypoint in the center or not.)

(see figure: All the detected keypoints in three views from the sugar bowl. But the images look rather textureless; what is the keypoint detector finding interesting in these images?)

We start by training a classifier using hand-annotated images with keypoints. This can be done by generating simple synthetic images where keypoints are unambiguously defined. The training set can be extended by running an initial keypoint detector on images and then augmenting the images with random geometric transformations. Then we can use the transformed keypoint coordinates together with the transformed images as new ground truth to train a more robust classifier. This is the approach proposed by SuperPoint.

[FIGURE:20cc53bc83ed338f | A grid of 32 small, zoomed-in image patches showing surface irregularities on a sugar bowl. Each patch features a central green dot marking a detected keypoint, highlighting subtle textures and...]

[FIGURE:549e4ecf64ea35ae | A grid of 32 small, zoomed-in image patches showing architectural details like window corners, wall edges, and decorative elements. Each patch features a single bright green dot marking a specific...]

Each patch shows a $65 \times 65$ image crop centered on a detected keypoint. The keypoint detector finds image regions with strong spatial changes. Those regions are also likely to be found on images of the same object but under different viewpoints. If a surface is smooth and textureless, the method would fail to detect any interesting points, and the whole pipeline for 3D reconstruction would fail. The advantage of hand-engineered detectors is that they are derived from first principles and do not require any training data. However, learning-based detectors can leverage unsupervised learning to achieve state of the art performance.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional hand-engineered keypoint detectors are derived from first principles but may lack robustness in complex scenes. Formulating detection as a learning problem allows models to leverage large datasets and unsupervised learning to achieve state-of-the-art performance and better stability under geometric transformations.
concepts.recap_md: - Detectors are trained as classifiers to identify whether an image patch is centered on a keypoint.

concepts.title: Local Image Descriptors

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Local image descriptors are vectors extracted at keypoint locations that allow for finding the same interest point across different images.
concepts.content:
Once we have trained a keypoint detector that finds image regions that are distinct and likely to be stable under geometric transformations, we run the detector in the set of images we want to match. We need now to extract at each location a descriptor that will allow finding the same keypoint across the different images.

Classical descriptors include SIFT, SURF, and ORB. (see figure: Examples of descriptors for three keypoints. For each keypoint, the figure shows the corresponding image patch and the computed descriptor. Each descriptor has a length of 256 values.) In this example, each descriptor is a vector of length 256.
concepts.motivation_md: Detecting a keypoint is only the first step; to reconstruct a scene, we must identify the same physical point in multiple images. Local descriptors provide a numerical representation of the area around a keypoint, making it possible to match points despite changes in viewpoint or lighting.
concepts.recap_md: - Descriptors are numerical vectors (e.g., length 256) representing the local image region around a keypoint.

concepts.title: Keypoint Matching across Viewpoints

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Keypoint matching identifies corresponding image regions across different viewpoints and illumination conditions using descriptors and matching algorithms.
concepts.content:
The keypoint detector and descriptor find image regions and their matches even under different viewpoints and illumination conditions. [FIGURE:867b7d3bf524344c | A sequence of six photographs showing a small reddish-brown clay pot from slightly different angles. A red dot with a black outline marks a specific interest point on the side of the pot in each...]

[FIGURE:79782851e8d2b5ec | A series of seven photographs of a historic stone building taken from different viewpoints and distances. In the top row, a red dot marks a specific keypoint on a window frame in each wide-angle...]

Matching keypoints across different viewpoints involves identifying the same physical feature, such as a window corner, across multiple views. For small numbers of images, brute-force matching can be performed, where features from one image are matched with features from every other image. Modern implementations may use graph network-based matchers like SuperGlue to establish these correspondences.
concepts.motivation_md: To perform 3D reconstruction, the system must know which pixels in different images represent the same point in 3D space. Matching algorithms use descriptors to find these correspondences reliably.
concepts.recap_md: - Matching identifies the same physical feature across multiple views and lighting conditions.

concepts.title: Incremental Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Incremental Structure from Motion estimates scene structure and camera parameters by adding images one by one and periodically running bundle adjustment.
concepts.content:
Incremental Structure from Motion (SFM) is a standard approach to minimize reprojection error by starting with a pair of images. The matches between those two images are used to compute the fundamental and essential matrices, accounting for outliers using RANSAC. An initial 3D reconstruction of the matched points is computed using triangulation. Then, another image is added and the process repeats until all images are incorporated. This results in a first set of approximated camera poses and 3D locations for a subset of the detected keypoints.

Online, or incremental-mode SFM approaches attempt to estimate scene structure and camera parameters as and when a new image arrives. In this mode, bundle adjustment is run periodically, whenever a sufficient number of points have been newly added. This is often used in applications where all images are not available a priori, or where real-time performance is desired.
concepts.motivation_md: Incremental SFM is useful for real-time applications or scenarios where images are captured sequentially, allowing for a growing reconstruction as new data becomes available.
concepts.recap_md: - Starts with an initial image pair to create a base 3D reconstruction via triangulation.

concepts.title: Batch Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Batch Structure from Motion computes the scene structure offline after processing all input images simultaneously.
concepts.content: Batch-mode SFM approaches compute the scene structure after processing all input images. In this mode, bundle adjustment only needs to be run once, albeit across a potentially large number of cameras and 3D points. This mode leverages images from all available viewpoints right from the outset. However, if new images are added, the entire SFM pipeline needs to be rerun.
concepts.motivation_md: Batch SFM is ideal for offline processing where all images are available at once, allowing the system to optimize the entire reconstruction globally for higher accuracy.
concepts.recap_md: - Processes all input images at once and typically runs bundle adjustment only once.

concepts.title: Sparse Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Sparse Structure from Motion computes 3D reconstructions for a small subset of reliably detectable image pixels.
concepts.content: Sparse SFM is the most popular variant of Structure from Motion used today. In this approach, the 3D reconstruction is computed only for a small subset of the image pixels—distinct points that may be detected reliably and repeatably across camera pose variations. While some approaches leverage lines, planes, or objects, point-based features remain the most popular choice due to their geometric simplicity and the availability of a wide range of point feature detectors and descriptors.
concepts.motivation_md: By focusing only on high-quality, distinct points, sparse SFM achieves high efficiency and robustness, making it suitable for large-scale reconstructions where processing every pixel would be computationally prohibitive.
concepts.recap_md: - Reconstructs 3D geometry using only a subset of distinct, repeatable keypoints.

concepts.title: Dense Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Dense Structure from Motion computes a 3D reconstruction for nearly every image pixel, typically by optimizing photometric error.
concepts.content: In dense SFM, the 3D reconstruction is computed for every (or most) of the image pixels. The resulting 3D reconstructions are rich and visually informative, making them useful for applications like robot navigation or mixed reality. Dense SFM approaches usually optimize photometric error—the difference in grayscale or RGB intensities of corresponding pixels across images—rather than the 3D reprojection error used in sparse methods. However, these techniques tend to be much slower than sparse methods and often require more assumptions, such as the scene being Lambertian or having a substantially smaller baseline motion.
concepts.motivation_md: While sparse SFM provides a skeleton of a scene, dense SFM provides a complete surface reconstruction, which is necessary for tasks like obstacle avoidance in robotics or realistic rendering in mixed reality.
concepts.recap_md: - Computes 3D data for almost every pixel to create rich, visually informative models.

concepts.title: Radiance Field
concepts.one_liner: A radiance field models a scene's optical content as a function mapping coordinates and viewing angles to color and density values.
concepts.motivation_md: Radiance fields allow for the representation of complex scenes with view-dependent effects like specular highlights, which traditional mesh-based or point-based reconstructions struggle to capture accurately.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps spatial coordinates and viewing angles to color ($r,g,b$) and density ($\sigma$).

concepts.title: Rigidity Assumption

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The rigidity assumption states that any set of elements undergoing a 2D transformation with a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such.
concepts.content: One major advance that allowed writing a mathematical formulation of the problem of structure from motion (SFM) was the rigidity assumption introduced by Shimon Ullman in 1979. Ullman writes: "Any set of elements undergoing a two dimensional transformation which has a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion." Since then, the 3D reconstruction of rigid objects from camera motion has been a rich area of work.
concepts.motivation_md: This assumption provides the necessary constraint to solve the inherently ambiguous problem of recovering 3D structure from 2D projections. Without assuming objects are rigid, an infinite number of non-rigid deformations could explain any given 2D motion.
concepts.recap_md:
- Proposes that 2D transformations should be interpreted as rigid 3D motion if a unique rigid interpretation exists.
 - Serves as the foundational constraint for most Structure from Motion (SFM) algorithms.

concepts.title: Sparse Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Sparse SFM reconstructs 3D structures by representing a sequence using the temporal trajectories of a sparse set of points.
concepts.content: Most works in the 3D reconstruction of rigid objects start by representing the sequence using as input the temporal trajectories of a sparse set of points (sparse SFM). (see figure: Early illustrations on the perceptual power of motion. (a) Nested cylinders by Shimon Ullman, 1979, illustrated how rigid motion elicits a strong 3D interpretation. (b) One frame from the point-light...) shows one frame from the nested cylinders sequence. In this sequence, there are a set of points placed on the surface of two nested cylinders. The cylinders are rotating. When viewing the sequence it is easy to see both cylinders, even though when seeing any single frame (as shown in (see figure: Early illustrations on the perceptual power of motion. (a) Nested cylinders by Shimon Ullman, 1979, illustrated how rigid motion elicits a strong 3D interpretation. (b) One frame from the point-light...)[a]) it is hard to see the cylinders or even to say which points are attached to the same surface.
concepts.motivation_md: Sparse SFM leverages the fact that human perception can easily identify 3D shapes from moving points, even when individual static frames are ambiguous. It simplifies the reconstruction problem by focusing on a manageable number of trackable features.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses temporal trajectories of discrete keypoints rather than dense pixel data.
 - Demonstrates how motion reveals 3D structure that is invisible in static 2D images.

concepts.title: Tomasi-Kanade SFM Algorithm

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The Tomasi-Kanade algorithm is an early SFM method that reconstructs 3D point locations from keypoint trajectories under a parallel projection assumption.
concepts.content: One of the first algorithms for structure from motion for rigid bodies was introduced by Tomasi and Kanade. For simplicity, their approach assumed parallel projection (orthographic camera) instead of perspective projection. The algorithm took as input a video sequence captured by a moving camera looking at a static scene. The video was first processed by extracting keypoints and tracking them over time. The input to the reconstruction algorithm was the keypoint trajectories and the output was the 3D locations of those points with respect to a reference world-coordinate system (usually defined by the first frame in the video). The model introduced by Tomasi and Kanade was later extended by Sturm and Triggs to handle perspective projection.
concepts.motivation_md: It provided a computationally tractable framework for SFM by using orthographic projection as a simplifying assumption, laying the groundwork for more complex perspective-based reconstruction methods.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes parallel (orthographic) projection for simplicity.
 - Inputs tracked keypoint trajectories to output 3D coordinates in a reference frame.

concepts.title: Correspondence in Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: A key problem in SFM is finding reliable image correspondences across multiple views, often captured from significantly different locations.
concepts.content: One of the key problems in SFM is to find correspondences across multiple images. Finding image correspondences is a fundamental topic in computer vision, related to stereo vision, homography, and optical flow estimation. SIFT made image matching more reliable, allowing structure from motion to work much better under difficult conditions, such as where views are captured by cameras at very different locations. This is a more difficult image matching task than when the views are consecutive frames from a single sequence.
concepts.motivation_md: To reconstruct a 3D point, the system must first identify which 2D pixels in different images represent the same physical location in space.
concepts.recap_md:
- Requires matching features across images with potentially large viewpoint changes.
 - Reliability was significantly improved by descriptors like SIFT.

concepts.title: General Structure from Motion from Unordered Collections

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: General SFM reconstructs 3D scenes from unordered collections of images taken by different cameras without assumptions about camera placement.
concepts.content: The task of SFM became more general, and instead of focusing on one moving camera, SFM was applied to the problem of reconstructing the 3D scene even from multiple images taken by different cameras and making no assumption about the placement of the cameras. The work by Snavely et al. was one of the first to produce spectacular registrations and camera pose estimates of images taken with many different cameras. They showed how one could reconstruct famous buildings from pictures taken by tourists.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach allows for the creation of 3D models from crowd-sourced data, such as internet photo collections, where camera types and positions are completely unknown and uncoordinated.
concepts.recap_md:
- Reconstructs scenes from unordered, heterogeneous image collections.
 - Does not require a continuous video sequence or a single camera.

concepts.title: Sparse SFM Problem Overview

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

Given a set of $M$ images with overlapping content, we want to recover the 3D structure of the scene and the location of the camera for each image. Figures (such as the sugar bowl and plaza examples) show sets of images representing very different scenarios that can be reconstructed with the same set of techniques.

concepts.title: Sparse SFM Problem Formulation

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The sparse SFM problem aims to recover 3D points and camera parameters from a set of corresponding 2D points matched across multiple views.
concepts.content: In the sparse SFM problem, we consider that in the scene there are $N$ distinct points that are matched across $M$ different views. We denote the $N$ 3D points as $\mathbf{P}_i$. For each of the $M$ views, we denote the projection of point $\mathbf{P}_i$ as seen by camera $j$ by $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$. Each view has camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$, and ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$. If all the images are captured by the same camera, then the matrices ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$ will be the same, though this assumption is not strictly necessary. The goal of the SFM problem is, given the set of corresponding 2D points $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$, recover 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$, the intrinsic camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, and the extrinsic camera parameters ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$ and ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$ for each camera $j$.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining the problem mathematically allows us to treat 3D reconstruction as an optimization task, where we minimize the error between observed 2D projections and the projections predicted by our 3D model.
concepts.recap_md:
- Inputs: Corresponding 2D points $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$ across $M$ views.
 - Outputs: 3D coordinates $\mathbf{P}_i$ and camera parameters (${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$, ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$).

concepts.title: SFM Notation

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: In SFM notation, capital letters denote quantities in 3D world coordinates, while lowercase letters denote image coordinates.
concepts.content: Notation reminder: we use capital letters for quantities measured in 3D world coordinates and lowercase for image coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Standardizing notation helps distinguish between the physical 3D world and its 2D projection on an image sensor, preventing confusion during derivation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Capital letters: 3D world coordinates (e.g., $\mathbf{P}_i$).
 - Lowercase letters: 2D image coordinates (e.g., $\mathbf{p}_i$).

concepts.title: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model a radiance field $L$ using a neural network $L_{\theta}$, typically a multilayer perceptron.
concepts.content: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) are a popular way of parameterizing a radiance field $L_{\theta}$. NeRFs model the radiance field $L$ with a neural network $L_{\theta}$. The neural network architecture in the original NeRF is a multilayer perceptron (MLP), but other architectures could be used as well. For the MLP formulation, evaluating the color-density at a single coordinate corresponds to a single forward pass through an MLP.
concepts.motivation_md: NeRFs provide a continuous, differentiable representation of a 3D scene's radiance and density, allowing for high-quality view synthesis using standard neural network architectures.
concepts.recap_md: - NeRFs parameterize the radiance field $L$ using a neural network $L_{\theta}$.

concepts.title: NeRF as 1x1 Convolutional Neural Network

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: When querying a grid of coordinates, a NeRF behaves like a convolutional neural network with 1x1 filters.
concepts.content:
Often we want to evaluate the color-density at multiple coordinate locations. To create an explicit representation of the field's values at a grid of coordinates, we can query the field on this grid. In this usage, the NeRF $L_{\theta}$ looks like a convolutional neural network (CNN) with 1x1 filters, as this is the architecture that results from applying an MLP to each position in a grid of inputs. We show this usage below, in @fig-nerfs-image_to_image_arch.

(see figure: NeRF architecture for computing the values at each position in an entire radiance field, sampled on a grid. The $\texttt{pos\_enc}$ refers to positional encoding. You can consider this architecture...)
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing NeRFs as 1x1 CNNs helps conceptualize how they process spatial grids and relates them to standard image processing architectures for efficient field evaluation.
concepts.recap_md: - Querying a NeRF on a grid of coordinates is equivalent to applying a 1x1 CNN.

concepts.title: Fourier Positional Encodings

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Fourier positional encodings transform raw coordinates into a representation that helps neural networks model high-frequency variations in radiance fields.
concepts.content:
NeRF includes a positional encoding layer to transform raw coordinates into a Fourier representation. In fact, the same positional encoding scheme is used as in transformers. @fig-nerfs-flatland_positional_encoding shows how this scheme translates the $XY$-coordinate field of Flatland to positional encodings:

(see figure: The first layer of NeRF applies positional encoding to the input coordinate values. Here we show the resulting positional codes for all possible input coordinate values $(X,Y)$ within some range.)

Fourier positional encodings are very effective for NeRFs because they help the network to model high frequencies variations, which are abundant in radiance fields. In regular Cartesian coordinates, the location $(0,0)$ is much closer to $(1,1)$ than it is to $(100,100)$, but this isn't necessarily the case with Fourier positional codes. Because of this, with Cartesian coordinates as inputs, an MLP will be biased to assign similar values to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and different values to $(0,0)$ and $(100,100)$. Conversely, with Fourier positional codes as input, this bias will be reduced. This makes it so the MLP has an easier time fitting high frequency functions that change in value rapidly, such as assigning very different output values to the locations $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard MLPs struggle to learn high-frequency details in 3D scenes (the 'spectral bias'). Positional encodings map inputs to a higher-dimensional space where these variations are easier to learn.
concepts.recap_md: - Fourier positional encodings reduce the bias of MLPs toward low-frequency functions.

concepts.title: Voxel-based Radiance Fields
concepts.one_liner: Voxel-based radiance fields parameterize 3D scenes using a grid-based volumetric representation.
concepts.content: One alternative to neural parameterization is to parameterize the radiance fields using a voxel-based representation.
concepts.motivation_md: Voxel-based representations can offer faster training and rendering times compared to pure MLP-based NeRFs by storing scene data in an explicit grid.
concepts.recap_md: - Voxel-based fields use a discrete grid (voxels) to store radiance and density values.

concepts.title: Gaussian Mixture Radiance Fields
concepts.one_liner: Gaussian mixture radiance fields approximate scene content using a collection of semi-transparent ellipsoids with specific colors and densities.
concepts.content: Another alternative is to use a mixture of Gaussians. In this case, each Gaussian represents a semi-transparent ellipsoid of some color $\mathbf{c}$ and some density $\sigma$. When many such Gaussians overlap, their sum can approximate scene content very well.
concepts.motivation_md: Using Gaussians allows for a more flexible, non-grid-aligned representation of geometry that can be more efficient than voxels for certain types of scene content.
concepts.recap_md: - Scenes are modeled as a sum of overlapping semi-transparent ellipsoids.

concepts.title: View Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: View synthesis is the process of rendering a scene from novel camera viewpoints using its underlying radiance field representation.
concepts.content: Radiance fields can be useful for many tasks in scene modeling, as they represent both appearance and geometry (density) of content in 3D. However, the main purpose they were introduced for is view synthesis. This is the problem of rendering what a scene looks like from different camera viewpoints.
