In the Flatland example, this is the problem of rendering the set of 1D images, $\{\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, shown on the left of @fig-nerfs-flatland_cameras_and_images. Once you have a radiance field for a scene, you can solve view synthesis by rendering images from it.
concepts.motivation_md: View synthesis allows for the creation of photorealistic images from angles where no original photos were taken, which is essential for VR, AR, and special effects.
concepts.recap_md: - View synthesis renders new camera viewpoints from a 3D scene representation.

concepts.title: Volume Rendering
concepts.one_liner: Volume rendering is a strategy for rendering images by integrating radiance values along camera rays through a volume of density.
concepts.content: Volume rendering is the strategy that methods like NeRFs use for rendering images from radiance fields. Volume rendering works by taking an integral of the radiance values along each camera ray. Think of it like looking into a hazy volume of colored dust. The integral adds up all the color values along the camera ray, weighted by a value related to the density of the dust. A cartoon visualization of the process is given in @fig-nerfs-flatland_volume_rendering, and several real results of rendering radiance fields are shown in @fig-nerfs-flatland_training.
concepts.motivation_md: Volume rendering provides a differentiable way to map a 3D volume (density and color) to a 2D image, which is necessary for training neural networks on image data.
concepts.recap_md: - Volume rendering integrates color along a ray, weighted by local density.

concepts.title: Volume Rendering Equation
concepts.one_liner: The volume rendering equation maps a radiance field to an image by integrating color and density along rays passing through pixels.
concepts.content:
The volume rendering equation is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \ell(r) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f}\alpha(t) \, \overbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}^{\text{density}} \, \overbrace{L^c(r(t),\mathbf{D})}^{\text{color}} \, dt\\
    \alpha(t) = \exp \Big(-\int_{t_n}^{t} \underbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}_{\text{density}} dt\Big)
\end{aligned}$$
where $r(t)$ gives the coordinates, in the radiance field, of a point $t$ distance along the ray, $\mathbf{D}$ is the direction of the ray (a unit vector), and $t_n$ and $t_f$ are the near and far cutoff points, respectively. We only integrate over the region of the ray within an interval sufficiently large to capture the scene content of interest. To render an image, we can apply this equation to the ray that passes through each pixel in the image. This procedure maps a radiance field $L$ to an image $\boldsymbol\ell$ as viewed by some camera.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation mathematically formalizes how light travels through and is absorbed by a semi-transparent medium, allowing for the calculation of final pixel colors from a 3D field.
concepts.recap_md:
- The equation integrates color $L^c$ and density $L^\sigma$ along a ray $r(t)$.
- The term $\alpha(t)$ represents the transmittance (how much light reaches the camera).

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Filtering

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: Spatiotemporal filtering uses the responses of velocity-tuned filters to estimate motion in image sequences.
concepts.content: Spatiotemporal filtering is a class of motion algorithms based on the principles of filter banks. These algorithms use the responses of velocity-tuned filters to estimate motion, often serving as an alternative to methods based on image correlations.
concepts.motivation_md: While many motion algorithms rely on simple image correlations, spatiotemporal filtering provides a principled way to estimate velocity by treating a video sequence as a 3D volume and applying filters tuned to specific orientations in space-time.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Spatiotemporal filtering estimates motion using velocity-tuned filter responses.",
  "- It treats motion as orientation within a space-time signal volume."
]

concepts.title: Fluted Square-Wave Motion Illusion

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: The fluted square-wave motion illusion demonstrates how the visual system's reliance on low-frequency spatiotemporal energy can lead to perceived motion opposite to actual pattern shifts.
concepts.content:
Adelson and Bergen proposed a motion illusion that distinguishes between classes of motion algorithms used by the visual system. The illusion involves temporal filtering, motion processing, and aliasing. (see figure: Space-time signals, building toward the fluted square-wave motion illusion. The first row shows a stationary sine wave. (a) Movie of a motionless sine wave. (b) Space-time plot shows only vertical structure. (c) Spatiotemporal Fourier transform shows all energy on the zero temporal frequency axis because nothing is moving. (d) The second row shows a moving sine wave. (e) In the space-time plot, speed corresponds to local orientation. (f) The Fourier transform energy is sheared according to the sine wave’s speed. (g–i) The third row shows a moving square wave. The additional harmonics required to form a square wave are visible in (i) the spatiotemporal Fourier transform.)

The spatiotemporal Fourier transform of a stationary sinusoid $f(x,y,t) = \cos(\pi \omega x)$ consists of impulses along the $w_t = 0$ line, indicating no motion. A moving sinusoid has energy along a line perpendicular to the moving structures in the spatiotemporal signal. A moving square wave adds extra harmonics to this structure. If a square wave moves in 1/4 period jumps, its spectrum is replicated over temporal frequencies and multiplied by a sinc function. (see figure: Derivation of the fluted square-wave motion illusion, continued from @fig-motionIllusion1 . Top row shows that the square wave moves in 1/4 wavelength jumps, instead of continuously. This staggered...)

Because orientation in space-time indicates motion direction, velocity-tuned filters respond to the lowest spatiotemporal frequency impulses. If the lowest spatial frequency sinusoid is removed, the dominant orientation of the remaining lowest frequency components points in the opposite direction. While a pattern-matching algorithm would see the signal moving left, the human visual system—examining the orientation of the lowest spatiotemporal frequency components—perceives the signal moving to the right. This supports spatiotemporal energy models for human motion processing.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion helps researchers determine whether the human visual system uses feature-matching (correlation) or spatiotemporal energy (filtering) to perceive motion, by creating a scenario where the two methods predict opposite directions.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Orientation in a space-time plot corresponds to the direction and speed of motion.",
  "- Removing the fundamental frequency from a jumping square wave can reverse the perceived motion direction.",
  "- The illusion supports the theory that human vision uses spatiotemporal energy filters rather than just pattern matching."
]

concepts.title: Vanishing Point (Motion)
concepts.one_liner: The vanishing point is the location in the image plane where a point moving in a straight line with constant velocity converges as time goes to infinity.
concepts.content:
Consider a point moving in a straight line in 3D with constant velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (V_X, V_Y, V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$. At any time $t$, the point location is $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X+V_Xt, Y+V_Yt, Z+V_Zt)^\mathsf{T}$. Its 2D projection is given by:

$$\begin{aligned} x(t) &= f \frac{X + V_X t}{Z + V_Z t}\\ y(t) &= f \frac{Y + V_Y t}{Z + V_Z t} \end{aligned}$$

If the velocity component in $Z$ is non-zero ($\dot{Z} \neq 0$), the projected point converges to a vanishing point as $t \to \infty$:

$$\begin{aligned} \lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) &= f \frac{V_X}{V_Z} = x_{\infty}\\ \lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) &= f \frac{V_Y}{V_Z} = y_{\infty} \end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Projection onto the camera plane of the sequence produced by a bird flying away. The bird will vanish at the **vanishing point**)

The location of the vanishing point $\mathbf{p}_{\infty}=(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})^\mathsf{T}$ is independent of the initial position of the point and depends only on the 3D velocity vector $\mathbf{V}$. Consequently, multiple points moving with the same velocity will converge to the same vanishing point.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding vanishing points in motion allows us to determine the direction of 3D travel from 2D image sequences, as all objects sharing a velocity vector will appear to head toward the same image coordinate.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- The vanishing point is the limit of a projected 3D point's position as time approaches infinity.",
  "- Its coordinates are determined by the ratio of the velocity components: $x_{\infty} = f V_X / V_Z$ and $y_{\infty} = f V_Y / V_Z$.",
  "- All points with the same 3D velocity vector share the same vanishing point regardless of their starting position."
]

concepts.title: Camera Translation Motion Field
concepts.one_liner: The camera translation motion field describes the 2D velocity of image points resulting from a camera moving in a straight line through a static scene.
concepts.content:
When a camera moves through a static scene with velocity $\dot{\mathbf{T}} = \mathbf{V} = (V_X,V_Y,V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$, every point $\mathbf{P}$ in the scene moves relative to the camera with velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = -\mathbf{V}$. The resulting 2D motion field in the image plane is:

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} -f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$

This relationship can be rearranged to make the contribution of the camera coordinates more explicit:

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \end{bmatrix} + \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} x\\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$

This provides a general expression for observed motion produced by camera translation without rotation.
concepts.motivation_md: By modeling how camera movement translates into image motion, we can separate the effects of the camera's own path from the movement of independent objects in a scene.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Camera translation creates a motion field where relative point velocity is $-\mathbf{V}$.",
  "- The 2D motion of a point depends on its depth $Z$ and its position $(x, y)$ in the image.",
  "- The motion field equation combines a lateral translation component and a forward expansion component."
]

concepts.title: Lateral Camera Motion
concepts.one_liner: Lateral camera motion occurs when a camera translates parallel to the image plane, causing image points to move in the opposite direction at speeds inversely proportional to their depth.
concepts.content:
Lateral camera motion occurs when a camera translates parallel to the camera plane, meaning the forward velocity $V_Z = 0$. (see figure: Lateral camera motion parallel to the camera plane.)

In this case, the relationship between the 3D velocity and the apparent 2D velocity in the image plane is:

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} V_X \\ V_Y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$

The motion field depends on the depth $Z$ at each location. Objects closer to the camera appear to move faster than objects farther away, while very distant objects appear stationary. This parallax effect is the same principle used in stereo vision to recover depth. The 2D motion in the image plane is always in the opposite direction to the camera's translation.

(see figure: Sketch of the motion field under lateral camera motion. Objects close to the camera will appear to be moving faster than objects farther away. Objects that are very far (like the cloud) will appear...)
concepts.motivation_md: Lateral motion is a common scenario (e.g., looking out a car window) where depth can be inferred from the relative speeds of objects, a phenomenon known as motion parallax.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Lateral motion occurs when $V_Z = 0$, resulting in image motion opposite to camera translation.",
  "- The speed of image points is inversely proportional to their depth $Z$.",
  "- This depth-dependent speed variation is known as the parallax effect."
]

concepts.title: Camera Forward Motion
concepts.one_liner: Camera forward motion occurs when a camera moves along its optical axis, resulting in a radial expansion of the image from a central point.
concepts.content:
For a camera moving forward along its optical axis, the lateral velocity components are zero ($V_X = V_Y = 0$) and the motion is only along the $Z$-axis ($V_Z \neq 0$). (see figure: Camera moving forward, along the camera axis.)

The resulting motion field is defined by:

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Forward motion is critical for navigation and obstacle avoidance, as it creates a characteristic expansion pattern that reveals the direction of travel and the proximity of objects.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Forward motion involves translation where $V_X = V_Y = 0$ and $V_Z \neq 0$.",
  "- The resulting image motion is radial, pointing away from the center of the image.",
  "- The velocity of image points is proportional to their distance from the image center."
]

concepts.title: Time to Contact
concepts.one_liner: Time to contact is the ratio of an object's depth to the camera's forward velocity, representing how long until the camera reaches that object.
concepts.content: The observed motion in a forward-moving camera depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact. The time to contact is the duration it will take the camera to reach an object located at distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$. Notably, the rate of expansion in the image does not depend on the focal length $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: Time to contact is a vital cue for biological and robotic systems to avoid collisions, as it can be estimated directly from the expansion of the image without knowing the absolute distance or speed.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Time to contact is defined as $Z/V_Z$.",
  "- It can be estimated from the rate of image expansion independently of focal length.",
  "- It represents the time remaining before the camera reaches a specific depth plane."
]

concepts.title: Focus of Expansion
concepts.one_liner: The focus of expansion is the point in the image plane where the observed motion is zero during forward camera translation.
concepts.content:
The observed motion is zero at the focus of expansion, located at $(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})$. (see figure: Sketch of the motion field when the camera approaches a planar surface. The motion field indicates the rate of expansion of the image, and it is a function of the time to contact. In this example...)

When a camera approaches a surface, points near the center (the point of impact) appear stationary, while points in the periphery appear to move faster and away from the center. This creates an effect where the whole image expands over time from the focus of expansion.
concepts.motivation_md: The focus of expansion identifies the exact direction the camera is heading, making it a fundamental reference point for visual navigation and steering.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- The focus of expansion is the stationary point in a radially expanding motion field.",
  "- It corresponds to the camera's heading or the point of future impact.",
  "- Image points move faster as their distance from the focus of expansion increases."
]

concepts.title: Direct Approach for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: The direct approach learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames without architectural priors.
concepts.content: The direct approach learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames. This architecture makes no assumptions about which architectural priors are needed to compute optical flow from images. The architecture is trained end-to-end using ground truth optical flow.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach aims to minimize human bias in architecture design by allowing a neural network to learn the necessary features and transformations for optical flow estimation directly from data, rather than relying on hand-crafted geometric priors.
concepts.recap_md:
- Estimates optical flow directly from a pair of input frames. 
- Avoids explicit architectural priors or traditional computer vision steps.
- Uses end-to-end training with ground truth optical flow data.

concepts.title: Modular Architecture for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Modular architectures for optical flow follow traditional steps like feature extraction and cost volume aggregation within a trainable neural network.
concepts.content:
Another common approach is to define an architecture that follows the same steps as traditional approaches:

- Extract features from each image using a pair of networks with shared weights. This can be done by a feature pyramid.

- Form a 3D cost volume indicating the local visual evidence of a match between the two images for each possible pixel position. This 3D cost volume can be referenced to the $H$ and $V$ positions of one of the input images (generally the first frame is the reference frame).

- Train and apply a CNN to aggregate (process) the costs over the cost volume in order to estimate a single best optical flow for each pixel position.

- Use a coarse-to-fine estimation procedure where optical flow estimated at a coarse scale is used to warp the features at a finer scale to compute a refined cost volume. Then, estimate an update to the optical flow to warp the features and the next finer level of the pyramid.

(see figure: Motion estimation. (1) Extract features from each image; (2) compute a 3D cost volume; and (3) aggregate the cost volume in order to estimate the best optical flow for each pixel.)

Other variations over this architecture incorporate concepts such as coarse-to-fine refinement, matching, and smoothing. Different approaches will differ in implementation details and training. The main building blocks can be implemented with convolutional neural networks or transformers. The main difference between the matching-based and gradient-based methods described earlier is that instead of using predefined functions, the architectures are trained end-to-end to minimize the optical flow error when compared with ground truth data.
concepts.motivation_md: By mirroring traditional computer vision pipelines (like cost volumes and pyramids), these architectures leverage geometric intuition while benefiting from the power of end-to-end deep learning to optimize performance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses shared-weight networks to extract feature pyramids from image pairs.
- Constructs a 3D cost volume to represent matching evidence between pixels.
- Employs coarse-to-fine refinement and warping to iteratively improve flow estimates.

concepts.title: Endpoint Error
concepts.one_liner: The endpoint error is the average distance between the estimated optical flow vector and the ground-truth vector across all pixels.
concepts.content:
In supervised optical flow estimation, the most common loss is the **endpoint error**, which is the average, over the whole image, of the distance between the estimated optical flow vector, $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ and the ground-truth vector, $(u,v)$:
$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \right) = \sum_{n,m} (\hat{u}[n,m] - u[n,m])^2 + (\hat{v}[n,m] - v[n,m])^2$$
The sum is over all the pixels in the image. Each pixel has an estimated optical flow $(\hat{u}[n,m],\hat{v}[n,m])$.

[FIGURE:94e55f574651d9ae | A vector diagram illustrating the endpoint error in optical flow estimation. Two vectors originate from the same point: a longer vector labeled (u,v) representing the ground truth, and a shorter...]
concepts.motivation_md: To train supervised models, a metric is needed to quantify the discrepancy between predicted motion and actual motion. Endpoint error provides a direct Euclidean measure of this accuracy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Measures the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth flow vectors.
- Summed or averaged over all pixel positions $(n,m)$ in the image.
- Serves as the primary loss function for supervised optical flow training.

concepts.title: Occlusion Detection in Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Occlusion detection identifies pixels that are hidden or revealed by moving objects, which is a significant challenge in optical flow estimation.
concepts.content:
One of the challenges for estimating optical flow is that, as objects move, they will occlude some pixels from the background and reveal new ones. Therefore, together with the estimated flow it is also convenient to detect occluded pixels. If we have ground truth data, we can train a function to estimate optical flow and the occlusion map from two frames:
$$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \hat{\mathbf{o}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: Standard optical flow assumes every pixel in frame one appears in frame two. Detecting occlusions allows models to handle areas where this assumption fails, improving overall motion estimation robustness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Addresses the problem of pixels being hidden (occluded) or revealed during motion.
- Predicts an occlusion map $\hat{\mathbf{o}}$ alongside the flow vectors $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$.
- Requires ground truth occlusion data for supervised training.

concepts.title: Synthetic Data for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Synthetic datasets provide perfect ground truth data for training optical flow models by rendering 3D scenes with known motion.
concepts.content: The largest existing datasets are synthetic 3D scenes with moving objects that can be rendered, which will give us perfect ground truth data to train the regression function. There are several examples of existing datasets such as this, like the Middelbury dataset, which contains six real and synthetic sequences with ground truth optical flow. The optical flow for the real sequences was obtained by tracking hidden fluorescent texture. The KITTI dataset contains real motion recorded from a moving car. The MPI Sintel contains synthetic sequences made with great effort to make the scenes look realistic. Finally, the Flying Chairs dataset is an interesting synthetic dataset that consists of pasting the image of a random number of chairs over a background image. Motion is created by applying different affine transformations to the background and the chairs. These sequences are easy to generate and pay little attention to their realism. This makes it possible to generate a very large number of sequences for training, allowing for competitive performance when used to train a neural network.
concepts.motivation_md: Obtaining ground truth optical flow for real-world video is extremely difficult and often requires specialized hardware. Synthetic data provides an infinite supply of perfectly labeled training examples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses rendered 3D scenes to provide perfect ground truth for flow regression.
- Ranges from highly realistic (MPI Sintel) to abstract and easy to generate (Flying Chairs).
- Enables the training of deep neural networks that generalize well to real motion.

concepts.title: Middlebury Dataset
concepts.one_liner: The Middlebury dataset contains six real and synthetic sequences with ground truth optical flow for motion estimation.
concepts.content: The Middelbury dataset contains six real and synthetic sequences with ground truth optical flow. The optical flow for the real sequences was obtained by tracking hidden fluorescent texture.
concepts.motivation_md: This dataset provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating optical flow algorithms using a mix of synthetic and carefully captured real-world data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Includes both real and synthetic image sequences.
- Real-world ground truth is obtained via hidden fluorescent texture tracking.
- Serves as a classic benchmark for optical flow accuracy.

concepts.title: KITTI Dataset
concepts.one_liner: The KITTI dataset provides real-world motion data recorded from a moving car for optical flow and autonomous driving research.
concepts.content: The KITTI dataset contains real motion recorded from a moving car. It is used for training and evaluating optical flow in real-world driving scenarios.
concepts.motivation_md: While synthetic data is useful, models must eventually perform on real-world data. KITTI provides the complex, noisy motion found in actual automotive environments.
concepts.recap_md:
- Features real-world motion captured from a vehicle.
- Essential for evaluating optical flow in autonomous driving contexts.
- Provides a bridge between synthetic training and real-world application.

concepts.title: MPI Sintel Dataset
concepts.one_liner: The MPI Sintel dataset consists of high-quality synthetic sequences designed to look realistic for optical flow training.
concepts.content: The MPI Sintel dataset contains synthetic sequences made with great effort to make the scenes look realistic. It is used to provide high-quality ground truth for complex motion and visual effects.
concepts.motivation_md: Sintel aims to provide the benefits of synthetic ground truth (perfection and density) while mimicking the visual complexity (blur, lighting, reflections) of real-world video.
concepts.recap_md:
- High-fidelity synthetic dataset based on an open-source animated film.
- Focuses on realistic visual effects and complex motion.
- Provides dense, perfect ground truth for supervised learning.

concepts.title: Flying Chairs Dataset
concepts.one_liner: The Flying Chairs dataset is a synthetic dataset created by pasting random chair images over background images with affine transformations to simulate motion.
concepts.content: The Flying Chairs dataset is a synthetic dataset that consists of pasting the image of a random number of chairs over a background image. Motion is created by applying different affine transformations to the background and the chairs. These sequences are easy to generate and pay little attention to their realism. This makes it possible to generate a very large number of sequences for training, allowing for competitive performance when used to train a neural network.
concepts.motivation_md: Generating realistic video data with ground-truth optical flow is difficult and expensive. This dataset provides a way to generate massive amounts of training data synthetically, which is sufficient for neural networks to learn motion estimation effectively.
concepts.recap_md: [FIGURE:fig-what_is_a_chair_with_text | What is a chair? The definition is based on affordances (i.e., something you can sit on) and on social conventions (i.e., some surfaces you can sit on are meant to be used to support other objects...]

concepts.title: Photometric Loss for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Photometric loss measures the reconstruction error between two frames by warping the first frame using predicted displacement to match the second.
concepts.content:
One typical formulation consists in learning to predict the displacement from frame 1 to frame 2, so that if we warp frame 1 we minimize the reconstruction error of frame 2. This is achieved by using the photometric loss:

$$L_{photo}(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= 
\sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_2 (x+\hat{u},y+\hat{v}) - \ell_1 (x,y)) \right| ^2$$
where now
$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] =  h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$.
concepts.motivation_md: In unsupervised or self-supervised motion estimation, we lack ground-truth flow. Photometric loss uses the brightness constancy assumption to provide a training signal based on how well the predicted flow aligns the images.
concepts.recap_md: - It calculates the squared difference between a warped first frame and the actual second frame.

concepts.title: Learning Photometric Loss for Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Motion estimation networks are trained by minimizing photometric loss over large video collections, potentially incorporating robust norms or occlusion weights.
concepts.content: The learning is done by searching over the parameter space for the parameters $\theta$ that minimize the photometric loss over a large collection of videos. The photometric loss can also be replaced by the L1 or other robust norms. If the network also predicts occlusions, the photometric loss can include a weight that cancels the contribution of occluded pixels to the loss. The network can also take as input multiple frames and not just two.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard photometric loss can be sensitive to outliers and occlusions. Using robust norms or occlusion masks helps the model focus on valid pixel correspondences during training.
concepts.recap_md: - Training involves minimizing the loss across large video datasets to optimize network parameters.

concepts.title: Object Recognition Tasks and Definitions
concepts.one_liner: Object recognition involves various tasks like classification, localization, and segmentation, where the approach depends on how the question of identity is answered.
concepts.content:
There are many tasks that researchers use to address the problem of recognition. Although the ultimate goal is to tell what something it is by looking at it, the way that you will answer the question will change the approach that you will use. For instance, you could say, "That is a chair" and just point at it, or we could ask you to indicate all of the visible parts of the chair, which might be a lot harder if the chair is partially occluded by other chairs producing a sea of legs. It can be hard to precisely delineate the chair if we cannot tell which legs belong to it. In other cases, identifying what a chair is might be difficult, requiring understanding of its context and social conventions.

(see figure: What is a chair? The definition is based on affordances (i.e., something you can sit on) and on social conventions (i.e., some surfaces you can sit on are meant to be used to support other objects...)

In this chapter we will study three tasks related to the recognition of objects in images (classification, localization, and segmentation). We will introduce the problem definitions and the formulation that lays the foundations for most existing approaches.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognition is not a single problem but a suite of tasks. Understanding the nuances between simple identification and precise delineation is necessary to choose the right computational framework.
concepts.recap_md: - Recognition tasks include classification, localization, and segmentation.

concepts.title: Recognition-by-Components Theory

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Recognition-by-components theory suggests humans recognize objects by decomposing them into a small set of geometric parts called Geons.
concepts.content:
One important theory of how humans represent and recognize objects from images is the recognition-by-components theory proposed by Irving Biederman in 1987. He started motivating his theory with the experiment illustrated in (Figure 1.1.6). The first observation is that novel objects can be decomposed into parts, often at regions of sharp concavity. The second observation is that these parts resemble known geometric primitives.

(see figure: What is this? This drawing from Biederman @Biederman1987, shows a novel object. After looking at this drawing we can conclude the following: (1) we have never seen this object before, (2) it can be...)

Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing the object into a small set of geometric components (e.g., blocks, cylinders, cones, and so on.) that he called **Geons**. He derived 36 different Geons that we can discriminate visually. Geons were defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature. An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists in a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations.
concepts.motivation_md: This theory explains how humans can recognize an infinite variety of objects from a finite set of parts, even when seeing a novel object for the first time.
concepts.recap_md: - Objects are decomposed into 36 basic geometric primitives called Geons.

concepts.title: Geons

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Geons are a set of 36 basic geometric components, such as blocks and cylinders, used to represent and recognize complex objects.
concepts.content: Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing the object into a small set of geometric components (e.g., blocks, cylinders, cones, and so on.) that he called **Geons**. He derived 36 different Geons that we can discriminate visually. Geons we defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature. An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists in a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations.
concepts.motivation_md: Geons provide a structural alphabet for visual recognition, allowing the brain to categorize objects based on their component shapes and spatial relationships rather than raw pixel data.
concepts.recap_md: - Geons are 36 discriminable geometric primitives like cones and blocks.

concepts.title: Compositionality in Vision

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Compositionality in vision refers to objects being formed by simpler, shared elements, though these components may vary in appearance across different classes.
concepts.content: One important aspect of his theory is that objects are formed by compositing simpler elements (Geons), which are shared across many different object classes. **Compositionality** in the visual world is not as strong as the one found in language, where a fix set of words are composed to form sentences with different meanings. In the visual world, components shared across different object classes will have different visual appearances (e.g., legs of tables and chairs share many properties but are not identical). Geons are great to represent artificial objects (e.g., tables, cabinets, and phones) but fail when applied to represent stuff (e.g., grass, clouds, and water) or highly textured objects such as trees or food.
concepts.motivation_md: Compositionality allows for efficient representation of the world; however, unlike language, visual components are often continuous and context-dependent, making a universal 'visual alphabet' difficult to define for natural textures.
concepts.recap_md: - Objects are composed of shared simpler elements like Geons.

concepts.title: Mental Rotation and Viewpoint Invariance

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Mental rotation is the hypothesized process where humans recognize objects in non-canonical poses by mentally rotating them to match a stored representation.
concepts.content:
One well studied property of the human visual system is its invariance to image and 3D rotations. Studies in human visual perception have shown that objects are recognized faster when they appear in canonical poses. In a landmark study, Roger N. Shepard and Jaqueline Metzler showed to participants pairs of drawings of three-dimensional objects. The result showed that participants had a reaction time proportional to the rotation angle between the two views. This supported the idea that participants were performing a **mental rotation** in order to compare both views.

(see figure: Two figures related by a 3D rotation. Modified from @Shepard1971aa)

Michael Tarr and Steven Pinker showed that similar results where obtained on a learning task. When observers learn to recognize a novel object from a single viewpoint they are able to generalize to new viewpoints but they do that at a cost: recognition time increases with the angle of rotation. When trained with multiple viewpoints, participants recognized equally quickly all the familiar orientations.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept explains why human recognition speed varies with viewpoint and suggests that our internal representations might be viewpoint-dependent rather than fully 3D-invariant.
concepts.recap_md: - Reaction time for recognition is proportional to the angle of rotation from a canonical or learned view.

concepts.title: Image Stitching and Panoramas
concepts.one_liner: Image stitching creates large panoramas by combining multiple pictures taken by a rotating camera without translation.
concepts.content: To create a large panorama from multiple pictures, the images need to be taken by a rotating camera without translation. To stitch together images, one needs to estimate the homography relating the images to be combined. While one could estimate the rotation and intrinsic camera matrices to compute the homography, it is usually simpler to use feature correspondences. For example, initial correspondences between each pair of images can be computed using speeded up robust features (SURF). (see figure: Two overlapping images and some found correspondences using SURF descriptors. A random set of four correspondences are highlighted.)
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for the creation of wide-angle panoramic views that exceed the field of view of a single camera shot by combining multiple overlapping images into a single seamless frame.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image stitching creates panoramas from multiple photos taken by a rotating camera without translation.
 - The process involves estimating the homography that relates overlapping image pairs.
 - Feature descriptors like SURF are used to find the initial point correspondences needed for estimation.

concepts.title: Direct Linear Transform (DLT) for Homography
concepts.one_liner: The Direct Linear Transform (DLT) algorithm estimates the homography matrix relating point correspondences across two camera views using a linear system of equations.
concepts.content: Given a set of point locations and their correspondences across two cameras, we can compute the homography relating the locations of imaged points using the direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm. This provides a linear set of equations for the parameters of the homography matrix in the form: $$\mathbf{A} 	ext{h} = \mathbf{0}$$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is a $2N \times 9$ matrix when given $N$ corresponding pairs. The vector $\mathbf{h}$ contains all the elements of the matrix $\mathbf{H}$ stacked as a column vector of length 9. Note that $\mathbf{h}$ only has 8 degrees of freedom as the results do not change for a global scaling of all the values. Therefore, we need at least four correspondences to estimate the homography between two sets of corresponding points. The solution is the vector that minimizes the residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} \|^2$, given by the eigenvector of the matrix $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$ with the smallest eigenvalue. In practice, it is useful to also minimize the reprojection error after initializing with the DLT solution.
concepts.motivation_md: DLT provides a mathematically straightforward way to solve for the homography matrix from point matches, serving as a necessary initialization step for more complex geometric optimizations.
concepts.recap_md:
- DLT solves for the homography matrix $\mathbf{H}$ using the linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$.
 - At least four point correspondences are required to solve for the 8 degrees of freedom in the homography.
 - The optimal linear solution is the eigenvector corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$.

concepts.title: RANSAC (Random Sampling with Consensus)
concepts.one_liner: RANSAC is a robust model-fitting algorithm that estimates parameters by iteratively sampling random subsets of data and identifying the set with the most consensus inliers.
concepts.content: Random sampling with consensus (RANSAC) is an algorithm used to fit models to data robustly, especially when feature point detection is noisy or contains mismatches. The procedure is simple: first, randomly select a sufficient set of datapoints to fit the parameters of a model, such as a line or a homography. Second, compute the model parameters from that randomly sampled set. Third, compute the inliers in the dataset—the datapoints that fit the model to within some tolerance. Repeat this procedure $N$ times. Finally, compute a model from the set of inlier points corresponding to the largest number of inlier datapoints. (see figure: RANSAC applied to robust estimation of line parameters. (a) Datapoints for which robust line estimation is sought. (b) Two points (in blue) are selected at random, sufficient to estimate line model...)
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world data often contains outliers or incorrect matches that would skew standard least-squares estimates; RANSAC ignores these outliers to find the true underlying model.
concepts.recap_md:
- RANSAC iteratively selects random minimal subsets of data to propose model candidates.
 - It identifies "inliers" that agree with the proposed model within a given tolerance $\epsilon$.
 - The final model is refined using the largest set of inliers found across all iterations.

concepts.title: RANSAC Iteration Heuristic
concepts.one_liner: The RANSAC iteration heuristic determines the number of trials $k$ needed to find a good model fit with a desired probability $p$ based on the expected outlier ratio.
concepts.content: A heuristic for the number of samples $S$ required to be assured a good model fit can be derived. Let $n$ be the number of datapoints required to specify the model, and let $w$ be the probability that any selected datapoint is an inlier. The probability that all selected points are inliers is $w^n$, and the probability that at least one selected point is an outlier is $1 - w^n$. The probability that in $k$ trials only bad models are selected is $(1 - w^n)^k$. If $p$ is the probability of selecting the correct model, we have $1-p = (1 - w^n)^k$. Solving for $k$, the number of RANSAC iterations required to find a good fit with probability $p$ is: $$k = \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^n)}$$ In practice, points should be selected without replacement to avoid degenerate fits, though this analysis assumes selection with replacement, which is legitimate when the number of points selected is small relative to the available set.
concepts.motivation_md: Since RANSAC is a randomized algorithm, this heuristic provides a statistical guarantee on how many iterations are necessary to ensure the algorithm succeeds with high confidence.
concepts.recap_md:
- The number of iterations $k$ depends on the desired confidence $p$ and the estimated inlier ratio $w$.
 - The formula $k = \log(1-p) / \log(1-w^n)$ calculates the trials needed to pick at least one all-inlier set.
 - This heuristic assumes selection with replacement, which is valid for small sample sizes relative to the dataset.

concepts.title: Image Stitching via Homography
concepts.one_liner: Image stitching uses DLT and RANSAC to compute homographies between image pairs and warp them into a single reference coordinate system.
concepts.content: Using DLT and RANSAC, we can compute the homography between each pair of images and align them with respect to a reference image. In practice, a middle image is often chosen as the reference. We can use the estimated homographies to warp all of the images into a single camera view to create a composite panorama. (see figure: Panoramic image composed by the three overlapping images from @fig-example_three_images)
concepts.motivation_md: This concept integrates point matching, robust estimation, and geometric warping to solve the practical problem of creating seamless wide-field-of-view images from standard photos.
concepts.recap_md:
- DLT and RANSAC are combined to find robust homography matrices between overlapping photos.
 - Images are aligned by warping them into the coordinate frame of a chosen reference image.
 - The final result is a single panoramic view synthesized from multiple individual captures.

concepts.title: Linear Perspective
concepts.one_liner: Linear perspective is a technique that uses parallel lines and vanishing points to infer 3D scene structure from 2D images.
concepts.content: Linear perspective uses parallel and orthogonal lines, vanishing points, the ground plane, and the horizon line to infer the 3D scene structure from a 2D image. The discovery of linear perspective is attributed to the Italian architect Filippo Brunelleschi in 1415. Linear perspective relies on specific assumptions about the scene; consequently, it is not a general cue useful in all scenes, but it is very powerful in most human-made environments.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear perspective provides a geometric framework for understanding how 3D depth is projected onto a 2D plane, which is essential for both realistic art and computer vision algorithms.
concepts.recap_md:
- It utilizes geometric features like vanishing points and horizon lines to recover 3D information.
 - The technique is particularly effective in man-made environments with many parallel and orthogonal lines.
 - It was historically pioneered by Filippo Brunelleschi during the Renaissance.

concepts.title: Leaning Tower Visual Illusion
concepts.one_liner: The leaning tower illusion occurs when the brain interprets identical side-by-side images as having different tilts because their parallel lines do not converge to a single vanishing point.
concepts.content: The human visual system makes use of vanishing points for 3D perception, which can lead to the leaning tower visual illusion. In this illusion, a pair of identical images of the Leaning Tower of Pisa are placed side by side. Despite being identical, they create an illusion of leaning with different angles, where the image on the right appears to have a greater tilt. One explanation is that the lines of each tower converge at a different vanishing point. If both towers were parallel in 3D, all the lines would converge to the same 2D vanishing point. Because they do not, our brain automatically interprets that the towers should have different 3D orientations. (see figure: The *leaning tower illusion* @Kingdom2017 involves two identical pictures placed side by side. The picture on the right appears to be more tilted than the one on the left.)
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion demonstrates how deeply the human brain relies on the geometry of vanishing points to reconstruct 3D scenes, even when that logic leads to an incorrect perception.
concepts.recap_md:
- Identical side-by-side images of a tower appear to tilt at different angles.
 - The illusion stems from the brain's automatic processing of vanishing points for 3D depth.
 - It highlights that our perception of orientation is relative to expected convergence points in a scene.

concepts.title: Vanishing Points in Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: In homogeneous coordinates, a vanishing point is the projection of a point at infinity, represented by a finite vector where the last coordinate is zero.
concepts.content: Homogeneous coordinates allow us to represent points at infinity with finite coordinates by setting the last element to 0. A 3D line can be written in parametric vector form as: $$\mathbf{P}_t = \begin{bmatrix} X_0 + t D_X\\ Y_0 + t D_Y\\ Z_0 + t D_Z\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X_0/t + D_X\\ Y_0 /t+ D_Y\\ Z_0/t + D_Z\\ 1/t \end{bmatrix}$$ In the limit $t \to \infty$, the fourth coordinate converges to 0, resulting in: $$\mathbf{P}_\infty = \begin{bmatrix} D_X\\ D_Y\\ D_Z\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{D}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ The vanishing point in homogeneous coordinates is the projection of $\mathbf{P}_\infty$ using the camera model $\mathbf{M}$: $$\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{P}_\infty = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{T} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{D}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{D}$$ This shows that vanishing point coordinates do not depend on camera translation $\mathbf{T}$, only on rotation $\mathbf{R}$ and intrinsics $\mathbf{K}$. If a scene is captured by two identical cameras translated from each other, their corresponding images will have the same vanishing points. If parallel projection is used instead of perspective projection, all vanishing points project at infinity in the image plane.
concepts.motivation_md: Using homogeneous coordinates simplifies the math of perspective projection by treating points at infinity (vanishing points) as standard vectors, making calculations for rotation and projection more elegant.
concepts.recap_md:
- Points at infinity are represented in homogeneous coordinates by a zero in the final coordinate.
 - Vanishing points are invariant to camera translation and depend only on camera rotation and intrinsics.
 - The vanishing point $\mathbf{v}$ is calculated as the product $\mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{D}$, where $\mathbf{D}$ is the direction of the 3D lines.

concepts.title: Levels of Categorization

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Categorization occurs at three levels of abstraction: superordinate, basic-level, and subordinate, allowing organisms to ignore irrelevant differences between stimuli.
concepts.content:
Categorization offers a number of advantages by allowing an organism not to differentiate one stimulus from others when that differentiation is irrelevant for the purposes at hand. Eleanor Rosch and her collaborators proposed that categorization occurs at three different levels of abstraction:

1. **Superordinate level**: Very general categories that provide a high degree of abstraction (e.g., Furniture, Tree).
2. **Basic level**: Corresponds to the most common level of abstraction (e.g., Chair, Oak).
3. **Subordinate level**: The most specific level of categorization (e.g., Kitchen chair, White oak).

Two objects belonging to the same superordinate category share fewer attributes than two objects belonging to the same subordinate category.
concepts.motivation_md: Categorization is essential for object recognition because it allows an organism to group equivalent objects together. By organizing information into levels of abstraction, we can efficiently process stimuli without being overwhelmed by irrelevant details.
concepts.recap_md: - Categorization happens at superordinate (general), basic (common), and subordinate (specific) levels.

concepts.title: Prototypes

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Prototypes are the clearest members of a category, used to define natural categories by their central examples rather than their fuzzy boundaries.
concepts.content: Natural categories tend to be fuzzy at their boundaries and inconsistent in the status of their constituent members. To address this, categories can be represented by prototypes, which are the clearest members of a category. Humans recognize categories by measuring the similarity of a stimulus to these prototypes. This approach makes it easier to work with continuous categories, as they are defined by "clear cases rather than its boundaries."
concepts.motivation_md: Natural categories often lack sharp boundaries. Prototypes provide a way to define and recognize categories based on central, ideal examples rather than rigid definitions.
concepts.recap_md: - Prototypes are the most representative or "clearest" members of a category.

concepts.title: Affordances and Contextual Meaning

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Object recognition is complicated by affordances, where an object's meaning or function changes based on the specific context in which it is used.
concepts.content:
Object recognition is not as straightforward as a simple categorization task because objects can have different affordances as a function of context. In linguistics, an expression has a standing meaning (its conventional definition) and an occasion meaning (its specific meaning in a particular context). The same principle applies to visual objects: an object's role can shift depending on its environment.

[FIGURE:cb0694462fa842df | A photograph of a plain cardboard box sitting on a blue carpeted floor in front of a whiteboard covered in complex mathematical equations and diagrams. The image illustrates the challenge of object...]

[FIGURE:e401ae49cd70f460 | A photograph of two yellow chairs facing each other in front of a whiteboard covered in complex mathematical and machine learning diagrams. Between the chairs is a cardboard box acting as a table...]
concepts.motivation_md: Standard categorization fails to capture how the function or 'meaning' of an object changes. Understanding affordances helps explain how a single object (like a box) can serve multiple roles (like a container or a table) depending on context.
concepts.recap_md: - Affordances describe the different uses or meanings an object has based on context.

concepts.title: Standing Meaning

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Standing meaning corresponds to the conventional, standard meaning of an expression or object.
concepts.content: A standing meaning corresponds to the conventional meaning of an expression.
concepts.motivation_md: To distinguish between the dictionary definition of a word (or the standard use of an object) and its specific use in a unique situation.
concepts.recap_md: - Standing meaning is the conventional or default definition of an expression.

concepts.title: Occasion Meaning

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Occasion meaning is the particular meaning an expression or object takes on when used in a specific context.
concepts.content: The occasion meaning is the particular meaning that an expression might have when used in a specific context. Therefore, when an expression is being used, it has an occasion meaning that differs from its conventional meaning. This concept also applies to visual objects, where their function changes based on the situation.
concepts.motivation_md: Context often changes the intended use or meaning of an object or word. Occasion meaning allows us to describe these situational variations.
concepts.recap_md: - Occasion meaning is situational and differs from conventional meaning.

concepts.title: Visual Memex
concepts.one_liner: The Visual Memex is a computer vision approach that attempts to understand images while avoiding traditional categorization.
concepts.content: The same object can have different occasion meanings depending on the context, such as a box being used as a table. Avoiding categorization altogether has been the focus of some computer vision approaches to image understanding, such as the Visual Memex by T. Malisiewicz and A. Efros.
concepts.motivation_md: Because categorization can be rigid and fail to account for contextual affordances, researchers developed the Visual Memex to explore image understanding without relying on fixed categories.
concepts.recap_md: - The Visual Memex is an approach to image understanding that avoids standard categorization.

concepts.title: Image Classification Formulation
concepts.one_liner: Image classification is mathematically formulated as a function mapping an input image ${\bf x}$ to an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$ representing class presence.
concepts.content:
We can formulate image classification mathematically by building a function that maps the input image ${\bf x}$ into an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$: $$\hat {\bf y} = f({\bf x})$$ For a single object, the output $\hat {\bf y}$ is a binary response where $1$ indicates the object is present and $0$ indicates it is not.

(see figure: Image classification: Is there a car in this image?)

In general, we want to classify an image according to multiple classes. We can do this by having an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$ of length $K$, where $K$ is the number of classes. Component $c$ of the vector $\hat {\bf y}$ indicates whether class $c$ is present or absent in the image. A training set consists of images and their corresponding class indicator vectors.

(see figure: Image classification: Is there a car in this image?)
concepts.motivation_md: To perform automated object recognition, we need a formal mathematical framework that translates raw pixel data into structured labels identifying which objects are present.
concepts.recap_md: - Classification is modeled as a function $f({\bf x}) = \hat {\bf y}$.

concepts.title: Exclusive Classes in Image Classification
concepts.one_liner: Exclusive class classification assumes exactly one category is present in an image, constrained by the sum of output probabilities equaling one.
concepts.content: One common assumption in image classification is that only one class, among $K$ possible classes, is present in the image. This is typical in settings where most images contain a single large object. Multiclass classification with exclusive classes results in the following constraint: $$\sum_{c=1}^K \hat{y}_c=1$$
concepts.motivation_md: In many datasets, images are centered on a single primary subject. Enforcing an exclusivity constraint simplifies the model's decision-making process and reflects the structure of the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes only one class is present per image.

concepts.title: Radial Distortion
concepts.one_liner: Radial distortion from lenses causes straight lines to appear curved and requires calibration to build an accurate camera model.
concepts.content: Modeling radial distortion requires introducing a skew parameter in $\mathbf{K}$. Radial distortion introduced by lenses is often an important and frequent source of issues that requires calibration. When there is radial distortion, straight lines will appear curved; in such cases, it is very important to correct for the distortion. Standardized tools for camera calibrations take into account these different aspects of the camera in order to build an accurate camera model.
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world lenses are not perfect pinholes; they often introduce radial distortion that causes straight lines in the scene to appear curved in the image. Calibration is necessary to correct these artifacts for accurate spatial measurements.
concepts.recap_md: - Radial distortion causes straight lines in the world to appear curved in the captured image. - Calibration tools account for lens distortion and skew parameters to build accurate camera models.

concepts.title: Camera-Extrinsic Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Extrinsic camera parameters, $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$, define the rotation and translation that relate the camera's coordinate system to the world.
concepts.content: In practice, placing the camera at an arbitrary location away from the world coordinate system is often necessary. The camera's position is defined by a translation vector $\mathbf{T}$ and its orientation by a rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}^\mathsf{T}$ relative to the world coordinate system. (see figure: World- and camera-coordinate systems. A 3D point expressed in world coordinates, $\mathbf{P}_W$, can be expressed in the camera-coordinate frame, $\mathbf{P}_c$, by applying the translation...) To find how a world point $\mathbf{P}_W$ projects into an image, we first change the coordinate system to the camera's frame. Using heterogeneous coordinates, this is described as $\mathbf{P}_C = \mathbf{R} (\mathbf{P}_W - \mathbf{T}) = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_W - \mathbf{R}\mathbf{T}$, where $\mathbf{R}$ is the inverse of the camera's rotation matrix. In homogeneous coordinates, we first translate by $-\mathbf{T}$ using matrix $\mathbf{M}_1$, then rotate using matrix $\mathbf{M}_2$, resulting in $\mathbf{P}_C = \mathbf{M}_2 \mathbf{M}_1 \mathbf{P}_W$. The product of these matrices is $\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & -\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T} \\ \mathbf{0}^\mathsf{T}& 1 \end{bmatrix}$. These parameters, $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$, are known as the extrinsic camera parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: In practice, cameras are rarely located at the world origin. Extrinsic parameters allow us to describe the camera's arbitrary location and orientation, enabling the projection of points from any world coordinate system into the camera's frame.
concepts.recap_md: - Extrinsic parameters consist of a rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$ and a translation vector $\mathbf{T}$. - These parameters transform coordinates from a world-coordinate system to the camera-centered coordinate system.

concepts.title: World to Camera Coordinate Transformation
concepts.one_liner: This transformation expresses world points in the camera's coordinate system by applying a translation followed by a rotation.
concepts.content: (see figure: World- and camera-coordinate systems. A 3D point expressed in world coordinates, $\mathbf{P}_W$, can be expressed in the camera-coordinate frame, $\mathbf{P}_c$, by applying the translation...) To project a world point $\mathbf{P}_W$ into an image, we must first express it with respect to the camera coordinate system. This requires initially translating and subsequently rotating the camera so that points are expressed in a coordinate system originating at the camera center. In heterogeneous coordinates, $\mathbf{P}_C = \mathbf{R} (\mathbf{P}_W - \mathbf{T}) = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_W - \mathbf{R}\mathbf{T}$, where $\mathbf{R}$ rotates the camera to be parallel to the world and $\mathbf{T}$ is the camera's position. In homogeneous coordinates, this is achieved by $\mathbf{P}_C = \mathbf{M}_2 \mathbf{M}_1 \mathbf{P}_W$, where $\mathbf{M}_1$ is a translation matrix by $-\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{M}_2$ is a rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$. The combined transformation matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & -\mathbf{R}\mathbf{T} \\ \mathbf{0}^\mathsf{T}& 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: To project a 3D world point onto an image plane, it must first be expressed relative to the camera's own coordinate system. This transformation bridges the gap between global world coordinates and local camera space.
concepts.recap_md: - The transformation is achieved by first translating the world point by $-\mathbf{T}$ and then rotating it by $\mathbf{R}$. - In homogeneous coordinates, this is expressed as $\mathbf{P}_C = \mathbf{M}_2 \mathbf{M}_1 \mathbf{P}_W$.

concepts.title: Full Camera Model
concepts.one_liner: The full camera model concatenates extrinsic and intrinsic matrices to transform 3D world coordinates into 2D pixel coordinates.
concepts.content: The concatenation of extrinsic and intrinsic transformation matrices yields a single matrix that transforms world coordinates to rendered pixel coordinates: $\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{M}_2 \mathbf{M}_1 \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Converting back to heterogeneous coordinates, the 2D pixel indices are $[x,y]^\mathsf{T}=[x'/w, y'/w]^\mathsf{T}$. The expanded form is $\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & a & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R_1 & R_2 & R_3 \\ R_4 & R_5 & R_6 \\ R_7 & R_8 & R_9 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & -T_X \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -T_Y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -T_Z \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, which is usually written compactly as $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} ~ \mid ~ -\mathbf{R} \mathbf{T} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}_W$. Different camera types, such as orthographic or affine cameras, can be modeled by replacing $\mathbf{K}$ with different intrinsic parameters. (see figure: Projection of a point into the image plane. This summary puts together @fig-pinholeGeometry2bis and @fig-camera_calibration. First, we change the world-coordinates system, in which the point is...)
concepts.motivation_md: A complete mathematical model is needed to automate the process of mapping any point in a 3D scene to its corresponding pixel location on a digital sensor, accounting for both camera placement and internal optics.
concepts.recap_md: - The model is expressed as $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{K} [\mathbf{R} \mid -\mathbf{R} \mathbf{T}] \mathbf{P}_W$. - It combines extrinsic parameters (camera pose) with intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point) into a single projection pipeline.

concepts.title: Horizon Line Projection
concepts.one_liner: The horizon line is the projection of points at infinity, located where $Z \rightarrow \infty$ in the camera model.
concepts.content: The horizon line is located at the points where $Z \rightarrow \infty$, which corresponds to $y=0$ in certain configurations. (see figure: If you hold the camera parallel to the ground at the height of your eyes and take a picture of a person standing in front of you with a similar height, their eyes will project near the middle portion...) For arbitrary camera angles $\theta$, the horizon line corresponds to the $y$ location for a point at infinity, $Z \rightarrow \infty$, and is located at $y = a \tan(\theta)$. If a picture is taken of people with a similar height $h$ to the camera, their eyes will be located at $y = a \tan(\theta)$ in the image, which is independent of their distance $Z$ and matches the vertical location of the horizon line. (see figure: Sketch showing a person taking a picture of two people standing at different distances from the camera. Their eyes will project to the same image row regardless of their distance to the camera.)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding where the horizon projects helps in determining camera orientation and the relative height of objects in a scene.
concepts.recap_md: - For a camera at an angle $\theta$, the horizon line is located at $y = a \tan(\theta)$. - Objects at the same height as the camera will have features project onto the horizon line regardless of their distance.

concepts.title: Camera Tilt Angle Estimation from Horizon
concepts.one_liner: A camera's tilt angle can be estimated from the vertical position of the horizon line in an image if the camera is calibrated.
concepts.content: If the camera is calibrated and the parameter $a$ is known, the camera tilt angle $\theta$ can be inferred by locating the horizon line in the image. Conversely, if $\theta$ is known, $a$ can be estimated. For example, using a calibrated iPhone 13 Pro with $a \simeq 3{,}103$, a horizon line at $y_h = -798$ results in an estimated angle of $\theta = \arctan(y_h/a) = 14.6$ degrees. Similarly, a horizon line at $y_h = 1{,}129$ results in an estimated angle of $\theta = 20$ degrees. These estimations can be verified by manual measurements of the camera angle.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for the recovery of camera pose information (specifically tilt) from image content alone, provided the internal camera parameters are known.
concepts.recap_md: - The tilt angle is calculated using the formula $\theta = \arctan(y_h/a)$, where $y_h$ is the horizon's vertical position. - This relationship allows for estimating the camera's angle or calibrating the focal parameter if the angle is known.

concepts.title: Reconciling Projection Models with Simple Visual Systems
concepts.one_liner: General projection models can be reconciled with simplified systems by applying specific geometric constraints and adapting to different coordinate conventions.
concepts.content: Reconciling general projection models with simple visual systems involves applying specific geometric constraints. For instance, if the world origin is the point where the optical axis intersects the ground, the constraint $\tan(\theta) = h/d$ applies, implying $d \sin(\theta) - h \cos(\theta) = 0$. In heterogeneous coordinates, this results in $x = -a X$ and $y = a \cos(\theta) Y - a \sin(\theta) Z$. These equations match simplified projection models, though the sign of $x$ may differ depending on the specific coordinate convention used in the text or publication.
concepts.motivation_md: Different textbooks and systems use varying conventions for axes and origins; reconciling these ensures that general camera models can be applied to specific, simplified scenarios correctly.
concepts.recap_md: - Specific constraints like $\tan(\theta) = h/d$ relate camera height and distance to the tilt angle. - Differences in coordinate sign conventions are common across literature and must be adapted per setting.

concepts.title: Purpose of Camera Calibration
concepts.one_liner: Camera calibration provides the intrinsic and extrinsic matrices needed to transform world coordinates to pixels without manual derivation.
concepts.content: Working with heterogeneous coordinates and deriving projection equations manually can be tedious. In practice, the camera matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and the projection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ are obtained through the camera calibration process. These matrices allow for the direct transformation of world coordinates to pixel coordinates without the need to derive their underlying equations for every setup.
concepts.motivation_md: Manual derivation of projection equations for every camera setup is impractical; calibration provides a standardized way to determine the parameters of a specific camera-lens system.
concepts.recap_md: - Calibration yields the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ and extrinsic parameters. - It simplifies the transformation of 3D points to 2D pixels by providing ready-to-use matrices.

concepts.title: Gradient Constraint Equation
concepts.one_liner: The gradient constraint equation $u \ell_x + v \ell_y + \ell_t = 0$ constrains local motion to a line perpendicular to the image gradient.
concepts.content: Combining the constancy brightness assumption and the Taylor expansion for motion, and ignoring higher order terms, we arrive at the gradient constraint equation: $$u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$$ This equation constrains the motion $(u,v)$ at location $(x,y)$ to be along a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell= \left( \ell_x, \ell_y \right)$ at that location. This is the same relationship described by the aperture problem, where the local gradient alone is insufficient to uniquely estimate motion.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation provides a mathematical link between temporal changes in image intensity and spatial gradients, serving as the fundamental basis for gradient-based optical flow estimation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Relates horizontal ($u$) and vertical ($v$) velocity to spatial and temporal image derivatives.
- Constrains motion to a line perpendicular to the image gradient, illustrating the aperture problem.

concepts.title: Harris Condition for Reliable Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: The Harris condition identifies image regions with sufficient texture variations where motion estimation is reliable.
concepts.content: Motion estimation can be unreliable in image regions without sufficient texture variations, such as the center of a square's side. The inverse of the motion matrix can only be computed reliably near corners. As in the Harris corner detector, the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue indicates the direction of smallest possible image change under translation; regions with a small minimum eigenvalue suffer from the aperture problem. To identify reliable regions, we use the quantity $R$, which relates to the conditioning of the matrix $\mathbf{A}$: $$R = \det (\mathbf{A}) - \lambda \mathrm{Tr}\hspace{1pt} (\mathbf{A})^2$$ where $\lambda=0.05$. This formulation avoids the computationally expensive step of calculating eigenvalues at every pixel. (see figure: Estimated optical flow in the regions with $R > 2$ (around *good features to track* @shi1994goodfeatures)
concepts.motivation_md: Gradient-based motion estimation fails in homogeneous or 1D-structured regions (the aperture problem). This technique identifies 'good features to track' where the motion is mathematically well-posed.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a response function $R$ to detect regions with high 2D texture variation.
- Helps avoid the aperture problem by selecting pixels where the motion matrix is well-conditioned.

concepts.title: Gaussian Pyramid for Large Displacements
concepts.one_liner: Gaussian pyramids handle large displacements by reducing motion magnitude at lower resolution scales.
concepts.content: One solution to the problem of large displacements is to compute a Gaussian pyramid for the input sequence. The low-resolution scales make the motion smaller and the gradient-based approach will work better.
concepts.motivation_md: Gradient-based methods rely on Taylor expansions which only hold for small displacements. Pyramids allow these methods to capture large movements by looking at them at a coarser scale.
concepts.recap_md:
- Reduces large pixel displacements into smaller, manageable motions at lower resolutions.
- Enables gradient-based optical flow to succeed on fast-moving objects.

concepts.title: Photometric Reconstruction Error
concepts.one_liner: Photometric reconstruction error measures the squared difference between a frame and its motion-compensated successor.
concepts.content: The gradient-based approach is efficient but it only provides an approximation to the motion field because it ignores higher order terms in the Taylor expansion. A different approach consists of directly minimizing the photometric reconstruction error: $$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: To overcome the inaccuracies of first-order Taylor approximations in standard gradient methods, this loss function directly measures how well the estimated motion aligns the actual pixel intensities.
concepts.recap_md:
- Defines a loss function based on the intensity difference between frames.
- Avoids the limitations of ignoring higher-order terms in Taylor expansions.

concepts.title: Iterative Refinement for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Iterative refinement improves optical flow accuracy by repeatedly updating motion estimates across a Gaussian pyramid.
concepts.content: We can run gradient descent on the photometric reconstruction loss. While one iteration is similar to standard gradient-based optical flow, adding iterations provides a more accurate estimate. At each iteration $n$, the estimated optical flow is used to compute the warped frame $\ell_1 (x+u_n,y+v_n,t+1)$ and we compute updates $\Delta u_n$ and $\Delta v_n$ such that $u_{n+1} = u_n+\Delta u_n$ and $v_{n+1}= v_n + \Delta v_n$. To improve results, this estimation is performed on a Gaussian pyramid. We run iterations on the lowest resolution scale, then upsample the estimated motion to initialize the next level, continuing until the highest resolution is reached. (see figure: Multiscale iterative refinement for optical flow. Optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid. (left) First, we run a few iterations on the lowest resolution scale of the pyramid (where the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Single-step gradient methods often fail to capture the true motion. Iterative refinement allows the algorithm to 'fine-tune' the alignment, while the multiscale approach prevents getting stuck in local minima.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses gradient descent to iteratively update the motion field $(u, v)$.
- Employs a coarse-to-fine strategy using a Gaussian pyramid for better convergence.

concepts.title: Horn and Schunck Objective
concepts.one_liner: The Horn and Schunck objective combines photometric reconstruction error with a regularization term to estimate optical flow.
concepts.content: The photometric reconstruction can incorporate a regularization term penalizing fast variations on the estimated optical flow: $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) + \lambda R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$$ This problem formulation was introduced by Horn and Schunck in 1981.
concepts.motivation_md: Optical flow is often an ill-posed problem (the aperture problem). Regularization adds a 'smoothness' constraint that allows for a unique and physically plausible solution across the entire image.
concepts.recap_md:
- Combines data fidelity (photometric error) with a regularization term $R$.
- Uses a parameter $\lambda$ to balance the influence of the regularization.

concepts.title: Slow Prior Regularization
concepts.one_liner: Slow prior regularization penalizes large velocities in the estimated optical flow.
concepts.content: There are several popular regularization terms. One penalizes large velocities (**slow prior**): $$R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( u(x,y) \right)^2 + \left( v(x,y)  \right)^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: In many physical scenarios, motion is expected to be small or conservative. This prior biases the optimization toward finding the smallest possible motion that explains the image change.
concepts.recap_md:
- Penalizes the magnitude of the velocity vectors.
- Encourages the solution to favor smaller displacements.

concepts.title: Smooth Prior Regularization
concepts.one_liner: Smooth prior regularization penalizes spatial variations in the optical flow field.
concepts.content: Another regularization term penalizes variations on the optical flow (**smooth prior**): $$R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}  \right)^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: Physical objects usually move as coherent units, meaning neighboring pixels should have similar velocities. This prior enforces spatial consistency in the motion field.
concepts.recap_md:
- Penalizes the partial derivatives of the flow components $u$ and $v$.
- Encourages neighboring pixels to have similar motion vectors.

concepts.title: Simplex in Multiclass Classification
concepts.one_liner: In multiclass classification with exclusive classes, valid prediction vectors are constrained to lie within a simplex where components are positive and sum to one.
concepts.content:
In multiclass classification with $K$ exclusive classes, the valid solutions for the predicted vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=[\hat{y}_1, \hat{y}_2, \dots, \hat{y}_K]^\mathsf{T}$ are constrained to lie within a simplex, where $0 < \hat{y}_c < 1$.
