[FIGURE:f4016c609bc00301 | A 3D coordinate system with axes $\hat{y}_1$, $\hat{y}_2$, and $\hat{y}_3$ representing the classes Car, Bike, and Bird respectively. A shaded triangular region, known as a 2-simplex, connects the...]

Under this formulation, the classification function $f$ is a mapping $f:\mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$ from the set of red-green-blue (RGB) images to the $(K-1)$-dimensional simplex, $\vartriangle^{K-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: When classes are mutually exclusive, the model's output should represent a valid probability distribution. The simplex constraint ensures that individual class scores are bounded between 0 and 1 and collectively sum to 100%, preventing logically impossible predictions.
concepts.recap_md: - The prediction vector for exclusive classes must reside on a $(K-1)$-dimensional simplex.

concepts.title: Softmax Regression Model
concepts.one_liner: The softmax regression model interprets the output of a function as a probability mass function over $K$ classes.
concepts.content:
The softmax regression model produces an output $f_{\theta}$ that can be interpreted as a probability mass function over $K$ classes:

$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(Y \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= \hat{\mathbf{y}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \end{aligned}$$

where $Y$ is the random variable indicating the single class per image. This relates to the classification probability model as:

$$\begin{aligned} p(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= p_{\theta}(Y=c \bigm | \mathbf{x}) \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Softmax regression allows a neural network to output a categorical probability distribution, making it suitable for multi-class decision making where we need to know the model's confidence in each mutually exclusive category.
concepts.recap_md: - Interprets the output vector as a probability mass function over $K$ classes.

concepts.title: Multilabel Classification
concepts.one_liner: Multilabel classification treats the problem as $K$ independent binary classification tasks where an image can belong to multiple classes simultaneously.
concepts.content:
When an image can have multiple labels simultaneously, the classification problem can be formulated as $K$ binary classification problems, where $K$ is the number of classes. 

In such a case, the function $f_\theta$ can be a neural network shared across all classes, and the output vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ of length $K$ is computed using a sigmoid nonlinearity for each output class. The output can still be interpreted as the probability $\hat{y}_c = p_\theta(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x})$, but without the constraint that the sum across classes is 1.

(see figure: Multilabel image classification system.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard multiclass classification assumes only one label is correct. Multilabel classification is necessary for complex scenes where multiple objects (e.g., a car, a person, and a tree) are present and all need to be identified.
concepts.recap_md: - Formulates classification as $K$ independent binary problems.

concepts.title: Misclassification Error
concepts.one_liner: Misclassification error is a measure of classification performance defined as the total number of incorrect class predictions across a dataset.
concepts.content:
In order to learn the model parameters, we define a loss function to capture the task. One natural measure of classification error is the misclassification error. The errors that the function $f$ makes are the number of misplaced ones over the dataset, which can be written as:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{c=1}^{K} \mathbb{1}(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \neq y^{(t)}_c ). \end{aligned}$$

where $T$ is the number of images in the dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: Misclassification error provides a direct, intuitive count of how many times the model was wrong. While useful for evaluation, its discrete nature makes it difficult to use directly for gradient-based optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the total count of incorrect predictions across all classes and samples.

concepts.title: Cross-Entropy Loss for Exclusive Classes
concepts.one_liner: Cross-entropy loss for exclusive classes is the negative log-likelihood of the ground truth labels, commonly used for differentiable optimization in image classification.
concepts.content:
If we interpret the function $f$ as estimating the probability $p(Y_c=1 \bigm | {\bf x}) = \hat{y}_c$, with $\sum_c \hat{y}_c =1$, the likelihood of the ground truth data is:

$$\prod_{t=1}^T \prod_{c=1}^K \left( \hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{y^{(t)}_c}$$

where $y^{(t)}_c$ is the ground truth value of $Y_c$ for image $t$. Maximizing this likelihood corresponds to minimizing the cross-entropy loss, obtained by taking the negative log of the likelihood, resulting in a total classification loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{cls}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} y^{(t)}_c \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)$$

The cross-entropy loss is differentiable and is commonly used in image classification tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Unlike raw misclassification error, cross-entropy is a smooth, differentiable function. This allows for the use of gradient descent to optimize model parameters by penalizing the model based on the confidence of its predictions.
concepts.recap_md: - Derived from maximizing the likelihood of the ground truth data.

concepts.title: Multiclass Binary Cross-Entropy Loss
concepts.one_liner: Multiclass binary cross-entropy loss is used for non-exclusive labels by applying a sigmoid layer and summing individual binary cross-entropy losses for each class.
concepts.content:
If classes are not exclusive, the likelihood of the ground truth data is:

$$\prod_{t=1}^T \prod_{c=1}^K \left( \hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{y^{(t)}_c} \left( 1-\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{1-y^{(t)}_c}$$

where the outputs $\hat{y}_c$ are computed using a sigmoid layer. Taking the negative log of the likelihood gives the multiclass binary cross-entropy loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{cls}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} y^{(t)}_c \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c) + (1-y^{(t)}_c) \log(1-\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)$$
concepts.motivation_md: In multilabel settings, each class prediction is an independent Bernoulli trial. This loss function allows the model to be penalized for every class it gets wrong independently, rather than assuming only one class can be correct.
concepts.recap_md: - Used for multilabel classification where classes are not mutually exclusive.

concepts.title: Top-1 Performance
concepts.one_liner: Top-1 performance measures the percentage of times the true class label matches the highest-scored prediction.
concepts.content:
Classification performance uses the output of the classifier, $f$, as a continuous value (the score $\hat{y}_c$) for each class. We can rank the predicted classes according to that value. The top-1 performance measures the percentage of times that the true class-label matches the highest scored prediction, $\hat{y} = \underset{c}{\mathrm{argmax}} ( \hat{y}_c )$, in the test set:

$$\text{TOP-1} = \frac{100}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = y^{(t)})$$

where $y^{(t)}$ is the ground truth class of image $t$. This evaluation metric only works for the exclusive class case since it assumes a single ground truth class per image. For the multilabel case, we may instead check if each label is predicted correctly.
concepts.motivation_md: Top-1 accuracy is the most standard and rigorous metric for classification, requiring the model to identify the single correct category as its most confident prediction.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures how often the highest-probability prediction is correct.

concepts.title: Top-5 Performance
concepts.one_liner: Top-5 performance measures the percentage of times the true label is among the five highest-scoring predictions.
concepts.content: In some benchmarks (such as ImageNet), researchers measure the top-5 performance, which is the percentage of times that the true label is within the set of five highest scoring predictions. Top-5 is useful in settings where the labels might be ambiguous, or where multiple labels for one image might be possible. The top-5 measure is less precise and it is used when the test set only contains one label despite that multiple labels might be correct. In the case of multiple labels, ideally, the test set should specify which labels are possible and evaluate only using those.
concepts.motivation_md: In large-scale datasets with hundreds of categories, some labels are very similar (e.g., different breeds of dogs). Top-5 performance provides a more lenient evaluation that accounts for such ambiguity or the presence of multiple valid objects in a single-label dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - Useful for benchmarks with ambiguous labels or many similar classes.

concepts.title: Next-pixel Softmax Regression
concepts.one_liner: Modeling the distribution of the next pixel in a sequence can be treated as a 256-way softmax regression problem conditioned on previous observations.
concepts.content: To model the distribution over a second grayscale pixel given the first, we model $p(\mathbf{x_2} \bigm | \mathbf{x_1})$ where $\mathbf{x_1}$ is the first pixel and $\mathbf{x_2}$ is the second. In this context, we index the first pixel as $\mathbf{x}_1$ rather than $\mathbf{x}_0$. Treating $\mathbf{x}_2$ as a categorical variable, we can use a softmax regression, as seen in @sec-intro_to_learning-image_classification. While that section modeled a $K$-way categorical distribution over object classes, we can use the same tools to model a 256-way distribution over the second pixel in a sequence. This logic extends via induction: modeling each next pixel in the sequence is a softmax regression problem that models $p(\mathbf{x}_n \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})$. The cross-entropy loss can be computed as shown in (see figure: Autoregressive prediction as next-pixel-classification.). This process looks almost identical to the diagram in @fig-softmax_regression_diagram from @sec-intro_to_learning.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows us to apply well-understood supervised learning tools, like softmax regression and cross-entropy loss, to the complex task of generative modeling by framing image generation as a sequence of classification problems.
concepts.recap_md: - Each pixel is treated as a categorical variable with 256 possible intensity values. - The model predicts the probability of the next pixel conditioned on all previously observed pixels in the sequence. - Standard cross-entropy loss is used to train the model to predict the correct pixel values.

concepts.title: Pixel Sequence Ordering
concepts.one_liner: Images can be modeled as sequences by vectorizing the 2D grid of pixels, typically by listing them row by row.
concepts.content: To model color images, we predict three values per pixel for the red, green, and blue channels in sequence. This involves predicting the red value as a 256-way classification problem, sampling it, and then predicting the green and blue values. To turn an image into a sequence of pixels, the simplest method is to vectorize the 2D grid by listing the first row of pixels, then the second row, and so forth. While any fixed ordering of the pixels into a sequence is valid, this simple raster-scan method is the most common.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models require a sequential input, so a consistent method for flattening 2D or 3D image data into a 1D sequence is necessary for the model to learn spatial dependencies.
concepts.recap_md: - Color images are handled by sequencing the red, green, and blue channels for each pixel. - The most common ordering method is raster order, which processes pixels row by row. - Any fixed sequence ordering is valid for defining the conditional dependencies in the model.

concepts.title: Chain Rule of Probability
concepts.one_liner: The chain rule of probability allows any joint distribution to be factorized into a product of conditional distributions.
concepts.content: According to the chain rule of probability, any joint distribution can be factorized into a product of conditionals as follows: $$\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{X}) &= p(\mathbf{x_n} \bigm | \mathbf{x_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-2}) \quad \ldots \quad p(\mathbf{x}_2 \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1)p(\mathbf{x}_1) \\ p(\mathbf{X}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1}) \end{aligned}$$ As a notational convenience, we define $p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1}) = p(\mathbf{x}_1)$ when $i=1$.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule provides the mathematical foundation for autoregressive models, enabling the decomposition of a complex high-dimensional joint distribution into a series of simpler, learnable conditional distributions.
concepts.recap_md: - Any joint probability distribution can be expressed as a product of conditional probabilities. - The probability of the first element is defined as the base case for the product. - This factorization justifies predicting sequences one element at a time.

concepts.title: Training Autoregressive Models
concepts.one_liner: Training an autoregressive model involves extracting supervised input-output pairs of pixel sequences and their corresponding next pixels from training images.
concepts.content: To train an autoregressive model, you extract supervised pairs of desired input-output behavior. For a pixel-based model, this means extracting sequences of pixels $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}$ and the corresponding observed next pixel $\mathbf{x}_n$. These can be extracted by traversing training images in raster order. The full training and testing setup is shown in (see figure: Training an autoregressive model, then sampling images from it.).
concepts.motivation_md: By converting unsupervised image data into supervised sequence-prediction tasks, we can use standard optimization algorithms to train models that learn the underlying structure of the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Training data consists of sequences of preceding pixels as inputs and the subsequent pixel as the target. - Training examples are generated by traversing images in a fixed order, such as raster order. - The model learns to predict the next pixel value based on the history of previous pixels.

concepts.title: Type 1 Training Batch (Independent Sequences)
concepts.one_liner: A type 1 training batch consists of independent sequence and completion pairs sampled from random starting locations in different random images.
concepts.content: One way to create a training batch is the type 1 batch: $$\begin{aligned} &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_k^{(i)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{k+n-1}^{(i)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_{k+n}^{(i)} \\ &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_l^{(j)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{l+n-1}^{(j)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_{l+n}^{(j)} \end{aligned}$$ In this setup, we sample supervised [sequence, completion] pairs that each come from a different random starting location (indexed by $k$ and $l$) in a different random image (indexed by $i$ and $j$).
concepts.motivation_md: This method ensures that the training batch is diverse and that the model sees a wide variety of contexts and starting points across the dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - Each example in the batch is an independent sequence and its next-token target. - Sequences are sampled from random images and random starting positions. - This approach provides a straightforward way to construct supervised training batches.

concepts.title: Type 2 Training Batch (Overlapping Sequences)
concepts.one_liner: Type 2 training batches use overlapping sequences to share computations, making the training process significantly more efficient.
concepts.content: Another way to set up batches is the type 2 batch, where the example sequences overlap: $$\begin{aligned} &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_1^{(i)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}^{(i)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_n^{(i)} \\ &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_2^{(i)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n}^{(i)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{(i)} \end{aligned}$$ This method is much more efficient because the representations computed for predicting $\mathbf{x}_n$ from $\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}$ can be reused for predicting the next item, $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}$. This is particularly useful in architectures like transformers with causal attention (@sec-transformers-masked_attention), where the representation of an item only depends on its predecessors. This allows the model to share computation between all overlapping predictions, as described in @eq-transformers-causal_training_batches.
concepts.motivation_md: Sequential prediction is computationally expensive; overlapping batches allow models to reuse intermediate calculations, drastically reducing the total compute required to process a dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - Training examples consist of overlapping segments from the same sequence. - Reusing hidden state representations across overlapping steps increases computational efficiency. - This batching style is standard for training transformers with causal masking.

concepts.title: Sampling from Autoregressive Models
concepts.one_liner: Sampling from an autoregressive model involves sequentially drawing values from the conditional distributions of each pixel.
concepts.content: Autoregressive models provide an explicit density function as seen in @eq-generative_models-autoregressive_likelihood. To sample from this density, we sample the first pixel from $p(\mathbf{x}_1)$, then, conditioned on this pixel, sample the second from $p(\mathbf{x}_2 \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1)$, and so forth. Since each of these densities is a categorical distribution, sampling is easy: one option is to partition a unit line segment into regions of length equal to the categorical probabilities and see where a
concepts.motivation_md: While training is often done in parallel, generating new data requires a sequential process to ensure each new element is consistent with the previously generated content.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling is done sequentially by drawing from conditional distributions. - Categorical distributions make the sampling process straightforward. - The process follows the factorization provided by the chain rule of probability.

concepts.title: Latent Variables in Autoregressive Models
concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive models lack latent variables, which prevents them from being used for tasks that require extracting or manipulating hidden representations.
concepts.content: uniform random draw along this line falls. Autoregressive models do not have latent variables $\mathbf{z}$, which makes them incompatible with applications that involve extracting or manipulating latent variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the limitations of autoregressive models helps in choosing the right architecture; if a task requires a compressed representation of data, other models like VAEs might be more appropriate.
concepts.recap_md: - Autoregressive models model the data distribution directly without hidden latent states. - The absence of latent variables means there is no compressed "code" for the data. - This makes them unsuitable for tasks like latent space interpolation or feature extraction.

concepts.title: Confusion Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The confusion matrix summarizes the overall performance of a classifier and the percentage of times that classes are confused with one another.
concepts.content:
For multiclass prediction problems, it is often useful to look at the structure of mistakes made by the model. The confusion matrix summarizes both the overall performance of the classifier and the percentage of times that two classes are confused. The diagonal elements represent the top-1 performance for each individual class, while the off-diagonal elements show the specific confusions. For instance, a classifier might confuse cats as dogs more frequently than other categories.

(see figure: Confusion matrix for a three-way classification task. The numbers are percentages.)

The elements of the confusion matrix are defined as:

$$C_{i,j} = 100 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = j)  \mathbb{1} (y^{(t)} = i)}{\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}(y^{(t)} = i)}$$

where $C_{i,j}$ measures the percentage of times that true class $i$ is classified as class $j$. In a typical example, 80 percent of cat images might be correctly classified, while 5 percent are classified as cars and 15 percent are classified as dogs.
concepts.motivation_md: In multiclass classification, simple accuracy doesn't reveal which specific classes the model struggles to distinguish. The confusion matrix provides a granular view of error patterns, helping developers identify if the model is systematically misidentifying one class as another.
concepts.recap_md: - The diagonal of the matrix represents the accuracy for each specific class.

concepts.title: Object Localization
concepts.one_liner: Object localization consists of localizing where an object is in an image, typically by finding a tight bounding box around it.
concepts.content: For many applications, saying that an object is present in the image is not enough. For example, in a visual system for an autonomous vehicle, simply knowing a person is in the image is insufficient for deciding how to navigate. Object localization consists of localizing where the object is in the image. There are many ways to specify where the object is. The most traditional way of representing the object location is using a bounding box, which involves finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each instance of class $c$ in the image $\bf x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Classification only identifies *what* is in an image; localization is necessary to determine *where* those objects are, which is critical for tasks like robotics, autonomous driving, and image editing.
concepts.recap_md: - Localization identifies the specific spatial coordinates of objects within an image.

concepts.title: Bounding Box
concepts.one_liner: A bounding box is a set of image coordinates defining a tight box around an object instance.
concepts.content: The most traditional way of representing an object's location is using a bounding box. This involves finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each of the instances of class $c$ in the image $\bf x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Bounding boxes provide a simple, standardized four-parameter representation of an object's spatial extent, making it computationally efficient to describe object locations compared to pixel-level masks.
concepts.recap_md: - A bounding box is defined by coordinates that tightly enclose a specific object instance.

concepts.title: Object Localization Formulation
concepts.one_liner: Object localization is formulated as a function mapping an image to a list of bounding boxes and their associated class vectors.
concepts.content:
Object detection is formulated as a function that maps the input image ${\bf x}$ into a list of bounding boxes $\hat {\bf b}_i$ and the associated classes to each bounding box encoded by a vector $\hat {\bf y}_i$.

(see figure: Car localization using bounding boxes. Each instance is shown with a different color.)

The class vector, $\hat {\bf y}_i$, has the same structure as in the image classification task but is applied to describe each bounding box. Bounding boxes are usually represented as a vector of length 4 using either the coordinates of the two corners, ${\bf b} = [x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2]$, or the center coordinates, width, and height, ${\bf b} = [x_c, y_c, w, h]$. The goal is to find a function $f$ such that: $${ \hat {\bf y}_i, \hat {\bf b}_i } = f({\bf x})$$
concepts.motivation_md: To solve object detection computationally, we must translate the visual task into a mathematical mapping where the output is a structured set of coordinates and class probabilities.
concepts.recap_md: - Detection outputs a set of pairs containing a class vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$ and a box vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$.

concepts.title: Three Steps of Object Detection
concepts.one_liner: Most object detection approaches involve proposing candidate boxes, classifying the patches within them, and postprocessing to remove redundancies.
concepts.content: Most approaches for object detection have three main steps. In the first step, a set of candidate bounding boxes are proposed. In the second step, we loop over all proposed bounding boxes, and for each one, we apply a classifier to the image patch inside the bounding box. In the third and final step, the selected bounding boxes are postprocessed to remove any redundant detections.
concepts.motivation_md: Processing every possible rectangular area in an image is computationally impossible; this three-step pipeline breaks the problem into manageable stages of proposal, verification, and refinement.
concepts.recap_md: - Step 1: Propose candidate bounding boxes.

concepts.title: Window Scanning Approach
concepts.one_liner: The window scanning approach turns classification into detection by sliding a classifier across the image at multiple scales.
concepts.content:
In its simplest form, the problem of object localization is posed as a binary classification task, namely distinguishing between a single object class and the background class. Such a classification task can be turned into a detector by sliding it across the image (or image pyramid) and classifying each local window.

(see figure: Window scanning approach using a multiscale image pyramid.)

The window scanning algorithm is as follows:

(see figure: Window scanning algorithm.)

In this approach, location and translation invariance are achieved by the bounding box proposal mechanism. Additional invariances, such as rotation invariance, can be added by proposing rotated bounding boxes.
concepts.motivation_md: If you already have a good image classifier, the simplest way to find objects is to apply that classifier to every possible sub-region of the image.
concepts.recap_md: - Detection is achieved by sliding a binary classifier across different locations and scales.

concepts.title: Selective Search
concepts.one_liner: Selective search efficiently proposes candidate bounding boxes using a fast selection mechanism before applying a more expensive classifier.
concepts.content:
The window scanning approach can be slow as the same classifier needs to be applied to tens of thousands of image patches. Selective search makes the process more efficient by proposing an initial set of bounding boxes that are good candidates to contain an object. This proposal mechanism is performed by a selection mechanism simpler than the object classifier.

(see figure: Selective search pipeline.)

This approach was motivated by the strategy used by the visual system in which attention is first directed toward image regions likely to contain the target. This first attentional mechanism is very fast but might be wrong; therefore, a second, more accurate but also more expensive, processing stage is required to take a reliable decision. The advantage of this cascade of decisions is that the most expensive classifier is only applied to a sparse set of locations, dramatically reducing the overall computational cost.

The algorithm for selective search only differs from the window scanning approach in how the list of candidate bounding boxes is generated. Some approaches also add a bounding box refinement step.

(see figure: Selective search algorithm.)
concepts.motivation_md: Exhaustive window scanning is computationally expensive. Selective search uses cheap image features to identify likely object regions, ensuring expensive neural networks only process the most promising areas.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a fast, simple mechanism to propose a sparse set of candidate regions.

concepts.title: Cascade of Decisions
concepts.one_liner: A cascade of decisions applies expensive classifiers only to a sparse set of locations selected by a cheaper initial mechanism.
concepts.content: A cascade of decisions is a strategy where the most expensive classifier is only applied to a sparse set of locations—specifically those selected by a cheap attentional mechanism. This approach dramatically reduces the overall computational cost of the system.
concepts.motivation_md: In real-time systems, we cannot afford to run complex models on every pixel. Cascading allows us to quickly discard irrelevant data using low-cost filters, saving resources for difficult cases.
concepts.recap_md: - Filters out unlikely candidates using a fast, inexpensive first stage.

concepts.title: Selective Search Pipeline
concepts.one_liner: The selective search pipeline uses a four-step process of candidate generation, classification, refinement, and nonmaximum suppression to detect objects in images.
concepts.content:
This algorithm consists of four main steps. First, it uses an efficient window scanning approach to produce a set of candidate bounding boxes. Second, the algorithm loops over these candidate boxes, crops and resizes them to a canonical size, and applies an object classifier to determine if the crop contains the target object. Third, the bounding boxes for crops classified as containing the object are refined. Finally, low-scoring boxes are removed and nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is used to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object, ensuring only one bounding box is output for each instance.

(see figure: A first classifier selects candidate bounding boxes. A second, stronger, classifier makes the final detections (e.g., cars). Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) removes overlapping detections.)

Bounding box proposal (represented as $f_0$ in @fig-selective_search_architecture) can be implemented in several ways, such as image segmentation, neural networks, or window scanning with a low-cost classifier. The classification and bounding box refinement, $f_1$, are implemented by a classifier and a regression function.

(see figure: Sketch of the selective search architecture. The image is first broken into candidate regions. Then each region is processed individually using a classifier and a regression.)
concepts.motivation_md: Object detection is computationally expensive if every possible window in an image is processed by a complex model. This pipeline solves the efficiency problem by filtering candidates through progressively more expensive stages, focusing resources only on promising regions.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Generate candidate bounding boxes using efficient scanning or segmentation.", "- Classify and refine candidates, discarding those unlikely to contain the target.", "- Apply nonmaximum suppression to ensure a single detection per object instance." ]

concepts.title: Nonmaximum Suppression (NMS)
concepts.one_liner: Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is an iterative algorithm used to discard overlapping bounding boxes and output a single detection for each object instance.
concepts.content:
Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is used to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object, so as to output only one bounding box for each instance present in the image. The algorithm takes as input a set of object bounding boxes and confidences, $S=\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$, and outputs a smaller set by removing overlapping boxes. 

It is an iterative algorithm as follows: 
(1) Take the highest confidence bounding box from the set $S$ and add it to the final set $S^*$.
(2) Remove from $S$ the selected bounding box and all the bounding boxes with an IoU larger than a threshold.
(3) Go to step 1 until $S$ is empty.
concepts.motivation_md: Detectors often produce multiple overlapping bounding boxes for the same object. NMS provides a systematic way to select the most confident box and suppress redundant detections based on spatial overlap.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Select the bounding box with the highest confidence score.", "- Remove all other boxes that have an Intersection over Union (IoU) above a specific threshold with the selected box.", "- Repeat the process until no boxes remain in the original set." ]

concepts.title: Cascade of Classifiers
concepts.one_liner: A cascade of classifiers divides object search into a sequence of functions with increasing computational complexity and accuracy.
concepts.content:
Trying to localize an object in an image is difficult because the object is usually small and surrounded by a complex background. Selective search reduces this complexity by dividing the search into two steps: a fast, cheap classification function to detect candidate locations, and a slow, expensive function to accurately classify the object in those subsets. A cascade of classifiers pushes this idea to the limit by dividing the search into a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

(see figure: Cascade of classifiers algorithm.)
concepts.motivation_md: Localizing objects is like finding a needle in a haystack. Cascades allow systems to quickly reject obvious background regions using simple tests, saving expensive computations for the most promising and difficult areas of the image.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Use a sequence of classifiers that grow more complex at each stage.", "- Reject negative regions early to minimize computational cost.", "- Apply the most accurate and expensive classifiers only to high-probability candidates." ]

concepts.title: Viola-Jones Face Detector
concepts.one_liner: The Viola-Jones detector is a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers introduced in 2001.
concepts.content: Cascades of classifiers became popular in computer vision when Paul Viola and Michael Jones introduced them in 2001 with a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers. In parallel, Fleuret and Geman also proposed a system that performs a sequence of binary tests at each location, where each test checks for the presence of a particular image feature. Early versions of this strategy were inspired by the game "Twenty Questions."
concepts.motivation_md: Before this approach, real-time face detection was computationally prohibitive. The Viola-Jones detector proved that a cascade of simple features could achieve high accuracy with enough speed for live video applications.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Utilizes a cascade of boosted classifiers for real-time performance.", "- Performs a sequence of binary tests to check for specific image features.", "- Inspired by the efficiency of the game \"Twenty Questions.\"" ]

concepts.title: Computational Allocation in Cascades
concepts.one_liner: In a cascade, computational power is concentrated on image regions likely to contain the target object while flat regions are rejected quickly.
concepts.content:
In a cascade, computational power is allocated into the image regions that are more likely to contain the target object, while regions that are flat or contain few features are rejected quickly with almost no computations. This results in a heat map of computational cost where the intensity is proportional to the number of levels in the cascade applied to each location.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)
concepts.motivation_md: Uniformly processing every pixel in an image is wasteful. This approach ensures that the 'computational budget' is spent where it matters most—on complex regions that resemble the target object.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Focuses processing resources on high-probability regions.", "- Quickly rejects featureless or flat areas to save time.", "- Visualizes efficiency through heat maps of computational levels per location." ]

concepts.title: YOLO (You Only Look Once)
concepts.one_liner: YOLO (You Only Look Once) is an object detection approach that makes predictions by looking at the image globally for higher computational efficiency.
concepts.content: YOLO is an example of an object detector that makes predictions by looking at the image globally. While it may not be as accurate as some scanning methods, it can be computationally more efficient.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional scanning methods are slow because they look at thousands of individual crops. YOLO treats detection as a single regression problem from image pixels to bounding box coordinates, enabling much faster inference.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Processes the entire image globally in one pass.", "- Prioritizes computational efficiency over maximum possible accuracy.", "- Avoids the repetitive window scanning typical of older detectors." ]

concepts.title: Object Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: Object localization loss combines classification loss and localization loss to evaluate how well a detector identifies and places bounding boxes.
concepts.content:
The object localization loss accounts for two complementary tasks: classification and localization. 

- Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$): Measures if the predicted label matches the ground truth for a detected bounding box.
- Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$): Measures how close the detected location is to the ground truth object location.

To evaluate an image, the detector's output set of bounding boxes $\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$ is associated with ground truth labels $\{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. Predicted boxes overlapping with ground truth are optimized to improve locations and labels. Boxes that do not overlap are assigned to the background class ($\mathbf{y}_i=0$), and the model is optimized to reduce their predicted class scores $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$. Multiple detections can be assigned to the same ground truth box.

(see figure: (left) Detector output (using a low threshold to generate many detections). (middle) Ground truth bounding boxes (one color per instance). (right) Detector outputs that overlap with ground truth...)
concepts.motivation_md: Object detection requires knowing both 'what' an object is and 'where' it is. A specialized loss function is needed to simultaneously penalize incorrect labels and imprecise spatial coordinates.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Combines classification accuracy and spatial localization precision.", "- Assigns predicted boxes to ground truth instances or the background class.", "- Optimizes parameters to refine box coordinates and suppress false positives." ]

concepts.title: Classification Loss
concepts.one_liner: Classification loss measures whether the predicted label for a detected bounding box matches the ground truth using cross-entropy.
concepts.content:
Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$) evaluates whether the predicted label matches the ground truth at a specific location for each detected bounding box. Since each bounding box can only belong to one class, cross-entropy loss is used:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$

where $K$ is the number of classes.
concepts.motivation_md: In object detection, once a region is proposed, the model must decide which category it belongs to. Cross-entropy loss provides a differentiable way to maximize the probability assigned to the correct class.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Measures the discrepancy between predicted and ground truth class labels.", "- Utilizes cross-entropy loss for single-class assignment per box.", "- Sums the log-probabilities of the predicted classes weighted by ground truth." ]

concepts.title: Precision
concepts.one_liner: Precision is the percentage of correct detections among all positive predictions for a given threshold.
concepts.content:
From the quantities of detections and ground truth, we compute the precision as the percentage of correct detections:

$$
Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Precision measures the accuracy of a model's positive predictions, helping to quantify how often a detection is actually correct rather than a false alarm.
concepts.recap_md:
- Precision calculates the ratio of true positives to the total number of predicted positives.
- It is computed for a specific decision threshold $\beta$.

concepts.title: Recall
concepts.one_liner: Recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are correctly detected for a given decision threshold.
concepts.content:
Recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are detected for a given decision threshold $\beta$:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Recall is used to determine how well a model finds all relevant instances in a dataset, highlighting the impact of misdetections or false negatives.
concepts.recap_md:
- Recall is the ratio of correctly detected instances to the total number of actual ground truth instances.
- It quantifies the model's ability to avoid missing detections.

concepts.title: Average Precision (AP)
concepts.one_liner: Average precision (AP) summarizes the entire non-monotonic precision-recall curve as the area under the curve.
concepts.content: The precision-recall curve is non-monotonic. The average precision (AP) summarizes the entire curve with one number. The AP is the area under the precision-recall curve, and it is a number between 0 and 1.
concepts.motivation_md: Since precision and recall change with different thresholds, AP provides a single, comprehensive metric to evaluate a model's performance across all possible thresholds.
concepts.recap_md:
- AP represents the area under the precision-recall curve.
- It provides a single-number summary of model performance between 0 and 1.

concepts.title: Stuff vs. Objects
concepts.one_liner: The distinction between 'stuff' (unbounded regions like sky) and 'objects' (discrete instances) helps determine appropriate image representations.
concepts.content:
It is useful to differentiate between stuff and objects. Stuff refers to things that do not have well-defined boundaries such as grass, water, and sky. However, the distinction between stuff and objects is not very sharp. In some images, object instances might be easy to separate, like the two trees in the left image below, or become a texture where instances cannot be detected individually (as shown in the right image). In cases with lots of instances, bounding boxes might not be appropriate and it is better to represent the region as "trees" than to try to detect each instance.

(see figure: Bounding boxes are not an appropriate representation of the location of trees. This is true for many object classes with extended shapes that are hard to approximate with a box.)
concepts.motivation_md: Differentiating between stuff and objects helps researchers choose between semantic segmentation (for stuff) and instance detection (for objects), especially when bounding boxes fail to capture amorphous shapes.
concepts.recap_md:
- 'Stuff' refers to entities without well-defined boundaries like grass or sky.
- 'Objects' are discrete instances, though the boundary between stuff and objects can be blurry depending on the image context.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation typically utilizes a neural network with an encoder-decoder structure to process images.
concepts.content:
Generally the function $f$ is a neural network with an encoder-decoder structure (@fig-segmentation_architecture), first introduced in @Badrinarayanan2015.

(see figure: Sketch of the encoder-decoder architecture for semantic segmentation.)
concepts.motivation_md: The encoder-decoder architecture allows a network to first compress image information into high-level features and then project those features back to the original image resolution for pixel-wise labeling.
concepts.recap_md:
- Segmentation models often use an encoder-decoder neural network structure.
- This architecture was popularized by early works like SegNet (Badrinarayanan et al., 2015).

concepts.title: Multiclass Semantic Segmentation Loss
concepts.one_liner: The multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to every pixel across all classes and training examples.
concepts.content:
Training this function requires access to a dataset of segmented images. Each image in the training set will be associated with a ground truth segmentation, $y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right]$ for each class $c$. The multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel:

$$\mathcal{L}_{seg}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} \sum_{n,m}  y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right] \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right])$$

where the sum is over all the training examples, all classes, and all pixel locations. This loss might focus too much on the large objects and ignore small objects. Therefore, it is useful to add a weight to each class that normalizes each class according to its average area in the training set.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard cross-entropy allows for pixel-wise classification, but class weighting is often necessary to prevent the model from being biased toward large, frequent background classes like 'sky' or 'road'.
concepts.recap_md:
- The loss is calculated as a pixel-wise cross-entropy sum across all classes and images.
- Class weighting is recommended to ensure small objects are not ignored in favor of large ones.

concepts.title: Mean IoU for Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Mean IoU provides a scale-invariant measure of segmentation quality by averaging the Intersection over Union across all classes.
concepts.content: In order to evaluate the quality of the segmentation, we can measure the percentage of correctly labeled pixels. However, this measure will be dominated by the large objects (sky, road, etc.). A more informative measure is the average IoU across classes. The IoU is a measure that is invariant to scale and will provide a better characterization of the overall segmentation quality across all classes.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple pixel accuracy is misleading because a model can achieve high scores by only predicting large background classes; Mean IoU forces the model to perform well on all classes regardless of their size.
concepts.recap_md:
- Mean IoU averages the Intersection over Union metric across all object classes.
- It is preferred over pixel accuracy because it is invariant to the scale of objects in the image.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation to output localized objects as pixel-level masks.
concepts.content:
We can combine the ideas of object detection and semantic segmentation into the problem of instance segmentation. Here the idea is to output a set of localized objects, but rather than representing them as bounding boxes we represent them as pixel-level masks as shown in @fig-instance_segmentation.

(see figure: Instance segmentation. Each instance of the class car is assigned to a different color.)
concepts.motivation_md: Instance segmentation is needed when we need to distinguish between individual occurrences of the same class (e.g., separate cars) while also knowing their precise shapes.
concepts.recap_md:
- It identifies individual object instances and provides a unique mask for each.
- It differs from semantic segmentation by distinguishing between different instances of the same class.

concepts.title: CLIP Training Procedure

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP is trained by maximizing the dot product between matched image-text pairs and minimizing it for mismatched pairs within a batch.
concepts.content:
CLIP training begins by sampling a batch of $N$ language-image pairs, ${\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N$. These text strings and images are embedded using a language encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$, respectively, producing a set of text embeddings ${\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_t}_{i=1}^N$ and image embeddings ${\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell}_{i=1}^N$. To compute the loss, the dot product $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\cdot \mathbf{z}^{(j)}_t$ is calculated for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$. Terms where $i == j$ represent positive pairs, and the objective is to maximize these dot products. Terms where $i \neq j$ are negative pairs, and the objective is to minimize these dot products.

(see figure: CLIP training for one batch of six language-image training examples. Green boxes are positive pairings (we seek to increase their value); these are the six training pairs. Red boxes are negative...)
concepts.motivation_md: CLIP aims to learn a robust representation of visual concepts by leveraging the rich semantic information available in natural language descriptions, rather than relying on fixed categorical labels.
concepts.recap_md: - Sample a batch of $N$ image-text pairs and embed them into a shared vector space.

concepts.title: Visualizing CLIP Embeddings with t-SNE

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: t-SNE visualization of CLIP encoders reveals that image layers transition from grouping by color to shape, while text encoders treat both features with similar ease.
concepts.content:
A trained CLIP model maps data to embeddings in a way that can be visualized using t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) for each encoder. For the image encoder, early layers tend to group images by color, while later layers group them more by shape. In contrast, for the text encoder, color words and shape words are equally easy to group. This difference may arise because color is a superficial feature in pixel-space whereas shape requires more processing to extract; however, in text-space, both concepts are represented by words that are equally accessible to the model.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning mapping diagram, using the same technique as described in @sec-neural_nets_as_distribution_transformers. To reduce dimensionality we apply t-SNE @tsne separately for the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizing the internal representations of CLIP helps researchers understand how different modalities (images vs. text) process features like color and shape at various stages of the network.
concepts.recap_md: - Use t-SNE to reduce the dimensionality of image and text embeddings for visualization.

concepts.title: CLIP Shared Embedding Space

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP aligns normalized image and text embeddings on a hypersphere, placing matching descriptions and images in close proximity.
concepts.content:
After passing data through the encoders, the final stage is to normalize the outputs and compute the alignment between the image and text embeddings. Once normalized, all embeddings lie on the surface of a hypersphere. In this shared space, text descriptions are embedded near the image embeddings that match those descriptions. Visualizing this $768$-dimensional space in 2D can be achieved using kernel principle component analysis with a cosine kernel, often removing the first principle component to account for the global offset between image and text modalities.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning joint embedding)
concepts.motivation_md: Normalizing embeddings to a hypersphere allows the model to use cosine similarity as a consistent metric for comparing how well a text description matches an image.
concepts.recap_md: - Normalize embeddings so they lie on a hypersphere for alignment.

concepts.title: Kernel Principle Component Analysis

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Kernel Principle Component Analysis is a technique used to visualize high-dimensional embeddings by applying a kernel to capture non-linear relationships.
concepts.content: Kernel principle component analysis is applied to embeddings, often using a cosine kernel. In the context of CLIP, the first principle component is sometimes removed because it codes for a global offset between the image embeddings and text embeddings, allowing for a clearer visualization of the alignment between the two modalities.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard PCA only captures linear relationships; Kernel PCA allows for the dimensionality reduction of data that lies on non-linear manifolds, such as embeddings on a hypersphere.
concepts.recap_md: - Apply PCA with a cosine kernel to high-dimensional embeddings.

concepts.title: Zero-Shot Classification with CLIP

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP enables zero-shot classification by leveraging the compositional power of language to describe and identify novel image categories without specific training.
concepts.content: Using language as one of the views in contrastive methods allows CLIP to connect the domain of images to the domain of language. This connection makes the powerful compositional abilities of language applicable to imagery. For example, CLIP can create a novel image classifier on the fly by describing a category in English, such as "striped red circles" versus "polka dotted green squares." CLIP leverages the ability of language to compose concepts to construct an image classifier for these categories without requiring explicit training on those specific labels.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional classifiers are limited to a fixed set of labels; zero-shot classification allows models to generalize to any concept that can be described in text.
concepts.recap_md: - Use natural language to define new conceptual categories on the fly.

concepts.title: CLIP Inference Procedure

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP performs inference by comparing the embedding of a query image to the embeddings of several candidate text descriptions to find the best match.
concepts.content:
To classify an image using CLIP, given a set of sentences ${\mathbf{t}^{a}, \mathbf{t}^{b}, \ldots}$ describing classes $a, b$, etc.:

1. Embed each sentence into a $\mathbf{z}$-vector: $\mathbf{z}_t^{a} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{a}), \mathbf{z}_t^{b} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{b})$, and so on.
2. Embed the query image into a $\mathbf{z}$-vector: $\mathbf{z}_{\ell}^{q} = f_{\ell}(\boldsymbol\ell^{q})$.
3. Determine which sentence embedding is closest to the image embedding; that is the predicted class.

(see figure: Making a ``striped red circles'' (class $a$) versus ``polka dotted green square'' (class $b$) classifier using a trained CLIP. The CLIP model parameters are frozen and not updated. Instead the...)
concepts.motivation_md: This procedure allows for flexible, open-vocabulary image classification where the model does not need to be retrained to recognize new classes.
concepts.recap_md: - Embed candidate text descriptions and the query image into the same space.

concepts.title: Custom Classifiers with CLIP

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Custom classifiers can be built in CLIP by comparing the angular distance between an image embedding and multiple text-based class vectors.
concepts.content:
Custom binary or multi-class classifiers can be created by describing classes with text strings (e.g., "triangle" versus "circle"). The embeddings of these text descriptions serve as class vectors. To classify an image, the system checks whether the image embedding is closer in angular distance to one text vector or another. This approach is extensible; adding more text vectors allows the space to be partitioned in more ways to accommodate additional classes.

[FIGURE:bbc557ba56150a05 | A scatter plot showing data points arranged in a circular pattern on a 2D coordinate system ranging from -1.0 to 1.0 on both axes. The points are represented by different shapes (triangles, squares...]
concepts.motivation_md: This enables users to build specialized classifiers for niche tasks instantly, without collecting or labeling a training dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - Define classes using text strings and convert them to embeddings.

concepts.title: Translating between Images and Text
concepts.one_liner: X2Y systems use deep networks to translate between disparate data modalities, such as images to text or music to lyrics.
concepts.content: It is possible to translate between entirely different data modalities using deep networks. For any data type X and any other type Y, "X2Y" (and "Y2X") systems can forge links between disparate domains of knowledge. Examples include translating between images and sounds, music and lyrics, or amino acid sequences and protein geometry. These systems are powerful because they allow tools and discoveries from one domain to become applicable to other linked domains.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-modal translation allows for the integration of knowledge across different formats, enabling tasks like image captioning, text-to-image generation, and cross-domain search.
concepts.recap_md: - Use deep networks to map one data modality (X) to another (Y).

concepts.title: Definition of Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow is an approximation to the 2D motion field computed by measuring the displacement of image brightness between consecutive frames.
concepts.content:
Optical flow is an approximation to the 2D motion field computed by measuring the displacement of image brightness. Given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3}$, the optical flow $[\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}] \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 2}$ indicates the relative position of each pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and its corresponding pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. Note that optical flow changes if the time direction is reversed. This definition assumes a one-to-one mapping between frames, which may fail if objects appear, disappear, or are occluded. It also assumes a single motion explains all brightness changes, an assumption violated by transparent objects or moving light sources.

(see figure: Two frames of a sequence, ground-truth optical flow (color coded), and the color code to read the vector at each pixel.)

Visualization of optical flow often uses color coding or arrows to represent the vector at each pixel.
concepts.motivation_md: Optical flow allows us to estimate the motion of objects in a video sequence without knowing the 3D geometry of the scene, providing a fundamental tool for video compression, tracking, and navigation.
concepts.recap_md: - Optical flow approximates the 2D motion field by measuring pixel brightness displacement.

concepts.title: Optical Flow vs. Motion Field
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow and the physical motion field can differ when changes in image brightness do not correspond to the actual motion of 3D points.
concepts.content: There are several scenarios where motion in image brightness does not correspond to the motion of 3D points in the scene. For example, a rotating Lambertian sphere with static illumination produces no image changes, while a moving light source near a static sphere creates the appearance of motion. Moving in front of a textureless wall produces no change, and waves in water appear to move horizontally while the water actually moves vertically. Additionally, rotating mirrors or moving cameras in front of specular surfaces produce motion fields that do not correspond to standard physical homographies. Motion estimation models should ideally assign physical causes to these variations, though many basic models do not.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the distinction between optical flow and the motion field is crucial for identifying edge cases where visual algorithms might fail to correctly interpret physical reality.
concepts.recap_md: - Optical flow measures brightness changes, which may not match physical 3D motion.

concepts.title: The Aperture Problem
concepts.one_liner: The aperture problem occurs when observing a 1D structure larger than the viewing window, making it impossible to determine the actual motion direction.
concepts.content:
The aperture problem is a classic limitation of motion estimation from images. It occurs when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure that is larger than the image frame. If the termination points of the structure are not within the observation window (the aperture), it is impossible to measure the actual image motion. In such cases, only the component of motion orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

(see figure: Aperture problem when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame. The actual motion of the bar is upward, but the perception, when vision is limited to what...)
concepts.motivation_md: The aperture problem explains why local motion sensors (like individual pixels or small patches) cannot uniquely determine velocity, necessitating the use of global constraints or feature tracking.
concepts.recap_md: - The aperture problem arises when viewing 1D structures without visible endpoints.

concepts.title: Barber-pole Illusion
concepts.one_liner: The barber-pole illusion is a visual demonstration of the aperture problem where a rotating pole appears to move downward.
concepts.content:
The Barber-pole illusion is a classic illustration of the aperture problem. While the barber pole is actually rotating horizontally, the diagonal stripes induce the visual illusion of downward motion.

[FIGURE:62969696d2b66d2a | A barber pole with diagonal red and blue stripes. A curved arrow at the top labeled 'Real motion' indicates the pole is rotating horizontally. A downward-pointing arrow on the side labeled 'Observed...]
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion provides a concrete example of how the human visual system (and computer vision algorithms) can be misled by local motion signals when global context is restricted.
concepts.recap_md: - The barber-pole illusion demonstrates the aperture problem through rotating diagonal stripes.

concepts.title: Dense Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Dense optical flow models motion as a sequence of images where every pixel is assigned a velocity vector $(u, v)$ at each time step.
concepts.content: Motion over time can be modeled as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$[u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t)]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. A limitation of this formulation is the lack of an explicit representation of the trajectory followed by scene points over time; as $t$ changes, the location $(x,y)$ may correspond to different scene elements.
concepts.motivation_md: Dense optical flow is used when a complete motion map of the entire scene is required, such as in video segmentation or dense 3D reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Dense optical flow assigns a velocity vector to every pixel in an image.

concepts.title: Sparse Set of Moving Points
concepts.one_liner: This representation models motion by tracking a discrete set of specific scene points, known as tracks, over time.
concepts.content: An alternative representation models motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$ This approach requires establishing the correspondence of the same scene point over time, a process known as tracking. Because the appearance of a 3D point changes due to perspective projection and illumination, maintaining these correspondences on a dense array is difficult. Consequently, most point-based representations use a sparse set of points.
concepts.motivation_md: Sparse tracking is more computationally efficient and robust than dense methods for tasks like camera motion estimation (SLAM) or object tracking.
concepts.recap_md: - Sparse motion models track a discrete set of points rather than every pixel.

concepts.title: Brightness Constancy Assumption
concepts.one_liner: The brightness constancy assumption states that the brightness of a scene element remains unchanged as it moves between consecutive image frames.
concepts.content:
The brightness constancy assumption posits that as a scene element moves, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time. Mathematically, for a sequence $\ell(x,y,t)$, this is expressed as:

$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  = \ell(x,y,t)$$

where $u$ and $v$ are the element displacements over one unit of time. This relationship is equivalent to $\ell(x, y, t + 1) = \ell(x-u,y-v,t)$. 

(see figure: Translation to the right of a simple $6 \times 6$ size image.)
concepts.motivation_md: This assumption provides the necessary mathematical constraint to solve for unknown velocity variables by relating spatial gradients to temporal changes in intensity.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes pixel intensity of a moving object remains constant over time.

concepts.title: Lucas-Kanade Gradient-Based Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: The Lucas-Kanade method is a gradient-based technique that estimates optical flow by solving a system of linear equations derived from the brightness constancy assumption.
concepts.content:
The Lucas-Kanade method, introduced in 1981, is a popular gradient-based method for optical flow estimation. It approximates the change between consecutive frames using a first-order Taylor expansion:
$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  \simeq \ell(x,y,t) + u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t$$

Combining this with the brightness constancy assumption yields the gradient constraint equation: $$u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$$ This constrains motion $(u,v)$ to a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell$. To uniquely solve for motion, the method assumes the motion field is constant over a local neighborhood. By minimizing a weighted loss $\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum g | u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t | ^2$ over a window $g$, we obtain a $2 \times 2$ system:

$$\begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x ^ 2  & \sum g \ell_x \ell_y \\ \sum g \ell_x \ell_y & \sum g \ell_y ^ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x \ell_t \\ \sum g \ell_y \ell_t \end{bmatrix}$$

If the matrix is invertible, the flow is uniquely defined; otherwise, the aperture problem persists.

(see figure: Gradient-based optical flow estimation using two input frames.)
concepts.motivation_md: Lucas-Kanade provides a robust way to overcome the aperture problem by combining local information from a small patch of pixels to find a single consistent velocity.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a Taylor expansion to linearize the brightness constancy constraint.

concepts.title: Scale Calibration from Known Distances

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: If we are given one real distance, we can calibrate a 3D reconstruction that otherwise has an arbitrary scaling.
concepts.content: The point cloud has an arbitrary scaling, so we cannot directly use it to make 3D measurements. However, if we are given one real distance, we can calibrate the 3D reconstruction.
concepts.motivation_md: 3D reconstructions from point clouds often lack absolute scale, meaning we know the relative positions but not the actual size. Providing a single known distance allows us to map the arbitrary units to real-world measurements.
concepts.recap_md: - Point clouds generated from images typically have an arbitrary scale.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Depth from a Single Image

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised methods learn to perceive depth from single images by using motion and temporal consistency as a supervisory signal instead of ground truth data.
concepts.content: Although supervised techniques can be very effective, unsupervised techniques are more likely to eventually reach higher accuracy as they can learn from much larger amounts of data and improve over time. Unsupervised techniques pose a grander intellectual challenge: How can a system learn to perceive depth from a camera without supervision? We assume that the camera is calibrated, meaning the intrinsic camera parameters are known. There are a number of approaches one could imagine; for instance, we could use some of the single view metrology techniques to generate supervisory data. A different, and likely simpler, approach would be to use motion and temporal consistency as a supervisory signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Supervised depth estimation requires massive amounts of ground truth data, which is hard to collect. Unsupervised methods solve this by using the inherent geometric consistency of video sequences as a self-supervisory signal.
concepts.recap_md: - Unsupervised depth estimation leverages large datasets without needing manual ground truth labels.

concepts.title: Image Prediction Formulation for Unsupervised Depth

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised depth learning can be formulated as an image prediction problem where pixel values between frames are related by scene structure and camera motion.
concepts.content: As a camera moves in the world, the pixel values between two images captured at two different time instants are related by the 3D scene structure and the relative camera motion between the two frames. Therefore, we can formulate the problem as an image prediction problem. Let's say we have a function $f_1$ that can estimate depth from a single image, and a function $f_2$ that takes as input two frames, $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$, and estimates the relative camera positions (the rotation and translation matrices, $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$) between the two frames, as shown in (see figure: System for unsupervised learning of camera motion and depth @Tinghui2017. The goal is to learn the parameters of the functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ by minimizing the reconstruction error. The function...): $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{z}} &= f_1(\boldsymbol\ell) \\ \left[ \hat{\mathbf{R}},\hat{\mathbf{T}} \right] &= f_2(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2) \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: By framing depth estimation as an image prediction task, we can use the difference between a predicted frame and an actual frame as a loss function, removing the need for explicit depth labels.
concepts.recap_md: - The system uses one function to estimate depth and another to estimate relative camera motion.

concepts.title: Backward Warping for Unsupervised Depth Supervision

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Backward warping uses estimated depth and camera motion to map pixels from a reference frame to a target frame, providing a geometric constraint for unsupervised learning.
concepts.content: If the estimations of the depth and camera motion were correct, then we could warp the pixels in $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ into the pixels of $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ as depth and camera motion is all we need to precisely predict how the corresponding 3D points will move between the two frames. Warping is a deterministic function ($f_3$ in @fig-unsupervised_depth_system) that takes as input a reference frame, the depth map, and the relative camera motion matrices and outputs an image: $$\boldsymbol\ell_{1 \rightarrow 2} = f_3(\boldsymbol\ell_1, \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{T})$$ The goal is to warp a reference frame into a target frame. For each pixel location $\mathbf{x}$ in the target frame $\boldsymbol\ell_2$, we compute the corresponding location on the reference frame $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ using these steps: 1. Express the image coordinates of the pixel in the target frame in homogeneous coordinates, $\mathbf{p}$. 2. Recover the 3D world coordinates of the target point, $\mathbf{P}$, using the known intrinsic camera matrix and the estimated depth: $\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$, where $\hat{\mathbf{z}} = f_1(\boldsymbol\ell_2)$. 3. Use the camera rotation and translation matrices to change the camera coordinates to those of the reference frame: $\mathbf{P}' = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{P}$. 4. Project the point $\mathbf{P}'$ into the image coordinates of the reference frame: $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{P}'$. 5. Translate the resulting coordinates $\mathbf{p}'$ back into heterogeneous coordinates. (see figure: Geometry between two images captured by a moving camera. The coordinates of corresponding points between the two frames are constrained by the 3D world coordinates of the point the relative camera...)
concepts.motivation_md: Backward warping allows us to synthesize a target image from a reference image using predicted geometry. The difference between this synthesized image and the real target image acts as the training signal.
concepts.recap_md: - Backward warping maps target frame pixels back to a reference frame using estimated depth and motion.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Depth Reconstruction Loss

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The unsupervised depth loss measures the pixel-wise difference between a target image and a reconstruction generated by warping a reference image.
concepts.content: Putting all these steps together, ignoring the transformations between homogeneous and heterogeneous coordinates, the reconstruction of $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ results in: $$\ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{p}) = \ell_1 \left( \mathbf{K} \hat{\mathbf{M}} \hat{z}(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p} \right)$$ where $\boldsymbol\ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}$ is the result of warping image $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ into $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. As the coordinates of the point $\mathbf{p}'$ will not be discrete, we use bilinear interpolation to estimate the pixel value. If the reconstruction is correct, we expect the difference $\left| \ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}(\mathbf{p}) - \ell_{2}(\mathbf{p}) \right|$ to be very small. The functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ can be neural networks and their parameters can be obtained by running back-propagation over the loss: $$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{n,m} v\left(n,m \right) \left( \ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}[n,m] - \ell_{2}[n,m] \right) ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: To train a model without ground truth depth, we need a proxy loss. The photometric error between the warped reference frame and the actual target frame serves as this proxy.
concepts.recap_md: - The loss function calculates the squared difference between the warped reference image and the target image.

concepts.title: Valid Pixel Masking in Depth Learning

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Valid pixel masking restricts the depth learning loss to pixels that are visible in both frames and not part of moving objects.
concepts.content: As only the pixels with coordinates $\mathbf{p}'$ inside the image can be reconstructed by warping, we compute the loss only over the valid set of pixels. This is done using the mask $v\left(n,m \right)$, which is 1 for valid pixels and 0 for pixels that lie outside the visible part of the reference frame. The mask could also exclude pixels that fall in moving objects as those will have displacements that cannot predicted by the motion of the camera alone.
concepts.motivation_md: Not all pixels in a target frame can be found in a reference frame due to camera motion or occlusions. Masking prevents the model from being penalized for errors it cannot geometrically resolve.
concepts.recap_md: - A binary mask $v(n,m)$ identifies which pixels should contribute to the reconstruction loss.

concepts.title: Camera Motion Requirements for Depth Learning

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Learning depth from single images requires complex camera motions in rich 3D environments to distinguish depth from simple image transformations.
concepts.content: Not all camera motions provide enough information to learn about the 3D world structure. As discussed in the context of homographies, if all the videos contain only sequences captured by a rotating camera, the points are related by a homography regardless of the 3D structure. Therefore, to learn depth from single images, we need to have complex camera motions inside environments with rich 3D structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Pure rotation doesn't produce parallax, which is the primary cue for depth. Without translation, a system cannot distinguish between a flat image and a 3D scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Purely rotating cameras produce homographies that do not reveal 3D scene structure.

concepts.title: Biological Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Biological motion refers to the unique movement patterns of living organisms that allow humans to recognize actions from just a few moving points.
concepts.content: In 1971, Gunnar Johansson, a Swedish psychologist working on gestalt laws of motion perception, created a series of videos recording the movements of a person with a set of lights attached to a few body joints (e.g., elbows, knees, feet, head, and hands as illustrated in @fig-demos_motivation_sfm[b]). He introduced the term **biological motion** to describe the typical motion of biological organisms. Johansson demonstrated that by watching the motion of only a few of those points, no more than 12, it was possible to clearly recognize the person's actions. By showing only moving points, Johansson dissociated the perception of form/shape from the motion pattern. These demonstrations have been used to argue about the importance of reliably tracking a few points over time.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights how motion alone, independent of static shape or form, carries significant information about the structure and intent of biological entities.
concepts.recap_md: - Humans can recognize complex actions from the motion of as few as 12 points on a body.

concepts.title: Writing a dynamite introduction
concepts.one_liner: A dynamite introduction must clearly state what the paper is about, the problem it solves, why it is interesting, what is new, and why it is neat.
concepts.content: Regarding paper introductions, Kajiya writes, "You must make your paper easy to read. You've got to make it easy for anyone to tell what your paper is about, what problem it solves, why the problem is interesting, what is really new in your paper (and what isn't), why it's so neat. And you must do it up front. In other words, you must write a dynamite introduction."
