concepts.motivation_md: The introduction is the first thing a reader encounters. If it fails to immediately communicate the paper's value and novelty, the reader may lose interest before reaching the core contributions.
concepts.recap_md: - Make the paper easy to read by stating the problem and solution up front.

concepts.title: Visualizing the main idea
concepts.one_liner: Showing a simple example that captures the main idea of a paper can be very helpful for reader comprehension.
concepts.content: When appropriate to the paper, it can be very helpful to show a simple example that captures the main idea of the paper. (see figure: Effect of translation on the wavelet representation of a signal (caption and figure after @Simoncelli92. (a) An input signal. (b-d) The high-, mid-, and low-frequency coefficients within a wavelet...) The figure above from a different paper conveys a main idea very simply. The paper's main idea was that wavelets lacked important desirable features for an image representation. @fig-wavelet shows the failure of a wavelet representation to form a translation invariant representation. The top row shows two versions of the same signal, differing only in a one-sample translation. The bottom three rows show the coefficients of the high-, mid-, and low-frequency bands of a wavelet representation of that signal. The figure points out in a simple way the drawback of a wavelet representation with aliased subbands that was the focus of the paper: as the signal translates, the signal representation energy moves to different frequency bands and changes form within the mid-frequency band.
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizations allow readers to grasp complex technical arguments quickly through concrete examples, making the paper's core thesis more accessible and memorable.
concepts.recap_md: - Use simple examples to visually capture the paper's main idea.

concepts.title: Experimental evidence in research papers
concepts.one_liner: Modern standards require that assertions in a research paper be backed up with quantitative experimental evidence.
concepts.content: In earlier days of computer vision research, good ideas could be presented with only plausibility arguments to support them. However, modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence. Readers will be expecting a table quantitatively comparing the performance of your algorithm with that of the previous state-of-the-art. If you are proposing a new task for which there aren't previous benchmarks, you should still compare with an algorithm that solves a related task, noting that the algorithm was designed for a different task. (see figure: prototypical table of results, from \cite{Owens2016} Rows are different algorithms, or ablations of a favored algorithm. Columns are datasets or tasks, and the numbers indicate performance, with the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Plausibility arguments are no longer sufficient in modern research; quantitative comparisons provide the objective proof needed to validate a new algorithm's effectiveness against existing methods.
concepts.recap_md: - Back up all claims with experimental evidence and quantitative data.

concepts.title: Strategies for ending a paper
concepts.one_liner: Instead of listing unfinished work, a paper should end by reviewing contributions and emphasizing how the research changes the field.
concepts.content: You should resist the temptation to describe the items that were left unfinished in a section on "Future Work." It is hard to imagine a weaker way to end the paper than to enumerate all the things the paper doesn't accomplish, providing a summary of where it falls short. Instead, the paper can finish with a review of what has been presented, emphasizing the contributions. How has the world changed, now that the reader has read this paper? What new research directions have been opened up; what can we do now that we couldn't do before?
concepts.motivation_md: Ending on a list of failures or uncompleted tasks leaves the reader with a negative impression. A strong conclusion reinforces the paper's value and its impact on future research.
concepts.recap_md: - Avoid ending with a "Future Work" section that highlights shortcomings.

concepts.title: Reader-centric writing principle
concepts.one_liner: The most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind, anticipating their needs and expectations.
concepts.content: Donald Knuth wrote, "Perhaps the most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind: What does the reader know so far? What does the reader expect next and why?" Our mental image is that of a great host, who anticipates every need of their house guest. At every moment, they know what you might be wanting and how to help you find it.
concepts.motivation_md: Writing is a form of communication; by anticipating the reader's questions and knowledge level, the author ensures the information is transmitted effectively and clearly.
concepts.recap_md: - Always consider what the reader knows and what they expect next.

concepts.title: Concise writing principle
concepts.one_liner: Vigorous writing is concise, containing no unnecessary words or sentences to ensure clarity and respect page limits.
concepts.content: In *The Elements of Style*, Strunk and White write, "Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts." Writing more concisely helps your paper in two ways. First, researchers are typically fighting against a page limit, particularly in conference submissions, so tighter text lets the author say more or add another figure. Second, concise text is usually clearer and easier to understand.
concepts.motivation_md: Conciseness improves readability and allows authors to fit more information into the strict page limits common in scientific publishing.
concepts.recap_md: - Eliminate unnecessary words and sentences to improve clarity.

concepts.title: Reader engagement and skimming
concepts.one_liner: Since many readers only skim papers, the title, figures, and abstract must be self-contained to convey the top-level message.
concepts.content: While we may imagine our reader reading every word of our paper, in our current era of many published papers, most of your readers will probably only skim your paper. (see figure: The conjectured readership of a computer science paper (conjectured relative amounts). Many people will read the title, but far fewer will read the abstract or look at the figures. Fewer still will...) You should write your paper so that readers will learn from it, even at reduced levels of engagement. The title should convey the top-level message of the paper. The figures and their captions should be self-contained and tell the story of the paper. The abstract should provide a good summary.
concepts.motivation_md: In a high-volume publishing environment, authors must optimize for skimmers to ensure their core message reaches the widest possible audience.
concepts.recap_md: - Design titles, figures, and abstracts to be informative even when skimmed.

concepts.title: Self-contained figure captions
concepts.one_liner: Figure captions should be self-contained so that readers can understand the main takeaway without reading the full paper.
concepts.content: Because you can assume that many of the readers of your figure captions will not be reading the full paper, the captions should be self-contained. They should point out what readers are supposed to notice about the figure, to help both the full-paper reader and the figures-only reader. (see figure: Figure and caption from \cite{FreemanShapetime}. The caption should be understandable by itself, and should point to what the reader should take away from the figure.)
concepts.motivation_md: Many readers browse figures before (or instead of) reading the text; self-contained captions ensure these readers still grasp the paper's key evidence and results.
concepts.recap_md: - Write captions that explain the figure's significance independently of the main text.

concepts.title: Writing with equations
concepts.one_liner: Your sentences should flow smoothly when all but the simplest formulas are replaced by 'blah' or some other grunting noise.
concepts.content: Equations interposed with text can pose a challenge to the reader, who must decide whether to stop to work through each equation or continue reading as if the equations were words. To address this, your sentences should flow smoothly even when complex formulas are replaced by a placeholder like "blah." Additionally, when referring to an equation, identify it by a descriptive phrase as well as a number. For example, instead of merely saying "inserting (2.47) and (3.51) into (5.13)," it is more helpful to say "inserting the form (2.47) of the electric field $E$ and the Lindhard form (3.51) of the dielectric function $\epsilon$ into the constitutive equation (5.13)."
concepts.motivation_md: Mathematical notation can disrupt the narrative flow of a technical paper. These guidelines ensure that readers can follow the logical argument of a text without being forced to decode every complex equation on their first pass.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ensure sentences remain grammatically coherent even if formulas are ignored.
 - Identify equations by both their reference number and a descriptive phrase.

concepts.title: Tone in scientific writing
concepts.one_liner: Develop a reputation for being clear and reliable by maintaining a generous, honest, and accurate tone in your writing.
concepts.content: The tone of your writing is critical; you should resist the pressure to oversell results, hide drawbacks, or disparage the work of others. If your work has a shortcoming, it is better to point it out yourself than to have someone else discover it later. Adopting a generous tone—viewing colleagues as good researchers doing their best—promotes long-lasting professional relationships and wins over readers. You should aim for a reputation of clarity and reliability by always conveying an accurate impression of an algorithm's performance. If a method fails in important cases, inform the reader, as documenting counterintuitive results or failures can prove valuable to the field in the long term.
concepts.motivation_md: Maintaining a professional and honest tone builds credibility with the scientific community and prevents future embarrassment when limitations are inevitably discovered.
concepts.recap_md:
- Be honest about shortcomings and failures in your own work.
 - Use a generous tone toward other researchers to build professional goodwill.
 - Prioritize accuracy and reliability over overselling your results.

concepts.title: Managing Public Speaking Nervousness
concepts.one_liner: Manage public speaking nervousness by practicing aloud and focusing on the information rather than yourself.
concepts.content: A great cure for nervousness is to practice the talk aloud, both by yourself and in front of friends. One approach to calming nerves is to remind yourself that the audience is there to hear the information, not to judge you personally; your role is simply to convey that information. As Dr. Rob Gilbert suggests, it is acceptable to have butterflies in your stomach as long as you get them to "fly in formation."
concepts.motivation_md: Nervousness is a common barrier to effective communication. Shifting focus from self-consciousness to information delivery helps speakers maintain composure.
concepts.recap_md:
- Practice your talk aloud multiple times to build confidence.
 - Focus on the goal of conveying information to the audience.
 - Channel nervous energy into a structured, controlled delivery.

concepts.title: Understanding the Distracted Audience
concepts.one_liner: Recognize that your audience is often distracted and prepare specifically to engage them.
concepts.content: Before giving a talk, you might imagine an audience listening to your every word, but in reality, most audiences are collections of people checking social media, looking at laptops, or feeling hungry and fidgety. To speak effectively to such a group, you must practice and prepare specifically to engage them and pull their attention back to your presentation.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the reality of audience behavior helps speakers move away from passive lecturing toward active engagement strategies.
concepts.recap_md:
- Accept that audiences are naturally prone to distraction.
 - Prepare your talk with the specific goal of capturing and holding attention.

concepts.title: Engaging the Audience with Questions
concepts.one_liner: Engage your audience by asking them questions and giving them sub-problems to solve.
concepts.content: One of the most effective techniques to get an audience more engaged in a talk is to ask them questions. The audience is like a sheepdog that wants to be working; you should give them something to work on while they listen. For instance, posing a sub-problem you encountered in your work encourages the audience to think about how they would solve it, making them more receptive to hearing your eventual solution.
concepts.motivation_md: Active participation prevents the audience from becoming passive observers and helps them internalize the logic of your research.
concepts.recap_md:
- Use questions to draw the audience into the presentation.
 - Present sub-problems to give the audience a task to work on mentally.

concepts.title: Layering the Talk with Verbal Cues
concepts.one_liner: Layer your talk with verbal cues to help both attentive and distracted listeners follow your structure.
concepts.content: It is easier for an audience to follow a talk if you layer it by providing verbal cues for new concepts and transitions between sections. These cues help attentive listeners follow the structure and prevent distracted listeners from becoming completely lost. By using phrases like "Now, how do we find the optimal value?" or "With these tools in hand, we can apply these methods," you provide verbal headings that allow even someone only partially listening to follow your main points.
concepts.motivation_md: Verbal signposting acts as a map for the listener, ensuring that even if they tune out for a moment, they can quickly re-orient themselves within the talk.
concepts.recap_md:
- Use verbal cues to signal transitions and new concepts.
 - Provide "verbal headings" to help distracted listeners track the main points.

concepts.title: Using Verbal Dynamics and Enthusiasm
concepts.one_liner: Use variations in speed, intensity, and personal enthusiasm to make your talk easier to follow.
concepts.content: Adding verbal dynamics—variations in speed or intensity—makes a talk more engaging. You should identify parts of your work that are particularly special to you and let your enthusiasm show. For example, expressing why a specific problem is beautiful or interesting can captivate an audience, as they enjoy watching a speaker who is genuinely excited about their subject matter.
concepts.motivation_md: Monotone delivery can lead to audience disengagement. Expressing genuine passion helps maintain interest and highlights the most important parts of the talk.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vary your speed and intensity to emphasize key points.
 - Show genuine enthusiasm for your subject to connect with the audience.

concepts.title: Engaging the Audience with Competing Conjectures
concepts.one_liner: Engage the audience by setting up a 'fight' between two competing conjectures.
concepts.content: Audiences love to watch a good fight, which can be facilitated by setting up a competition between two conjectures. For example, you might contrast the predictions of a flat earth theory against a round earth theory regarding how ships appear on the horizon. By showing the expected results for each theory—as in (see figure: The appearance of ships approaching a port, from the flat-earth theory.) and (see figure: Their appearance as predicted by the round-earth theory.)—you build anticipation. The audience then waits to see the experimental evidence, such as (see figure: The experimental evidence: a photograph of ships approaching a port.), which reveals the winning theory.
concepts.motivation_md: Framing research as a choice between competing ideas creates narrative tension and makes the eventual results more satisfying and memorable.
concepts.recap_md:
- Frame your research as a competition between different theories.
 - Use visual evidence to reveal which conjecture is correct.

concepts.title: Color Appearance of Different Spectral Bands
concepts.one_liner: The visible spectrum can be divided into three 100 nm bands—blue, green, and red—whose combinations determine the approximate color appearance of light.
concepts.content: The visible spectrum lies roughly in the range between 400 and 700 nm. We can divide the visible spectrum into three 100 nm bands and study the appearance of light power spectra where power is present or absent from each of those three bands. (see figure: The approximate color appearance of light over different spectral regions.) Light with spectral power distributed in just the 400–500 nm wavelength band will look some shade of blue, while light in the 500–600 nm band will appear greenish. Most distributions within the 600–700 nm band will look red. White light is a mixture of all spectral colors; a spectrum containing power evenly distributed over 400–700 nm would appear approximately white. Light with no power in any of those three bands, that is, darkness, appears black. There are three other spectral classes in this simplified grouping: spectral power present in two bands but missing in the third. Cyan is a combination of blue and green (roughly 400–600 nm), sometimes called minus red. Magenta is a combination of blue and red (400–500 nm and 600–700 nm), or minus green. Red and green together (500–700 nm) make yellow, or minus blue. (see figure: For coarse orientation only, this cartoon model gives the color appearance of different spectral bands of the spectrum of visible light.)
concepts.motivation_md: Developing a feel for how different spectral bands contribute to perceived color helps simplify the complex relationship between physical light spectra and subjective human vision.
concepts.recap_md: - The visible spectrum (400–700 nm) can be simplified into three primary bands: blue, green, and red.

concepts.title: Diffuse Surface Reflection Model
concepts.one_liner: The diffuse reflection model describes the reflected power spectrum as the wavelength-by-wavelength product of incident light and a surface's reflectance spectrum.
concepts.content: When light reflects off a surface, the power spectrum alters in ways that depend on the surface's characteristics and geometry. While reflections can be complex and described by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF), many matte reflections are characterized by a diffuse reflection model. In this model, the power spectrum of the reflected light, $r(\lambda)$, is proportional to the wavelength-by-wavelength product of the power spectrum of the incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and a reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of the surface: $$r(\lambda) = k \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) s(\lambda),$$ where the proportionality constant $k$ depends on the reflection geometry. This wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is also a good model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through an attenuating filter, where the incident power spectrum is multiplied by a transmittance spectrum. (see figure: Reflectance spectra from two flowers @Arnold2010. The blue *Hepatica nobilis* flower @nobilis and the orange flower, *Pyrostegia venusta* @venusta}.)
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling how surfaces modify light spectra is essential for understanding how we perceive object colors and for simulating realistic light-surface interactions in computer graphics.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffuse reflection is modeled as the product of the incident light spectrum and the surface's reflectance spectrum at each wavelength.

concepts.title: Reflectance Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: A reflectance spectrum $s(\lambda)$ represents the proportion of incident light a surface reflects at each wavelength.
concepts.content: The reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of a surface is used to determine the reflected light spectrum. In the diffuse reflection model, the reflected power spectrum is proportional to the wavelength-by-wavelength product of the incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and this reflectance spectrum.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a physical description of a material's color properties independent of the light source illuminating it.
concepts.recap_md: - The reflectance spectrum $s(\lambda)$ defines a surface's intrinsic color characteristics.

concepts.title: Transmittance Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: A transmittance spectrum describes the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling of light as it passes through an attenuating filter.
concepts.content: The transmittance spectrum of an attenuating filter describes how the incident power spectrum is multiplied at each wavelength as light passes through it. This wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is a model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through such a filter.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding transmittance is crucial for designing filters and understanding how transparent or translucent materials alter the color of light.
concepts.recap_md: - Transmittance spectra characterize how filters or materials attenuate light at different wavelengths.

concepts.title: Color Constancy and Illumination Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Color constancy is the visual system's ability to estimate surface reflectance by accounting for the unknown spectrum of the illumination.
concepts.content: To estimate surface colors, a vision system must estimate the illumination spectrum and the surface reflectance spectra from observations of only their products. When the illumination is white light, the observed reflected spectrum is proportional to the reflectance spectrum of the material. However, under unknown illumination, a visual system must estimate the surface reflectance spectrum by taking the context of nearby image information into account. Algorithms to do this range from simple heuristics to statistical and neural network approaches. Humans do not solve this perfectly, as seen in the viral optical illusion of "The Dress." (see figure: A photograph of a striped dress that became a famous viral optical illusion. The dress features horizontal bands of lace and fabric that appear to some as blue and black, and to others as white and...) (see figure: A diagram illustrating the color constancy ambiguity of 'The Dress'. A central image of a striped dress is shown twice: once on the left under yellow 'warm illumination' where it appears as blue and...) The perceived colors of the dress depend on the assumed color of the illumination. Assuming warm, yellowish illumination leads to a perception of blue and black material, while assuming cool, blueish illumination leads to a perception of white and gold.
concepts.motivation_md: Color constancy allows organisms to recognize objects consistently across different lighting conditions, such as direct sunlight versus shade.
concepts.recap_md: - Color constancy involves disentangling the contribution of the light source from the intrinsic reflectance of a surface.

concepts.title: The Machinery of the Eye
concepts.one_liner: The human eye reduces the high-dimensional light spectrum into a three-dimensional description using three classes of cone photoreceptors.
concepts.content: While instruments like spectrographs can measure light power at hundreds of wavelengths, the human visual system obtains a useful description of the world from a much lower dimensional representation. The retina contains photoreceptors called rods and cones. Rods are used in low-light levels, while cones are used in color vision. The human visual system analyzes the incident light power spectrum with only three different classes of photoreceptors, called the L, M, and S cones because they sample at the long, medium, and short wavelengths. This gives the visual system a three-dimensional (3D) description of light, with each photoreceptor class taking a different weighted average of the incident light power spectrum. (see figure: A diagram showing a mosaic of red, green, and blue circles representing the spatial distribution of L, M, and S cones in a human retina. The red and green circles are most numerous and are arranged...) (see figure: A graph showing the normalized spectral sensitivity curves for the three types of human cone cells: S (short-wavelength, blue curve), M (medium-wavelength, green curve), and L (long-wavelength, red...) In the retina, cones are close-packed in a hexagonal pattern, particularly near the fovea, with a stochastic assignment of classes. Notably, the spatial sampling of S cones is much sparser than that of L or M cones.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the biological constraints of the eye explains why we perceive color the way we do and provides the basis for three-component color models like RGB.
concepts.recap_md: - Human color vision is trichromatic, based on three types of cone cells (L, M, and S).

concepts.title: Rods and Cones
concepts.one_liner: Rods and cones are the two types of photoreceptors in the retina, responsible for low-light vision and color vision, respectively.
concepts.content: The retina contains photoreceptors called rods and cones. Rods are used in low-light levels, and the cones are used in color vision. In low-light, only the rods operate and our vision becomes black and white.
concepts.motivation_md: This dual-receptor system allows the eye to function across a vast range of light intensities, from dim starlight to bright sunlight.
concepts.recap_md: - Rods provide high sensitivity for vision in low-light environments but do not perceive color.

concepts.title: L, M, and S Cones
concepts.one_liner: L, M, and S cones are the three classes of photoreceptors that sample long, medium, and short wavelengths to enable trichromatic color vision.
concepts.content: The human visual system analyzes the incident light power spectrum with three classes of photoreceptors: the L, M, and S cones, which sample long, medium, and short wavelengths respectively. This results in a three-dimensional (3D) description of light, where each class takes a different weighted average of the spectrum. (see figure: A diagram showing a mosaic of red, green, and blue circles representing the spatial distribution of L, M, and S cones in a human retina. The red and green circles are most numerous and are arranged...) (see figure: A graph showing the normalized spectral sensitivity curves for the three types of human cone cells: S (short-wavelength, blue curve), M (medium-wavelength, green curve), and L (long-wavelength, red...) These cones are arranged in a hexagonal packing in the retina, with L and M cones being much more numerous than the sparser S cones. This sampling pattern is most dense near the fovea.
concepts.motivation_md: These specific receptors define the spectral sensitivity of human vision and determine which wavelengths of light we can distinguish as different colors.
concepts.recap_md: - L, M, and S cones respond to long, medium, and short wavelengths, respectively.

concepts.title: Direct Approach to Generative Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The direct approach to generative modeling learns the function $G: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$ to map latent variables to data.
concepts.content: There are two general approaches to forming data generators. The direct approach involves learning the function $G: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. In the generative modeling literature, the direct approach is sometimes called an implicit model because the probability density is never explicitly represented. However, this model explicitly describes the way data is generated. The direct approach has recently become popular with models like generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models, as schematized in @fig-generative_models-gen_model_training_vs_sampling.
concepts.motivation_md: The direct approach simplifies generative modeling by learning a straight mapping from a simple noise source to complex data. This avoids the need to explicitly define or compute complex probability densities, enabling the high-fidelity synthesis seen in modern GANs and diffusion models.
concepts.recap_md: - Learns a direct mapping function $G: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$ from latent space to data space. - Does not explicitly represent the probability density of the data. - Includes modern architectures like GANs and diffusion models.

concepts.title: Indirect Approach to Generative Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The indirect approach learns a function $E: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and generates samples by finding values for $\mathbf{x}$ that score highly under this function.
concepts.content: There are two general approaches to forming data generators. The indirect approach involves learning a function $E: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and generating samples by finding values for $\mathbf{x}$ that score highly under this function. This classical approach describes many statistical image models and comes in two general flavors: density models and energy models. Both follow the schematic given in @fig-generative_models-gen_model_training_vs_sampling_indirect: (see figure: The indirect approach to generative modeling. The scoring function can be either a probability density or an energy function. The models we learned about in @sec-stat_image_models.) Samples are produced from the scoring function as output.
concepts.motivation_md: The indirect approach allows us to define what constitutes 'good' data through a scoring or density function. This provides a classical framework for modeling data that is useful for both generating new samples and evaluating the quality of existing ones.
concepts.recap_md: - Learns a scoring function $E: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ rather than a direct mapping. - Generates samples by finding values that score highly under the learned function. - Includes density models and energy models as its two primary flavors.

concepts.title: Implicit Model
concepts.one_liner: An implicit model is a direct approach to generative modeling where the probability density is never explicitly represented.
concepts.content: In the generative modeling literature, the direct approach is sometimes called an implicit model. This is because the probability density is never explicitly represented. However, note that this "implicit" model explicitly describes the way data is generated.
concepts.motivation_md: Implicit models focus entirely on the data generation process rather than calculating probabilities. This allows for more flexible and complex model architectures, like GANs, which can produce high-quality samples without the mathematical constraints of explicit density estimation.
concepts.recap_md: - A generative model that describes the data generation process without an explicit density function. - Another term for the direct approach to generative modeling. - Examples include GANs and diffusion models.

concepts.title: Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Density models are generative models that yield a probability density function $p_{\theta}$ fit to the training data.
concepts.content: Some generative models not only produce generators but also yield a probability density function $p_{\theta}$, fit to the training data. This density function may play a role in training the generator (e.g., we want the generator to produce samples from $p_{\theta}$), or the density function may be the goal itself (e.g., we want to be able to estimate the probability of datapoints in order to detect anomalies). Some generative models only produce a density $p_{\theta}$ and do not learn any explicit generator function; instead, samples can be drawn from $p_{\theta}$ using a sampling algorithm that takes a density as input and produces samples from it as output. This is a form of the indirect approach to synthesizing data.
concepts.motivation_md: Beyond just creating new samples, we often need to know how likely a specific data point is. Density models solve this by providing an explicit probability function, which is critical for applications like detecting outliers or understanding the underlying structure of the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models that explicitly fit a probability density function $p_{\theta}$ to training data. - Useful for estimating the likelihood of points and detecting anomalies. - May rely on sampling algorithms like MCMC to synthesize new data.

concepts.title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a sampling algorithm that takes a density as input and produces samples from it as output.
concepts.content: Samples can be drawn from a density $p_{\theta}$ using a sampling algorithm, such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), that takes a density as input and produces samples from it as output. This is a form of the indirect approach to synthesizing data.
concepts.motivation_md: Many powerful generative models define a probability density but do not provide a direct way to generate new data points. MCMC sampling solves this by providing a general-purpose algorithm to produce samples from any given density function.
concepts.recap_md: - A sampling algorithm that produces data points from a given probability density function. - Enables the indirect approach to generative modeling. - Essential for models that provide a density but lack a direct generation function.

concepts.title: Divergence between Distributions
concepts.one_liner: A divergence measures the closeness between two distributions and is defined by nonnegativity and the property that $D(p,q) = 0 \iff p=q$.
concepts.content: To measure closeness between a model distribution $p_{\theta}$ and the data distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}$, we can define a divergence $D$ and solve the optimization problem $\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} D(p_{\theta}, p_{\texttt{data}})$. Since we only have samples $\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$, we need a divergence $D$ that measures the distance between $p_{\theta}$ and $p_{\texttt{data}}$ while only accessing samples. A divergence need not be a proper distance metric; it can be nonsymmetric and need not satisfy the triangle inequality. It is defined by just two properties: nonnegativity and $D(p,q) = 0 \iff p=q$.
concepts.motivation_md: In generative modeling, we need a way to quantify how closely our model's distribution matches the true data distribution. Since we only have access to samples of the real data, we require a mathematical measure—a divergence—that can be estimated from those samples to guide the optimization process.
concepts.recap_md: - A mathematical measure of the difference between two probability distributions. - Defined by nonnegativity and being zero only when the distributions are identical. - Does not need to be symmetric or satisfy the triangle inequality.

concepts.title: Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
concepts.one_liner: The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is a measure of distribution closeness that, when minimized, is equivalent to maximizing the expected log likelihood of the training data.
concepts.content: A common choice for measuring distribution closeness is the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, defined as follows: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}^* &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right)\\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\Big[-\log \frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}{p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})}\Big]\\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})\big]\\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] \quad \triangleleft \quad\text{dropped second term since no dependence on $p_{\theta}$} \\ &\approx \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$ The final line is an empirical estimate of the expectation by sampling over the training dataset. This is the expected log likelihood of the training data under the model's density function. $\mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right)$ is sometimes called the forward KL divergence, measuring the probability of the data under the model distribution, while the reverse KL divergence $\mathrm{KL}\left(p_\theta \| p_{\text {data }}\right)$ measures the probability of the model's samples under the data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: KL divergence provides a principled information-theoretic way to measure the difference between distributions. Its forward form is particularly useful because it simplifies into the maximum likelihood objective, which is the standard method for fitting statistical models to observed data.
concepts.recap_md: - A divergence measure used to quantify the difference between two probability distributions. - Minimizing forward KL divergence is equivalent to maximizing the log likelihood of the data. - Can be estimated empirically by averaging log probabilities over a training dataset.

concepts.title: Forward KL Divergence
concepts.one_liner: Forward KL divergence, $\mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right)$, measures the probability of the data under the model distribution.
concepts.content: $\mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right)$ is sometimes called the forward KL divergence, and it measures the probability of the data under the model distribution. The reverse KL divergence, $\mathrm{KL}\left(p_\theta \| p_{\text {data }}\right)$, does the converse, measuring the probability of the model's samples under the data distribution; because we do not have access to the true data distribution, the reverse KL divergence usually cannot be computed.
concepts.motivation_md: While there are multiple ways to measure the distance between distributions, the forward KL divergence is the most practical for training models on real-world datasets because it can be estimated using only the available data samples, unlike the reverse KL divergence.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the probability of the observed data under the model distribution. - Computationally feasible because it only requires samples from the true data distribution. - Contrasts with reverse KL divergence, which is typically impossible to compute.

concepts.title: Robustness vs. accuracy tradeoff
concepts.one_liner: Hand-crafted models offer high accuracy within specific assumptions, while learning-based models provide greater robustness and generalization across diverse conditions.
concepts.content:
While hand-crafted algorithms can produce highly accurate 3D reconstructions when images fit specific world assumptions, they are often fragile. For instance, poor illumination can break edge detectors, resulting in a cascade of errors. A hand-crafted approach may completely fail if a small change occurs, such as changing the ground plane color. 

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)

In contrast, learning-based models like MiDaS may lose some precision—cubes' edges might not be perfectly straight or surfaces perfectly flat—but they gain significantly in robustness and generalization. These models produce results of consistent quality regardless of conditions, even when applied to simple worlds dissimilar to their natural-image training data.

(see figure: Out of domain generalization. For the pretrained model, these images might still be within the domain of the training, as it contained a very diverse set of natural images. The simple system model...)
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains the fundamental tension between specialized precision and general-purpose reliability. It helps engineers decide whether to use rigid, rule-based systems or flexible, data-driven models based on the variability of the environment.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Hand-crafted models are precise under ideal conditions but fragile to environmental changes like lighting.", 
  "- Learning-based models generalize better to new domains and offer higher robustness at the cost of some geometric accuracy."
]

concepts.title: LLM-based scene understanding
concepts.one_liner: Large language models like GPT-4V can interpret visual scenes by leveraging learned rules of perspective geometry and feature detection.
concepts.content:
GPT-4V can be used to interpret scenes by taking images as input and answering questions about them. At one level, it is a transformer trained on massive data using an autoregressive modeling objective. At another level, the transformer learns rules similar to classical vision: it detects edges in early layers, uses filters that act like wavelets tiling Fourier space, and reasons about perspective geometry to find vanishing points and estimate shape.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)
concepts.motivation_md: Explains how modern multimodal LLMs bridge the gap between raw pixel data and semantic/geometric understanding, showing that they often 're-discover' classical vision principles through massive data training.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- GPT-4V uses an autoregressive transformer architecture to interpret and describe visual scenes.", 
  "- The model learns to perform edge detection and geometric reasoning similar to hand-crafted vision systems."
]

concepts.title: Limitations of LLM-based scene reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: Current LLMs often fail to perfectly reconstruct images from text descriptions, revealing gaps in their fundamental understanding of scene consistency.
concepts.content:
Despite their accuracy in description, LLM-based scene reconstruction is not fully solved. When attempting to reconstruct an image from a text description, the output often looks incorrect, as seen in @fig-chatgpt_blockworld2. These failures provide important clues regarding the next fundamental questions that need to be addressed in the field as it moves forward.

(see figure: Output by ChatGPT when asked to render a new image with the same elements as in @fig-chatgpt_blockworld This conversation is a continuation of the same chat from @fig-chatgpt_blockworld)
concepts.motivation_md: Highlights the current boundaries of AI capabilities, encouraging researchers to look at specific failure modes as opportunities for the next wave of innovation.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Reconstructing a scene from an LLM's text description often results in visual inconsistencies.", 
  "- Identifying these failures helps define the next set of fundamental problems in computer vision."
]

concepts.title: Unsolved solved computer vision problems
concepts.one_liner: Many computer vision problems that appear solved are actually illusions, with deeper challenges remaining hidden in the background.
concepts.content: Computer vision is making amazing progress, but one must beware of the "unsolved solved computer vision problems." For some vision tasks, it might appear as if a single method perfectly resolves the task or that foundational problems are solved. Often, this is just an illusion, and the problem was not really solved at all. Even when a problem is genuinely solved, there are many unsolved problems lurking in the background. Advances result from exploring new directions with an open mind and using creativity as a powerful tool.
concepts.motivation_md: Warns against complacency in research and engineering, reminding students that 'solved' benchmarks often hide edge cases and deeper complexities.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Apparent solutions to foundational vision problems are often incomplete or illusory.", 
  "- Progress in the field requires an open mind and the exploration of new, creative directions."
]

concepts.title: Hand-crafted vs. learning-based paradigms
concepts.one_liner: Hand-crafted models provide transparency and require no training data, while learning-based models offer superior generalization and robustness to environmental changes.
concepts.content:
Hand-crafted models provide a comprehensive understanding of system mechanisms, assumptions, and limitations. They require no training data and work immediately, but they are fragile and do not generalize outside their specific assumptions. When they fail, the cause is easy to identify, but that knowledge doesn't necessarily make the system work better.

Conversely, pretrained learning-based systems generalize to new settings and handle configurations outside their original modeling assumptions. They are robust to changes in illumination and do not rely on fragile, explicit operations like edge detection, though they may learn equivalent internal heuristics. Understanding these networks often requires experimental approaches similar to psychophysics in humans.

[FIGURE:2d5b0345de81fa09 | A split-screen conceptual illustration comparing two computer vision paradigms. The left side represents a hand-crafted model with rigid, mechanical gears, cogs, and circuit-like lines on a light...]

While GPT-4V can recognize geometric figures, its integration with rendering engines remains fragile. The field is evolving quickly, and the priority is to challenge existing approaches and identify relevant questions for new systems.

[FIGURE:a9cf6077c82fad75 | A simple black-and-white line drawing of a bird in flight, shown from a side profile. The bird has a pointed beak, a small dot for an eye, and outstretched wings and tail, rendered with a thick...]
concepts.motivation_md: Compares the two dominant approaches in computer vision to help students understand the trade-offs between interpretability (hand-crafted) and performance (learning-based).
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Hand-crafted models are transparent and data-efficient but fail to generalize beyond strict assumptions.", 
  "- Learning-based models are robust and flexible but act as 'black boxes' requiring experimental analysis to understand."
]

concepts.title: Recovering 3D World Coordinates from Depth
concepts.one_liner: 3D world coordinates for a pixel can be recovered from its image coordinates and depth using the inverse of the camera matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows us to map 2D image pixels back into their original 3D spatial positions, which is essential for tasks like 3D reconstruction, navigation, and spatial reasoning in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Use the inverse camera matrix $\mathbf{K}^{-1}$ to back-project 2D coordinates.

concepts.title: Camera Matrix Decomposition (K = MR)
concepts.one_liner: The camera matrix $\mathbf{K}$ accounts for focal length, image size, camera center, and rotation relative to world coordinates.
concepts.content:
The camera parameters will have to account for the focal length, image size, camera center, and the camera rotation with respect to the world coordinates:
$$\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{R}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Decomposing the camera matrix into intrinsic and extrinsic components allows for a modular understanding of how internal camera properties and external orientation separately affect the image formation process.
concepts.recap_md: - The camera matrix $\mathbf{K}$ is the product of intrinsic parameters $\mathbf{M}$ and rotation $\mathbf{R}$.

concepts.title: Intrinsic Camera Parameters for Perspective Projection
concepts.one_liner: Intrinsic camera parameters for perspective projection are represented by a matrix $\mathbf{M}$ containing focal and center point information.
concepts.motivation_md: Intrinsic parameters define the internal geometry of the camera, such as how light is focused onto the sensor and where the optical center lies, which is necessary for accurate 3D-to-2D mapping.
concepts.recap_md: - The matrix $\mathbf{M}$ encodes the focal length $a$ and the camera center $(n_0, m_0)$.

concepts.title: Extrinsic Camera Parameters for 3D Rotation
concepts.one_liner: Extrinsic camera parameters model the 3D rotation of the camera, often focusing on the rotation around the X-axis.
concepts.motivation_md: Extrinsic parameters describe the camera's position and orientation in the world, allowing the system to relate the camera's local view to a global coordinate frame.
concepts.recap_md: - The rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$ defines the camera's orientation relative to the world.

concepts.title: Heuristic Parameter Selection for Depth Mapping
concepts.one_liner: Heuristic parameter selection provides a simpler alternative to formal calibration for defining camera constants.
concepts.content:
In order to apply the recovery of world coordinates, we need to define certain parameters: $d_0$, $n_0$, $m_0$, $a$, and $\theta$. Although we could determine these parameters using a calibration image, in this case, we'll opt for a simpler heuristic approach:

- $d_0$: We will set this value to 0.
- $n_0, m_0$: Defines the camera center point, where $n_0=N/2$ and $m_0=M/2$, when $N \times M$ is the input image size.
- $a$: Accounts for the image size and the camera focal length. One standard setting is to make $a = N$, where $N$ is the image width.
concepts.motivation_md: Formal camera calibration can be complex and requires specific calibration targets; heuristics provide a 'good enough' starting point for 3D reconstruction when exact parameters are unknown.
concepts.recap_md: - Set the camera center $(n_0, m_0)$ to the midpoint of the image dimensions.

concepts.title: Ground plane angle theta
concepts.one_liner: The parameter $\theta$ represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane.
concepts.content: $\theta$ represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane. It would be possible to estimate this angle accurately by determining the direction of the surface normal in pixels corresponding to the ground and measuring the angle with respect to the vertical axis. However, for our purposes, we will simply set it to $\theta = \pi / 4$, as this is approximately the angle at which the pictures were taken.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the tilt of the camera relative to the ground is crucial for correctly orienting the reconstructed 3D scene so that 'down' in the model matches 'down' in the real world.
concepts.recap_md: - $\theta$ is the angle between the camera's optical axis and the ground.

concepts.title: Learning-based 3D reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based 3D reconstruction uses neural networks to directly transform images into world coordinates without manual feature detection.
concepts.content: Learning-based 3D reconstruction involves applying a neural network to an input image to obtain the output disparity and then transforming that disparity into world coordinates. Unlike traditional methods, we do not have to detect edges or any other manual features. Instead, the neural network learns to compute whatever features it deems necessary to solve the task. In this approach, we do not retrain the network using images from our simple visual world, but rely on its learned representations.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional 3D reconstruction relies on hand-crafted features like edges, which can be fragile; neural networks can learn more robust features automatically from large datasets.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural networks can output disparity maps directly from raw images.

concepts.title: 3D structure validation via re-rendering
concepts.one_liner: Re-rendering an inferred 3D structure from different viewpoints validates the accuracy of the 3D interpretation.
concepts.content:
To show that the algorithm for 3D interpretation gives reasonable results, we can re-render the inferred 3D structure from different viewpoints.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using a pretrained model. The images show multiple view points of the reconstructed 3D scene from @fig-simplesystem_revisited_img1)
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizing a 3D model from angles not present in the original 2D image helps confirm that the depth and geometry were correctly inferred rather than just 'looking right' from one perspective.
concepts.recap_md: - Re-rendering from new viewpoints serves as a qualitative check for 3D models.

concepts.title: Reconstruction of Impossible Figures
concepts.one_liner: The reconstruction of impossible figures demonstrates how vision systems attempt to approximate 3D constraints even when they cannot be exactly satisfied.
concepts.content: The reconstruction of *impossible steps* illustrates how 3D perception handles conflicting visual cues. On one side, a shape may look rectangular with stripes painted on the surface, while on the other side, it appears to have steps where the stripes correspond to shading from surface orientation. In the middle, the shape remains ambiguous. When a system attempts to reconstruct the 3D scene for such an unlikely image, it tries to approximate the constraints; however, for these shapes, it is not possible to exactly satisfy all constraints simultaneously.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explores the limits of 3D reconstruction and human perception. By studying how we (and computer systems) interpret 'impossible' objects, we learn how the brain and algorithms prioritize certain geometric constraints over others to form a coherent, though sometimes flawed, 3D model.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vision systems attempt to satisfy 3D constraints even when an image is geometrically impossible.
 - Ambiguous shapes can be perceived differently depending on which local features are prioritized.
 - Reconstructions of impossible figures represent the best possible approximation of conflicting visual data.

concepts.title: Model-Based Scene Interpretation
concepts.one_liner: Model-based scene interpretation uses predefined object models to detect presence and recover parameters like pose and color in an image.
concepts.content: Model-based scene interpretation is an approach where a system utilizes a set of predefined models of objects that may be present in a scene. The system attempts to decide if these objects are present in the image and subsequently recovers their specific parameters, such as pose and color.
concepts.motivation_md: Instead of building a scene from scratch using low-level features, this technique leverages prior knowledge. It simplifies the vision problem by turning it into a search or matching task against known templates.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses predefined models of objects to guide image interpretation.
 - Aims to detect the presence of specific objects within a scene.
 - Recovers object-specific parameters like pose and color.

concepts.title: Pixel Recognition and Context
concepts.one_liner: The recognition of individual pixels depends on the context of the whole image rather than just local intensity.
concepts.content: Before building systems that can see, it is useful to look at images and pay attention to individual pixels. Even in a tiny $32 \times 32$ pixel image, we can often recognize content despite the low resolution. For example, a single dark gray pixel surrounded by white pixels might be identified as a pen, even if the pen is only three pixels long. Recognition of the meaning of that pixel cannot come just from the intensity of that pixel or the few pixels nearby, as many different objects could map to similar intensities. Instead, it is the whole image and the context that provides the necessary information. Taken in isolation, such pixels are impossible to recognize.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights that vision is not just a bottom-up process of identifying colors. It demonstrates the necessity of global context in resolving local ambiguities in low-resolution data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Individual pixel intensities are often insufficient for object recognition.
 - Global context allows the brain to assign meaning to ambiguous local features.
 - Recognizable images can be formed with surprisingly few pixels if context is preserved.

concepts.title: Vision as a Dynamical System

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: Vision is a dynamical system where the longer one looks at an image, the more details and understanding are extracted.
concepts.content:
Visual perception cannot be formulated as a simple input-output function over predefined domains. Vision is a dynamical system, even when looking at a static image. The longer you look at an image, the more details you see and the better you understand the scene.

(see figure: A street in Paris. Is everything fine in this picture?)

However, this feeling of unlimited and effortless understanding is often an illusion. We may not truly understand everything we see; for example, in a manipulated image of a street in Paris, some chair legs might not correspond to any actual chair, challenging our initial perception of the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: To understand that vision is an active, temporal process rather than a single snapshot. It explains why we miss details initially and how our brain 'fills in' gaps that might not actually make sense.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vision is an active process that evolves over time even for static images.
 - Increased observation time leads to the extraction of finer scene details.
 - Perception can be illusory, masking inconsistencies in a scene through a sense of effortless understanding.

concepts.title: Visual Cognitive Load

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: Visual cognitive load refers to the increased likelihood of making judgment mistakes as the complexity of a visual task grows.
concepts.content: When solving a task, as the **visual cognitive load** increases, we are more likely to make judgment mistakes.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the limits of human visual processing is crucial for designing interfaces and safety systems where information overload can lead to critical errors.
concepts.recap_md:
- Higher visual cognitive load correlates with an increase in judgment errors.
 - It represents the mental effort required to process visual information for a specific task.

concepts.title: Image Patches as a Dataset

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: A single large image can be treated as a dataset by dividing it into thousands of tiny image patches.
concepts.content: Each patch within a larger image is essentially a small photo in its own right. Consequently, a single large image contains thousands of tiny images within it. This allows a single photo to be treated as *big data*; by chopping up the photo, you create a large dataset of tiny images. A common trick in computer vision is to take a method developed for processing a dataset and apply it to the set of patches in an image, or vice versa.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows researchers to apply statistical learning methods to single images, which is useful for tasks like texture synthesis, super-resolution, or training models when data is scarce.
concepts.recap_md:
- Large images can be decomposed into a dataset of smaller image patches.
 - Enables the application of dataset-oriented algorithms to individual images.
 - Treats local image regions as independent samples for analysis.

concepts.title: Learning to See Through Painting
concepts.one_liner: Learning to paint helps one understand the world by focusing on why objects look a certain way rather than just what they represent.
concepts.content: Learning to paint is an effective way of learning to see. Starting from a blank canvas and a finite set of paints, the goal is to replicate shadows, 3D shapes, and reflections to make an object look real. Artists learn to see the world not just by what it represents, but by why it looks the way it does. In the process of painting, such as a strawberry, realism may not increase monotonically; certain strokes might initially look less realistic but eventually provide the shading necessary to make the object appear three-dimensional.
concepts.motivation_md: By attempting to reconstruct an image from scratch, one gains a deeper appreciation for the physics of light, shading, and geometry that the visual system usually processes subconsciously.
concepts.recap_md:
- Painting requires understanding the 'why' of appearance (light, shadow, shape).
 - Realism in a visual representation may decrease temporarily to build necessary depth cues.
 - The process of artistic creation mirrors the decomposition of visual scenes into constituent elements.

concepts.title: Natural Pinhole Cameras in Tree Shadows
concepts.one_liner: Small gaps between tree leaves act as natural pinhole cameras, projecting images of the sun onto the ground.
concepts.content: Under the shadow of a tree on a sunny day, light rays passing through holes between leaves create spots on the floor. While one might expect these spots to have irregular shapes matching the gaps, they are actually circular and of similar size. This occurs because the gaps act as **pinhole cameras**. When the openings are small enough, the shape of the projected light is dominated by the shape of the light source—the sun—rather than the shape of the opening. This effect is most clearly observed during a solar eclipse, where the tree's shadow contains many crescent-shaped images of the eclipsed sun.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces the fundamental principles of image formation and the pinhole camera model using a common natural phenomenon, illustrating how light travels and projects images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaps between leaves function as natural pinhole apertures.
 - The shape of the projected light spot reflects the shape of the light source (the sun).
 - During an eclipse, these natural pinholes project crescent shapes instead of circles.

concepts.title: Toy models (TSTMTCTMI)
concepts.one_liner: A toy model is the simplest possible version of a problem that still captures its main idea.
concepts.content:
A toy model is "the simplest toy model that captures the main idea" (TSTMTCTMI). Simple toy models help build intuition about what matters, which provides a significant advantage in research. 

For example, the color constancy problem involves estimating surface reflectance colors from the product of surface reflectance and an unknown illuminant spectrum. A toy model for this is estimating scalars $a$ and $b$ from their product $y = a \times b$. This simple problem allows one to think through loss functions and Bayesian decision theory.

(see figure: A toy model for the color constancy problem: $y = a \times b$. The plot shows the possible solutions for $a$ and $b$ when $y=1$.)

Another example is using a single bump as a proxy for complicated shaded surfaces. Having the intuitions gained from working with toy problems allows you to figure out what will work by thinking it through with the model.
concepts.motivation_md: Complex research problems often have too many variables to build immediate intuition. Toy models strip away non-essential details, allowing researchers to test logic and decision-making frameworks in a manageable environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Use the simplest model possible that still captures the core problem (TSTMTCTMI).

concepts.title: Parable of the two students
concepts.one_liner: Strong researchers explore small variations around a failed proposal to find a solution that actually works.
concepts.content:
In this parable, a weak and a strong graduate student are both asked by their advisor to try a particular approach to a research problem. The weak student does exactly what the advisor asked; when the solution fails, the student simply reports that failure. The strong student starts with the advisor's request but, upon seeing it doesn't work, looks within an epsilon ball of the original proposal to find what does work and reports that successful solution.

(see figure: The parable of the two students.)
concepts.motivation_md: This parable illustrates the difference between passive execution and active problem-solving. It encourages students to take agency and use their advisor's suggestions as a starting point rather than a rigid boundary.
concepts.recap_md: - Don't just report failure if an advisor's specific suggestion doesn't work.

concepts.title: Independent thinking vs. literature review
concepts.one_liner: Balance the freedom of thinking others are off-track with the necessity of knowing the existing literature.
concepts.content:
Sometimes it is useful to think that everyone else is completely off-track, as this allows you to pursue directions no one else is doing. When doing so, it is best to remain humble in communication, perhaps saying, "Oh, I just thought I'd try out this direction."

Conversely, it is also useful to remember that many smart people have worked on related problems and recorded their results. You should avoid being caught flat-footed by a large body of closely related literature that you are unfamiliar with.
concepts.motivation_md: Researchers must balance two extremes: being so influenced by existing work that they can't innovate, and being so isolated that they reinvent the wheel or ignore known pitfalls.
concepts.recap_md: - Use independent thinking to explore unique directions others might ignore.

concepts.title: Personal branding and reputation
concepts.one_liner: Build a personal brand by consistently producing great work and playing to your specific strengths.
concepts.content: In research, you have a brand: yourself. You should aim to build positive impressions—that you do great work, have good ideas, give great talks, and write wonderful software. Promote your brand by consistently behaving in the way you would like to be perceived. Additionally, cultivate and play to your specific strengths, whether those include being broad, creative, a great implementer, or skilled at theory.
concepts.motivation_md: A researcher's reputation (or 'brand') affects their opportunities for collaboration, funding, and employment. Consciously cultivating strengths helps a researcher stand out in a competitive field.
concepts.recap_md: - Consistently behave in the way you want to be perceived by the community.

concepts.title: Communication with your research advisor
concepts.one_liner: Maintain active and insistent communication with your research advisor.
concepts.content: Do not hide from your advisor. It is important to talk regularly. Advisors often appreciate it when students track them down and insist on meeting, especially if the advisor has been busy or traveling.
concepts.motivation_md: Regular communication prevents students from getting stuck for long periods and ensures that the advisor's expertise is being utilized effectively.
concepts.recap_md: - Avoid hiding from your advisor; insist on regular meetings to stay on track.

concepts.title: Collaboration and authorship in research
concepts.one_liner: Collaboration is a team sport where the impact of the work matters more than the number of authors.
concepts.content:
Science is generally a team sport. What matters in a collaboration is whether the work is insightful, foundational, or impactful, regardless of how many people were involved. It is better to be one of many contributors to a great paper than the sole author of an unimportant one. Furthermore, collaborations often lead to lifelong professional friendships.

Regarding authorship, everyone who contributed to the paper should be included. Contributions can include experimentation, providing a seminal idea, helping with writing, or even exploring a research direction that ultimately did not work. If authorship is uncertain, it is often best to ask the person directly and follow their preference.
concepts.motivation_md: Modern research is often too complex for individuals. Understanding how to collaborate and fairly assign credit is essential for maintaining professional relationships and producing high-impact work.
concepts.recap_md: - Prioritize being part of impactful, high-quality work over sole authorship.

concepts.title: Relationship between paper quality and impact
concepts.one_liner: Only high-quality papers significantly impact a research career, so prioritize quality over quantity.
concepts.content:
While the number of papers is a rough measure of productivity, in the eyes of mentors, search committees, and managers, only the good papers count. This relationship is illustrated in @fig-impact, which shows that only high-quality papers have a significant impact on one's career. Therefore, it is essential to learn how to write the best possible paper from any given piece of research.

(see figure: Plot of conjectured data showing the impact of a paper on one's career, as a function of paper quality.)
concepts.motivation_md: Students often feel pressured to publish frequently, but a resume full of mediocre papers is less effective than one with a few truly excellent contributions.
concepts.recap_md: - Focus on making every paper as good as possible rather than just increasing your paper count.

concepts.title: Standard paper organization structure
concepts.one_liner: A standard research paper structure moves from problem definition and existing solutions to your own method and results.
concepts.content:
A successful research paper typically follows a specific logical progression:

- Start by stating the problem and why the audience should care about it.
- Briefly state existing solutions and explain why they are unsatisfactory.
- Explain your own solution, compare it to others, and demonstrate why it is better.
- Conclude by discussing related work that uses similar techniques for different problems.

This structure often maps to standard section headings: Introduction, Related Work, Main Idea, Algorithm (with specific sub-steps), Experiments, and Discussion.
concepts.motivation_md: Standardized organization helps readers quickly find information and understand the value proposition of the research relative to existing work.
concepts.recap_md: - Clearly state the problem and why existing solutions fail before presenting your own.

concepts.title: Line Equation in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: In homogeneous coordinates, a 2D line is represented by a vector such that its dot product with any point on the line equals zero.
concepts.content: The equation of a line $ax+by+c=0$ can be written in homogeneous coordinates as: $$ax+by+c=0 \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 0$$ In this system, the equation of a line is the dot product $\boldsymbol{l} ^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p} = 0$ where $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [a, b, c\right ]$. A point $\mathbf{p}$ belongs to the line when $\boldsymbol{l}$ and $\mathbf{p}$ are perpendicular. This representation is scale invariant, meaning $\left [a, b, c\right ]$ represents the same line as $\left [a/c, b/c, 1\right ]$. It is also useful to describe the line using $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [n_x, n_y, -d\right ]$, where $(n_x,n_y)$ is the normal to the line and $d$ is the distance to the origin.
concepts.motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates provide a scale-invariant representation of lines, simplifying geometric operations into linear algebra. This allows for a unified treatment of points and lines through dot products and perpendicularity.
concepts.recap_md: - A line is defined by a vector $\boldsymbol{l}$ such that $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p} = 0$ for all points $\mathbf{p}$ on it.

concepts.title: Line from Two Points

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: The line passing through two points in homogeneous coordinates is calculated as the cross product of the points' vectors.
concepts.content: Using homogeneous coordinates makes obtaining geometric properties of points and lines very easy. Given two points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ in homogeneous coordinates, the line that passes by both points is the cross product: $$\boldsymbol{l} = \mathbf{p}_1 \times \mathbf{p}_2$$ (see figure: Using homogeneous coordinates to get the line that passes by two points, and to obtain the intersection of two lines. Both operations are analogous.) This is because if the line passes by both points, it has to verify that $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}_1=0$ and $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}_2=0$. That is, the vector $\mathbf{l}$ has to be perpendicular to both $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$, and the cross product between $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ provides such a vector.
concepts.motivation_md: Determining the unique line connecting two points is a fundamental task in geometry; homogeneous coordinates reduce this problem to a simple cross-product operation.
concepts.recap_md: - The line $\boldsymbol{l}$ connecting points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ is given by $\boldsymbol{l} = \mathbf{p}_1 \times \mathbf{p}_2$.

concepts.title: Intersection of Two Lines

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: The intersection point of two lines in homogeneous coordinates is found by taking the cross product of the vectors representing the lines.
concepts.content: Given two lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$, the intersection point between them is the cross product: $$\mathbf{p} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \boldsymbol{l}_2$$ (see figure: Using homogeneous coordinates to get the line that passes by two points, and to obtain the intersection of two lines. Both operations are analogous.) The coordinates of $\mathbf{p}$ computed this way will be in homogeneous coordinates. To get the actual point coordinates in heterogeneous (Cartesian) coordinates, you must divide by the third component.
concepts.motivation_md: Finding where two lines meet is a common problem in computer vision and graphics. Homogeneous coordinates allow this to be solved using the same cross-product logic used to find lines from points.
concepts.recap_md: - The intersection point $\mathbf{p}$ of lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ is $\mathbf{p} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \boldsymbol{l}_2$.

concepts.title: Colinearity Condition

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: Three points are colinear if the determinant of the matrix formed by their homogeneous coordinate vectors is zero.
concepts.content: If three 2D points are colinear, then the determinant of the matrix formed by concatenating the three vectors, in homogeneous coordinates, as columns is equal to zero: $\det( [\mathbf{p}_1~\mathbf{p}_2~\mathbf{p}_3 ])=0$. Similarly, if three lines intersect in the same point, we have a similar relationship: $\det( [\boldsymbol{l}_1~\boldsymbol{l}_2~\boldsymbol{l}_3 ])=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This condition provides a simple algebraic test to verify if points lie on a single line or if multiple lines are concurrent at a single point.
concepts.recap_md: - Points are colinear if the determinant of their concatenated homogeneous vectors is zero.

concepts.title: Plane Equation in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: A 3D plane is represented in homogeneous coordinates by a vector such that its dot product with any point on the plane is zero.
concepts.content: We can represent planes in 3D using a method analogous to 2D lines. The equation of a 3D plane is $aX+bY+cZ+d=0$, which can be written in homogeneous coordinates as: $$\mathbf{\pi}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P} = 0$$ where $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$ are the plane parameters and $\mathbf{P}=[X,Y,Z,1]^\mathsf{T}$ are the 3D point homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Extending homogeneous coordinates to 3D allows for a consistent algebraic framework to handle points and planes, mirroring the simplicity of 2D point-line operations.
concepts.recap_md: - A 3D plane is defined by the vector $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$.

concepts.title: Forward Mapping
concepts.one_liner: Forward mapping transforms an image by applying a transformation to each source pixel and recording its color at the resulting destination coordinates.
concepts.content: Forward mapping is an algorithm for transforming an image where every pixel in the original image, represented as $[\ell_i,x_i,y_i]$, has a transformation $\mathbf{M}$ applied to its coordinates. The pixel color is then recorded into the resulting coordinates in the target image. (see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.) As coordinates might result in non-integer values, the result can be rounded to the closest pixel coordinate using nearest neighbor interpolation. While intuitive, forward mapping is generally not a good idea because it produces artifacts such as missing values and aliasing. (see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping. Forward mapping produces many artifacts. In both cases we use nearest neighbor interpolation.)
concepts.motivation_md: Forward mapping is the most intuitive approach to image warping, but it is rarely used because it often leaves 'holes' in the destination image when source pixels do not map to every target pixel.
concepts.recap_md: - Forward mapping iterates through source pixels and maps them to the destination.

concepts.title: Backward Mapping
concepts.one_liner: Backward mapping iterates over target image pixels and uses the inverse transformation to sample color values from the source image.
concepts.content: (see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.) The best approach for image warping is backward mapping, which consists of looping over all the pixels of the target image and applying the inverse geometric transform, $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. Interpolation is then used to get the correct color value from the source image. This process guarantees that there will be no missing values, provided the coordinates stay within the input image frame. To avoid aliasing, blurring the input image might be necessary if the target image has a lower pixel density than the input. (see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping. Forward mapping produces many artifacts. In both cases we use nearest neighbor interpolation.)
concepts.motivation_md: Backward mapping solves the 'missing value' problem of forward mapping by ensuring that every pixel in the destination image is assigned a color sampled from the source.
concepts.recap_md: - Backward mapping iterates through destination pixels and uses the inverse transform $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ to find source colors.

concepts.title: MIP-mapping
concepts.one_liner: MIP-mapping uses a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently determine the best neighborhood for high-quality interpolation during image warping.
