concepts.content: MIP-mapping is a technique for high quality and efficient interpolation. It relies on a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently compute the best neighborhood structure needed to perform the interpolation at each location. This technique is particularly useful when warping an image onto a curved surface.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard interpolation can be slow or cause aliasing when scaling images; MIP-mapping uses pre-calculated image scales to make the process both faster and visually smoother.
concepts.recap_md: - MIP-mapping utilizes a multiscale image pyramid for efficient interpolation.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation Pipeline
concepts.one_liner: Instance segmentation can be achieved by applying a binary semantic segmentation function to the cropped image within each proposed and labeled bounding box.
concepts.content:
One approach to instance segmentation is to follow the object localization pipeline but, after the bounding boxes have been proposed and labeled, feed the cropped image within each bounding box to a binary semantic segmentation function. This function predicts, for each pixel in box $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$, whether it belongs to the object or not, resulting in an instance mask for each box. Such an approach was introduced in @he2017. The architecture is illustrated in @fig-instance_segmentation_architecture.

(see figure: Architecture for instance segmentation. This architecture combines several of the components we have seen previously. The image is first broken into overlapping regions, and then class segmentation...)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard object detection only provides bounding boxes, which lack pixel-level precision. This pipeline extends localization to provide exact masks for individual object instances, which is necessary for tasks requiring precise boundaries.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- The pipeline starts with object localization to propose and label bounding boxes.", 
  "- Each cropped box is processed by a binary segmentation function to create a pixel-wise mask.", 
  "- This method produces distinct instance masks for every detected object in the image." 
]

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation Loss
concepts.one_liner: The instance segmentation loss combines classification, localization, and segmentation losses into a single weighted objective function.
concepts.content:
The loss can be written as a combination of the classification, localization, and segmentation losses:
$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \left( 
     \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
     +
     \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i, \mathbf{s}_i)
     \right)
$$

The first classification loss corresponds to the classification of the crop as containing the object or not. If the object is present, the second term measures the accuracy of the bounding box, and the third term measures whether the segmentation, $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i$, inside each bounding box matches the ground truth instance segmentation, $\mathbf{s}_i$. The parameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ control how much weight each loss has on the final loss.
concepts.motivation_md: To train a model that performs multiple tasks simultaneously—identifying, locating, and masking objects—a multi-task loss function is needed to balance the accuracy of each component.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- The total loss is a weighted sum of classification, localization, and segmentation errors.", 
  "- Localization and segmentation losses are only calculated if an object is actually present.", 
  "- Hyperparameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ adjust the relative importance of the different loss terms." 
]

concepts.title: Summary of Object Recognition Methods
concepts.one_liner: Object representation methods in images utilize a common set of building blocks including classifiers, region proposals, and bounding box regression.
concepts.content:
The different methods used to represent objects in images rely on a common set of building blocks: image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression. @fig-pictorialsummary shows a pictorial summary of these different approaches.

(see figure: A family of object recognition definitions.)
concepts.motivation_md: Summarizing these methods helps clarify how complex vision tasks are built from a standard set of modular components.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Object recognition methods share core components like image and pixelwise classifiers.", 
  "- Region proposals and bounding box regression are essential for localization tasks.", 
  "- These building blocks are combined in various ways to define different recognition paradigms." 
]

concepts.title: Limitations of Language-Based Object Recognition
concepts.one_liner: Language-based object representations are often insufficient for robotics and autonomous systems that require 3D modeling, physical properties, and dynamic understanding.
concepts.content:
The representations described in this chapter feel incomplete for applications like robotics or autonomous vehicles, where object representations are hard to act on. A robot planning to grasp an object needs accurate 3D modeling and an understanding of physical properties to plan grasping points. Similarly, autonomous vehicles require 3D descriptions of object locations and their dynamics. Therefore, object segmentation and classification provide only part of the necessary information.

Techniques relying on language to define objects (e.g., tagging, captioning) leave many questions unanswered, such as:
- Is this piece of matter an object or a random arrangement?
- What is its 3D shape and how is it supported?
- What are its mechanical properties (soft, rigid, deformable)?
- How will it react to external actions or grasping?
- What is its utility or physical origin?
- Is it stable or alive?

A computer vision system should behave as a scientist, formulating hypotheses and performing experiments to answer these questions. While language can answer some, it does not need to be the only internal representation used.
concepts.motivation_md: While naming and masking objects is useful, real-world interaction requires deeper physical and spatial understanding that simple labels cannot provide.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Language-based labels lack the 3D and physical data needed for robotic manipulation.", 
  "- Vision systems should investigate properties like stability, mechanical behavior, and utility.", 
  "- Future systems may need to act like scientists, using more than just language for internal representations." 
]

concepts.title: Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
concepts.one_liner: Vision-language models (VLMs) are systems designed to understand and relate information across both visual and textual modalities.
concepts.content: In order to understand vision-language models (VLMs), it is first necessary to understand the fundamentals of language models.
concepts.motivation_md: VLMs bridge the gap between seeing and describing, allowing AI to perform tasks like image captioning and visual question answering.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual data with linguistic information.", 
  "- Understanding VLMs requires a foundational knowledge of how language models operate." 
]

concepts.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
concepts.one_liner: Natural language processing (NLP) is the field dedicated to the study and modeling of language.
concepts.content: Natural language processing (NLP) is the field that studies the various ways to model language.
concepts.motivation_md: NLP provides the tools and frameworks necessary for computers to process, interpret, and generate human language.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- NLP is the primary academic and technical field for language modeling.", 
  "- It encompasses various strategies for representing and processing text computationally." 
]

concepts.title: Word-level Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Word-level encoding represents text by mapping each unique word in a vocabulary to a specific one-hot code.
concepts.content: One option for representing text as numbers is to use a word-level encoding scheme. This involves mapping each word in a vocabulary to a unique one-hot code. For a vocabulary containing $K$ different words, this requires $K$-dimensional one-hot codes.
concepts.motivation_md: To process text with neural networks, words must be converted into a numerical format that the model can interpret.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Each unique word is assigned a distinct one-hot vector.", 
  "- The dimensionality of the vector is equal to the size of the vocabulary $K$." 
]

concepts.title: Character-level Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Character-level encoding assigns a one-hot code to each individual character rather than to entire words.
concepts.content: Character-level encoding is a strategy where a one-hot code is assigned to each character in the vocabulary rather than to each unique word. If all alphanumeric characters and common punctuation marks are represented this way, it may only require a few dozen codes. However, the disadvantage is that representing a single word now requires a sequence of one-hots, which necessitates modeling that sequence.
concepts.motivation_md: Character-level encoding significantly reduces the vocabulary size compared to word-level encoding and can handle out-of-vocabulary words more gracefully.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- One-hot codes are assigned to individual characters and punctuation marks.", 
  "- This approach uses a much smaller vocabulary size than word-level encoding.", 
  "- It requires modeling sequences of characters to represent and understand words." 
]

concepts.title: Modular Encoder-Decoder Translation
concepts.one_liner: One approach to solving X-to-Y translation problems is to hook up an encoder for domain X to a decoder for domain Y.
concepts.content: One approach to solving X-to-Y translation problems is to do it in a modular fashion by hooking up an encoder for domain X to a decoder for domain Y. This approach is popular because powerful encoder and decoder architectures, as well as pretrained models, exist for many domains. If we have an encoder $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ and a decoder $g: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, then we can create a translator simply by function composition, $g \circ f$.
concepts.motivation_md: Translation between different modalities (like text and images) is complex. By using a modular approach, researchers can leverage specialized, pre-existing models for each domain and combine them into a single system, rather than training a massive end-to-end model from scratch for every specific pair of domains.
concepts.recap_md: - Translation can be achieved by composing an encoder $f$ and a decoder $g$ into a single function $g \circ f$.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder Alignment Strategies
concepts.one_liner: Alignment strategies ensure that the output of an encoder is interpretable as a proper input to a specific decoder.
concepts.content:
The output of an encoder might not be interpretable as a proper input to the selected decoder. For example, if $f$ is a text encoder and $g$ is an image decoder, the generated image $\boldsymbol\ell= g(f(\mathbf{t}))$ from text input $\mathbf{t}$ is not guaranteed to semantically match the text.

To align the encoder and decoder, several strategies can be followed. One is to finetune the composition $g \circ f$ on paired examples of the target translation problem, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Another option is to freeze $f$ and $g$ and instead train a translation function in latent space, $h: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, so that $g \circ h \circ f$ correctly maps each training point $\mathbf{t}^{(i)}$ to the target output $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Even if we have a good encoder and a good decoder, their latent spaces may not naturally match. Alignment strategies are necessary to bridge the gap between these representations so that the decoder correctly interprets the information provided by the encoder.
concepts.recap_md: - Alignment can be achieved by finetuning the entire composed model on paired data.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: Text-to-image synthesis is the process of generating an image from a text description using conditional generative models.
concepts.content:
One amazing ability of modern generative models is to synthesize an image just from a text description, a problem called text-to-image. This can be achieved using conditional generative models by finding an effective way to use text as the conditioning information. (see figure: Text-to-image.)

This mapping from the space of text to the space of images allows a system to translate input text $\mathbf{t}$ to an output image $\hat{\boldsymbol\ell}$ that matches what the text describes. This problem is closely related to concepts in representation learning and generative modeling.
concepts.motivation_md: Text-to-image synthesis allows for the creation of visual content through natural language, making generative AI accessible for creative tasks, design, and visual communication.
concepts.recap_md: - Text-to-image synthesis maps text descriptions to corresponding visual representations.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image with Conditional Variational Autoencoders
concepts.one_liner: A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) for text-to-image uses a text encoder to provide conditioning vectors for image generation.
concepts.content:
A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) can be used for text-to-image synthesis, an architecture notably used by the DALL-E 1 model. A cVAE for text-to-image is trained like a regular cVAE, but specifically uses a text encoder—a neural network that maps text to a vector embedding.

(see figure: Training a cVAE to perform text-to-image. The dotted lines indicate that the image encoder is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path. In this cartoon we draw the output...)

After training, we can sample from the model by discarding the image encoder. Instead, we input a random Gaussian vector to the decoder and provide the decoder with the text embedding to generate the image.

(see figure: Sampling from a trained cVAE.)
concepts.motivation_md: The cVAE framework provides a structured way to learn a latent space that is conditioned on text, allowing for diverse image generation from the same prompt by sampling from a distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Text-to-image cVAEs use a text encoder to condition the image generation process.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image with Conditional Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models generate images from text by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise conditioned on text embeddings.
concepts.content:
Text-to-image generation can also be performed using a conditional diffusion model, an approach used by DALL-E 2 and other popular systems. A key challenge is effectively inserting text embeddings into the decoder. One method is to insert text embedding vectors into each denoising U-Net, and even into multiple layers of each U-Net, allowing the model to condition all decisions on the text information.

(see figure: A text-to-image diffusion model.)

At sampling time, both conditional diffusion models and cVAEs take text and Gaussian noise as input. While a VAE uses a network that maps these inputs to an image in a single forward pass, a diffusion model maps to an image via a chain of denoising steps, each being a forward pass through a neural network.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffusion models often produce higher-quality and more detailed images than VAEs. By conditioning the iterative denoising process on text, the model can refine the image to better match the description at multiple scales.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffusion models generate images through iterative denoising steps rather than a single forward pass.

concepts.title: Image-to-Text (Image Captioning)
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-text, or image captioning, translates visual information into natural language descriptions.
concepts.content:
Naturally, we can also translate in the opposite direction using an image encoder and a text decoder. This problem is called image-to-text or image captioning. This translation is useful because language serves as a general-purpose interface for human knowledge; translating images to text links imagery to many other domains.

One example of an image-to-text system uses a transformer to map the input image to a set of tokens, which are then fed into an autoregressive text decoder implemented with another transformer.

(see figure: Image-to-text using a small transformer with cross-attention. The edges in gray are cross-attention edges. Many variations of this architecture are possible. For example, each layer of the text...)
concepts.motivation_md: Image captioning allows machines to describe the visual world in human terms, enabling applications like accessibility for the visually impaired, automated content indexing, and visual question answering.
concepts.recap_md: - Image captioning uses an image encoder and a text decoder to generate descriptions.

concepts.title: Cross-Attention Layer
concepts.one_liner: The cross-attention layer allows text tokens to attend to image tokens, integrating visual information into a text decoder.
concepts.content: The cross-attention layer (`cross-attn`) addresses the question of how to insert image tokens into a text model. In this layer, text tokens attend to image tokens. The image tokens emit their value vectors, which are mixed with the text token value vectors according to the attention weights to produce the next layer of tokens in the text decoder.
concepts.motivation_md: In multimodal tasks, the model needs a way to relate information from one modality (like an image) to another (like text). Cross-attention provides a mechanism for the text generation process to 'look at' specific parts of the image representation.
concepts.recap_md: - Cross-attention enables interaction between different modalities by letting one set of tokens attend to another.

concepts.title: Cross-Attention Equations
concepts.one_liner: Cross-attention equations define how queries from text tokens interact with keys and values from image tokens.
concepts.motivation_md: Formalizing cross-attention with equations allows for the precise implementation of multimodal transformers, where text and image features must be mathematically combined through a shared attention mechanism.
concepts.recap_md: - Cross-attention uses text-based queries $\mathbf{Q}_t$ and image-based keys $\mathbf{K}_\ell$ and values $\mathbf{V}_\ell$.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Text Decoding for Image Captioning
concepts.one_liner: An autoregressive text decoder uses causal attention to predict the next word in a sentence based on the sequence of previously generated words.
concepts.content: The text decoder is an autoregressive model that uses causal attention to predict the next word in the sentence given the previous words generated so far. In this strategy, the input to the text decoder is the tokens representing the previous words in the training data caption that describes the image. At sampling time, the model is run sequentially, where for each next word generated it autoregressively repeats, with that word being added to the input sequence of tokens. The text tokens themselves are produced by tokenizing the input words, for example, via byte-pair encodings or word-level encodings.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive decoding allows models to generate coherent, variable-length text descriptions by building sentences one token at a time, ensuring each word is contextually relevant to the preceding ones.
concepts.recap_md: [ - The model predicts the next word by attending to all previously generated tokens in the sequence. , - During sampling, the process repeats sequentially as each new word is appended to the input. , - Input words are converted into tokens using methods like byte-pair or word-level encoding. ]

concepts.title: Text as a Visual Representation
concepts.one_liner: Text can be viewed as a visual representation that describes an image's content in a format compatible with language models for reasoning.
concepts.content: One way of thinking about image-to-text is as yet another visual encoder, where text is the visual representation. Just like we can represent an image in terms of its frequencies (Fourier transform), its semantics and geometry (scene understanding), or its feature embeddings (DINO, CLIP, and others), we can also represent it in terms of a textual description of its content. In @fig-vision_and_language-different_visual_representations we show an image represented in several ways: (see figure: Four representations computed from the input on the left. The input image itself (its pixel values) is in fact a fifth representation of the scene.) Text is a powerful visual representation because it interfaces with language models. This means that after translating an image into text we can use language models to reason about the image contents.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing images as text allows computer vision systems to leverage the vast reasoning and knowledge-retrieval capabilities of large language models.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Text serves as a high-level visual representation alongside methods like Fourier transforms or feature embeddings. , - Using text as a representation enables the use of language models to reason about visual content. ]

concepts.title: Visual Question Answering (VQA)
concepts.one_liner: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a task where a system maps an image and a textual question to a corresponding textual answer.
concepts.content: Visual question answering (VQA) is a formulation of the goal to create a fully general vision algorithm that can answer any question about an image. The problem statement in VQA is to make a system that maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer, as shown in @fig-vision_and_language-VQA_examples. (see figure: An example VQA system.) Creating a VQA system requires a text encoder for the question, an image encoder for the image, and a text decoder for the answer. These components are connected using standard multimodal tools, and the model is trained on tuples consisting of a question, an image, and the correct answer.
concepts.motivation_md: VQA serves as a "Turing test" for visual intelligence, challenging AI to demonstrate a deep, general-purpose understanding of visual scenes through natural language interaction.
concepts.recap_md: [ - VQA systems map a combination of an image and a text question to a text-based answer. , - The architecture typically combines an image encoder, a text encoder, and a text decoder. , - Training requires datasets structured as tuples of questions, images, and ground-truth answers. ]

concepts.title: Language as a Perceptual Representation
concepts.one_liner: Language is a low-dimensional, abstracted perceptual representation that evolved to describe sensory information and interface with human knowledge.
concepts.content: From the perspective of vision, language is a perceptual representation. It is a way of describing "what is where" and much more in a low-dimensional and abstracted format that interfaces well with other domains of human knowledge. While theories of language evolution often focus on communication or reasoning, it can also be suggested that language is the result of perceptual representation learning over the course of human evolution and cultural development. It is one of the primary formats brains have developed to represent the complex sensory array around us. As David Marr defined it, vision is the process of knowing "what is where by looking."
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective frames language not just as a communication tool, but as an efficient, learned encoding of the physical world that facilitates cross-domain reasoning.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Language acts as an abstracted, low-dimensional format for representing visual and sensory information. , - It may be viewed as a product of perceptual representation learning throughout human evolution. , - This format allows sensory data to interface effectively with broader domains of knowledge and reasoning. ]

concepts.title: Slow down to speed up
concepts.one_liner: In research, taking the time to verify assumptions and understand algorithms deeply leads to faster progress than rushing through experiments without comprehension.
concepts.content: The advice "slow down to speed up" highlights a key difference between structured classroom learning and research. In research, there is no guaranteed correct answer or immediate feedback to identify mistakes. To handle this uncertainty, one should take things slowly by verifying assumptions and deeply understanding the program, algorithm, or proof. When conducting experiments, change only one variable at a time to ensure the results are interpretable. While this approach may feel slow, it prevents the lack of progress that comes from flailing around without understanding the system. (see figure: Research advice for a bumper sticker.)
concepts.motivation_md: Research lacks the clear structure and immediate feedback of coursework, making careful, methodical verification essential to avoid getting lost in complex, unidentifiable errors.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Research requires a slower, more deliberate pace than coursework because correct answers are not pre-defined. , - Verify every assumption and change only one variable at a time during experimentation. , - Deep understanding of the underlying system is more productive than rapid, unguided trial and error. ]

concepts.title: Reporting failures and progress effectively
concepts.one_liner: Effective progress reporting involves narrowing down where a system fails and ruling out potential causes rather than simply stating that it does not work.
concepts.content: When reporting issues, avoid simply stating that a system "doesn't work." Instead, identify the specific step where the failure occurs and demonstrate that previous steps are functioning as expected. Effective reporting includes ruling out specific causes and analyzing why a particular instance fails or if the issue is categorical. If a solution isn't immediate, try to create a simpler case that does work or a case that fails more dramatically to better understand the system's limits. Progress in research includes showing why something doesn't work, simplifying tasks, or spending time reading to build necessary understanding.
concepts.motivation_md: Precise failure reporting accelerates debugging and collaboration by allowing mentors and peers to focus on specific, isolated problems rather than the entire system.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Isolate failures to specific steps and provide evidence of where the system still functions correctly. , - Use simplified cases or extreme failure examples to probe the boundaries of the problem. , - Define progress broadly to include learning why a method fails or gaining necessary theoretical background. ]

concepts.title: Hard work and work-life balance in research
concepts.one_liner: Success in graduate-level research is driven by sustained hard work and a passion for the problem rather than just innate intelligence.
concepts.content: In graduate school, hard work is often what distinguishes successful researchers, as most peers are already highly intelligent. Similar to great athletes, the best researchers are often those who dedicate the most time to their practice. However, it is equally important to maintain a sustainable pace and a healthy work-life balance to protect the time needed for high-quality research. The most effective way to sustain this effort is to choose a research topic you love; if you enjoy the work, the necessary time and effort follow naturally.
concepts.motivation_md: Research is a marathon that requires consistent effort over long periods; understanding the role of persistence and passion helps students manage the transition from competitive schooling to open-ended discovery.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Hard work and persistence are primary drivers of success in research environments where everyone is smart. , - Maintain a sustainable pace by balancing intense work with time for relationships and relaxation. , - Choosing a research topic you are passionate about makes the required hard work feel more natural. ]

concepts.title: Steering and time management
concepts.one_liner: Steering involves periodically stepping back from hard work to ensure that efforts are being directed toward the right research problems.
concepts.content: While hard work provides the "motor" for research, "steering" provides the rudder. Steering means stepping back periodically to evaluate whether you are working on the right problems. Hard work alone is insufficient if the effort is misdirected. Utilizing time management strategies can be highly beneficial in learning how to prioritize and solve the most impactful problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Without periodic evaluation, a researcher might spend significant effort on low-impact or irrelevant tasks; steering ensures that hard work translates into meaningful progress.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Hard work is the motor of research, but steering is the rudder that ensures you are moving in the right direction. , - Periodically step back to evaluate if your current tasks are the most important ones to solve. , - Time management techniques are essential tools for effective steering and prioritization. ]

concepts.title: Optimality of Gabor Localization
concepts.one_liner: Gabor functions are the optimal functions for achieving the best simultaneous localization in both the spatial and frequency domains.
concepts.content: Gabor functions are localized in both the spatial and frequency domain. One remarkable property of the Gabor function is that it is the optimal function that achieves the best simultaneous localization in space and frequency.
concepts.motivation_md: In signal processing, there is a fundamental trade-off between resolution in time (or space) and resolution in frequency. Gabor functions are significant because they mathematically reach the lower bound of this uncertainty principle, providing the most precise possible representation across both domains.
concepts.recap_md: - Gabor functions provide simultaneous localization in space and frequency.

concepts.title: 2D Complex Gabor Function
concepts.one_liner: A 2D complex Gabor function is formed by multiplying a complex Fourier basis function by a spatially localized 2D Gaussian window.
concepts.content:
Gabor functions can be extended to two dimensions by using 2D Gaussians and waves. Using complex waves provides a more general form of the Gabor function. We can multiply a complex Fourier basis function, $\exp{ \left(j  \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right)  \right)}$, by a spatially localized 2D Gaussian window, $\exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$ to obtain a Gabor function, $\psi(x,y)$:
$$\psi(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \exp{ \left( j \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) \right)}$$
concepts.motivation_md: While simple sinusoids have perfect frequency localization but no spatial localization, and Gaussians have spatial localization but poor frequency specificity, the complex Gabor function combines both to analyze specific frequencies at specific locations in an image.
concepts.recap_md: - The 2D Gabor function is the product of a 2D Gaussian and a complex exponential.

concepts.title: Cosine and Sine Phase Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: The real and imaginary components of a complex Gabor function define the cosine and sine phase Gabor filters, respectively.
concepts.content:
A complex Gabor function is a complex-valued function of location and frequency. We can get the cosine and sine waves by looking at the real and imaginary components, $\psi(x,y;u_0,v_0) =  \psi_r(x,y;u_0,v_0) + j \psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0)$ with:
$$\psi_r(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \cos{ \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) }$$
$$\psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2} \exp{\left(-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right)} \sin{ \left(u_0 x + v_0 y \right) }$$
Where $\psi_r(x,y;u_0,v_0)$ and $\psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0)$ are the cosine and sine phase Gabor filters. (Figure 1.1.6) shows the Gaussian window and the real and imaginary parts of the Gabor function.

(see figure: 2D Gabor functions. (a) The localizing Gaussian window ($\sigma=1$), which can be thought of as a Gabor function for a zero frequency sinusoid. (b) Cosine, and (c) sine phase Gabor functions with...)
concepts.motivation_md: Splitting the complex Gabor filter into real (cosine) and imaginary (sine) parts allows for the detection of features with different symmetries, such as lines (even symmetry) and edges (odd symmetry).
concepts.recap_md: - The real part of a complex Gabor function corresponds to a cosine phase filter.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of a complex Gabor function is a Gaussian in the frequency domain shifted by the filter's central frequency.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform of a complex Gabor function is a Gaussian in the Fourier domain shifted with respect to the origin:
$$\Psi(u,v; u_0,v_0) = \exp{ \left( -  \left((u-u_0)^2 + (v-v_0)^2 \right) \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right) }$$

(see figure: (a) Cosine and (b) sine Gabor functions. (c) Magnitude of the Fourier transform of both the cosine and sine Gabor functions (their FT only differs in the phase). (d) FT of the complex Gabor function...)

(Figure 1.1.7) shows the magnitude of the Fourier transform of the Gabor filters. (Figure 1.1.7a) shows the cosine phase Gabor function, $\psi_r(x,y;u_0,v_0)$, and (Figure 1.1.7b) shows the sine phase Gabor function, $\psi_i(x,y;u_0,v_0)$. (Figure 1.1.7c) shows the Fourier transform of the cosine phase Gabor function, $\Psi_r(u,v;u_0,v_0)$, and (Figure 1.1.7d) shows the Fourier transform of the complex Gabor function, $\Psi(u,v;u_0,v_0)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the Fourier transform of a Gabor filter reveals its band-pass nature, showing exactly which range of spatial frequencies and orientations the filter will respond to.
concepts.recap_md: - The Fourier transform of a Gabor function is a shifted Gaussian.

concepts.title: Gabor Filter as Oriented Band-pass Filter
concepts.one_liner: The Gabor filter is an oriented band-pass filter.
concepts.content: The Gabor filter is an oriented band-pass filter.
concepts.motivation_md: Images contain information at many scales and directions. An oriented band-pass filter allows us to isolate specific textures or edges that align with a particular direction and frequency range.
concepts.recap_md: - Gabor filters act as oriented band-pass filters in image processing.

concepts.title: Gabor Filter Parameters
concepts.one_liner: The Gabor filter's behavior is determined by its central frequency, which sets orientation, and its width, which determines spatial locality.
concepts.content:
The Gabor function changes when modifying its parameters: the central frequency $(u_0,v_0)$ and the width $\sigma$. The value of $\sigma$ sets the locality of the window of analysis, while the values of $(u_0,v_0)$ adjust the orientation and frequency of the Gabor function. A large $\sigma$ makes the spatial extent large and the frequency extent small; a small value of $\sigma$ has the opposite behavior. Analyzing an image with a set of Gabor functions with a large $\sigma$ is similar to computing the Fourier transform of the image.

(see figure: Cosine phase Gabor functions tuned to different widths, frequencies, and orientations, and their corresponding Fourier transforms (only the magnitude is shown).)
concepts.motivation_md: By tuning $\sigma$ and $(u_0,v_0)$, we can control the resolution of our analysis. This allows us to choose between high spatial precision (small $\sigma$) or high frequency precision (large $\sigma$) depending on the image features we want to extract.
concepts.recap_md: - $\sigma$ controls the trade-off between spatial locality and frequency resolution.

concepts.title: Biological Motivation for Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Gabor filters are motivated by their similarity to cortical receptive fields in the mammalian visual system.
concepts.content: One important characteristic of Gabor filters is that they are very similar to the shape of some cortical receptive fields found in the mammalian visual system. This similarity suggests that these filters are an effective way to build image representations, reflecting the simple and complex cells found in the visual system.
concepts.motivation_md: Computer vision often looks to biological systems for efficient ways to process visual information. Since mammalian brains use Gabor-like structures to process scenes, using them in algorithms is a biologically-inspired approach to feature detection.
concepts.recap_md: - Gabor filters mimic the receptive fields of simple cells in the mammalian primary visual cortex.

concepts.title: Convolution with Gabor Filters
concepts.one_liner: Convolving an image with a Gabor filter produces an output that represents the image's content at a specific location, frequency, and orientation.
concepts.content:
The convolution of the Gabor function with an image, $\ell(x,y)$, results in an output image that depends on both space, $(x,y)$, and frequency, $(u,v)$:
$$\ell_{\psi} \left(x,y,u,v \right) = \ell\left(x,y\right) \circ \psi(x,y;u,v)$$

(see figure: Zebra picture filtered by cosine and sine Gabor functions at three scales with $\sigma = 2,4,8$ and $u_0 = 1/(2\sigma)$, $v_0=0$. Each row shows one scale. (a) Cosine and sine Gabor filters. (b)...)

(Figure 1.1.9) shows the result of the convolution between a picture and the cosine and sine phase Gabor functions at three different scales ($\sigma = 2,4,8$). In this example, the Gabor filters are tuned to detect vertical edges. Gabor filters are useful for analyzing line or edge phase structures in images, and they provide further benefits when combined in quadrature pairs.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution allows us to apply the Gabor filter across an entire image to create a 'feature map.' This map highlights where specific textures or edges occur, which is a foundational step in tasks like object recognition or texture analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - Convolution with Gabor filters extracts localized frequency information from an image.

concepts.title: Clustering
concepts.one_liner: Clustering is the process of quantizing a signal into discrete categories by mapping members of a dataset to a set of integer classes.
concepts.content:
Clustering is a method of signal compression that quantizes data into discrete categories. Mathematically, clustering is defined as a function $f: \{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N \rightarrow \{1,\dots,k\}$, which maps members of a dataset $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ to $k$ integer classes, where $k$ can potentially be unbounded. This operation can be visualized as a mapping from data points to one-hot codes.

(see figure: You can think of clustering as being just like image labeling, except that that labels are self-discovered rather than being predefined.)
concepts.motivation_md: Clustering serves as a form of dimensionality reduction and compression. By summarizing complex signals into discrete category labels, it creates a lighter weight and more abstracted substrate for further reasoning and computation.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is a mapping $f$ from a dataset to a set of $k$ discrete integer classes.
 - It acts as a form of signal quantization and compression.
 - It can be viewed as self-discovered labeling of data.

concepts.title: Vector quantization
concepts.one_liner: Vector quantization is an alternative name for clustering commonly used in representation learning literature.
concepts.content: Another name for clustering, more common in the representation learning literature, is **vector quantization**.
concepts.motivation_md: This term is used to describe the process of mapping continuous vectors to a discrete set of representative vectors, emphasizing its role in signal processing and compression.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is synonymous with clustering.
 - The term is frequently used in representation learning contexts.

concepts.title: Clustering as compression
concepts.one_liner: Clustering follows the principle of compression, where discrete category labels summarize complex data to facilitate reasoning.
concepts.content: Clustering follows from the principle of compression: if we can summarize a signal with a discrete category label, then this summary serves as a lighter weight and more abstracted substrate for further reasoning. This is analogous to how natural language uses words like "antelope" or "zebra" as discrete category labels to summarize huge, diverse conceptual sets. In this sense, words are clusters—mappings from data to integers—and clustering is the problem of making up new words for things. Just as words gain structure through grammar and connotation, additional structure can be added on top of visual clusters.
concepts.motivation_md: The goal is to reduce complex, high-dimensional data into a manageable set of discrete symbols (like words) that retain the essential meaning of the original signal for easier processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Clustering summarizes signals into discrete labels to enable more efficient reasoning.
 - It is conceptually similar to how language uses words to categorize diverse entities.
 - These discrete labels act as a compressed representation of the original data.

concepts.title: Code vector
concepts.one_liner: A code vector is a representation of the data within a specific cluster, most commonly defined as the cluster center or mean.
concepts.content: Many clustering algorithms compute a representation of the data within each cluster known as a **code vector**. The most common code vector is the **cluster center**, $\mu$, which is the mean value of all datapoints assigned to that cluster. While clusters can be represented by other statistics such as variance or arbitrary embedding vectors, these are less common. The set of cluster centers, $\{\mu_i\}_{i=1}^k$, represents the whole dataset by summarizing its main modes of behavior.
concepts.motivation_md: Code vectors provide a way to represent a group of data points with a single prototypical value, enabling efficient data summarization and reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:
- A code vector represents the data points belonging to a specific cluster.
 - The most common type of code vector is the cluster mean (cluster center).
 - The collection of all code vectors summarizes the main behaviors of a dataset.

concepts.title: Cluster center
concepts.one_liner: A cluster center is the mean value of all datapoints assigned to a cluster, serving as its prototypical representation.
concepts.content: A **cluster center**, $\mu$, is the most common type of **code vector**. It is defined as the mean value of all datapoints assigned to a specific cluster. Although clusters can occasionally be represented by other statistics like variance or embedding vectors, the mean is the standard representation. The set of cluster centers $\{\mu_i\}_{i=1}^k$ summarizes the main modes of behavior in a dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: Using the mean as a cluster center minimizes the squared distance between the center and the points in the cluster, providing an optimal central representative.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is the mean value of all points within a cluster.
 - It is the standard form of a code vector.
 - A set of centers provides a summary of the entire dataset's modes.

concepts.title: K-means algorithm
concepts.one_liner: K-means is a popular clustering algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by minimizing the distance between points and their assigned cluster code vectors.
concepts.content:
$K$-means is a clustering algorithm that partitions data into $k$ clusters. Each datapoint $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ is assigned to a cluster indexed by an integer $a_i \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$, and each cluster is associated with a code vector $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^M$. The algorithm seeks to minimize the $k$-means objective, which is the sum of squared distances between datapoints and their assigned code vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{kmeans}} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \left\lVert\mathbf{z}_{a_i} - \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert^2_2
\end{aligned}
$$

The algorithm optimizes two sets of parameters: the cluster assignments (represented by an encoder function $f$) and the code vectors (represented by a decoder function $g$). Because cluster assignments are discrete, gradient descent is not suitable; instead, $k$-means uses an iterative process: compute cluster means based on current assignments, then reassign points to the nearest mean until convergence.

[FIGURE:83e2c20af43a1fa5 | A learning diagram for k-means ($L_2$) clustering. It shows an input 'Data' represented as {x^(i)} entering a central box via an arrow. Inside the box, the 'Objective' is...]

(see figure: A scatter plot on x_1 and x_2 axes showing several clusters of colored data points. Five distinct clusters are visible: yellow, blue, red, orange, and maroon. Large 'X' markers in corresponding...)

(see figure: A 2D scatter plot on x_1 and x_2 axes showing five distinct clusters of data points, each colored differently: yellow, blue, red, orange, and maroon. Each cluster has a large 'X' mark of the same...)

(see figure: A 2D scatter plot on x_1 and x_2 axes showing five distinct clusters of data points, each colored differently: yellow, blue, red, brown, and orange. Each cluster contains a large 'X' marker of...)

(see figure: A scatter plot on a 2D plane with axes x_1 and x_2 showing five distinct clusters of data points. Each cluster is colored differently (blue, yellow, red, maroon, and orange) and has a large 'X'...)
concepts.motivation_md: K-means provides a simple and efficient way to find a faithful but compressed representation of a dataset by approximating data points with a small set of prototypical vectors.
concepts.recap_md:
- Partitions data into $k$ clusters by minimizing squared Euclidean distance to cluster centers.
 - Iteratively updates cluster assignments and code vectors (means).
 - Functionally similar to an autoencoder with a discrete bottleneck.

concepts.title: K-means objective
concepts.one_liner: The k-means objective is to minimize the sum of squared distances between each datapoint and its assigned cluster's code vector.
concepts.content:
The $k$-means objective, $J_{\texttt{kmeans}}$, is defined as the sum of the squared $L_2$ distances between each datapoint $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ and the code vector $\mathbf{z}_{a_i}$ of the cluster it is assigned to:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{kmeans}} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \left\lVert\mathbf{z}_{a_i} - \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert^2_2
\end{aligned}
$$

By minimizing this objective, the code vector assigned to each datapoint becomes a good approximation of that point, resulting in a faithful but compressed representation of the dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: This objective function quantifies the reconstruction error of the compression; minimizing it ensures that the discrete cluster labels and their centers represent the original data as accurately as possible.
concepts.recap_md:
- Measures the total squared error between data points and their assigned cluster centers.
 - Minimizing this objective leads to a compressed representation that approximates the original data.
 - It is the central loss function optimized by the k-means algorithm.

concepts.title: Block coordinate descent for k-means
concepts.one_liner: K-means uses block coordinate descent to alternate between minimizing the objective with respect to cluster assignments and cluster code vectors.
concepts.content:
$K$-means employs an optimization strategy known as **block coordinate descent**. This algorithm divides the optimization parameters into subsets, or blocks, and alternates between fully minimizing the objective for each block while keeping others fixed. In $k$-means, the two blocks are the cluster assignments $\{a_i\}_{i=1}^N$ and the code vectors $\{\mathbf{z}_j\}_{j=1}^k$. 

The update rules are:
1. **Assign datapoints to the nearest cluster**:
$$\begin{aligned}
    a_i &\leftarrow \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,k\}} \left\lVert\mathbf{z}_j - \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2
\end{aligned}$$
2. **Set code vectors to the cluster centers**:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{z}_j &\leftarrow \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}(a_i = j)\mathbf{x}^{(i)}
\end{aligned}$$

These steps repeat until a fixed point is reached, where all points are closest to their assigned cluster's code vector.
concepts.motivation_md: Since the cluster assignment parameters are discrete, standard gradient descent cannot be used. Block coordinate descent provides a robust alternative by solving simpler sub-problems iteratively.
concepts.recap_md:
- Alternates between updating cluster assignments and updating cluster centers.
 - Each step fully minimizes the objective with respect to one set of parameters.
 - Convergence is reached when assignments no longer change.

concepts.title: Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: Localization loss measures how close a detected location is to the ground truth object location.
concepts.content: Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$) measures how close the detected location is to the ground truth object location. It is used to quantify the error in the predicted bounding box coordinates $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$ relative to the actual coordinates $\mathbf{b}_i$.
concepts.motivation_md: In object detection, identifying that an object exists is not enough; we must also accurately determine its spatial position. Localization loss provides a differentiable metric to optimize the precision of predicted bounding box coordinates during training.
concepts.recap_md: - Localization loss measures the spatial discrepancy between predicted and ground truth bounding boxes.

concepts.title: Intersection over Union (IoU)
concepts.one_liner: Intersection over Union (IoU) is a typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes.
concepts.content: A typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes is the Intersection over Union (IoU). [FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.] The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates no overlap and 1 indicates that both bounding boxes are identical.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard distance metrics like L2 distance don't account for the area of overlap relative to the total area covered. IoU provides a normalized metric that intuitively represents how well two boxes align regardless of their absolute size.
concepts.recap_md: - IoU measures the overlap between two bounding boxes as a value between 0 and 1.

concepts.title: IoU Loss
concepts.one_liner: IoU loss is defined as one minus the Intersection over Union between predicted and ground truth bounding boxes.
concepts.content: Since IoU is a similarity measure, the localization loss can be defined as: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$ The IoU is translation and scale invariant, and it is frequently used to evaluate object detectors. However, the IoU loss becomes 1 when the two bounding boxes do not overlap, which means that there will be no gradient information when running backpropagation.
concepts.motivation_md: While IoU is a good evaluation metric, it needs to be converted into a loss function for training. By using $1 - IoU$, we create a minimization objective that is scale-invariant, though it suffers from vanishing gradients when boxes don't overlap.
concepts.recap_md: - IoU loss is calculated as $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} = 1 - IoU$.

concepts.title: L2 Regression Loss
concepts.one_liner: L2 regression loss is a simple optimization objective that sums the squared differences of bounding box coordinates.
concepts.content: A simpler loss to optimize than IoU is the L2 regression loss: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$ The L2 regression loss is translation invariant, but it is not scale invariant; the loss is larger for big bounding boxes. The following graph compares the IoU loss and the L2 regression loss for two square bounding boxes, with an area equal to 1, as a function of the relative $x$-displacement: (see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)
concepts.motivation_md: L2 loss is computationally simple and provides gradients even when boxes are far apart. However, its lack of scale invariance means large objects contribute disproportionately to the total loss compared to small objects.
concepts.recap_md: - L2 loss sums the squared differences of the four bounding box coordinates.

concepts.title: Overall Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: The overall loss combines classification and localization losses, weighted by a parameter and an indicator function.
concepts.content: The overall loss is computed by combining the classification and the localization loss: $$ \mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) + \lambda \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i) $$ where the indicator function $\mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)$ sets to zero the location loss for the bounding boxes that do not overlap with any of the ground truth bounding boxes. The parameter $\lambda$ can be used to balance the relative strength of both losses. This loss makes it possible to train the whole detection algorithm end-to-end, although it is also possible to train the localization and classification stages independently.
concepts.motivation_md: Object detection requires solving two tasks simultaneously: identifying what an object is and where it is. A multi-task loss function allows the model to optimize both objectives in a single training pass.
concepts.recap_md: - The total loss is the sum of classification loss and a weighted localization loss.

concepts.title: Precision-Recall Evaluation
concepts.one_liner: The most common approach for evaluating object localization is measuring the average precision-recall.
concepts.content: There are several ways of evaluating object localization approaches. The most common approach is measuring the average precision-recall. Just as when defining the localization loss, we need to assign detection outputs to ground truth labels. This assignment can be done in several ways, and they can result in different measures of performance. The methodology introduced in the PASCAL challenge used a specific procedure for this assignment.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple accuracy is insufficient for object detection because it doesn't account for the trade-off between finding all objects (recall) and ensuring detections are correct (precision).
concepts.recap_md: - Average precision-recall is the standard metric for evaluating object localization.

concepts.title: Assigning Detections to Ground Truth Labels
concepts.one_liner: Detections are assigned to ground truth labels by matching high-confidence boxes to the highest IoU ground truth.
concepts.content: To assign detections to ground truth labels, first sort all detections by their score, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$. Then, loop over the sorted list in decreasing order. For each bounding box, compute the IoU with all ground truth bounding boxes and select the one with the highest IoU. If the IoU is larger than a predefined threshold (typically 0.5), mark the detection as correct and remove that ground truth bounding box from the list to avoid double counting. If the IoU is below the threshold, mark the detection as incorrect and do not remove the ground truth label. Repeat until all detections are evaluated, and mark any remaining ground-truth bounding boxes as missed detections.
concepts.motivation_md: In evaluation, we need to know which predicted box corresponds to which real object. This greedy matching process ensures that each object is only counted once and that high-confidence predictions are prioritized.
concepts.recap_md: - Detections are matched to ground truth boxes based on the highest IoU above a threshold.

concepts.title: Precision-Recall Curve
concepts.one_liner: The precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold.
concepts.content: The precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold $\beta$. As each bounding box comes with a confidence score $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$, the threshold $\beta$ is used to decide if an object is present at the bounding box location $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$. Given a threshold $\beta$, the number of detections is $\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)$ and the number of correct detections is $\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i$. Both precision and recall are quantities between 0 and 1, where high values correspond to high performance. (see figure: Example of a precision-recall curve. This is a standard plot to evaluate detection algorithms. It is usually summarized by the area under the curve. In this example, note that recall stops around...)
concepts.motivation_md: A single precision or recall value only describes performance at one specific threshold. The curve shows the full trade-off, allowing researchers to see how the model behaves across all possible confidence levels.
concepts.recap_md: - The curve plots precision against recall as the confidence threshold $\beta$ varies.

concepts.title: L2 Normalization
concepts.one_liner: $L_2$ normalization projects the inputs onto the unit hypersphere, which is useful for bounding the activations to unit vectors.
concepts.content: L2 normalization projects the inputs onto the unit hypersphere, which is useful for bounding the activations to unit vectors: $$ \begin{aligned} \textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{out}}}[i] &= \frac{\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{in}}}[i]}{\left\lVert\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}}\right\rVert_2} & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{L2-norm} \end{aligned} $$
concepts.motivation_md: It is used to bound activations to unit vectors by projecting them onto a unit hypersphere.
concepts.recap_md: - Projects input activations onto the unit hypersphere. - Bounds activations to unit vectors using the $L_2$ norm.

concepts.title: Layer Normalization (Layernorm)
concepts.one_liner: Layer normalization standardizes the vector of input activations for each datapoint independently, mapping them to a hypersphere while centering, scaling, and shifting them.
concepts.content: Layernorm standardizes the vector of input activations: $$ \begin{aligned} \mu &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{in}}}[i] \\ \sigma^2 &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{in}}}[i] - \mu\right)^2 \\ \textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{out}}}[i] &= \textcolor[rgb]{0.2, 0.6, 1.0}{\gamma} \frac{\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{in}}}[i] - \mu}{\sigma} + \textcolor[rgb]{0.2, 0.6, 1.0}{\beta} & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{layernorm} \end{aligned} $$ Like $L_2$-normalization, layernorm maps the activation vector to the surface of a hypersphere, but it also centers the activations to have zero mean, and then scales and shifts them via $\gamma$ and $\beta$. As an exercise, see if you can write layernorm using $L_2$-normalization as one of the steps. Layernorm computes a mean and variance over elements of a datapoint $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ separately for each datapoint in a batch, whereas batchnorm computes the mean and variance per channel over datapoints in a batch. (see figure: Batchnorm vs layernorm. Gray indicates the region over which mean and variance are computed. See also Figure 2 of \cite{wu2018group} for more such visualizations.) Batchnorm standardizes each element of a tensor by the mean and variance of its column, while layernorm standardizes by the mean and variance of its row. One issue with batchnorm is that it requires processing a batch of datapoints all at once and introduces a dependency between them, violating the principle that datapoints should be processed independently and identically (iid). Layernorm does not have this problem and processes each datapoint in an iid fashion.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a way to standardize activations independently for each datapoint, avoiding the inter-batch dependencies and iid violations found in batch normalization.
concepts.recap_md: - Standardizes activations across the features of a single datapoint independently. - Centers activations to zero mean and applies learnable scaling and shifting. - Avoids inter-datapoint dependencies, maintaining the iid assumption.

concepts.title: Neural networks as distribution transformers

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: A deep net can be thought of as transforming an input data distribution into an output data distribution layer by layer through a sequence of embeddings.
concepts.content: A deep net transforms an input data distribution, $p_{\text {data }}$, into an output data distribution, $p_{\text {out}}$, layer by layer. Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data, and we can consider the distribution of activations on some layer $\ell$ to be $p_{\ell}$. The goal of a binary softmax classifier, for example, is to move the datapoints around until all the class 0 points end up moved to $(1,0)$ on the output layer and all the class 1 points end up moved to $(0,1)$. (see figure: Mapping plot for a `linear`-`relu` stack.) Most loss functions can also be interpreted from this angle: they penalize the divergence, in one form or another, between the output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective helps explain how complex networks achieve classification or regression by geometrically reshaping data distributions into separable or target-aligned configurations.
concepts.recap_md: - Views a deep network as a sequence of transformations on a data distribution. - Represents each layer's activations as a distinct embedding $p_{\ell}$. - Maps the input distribution $p_{\text{data}}$ toward a target output distribution $p_{\text{out}}$.

concepts.title: Goal of a binary softmax classifier

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: The goal of a binary softmax classifier is to move datapoints until class 0 points end up at $(1,0)$ and class 1 points end up at $(0,1)$.
concepts.content: An incoming data distribution can be reshaped layer by layer into a desired configuration. The goal of a binary softmax classifier, for example, is to move the datapoints around until all the class 0 points end up moved to $(1,0)$ on the output layer and all the class 1 points end up moved to $(0,1)$. This is because the one-hot code for the integer 0 is $[1,0]$ and the one-hot code for the integer 1 is $[0,1]$.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a geometric interpretation of classification as the process of moving data points to specific locations in the output space.
concepts.recap_md: - Aims to map class 0 points to the coordinate $(1,0)$. - Aims to map class 1 points to the coordinate $(0,1)$.

concepts.title: Embedding

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data.
concepts.content: Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data. We can think of a deep net as transforming an input data distribution, $p_{\text {data }}$, into an output data distribution, $p_{\text {out}}$, through a sequence of these embeddings. We can consider the distribution of activations on some layer $\ell$ to be $p_{\ell}$. Layer by layer, a deep net transforms $p_{\text {data }}$ into $p_{\texttt{1}}$ into $p_{\texttt{2}}$, and so on until finally transforming the data to the distribution $p_{\text {out}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Embeddings allow the network to transform raw input into increasingly useful, high-level representations for the task at hand.
concepts.recap_md: - Defines an embedding as the representation of data at a specific network layer. - Treats layer activations as a distribution $p_{\ell}$ in a sequence of transformations.

concepts.title: Loss function as distribution divergence

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: Most loss functions can be interpreted as penalizing the divergence between the output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$.
concepts.content: Most loss functions can be interpreted as penalizing the divergence, in one form or another, between the output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ of a neural network and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$. This perspective treats the deep net as a transformer of the input data distribution $p_{\text {data }}$ into an output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ through intermediate layer embeddings $p_{\ell}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective links optimization objectives to information theory and the geometric transformation of data distributions.
concepts.recap_md: - Interprets loss functions as measuring the divergence between $p_{\text{out}}$ and $p_{\text{target}}$. - Frames training as the process of aligning output and target distributions.

concepts.title: Visualizing 2D-to-2D mappings

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: Visualizing 2D-to-2D mappings provides insight into how neural net layers act to transform a Gaussian blob of data.
concepts.content: Visualizing two-dimensional (2D)-to-2D mappings extends to visualizing the $N$-dimensional (ND)-to-ND mappings performed by real deep nets. Already 2D-to-2D visualizations can give a lot of insight into the general case. In @fig-neural_nets_as_data_transformations-2D_mapping_diagrams, we show how three common neural net layers may act to transform a Gaussian blob of data centered at the origin. (see figure: 2D mapping diagrams for several neural layers. The `linear` layer mapping will shift, stretch, and rotate depending on its weights and biases.)
concepts.motivation_md: Since high-dimensional transformations are difficult to visualize, 2D mappings serve as a useful proxy for understanding the geometric effects of different layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses 2D-to-2D diagrams to visualize how layers transform Gaussian data blobs. - Provides intuition for high-dimensional transformations that are difficult to plot.

concepts.title: Sparsity in high-dimensional ReLU networks

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: In high-dimensional ReLU networks, almost the entire space gets mapped to the axes, resulting in very sparse representational geometry.
concepts.content: The relu layer maps many points to the axes of the positive quadrant. In general, with relu-nets, a lot of data density will build up along these axes, because any point not in the positive quadrant snaps to an axis. This effect becomes exaggerated in real networks with high-dimensional embeddings. In particular, for a width-$N$ layer, the region that is strictly positive occupies only $\frac{1}{2^N}$ proportion of the embedding space, so almost the entire space gets mapped to the axes after a relu layer. The geometry of high-dimensional neural representations may become very sparse because of this, where most of the volume of representational space is not occupied by any datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Explains the geometric origin of sparsity in ReLU-based networks and how high dimensionality affects the occupancy of the representation space.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps non-positive inputs to axes, concentrating data density along them. - Results in extremely sparse representations in high dimensions where only $\frac{1}{2^N}$ of the space is positive.

concepts.title: Euler Angles (Yaw, Pitch, Roll)
concepts.one_liner: Euler angles decompose a camera's rotation into yaw, pitch, and roll along the three coordinate axes.
concepts.content: To derive the rotation, we consider the Euler angles and decompose the rotation using rotations along the three axes (yaw, pitch, roll): (see figure: Rotation expressed by Euler angles (yaw, pitch, roll).) Each angle measures the rotation along the camera-coordinate axes. Using this representation of the rotation, the rotation matrix can be written as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Z & \sin \theta_Z & 0\\ -\sin \theta_Z & \cos \theta_Z & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Y & 0 & -\sin \theta_Y\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ \sin \theta_Y & 0 & \cos \theta_Y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \cos \theta_X & \sin \theta_X \\ 0 & -\sin \theta_X & \cos \theta_X \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ In this equation, the sign of the angles are chosen to reflect that a rotation of the camera is equivalent to the opposite rotation of the 3D point.
concepts.motivation_md: Euler angles provide an intuitive way to represent complex 3D rotations as a sequence of three independent rotations around the principal axes, which is essential for modeling camera movement in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Euler angles decompose a 3D rotation into yaw, pitch, and roll components.

concepts.title: Small Motion Rotation Approximation
concepts.one_liner: For small time intervals, rotation matrices can be approximated using small-angle assumptions to simplify the relationship between 3D points and motion.
concepts.content: For a small $\Delta t$, the angles will be small, and we can approximate the trigonometric functions by $\cos \alpha \approx 1$ and $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$. We can also approximate the product $\sin \alpha \sin \beta \approx 0$ as it results in a second-order term. Under these assumptions, the rotation matrix simplifies to: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta_Z & 0\\ -\theta_Z & 1& 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -\theta_Y\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ \theta_Y & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & \theta_X \\ 0 & -\theta_X & 1 \end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta_Z & -\theta_Y\\ -\theta_Z & 1 & \theta_X \\ \theta_Y & -\theta_X & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ The change in position of a point $\mathbf{P}$ is then: $$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} + (\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} - \mathbf{I}) \mathbf{P}_t = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\theta_Z & \theta_Y\\ \theta_Z & 0 & -\theta_X \\ -\theta_Y & \theta_X & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}_t$$ The last term corresponds to the cross product in matrix form, allowing the expression to be rewritten as: $$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t$$
concepts.motivation_md: Linearizing rotation for small displacements simplifies complex trigonometric equations into a linear form involving cross products, making it computationally efficient to estimate motion in real-time applications.
concepts.recap_md: - Small angles allow the approximations $\cos \alpha \approx 1$ and $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$.

concepts.title: General 2D Motion Field Equation
concepts.one_liner: The general 2D motion field equation relates image plane velocity to the camera's translational and rotational velocities.
concepts.content: Substituting the small motion approximation into the general camera motion equation, we obtain the motion of a 3D point: $$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = - \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{W} \times \mathbf{P}_t = -\begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -W_Z Y + W_Y Z\\ W_Z X - W_X Z \\ -W_Y X + W_X Y \end{bmatrix}$$ where $\mathbf{W}=(W_X,W_Y,W_Z)$ is the angular velocity. Using the projection equations $x=f \, X/Z$ and $y=f \, Y/Z$, the 2D motion field is: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} -f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix} + \frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} xy & -f^2-x^2) & f y \\ f^2+y^2 & -xy & -f x \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} W_X\\ W_Y \\ W_Z \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ This expression relates the 2D motion field with camera velocity and rotation. The matrices are functions of intrinsic camera parameters (focal length $f$) and camera coordinates. Note that this expression is only valid for small displacements.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation is fundamental for computer vision as it provides a mathematical link between the observed flow of pixels and the physical movement of the camera in 3D space.
concepts.recap_md: - The motion field is the sum of a translational component and a rotational component.

concepts.title: Camera Rotation Motion Field
concepts.one_liner: When a camera only rotates, the resulting 2D motion field depends solely on rotational velocity and camera parameters, independent of scene depth.
concepts.content: In the case where there is only camera rotation ($V_X=V_Y=V_Z=0$), the motion field equation simplifies to: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} xy & -f^2-x^2) & f y \\ f^2+y^2 & -xy & -f x \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} W_X\\ W_Y \\ W_Z \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ The 2D motion field does not depend on the 3D scene structure $Z$ and is only a function of the rotational velocity and the camera parameters. Therefore, under pure camera rotation, we cannot learn anything about the scene structure by observing the motion field. The only information that can be extracted from the 2D motion field is the motion of the camera itself.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding pure rotation is crucial because it reveals a fundamental limitation: rotation alone provides no information about the distance to objects in the scene, unlike translation.
concepts.recap_md: - Pure rotational motion fields are independent of the scene's depth $Z$.

concepts.title: Rotation Around Optical Axis
concepts.one_liner: Rotation around the camera's optical axis creates a motion field where vectors are orthogonal to the radial vector from the image origin.
concepts.content: Consider rotation along the camera optical axis, where $W_X=W_Y=0$. In this case, the motion field is: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} y \\ -x \end{bmatrix} W_Z \end{aligned}$$ The 2D motion field at each location $(x,y)$ points in the orthogonal direction to the vector that connects that point with the origin (see figure: Motion field for a rotating camera around the optical axis, $W_X=W_Y=0$.). This motion field does not depend on the focal length $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: This case isolates the effect of 'roll' on the image, showing that it produces a simple circular flow pattern that is invariant to the camera's focal length.
concepts.recap_md: - Rotation around the $Z$-axis (optical axis) results in a circular motion field.

concepts.title: Rotation Around Y-Axis
concepts.one_liner: Rotation around the Y-axis produces a motion field heavily influenced by focal length, appearing as lateral translation for large focal lengths.
concepts.content: If $W_Z=0$ and $W_X=0$, rotation along the $Y$-axis ($W_Y$) produces the following motion field: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} f^2+x^2 \\ xy \end{bmatrix} W_Y \end{aligned}$$ The focal length $f$ has a strong effect on the appearance of this motion field. For very large $f$, the 2D motion field can be approximated by $\dot{x} \approx f W_Y$ and $\dot{y} \approx 0$, which looks like lateral translation. For very small $f$, the field is similar to a homography and differs significantly from lateral camera motion. The flows shown in (see figure: Motion flows corresponding to a rotation around the Y-axis.) correspond to $f=1/3$, $f=1$, and $f=3$. Camera rotation around the $Y$-axis does not inform about scene structure, but it does inform about camera parameters. The magnitude of $W_Y$ only affects the scaling of the motion vectors, but it does not change their orientation.
concepts.motivation_md: Analyzing Y-axis rotation (yaw) helps distinguish between true camera translation and rotation, especially since they can look similar at high zoom levels.
concepts.recap_md: - Rotation around the $Y$-axis produces a motion field sensitive to focal length $f$.

concepts.title: Motion under Varying Focal Length
concepts.one_liner: Changing the focal length of a static camera creates a motion field that scales the image without providing depth information.
concepts.content: Consider a static camera observing a static scene where the focal length $f$ changes over time. This produces motion in the image plane; an increasing focal length results in a zoom effect. Starting from the perspective projection equation: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ Computing the temporal derivative where only $f$ varies gives: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{f} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ This expression shows that changing the focal length results in a scaling of the projected image on the image plane. It does not create parallax. Because the sensor has a finite size, changing the focal length results in a zoom and a crop. Crucially, the motion field does not depend on the 3D scene structure $Z$, meaning images taken from the same viewpoint with different focal lengths do not provide depth information.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why 'zooming' is fundamentally different from 'moving forward'—zooming is a purely 2D image transformation that lacks the depth cues (parallax) provided by physical camera movement.
concepts.recap_md: - Changing focal length (zooming) creates a radial motion field from the image center.

concepts.title: Perspective Projection Equations for Motion
concepts.one_liner: The temporal derivative of the perspective projection equation describes how image coordinates change when the focal length varies.
