concepts.content: Starting from the perspective projection equation: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ If we compute the temporal derivative where only the focal length $f$ varies over time, we obtain: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \end{bmatrix} = \frac{\dot{f}}{f} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: These equations provide the mathematical basis for understanding how optical zoom affects the position of points on the image sensor over time.
concepts.recap_md: - The motion field $(\dot{x}, \dot{y})$ is proportional to the current coordinates $(x, y)$ when only $f$ changes.

concepts.title: Goal of Vision: Interpretation vs. Measurement
concepts.one_liner: The goal of vision is to provide an interpretation of the world in terms of "meaningful" surfaces, objects, and materials to extract relevant elements.
concepts.content: If the goal of vision were simply to measure the light intensity coming from a particular direction of space like a photometer, then things would be easy. However, the goal of vision is to provide an interpretation of the world in terms of "meaningful" surfaces, objects, and materials to extract all the different elements that compose the scene. This problem is hard because most information is lost, requiring the visual system to make assumptions about the structure of the world to recover information from a small sample of the plenoptic function. It is also difficult because our understanding of what is relevant for the observer is incomplete.
concepts.motivation_md: Vision exists to help observers interact with their environment by identifying objects and surfaces, which is much more complex than simple light measurement.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision interprets the world as meaningful objects and materials rather than just measuring light intensity. - The visual system uses assumptions to recover lost information from the environment.

concepts.title: Recovery of Scene Properties
concepts.one_liner: The human visual system extracts scene properties relevant for the observer by automatically interpreting images as pictures of real three-dimensional scenes.
concepts.content: The goal of vision is to extract scene properties relevant for the observer rather than just measuring light intensities. @fig-measuringScene shows images illustrating that the human visual system tries to recover the scenes that cause those images. In @fig-measuringScene (a), we perceive an occluded blue square rather than an L-shaped figure because we assume squares and occlusions are common. In @fig-measuringScene (b), the "turning tables illusion" shows that the visual system interprets 2D shapes as 3D objects, making one table appear longer. In @fig-measuringScene (c), the "checkershadow illusion" shows the system removing the effect of shadows to infer true surface reflectance, causing squares with identical intensity to be perceived differently.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how our brains resolve ambiguity in 2D images by applying prior knowledge about the 3D world.
concepts.recap_md: - The visual system automatically recovers 3D scene properties like shape and reflectance from 2D images. - Prior assumptions about the world, such as the prevalence of squares and shadows, guide visual interpretation.

concepts.title: Turning Tables Illusion
concepts.one_liner: The turning tables illusion demonstrates how the visual system's automatic 3D interpretation makes two identical 2D shapes appear to have different lengths.
concepts.content: The "turning tables illusion" by Roger Shepard demonstrates that we cannot shut down the automatic mechanisms that interpret images as pictures of real three-dimensional (3D) scenes. In this illusion, both table tops have the same shape and size but one is rotated with respect to the other. The visual system insists in interpreting these objects as 3D objects, giving the impression that the left table is longer than the table on the right. This perception cannot be shut down even if we know exactly how this image has been generated.
concepts.motivation_md: It illustrates the persistence of 3D interpretation mechanisms in the human brain, even when they lead to incorrect conclusions about 2D geometry.
concepts.recap_md: - The turning tables illusion makes identical 2D shapes appear different by forcing a 3D interpretation. - This automatic 3D perception is persistent and cannot be consciously suppressed.

concepts.title: Checkershadow Illusion
concepts.one_liner: The checkershadow illusion shows how the visual system infers true surface reflectance by removing the effects of shadows from its perception.
concepts.content: The "checkershadow illusion" by Adelson illustrates that the visual system interprets images as pictures of real three-dimensional (3D) scenes rather than just light patterns. In this figure, the squares marked with A and B have the exact same intensity values. However, the visual system tries to measure the surface reflectance of the squares, removing the effect of the shadow to infer the true gray value of each square. As a result, the square in the shadow is perceived as being lighter than the square outside the shadow region, even though both have the same gray levels.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion highlights the brain's ability to achieve lightness constancy by accounting for illumination conditions like shadows.
concepts.recap_md: - The checkershadow illusion shows the brain discounting shadows to estimate true surface reflectance. - Identical intensity values are perceived as different shades based on their environmental context.

concepts.title: Tasks in Computer Vision
concepts.one_liner: Computer vision tasks range from motion estimation and object recognition to building 3D models and understanding animal behavior.
concepts.content: The goal of vision is to provide the observer with information relevant to understanding the outside world and to enable tasks such as navigating, interacting with agents, and finding food. Tasks within computer vision include detecting changes in the environment, motion estimation, object recognition and localization, and recognizing materials. Other tasks include reading text, building 3D models, finding free space to move, finding other people, deciding if food is in a good state, and understanding the behavior of animals. Some tasks seem to require significant external knowledge, while others may be solvable from the images alone.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining these tasks helps organize the field of computer vision into specific problems that can be solved algorithmically.
concepts.recap_md: - Computer vision tasks include motion estimation, object recognition, and 3D modeling to help observers interact with the world. - Tasks range from those solvable by image data alone to those requiring extensive external knowledge.

concepts.title: Gibson's Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
concepts.one_liner: Gibson's ecological approach suggests that vision should be studied in the context of the observer's body and their natural environment.
concepts.content: James J. Gibson postulated that understanding vision requires an ecological approach to visual perception, studying the eye in the context of the body and the world it lives in. While simple visual stimuli in controlled labs allow for reproducible findings, they are too limiting to unravel the true nature of the visual system. Gibson argued that the environment should be studied by means of ecological properties, such as medium (air or water), substances (rocks, metal, wood), and surfaces, together with the notions of change and persistence. These concepts are considered more relevant to perception than the notions of space, matter, and time found in classical physics.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach shifted the focus of perception research from abstract physics to the functional relationship between an organism and its environment.
concepts.recap_md: - The ecological approach studies vision within the context of the observer's body and natural environment. - Perception is understood through ecological properties like medium and surfaces rather than abstract physical laws.

concepts.title: The Ground Plane in Perception
concepts.one_liner: The ground plane is the most important surface for terrestrial animals, serving as the center of their perception and behavior and providing a reference for action.
concepts.content: The ground plane is the most important surface for terrestrial animals, serving as the center of their perception and behavior. The ground provides the support for action and a reference for perception. Other notions of ecological importance include the concepts of layout, place, and enclosure. [FIGURE:ec27a980e52fb1da | A series of converging lines representing an optic flow pattern. The lines originate from the top and right edges and fan out towards the bottom and left, creating a sense of perspective and forward...]
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying the ground plane is a fundamental task for navigation and spatial orientation in terrestrial environments.
concepts.recap_md: - The ground plane acts as the primary reference for perception and behavior in terrestrial animals. - It provides the necessary support for physical action and spatial layout.

concepts.title: Ecological Optics
concepts.one_liner: Ecological optics studies the light that converges into the observer, which is the result of countless interactions with all the surfaces in a messy environment.
concepts.content: Gibson made a distinction between the light studied by optical physics and ecological optics, which is the light relevant for perception. While physicists study light in simplified settings like point sources, ecological optics studies the light that converges into the observer as a result of countless interactions with surfaces in a messy environment. The ambient optic array is the set of light rays that converge into a point of observation. As shown in @fig-gibson_bird, this moving ambient optic array contains information about the environment and also about the observer themselves.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept provides a framework for understanding how moving through the world generates visual information that guides behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Ecological optics focuses on the complex light patterns reaching an observer in real-world settings. - The ambient optic array contains information about both the environment and the observer's own movement.

concepts.title: Colored Particle Model
concepts.one_liner: A model that treats volume as being filled with colored particles, where observed color depends on the probability of a ray hitting particles along its path.
concepts.content: This model is based on the idea that space is filled with colored particles. When a ray is traced from the camera into the scene, it may hit one of these particles, determining the observed color. For any given increment along the ray, there is a chance of not hitting a particle. This is modeled by the density function $L^\sigma$, representing the differential probability of hitting a particle. The probability of not hitting a particle up to distance $t$ is given by $\alpha$, a cumulative integral of densities. The integral in @eq-nerfs-vol_rendering_integral averages over the colors of all the particles we might hit along the ray, weighted by the probability of hitting them.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a physical intuition for volume rendering by treating space as a probabilistic medium of particles rather than just abstract mathematical integrals.
concepts.recap_md: - Space is modeled as being filled with colored particles with a specific density $L^\sigma$.

concepts.title: Ray Casting
concepts.one_liner: A special case of volume rendering where the ray terminates at the first solid surface it hits.
concepts.content: Ray casting is a special case of volume rendering that occurs when particle density is either zero (empty space) or infinite (solid objects). In empty space, the density is zero and contributes nothing to the integral. When a ray hits a solid object with infinite density, the transparency $\alpha$ immediately goes to zero, and the ray terminates at the surface. Consequently, if a scene consists only of solid objects and empty space, volume rendering reduces to measuring the color of the first surface hit by each ray exiting the camera. This simple model is how many basic renderers work, including standard rasterization pipelines @shirley2009fundamentals.
concepts.motivation_md: It simplifies complex volume rendering into a more intuitive model for scenes containing only solid objects, serving as the basis for many standard renderers.
concepts.recap_md: - Ray casting occurs when volume rendering is applied to scenes with only solid objects and empty space.

concepts.title: Quadrature Rule for Volume Rendering
concepts.one_liner: A discrete approximation of the volume rendering integral using a sum of samples along a ray.
concepts.content: To compute the volume rendering integral, it can be approximated as a discrete sum using a quadrature rule (see @max1995optical, @max2005local). The approximation is given by: $$\begin{aligned} \ell(r) &\approx \sum_{i=1}^T \alpha_i \, (1-e^{-L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_i)\delta_i}) \, L^c(\mathbf{R}_i, \mathbf{D})\\ \alpha_i &= \exp\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_j)\delta_j\Big)\\ \delta_i &= t_{i+1} - t_i \end{aligned}$$ Here, the continuous radiance field is replaced by a discrete vector of samples $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$, where $\mathbf{R}_t = r(t)$ is the world coordinate at distance $t$ along ray $r$. (see figure: Volume rendering of our Flatland radiance field.) In this procedure, rays are sampled at specific points (circles). The size of each circle indicates the $\alpha$ value, while the color and transparency indicate the radiance field's density and color at that point. For solid objects, density is infinite, causing $\alpha$ to go to zero for all subsequent points along the ray.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous integrals cannot be computed directly by computers, so a discrete quadrature rule is necessary to numerically estimate the light accumulated along a ray.
concepts.recap_md: - The continuous volume rendering integral is approximated using a discrete sum of samples along the ray.

concepts.title: Stochastic Sampling Along Rays
concepts.one_liner: A sampling strategy that divides a ray into intervals and samples one point uniformly from each to ensure continuous coverage.
concepts.content: Instead of taking samples at evenly spaced increments, as suggested in @mildenhall2020nerf, the ray is divided into $T$ evenly spaced intervals, and one point is sampled uniformly within each interval. This ensures that all continuous coordinates have a probability of being sampled. Over multiple iterations of an optimization loop, every point in the continuous space will eventually be supervised. For a ray with origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$, the sampled coordinates $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$ are computed as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_i &= \mathbf{O} + t_i\mathbf{D}\\ t_i &\sim \mathcal{U}[i-1,i]*\frac{t_f-t_n}{T}+t_n \end{aligned}$$ where $\mathcal{U}[a,b]$ is the uniform distribution over the interval $[a,b]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Fixed-step sampling can miss details between samples; stochastic sampling ensures that the entire volume is eventually seen and supervised during the training process.
concepts.recap_md: - The ray is partitioned into $T$ equal segments, with one point sampled randomly from each.

concepts.title: Volume Rendering Computation Graph
concepts.one_liner: A modular pipeline that maps pixel coordinates to color values through ray generation, sampling, and volume integration.
concepts.content: The full volume rendering pipeline is defined as a series of computational modules. To find the color of a pixel $\boldsymbol\ell[n,m,:]$ at camera coordinates $n,m$, the first step is to determine the ray (origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$) passing through it. This uses the camera origin $\mathbf{O}_{\texttt{cam}}$ and the camera matrix $\mathbf{K}_{\texttt{cam}}$, which maps pixel coordinates to world coordinates (see @sec-pixel_to_rays). (see figure: Module for mapping from pixel coordinates to the world coordinates of a ray through that pixel.) RGB images are represented as $N \times M \times 3$ dimensional arrays. Next, world coordinates are sampled along the ray (see figure: Module for sampling coordinates along a ray.) Finally, the volume rendering integral is computed using a quadrature rule to determine the pixel's color (see figure: Module for volume rendering of a single ray.) This pipeline maps pixel coordinates to $r,g,b$ color values.
concepts.motivation_md: Organizing the rendering process into a modular computation graph allows for the use of automatic differentiation and backpropagation to optimize scene representations.
concepts.recap_md: - The pipeline maps pixel coordinates to rays, samples points along those rays, and integrates their colors.

concepts.title: Fitting Radiance Fields as an Inverse Problem

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: The process of inferring a 3D radiance field from 2D images by treating rendering as an inverse problem.
concepts.content: The goal is to find a radiance field $L_{\theta}$ that explains a set of observed images. While rendering a radiance field into images (view synthesis) is a graphics problem, inferring the field from images is a vision problem, specifically an inverse problem. This is the task denizens of Flatland solve as they walk around their world to represent the scene they see. The fitting procedure takes a set of images $\{\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}, \mathbf{K}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}, \mathbf{O}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}\}_{i=1}^N$ as input to produce a parameterized radiance field $L_{\theta}$. The objective is to ensure that when the resulting radiance field is rendered using the input camera parameters, the output matches the original images as closely as possible.
concepts.motivation_md: To reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D photos, we must treat the rendering process as a function to be inverted, allowing us to solve for the underlying scene parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision is treated as the inverse problem of graphics: inferring the scene from its rendered images.

concepts.title: Full NeRF Rendering Pipeline

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: A differentiable computation graph that uses volume rendering to generate images from a parameterized radiance field.
concepts.content: Given a parameterized radiance field $L_{\theta}$, an image is rendered using the volume rendering process described previously. The entire computation graph is differentiable, which is critical for fitting parameters to data. (see figure: Full NeRF pipeline for rendering an image.) Camera parameters are input into the $\texttt{pixel2ray}$ module, and $\texttt{vrender}$ takes the direction $\mathbf{D}$ and sampling points $\mathbf{t}$ computed by $\texttt{ray2coords}$ to produce the final output.
concepts.motivation_md: A fully differentiable pipeline allows for the use of gradient-based optimization to learn the parameters of a radiance field from image data.
concepts.recap_md: - The pipeline is composed of differentiable modules, enabling end-to-end optimization via backpropagation.

concepts.title: Pattern Matching Methods

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: A class of algorithms used by visual systems for motion detection, typically based on image correlations.
concepts.content: Pattern matching methods are a class of algorithms that the visual system may use, often based on image correlations (see @Adelson85). These methods represent one approach to processing visual information, such as motion.
concepts.motivation_md: Pattern matching provides a way to understand how biological or artificial systems can identify motion or objects by comparing correlations between image regions.
concepts.recap_md: - Pattern matching methods are a category of algorithms used by visual systems for tasks like motion detection.

concepts.title: Camera-Intrinsic Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Camera-intrinsic parameters model the image formation process by capturing the relationship between 3D scene coordinates and 2D image pixels.
concepts.content: Camera-intrinsic parameters are used to construct a model that captures the image formation process. While cameras translate the world into pixels, the relationship between the 3D scene and the 2D image is not always straightforward. The world is measured in units of meters, while points in images are measured in pixels. A camera model must account for factors such as geometric distortions and the scaling between physical units and pixel coordinates to accurately represent this relationship.
concepts.motivation_md: We need intrinsic parameters because cameras do not just capture raw 3D coordinates; they transform physical distances into digital pixels and introduce geometric distortions. Modeling these internal properties is essential for accurately mapping between the 3D world and 2D images.
concepts.recap_md: - Intrinsic parameters model the internal characteristics of a camera's image formation process.

concepts.title: Scaling from Meters to Pixels
concepts.one_liner: Scaling from meters to pixels accounts for the perspective projection of a 3D point onto a sensor plane by relating physical focal length to pixel dimensions.
concepts.content:
(see figure: An image is projected into the sensor. World coordinates are transformed into pixels at the sensor. The focal length is $f$, and the physical width of the sensor is $w$. The sensor has $N \times M$...) 

The units of the position in pixel space may be different than those of the world coordinates, which scales the focal length, $f$, to some other value $a$: 
$$\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & a & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ 
where the constant $a$ is related to the physical camera parameters in the following way: $$a = f \, N / w$$ where $f$ is the focal length (in meters), $w$ is the width of the sensor in meters, and $N$ is the image width in pixels. The ratio $N/w$ is the number of pixels per meter in the sensor.
concepts.motivation_md: Since world coordinates are measured in meters and digital images are measured in pixels, we need a scaling factor to bridge the two. This allows the perspective projection equations to work directly with pixel coordinates.
concepts.recap_md: - The scaling factor $a$ relates the physical focal length $f$ to the pixel-based focal length.

concepts.title: Principal Point Offset
concepts.one_liner: The principal point offset applies a translation to the intrinsic matrix so that 3D points on the optical axis project to the image center.
concepts.content:
The image center might not be the pixel $[0,0]^\mathsf{T}$. If the optical axis coincides with the image center, we need to apply a translation so that a 3D point on the optical axis (i.e., $X=Y=0$) projects to $[c_x, c_y]^\mathsf{T}$. For example, for an image of size $N \times M$ we will have $c_x=N/2$ and $c_y=M/2$: 
$$\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 & c_x & 0 \\ 0 & a & c_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.motivation_md: In digital images, the origin (0,0) is usually at the top-left corner, but the optical axis of the lens usually passes through the center of the sensor. The principal point offset shifts the coordinate system so that the projection math aligns with standard image indexing.
concepts.recap_md: - The principal point $[c_x, c_y]^\mathsf{T}$ represents the pixel coordinates where the optical axis intersects the image plane.

concepts.title: Non-square Pixels Scaling
concepts.one_liner: Non-square pixel scaling accounts for different physical dimensions along the horizontal and vertical axes of a camera sensor.
concepts.content:
It is also possible that the pixels are not square, in which case we have to account for different scaling along both axis: 
$$\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 & c_x & 0 \\ 0 & b & c_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.motivation_md: While most modern sensors have square pixels, some specialized or older hardware may have rectangular pixels. Using a single focal length for both dimensions would cause stretching or compression in the image, so separate scaling factors are required.
concepts.recap_md: - Non-square pixels require separate scaling factors $a$ and $b$ for the $x$ and $y$ axes.

concepts.title: Image Coordinate System Conventions
concepts.one_liner: Image coordinate conventions define the orientation of the axes and the location of the origin, typically placing the origin at the top-left.
concepts.content: The signs of $a$ and $b$ can be positive or negative. With the convention used in this book, where the camera optical axis coincides with the $Z$-axis and the camera looks in the direction of positive $Z$, the sign of $a$ has to be negative. If $n$ and $m$ are indices into an array, then the image origin is located at the top-left of the array, which means the signs of $a$ and $b$ will be negative. This is the convention used by Python and OpenCV.
concepts.motivation_md: Different software libraries and mathematical frameworks use different coordinate systems. Standardizing these conventions is necessary to ensure that 3D-to-2D projections align correctly with how image data is stored in memory.
concepts.recap_md: - Python and OpenCV typically use a convention where the origin is at the top-left of the image.

concepts.title: Deriving Rays from Pixels
concepts.one_liner: Deriving rays from pixels allows for the reconstruction of a 3D line from a 2D image point by scaling the image coordinates by the focal length.
concepts.content:
If you have a calibrated camera, we can derive the equation of the ray that leaves the image at one point. This allows us to answer the following: if we know $Z$ for an image pixel with camera-coordinates $x,y$, can we get the point world-coordinates $X$ and $Y$? 

We can relate the point in the image plane, $\mathbf{p}$, with the 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ in world-coordinates. To do this, we express the 2D point $\mathbf{p}$ in 3D coordinates. The point $\mathbf{p}$ is contained in the image plane which is located at a distance $f$ of the origin along the $Z$-axis. Therefore, in 3D, the 2D point $\mathbf{p}$ is a point located at coordinates $Z_c=f$, $X_c=x$, and $Y_c=y$. 

(see figure: The 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ is obtained by scaling the point $\mathbf{p}=(x,y,f)$ with a scaling factor $Z/f$. The ray that passes by the point $\mathbf{p}$ is the line defined by $\lambda (x,y,f)$...) 

The ray that connects the camera center and the point $\mathbf{p}$ is $\lambda (x,y,f)$, with $\lambda$ being a positive real number. Any 3D point along this line will project into the same image point $\mathbf{p}$ under perspective projection. The 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ is obtained by scaling the ray that passes by $\mathbf{p}$ with a scaling factor $\lambda = Z/f$: 
$$\frac{Z}{f} \begin{pmatrix} x\\ y\\ f \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{pmatrix}$$ 
We should use $a$ instead of $f$ if we are using coordinates in pixels.
concepts.motivation_md: While projection maps 3D to 2D, we often need to go the other way. Since a single pixel corresponds to an infinite line in space, deriving the ray equation is the first step in 3D reconstruction or determining the physical location of an object given its depth.
concepts.recap_md: - A 2D image point $(x, y)$ defines a 3D ray $\lambda(x, y, f)$ originating from the camera center.

concepts.title: Simple Camera Calibration Method
concepts.one_liner: A simple camera calibration method uses a physical object like a checkerboard to estimate unknown parameters like focal length and sensor size.
concepts.content:
Camera calibration relies on a series of parameters (i.e., focal length, sensor size) that will be unknown in general. A simple and intuitive method for camera calibration involves using a checkerboard pattern. While not very accurate, it provides a good sanity check before doing more precise calibrations. 

[FIGURE:3add6249a5e2efb6 | A photograph demonstrating a simple camera calibration setup. A smartphone is held at one end of a metal ruler, which measures the distance to a $7 \times 9$ black-and-white checkerboard pattern...] 

[FIGURE:b8af96b4500a24bd | A photograph showing a $7 \times 9$ black and white checkerboard pattern printed on paper and mounted on a piece of cardboard. A label above the pattern states it is for camera calibration and that...] 

A simple calibration setting requires specific ingredients to estimate the internal properties of the camera.
concepts.motivation_md: Most cameras do not come with their internal geometric properties pre-documented. Calibration is the process of measuring these properties so that the camera can be used for precise 3D measurements or computer vision tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Calibration estimates unknown internal parameters like focal length and sensor size.

concepts.title: Camera Skew Parameter
concepts.one_liner: The camera skew parameter accounts for pixels that are arranged along non-perpendicular axes within the intrinsic matrix.
concepts.content: There are other important aspects of a camera that require precise calibration. In some rare cases, pixels might not be square, or might be arranged along non-perpendicular axes, which requires introducing a skew parameter in $\mathbf{K}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Ideal sensors have perfectly rectangular grids. However, manufacturing imperfections can result in a 'skewed' grid where the x and y axes are not perfectly 90 degrees apart. The skew parameter corrects for this geometric distortion.
concepts.recap_md: - The skew parameter is used when the pixel axes are not perfectly perpendicular.

concepts.title: Steering Rule for Polynomials
concepts.one_liner: For an $N$-th order polynomial with even or odd symmetry, $N+1$ basis functions are sufficient for steering when combined with radially symmetric window functions.
concepts.content: Sometimes it is more convenient to think of filters as polynomials multiplied by radially symmetric window functions, which is the case for high-order Gaussian derivatives. For an $N$-th order polynomial with even or odd symmetry, $N+1$ basis functions are sufficient to achieve steerability.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule provides a clear mathematical bound on the number of basis functions required to steer a filter, simplifying the design of steerable filters for complex shapes like high-order derivatives.
concepts.recap_md:
- Filters can be represented as polynomials times radially symmetric window functions.
 - An $N$-th order symmetric polynomial requires only $N+1$ basis functions for steering.

concepts.title: Steerability Sampling Invariance
concepts.one_liner: Steerability is preserved after sampling because spatial sampling and the weighted summation of basis functions are interchangeable operations.
concepts.content: Although steerability is typically derived in the continuous domain, it is a property that still holds after sampling the filter function. This is because spatial sampling and steerability are interchangeable: the weighted sum of spatially sampled functions is equal to the spatial sampling of the same weighted sum of continuous basis functions.
concepts.motivation_md: This ensures that steerable filter theory, which is often developed for continuous functions, remains mathematically valid when implemented on discrete digital grids.
concepts.recap_md:
- Steerability is a property that holds even after a filter function is sampled.
 - Spatial sampling and the weighted summation of basis functions are interchangeable operations.

concepts.title: Separable Basis Filters for Steering
concepts.one_liner: Using $x-y$ separable functions as basis filters improves computational efficiency for steering operations.
concepts.content: For computational efficiency, it is more convenient to have the basis filters all be $x-y$ separable functions. In many cases, it is straightforward to find such basis functions; where it is not, simple numerical methods can be used to find the best-fitting $x-y$ separable basis set.
concepts.motivation_md: Separable filters significantly reduce the number of operations required for convolution, making real-time steering of filters computationally feasible in image processing applications.
concepts.recap_md:
- Using $x-y$ separable basis filters enhances the computational efficiency of steering.
 - Numerical methods can approximate a separable basis set if an exact one is not available.

concepts.title: Steerable Quadrature Pairs
concepts.one_liner: Steerable quadrature pairs are filter sets that allow for arbitrary shifts in both orientation and phase.
concepts.content: As in the case of Gabor filters, it is useful to build quadrature pairs of steerable filters. Steerable-quadrature filters allow for arbitrary shifts both in orientation and in phase.
concepts.motivation_md: These pairs are essential for analyzing local image structure independently of phase, which is useful for tasks like edge and line detection where the exact position relative to the filter center may vary.
concepts.recap_md:
- Steerable quadrature pairs allow for simultaneous control over orientation and phase.
 - They are analogous to Gabor filters but designed within the steerable filter framework.

concepts.title: Hilbert Transform Steerable Approximation
concepts.one_liner: The Hilbert transform of a second-order Gaussian derivative can be approximated using a third-order odd polynomial to create a steerable quadrature pair.
concepts.content:
Consider the second-order derivatives of a Gaussian with $\sigma^2=1/2$, normalized so that the integral over all space of its squared magnitude equals 1:

$$\begin{split}
g_{xx}(x,y) &= 0.9213(2x^2-1) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
g_{xy}(x,y) &= 1.843 (x y) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
g_{yy}(x,y) &= 0.9213(2y^2-1) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right)
\end{split}$$

It is possible to get a good approximation to its Hilbert transform using a Gaussian times a third-order odd polynomial. The approximation to the Hilbert transform of $g_{xx}(x,y)$ is:

$$h_{xx}(x,y) = -0.9780 (-2.254 x+x^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right)$$

where $g_{xx}(x,y)$ and its Hilbert transform $h_{xx}(x,y)$ have the same spectral content but opposite phase. (see figure: Quadrature pair, $g_{xx} \left[n,m \right)$ and $h_{xx} \left[n,m \right]$. The filters are sampled in space and cropped into a window of $13\times13$ pixels.] To steer $h_{xx}(x,y)$ to an angle $\theta$, this approximation requires four basis functions, rather than three as for the second-order derivative of a Gaussian. The other three functions needed are:

$$\begin{split}
h_2(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+x^2) y \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
h_3(x,y) &= -0.9780(-0.7515+y^2) x \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) \\
h_4(x,y) &= -0.9780 (-2.254 y+y^3) \exp \left(-(x^2+y^2) \right) 
\end{split}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Since the exact Hilbert transform of a Gaussian derivative is not steerable with a finite basis, this polynomial approximation allows for the practical implementation of steerable quadrature pairs.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Hilbert transform of $g_{xx}$ is approximated by a third-order odd polynomial times a Gaussian.
 - Steering the approximated Hilbert transform requires a set of four basis functions.

concepts.title: Non-uniqueness of Steerable Basis Functions
concepts.one_liner: Steerable basis functions are not unique; a space can be spanned by different sets, such as $x-y$ separable filters or rotated versions of the same function.
concepts.content: The basis functions for steerability are not unique. For instance, the space spanning all rotations of $g_{xx}$ can be represented by $x-y$ separable filters ($g_{xx}$, $g_{xy}$, and $g_{yy}$) or by three rotated versions of $g_{xx}$ at 0, 60, and 120 degrees. The latter is a non-separable basis spanning the same space as the separable filters. Similarly, different basis functions can span all rotations of $h_{xx}$. Spatial scaling of these filters results in changing the parameter $\sigma$. (see figure: (a) Second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ separable steerable basis set. b) Approximation to Hilbert transform of second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ steerable basis set. (c) Nonseparable basis equivalent to (a). (d) Nonseparable basis set equivalent to (b).)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding non-uniqueness allows designers to choose basis sets that optimize for specific criteria, such as computational efficiency through separability or geometric intuition through rotated versions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multiple different sets of basis functions can span the same space of rotated filters.
 - Common choices include $x-y$ separable sets or sets of rotated versions of the primary filter.

concepts.title: Oriented Energy
concepts.one_liner: Oriented energy is calculated as the sum of the squared responses of a steerable quadrature pair at a specific angle.
concepts.content: (see figure: (a) Second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ separable steerable basis set. b) Approximation to Hilbert transform of second derivative of Gaussian, $x-y$ steerable basis set. (c) Nonseparable basis equivalent to (a). (d) Nonseparable basis set equivalent to (b).) Oriented energy can be computed as a function of angle $\theta$, for all angles, from the basis filter responses. Using the $g_{xx}$ and $h_{xx}$ filters, the oriented energy is defined as: $$E(x,y,\theta) = g_{xx}(x,y,\theta)^2 + h_{xx}(x,y,\theta)^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: Oriented energy provides a phase-invariant measure of local image structure, allowing for the detection of edges and lines regardless of their specific intensity profile or polarity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Oriented energy is the sum of squared responses from even and odd phase steerable filters.
 - It allows for the continuous calculation of energy across all possible orientations.

concepts.title: Oriented Energy Cross-terms
concepts.one_liner: When multiple oriented structures exist within a filter's passband, squaring the responses introduces cross-terms that prevent simple linear superposition of energies.
concepts.content: Polar plots of oriented energy as a function of angle can reveal artifacts at intersections when using $g_{xx}$ and $h_{xx}$ filters. This issue is not due to insufficient angular resolution, but rather a non-linear interaction. When there are two oriented structures within the passband of the quadrature pair filters, the sum of the energies of the individual structures is not the same as the energy of the sum of the structures. (see figure: (Polar plots of orientation energy as a function of angle, computed using $g_{xx}$, $h_{xx}$ filters. (a) Note the non-superposition of oriented energies near the junction of the two lines. (b)...) Because energy is found by squaring, the combination of multiple structures is not linear. When two oriented structures are within the passband, the convolution in the Fourier domain picks up extra cross-terms from the interaction between the structures, in addition to the desired terms from squaring individual frequency responses.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing the presence of cross-terms is crucial for interpreting oriented energy plots, as it explains why energy may not perfectly represent the sum of independent components in complex regions like junctions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Squaring filter responses to find energy makes the combination of multiple structures non-linear.
 - Interaction between structures in the filter passband creates cross-terms in the Fourier domain.

concepts.title: Weight Decay
concepts.one_liner: In the context of neural networks, weight decay is a regularizer that penalizes the size of the parameters.
concepts.content: In the context of neural networks, this regularizer is called weight decay. When $p=1$, the regularizer is based on the $L_1$ norm.
concepts.motivation_md: Weight decay is used to prevent overfitting in neural networks by penalizing large parameter values, effectively encouraging the model to find simpler solutions that generalize better.
concepts.recap_md: - Weight decay is a common term for parameter regularization in neural networks.

concepts.title: Regularizers as Probabilistic Priors
concepts.one_liner: Regularizers can be interpreted as probabilistic priors that prefer certain solutions over others before looking at the data.
concepts.content: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori (before looking at the data), some solutions over others. Under this interpretation, the data fit loss (e.g., $L_2$ loss) is a likelihood function $p(\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1} \bigm | \{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}, \theta)$ and the regularizer is a prior $p(\theta)$. Bayes' rule then states that the posterior $p(\theta \bigm | \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1})$ is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood. The log posterior is then the sum of the log likelihood and the log prior, plus a constant. Hence we arrive at the form of a regularized objective function.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective provides a formal statistical foundation for regularization, allowing us to use Bayesian inference to justify why we add penalty terms to our loss functions.
concepts.recap_md: - Regularizers act as a prior probability distribution $p(\theta)$ over the model parameters.

concepts.title: Bayesian Occam's Razor
concepts.one_liner: The Bayesian Occam's razor suggests that simpler hypotheses are more likely because complex hypothesis spaces must spread their prior probability mass more thinly.
concepts.content: These priors are not arbitrarily chosen. The notion of the Bayesian Occam's razor derives such priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces must cover more possible hypotheses, and therefore must assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis. This is because the prior probability of all possible hypotheses in the hypothesis space must sum to 1. This is why, probabilistically, simpler hypotheses are more likely to be true.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a mathematical justification for the principle of parsimony, explaining why we should prefer simpler models unless the data strongly supports a complex one.
concepts.recap_md: - Complex models assign less prior probability to any single hypothesis because they cover a larger space.

concepts.title: Model Capacity
concepts.one_liner: Model capacity refers to the expressivity of a hypothesis space, for which the number of parameters is only a rough proxy.
concepts.content: A recent empirical finding is that some seemingly complex hypothesis spaces, such as deep nets, tend not to overfit, even though they have many more free parameters than the number of datapoints they are fit to. The number of parameters is just a rough proxy for model capacity (i.e., the expressivity of the hypothesis space). A single parameter that has infinite numerical precision can parameterize an arbitrarily complex function, defining a very expressive hypothesis space capable of overfitting. Conversely, if we have a million parameters that are regularized so that almost all are zero, they may define a simple class of functions which does not overfit. While the number of parameters is a rough estimate of model capacity, it is not the full story.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding capacity helps explain why large models like neural networks can sometimes generalize well despite having millions of parameters, and why regularization is essential.
concepts.recap_md: - Model capacity measures the expressivity of the hypothesis space.

concepts.title: Three Tools for Generalization: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Learning and generalization can be viewed as a search for truth using three primary tools: data, priors, and the hypothesis space.
concepts.content:
Learning can be considered as akin to searching for a needle (the "truth" or true function) in a haystack (the hypothesis space). We have three tools to pinpoint this location:

1. Data: Observations of the world that provide explanations consistent with observed facts.
2. Priors: Also known as regularizers, these prefer some solutions over others a priori.
3. Hypotheses: The set of functions under consideration. The hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ constrains which solutions we can possibly find; if the truth is not in our space, no amount of data can find it.

Together these three tools allow us to pinpoint good solutions in the space of all possibilities.

(see figure: A cartoon of the tools for honing in on the truth.)

In this framework, the hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ (white circle) places a hard constraint, the prior (yellow ellipse) places a soft constraint on preferred mappings, and the data (green ellipse) places a soft constraint preferring mappings that fit the observations. While approximation error is low in the data-fitting region, we bias our picks toward the prior region to improve generalization. A learning algorithm searches over $\mathcal{F}$ to maximize the likelihood times the prior.
concepts.motivation_md: This framework helps conceptualize how different components of machine learning—the model architecture, the loss function, and the dataset—interact to find a generalizable solution.
concepts.recap_md: - Data, priors, and hypothesis spaces act as constraints to narrow down the search for the true function.

concepts.title: Effect of Priors on Learning

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Priors act as soft constraints that pull learned solutions toward preferred regions of the parameter space, such as the origin.
concepts.content:
The effect of priors can be observed using an objective function like $J(\theta; \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \left\lVert f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2 + \lambda \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$ with a linear hypothesis space $f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x$. The ridge regularizer $\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$ prefers solutions with small parameter norms, placing a quadratic bowl around the origin in the energy landscape. As the regularization strength $\lambda$ increases, the solution is pulled closer to the origin.

(see figure: More regularization, more (soft) constraints.)

Lessons from this effect include:
1. Priors help only when they are good guesses as to the truth.
2. Overreliance on the prior means ignoring the data, which is generally detrimental.
3. There is an optimal "sweet spot" for the strength of any given prior.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the effect of priors allows practitioners to balance the trade-off between fitting the training data and adhering to pre-existing beliefs about the model parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - Priors pull the learned solution toward a preferred region, such as small parameter values.

concepts.title: Ridge Regularization

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Ridge regularization adds a penalty proportional to the squared norm of the parameters to the objective function.
concepts.content:
The ridge regularizer $\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$ prefers solutions with small parameter norms. Its contribution to the energy landscape is to place a quadratic bowl around the origin. As the regularization parameter $\lambda$ increases, the effect of the regularizer becomes stronger and pulls the learned solution closer and closer to the origin.

(see figure: More regularization, more (soft) constraints.)
concepts.motivation_md: Ridge regularization is a standard technique to prevent overfitting by discouraging large weights, which often leads to more stable and generalizable models.
concepts.recap_md: - Ridge regularization uses the squared $L_2$ norm of parameters as a penalty.

concepts.title: Effect of Hypothesis Space on Learning

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: The choice of hypothesis space acts as a hard constraint on learning, where smaller spaces can accelerate search but may exclude the true solution.
concepts.content:
The hypothesis space itself acts as a tool for learning. Consider three spaces: quadratic ($f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 x + \theta_1 x^2$), linear ($f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 x$), and constant ($f_{\theta}(x) = 0$).

(see figure: Fewer hypotheses, more (hard) constraints)

If the true function is linear, both the quadratic and linear spaces contain the truth. However, the linear space is much smaller, allowing the learning process to ignore large regions of parameter space (e.g., where $\theta_1 \neq 0$), which can accelerate the search. Conversely, a space can be too small; the constant hypothesis space makes search trivial but fails if the truth is not a constant zero function.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing the right hypothesis space is a fundamental trade-off: a larger space is more likely to contain the truth but is harder to search and prone to overfitting, while a smaller space is easier to optimize but may suffer from bias.
concepts.recap_md: - Smaller hypothesis spaces provide hard constraints that can speed up learning.

concepts.title: Laplacian Pyramid
concepts.one_liner: The Laplacian pyramid represents the fine image details lost at each level of a Gaussian pyramid by calculating the difference between adjacent levels.
concepts.content: The Laplacian pyramid represents, at each level, what is present in a Gaussian pyramid image of one level, but not present at the level below it. This is calculated by expanding the lower-resolution Gaussian pyramid image to the same pixel resolution as the neighboring higher-resolution Gaussian pyramid image, then subtracting the two. This calculation is made in a recursive, telescoping fashion. To compute a Laplacian pyramid with $N$ levels, we need to first compute the Gaussian pyramid of the input image with $N+1$ levels. The last level of this pyramid is the smallest level of the Gaussian pyramid used to compute the Laplacian pyramid and is called the low-pass residual. [FIGURE:21bbe2abae2fa724 | A stylized photograph of a lighthouse and an adjacent house, processed with a high-pass or edge-detection filter that emphasizes outlines and textures while muting colors to a gray palette. This...] [FIGURE:bf4041c8114a024e | A processed photograph of a lighthouse and adjacent house, characterized by high-frequency edge enhancement and ringing artifacts typical of a Laplacian pyramid level. The image highlights sharp...] [FIGURE:8ce429b4063e6442 | A pixelated, low-resolution image of a white lighthouse and an adjacent white house with a red roof, set against a gray sky. The image appears to be a low-pass residual or a coarse level from a...] [FIGURE:33d68ea479503ac6 | A heavily pixelated, low-resolution photograph of a building with a white facade and a red roof, featuring a tall tower on the right side. The image demonstrates the visual effect of extreme...] [FIGURE:66e8f7c4465d2592 | A very small, low-resolution thumbnail image representing the fifth and smallest level of a Laplacian pyramid. It appears as a tiny square of blurred pixels with muted gray and brown tones.] [FIGURE:c461ed1161f48fdc | A highly pixelated, low-resolution version of an image, representing a deep level in a Gaussian pyramid where the original image has been repeatedly blurred and downsampled.] The Laplacian pyramid includes the tiny low-pass residual as the last image and is built for each color channel independently.
concepts.motivation_md: While Gaussian pyramids provide multi-scale representations, they lose fine details at each level; the Laplacian pyramid captures these missing high-frequency details, enabling perfect reconstruction and better image analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- It captures the difference between a Gaussian pyramid level and its expanded, lower-resolution neighbor.",
  "- The representation includes a series of detail levels and a final low-pass residual."
]

concepts.title: Laplacian Pyramid Coefficients Calculation
concepts.one_liner: Laplacian pyramid coefficients are calculated by subtracting an upsampled and blurred version of a lower-resolution Gaussian level from the current Gaussian level.
concepts.content: Calculating a Laplacian pyramid involves computing the difference between $\mathbf{g}_k$ and $\mathbf{g}_{k+1}$. To do this, we first upsample the image $\mathbf{g}_{k+1}$ so that it has the same size as $\mathbf{g}_k$. Let $\mathbf{F}_k = \mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{U}_k$ be the upsample-and-blur operator for pyramid level $k$. The operator $\mathbf{F}_k$ applies first the upsampling operator $\mathbf{U}_k$, which inserts zeros between samples, followed by blurring by the same filter $\mathbf{B}_k$ used for the Gaussian pyramid. The Laplacian pyramid coefficients, $\mathbf{l}_k$, at pyramid level $k$, are: $$\mathbf{l}_{k} =  \mathbf{g}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{g}_{k+1} =  (\mathbf{I}_k - \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{G}_k) \mathbf{g}_{k} = \mathbf{L}_k \mathbf{g}_{k}$$ [FIGURE:1378d35f4fd51217 | A block diagram showing the computation of a Laplacian pyramid level. An input image $\mathbf{g}_k$ passes through a block $\mathbf{G}_k$ to produce $\mathbf{g}_{k+1}$. Simultaneously...]
concepts.motivation_md: This mathematical formulation provides a precise way to isolate high-frequency information, such as edges and fine textures, that is discarded during the downsampling process of a Gaussian pyramid.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Coefficients $\mathbf{l}_k$ represent the difference between a level and its predicted version from a coarser scale.",
  "- The process uses an upsampling and blurring operator $\mathbf{F}_k$ to align image dimensions."
]

concepts.title: Laplacian Pyramid Reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: The original image can be perfectly reconstructed from a Laplacian pyramid by recursively adding detail coefficients back to upsampled lower-resolution levels.
concepts.content: The Laplacian pyramid is an invertible transform, but only if we keep the low-pass residual. We can reconstruct the original image from the Laplacian pyramid by using the low-pass residual signal to recursively reconstruct the corresponding Gaussian pyramid. Since Gaussian pyramid level 1 is the original image itself, we can use this process to recover the input signal $\boldsymbol\ell=\mathbf{g}_0$. The reconstruction is performed by recursively applying the following from $k=N-1$ to $k=0$: $$\mathbf{g}_k = \mathbf{l}_k + \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{g}_{k+1}$$ The reconstruction uses the Laplacian pyramid $\mathbf{l}_0,\mathbf{l}_1,...,\mathbf{l}_2$ and the low pass residual $\mathbf{g}_3$ for a three-level pyramid.
concepts.motivation_md: Invertibility is crucial for applications like image compression or editing, where one needs to transform an image into a detail-oriented representation and then accurately return to the pixel domain.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Reconstruction is possible only if the low-pass residual is preserved alongside the Laplacian coefficients.",
  "- The process is recursive, moving from the coarsest level back to the original image resolution."
]

concepts.title: Pyramid Encoder and Decoder Networks
concepts.one_liner: The Laplacian pyramid architecture functions as an encoder-decoder system, transforming an image into an overcomplete representation of details and a residual for reconstruction.
concepts.content: This architecture has two parts: (1) the analysis network (or encoder) that transforms the input image $\mathbf{x}$ into a representation composed of $\mathbf{l}_0, \mathbf{l}_1, ...$ and the low pass residual $\mathbf{x}_n$; and (2) the synthesis network (or decoder) that reconstructs the input from the representation. The Laplacian pyramid is an overcomplete representation, meaning the dimensionality of the representation is higher than the dimensionality of the input because it contains more coefficients than pixels. Encoder and decoder networks are also common building blocks of deep neural networks, and the Laplacian pyramid can be considered as a special type of deep neural net.
concepts.motivation_md: Framing the pyramid as an encoder-decoder helps relate classical multi-scale signal processing to modern deep learning architectures used for feature extraction and generative modeling.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- The encoder transforms the input into multi-scale detail coefficients and a residual.",
  "- The decoder performs the inverse operation to synthesize the original image.",
  "- It is an overcomplete representation because it uses more coefficients than the original pixel count."
]

concepts.title: Image Blending with Laplacian Pyramids
concepts.one_liner: Laplacian pyramid blending creates seamless composites by transitioning between images across multiple spatial scales using a Gaussian pyramid of a mask.
concepts.content: Image blending (or image compositing) consists in introducing elements of one image inside another using a mask, $\mathbf{m}$, that specifies how the images will be combined. A naive solution using linear blending often results in a sharp, unpleasing transition. [FIGURE:1a6744bb03a38c89 | A close-up photograph of a single ripe orange hanging from a branch with green leaves. The orange is brightly lit by sunlight, highlighting its textured peel, and serves as a source image for the...] [FIGURE:d0117de8048c2287 | A close-up photograph of a single red apple hanging from a tree branch, surrounded by green leaves. The apple has a deep red skin with small yellow speckles (lenticels).] [FIGURE:0221968e4f64f996 | A binary mask image for image blending, consisting of a solid white rectangle on the left half and a solid black rectangle on the right half, divided by a sharp vertical line.] (see figure: Resulting blended image from @fig-orange_apple_mask. This result is not very pleasing.) The Burt and Adelson algorithm uses Laplacian pyramids to achieve a smooth transition by transitioning from one image to the next over many different spatial scales. First, build the Laplacian pyramid for the two input images, keeping the last low-pass residual. (see figure: Laplacian pyramids (seven levels and Gaussian residual) for both input images.) Second, build the Gaussian pyramid of the mask. (see figure: Gaussian pyramid of the mask.) Third, combine the three pyramids to compute the Laplacian pyramid of the blended image using: $$\mathbf{l}_k = \mathbf{l}_k^A * \mathbf{m}_k + \mathbf{l}_k^B * (1-\mathbf{m}_k)$$ Finally, collapse (decode) the resulting pyramid to produce the blended image. (see figure: Image compositing with the Laplacian pyramid. Example inspired by @{Burt83}.) This method produces a pleasing blending with smooth transitions, though it may fail when blending requires geometric image transformations.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple cut-and-paste blending creates visible seams; by blending different frequency bands separately, this technique ensures that sharp edges and smooth gradients are merged naturally.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- It blends images level-by-level using a Gaussian-blurred version of the selection mask.",
  "- High-frequency details are blended over narrow regions, while low-frequency components are blended over wider regions."
]

concepts.title: Steerable Pyramid
concepts.one_liner: The steerable pyramid is a multiscale, oriented image representation that captures orientation information while remaining translation-invariant and self-invertible.
concepts.content: The steerable pyramid provides a richer representation than the Gaussian pyramid by adding information about image orientation. It is a multiscale oriented representation that is translation-invariant, non-aliased, and self-invertible. Ideally, this image transformation is shiftable, meaning one can perform interpolations in position, scale, and orientation using linear combinations of a set of basis coefficients. The steerable pyramid is a self-inverting overcomplete representation, containing more coefficients than pixels. (see figure: Steerable pyramid representation (three levels and four orientations). Why is that each orientation subband seems to indicate a different time?)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard pyramids are poor at capturing directional features; steerable pyramids solve this by decomposing images into specific orientations, which is vital for texture analysis and edge detection.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- It decomposes an image into multiple scales and multiple orientation subbands.",
  "- The representation is translation-invariant and allows for linear interpolation of orientation."
]

concepts.title: Steerable Pyramid Construction
concepts.one_liner: Steerable pyramids are constructed using a steerable filter bank for orientation analysis and recursive low-pass filtering for scale decomposition.
concepts.content: Orientation is analyzed using a steerable filter bank. A decomposition in scale is formed by introducing a low-pass filter designed to work with selected bandpass filters, and recursively breaking the low-pass filtered component into angular and low-pass frequency components. To remove aliasing, pyramid subsampling steps are preceded by sufficient low-pass filtering. (see figure: Oriented filters and the low-pass kernel used in the steerable pyramid.) [FIGURE:23144f4d582c7514 | A block diagram showing a single stage of a steerable pyramid architecture. An input signal $g_k$ is branched into four parallel paths: three paths lead through bandpass filters $B_0, B_1, \dots...]
concepts.motivation_md: This specific construction ensures that orientation information is captured without introducing artifacts like aliasing, which would occur with simpler subsampling methods.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Uses a bank of oriented bandpass filters to capture directional details.",
  "- Employs recursive low-pass filtering and subsampling to create the scale hierarchy."
]

concepts.title: Steerable Pyramid Reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: Perfect reconstruction in steerable pyramids is achieved by designing filters that tile the frequency domain and applying them during synthesis to ensure a flat response.
concepts.content: To ensure that the image can be reconstructed from the steerable filter transform coefficients, the filters must be designed so that their sums of squared magnitudes tile in the frequency domain. Reconstruction is performed by applying each filter a second time to the steerable filter representation; for perfect reconstruction, the final system frequency response must be flat. The architecture consists of: (1) the analysis network (or encoder) that transforms the input image $x$ into a representation $r=\left[ b_{0,0},...,b_{0,n}, b_{1,0},...b_{1,n},...,b_{k-1,0},...b_{k-1,n} \right]$ and the low pass residual $g_{k-1}$; and (2) the synthesis network (or decoder) that reconstructs the input from the representation $r$. (see figure: Steerable pyramid architecture.)
concepts.motivation_md: For a representation to be useful in image editing or compression, it must be possible to perfectly reconstruct the original signal from its oriented components.
concepts.recap_md:
[ 
  "- Requires filters that tile the frequency domain to avoid gaps or overlaps in information.",
  "- The synthesis process mirrors the analysis process to achieve a flat frequency response."
]

concepts.title: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
concepts.one_liner: Byte-pair encoding is an approach that assigns one-hot codes to common substrings or small chunks of text.
concepts.content: A happy middle ground can be achieved using byte-pair encodings @gage1994new. In this approach, we assign a one-hot code to each small chunk of text. The chunks are common substrings found in text, like "th" or "ing." This strategy is popular in language models like the generative pretrained transformer (GPT) series @brown2020language and the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) model @radford2021learning that we will learn about in @sec-VLMs-CLIP.
concepts.motivation_md: BPE balances vocabulary size and representation granularity by encoding common character sequences rather than just individual characters or full words.
concepts.recap_md: - It assigns one-hot codes to common substrings like "th" or "ing".\n- It provides a middle ground between character-level and word-level encoding.

concepts.title: Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT)
concepts.one_liner: The generative pretrained transformer (GPT) is a series of language models often used in conjunction with byte-pair encoding.
concepts.content: The generative pretrained transformer (GPT) series and contrastive language-image models are examples of architectures that utilize advanced text encoding.
concepts.motivation_md: GPT models are designed to learn general-purpose language representations through large-scale pretraining on diverse text data.
concepts.recap_md: - It refers to the generative pretrained transformer series of language models.\n- These models are frequently used in conjunction with byte-pair encoding.

concepts.title: Text Tokenization
concepts.one_liner: Text tokenization converts one-hot encoded text into token vectors via a projection to a target dimensionality.
concepts.content: Once we have converted text into a sequence of one-hot codes, the next step is to convert these into tokens via a projection, $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{tokenize}}$, from the one-hot dimensionality ($K$) to a target dimensionality for token code vectors ($d$). @fig-VLMs-tokenizing_text shows these steps for converting an input string to tokens. For simplicity, we show word-level one-hot encoding rather than byte-pair encoding. (see figure: Tokenizing text. Note that these steps can be implemented with a lookup table that simply stores the token code vector for each unique item in our vocabulary.)
concepts.motivation_md: Tokenization transforms discrete text representations into continuous vector spaces that neural networks can process effectively.
concepts.recap_md: - It converts one-hot encoded text into token vectors via a projection matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{tokenize}}$.\n- The process maps the one-hot dimensionality $K$ to a target dimensionality $d$.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Language Modeling

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive language modeling predicts each next item in a vocabulary given the sequence generated so far.
concepts.content: To handle the output side where text is produced, tokens must be converted back to text. The most common method is an autoregressive model that predicts each next item in the vocabulary—such as a word, character, or byte-pair—given the sequence generated so far. Each prediction step is modeled as a softmax over all $K$ possible items in the vocabulary.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive modeling allows systems to generate coherent, sequential text by conditioning each new token on the previous context.
concepts.recap_md: - It predicts the next item in a vocabulary based on the sequence generated so far.\n- Each step is modeled using a softmax function over all possible vocabulary items.

concepts.title: Language Supervision as a Pretext Task

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Language supervision uses linguistic structures, such as free-form natural language, as a pretext task for learning visual representations.
concepts.content: Language association can serve as a pretext task for representation learning. Historically, image classification has been a popular pretext task where an image is associated with one of $K$ nouns, effectively supervising visual representations from language. However, human language contains richer structures like adjectives and verbs. Research indicates that using all the structure in language by associating images with free-form natural language works best when scaled with data and compute.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach leverages the rich semantic information in natural language to provide more nuanced supervision for vision systems than simple category labels.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses language association as a pretext task to learn visual representations.\n- Training on free-form natural language captures more structural information than simple classification.

concepts.title: Image Classification as a Pretext Task

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Image classification is a pretext task where an image is associated with one of $K$ nouns to supervise visual representations.
concepts.content: Historically, one of the most popular pretext tasks has been image classification, where an image is associated with one of $K$ nouns. This approach serves as a way of supervising visual representations from language.
concepts.motivation_md: Classification tasks provide a structured way for models to learn features that distinguish between different semantic categories.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a pretext task where images are associated with one of $K$ nouns.\n- It serves as a foundational method for supervising visual learning through language.

concepts.title: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP)

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP is a contrastive learning system that associates images with natural language captions using a symmetric objective.
concepts.content: CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) is a contrastive method where one data view is an image and the other is a caption describing that image. Specifically, CLIP is a form of contrastive learning from co-occurring visual and linguistic views that is formulated as follows: [FIGURE:7d5ab02809b91736 | A diagram illustrating the CLIP training process. It shows input data as a set of pairs \{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol{\ell}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ entering a box labeled 'CLIP'. Inside the box, the...] where $\boldsymbol\ell$ represents an image, $\mathbf{t}$ represents text, $\mathbb{S}^{d_z}$ represents the space of unit vectors of dimensionality $d_z$ (i.e., the surface of the $[d_z-1]$-dimensional hypersphere), $f_{\ell}$ is the image encoder, $f_t$ is the text encoder, image inputs are represented as $[3 \times N \times M]$ pixel arrays, text inputs are represented as $d_t$ dimensional tokens, and $d_z$ is the embedding dimensionality. Notice that the objective is a symmetric version of the InfoNCE loss defined in @eq-representation_learning-infonce. Also notice that $f_\ell$ and $f_t$ both output unit vectors (which is achieved using $L_2$-normalization before computing the objective); this ensures that the denominator cannot dominate by pushing negative pairs infinitely far apart.
concepts.motivation_md: CLIP enables models to learn robust visual representations by aligning them with natural language descriptions in a shared embedding space.
concepts.recap_md: - It aligns image and text encoders using a contrastive objective on co-occurring views.\n- The model optimizes a symmetric InfoNCE loss using $L_2$-normalized unit vectors.

concepts.title: Image Captioning as a Pretext Task

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Visual learning by image captioning is a pretext task with a long history of associating images with descriptive text.
concepts.content: The idea of visual learning by image captioning has a long history before CLIP, as seen in early work such as @ordonez2011im2text.
concepts.motivation_md: Captioning provides a richer signal for visual learning than discrete labels, allowing models to capture complex scenes and relationships.
concepts.recap_md: - It involves learning visual features by associating images with descriptive captions.\n- This approach has a significant history in visual learning that predates the CLIP system.

concepts.title: GAN Discriminator
concepts.one_liner: A discriminator is a function $d_{\phi}$ that attempts to classify whether data is synthesized by a generator or comes from a real dataset.
concepts.content: A discriminator, $d_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \Delta^1$, is a component of a generative adversarial network that tries to classify between synthesized data and real data.
concepts.motivation_md: To train a generative model effectively, we need a mechanism to evaluate how realistic its outputs are; the discriminator provides this feedback by learning to distinguish real data from synthetic samples.
concepts.recap_md: - The discriminator $d_{\phi}$ maps input data to a probability indicating whether it is real or synthetic.

concepts.title: GAN Minimax Game
concepts.one_liner: GAN training is a minimax game where a generator tries to fool a discriminator while the discriminator learns to detect synthetic data.
concepts.content: The generator $g_{\theta}$ and discriminator $d_{\phi}$ play an adversarial game in which $g_{\theta}$ tries to become better at generating synthetic images while $d_{\phi}$ tries to become better at detecting errors $g_{\theta}$ is making. The learning problem can be written as a minimax game: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_\theta\max_\phi \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$. Schematically, the generator synthesizes images that are then fed as input to the discriminator. The discriminator tries to assign a high score to generated images (classifying them as synthetic) and a low score to real images from some training set (classifying them as real). (see figure: Architecture of a GAN being trained to generate images of flamingos. The synthetic image in this example is generated by BigGAN @brock2018large)
concepts.motivation_md: This framework allows for training generative models without a hand-crafted loss function, instead using a learned adversary to define what "realistic" data looks like.
concepts.recap_md: - The generator aims to minimize the objective while the discriminator aims to maximize it.

concepts.title: Alternating Gradient Descent for GANs
concepts.one_liner: GAN optimization alternates between updating the discriminator to maximize classification accuracy and updating the generator to minimize it.
concepts.content: Given a particular generator $g_{\theta}$, $d_{\phi}$ tries to maximize its ability to discriminate between real and synthetic images. The objective of $d_{\phi}$ is logistic regression between a set of real data $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and synthetic data $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, where $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{(i)})$. The optimal discriminator $d_{\phi}^*$ is defined as: $$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$. From the perspective of $g_{\theta}$, it tries to solve: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}^*(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$. Because $d_{\phi}^*$ depends on the current behavior of $g_{\theta}$, updating the generator requires re-solving for the discriminator. To optimize a GAN, we alternate between taking one gradient step on the generator objective and $K$ gradient steps on the discriminator objective. In practice, setting $K=1$ is often sufficient.
concepts.motivation_md: Since the two components have opposing goals, standard joint optimization is difficult; alternating gradient descent provides a practical way to reach a stable equilibrium.
concepts.recap_md: - The discriminator is updated to better distinguish real from fake samples using logistic regression.

concepts.title: GANs as Statistical Image Models
concepts.one_liner: GANs are learned statistical image models that amortize the optimization of matching data statistics by learning a mapping from latent noise to samples.
concepts.content: GANs are related to statistical image and texture models where images are synthesized with the same statistics as a source texture. In traditional models like Heeger-Bergen, this is an optimization problem where pixels are adjusted until subband histograms match a training image. In the language of GANs, the loss checking for such a match is a kind of discriminator, but it is hand-defined rather than learned. Additionally, GANs amortize the optimization via learning; they learn a mapping $g_{\theta}$ from latent noise to samples rather than arriving at samples via an optimization process that starts from scratch each time a new sample is needed.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional texture synthesis requires a new optimization for every image; GANs solve this by learning a generator that can instantly produce new samples.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs replace hand-defined statistical matching with a learned discriminator.

concepts.title: Generative Modeling and Representation Learning as Inverses
concepts.one_liner: Generative modeling and representation learning are inverse processes that map between simple base distributions and complex data.
concepts.content: Generative modeling and representation learning are models that learn mappings both to and from data. Generative models map a simple base distribution (noise) to data, whereas representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations called embeddings. These two problems are essentially inverses of each other. Deep learning can be viewed as representation learning, mapping raw data to abstracted representations layer by layer, or as generative modeling, mapping from abstracted representations to concrete data. Both modeling directions are valid. (see figure: The relationship between representation learning and generative modeling. Here we label one side as "Data" and the other as "Embedding"; but what's the precise difference between these two things?...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the inverse relationship between these two fields allows for the development of models that can both understand data (encoding) and create it (decoding).
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models map from simple noise or embeddings to complex data.

concepts.title: Embeddings
concepts.one_liner: Embeddings are simple underlying representations of data produced by mapping complex data to a lower-dimensional space.
concepts.content: Representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations known as embeddings. This process is the inverse of generative modeling, which maps a simple base distribution (noise) to data.
