Many algorithms explicitly treat these as inverse problems, where solving the problem in one direction can inform the solution in the other direction.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw data is often high-dimensional and noisy; embeddings provide a compressed, meaningful space that makes downstream tasks like classification or generation easier.
concepts.recap_md: - Embeddings are the output of representation learning mappings.

concepts.title: Latent Variables as Representations
concepts.one_liner: Latent variables in generative models act as representations that specify unobserved factors and control the properties of generated data.
concepts.content: Latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ specify all unobserved factors that might affect the output of a model. For example, if a model predicts the color of a black and white photo, it is a mapping $g: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$, where $\mathbf{x}$ is the black and white input, $\mathbf{y}$ is the color output, and $\mathbf{z}$ represents information like the color of a t-shirt which cannot be inferred from the input alone. In unconditional generative models, latent variables are a complete representation of the data, meaning all information in the data is represented in the latent variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Latent variables allow models to handle ambiguity and multi-modality by capturing information not present in the input, serving as a complete representation of the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Latent variables capture unobserved or stochastic factors in data generation.

concepts.title: Technical Setting for Generative and Representation Learning
concepts.one_liner: The technical framework for joint learning involves an encoder and decoder trained to be approximate inverses of each other.
concepts.content: Consider random variables $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ related as follows, with $g$ being a deterministic generator (decoder) and $f$ being a deterministic encoder: $$\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}} &\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}} \\ &\hat{\mathbf{z}} = f(\mathbf{x}) &\hat{\mathbf{x}} = g(\mathbf{z}) \end{aligned}$$ The functions $f$ and $g$ are trained so that $g \approx f^{-1}$, which means that $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \approx \mathbf{x}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{z}} \approx \mathbf{z}$. Generative modeling performs the opposite mapping from representation learning, as shown in (see figure: Generative modeling performs the opposite mapping from representation learning.). In most generative models, we assume the distribution $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ is known, typically as a simple form such as a unit Gaussian. Knowing this distribution allows us to sample from it and then generate images via $g$.
concepts.motivation_md: By enforcing an inverse relationship between encoding and decoding, models can learn to map data to a structured latent space that is easy to sample from.
concepts.recap_md: - The encoder $f$ maps data to latent space, while the generator $g$ maps latent variables to data.

concepts.title: Connecting with the Audience
concepts.one_liner: Connecting with the audience involves showing your excitement for the topic and engaging them through shared enthusiasm.
concepts.content: Connecting with the audience is a vital component of scientific presentations. Engaging in improvisational theater exercises can help speakers prime themselves to connect with others, making their technical talks more vibrant. Generally, an audience wants three things from a talk: for the content to follow a logical sequence, to learn something new, and to connect with the speaker. They want to share in the speaker's excitement and watch them demonstrate a genuine love for their subject.
concepts.motivation_md: Technical talks often fail when they are dry or disconnected. This concept emphasizes that human connection and shared enthusiasm are just as important as the data being presented for a talk to be effective and memorable.
concepts.recap_md: - Audiences value logical flow, learning, and a personal connection with the speaker.

concepts.title: How to End a Technical Talk Effectively
concepts.one_liner: End a talk with "Thank you" to clearly signal the audience to applaud before transitioning to questions.
concepts.content: The way a talk ends significantly impacts the audience's response. A common but awkward approach is to end by asking, "Are there any questions?" which often results in scattered applause because the audience is unsure whether to clap or ask. A more effective method is to close with "Thank you," which provides a clear cue for the audience to applaud, after which you can invite questions. However, some speakers, like Patrick Winston, disagree with this approach; he preferred to end by reminding the audience of the promises kept regarding what they would learn, rather than implying the audience did a favor by attending.
concepts.motivation_md: Ending a talk effectively ensures a clear transition from the presentation to the Q&A session, avoiding the awkward silence or confusion that occurs when an audience doesn't know when to applaud.
concepts.recap_md: - Closing with "Thank you" provides a clear signal for the audience to applaud.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks on Giving Talks
concepts.one_liner: Preparation and rehearsal are the best cures for nervousness and ensure an enjoyable presentation for the audience.
concepts.content: Preparation and practice are essential for giving a successful talk. During the presentation, it is important to let the audience see your enjoyment of the work. Engaging with various resources and tips can help you find a personal style that works best. Ultimately, thorough preparation and rehearsal are the most effective ways to manage nervousness about public speaking.
concepts.motivation_md: Public speaking is a common source of anxiety. This concept provides a practical solution: rigorous preparation and the outward expression of enthusiasm to improve both the speaker's confidence and the audience's experience.
concepts.recap_md: - Preparation and rehearsal are the primary cures for public speaking nervousness.

concepts.title: Introduction to the Revisited Simple Vision System
concepts.one_liner: Modern computer vision leverages large-scale pretrained models to solve complex visual tasks with minimal fine-tuning.
concepts.content: The emergence of large-scale pretrained models like DALL-E, GPT, and ChatGPT has shifted the approach to computer vision. These models are trained on massive, diverse datasets, allowing them to generalize across domains such as natural language processing, image generation, and depth perception. They can be used as standalone systems or as building blocks in more complex architectures. While these models produce astonishing results, a gap remains in building truly reliable and robust systems, raising the question of whether current optimism in the field is well-founded or premature.
concepts.motivation_md: The field of computer vision has moved from hand-crafted algorithms to leveraging massive pretrained models. Understanding this shift is crucial for using state-of-the-art tools effectively while remaining aware of their current limitations.
concepts.recap_md: - Large-scale pretrained models can solve diverse tasks with little to no fine-tuning.

concepts.title: MiDaS Model for 3D Perception
concepts.one_liner: MiDaS is a state-of-the-art neural network trained end-to-end to recover 3D scene structure from a single image.
concepts.content:
The MiDaS model represents the current state of the art for recovering three-dimensional (3D) structure from a single image. Unlike traditional algorithms derived from first principles of image formation, MiDaS is a neural network trained end-to-end using diverse real-world images with ground truth depth information and stereo images. From a user's perspective, it functions as a simple call, though utilizing it effectively requires understanding its training, output format, and how to adapt it to specific tasks.

(see figure: Image from the simple world.)
concepts.motivation_md: Recovering 3D information from a 2D image is an under-determined problem. MiDaS provides a powerful, pretrained solution that bypasses the need to manually derive complex geometric algorithms for every new scene.
concepts.recap_md: - MiDaS is a pretrained neural network for single-image depth estimation.

concepts.title: Invariant Loss in Depth Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Invariant loss allows models to be trained on diverse datasets by ignoring ambiguities in scale and camera parameters.
concepts.content:
When training a model on a mix of diverse datasets, ambiguities arise regarding overall scale, camera parameters, and stereo baselines. To handle this, an invariant loss is used, which makes the training process more robust to these variations. While this improves the model's ability to learn from varied data sources, it also results in an output that is less convenient to use directly because the absolute scale is not preserved.

(see figure: Images and depth maps from the training set. *Source*: Image from @Ranftl2022)
concepts.motivation_md: Different depth datasets use different scales and cameras. Invariant loss allows a single model to learn from all of them simultaneously without being confused by these technical inconsistencies.
concepts.recap_md: - Invariant loss handles ambiguities in scale and camera parameters across datasets.

concepts.title: Disparity Prediction in Neural Networks
concepts.one_liner: The model predicts disparity, which is inverse depth up to an unknown scale and shift.
concepts.content: To manage the ambiguities inherent in diverse training data, the model is designed to predict disparity rather than absolute depth. Disparity is defined as inverse depth up to an unknown scale and shift. Because of this, the raw output of the model cannot be used directly as a physical measurement and must first be converted into world coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Predicting absolute depth is difficult when training data lacks a consistent scale. Predicting disparity allows the model to focus on relative depth relationships, which are more consistent across different images.
concepts.recap_md: - Disparity is the inverse of depth, subject to an unknown scale and shift.

concepts.title: Converting Disparity to Depth Values
concepts.one_liner: To convert disparity to depth, the inverse of the disparity plus an unknown constant is calculated.
concepts.content:
MiDaS returns disparity values that are accurate only up to an unknown constant ($d_0$). To transform these values into world coordinates ($X, Y, Z$), we must apply camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. Specifically, to translate the returned disparity for a pixel $d[n,m]$ into a depth value $z[n,m]$, the disparity must be inverted after adding the constant:

$$\begin{aligned}z [n,m] = \frac{1}{ d [n,m] + d_0}\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Raw model outputs are often in a relative format (disparity). This technique is necessary to recover actual physical distances (depth) required for 3D reconstruction or robotics applications.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth is calculated by inverting the sum of the predicted disparity and a constant $d_0$.

concepts.title: Layer-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Represents the 2D motion field as a collection of superimposed layers, each containing a rigid object with its own motion parameters.
concepts.content: If a scene is composed of rigid objects, we can assume that the motion field within each object follows the form described by equation (@eq-2d_motion_field_from_translation_and_rotation). In this case, the 2D motion field can be represented as a collection of superimposed layers, where each layer contains one object and occludes the layers below. Each layer is described by a different set of motion parameters. This parametric motion field can be incorporated into gradient-based approaches and estimated iteratively using an expectation-maximization (EM) style algorithm. At each step, the algorithm estimates which layer each pixel likely belongs to and then estimates the motion parameters of each layer. The idea of using layers to represent motion was first introduced by Wang and Adelson in 1994.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional motion estimation often ignores 3D scene properties; layer-based estimation incorporates these by assuming the scene consists of rigid objects with distinct motion patterns.
concepts.recap_md: - Models the motion field as a set of superimposed layers representing individual rigid objects. - Uses an EM-style algorithm to iteratively assign pixels to layers and estimate motion parameters.

concepts.title: Superimposed Layers
concepts.one_liner: A representation of the 2D motion field where each layer contains one object and occludes the layers below.
concepts.content: The 2D motion field can be represented as a collection of superimposed layers, where each layer contains one object and occludes the layers below. Each layer is described by its own set of motion parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: This representation allows for handling occlusions and multiple distinct moving objects within a single scene by treating them as separate, overlapping entities.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents the 2D motion field as a stack of layers where each layer contains a single object. - Models occlusions by allowing higher layers to cover layers positioned below them.

concepts.title: Parametric Motion Field
concepts.one_liner: A motion field where each layer is described by a specific set of motion parameters.
concepts.content: In a layer-based representation, each layer is described by a different set of motion parameters. This collection of parameters defines the parametric motion field for the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Using parameters to describe motion reduces the complexity of the estimation problem and enforces physical consistency within objects.
concepts.recap_md: - Describes motion using a set of parameters for each layer rather than independent pixel vectors. - Provides a structured way to incorporate 3D scene assumptions into 2D motion estimation.

concepts.title: EM-style Algorithm for Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: An iterative algorithm that estimates which layer each pixel belongs to and the motion parameters of each layer.
concepts.content: Motion parameters can be estimated iteratively using an expectation-maximization (EM) style algorithm. At each step, the algorithm estimates which layer each pixel is likely to belong to and then estimates the motion parameters of each layer.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach solves the chicken-and-egg problem of needing to know which pixels belong to an object to find its motion, and vice versa.
concepts.recap_md: - Iteratively estimates pixel-to-layer assignments and the motion parameters for each layer. - Alternates between determining layer membership and optimizing the parameters of the motion field.

concepts.title: Learning-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: An approach to motion estimation that uses data to learn properties and semantic cues that models cannot easily capture.
concepts.content: Learning-based methods for motion estimation address the limitations of model-based methods, which often rely on assumptions like brightness constancy that do not always hold. Modeling errors can occur due to occlusions, shadows, illumination changes, or deformable surfaces. Learning-based models can implicitly exploit semantic properties and motion-relevant cues, such as monocular depth or priors about familiar objects (e.g., buildings do not move, people are deformable). These methods can also account for approximations made in traditional computations, such as those used in calculating derivatives.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional models often fail in complex real-world scenarios due to rigid assumptions; learning-based methods can adapt to these complexities and utilize semantic context.
concepts.recap_md: - Addresses modeling errors caused by failures in assumptions like brightness constancy or rigid motion. - Exploits semantic cues and priors about object motion that are difficult to model from first principles.

concepts.title: Supervised Models for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Models that learn to estimate motion using a database of training examples.
concepts.content: Supervised models learn to estimate motion using a database of training examples.
concepts.motivation_md: Supervised learning allows models to directly learn the mapping from image intensity changes to motion vectors using labeled data.
concepts.recap_md: - Requires a database of training examples with known ground truth motion. - Learns to estimate optical flow by minimizing the error against provided labels.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Models for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Models that learn to estimate motion without training data.
concepts.content: Unsupervised models learn to estimate motion without training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Obtaining ground truth optical flow for real-world video is extremely difficult; unsupervised methods circumvent this by learning from the data itself.
concepts.recap_md: - Learns motion estimation from image sequences without requiring ground truth training data. - Typically relies on internal consistency or reconstruction loss to guide the learning process.

concepts.title: FlowNet
concepts.one_liner: A neural network architecture that estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames using end-to-end supervised training.
concepts.content: FlowNet was one of the first approaches to use the formulation $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$ with neural networks. The architecture is simple and estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames. (see figure: In FlowNet the direct approach estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames.) This direct approach, depicted in @fig-supervised_estimation, learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames without making assumptions about architectural priors. The architecture is trained end-to-end using ground truth optical flow.
concepts.motivation_md: FlowNet demonstrated that deep convolutional networks could learn the complex task of optical flow estimation directly from raw pixels, bypassing traditional hand-crafted algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - Estimates optical flow $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right]$$ directly from two input frames. - Uses an end-to-end supervised training regime with ground truth data.

concepts.title: Pinhole-Lens Sharpness-Brightness Tradeoff
concepts.one_liner: Pinhole cameras can only increase light intake at the expense of image sharpness, a tradeoff that lenses overcome by focusing rays from a single point to a single sensor position.
concepts.content: Pinhole cameras allow more light to enter the camera aperture only at the expense of image sharpness. Lenses overcome that tradeoff by focusing all the rays passing through the lens from a point on a surface to a single position on the sensor plane, creating an image that is both sharp and bright.
concepts.motivation_md: Pinhole cameras face a fundamental physical limit where a larger aperture increases brightness but blurs the image; lenses are necessary to achieve both high light sensitivity and high resolution.
concepts.recap_md: - Pinhole cameras trade off image sharpness for light intake. - Lenses focus multiple rays from a single scene point onto a single sensor point. - This mechanism allows for images that are simultaneously bright and sharp.

concepts.title: Lens Shape Derivation
concepts.one_liner: Using small-angle and thin-lens approximations, a lens surface must have a parabolic or spherical shape to focus light rays effectively.
concepts.content: Using small-angle and thin-lens approximations, a lens surface can be designed to have specific focusing properties. This derivation shows that the lens must have a parabolic or spherical shape to focus rays from a point to a single position.
concepts.motivation_md: To create a lens that effectively focuses light, we need a mathematical model to determine the physical geometry required for the lens surface.
concepts.recap_md: - Small-angle and thin-lens approximations are used to design lens surfaces. - The ideal focusing property requires a parabolic or spherical lens shape.

concepts.title: Linearity of Imaging Systems
concepts.one_liner: Because optical elements often respond linearly to light, cameras can be described using linear algebra to recover interpretable images from recorded data.
concepts.content: Optical elements of imaging systems are often linear in their response to light. Consequently, it is convenient and powerful to describe such general cameras using linear algebra. This formulation provides a powerful machinery to recover an interpretable image from the recorded data, helps build intuitions about how cameras work, and allows for the conceptualization of new types of cameras.
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling cameras as linear systems allows us to apply the robust tools of linear algebra to solve complex image reconstruction problems and design novel imaging hardware.
concepts.recap_md: - Imaging systems often exhibit a linear response to light. - Linear algebra provides the mathematical framework for image recovery. - This model aids in understanding current cameras and designing new ones.

concepts.title: Light Field
concepts.one_liner: The light field represents light intensities at various positions and directions, allowing for the linear algebraic modeling of scenes with complex spatial structures.
concepts.content: Let the light intensities in the world be represented by a column vector, $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$, where the $n$-th component gives the intensity of the light at position $n$ heading in the direction of the camera. In simple models, the axis in the camera sensor is reversed, and the scene is modeled as a line at a fixed depth. However, if the scene has a more complex spatial structure, the light field must be used to apply the same linear algebra to model cameras.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard 2D image representations fail to capture the full complexity of light rays in a 3D scene; light fields provide a more complete description necessary for advanced reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Light intensities are represented as a column vector $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$. - The light field accounts for both position and direction of light rays. - It enables linear algebraic modeling of complex 3D spatial structures.

concepts.title: Discrete Light Ray Approximation
concepts.one_liner: Approximating input light as a discrete set of rays rather than a continuous wave allows the imaging process to be described using linear algebra.
concepts.content: The input light can be approximated by a discrete and finite set of light rays instead of a continuous wave. This approximation allows for the use of linear algebra to describe the imaging process.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous wave optics is mathematically complex; discretizing light into rays simplifies the physics into a system of linear equations that computers can solve efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - Light is modeled as a finite set of discrete rays. - This replaces the more complex continuous wave model of light. - The approximation facilitates the use of linear algebra in imaging.

concepts.title: Linear Imaging Model
concepts.one_liner: A camera can be modeled as a linear system where sensor measurements are a linear combination of scene intensities via a camera matrix.
concepts.content: Cameras can be modeled as linear systems. Let the sensor measurements be $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}$ and the unknown scene be $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$. If the camera sensors respond linearly to the light intensity, their measurements will be a linear combination of the light intensities given by the matrix $\mathbf{A}$: $$\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}} = \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$$ We represent the camera by matrix $\mathbf{A}$. For pinhole cameras or conventional lens cameras, $\mathbf{A}$ is approximately an identity matrix because each sensor depends only on the value of a single scene element. For more general cameras, $\mathbf{A}$ may be very different from an identity matrix, requiring the estimation of $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$ from $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}$. (see figure: Figure: (a) Schematic drawing of a small-hole 1D pinhole camera, and (b) the visualization of its imaging matrices $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$, and the regularized inverse $\mathbf{B}$. For the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Expressing the imaging process as a matrix multiplication allows us to use standard inverse problem techniques to reconstruct scenes from distorted or encoded sensor data.
concepts.recap_md: - The imaging process is defined by the equation $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}} = \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$. - The matrix $\mathbf{A}$ represents the specific optical characteristics of the camera. - Reconstruction involves estimating the scene $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$ from measurements $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}$.

concepts.title: Regularized Image Reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: Regularized reconstruction solves for the scene by minimizing an objective function that balances data fidelity with a regularization term to handle noise and ill-conditioned matrices.
concepts.content: In the presence of noise, there may not be a solution $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$ that exactly satisfies the imaging model in a least squares sense. Because the camera matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is often not invertible or is poorly conditioned, it is useful to introduce a regularizer as an additional term in the objective function. If the regularization term favors a small world $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$, the objective function $E$ to minimize is: $$E = \lVert \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}- \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}\rVert ^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}\rVert ^2$$ The regularization parameter, $\lambda$, determines the trade-off between explaining the observations and satisfying the regularization term. (see figure: Figure: (a) Schematic drawing of a small-hole 1D pinhole camera, and (b) the visualization of its imaging matrices $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$, and the regularized inverse $\mathbf{B}$. For the...) Setting the derivative of the objective function with respect to the vector $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$ equal to zero, we have: $$\begin{align} 0 &= \bigtriangledown_{\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}} \lVert \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}- \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}\rVert ^2 + \bigtriangledown_{\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}} \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}\rVert ^2 \\ &= \mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}- \mathbf{A}^T \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}+ \lambda \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}} \end{align}$$ or $$\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}= (\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world imaging data is noisy and the camera matrix is often ill-conditioned; regularization prevents noise amplification and provides stable solutions for image reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Regularization handles noise and ill-conditioned camera matrices $\mathbf{A}$. - The parameter $\lambda$ balances data fidelity against the regularization term. - The solution is found by minimizing the objective function $E = \lVert \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}- \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}\rVert ^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}\rVert ^2$.

concepts.title: Regularized Inverse
concepts.one_liner: The regularized inverse is the matrix $\mathbf{B}=(\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{A}^T$ used to estimate the scene from sensor measurements.
concepts.content: The matrix $\mathbf{B}=(\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{A}^T$ is the regularized inverse of the imaging matrix $\mathbf{A}$.
concepts.motivation_md: When a direct inverse of the camera matrix does not exist or is unstable, the regularized inverse provides a robust linear operator to reconstruct the scene.
concepts.recap_md: - The regularized inverse is defined as $\mathbf{B}=(\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{A}^T$. - It provides a stable way to compute the scene estimate $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$ from measurements $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{s}}$.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Model Connection
concepts.one_liner: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an autoregressive model, a class of models that can be used in conjunction with deep networks for texture synthesis.
concepts.content: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an autoregressive model. This class of models can be used in conjunction with deep networks to generate textures and other data by modeling the probability of a pixel or element conditioned on previous ones.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models provide a structured way to generate complex data like textures by breaking the generation process into a sequence of conditional steps.
concepts.recap_md: - The Efros-Leung algorithm serves as a specific instance of an autoregressive model.

concepts.title: Diffusion Models Connection
concepts.one_liner: The iterative optimization of the Heeger-Bergen algorithm is a type of denoising process, similar to the strategy used in diffusion models.
concepts.content: The iterative optimization of the Heeger-Bergen algorithm is a type of denoising process: it starts with a noise image and little by little transforms it into an image of a texture. This general idea reappears in the context of diffusion models, which follow this same strategy.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the iterative refinement in early texture algorithms helps motivate the denoising strategies used in modern generative diffusion models.
concepts.recap_md: - Heeger-Bergen uses iterative optimization to transform noise into texture.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) Connection
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and the Heeger-Bergen algorithm both aim to match the statistics of a generated image to those of exemplar images.
concepts.content: The Heeger-Bergen algorithm is connected to generative adversarial networks (GANs). The objective of Heeger-Bergen is to make a texture that has the same histogram statistics as an exemplar. Similarly, a GAN makes images that have the same statistics as a set of exemplars; however, the statistics we seek to match in a GAN are learned by a discriminator neural network rather than being hand-defined subband statistics.
concepts.motivation_md: This connection highlights the evolution from hand-crafted statistical matching to learned feature matching in generative modeling.
concepts.recap_md: - Both Heeger-Bergen and GANs seek to match the statistics of exemplar images.

concepts.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way to reason about complicated visual situations.
concepts.content: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way that allows us to reason about the visual world even when we're modeling very complicated situations. These models are useful in vision, where we often need to exploit modularity to make computations tractable.
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling complex joint distributions directly is often computationally impossible; graphical models provide a modular framework to make these calculations tractable.
concepts.recap_md: - They provide a modular way to describe joint probability distributions.

concepts.title: Undirected Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: An undirected graphical model is a graph with nodes representing variables and line segments representing shared structure in a probability distribution.
concepts.content: A probabilistic graphical model is a graph that describes a class of probability distributions sharing a common structure. The graph has nodes, drawn as circles, indicating the variables of the joint probability. It has edges, drawn as lines connecting nodes to other nodes. In undirected graphical models, the edges are line segments without arrowheads.
concepts.motivation_md: Undirected graphs are used to represent symmetric relationships between variables where no specific causal direction is assumed.
concepts.recap_md: - Nodes represent variables in a joint probability distribution.

concepts.title: Conditional Independence in Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: In undirected graphical models, the absence of an edge between nodes indicates that the corresponding variables are conditionally independent.
concepts.content: In undirected graphical models, the edges indicate the conditional independence structure of the nodes of the graph. If there is no edge between two nodes, then the variables described by those nodes are independent, conditioned on the values of intervening nodes in any path between them in the graph. If two nodes do have a line between them, then we cannot assume they are independent.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying conditional independence allows for the factorization of complex joint distributions, significantly simplifying probabilistic inference.
concepts.recap_md: - Missing edges signify conditional independence between variables.

concepts.title: Hammersley-Clifford Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Hammersley-Clifford theorem states that a positive joint probability distribution must be a product of functions over the maximal cliques of its graphical model.
concepts.content: The Hammersley-Clifford theorem defines the form the joint probability must have for any given graphical model. It states that a positive probability distribution has the independence structure described by a graphical model if and only if it can be written as a product of functions over the variables of each maximal clique: $$p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N) = \prod_{x_c \in x_i} \Psi_{c} (x_c),$$ where the product is over all maximal cliques $x_c$ in the graph $x_i$. A clique is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the clique. A maximal clique is a clique that can't include more nodes of the graph without losing the clique property. [FIGURE:a834d415de54d03b | A maximal clique is the largest possible clique.]
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the mathematical bridge between the visual structure of a graph and the algebraic factorization of its probability distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Joint probability is the product of functions over maximal cliques.

concepts.title: Clique
concepts.one_liner: A clique is a set of nodes in a graph where every node is connected to every other node in the set.
concepts.content: A clique is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the clique.
concepts.motivation_md: Cliques are the fundamental building blocks used to define local dependencies and factorize joint distributions in graphical models.
concepts.recap_md: - Every node in a clique is connected to all other nodes in that clique.

items.title: Example: Learning the star symbol
items.prompt_md:
Imagine you find an ancient mathematics text, with marvelous looking proofs, but there is a symbol you do not recognize, "$\star$". You see it being used here and there in equations, and you note down examples of its behavior: 
$$\begin{aligned}
    2 \star 3 &= 36\nonumber \\
    7 \star 1 &= 49\nonumber \\
    5 \star 2 &= 100\nonumber \\
    2 \star 2 &= 16\nonumber
\end{aligned}
$$ 

What do you think $\star$ represents? What function is it computing? Do you have it? Let's test your answer: what is the value of $3 \star 5$? (The answer is in the figure below.)
items.solution_md:
It may not seem like it, but you just performed learning! You *learned* what $\star$ does by looking at examples. In fact, @fig-star_symbol_learning shows what you did:

items.title: Querying sensitive information using coin flips for differential privacy
items.prompt_md: Describe a procedure to query a set of adults to determine what fraction of them have cheated on their partner using differential privacy (coin flips).
items.solution_md:
averaging over the many data samples. A simple example of this approach, described in @Kearns2020, is the following procedure to query a set of adults to determine what fraction of them have cheated on their partner. Each surveyed adult is instructed to flip a coin. If the coin shows heads, they are instructed to answer the question, "Have you cheated on your partner?", truthfully. If the coin shows tails, they are asked to answer "yes" or "no" at random, by flipping the coin again and answering "yes" if heads and "no" if tails. The resulting responses for each individual are stored.

If the stored data were hacked, or accidentally leaked, no harm would come to the surveyed individuals even though their data from this sensitive survey had been revealed. Any "yes\" answer could very plausibly be explained as being a result of the subject having been instructed by the protocol to flip a coin to select the answer. Yet it is still possible to infer the true percentage of "yes\" answers in the surveyed population from the stored data: the expected value of the measured percentages will be the true "yes\" and "no\" answers in the population. The price for this differential privacy is that more data must be collected to obtain the same accuracy guarantees in the estimate of the true population averages.

items.title: Ethical Issues in Computer Vision
items.prompt_md:
The following are an (incomplete) set of questions that researchers and engineers may keep in mind:

-   Would you prefer that a person identify someone from a photograph, with the potential biases and assumptions that the individual may have, or for an algorithm to do so, based on training from a dataset which may include biases of its own? See @Kearns2020, @Mullainathan2019 for related discussions.

-   What privacy safeguards must be in place to accept always-on camera and voice recording inside people's homes? Inside your own home?

-   Traffic fatalities in the US currently result in the tragedy of approximately 30,000 deaths annually, with most of those fatalities being caused by driver error. If every vehicle were self-driving, fatalities caused by human error could fall dramatically, yet there will surely still be fatalities caused by machine errors, albeit far fewer than had been caused by humans. Is that a tradeoff society should make? What should be our threshold of fatalities caused by machine? This moral question is a societal-scale version of "the trolley problem" @Thomson1985: A bystander can choose to divert a trolley from the main track to a side track, saving five people who are on that main track, but killing one person who is on the side track. Should the bystander actively divert the trolley, intentionally killing the person on the side track, who would otherwise have been spared if no action were taken? These issues are also present for automobile airbags, which save many lives but sometimes injure a small number of people @Dalmotas1995, and in other public health issues.

-   Algorithms will never perform exactly as well among all groups of people. Within what tolerance must the performance of human analysis algorithms be for an algorithm to be considered fair? Is algorithmic bias being less than human bias sufficient for deployment?

-   Some image datasets have contained offensive material @Birhand2021, @Barber2019. How should we decide which concepts or images can be part of a training set? Is there any need for algorithms to understand offensive words or concepts?

-   Could potential categorization tasks of humans in photographs (e.g., gender identity, skincolor, age, height) bring harm to individuals, and how?

-   Should computer vision systems ever be used in warfare? In policing? In public surveillance?

-   What is the role of machines in society? Regarding decisions of person identification, do we want people making decisions, with their own difficult-to-measure biases, or do we want machines involved, with biases that may be measurable?

-   Do face recognition algorithms suppress public protests? Consider a world where any face shown in public is always recorded and identifiable. (We are almost in that world). What are the consequences of that for personal safety, speech, assembly, and liberties?

-   What are the most beneficial uses of computer vision?

-   Which uses have the most potential for harm, or currently cause the most harm?

-   Is it ok to use computer vision to monitor workers in order to improve their productivity? In order to improve workplace safety? In order to prevent workplace harassment?

-   What criteria would you use to evaluate the pros and cons of using machines or humans for a given task?

-   Should datasets represent real-world disparities, or represent the world as we want it to be? How might these choices amplify existing economic disparities?

-   When should consent be required (and from whom) before using an image to train a computer vision algorithm?

items.title: Binary Classifier Example
items.prompt_md:
Consider a multilayer perceptron (MLP) that performs binary classification formulated as two-way softmax regression. The input datapoints are each in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the target outputs are in $\vartriangle^1$, with layer structure $\texttt{linear}-\texttt{relu}-\texttt{linear}-\texttt{relu}-\texttt{linear}$. This network is drawn below in @fig-neural_nets-simple_MLP_network2.

(see figure: An MLP with three linear layers and two outputs, suitable for performing binary softmax regression.)

Or expressed in math as follows:

$$
\begin{align}
    \mathbf{z}_1 &= \mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1 &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{linear}\\
    \mathbf{h}_1 &= \texttt{relu}(\mathbf{z}_1) &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{relu}\\
    \mathbf{z}_2 &= \mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{h}_1 + \mathbf{b}_2 &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{linear}\\
    \mathbf{h}_2 &= \texttt{relu}(\mathbf{z}_2) &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{relu}\\
    \mathbf{z}_3 &= \mathbf{W}_3\mathbf{h}_2 + \mathbf{b}_3 &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{linear}\\
    \mathbf{y} &= \texttt{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_3) &\triangleleft \quad \text{\texttt{softmax}}
\end{align}
$$

Now we wish to train this net to classify between two data distributions. The goal is to transform the input distribution into a target distribution that separates the classes, as shown below in @fig-neural_nets_as_data_transformations-goal_of_classifier.

(see figure: The goal of a neural net classifier is to rearrange the input data distribution to match the target label distribution. (left) Input dataset with two classes in red and blue. (right) Target output...)

In this example, the target output places all the red dots at $(0,1)$ and all the blue dots at $(1,0)$. These are the coordinates of one-hot codes for our two classes. Training the network consists of find the series of geometric transformations that rearrange the input distribution to this target output distribution.

We will visualize how the net transforms the training dataset, layer by layer, at four **checkpoints** over the course of training.
items.solution_md:
A checkpoint is a record of the parameters at some iteration of training, that is, if iterates of the parameter vector are $\theta^0, \theta^1, \ldots, \theta^T$, then any $\theta^k$ can be recorded as a checkpoint.

In @fig-neural_nets-nn_training_viz, we plot this as a 3D visualization of $\mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ mappings. Each dotted line connects the representation of a datapoint at one layer to its representation at the next. The gray lines show, for each layer, how a square region around the origin gets stretched, rotated, or squished to map to a transformed region on the next layer.

(see figure: How a deep net remaps input data layer by layer. The target output is to move all the red points to $(0,1)$ and all the blue points to $(1,0)$ (one-hot codes for the two classes). As training...)

Of course, ``stretched, rotated, or squished'' is just an intuitive way to think about it, but we can be more precise. The linear layers perform an affine transformation of the space, while the relus project all negative values to the boundaries of the cone whose dimensions are strictly positive. Layer by layer, over the course of training, the net learns to disentangle these two classes and pull the points toward vertices of the one-simplex, achieving a correct classification of the points!

items.title: Snell's Law
items.prompt_md:
interface surface, according to **Snell's Law** @Hecht2016, given in the
equation below. Both the wavelength and the speed of light in a medium
are inversely proportional to the **index of refraction** of that
medium, denoted as $n$. The $n$ for a vacuum is 1. At a material
boundary, for the geometry illustrated in @fig-snell, we have
$$n_1 \sin(\theta_1) = n_2 \sin(\theta_2)$$
where $\theta_1$ and
$\theta_2$ are the angles with respect to the surface normal of the
incident and outgoing light rays, and $n_1$ and $n_2$ are the indices of
refraction of the materials in region 1 and region 2. Snell's law can be
derived by matching the wavelength of light projected along the material
interface boundary across each side of the boundary.

items.title: Snell's Law and Refraction Demonstration
items.caption_md: (a) Snell's law describes the bending of light at interfaces of differing indices of refraction, $n_1$ and $n_2$, in terms of the angles, $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, relative to the interface, or surface, normal. (b) Straw below water surface appears distorted due to refraction at the air/water boundary.

items.title: Example: Image inpainting function
items.prompt_md: From the three examples in @fig-intro_to_learning-inpainting_example, can you figure out what the operator $F$ does?
items.solution_md:
We were able to model the behavior of $\star$, on the examples we were
given, with a simple algebraic equation. Let's try something rather more
complicated. From the three examples in @fig-intro_to_learning-inpainting_example, can you figure out what the operator $F$ does?

(see figure: A complicated function that could be learned from examples. This example is from @hays2007scene.)

You probably came up with something like "it fills in the missing
pixels." That's exactly right, but it's sweeping a lot of details under
the rug. Remember, we want to learn an *algorithm*, a procedure that is
completely unambiguous. How exactly does $F$ fill in the missing pixels?

It's hard to say in words. We may need a very complex algorithm to
specify the answer, an algorithm so complex that we could never hope to
write it out by hand. This is the point of machine learning. The machine
writes the algorithm for us, but it can only do so if we give it many
examples, not just these three.
items.answer: It fills in the missing pixels.

### Example 1: Linear Least-Squares Regression {#sec-intro_to_learning-least_squares}

One of the simplest learning problems is known as **linear least-squares
regression**. In this setting, we aim to model the relationship between
two variables, $x$ and $y$, with a line.

As a concrete example, let's imagine $x$ represents the temperature
outside, and $y$ represents the number people at the beach. As before,
we train (i.e., fit) our model on many observed examples of
{`temperature outside`, `number of people at the beach`} pairs, denoted
as $\{x^{(i)},y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. At test time, this model can be
applied to predict the $y$ value of a new query $x'$, as shown in
@fig-intro_to_learning-ols_train_test.

(see figure: The goal of learning is to use the training data to predict the $y$ value of the test query. In our example we find that for every 1 degree increase in temperature, we can expect $\sim 10$ more...)

Our *hypothesis space* is linear functions, that is, the relationship
between $x$ and our predictions $\hat{y}$ of $y$ has the form
$\hat{y} = f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$. This hypothesis space
is parameterized by a two scalars, $\theta_0, \theta_1 \in \mathbb{R}$,
the intercept and slope of the line. In this book, we will use $\theta$
in general to refer to any parameters that are being learned. In this
case we have $\theta = [\theta_0, \theta_1]$. Learning consists of
finding the value of these parameters that maximizes the objective.

Our *objective* is that predictions should be near ground truth targets
in a least-squares sense, that is, $(\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)})^2$ should
be small for all training examples $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. We
call this objective the $L_2$ loss: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    J(	heta) &= \sum_i \mathcal{L}(\hat{y}^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\\
    &\quad \mathcal{L}(\hat{y}, y) = (\hat{y} - y)^2 \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad L_2 \text{ loss}
\end{aligned}$$ 


We will use $J(\theta)$ to denote the total objective, over all training datapoints, as a function of the parameters; we will use $\mathcal{L}$ to denote the loss per datapoint. That is, $J(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}), y^{(i)})$.


The full learning problem is as follows: 
$$\begin{aligned}
    \theta^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N (\theta_1 x^{(i)} + \theta_0 - y^{(i)})^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

We can choose any number of optimizers to solve this problem. A first idea might be "try a bunch of random values for $\theta$ and return the one that maximizes the objective." In fact, this simple approach works, it just can be rather slow since we are searching
for good solutions blind. A better idea can be to exploit *structure* in the search problem. For the linear least-squares problem, the tools of calculus give us clean mathematical structure that makes solving the optimization problem easy, as we show next.

From calculus, we know that at any maxima or minima of a function, $J(\theta)$, with respect to a variable $\theta$, the derivative $\frac{\partial{J(\theta)}}{\partial{\theta}} = 0$. We are trying to find the minimum of the objective $J(\theta)$: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    J(	heta) = \sum_{i=1}^N (\theta_1 x^{(i)} + \theta_0 - y^{(i)})^2.
\end{aligned}$$ 

This function can be rewritten as 
$$\begin{aligned}
    J(	heta) = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\theta)^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\theta)
\end{aligned}
$$ 
with 
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X} = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & x^{(1)}  \\
    1 & x^{(2)} \\
    \vdots & \vdots \\
    1 & x^{(N)}
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\mathbf{y} = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    y^{(1)}  \\
    y^{(2)} \\
    \vdots \\
    y^{(N)}
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\theta = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    \theta_0 \\
    \theta_1
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$$

The $J$ is a quadratic form, which has a single global minimum where the derivative is zero, and no other points where the derivative is zero. Therefore, we can solve for the $\theta^*$ that minimizes $J$ by finding the point where the derivative is zero. The derivative is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial J(\theta)}{\partial \theta} =  2(\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X} \theta - \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}).
\end{aligned}
$$ 

We set this derivative to zero and solve for $\theta^*$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
    2(\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X} \theta^* - \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}) &= 0\\
\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X} \theta^* &= \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}\\
\theta^* &= (\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The $\theta^*$ defines the best fitting line to our data, and this line
can be used to predict the $y$ value of future observations of $x$
(@fig-intro_to_learning-ols_fit).

(see figure: A best fit line is a visualization of a function $f_{\theta}$, that predicts the $y$-value for each input $x$-value.)

We can now summarize the entire linear least-squares learning problem as
follows:

(see figure: Linear regression finds a line that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.)

In these diagrams, we will sometimes describe the objective just in terms of $\mathcal{L}$, in which case it should be understood that this implies $J(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}), y^{(i)}).

items.title: Experiment 1: Effect of Data

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

items.prompt_md: Look at how data shapes the objective function $J$ for the following empirical risk minimization problem: $$\begin{aligned} J(\theta; \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}) &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \lvert f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\rvert^{0.25} \\ f_{\theta}(x) &= \theta_0 x + \theta_1 \sin(x) \end{aligned}$$
items.solution_md:
Training data is the main source of information for a learner, and a learner is just like a detective: as it observes more and more data, it gets more and more evidence to narrow in on the solution. ... We use the exponent $0.25$, rather than the more common squared error, just so that the plots in @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_data_more_constraints show more clearly the linear constraints (the dark lines) added by each datapoint to the objective $J$.

In @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_data_more_constraints, bottom row, we plot $J$ as a heatmap over the values obtained for different settings of $\theta$. On the top row we plot the data being fit, $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$, along with the function $f_{\theta}$ that achieves the best fit, and a sample other settings of $\theta$ that achieve within 0.1 of the cost of the best fit. Each column corresponds to some amount of training data $N$. Moving to the right, we increase $N$.

The heatmaps here are reminiscent of a classic computer vision algorithm called the Hough transform @hough1959machine, @duda1972use. This transform can be used to find geometric primitives that fit feature points in images. In fact, the bottom row is \textit{exactly} the generalized Hough transform~\cite{duda1972use} of the data points in the top row, using $\theta_0 x + \theta_1 \sin(x)$ as the family of geometric primitives we are fitting.

The first thing to look at is the leftmost column, where $N=1$. For a single datapoint, there are an infinite number of functions in our hypothesis space that perfectly fit that point. This shows up in the heatmaps as a *line* of settings of $\theta$ that all achieve zero loss. The learning algorithm we used in this example picks a random solution from the set of solutions that achieve zero loss. Unfortunately, here it got unlucky and picked a solution that happens to be far from the true solution.

Next, look at the second column where we have $N=5$ training points. Ideally we want to find a curve that exactly passes through each point. Each *single* datapoint adds one constraint to this problem, and each constraint shows up as a line in the heatmap for $J$ [the line of solutions that satisfy the constraint $y^{(i)} = \theta_0 x^{(i)} + \theta_1 \sin(x^{(i)})$ for that datapoint $i$]. The *intersection* of all these constraints pinpoints the setting of parameters that fits *all* that data. In this example, with five datapoints, there is no location where all the constraint lines intersect, which means there is no curve in our hypothesis space that can perfectly fit this data. Instead we settle for the curve that best approximates the data, according to our loss function. Notice that the learned solution is now pretty close to the true function that generated the data. It is not an exact match, because the data is generated by taking *noisy* samples from the true data generating function.

Finally, let's look at the third column, where we are fitting 20 datapoints. Now the intersection (or, more precisely, average) of the losses for all the datapoints gives a relatively smooth cost function $J(\theta)$, and the learned solution is almost right on top of the true solution. This illustrates a very important point:

*The more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools.*

With enough data, the true solution will be pinpointed by data alone. However, when we don't have enough data, or when the data is noisy or incorrectly labeled, we can turn to our two other tools, which we will see next.

items.title: Experiment 2: Effect of Priors

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

items.prompt_md: Analyze the effect of priors using a ridge regularizer $\lambda \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$ in the following empirical risk minimization problem: $$\begin{aligned} J(\theta; \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}) &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \left\lVert f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2 + \lambda \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2 \\ f_{\theta}(x) &= \theta_0 + \theta_1 x \end{aligned}$$
items.solution_md:
Now we will run a similar experiment to look at the effect of priors. ... We will look at the effect of the ridge regularizer $\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$. We plot the energy landscape and function fit for this problem in @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_regularizer_more_constraints, fitting to a single datapoint. The ridge regularizer prefers solutions with small parameter norm, so its contribution to the energy landscape is to place a quadratic bowl around the origin. As we increase $\lambda$ (moving left to right in the subplots), the effect of the regularizer becomes stronger and pulls the learned solution closer and closer to the origin.

(see figure: More regularization, more (soft) constraints.)

In this example, the true solution lies near the origin, so adding some regularization gets us closer to the truth. But using too strong a $\lambda$ overregularizers; the true solution is not *exactly* $\theta=0$. The middle column is the Goldilocks solution, where the strength of the regularizer is just right.

You can take away a few lessons from this example:

1.  Priors help only when they are good guesses as to the truth.

2.  Overreliance on the prior means ignoring the data, and this is generally a bad thing.

3.  For any given prior, there is a sweet spot where the strength is optimal. Sometimes this ideal strength can be derived from modeling assumptions and other times you may need to tune it as a hyperparameter.

items.title: Parseval's Theorem
items.prompt_md:
As the DFT is a change of basis, the dot product between two signals and
the norm of a vector is preserved (up to a constant factor) after the
basis change. This is stated by Parseval's theorem:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \ell_1 \left[n,m \right] \ell_2^* \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v \right] \mathscr{L}_2^* \left[u,v \right]$$

items.title: Plancherel Theorem
items.prompt_md:
In particular, if $\ell_1=\ell_2$ this reduces to the **Plancherel
theorem**:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \ell\left[n,m \right] \|^2 = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \|^2$$

items.title: Linearity of Gradients
Example: Backpropagation for an MLP
items.prompt_md: Derive the backpropagation operations (gradients with respect to inputs and parameters) for the standard layers of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), specifically linear layers, pointwise nonlinearities (like ReLU), and loss layers (like $L_2$ loss).
items.solution_md:
In order to fully describe backprop for any given architecture, we need
$\mathbf{L}$ for each layer in the network. One way to do this is to
define the derivative $f^{\prime}$ for all atomic functions like
addition, multiplication, and so on, and then expand every layer into a
computation graph that involves just these atomic operations. Backprop
through the expanded computation graph will then simply make use of all
the atomic $f^{\prime}$s to compute the necessary $\mathbf{L}$ matrices.
However, often there are more efficient ways of writing `backward` for
standard layers. In this section we will derive a compact `backward` for
linear layers and relu layers --- the two main layers in MLPs.

### Backpropagation for a Linear Layer

The definition of a linear layer, in forward direction, is as follows:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}
\end{aligned}$$ We have separated the parameters into $\mathbf{W}$ and
$\mathbf{b}$ for clarity, but remember that we could always rewrite the
following in terms of $\theta = \texttt{vec}[\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{b}]$.
Let $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ be $N$-dimensional and
$\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ be $M$-dimensional; then $\mathbf{W}$ is an
$[M \times N]$ dimensional matrix and $\mathbf{b}$ is an $M$-dimensional
vector.

Next we need the gradients of this function, with respect to its inputs
and parameters, that is, $\mathbf{L}$. Matrix algebra typically hides
the details so we will instead first write out all the individual scalar
gradients:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}[i,j] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial x_{\texttt{in}}[j]} = 
    \frac{\partial \sum_l \mathbf{W}[i,l] x_{\texttt{in}}[l]}{\partial x_{\texttt{in}}[j]} = \mathbf{W}[i,j]
\end{aligned}$${#eq-lingrad1}


$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{W}}[i,jk] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial \mathbf{W}[j,k]} = \frac{\partial \sum_l \mathbf{W}[i,l] x_{\texttt{in}}[l]}{\partial \mathbf{W}[j,k]} = 
    \begin{cases}
        x_{\texttt{in}}[k], &\text{if} \quad i == j\\
        0,      & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases} \label{lingrad2}\\
    \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}}[i,j] &= \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial \mathbf{b}[j]} = 
    \begin{cases}
        1, &\text{if} \quad i == j\\
        0, & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases} 
\end{aligned}$${#eq-lingrad3}

@eq-lingrad1 and @eq-lingrad3 imply: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    \boxed{\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{W}} &\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad [M \times N]\\
    \boxed{\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{I}} &\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad [M \times M]
\end{aligned}$$ 

There is no such simple shorthand for $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{W}$, but that is no matter, as we can proceed at this point to implement `backward` for a linear layer by plugging our
computed $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{x}$ into @eq-backpropagation-backward, and
$\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{b}$ into
@eq-backpropagation-djdtheta. 

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}\\
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}} &=  \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{W}}\\
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{b}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}
\end{aligned}$${#eq-backpropagation-linear_backward_costgrad} 

To get an intuition for
@eq-backpropagation-linear_backward_costgrad, it can help to draw the
matrices being multiplied. Below, in
@fig-backpropagation-linear_forward_backward_matrices, on the left we
have the forward operation of the layer (omitting biases) and on the
right we have the backward operation in
@eq-backpropagation-linear_backward_costgrad.


(see figure: The forward and backward matrix multiples for a linear layer.)

Unlike the other equations, at first glance
$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}}$ does not seem to have a simple
form. A naive approach would be to first build out the large sparse
matrix $\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{W}}$ (which is $[M \times MN]$, with zeros
wherever $i \neq k$ in $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{W}[i,jk]$), then do the
matrix multiply $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{W}}$. We
can avoid all those multiplications by zero by observing the following
simplification: 

$$\begin{aligned}    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}[i,j]} 
        &= \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \mathbf{W}[i,j]} \quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad[1 \times M][M \times 1] \rightarrow [1 \times 1]\\
        &= \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} \Big[\frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[0]}{\partial \mathbf{W}[i,j]}, \ldots ,\frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[M-1]}{\partial \mathbf{W}[i,j]} \Big]^\mathsf{T}\\
        &= \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} \Big[\ldots , 0, \ldots , \frac{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}{\partial \mathbf{W}[i,j]}, \ldots, 0, \ldots \Big]^\mathsf{T}\\
        &= \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} \Big[\ldots , 0, \ldots , x_{\texttt{in}}[j], \ldots, 0, \ldots \Big]^\mathsf{T}\\
        &= \frac{\partial J}{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[i]}x_{\texttt{in}}[j] \quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad[1 \times 1][1 \times 1] \rightarrow [1 \times 1]
\end{aligned}$$ 

In matrix equations, it's very useful
to check that the dimensions all match up. To the right of some
equations in this chapter, we denote the dimensionality of the matrices
in the product, where $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ is M dimensions,
$\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ is N dimensions, and the loss $J$ is always
a scalar.

Now we can just arrange all these scalar
derivatives into the matrix for $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}}$, and obtain the following:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}} & = 
        \begin{bmatrix}
            \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}[0,0]} & \ldots & \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}[N-1,0]} \\
            \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
            \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}[0,M-1]} & \ldots & \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}[N-1,M-1]} \\
        \end{bmatrix}\\
        & = 
        \begin{bmatrix}
            \frac{\partial J}{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[0]}x_{\texttt{in}}[0] & \ldots & \frac{\partial J}{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[N-1]}x_{\texttt{in}}[0] \\
            \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
            \frac{\partial J}{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[0]}x_{\texttt{in}}[M-1] & \ldots & \frac{\partial J}{\partial x_{\texttt{out}}[N-1]}x_{\texttt{in}}[M-1] \\
        \end{bmatrix}\\
        & = \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}\\
        &= \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}
\end{aligned}$$ 

Note, we are using the convention of
zero-indexing into vectors and matrices.

So we see that in
the end this gradient has the simple form of an outer product between
two vectors, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$
(@fig-backpropagation-parameter_grad_linear_matrices).


(see figure: Matrix multiply for parameter gradient of a linear layer.)

We can summarize all these operations in the `forward` and `backward`
diagram for linear layer in @fig-backpropagation-linear_layer_backprop.




(see figure: Linear layer forward and backward.)

Notice that all these operations are simple expressions, mainly
involving matrix multiplies. `Forward` and `backward` for a linear layer
are also very easy to write in code, using any library that provides
matrix multiplication (`matmul`) as a primitive.
@fig-backpropagation-backprop_code gives Python pseudocode for this
layer.


```python
class linear():
    def __init__(self, W, b, lr):
        self.W = W
        self.b = b
        self.lr = lr # learning rate
        
    def forward(self, x_in):
        self.x_in = x_in
        return matmul(W,x)+b
    
    def backward(self,J_out):
        J_in = matmul(J_out,W)
        dJdW = matmul(self.x_in,J_out)
        dJdb = J_out
        return J_in, dJdW, dJdb
    
    def update(self, dJdW, dJdb):
        self.W -= self.lr*dJdW.transpose()
        self.b -= self.lr*dJdb
```
Pytorch-like pseudocode for a linear layer with `forward` and `backward`.


### Backpropagation for a Pointwise Nonlinearity

Pointwise nonlinearities have very simple `backward` functions. Let a
(parameterless) scalar nonlinearity be
$h: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with derivative function
$h^{\prime}: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. Define a pointwise
layer using $h$ as
$f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = [h(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}$.
Then we have $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &= f^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = \texttt{diag}([h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}) \triangleq \mathbf{H}^\prime
\end{aligned}$$  

The $\texttt{diag}$ operator is the operator that places a vector on the diagonal of a matrix, whose other entries are all zero.

There are no parameters to update, so we just
have to calculate $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ in the `backward`
operation, using @eq-backpropagation-backward: $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{H}^\prime
\end{aligned}$$

As an example, for a `relu` layer we have: $$\begin{aligned}
    h^\prime(x) = 
        \begin{cases}
            1 &\text{if} \quad x \geq 0\\
            0 &\text{otherwise}
        \end{cases}
\end{aligned}$$ As a matrix multiply, the `backward` operation is shown
in @fig-backpropagation-pointwise_backward_matices.



(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)

with $a = h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[0])$,
$b = h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[1])$, and
$c = h^\prime(x_{\texttt{in}}[2])$. We can simplify this equation as
follows: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}[i] = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[i]h^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[i]) \quad \forall i 
\end{aligned}$${#eq-backpropagation-pointwise_costgrad}



The full set of operations for a pointwise layer is shown next in
@fig-backpropagation-pointwise_layer_backprop.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for \texttt{backward} of a pointwise layer.)


### Backpropagation for Loss Layers

The last layer we need to define for a complete MLP is the loss layer.
As a simple example, we will derive backprop for an $L_2$ loss function:
$\left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2$, where
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the output of the network (prediction) and
$\mathbf{y}$ is the ground truth.

This layer has no parameters so we only need to derive
@eq-backpropagation-backward for this layer: $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} &= \frac{\partial \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert^2_2}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{y}}} = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad [1 \times |\mathbf{y}|]\\
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}*2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}$$ Here we have made use of the fact that
$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1$,
since the output of the loss layer *is* the cost $J$.

So, the backward signal sent by the $L_2$ loss layer is a row vector of
per-dimension errors between the prediction and the target.

This completes our derivation of $\texttt{forward}$ and
$\texttt{backward}$ for a $L_2$ loss layer, yielding
@fig-backpropagation-L2_loss_layer_backprop.



(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of an $L_2$ loss layer.)

### Putting It All Together: Backpropagation through an MLP

Let's see what happens when we put all these operations together in an
MLP. We will start with the MLP in @fig-backpropagation-simple_MLP. For
simplicity, we will omit biases. Let $\mathbf{x}$ be four-dimensional
and $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{h}$ be three-dimensional, and
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ be two-dimensional. The forward pass for this network
is shown below in @fig-backpropagation-forward_pass_MLP.


(see figure: Forward pass through an MLP.)

For the backward pass, we will here make a slight change in convention,
which will clarify an interesting connection between the forward and
backward directions. Rather than representing gradients $\mathbf{g}$ as
row vectors, we will transpose them and treat them as column vectors.
The `backward` operation for transposed vectors follows from the matrix
identity that
$(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^\mathsf{T}= \mathbf{B}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}$:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{in}} = (\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W})^\mathsf{T}= \mathbf{W}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{out}}
\end{aligned}$$

Now we will draw the backward pass, using these transposed
$\mathbf{g}$'s, in @fig-backpropagation-backward_pass_MLP.


(see figure: Backward pass through an MLP.)

This reveals an interesting connection between `forward` and `backward`
for linear layers: `backward` for a linear layer is the same operation
as `forward`, just with the weights transposed! We have omitted the bias
terms here, but recall from
@eq-backpropagation-linear_backward_costgrad that the backward pass to
the activations ignores biases anyway.

In contrast, the `relu` layer is not a `relu` on the backward pass.
Instead, it becomes a sort of gating matrix, parameterized by functions
of the activations from the forward pass ($a$, $b$, and $c$). This
matrix is all zeros except for ones on the diagonal where the activation
was nonnegative. This layer acts to mask out gradients for variables on
the negative side of the $\texttt{relu}$. Notice that this operation is
a matrix multiply --- in fact, *all* `backward` operations are matrix
multiplies, no matter what the `forward` operation might be, as you can
observe in algorithm @alg-backpropagation-backprop_for_chains.

In the diagrams above, we have not yet included the computation of the
parameter gradients. At each step of the backward pass, these are
computed as an outerproduct between the activations input to that layer,
$\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$, and the gradients being sent back,
$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ (see
@fig-backpropagation-parameter_grad_linear_matrices).

items.title: Convolution Property
items.prompt_md:
Consider a signal $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$ that is the result of applying (circular) convolution of two signals, $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$, both of size $N \times M$: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \ell_1 \circ \ell_2$$

The question is; how does the Fourier transform of the signal $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$ relates to the Fourier transforms of the two signals $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$?

$$\ell_1 [n,m] \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 [n,m] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}_1 [u,v] \mathscr{L}_2 [u,v]$$
items.proof_md: If we take the Fourier transform of both sides, and use the definition of the Fourier transform, we obtain $$\begin{split} \mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] & =  \mathcal{F}  \left\{ \ell_1 \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 \right\} \\ & =   \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}  \sum_{m=0}^{M-1}  \left\{ \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1}  \ell_1 \left[n-k, m-l \right] \ell_2 \left[k,l \right] \right\} \exp \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{nu}{N} + \frac{mv}{M} \right) \right) \end{split}$$ In these sums, the finite signal $\ell_1 \left[n, m \right]$ of size $N \times M$ is extended periodically infinitely. The periodic extension allows us to drop the modulo operators. Changing the dummy variables in the sums (introducing $n' = n - k$ and $m' = m - l$), we have $$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1}  \ell_2 \left[k,l \right] \sum_{n'=-k}^{N-k-1}  \sum_{m'=-l}^{M-l-1}  \ell_1 \left[n', m' \right]  \exp{ \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{(n'+k)u}{N} + \frac{(m'+l)v}{M} \right) \right)}$$ Recognizing that the last two summations give the DFT of $x\left[n,m\right]$, using circular boundary conditions, gives $$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1}  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \exp{ \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{ku}{N}+\frac{lv}{M} \right ) \right)} \ell_2 \left[k,l\right]$$ Performing the DFT indicated by the second two summations gives the desired result: $$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v\right] = \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$

items.title: Dual Convolution Property
items.prompt_md:
The Fourier transform of the product of two images is the (circular) convolution of their DFTs:

$$\ell_1 [n,m] \ell_2 [n,m] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \frac{1}{NM} \mathscr{L}_1 [u,v] \circ \mathscr{L}_2 [u,v]$$

items.title: Shift Property
items.prompt_md:
A shift corresponds to a translation in space. Translating a signal in the spatial domain results in multiplying its Fourier transform by a complex exponential. Consider an image $\ell[n,m]$, with Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$ and period $N,M$. When displacing the image by $(n_0, m_0)$ pixels, we get $\ell[n-n_0,m-m_0]$ and its Fourier transform is:
$$\mathcal{F} \{ \ell[n-n_0,m-m_0] \} = \mathscr{L}[u,v] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)}$$
items.proof_md: $$\begin{split} \mathcal{F} \left\{ \ell\left[n-n_0,m-m_0 \right] \right\} &= \\  & = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n-n_0,m-m_0 \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} = \\ & =  \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n,m \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, (n+n_0)}{N} + \frac{v\, (m+m_0)}{M} \right) \right)}  = \\ & =   \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)}    \end{split}$$

items.title: Modulation Property
items.prompt_md:
If we multiply an image with a complex exponential, its Fourier transform is translated:

$$\ell\left[n,m \right]  \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)}\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}}\mathscr{L}\left[u-u_0,v-v_0 \right]$$

A related relationship is as follows:

$$\ell\left[n,m \right]  \cos{ \left( 2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)}\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}\left[u-u_0,v-v_0 \right] + \mathscr{L}\left[u+u_0,v+v_0 \right]$$
items.proof_md: This can be proven using the dual convolution property from section -sec-dualconv. Note that now the result in equation (@eq-modulation_exp) is not a real signal, and for this reason its Fourier Transform does not have symmetries around $u,v=0$.

items.title: Example 2: Program Induction
items.prompt_md: Contrast linear least-squares with Python program induction as learning algorithms.
items.solution_md:
At the other end of the spectrum we have what is known as **program
induction**, which is one of the broadest classes of learning algorithm.
In this setting, our hypothesis space may be all Python programs. Let's
contrast linear least-squares with Python program induction.
@fig-intro_to_learning-ols_system_diagram shows what linear
least-squares looks like.

(see figure: Linear regression finds a line that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.)

The learned function is an algebraic expression that maps $x$ to $y$.
Learning consisting of searching over two scalar parameters, $\theta_0$
and $\theta_1$.

@fig-intro_to_learning-program_induction_system_diagram shows Python
program induction solving the same problem. In this case, the learned
function is a Python program that maps $x$ to $y$. Learning consisted of
searching over the space of all possible Python programs (within some
max length). Clearly that's a much harder search problem than just
finding two scalars. In chapter @sec-problem_of_generalization, we will see some pitfalls of using too powerful a hypothesis space when a simpler one will do.

(see figure: Python program induction finds a Python program that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.)
